clues: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe chest pain that began abruptly while he was watching television.
He has a long history of poorly controlled hypertension. He says the pain was at its worst the instant it started, not building gradually.
Blood pressure is 210/120 in the right arm and 155/90 in the left arm. A diastolic murmur is heard that was not present on prior exams.
Chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum with blunting of the aortic knob. Troponin is negative.
CT angiography shows a linear intimal tear with a false lumen extending from the ascending aorta past the left subclavian artery.
explanation: A tear in the aortic intima allows blood to dissect into the media, creating a false lumen. The flap can obstruct branch vessels (causing stroke, limb ischemia, mesenteric ischemia) or rupture into the pericardium (tamponade).
keyFact: Tearing pain maximal at onset + blood pressure difference between arms = dissection. Type A (ascending) = surgery. Type B (descending only) = medical management. Associations: hypertension, Marfan, bicuspid aortic valve, cocaine.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocardial Infarction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MI pain crescendos over minutes. Dissection pain is maximal at onset. The blood pressure differential and new AR murmur point to dissection.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE causes pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea but without the tearing quality, blood pressure differential, or intimal flap on imaging.

wrongAnswers.name: Musculoskeletal Chest Pain
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Musculoskeletal pain is reproducible with palpation and doesn't cause blood pressure differential, aortic regurgitation, or a false lumen on CT.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and awareness of a forceful pounding heartbeat, especially when lying on his left side.
He had rheumatic fever as a teenager growing up in India.

Exam reveals bounding pulses with a wide pulse pressure of 168/52, a laterally displaced hyperdynamic apical impulse, and a high-pitched blowing decrescendo diastolic murmur along the left sternal border.
His head bobs visibly with each heartbeat, and his nail beds pulsate when gentle pressure is applied.
Echocardiography demonstrates a broad jet of blood flowing backward from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole with progressive left ventricular dilation.
explanation: The valve fails to seal during diastole, so blood leaks back into the ventricle. The heart must pump the regurgitant volume plus the forward output, creating a volume overload.
keyFact: Wide pulse pressure (high systolic from large stroke volume, low diastolic from leak-back) is the hemodynamic fingerprint. Chronic AR is tolerated for years. Acute AR (endocarditis, dissection) is a surgical emergency.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AS has a SYSTOLIC crescendo-decrescendo murmur with NARROW pulse pressure and slow-rising pulse — hemodynamic opposites of AR.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS has a diastolic rumble at the APEX with an opening snap, not a decrescendo diastolic murmur at the LEFT STERNAL BORDER.

wrongAnswers.name: Patent Ductus Arteriosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PDA has a continuous machinery murmur at the left infraclavicular area and wide pulse pressure, but the murmur is continuous (not purely diastolic).

clues: A 72-year-old man presents with exertional chest pain that resolves with rest.
He recently fainted during exercise and has been getting more short of breath climbing stairs.
Auscultation reveals a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to the carotids.
Carotid upstrokes are weak and delayed, and the murmur increases with squatting and decreases with standing.
Echocardiogram shows a heavily calcified trileaflet valve with a mean gradient of 52 mmHg and a valve area of 0.7 cm².
explanation: Progressive calcification narrows the valve opening, creating a pressure overload that causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. The ventricle compensates until it can't.
keyFact: The slow-rising pulse (parvus et tardus) is the physical exam hallmark. The symptom triad of angina, syncope, and heart failure progresses in that order with worsening survival. Severe = gradient >40 mmHg or area <1.0 cm².

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM causes a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva (decreased preload), while AS decreases. HCM also has a brisk bisferiens pulse, not the slow-rising pulse.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sclerosis produces a similar murmur but without significant gradient or valve narrowing — the carotid pulse is normal and symptoms are absent.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MR is a holosystolic (not crescendo-decrescendo) murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, not at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids.

clues: A 72-year-old man presents with palpitations he describes as his heart beating 'all over the place.'
He reports dizziness and exertional dyspnea that started two days ago; he has no prior cardiac history.
Exam reveals an irregularly irregular pulse at 142 with variable intensity of S1.
ECG shows an irregularly irregular ventricular response with a narrow QRS complex and a chaotic, undulating baseline.
No discernible P waves are present on any lead of the 12-lead ECG, only a chaotic fibrillatory baseline.
explanation: Disorganized electrical activity in the atria replaces coordinated contraction with chaotic fibrillation, producing an irregularly irregular ventricular response and loss of effective atrial contraction.
keyFact: Irregularly irregular rhythm + absent P waves = AFib. The biggest risk is stroke from atrial thrombus (especially left atrial appendage). Rate control (beta-blocker, CCB) vs rhythm control (cardioversion, antiarrhythmics) is a key management decision.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrial Flutter
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Flutter has a regular (not irregular) ventricular response and shows sawtooth flutter waves on ECG, not absent P waves.

wrongAnswers.name: Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MAT has 3+ different P-wave morphologies with an irregular rhythm, but P waves ARE present. AFib has NO discernible P waves.

wrongAnswers.name: Frequent Premature Atrial Contractions
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PACs cause an irregular rhythm but with identifiable (though premature) P waves and a regular underlying rhythm.

clues: A 50-year-old woman presents with episodes of lightheadedness that worsen in certain body positions.
She has had intermittent fevers, elevated ESR, and unexplained weight loss for months without an identifiable infectious cause.
Exam reveals a low-pitched diastolic sound that changes in intensity with body position.
Echocardiogram reveals a pedunculated mobile mass prolapsing through the mitral valve during diastole.
The mass is attached to the interatrial septum at the fossa ovalis and arises from the left atrium.
explanation: The benign gelatinous tumor dangles from a stalk and can prolapse into the mitral valve opening, intermittently obstructing flow and causing the position-dependent symptoms.
keyFact: Left atrium, fossa ovalis, pedunculated, positional symptoms. The constitutional symptoms (fever, elevated ESR, anemia, weight loss) mimic endocarditis or autoimmune disease. 'Tumor plop' is the diastolic sound of the mass hitting the mitral valve.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mitral stenosis causes a diastolic murmur but it doesn't change with position, and echo shows a thickened calcified valve, not a mobile mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Infective Endocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Endocarditis causes fever, elevated ESR, and cardiac findings, but echo shows vegetations on valve leaflets, not a pedunculated mass on the atrial septum.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE causes dyspnea and syncope but without a positional diastolic sound or an intracardiac mass on echo.

clues: A 35-year-old woman has a murmur found on routine exam and reports mild exertional dyspnea she attributed to being out of shape.
She has never had heart failure or cyanosis and has no family history of congenital heart disease.
Auscultation reveals that the second heart sound splits by the SAME amount with every breath — the split does not widen with inspiration as it normally should.
ECG shows right axis deviation and an incomplete right bundle branch block pattern.
Echocardiography with agitated saline shows microbubbles crossing from the right atrium to the left through a defect in the interatrial septum.
explanation: The hole allows left-to-right shunting, volume-overloading the right side. Both ventricles always receive similar volumes regardless of breathing, so the split of S2 doesn't change with respiration.
keyFact: FIXED split S2 is pathognomonic. The murmur is actually from increased flow across the pulmonic valve, not from the hole itself. Right axis deviation and RBBB pattern reflect chronic right ventricular volume overload.

wrongAnswers.name: VSD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VSD produces a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border without fixed splitting of S2.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonic Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PS causes a systolic ejection murmur with WIDE physiologic splitting that DOES change with respiration — not fixed.

wrongAnswers.name: Innocent Flow Murmur
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Innocent murmurs vary with position and have a normal S2. The fixed split S2, right axis, and bubble study findings rule out a benign cause.

clues: A 35-year-old previously healthy man is resuscitated after cardiac arrest that occurred during sleep.
He has no structural heart disease, no coronary disease, and no drug use. His father died suddenly in his sleep at age 40.
Physical exam and echocardiogram are completely normal with no structural heart disease identified.
Resting ECG shows a right bundle branch block pattern with ST-segment changes in leads V1-V3.
The ST elevation in V1-V3 has a distinctive coved (type 1) morphology with a downsloping ST segment ending in a negative T wave.
explanation: A sodium channel mutation causes abnormal repolarization that predisposes to ventricular fibrillation, particularly during sleep or vagal states when heart rate slows.
keyFact: Classic demographics: young Southeast Asian males dying in their sleep (historically called 'sudden unexpected nocturnal death syndrome'). The ECG pattern is intermittent and can be provoked with ajmaline or procainamide challenge.

wrongAnswers.name: Long QT Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Long QT shows prolonged QT interval and triggers include exercise and startle. Brugada shows coved ST elevation in V1-V3 and events occur during sleep.

wrongAnswers.name: WPW Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: WPW shows a delta wave and short PR interval from an accessory pathway. Brugada shows coved ST elevation without a delta wave.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocardial Infarction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MI causes ST elevation but in a coronary territory distribution with troponin elevation. This patient has normal coronaries and the ST pattern is limited to V1-V3.

clues: A 55-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer presents with progressive dyspnea and a sense of impending doom.
He has been feeling lightheaded and his voice seems quieter over the past few days.
Exam reveals distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, and hypotension, with systolic blood pressure dropping more than 10 mmHg during inspiration.
ECG shows low voltage QRS complexes with beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude.
Echocardiogram reveals a large pericardial effusion with right atrial and right ventricular diastolic collapse.
explanation: Fluid accumulating in the pericardial space compresses the heart, preventing diastolic filling. The ventricles cannot fill, so cardiac output drops and the patient progresses to shock.
keyFact: The three classic findings (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds) + the paradoxical rise of JVP with inspiration + exaggerated blood pressure drop during inspiration (pulsus paradoxus) = this diagnosis. Emergency pericardiocentesis is life-saving.

wrongAnswers.name: Tension Pneumothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tension pneumothorax also causes hypotension with JVD, but there are absent breath sounds on one side and the trachea deviates — not muffled heart sounds with a pericardial effusion.

wrongAnswers.name: Right Heart Failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Right heart failure causes JVD and hypotension but develops gradually with peripheral edema and hepatomegaly — not the acute hemodynamic collapse with muffled sounds and pulsus paradoxus.

wrongAnswers.name: Constrictive Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Constriction is chronic with a thickened calcified pericardium. This is acute fluid accumulation with right ventricular diastolic collapse requiring emergent drainage.

clues: A 68-year-old man who had a large heart attack 6 hours ago is now cold, confused, and hypotensive despite IV fluids.
He is making less than 20 mL of urine per hour, and his extremities are cold and mottled.
Exam reveals blood pressure of 72/50, heart rate of 118, bibasilar crackles, distended neck veins, and an S3 gallop.
Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 15% with more than half the left ventricle akinetic.
Pulmonary artery catheter shows a cardiac index of 1.4, elevated wedge pressure, and systemic vascular resistance of 2800.
explanation: Too much heart muscle died, and the remaining muscle cannot generate enough output to perfuse organs. The body vasoconstricts to compensate, which further increases the workload on the failing heart.
keyFact: Low output + high filling pressures + high SVR = this type of shock. Cold extremities with pulmonary edema = the heart is both too weak to pump AND overloaded. Treatment: inotropes, vasopressors, mechanical support.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic Shock
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic shock has LOW SVR (warm, vasodilated) with HIGH cardiac output early. This has HIGH SVR (cold, clamped) with LOW cardiac output.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypovolemic Shock
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypovolemic shock has LOW filling pressures (empty tank). This has HIGH filling pressures (overfull tank) — the pump has failed.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Massive PE causes right heart failure with elevated right-sided pressures but LOW left-sided pressures. Here LEFT-sided filling pressures are high.

clues: A 16-year-old boy is found to have elevated blood pressure during a sports physical.
He reports frequent headaches, occasional nosebleeds, and bilateral leg cramps during exercise.
Blood pressure in the right arm is 158/94 but in the left leg is only 104/70, and femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared to radial pulses.
Chest X-ray shows notching along the inferior surfaces of several ribs bilaterally.
CT angiography reveals a discrete narrowing of the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery takeoff.
explanation: A discrete narrowing in the aorta creates high pressure above (upper body) and low pressure below (lower body). Collateral vessels through intercostal arteries enlarge to bypass the blockage.
keyFact: Upper extremity hypertension + lower extremity hypotension with weak femorals = this diagnosis. Associated with bicuspid aortic valve (~50%) and Turner syndrome. The infantile preductal form presents with heart failure in neonates.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Artery Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RAS causes secondary hypertension but pressures are equal in arms and legs — no arm-to-leg gradient.

wrongAnswers.name: Takayasu Arteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Takayasu causes pulse deficits from inflammatory arterial narrowing in young women, not the congenital discrete narrowing with rib notching.

wrongAnswers.name: Essential Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Essential hypertension produces equal pressures in all extremities. A 50-point arm-leg gradient means mechanical obstruction.

clues: A 75-year-old man presents with syncope and a heart rate of 35 that does not increase with exertion.
He lost consciousness while walking upstairs and had a brief witnessed collapse.
Exam reveals bradycardia, intermittent cannon 'a' waves in the jugular venous pulse, and variable intensity of S1.
ECG shows P waves and QRS complexes each occurring at regular but independent rates — the atrial rate is 78 and the ventricular rate is 35.
No fixed relationship exists between P waves and QRS complexes; the PR interval varies randomly from beat to beat.
explanation: Complete failure of electrical conduction from atria to ventricles means the atria and ventricles beat independently — the atria at their intrinsic rate (~60-100) and the ventricles at a much slower escape rate (~30-40).
keyFact: P waves and QRS complexes with NO fixed relationship (AV dissociation) defines complete heart block. The cannon 'a' waves occur when the atria contract against closed tricuspid valve. Causes: fibrotic degeneration, inferior MI, Lyme disease, medications.

wrongAnswers.name: Second-Degree Type II Block
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Type II has some P waves conducted and some dropped, but the PR interval is fixed for conducted beats. In complete block, NO P waves are conducted.

wrongAnswers.name: Sinus Bradycardia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sinus bradycardia is a slow rate with normal 1:1 P-QRS relationship. Complete block shows independent atrial and ventricular rhythms.

wrongAnswers.name: Vasovagal Syncope
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vasovagal syncope causes transient bradycardia with prodrome, but the ECG is normal between events. This patient has persistent AV dissociation.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department because he keeps waking up gasping for air at 2 AM.
He has a history of a prior myocardial infarction. He sleeps propped on 3 pillows and has gained 12 pounds in 2 weeks without eating more.
Exam reveals distended neck veins, an S3 gallop, and crackles extending to mid-lung bilaterally.
BNP is 1,840, and chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with bilateral pleural effusions and cephalization of pulmonary vessels.
Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 25% with anterior wall akinesis corresponding to his prior infarct territory.
explanation: His prior infarction killed enough muscle that the remaining heart cannot maintain adequate output. Fluid retention from neurohormonal activation causes the congestion.
keyFact: S3 gallop = blood slamming into an overfilled ventricle. Low sodium (dilutional hyponatremia) is a poor prognostic sign. The four pillars: ARNI + beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2 inhibitor.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD Exacerbation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes dyspnea with wheezes and hyperinflated lungs. This has CRACKLES, S3, elevated JVP, and BNP of 1,840 — a failing pump, not air trapping.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bilateral pneumonia causes crackles, but without cardiomegaly, S3, JVD, and massively elevated BNP.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nephrotic syndrome causes edema from protein loss, but without cardiomegaly, S3, or elevated BNP.

clues: A 65-year-old man on supplemental oxygen presents with worsening leg swelling over several weeks.
He has severe COPD and has been on home oxygen for years. His belly has been distending and he gets winded despite using his oxygen.
Exam reveals elevated jugular venous pressure, a right ventricular heave, a loud P2, and hepatomegaly.
ABG shows a PaO2 of 52 mmHg on his current oxygen. Echocardiogram shows right ventricular dilation with elevated pulmonary artery pressures.
The left ventricle is normal in size and function on echocardiogram, and right heart catheterization confirms a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mmHg.
explanation: Chronic hypoxemia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, which increases resistance in the pulmonary vasculature. The right ventricle hypertrophies trying to pump against the increased resistance, then eventually dilates and fails.
keyFact: Right heart failure from LUNG disease = cor pulmonale. The left ventricle is normal — the problem originates in the pulmonary vasculature. Long-term supplemental oxygen is one of the few treatments proven to improve survival in COPD.

wrongAnswers.name: Congestive Heart Failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Biventricular CHF causes similar edema and JVD but the LEFT ventricle is also dilated and dysfunctional. Here the left ventricle is normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Constrictive Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Constrictive pericarditis causes right-sided heart failure signs but with pericardial thickening, a pericardial knock, and characteristic hemodynamics — not elevated pulmonary pressures from lung disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatic Cirrhosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cirrhosis causes edema and ascites from portal hypertension but without elevated JVP, right ventricular hypertrophy, or elevated pulmonary pressures.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician because her left leg has been aching and feels 'heavier than usual' for the past few days.
She returned from a 14-hour international flight one week ago and takes oral contraceptives. She has no prior history of blood clots.
The left calf is 3 cm larger than the right, with warmth, pitting edema, and tenderness along the deep venous tract.
D-dimer returns at 4,200 ng/mL. There is no erythema with distinct borders and no fever.
Compression ultrasonography shows a noncompressible left popliteal vein with absent flow on Doppler.
explanation: Venous stasis during the flight combined with estrogen-induced hypercoagulability created the conditions for clot formation in the deep veins.
keyFact: Virchow's triad: stasis + endothelial injury + hypercoagulability. Noncompressible vein on ultrasound is the diagnostic standard. The major danger is embolization to the lungs (PE). Unprovoked DVT in a young patient should prompt hypercoagulability workup.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis causes unilateral leg erythema and warmth but without the deep venous tenderness or noncompressible vein on ultrasound.

wrongAnswers.name: Baker Cyst Rupture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ruptured Baker cyst causes acute calf swelling mimicking DVT, but ultrasound shows the cyst rather than a noncompressible vein.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphedema causes chronic painless swelling with non-pitting edema. This is acute, painful, pitting edema with a noncompressible vein.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath over 3 months and difficulty lying flat at night.
He has a 20-year history of heavy alcohol use. He can no longer walk up a flight of stairs without stopping, and his legs are swollen.
Exam reveals an irregularly irregular pulse, an S3 gallop, bibasilar crackles, and bilateral pitting edema.
Chest X-ray shows a massively enlarged cardiac silhouette with pulmonary vascular congestion.
Echocardiogram reveals all four chambers dilated with an ejection fraction of 18% and diffuse global hypokinesis.
explanation: Toxic, infectious, or genetic damage weakens the myocardium globally. The ventricle dilates as it fails, creating a thin-walled, poorly contracting chamber.
keyFact: Diffuse hypokinesis (vs regional = ischemic). Causes: alcohol, viral myocarditis, peripartum, Chagas, familial. Leads to eccentric hypertrophy (dilation). Management same as HFrEF — the four-pillar drug regimen.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM has a thick-walled ventricle with preserved or hyperdynamic systolic function. This has a thin-walled dilated ventricle with severely reduced function.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic cardiomyopathy shows REGIONAL wall motion abnormalities corresponding to coronary territories. This shows DIFFUSE global hypokinesis.

wrongAnswers.name: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Restrictive cardiomyopathy has normal or small chamber size with preserved systolic function but impaired filling. This has massively dilated chambers with severely reduced systolic function.

clues: A 60-year-old man presents with sharp chest pain that worsens with inspiration and lying flat, 4 weeks after a heart attack.
The pain improves when he sits up and leans forward; he has had low-grade fevers for several days.
Exam reveals a three-component pericardial friction rub, low-grade fever, and a small pericardial effusion on bedside echo.
ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression in a pattern distinct from the territorial changes of his prior infarction.
Labs show elevated ESR, elevated CRP, and a new small pericardial effusion on echocardiogram appearing weeks after documented myocardial injury.
explanation: Damaged myocardial tissue exposes intracellular antigens that trigger an autoimmune pericarditis weeks after the initial injury.
keyFact: Pericarditis weeks after MI (or cardiac surgery) with fever, friction rub, and effusion = Dressler syndrome. The diffuse ST elevation pattern distinguishes pericarditis from a new territorial infarction. Treatment: NSAIDs and colchicine. Avoid anticoagulation if effusion is large (risk of hemorrhagic conversion).

wrongAnswers.name: Reinfarction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reinfarction causes territorial ST elevation matching a coronary distribution with rising troponin. This has DIFFUSE ST elevation with PR depression — the pericarditis pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE can occur post-MI and causes pleuritic pain, but without the friction rub, diffuse ST changes, or the autoimmune mechanism.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The presentation IS pericarditis — but the specific post-MI timing and autoimmune mechanism define Dressler syndrome as a distinct entity.

clues: A 17-year-old athlete collapses during a basketball game and is resuscitated on the sideline.
His father had a cardiac device placed at age 40 for a heart condition; a paternal uncle died suddenly.
Exam reveals a harsh systolic murmur that gets louder when standing or during Valsalva, and gets quieter when squatting.
Echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy of 22 mm with dynamic outflow obstruction during systole.
Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve leaflet toward the septum is visualized on echo, contributing to the obstruction.
explanation: The thickened septum narrows the outflow tract. The mitral valve is pulled into the outflow stream during systole, worsening the obstruction. Anything that decreases ventricular volume worsens it.
keyFact: Murmur increases with decreased preload (standing, Valsalva, dehydration). Decreases with increased preload (squatting, leg elevation). Opposite of most murmurs. Autosomal dominant — screen first-degree relatives.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AS murmur decreases with Valsalva. HCM increases. AS has a fixed obstruction; HCM's obstruction is dynamic and volume-dependent.

wrongAnswers.name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DCM has a dilated, thin-walled ventricle with systolic failure. This has a thick, hypertrophied ventricle with diastolic dysfunction.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myocarditis causes acute heart failure from inflammation with a dilated ventricle, not the chronic asymmetric septal hypertrophy with dynamic obstruction.

clues: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the ER after collapsing during swim practice and being pulled from the pool unconscious.
She has had two prior fainting episodes — once while startled by an alarm and once during exercise. Her older brother died suddenly at age 14.
Exam after regaining consciousness is unremarkable with no murmurs or neurologic deficits.
Echocardiogram and cardiac MRI are structurally normal with no evidence of cardiomyopathy.
Resting ECG shows a corrected QT interval of 520 ms with broad-based T waves in multiple leads.
explanation: Mutations in cardiac ion channels delay ventricular repolarization, creating a vulnerable window for a potentially fatal arrhythmia (torsades de pointes) that presents as syncope or sudden death.
keyFact: Triggers vary by subtype: swimming (type 1), auditory startle (type 2), sleep/rest (type 3). Many common medications prolong QT and can trigger events. Family history of sudden death in young relatives is a red flag.

wrongAnswers.name: Epilepsy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Seizures can cause loss of consciousness during exercise, but the prolonged QT interval on ECG and family history of sudden death point to a cardiac channelopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM causes exertional syncope and sudden death in young athletes, but with a murmur that changes with Valsalva and septal hypertrophy on echo — not a prolonged QT.

wrongAnswers.name: Vasovagal Syncope
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vasovagal syncope is benign with prodromal lightheadedness, not sudden collapse during exercise with a family history of sudden death and prolonged QT.

clues: A 60-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and orthopnea that has worsened over the past year.
She has a history of a prior heart attack that damaged the papillary muscle.
Exam reveals a laterally displaced apical impulse and a blowing holosystolic murmur at the apex that radiates to the left axilla.
The murmur does NOT change with Valsalva maneuver or inspiration.

Echocardiography shows failure of the valve leaflets to coapt with a regurgitant jet directed posteriorly into the left atrium, and the left atrium and left ventricle are both dilated from volume overload.
explanation: The valve fails to close properly during systole, allowing blood to regurgitate from the ventricle back into the atrium. The atrium and ventricle both dilate to accommodate the extra volume.
keyFact: Holosystolic at apex radiating to axilla = this murmur. Acute MR (papillary rupture after MI, chordae rupture) is a surgical emergency with flash pulmonary edema. Chronic MR is tolerated until the LV begins to fail.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AS is a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the RIGHT upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, not a holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.

wrongAnswers.name: Tricuspid Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TR is a holosystolic murmur at the LEFT LOWER sternal border that INCREASES with inspiration. MR is at the APEX and does not increase with inspiration.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Valve Prolapse
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MVP causes a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur. This is a HOLOsystolic murmur without a click — the valve is not clicking and prolapsing, it's simply failing to close.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and reports coughing up blood-tinged sputum.
She had rheumatic fever as a child, and she has recently developed an irregular heartbeat.
Auscultation reveals an irregularly irregular pulse, a loud opening snap after S2, and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex best heard with the bell.
ECG shows atrial fibrillation, and echocardiography shows a thickened immobile valve with a valve area of 1.2 cm2.
The valve has a fish-mouth appearance on echocardiography with commissural fusion and diastolic doming of the leaflets.
explanation: Rheumatic inflammation fuses the valve commissures, narrowing the opening. The left atrium dilates from chronic pressure overload, predisposing to atrial fibrillation and mural thrombus formation.
keyFact: Opening snap followed by diastolic rumble at the apex is pathognomonic. Rheumatic heart disease is the overwhelmingly dominant cause. Atrial fibrillation + hemoptysis + embolic stroke risk make anticoagulation essential.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MR is a holoSYSTOLIC murmur at the apex. This is a DIASTOLIC rumble — different phase of the cardiac cycle.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AR is a diastolic murmur but at the LEFT STERNAL BORDER with wide pulse pressure. This diastolic murmur is at the APEX with an opening snap.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrial Myxoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atrial myxoma can mimic mitral stenosis by obstructing the valve, but imaging shows a pedunculated mass rather than valve fusion.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe substernal pressure for 45 minutes that started while he was sitting at his desk.
He is a smoker with hypertension and diabetes. He is diaphoretic and nauseated, and sublingual nitroglycerin provided no relief.
Exam reveals an anxious, pale, diaphoretic man with blood pressure of 92/68 and heart rate of 104.
ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1-V4 with reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads, and troponin I is 12.4.
Emergent catheterization reveals a 100% thrombotic occlusion of the left anterior descending artery.
explanation: A ruptured atherosclerotic plaque triggered a thrombus that completely occluded the coronary artery. Heart muscle downstream began dying within minutes.
keyFact: The LAD supplies the anterior wall and is called the widowmaker. ST elevation in a territorial pattern = emergent catheterization, no waiting. Time is muscle — every 30 minutes of delay loses more tissue.

wrongAnswers.name: Unstable Angina
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Unstable angina causes similar pain but WITHOUT ST elevation or troponin rise — the artery is critically narrowed but not completely occluded.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Dissection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dissection causes tearing chest/back pain with blood pressure differences between arms. The ST elevation and troponin here confirm coronary occlusion.

wrongAnswers.name: Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pericarditis causes diffuse ST elevation in almost every lead. This has ST elevation only in V1-V4 with reciprocal changes — a territorial pattern.

clues: A premature infant born at 28 weeks develops worsening respiratory distress and a widened pulse pressure in the first week of life.
The infant has bounding peripheral pulses and a hyperdynamic precordium on palpation.
Auscultation reveals a continuous machinery-like murmur heard best in the left infraclavicular area.
Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings bilaterally.
Echocardiography confirms a persistent vascular connection between the aorta and pulmonary artery with continuous left-to-right shunting.
explanation: The fetal connection between the aorta and pulmonary artery fails to close after birth. Blood shunts from the high-pressure aorta to the lower-pressure pulmonary artery, overloading the lungs.
keyFact: Continuous machinery murmur (heard in both systole and diastole) at the left infraclavicular area with bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure. NSAIDs close it (inhibit prostaglandin). Prostaglandin keeps it open (needed in ductus-dependent lesions like TGA).

wrongAnswers.name: VSD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VSD produces a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border — NOT the continuous machinery murmur heard here.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AR causes wide pulse pressure and a diastolic murmur but NOT a continuous murmur spanning both systole and diastole.

wrongAnswers.name: ASD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD produces a fixed split S2 with a systolic ejection murmur, not a continuous machinery murmur.

clues: A 28-year-old man presents with sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breathing and lying flat but improves sitting up and leaning forward.
He had a viral upper respiratory illness one week ago with fever, myalgias, and malaise.
Auscultation reveals a scratchy, grating sound heard best with the diaphragm at the left lower sternal border with the patient leaning forward.
ECG shows PR depression across multiple leads with diffuse concave-upward ST segment elevation.
ECG also shows diffuse ST elevation in nearly all leads with no reciprocal ST depression.
explanation: Viral infection inflames the pericardial layers, causing friction between them (producing the rub) and chest pain that varies with body position because the inflamed layers slide against each other.
keyFact: Positional chest pain (worse supine, better leaning forward) + friction rub + diffuse ST elevation with PR depression = pericarditis. Diffuse (all leads) vs territorial (specific coronary distribution) is the ECG key.

wrongAnswers.name: STEMI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: STEMI shows ST elevation in a specific coronary territory with reciprocal changes. This has DIFFUSE ST elevation with no reciprocal depression.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE causes pleuritic chest pain but without the friction rub, positional relief, or diffuse ST elevation.

wrongAnswers.name: Cardiac Tamponade
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tamponade is a complication of pericarditis but presents with hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds — not the chest pain and friction rub.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with aching in both calves when walking two blocks that goes away within minutes of stopping.
He has diabetes and a 40-pack-year smoking history. He also reports a nonhealing sore on his right great toe present for three weeks.
Exam reveals absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally, cool hairless skin, and a shallow ulcer on the right first toe.
Ankle-brachial index is 0.55 on the right and 0.62 on the left. Pedal pulses remain absent bilaterally.
CT angiography reveals diffuse atherosclerotic narrowing of the bilateral superficial femoral and popliteal arteries.
explanation: Atherosclerosis narrows the arteries supplying the legs. At rest, enough blood gets through. During exercise, the muscles demand more oxygen than the narrowed vessels can deliver, causing ischemic pain.
keyFact: Claudication = predictable exercise-induced leg pain relieved by rest. Critical limb ischemia = rest pain, nonhealing ulcers, gangrene. ABI <0.9 confirms PAD. ABI >1.3 suggests calcified incompressible vessels (common in diabetes).

wrongAnswers.name: Spinal Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Spinal stenosis causes 'neurogenic claudication' with leg pain during walking, but it's relieved by FLEXION (bending forward, sitting), pulses are normal, and ABI is normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DVT causes leg swelling and pain but from venous obstruction, not arterial insufficiency. Pulses are present and ABI is normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetic Neuropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diabetic neuropathy causes chronic burning/tingling in feet but not the exercise-induced cramping pattern with absent pulses and low ABI.

clues: A 30-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and occasional fainting during exercise over 6 months.
She has no history of lung disease, sleep apnea, or blood clots. A young woman in her family died suddenly during pregnancy.
Exam reveals elevated jugular venous pressure, a right ventricular heave, and a loud pulmonic component of S2.
Echocardiogram shows a dilated right ventricle with estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 68 mmHg and a normal left ventricle.
Right heart catheterization confirms mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mmHg with a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 10 mmHg.
explanation: Abnormal proliferation and vasoconstriction of the pulmonary arterioles increases resistance in the pulmonary vasculature, overloading the right ventricle. Unlike secondary causes, no underlying lung or left heart disease is identified.
keyFact: Normal wedge pressure distinguishes pulmonary arterial hypertension (pre-capillary, group 1) from pulmonary venous hypertension due to left heart disease (post-capillary, elevated wedge, group 2). Vasodilator testing during catheterization identifies calcium channel blocker responders.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) causes similar findings but CT angiography or V/Q scan shows thrombus. This patient has no thromboembolic history.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mitral stenosis causes pulmonary hypertension but the wedge pressure is ELEVATED (left atrial pressure backup). The wedge is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes pulmonary hypertension from hypoxic vasoconstriction, but PFTs and lung imaging would be abnormal. This patient has no lung disease.

clues: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden onset of dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain 10 days after hip replacement surgery.
He has tachycardia at 112 bpm, and his oxygen saturation is 88% on room air despite no prior lung disease.
Exam reveals tachypnea, clear lungs, and a prominent pulmonic component of the second heart sound.
D-dimer is elevated, troponin is mildly elevated, and ECG shows sinus tachycardia with new right axis deviation and a strain pattern in the right precordial leads.
CT pulmonary angiography shows filling defects in the right main and left lower lobe pulmonary arteries.
explanation: A clot from the deep leg veins embolizes to the pulmonary arteries, blocking blood flow and creating dead space ventilation. The right heart must pump against the sudden obstruction.
keyFact: Clear lungs with hypoxia after surgery = think PE. The loud P2 reflects pulmonary hypertension from the obstruction. Massive PE with hemodynamic instability may require thrombolytics or surgical embolectomy.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pneumonia causes fever with focal crackles and consolidation on imaging, not clear lungs with filling defects in pulmonary arteries.

wrongAnswers.name: Heart Failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HF causes bilateral crackles with elevated BNP and cardiomegaly, not clear lungs with acute right heart strain.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pneumothorax causes unilateral absent breath sounds with hypoxia but the CT shows vascular filling defects, not air in the pleural space.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with exertional dyspnea and markedly elevated jugular venous pressure that rises further with inspiration.
He has bilateral leg edema, fatigue, and difficulty lying flat.
Exam reveals Kussmaul sign (JVP rises with inspiration — the opposite of normal), an S4 gallop, and hepatomegaly.
Echocardiogram shows normal ventricular cavity size, PRESERVED systolic function, but severely impaired DIASTOLIC filling with biatrial enlargement.
The stiff ventricles fill normally in early diastole but then abruptly halt — the catheterization shows a 'dip and plateau' (square root sign) pattern on the ventricular pressure tracing.
explanation: Infiltration or scarring of the myocardium makes the walls stiff, impairing diastolic filling while systolic function is maintained. The classic infiltrative cause produces the sparkling echo texture.
keyFact: Normal systolic function with diastolic failure = restriction. The sparkling myocardium suggests infiltration by abnormal protein fibrils. Must distinguish from constrictive pericarditis — both cause right-sided failure with preserved EF, but treatment is completely different.

wrongAnswers.name: Constrictive Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Constrictive pericarditis has a similar hemodynamic profile but from a thickened calcified pericardium that restricts filling from the outside. The sparkling myocardium and tongue/eye findings point to an infiltrative myocardial process.

wrongAnswers.name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DCM has dilated chambers with reduced systolic function. This has normal-sized chambers with preserved systolic function but impaired diastolic filling.

wrongAnswers.name: Heart Failure with Preserved EF
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HFpEF from hypertension or aging has diastolic dysfunction too, but without the sparkling myocardium, macroglossia, or periorbital purpura that identify an infiltrative cause.

clues: A 70-year-old woman presents with acute chest pain after receiving news of her husband's sudden death.
She has no prior cardiac history, and her symptoms began within hours of the emotional shock.
ECG shows ST elevation in the anterior leads, and troponin is mildly elevated but modestly so for the ECG changes.
Coronary angiography reveals completely normal coronary arteries with no obstructive lesions.
Ventriculography shows apical ballooning with wall motion abnormalities extending beyond a single coronary artery territory.
explanation: An intense catecholamine surge from emotional or physical stress causes transient myocardial stunning, predominantly affecting the apex where beta-adrenergic receptor density is highest.
keyFact: Postmenopausal woman + acute emotional/physical stress + MI presentation + NORMAL coronaries + apical ballooning + full recovery = takotsubo. The wall motion extends beyond one coronary territory — this is the key distinguishing feature from true MI.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute MI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MI causes ST elevation with troponin rise from coronary occlusion. This has normal coronaries with wall motion crossing coronary territories.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myocarditis causes troponin elevation with wall motion abnormalities, but it's typically post-viral with diffuse (not apical) dysfunction and MRI shows late gadolinium enhancement.

wrongAnswers.name: Panic Attack
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Panic causes chest pain after emotional stress but ECG, troponin, and ventriculogram are normal.

clues: A 6-month-old infant turns blue and becomes limp during a crying spell. The mother calms him by holding his knees to his chest.
He was noted to have a murmur at birth and turns blue intermittently with agitation or feeding.
Exam reveals central cyanosis, a right ventricular heave, and a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border that gets quieter during cyanotic episodes.
Chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart silhouette with decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
Echocardiography shows a ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
explanation: The right ventricular outflow obstruction forces deoxygenated blood across the VSD into the aorta. During spells, the obstruction worsens and the murmur quiets because LESS blood flows through the narrowed area.
keyFact: The murmur gets QUIETER during tet spells — counterintuitive because less flow through the obstruction means less turbulence. Squatting/knee-to-chest increases SVR, forcing more blood through the lungs. Most common cyanotic congenital heart defect.

wrongAnswers.name: Transposition of the Great Arteries
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TGA causes cyanosis from birth with an egg-on-a-string heart shape and requires a mixing lesion. This has a boot-shaped heart with the obstruction-VSD physiology.

wrongAnswers.name: VSD Alone
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Isolated VSD causes a left-to-right shunt without cyanosis (acyanotic). The right ventricular outflow obstruction here reverses the shunt direction, causing cyanosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Atresia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pulmonary atresia causes cyanosis but with NO forward flow through the pulmonary valve and the infant is ductus-dependent — a different physiology.

clues: A newborn turns profoundly blue within hours of birth despite appearing normal at delivery.
The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and oxygen saturations do not improve despite 100% supplemental oxygen.
The infant is deeply cyanotic with tachypnea but no respiratory distress, and there is no significant murmur.
Chest X-ray shows an egg-shaped cardiac silhouette on a narrow mediastinal stalk with increased pulmonary vascular markings.
Echocardiography shows the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle.
explanation: The aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left, creating two parallel circuits with no mixing. Deoxygenated blood recirculates through the body and oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs.
keyFact: The egg-on-a-string silhouette from the narrow mediastinum is classic. PGE1 keeps the ductus open for mixing. Balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) creates an emergency mixing hole. Definitive repair is the arterial switch operation.

wrongAnswers.name: Tetralogy of Fallot
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TOF causes cyanotic spells but not from birth — they develop over months as the outflow obstruction worsens. This is cyanosis from the first hours of life.

wrongAnswers.name: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PPHN causes neonatal cyanosis from right-to-left shunting across the PDA/foramen ovale but the great vessels are normally connected.

wrongAnswers.name: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TAPVR causes cyanosis with a snowman-shaped heart silhouette, not the egg-on-a-string appearance.

clues: A 2-month-old infant presents with poor feeding and sweating during breastfeeding.
The baby runs out of energy after a few minutes of nursing and is not gaining weight appropriately.
Exam reveals tachypnea, a palpable thrill on the left side of the sternum, and a loud harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings.
Echo confirms a hole between the two pumping chambers with blood flowing from left to right and a shunt ratio of 2.5.
explanation: Blood shunts from the high-pressure left ventricle to the right ventricle, overloading the pulmonary circulation. Small muscular defects often close spontaneously.
keyFact: Holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border with thrill. Large shunts cause heart failure in infancy. If untreated, chronic pulmonary overcirculation leads to irreversible pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger syndrome).

wrongAnswers.name: ASD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD has a fixed split S2 with a systolic ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border — not the holosystolic murmur at the lower border.

wrongAnswers.name: PDA
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PDA produces a continuous machinery murmur at the left infraclavicular area, not a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.

wrongAnswers.name: Innocent Murmur
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Innocent murmurs don't cause failure to thrive, cardiomegaly, or a palpable thrill.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with sudden-onset palpitations and dizziness with a heart rate of 210 bpm that began during exercise.
He has had similar episodes since adolescence that start and stop abruptly, lasting 10-30 minutes.
Between episodes, his physical exam is completely normal with no murmurs or abnormal sounds.
Baseline ECG shows a PR interval under 120 ms, a widened QRS complex, and no ischemic changes.
A slurred upstroke (delta wave) is visible at the beginning of each QRS complex on the resting ECG.
explanation: An extra electrical connection between the atria and ventricles conducts impulses faster than the normal pathway, shortening the PR interval and producing the characteristic slurred upstroke (delta wave).
keyFact: Short PR + delta wave + wide QRS on baseline ECG is the diagnostic triad. The biggest danger is atrial fibrillation conducting rapidly down the accessory pathway — AV nodal blocking drugs (digoxin, verapamil, beta-blockers) are CONTRAINDICATED because they force all conduction down the bypass tract.

wrongAnswers.name: AV Nodal Reentrant Tachycardia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AVNRT causes similar paroxysmal tachycardia but the baseline ECG is NORMAL — no short PR, no delta wave. The reentry circuit is within the AV node, not through an accessory pathway.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrial Flutter
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Flutter causes regular tachycardia but with sawtooth flutter waves on ECG, not a delta wave on baseline tracing.

wrongAnswers.name: Ventricular Tachycardia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VT causes wide complex tachycardia but the baseline ECG doesn't show a delta wave or short PR interval.

clues: A 40-year-old nonsmoker presents with progressive dyspnea and a productive cough, with a family history of emphysema at a young age.
He has never smoked and has no occupational exposures, yet he has the lung findings of someone who smoked for decades.
Exam reveals a barrel-shaped chest with diminished breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion bilaterally.
Pulmonary function tests show severe obstruction with markedly decreased diffusing capacity, and CT shows emphysematous destruction predominantly in the LOWER lobes.
Serum level of the protease inhibitor is 28 mg/dL (normal 100-300), and liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules of misfolded protein accumulating in hepatocytes.
explanation: The misfolded protease inhibitor cannot leave the liver (causing cirrhosis from accumulation) and cannot reach the lungs (allowing unopposed neutrophil elastase to destroy alveolar walls).
keyFact: LOWER lobe emphysema (vs upper lobe in smoking). PAS-positive globules in hepatocytes = accumulated misfolded protein. Can cause both emphysema AND cirrhosis — lung damage from absence, liver damage from accumulation.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD from Smoking
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Smoking causes UPPER lobe emphysema. This patient has LOWER lobe emphysema as a nonsmoker — the distribution is reversed.

wrongAnswers.name: Asthma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asthma causes reversible airflow obstruction. This is irreversible structural emphysema with severely decreased diffusing capacity.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IPF causes restriction with lower lobe involvement, but the pattern here is OBSTRUCTION with emphysema on CT — not fibrosis.

clues: A 14-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of wheezing and chest tightness that are worst at night and during exercise.
He has a history of eczema as an infant and allergic rhinitis, and his mother has a similar breathing condition.
Exam during an episode reveals diffuse bilateral expiratory wheezes with a prolonged expiratory phase.
Pulmonary function testing shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.65 with an obstructive pattern.
After inhaled bronchodilator, FEV1/FVC improves to 0.82 with a greater than 12% increase in FEV1.
explanation: Airway inflammation with smooth muscle hyperreactivity causes episodic bronchoconstriction with mucus plugging. The inflammation is driven by Th2 cytokines, eosinophils, and IgE.
keyFact: Reversible airflow obstruction (>12% improvement with bronchodilator) distinguishes this from COPD (irreversible). The atopic triad: eczema → asthma → allergic rhinitis. Inhaled corticosteroids reduce inflammation and are the cornerstone of long-term control.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes airflow obstruction that does NOT reverse with bronchodilators. This patient has significant reversibility — from 0.65 to 0.82.

wrongAnswers.name: Vocal Cord Dysfunction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VCD causes wheezing and dyspnea but the obstruction is INspiratory (not expiratory) and PFTs show flattening of the inspiratory loop.

wrongAnswers.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Foreign body causes unilateral wheezing localized to one lung, not bilateral diffuse wheezing with reversibility on PFTs.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with chronic productive cough producing copious foul-smelling purulent sputum daily.
She has a history of recurrent pneumonias since childhood with 5 hospitalizations for lung infections in the past 3 years, and reports intermittent hemoptysis.
Exam reveals bibasilar coarse crackles that do not clear with coughing, and digital clubbing is present.
High-resolution CT shows thickened airway walls in a 'tram track' pattern with scattered areas of mucus plugging.
The affected airways are permanently dilated and do not taper as they extend toward the lung periphery.
explanation: Repeated cycles of infection, inflammation, and healing destroy the elastic and muscular components of the airway wall, leaving them permanently dilated and unable to clear secretions.
keyFact: The most common cause worldwide is prior severe infection. In developed countries, cystic fibrosis is the leading cause in young patients. Other causes: primary ciliary dyskinesia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, immunodeficiency, and post-obstructive. Pseudomonas colonization is common.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes chronic cough and dyspnea from smoking but without the copious daily purulent sputum production and permanently dilated airways on CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Bronchitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic bronchitis causes productive cough for ≥3 months per year, but CT shows airway wall thickening without the permanent dilation and tram tracking.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A lung abscess causes foul-smelling sputum but is a focal cavity on imaging, not diffuse permanent airway dilation.

clues: A 4-month-old infant presents in January with nasal congestion and progressive wheezing.
He had a runny nose for 2 days before the wheezing began and is now feeding poorly.
Exam reveals tachypnea, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and widespread bilateral wheezes and crackles.
Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with peribronchial thickening and flattened diaphragms.
RSV rapid antigen test from a nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive in this previously healthy infant.
explanation: RSV (most common cause) infects the bronchiolar epithelium, causing inflammation, edema, and mucus plugging of the small airways with air trapping.
keyFact: Infant <12 months + winter season + preceding URI + wheezing + hyperinflation on CXR = bronchiolitis. First-time wheezing in an infant is almost always infectious bronchiolitis, NOT asthma. Palivizumab prophylaxis is given to high-risk infants (premature, congenital heart disease).

wrongAnswers.name: Asthma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asthma is NOT typically diagnosed in infants <12 months. First-time wheezing with a viral URI in this age group is bronchiolitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pneumonia causes focal findings (consolidation) with high fever. Bronchiolitis causes diffuse bilateral wheezing with mild fever.

wrongAnswers.name: Foreign Body
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Foreign body causes sudden-onset unilateral wheezing in a toddler. This is an infant with bilateral findings after a viral prodrome.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath on exertion and a productive cough that has persisted for the past three years.
He has a 45-pack-year smoking history. He now gets winded walking one block and has been using more pillows at night to breathe.
Exam reveals a barrel-shaped chest, diminished breath sounds bilaterally, prolonged expiratory phase, and scattered wheezes.
Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55, FEV1 of 42% predicted, with no significant improvement after bronchodilator administration.
Chest X-ray shows hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and increased retrosternal airspace.
explanation: Chronic cigarette smoke exposure causes both airway inflammation with mucus hypersecretion (chronic bronchitis component) and destruction of alveolar walls with air trapping (emphysema component).
keyFact: The fixed low FEV1/FVC ratio that does NOT reverse with bronchodilators distinguishes COPD from asthma (which is reversible). Smoking cessation is the single most important intervention to slow decline.

wrongAnswers.name: Asthma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asthma causes airflow obstruction but it REVERSES with bronchodilators (>12% improvement). The obstruction here is fixed.

wrongAnswers.name: Congestive Heart Failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CHF causes dyspnea and orthopnea but with crackles (not diminished sounds), an enlarged heart, and elevated BNP.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IPF causes progressive dyspnea but with RESTRICTIVE physiology (low FVC with normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio), not obstructive.

clues: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent lower respiratory infections requiring two hospitalizations.
His first bowel movement was delayed at birth and required surgical intervention.
His stools are pale, greasy, and foul-smelling despite adequate caloric intake.
Sputum culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is very unusual for an infant this age.
Genetic testing confirms homozygosity for a three-nucleotide deletion in a chloride channel gene on chromosome 7.
explanation: A defective chloride channel produces thick dehydrated secretions in every exocrine organ. Lungs get colonized because thick mucus cannot be cleared, and pancreatic ducts are blocked causing maldigestion.
keyFact: Pseudomonas colonization is the hallmark lung pathogen. Meconium ileus at birth occurs in ~15%. Male infertility in >95% from absent vas deferens. CFTR modulators have transformed prognosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PCD causes recurrent sinopulmonary infections but from immotile cilia, not thick secretions. Sweat chloride is normal, and 50% have situs inversus.

wrongAnswers.name: Immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Recurrent infections in an infant raise immune concerns, but the steatorrhea, elevated sweat chloride, and Pseudomonas point to a secretion disorder.

wrongAnswers.name: Celiac Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Celiac causes steatorrhea but only after gluten introduction, with normal sweat chloride and no lung infections.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with cough and dyspnea that begin several hours after working in an enclosed environment.
She breeds pigeons and symptoms improve when she is away from her birds for several days but recur each time she returns.
Exam during an acute episode reveals diffuse fine crackles without wheezing and a temperature of 100.8 F.
CT shows ground-glass opacities with centrilobular nodules predominantly in the upper and middle lung zones.
Bronchoalveolar lavage shows markedly elevated lymphocytes with a predominance of CD8+ T cells.
explanation: Repeated inhalation of organic antigens triggers an immune-mediated inflammatory reaction in the alveoli and small airways. Acute episodes are type III (immune complex) and type IV (T-cell mediated) hypersensitivity reactions.
keyFact: Temporal relationship to antigen exposure is key: symptoms 4-8 hours after exposure, improve with avoidance. Common antigens: bird proteins, thermophilic actinomycetes (farmer's lung), mold. Upper/middle lobe predominance distinguishes from IPF (lower lobe).

wrongAnswers.name: Asthma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asthma causes wheezing and airflow obstruction that responds to bronchodilators. HP causes crackles with restrictive physiology and lymphocytic BAL.

wrongAnswers.name: IPF
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IPF is idiopathic with LOWER lobe honeycombing and no antigen exposure. HP has an identifiable trigger and UPPER/MIDDLE lobe predominance.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with noncaseating granulomas and is not temporally related to antigen exposure.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and a persistent dry cough over 2 years.
He has no occupational exposures, no medication use associated with lung fibrosis, and no connective tissue disease symptoms.
Exam reveals fine bibasilar inspiratory crackles that sound like Velcro being pulled apart, and digital clubbing.
PFTs show a restrictive pattern with reduced FVC, reduced DLCO, and a normal FEV1/FVC ratio.
High-resolution CT shows bibasilar peripheral honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis in a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern.
explanation: Progressive fibrosis replaces normal lung parenchyma from the bases upward, stiffening the lungs (restrictive physiology) and impairing gas exchange (low DLCO).
keyFact: The UIP pattern on HRCT (basal, peripheral, honeycombing) in the right clinical context is diagnostic without biopsy. Velcro crackles + clubbing + restrictive PFTs in an older man = IPF. Pirfenidone and nintedanib slow progression. Lung transplant is the only cure.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes OBSTRUCTIVE physiology (low FEV1/FVC) with hyperinflation. This is RESTRICTIVE with honeycombing.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with upper lobe predominance and noncaseating granulomas. IPF is basal-predominant with honeycombing and no granulomas.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HP causes fibrosis but has an identifiable antigen exposure (birds, mold), upper/middle lobe predominance, and air trapping on imaging. IPF is idiopathic with lower lobe predominance.

clues: A 55-year-old woman who has never smoked presents with a chronic cough, and an incidental peripheral nodule is found on chest X-ray.
She has no occupational exposures and no family history of cancer. She has had mild unintentional weight loss.
Exam is unremarkable except for digital clubbing of the fingers, noted bilaterally.
CT shows a 2.5-cm spiculated peripheral nodule in the right upper lobe with avid PET uptake suggesting malignancy.
Biopsy reveals malignant glandular cells forming acinar structures, positive for TTF-1 and harboring an EGFR exon 19 deletion.
explanation: This is the most common lung cancer overall and the most common type in never-smokers. It typically arises peripherally and can harbor targetable driver mutations.
keyFact: Peripheral + non-smoker (or any smoker) + glandular histology + TTF-1 positive = adenocarcinoma. It's the most common lung cancer overall. Targetable mutations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1) are more common in never-smokers and can dramatically alter treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Squamous cell is CENTRAL, strongly associated with smoking, and produces keratin pearls — not peripheral with glandular mucin-producing cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Small Cell Lung Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCLC is CENTRAL, neuroendocrine, and almost exclusively occurs in heavy smokers. This is a peripheral adenocarcinoma in a never-smoker.

wrongAnswers.name: Carcinoid Tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoids are neuroendocrine tumors that are typically endobronchial and well-differentiated. This is a peripheral glandular tumor with EGFR mutation.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea and dull chest pain over 4 months.
He worked as a shipyard insulator for 30 years and has a large unilateral pleural effusion on the right that reaccumulates after each drainage.
Exam reveals dullness and decreased breath sounds over the entire right hemithorax.
CT shows circumferential nodular pleural thickening encasing the right lung with calcified pleural plaques bilaterally.
Pleural biopsy shows malignant spindle and epithelioid cells that stain positive for calretinin and negative for TTF-1.
explanation: Inhaled mineral fibers lodge in the pleural surface and cause chronic irritation that leads to malignant transformation of mesothelial cells decades later.
keyFact: The long latency (20-40 years) means current cases reflect exposures decades ago. The calcified plaques indicate prior exposure but are themselves benign — the malignant component is the nodular pleural thickening. Calretinin positivity distinguishes mesothelioma from adenocarcinoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Adenocarcinoma with Pleural Metastasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lung cancer can cause pleural effusion and thickening, but there would be a parenchymal lung mass and the biopsy would show adenocarcinoma markers (TTF-1), not mesothelial markers (calretinin).

wrongAnswers.name: Empyema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Empyema causes a unilateral pleural collection with fever and purulent fluid, not the chronic nodular pleural thickening with malignant cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Asbestosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asbestosis is interstitial PULMONARY fibrosis from asbestos (affects the lung parenchyma). Mesothelioma is a PLEURAL malignancy. They share the exposure but are different diseases.

clues: A premature infant born at 30 weeks develops grunting, nasal flaring, and intercostal retractions within hours of birth.
The mother did not receive antenatal corticosteroids because she presented in active preterm labor.
The infant has tachypnea with audible grunting and subcostal retractions, with cyanosis that improves on supplemental oxygen.
Chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms and low lung volumes.
Lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio from tracheal aspirate is less than 2, and lamellar body count is low.
explanation: Premature type II pneumocytes have not yet produced adequate surfactant, which normally reduces alveolar surface tension. Without it, alveoli collapse with each breath and the lungs become progressively more difficult to inflate.
keyFact: Surfactant production begins around 24-28 weeks and is adequate by ~35 weeks. Antenatal betamethasone given to the mother accelerates surfactant production and dramatically reduces incidence. Lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio >2 on amniocentesis predicts lung maturity.

wrongAnswers.name: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTN causes respiratory distress in near-term infants from retained lung fluid, but it's self-limited within 24-48 hours and X-ray shows fluid in fissures, not the diffuse ground-glass of surfactant deficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: Meconium Aspiration
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meconium aspiration occurs in term or post-term infants with meconium-stained fluid, showing patchy asymmetric infiltrates, not the symmetric ground-glass pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Neonatal pneumonia (GBS) can look similar but presents with sepsis markers, asymmetric infiltrates, and positive cultures.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with excessive daytime drowsiness despite reportedly getting 8 hours of rest each night.
He is obese with a BMI of 38. His wife describes loud snoring and episodes where he stops breathing during the night.
Exam reveals a thick neck circumference of 19 inches and a crowded oropharynx with a Mallampati class IV airway.
Polysomnography shows 32 apnea-hypopnea events per hour with oxygen desaturations to 78%.
During the study, all apnea events show continued chest and abdominal wall effort against a closed airway with no central pauses.
explanation: The upper airway collapses repeatedly during sleep due to loss of muscle tone, causing intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation. The obesity and large neck circumference contribute to airway narrowing.
keyFact: Excessive daytime sleepiness + witnessed apneas + snoring + obesity = OSA until proven otherwise. Untreated OSA increases risk of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, stroke, and motor vehicle accidents. An AHI ≥5 with symptoms or ≥15 regardless confirms the diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Narcolepsy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Narcolepsy causes excessive daytime sleepiness with cataplexy and sleep-onset REM, but without snoring, apneic episodes, or obesity.

wrongAnswers.name: Central Sleep Apnea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Central apnea is from absent respiratory drive (no chest/abdominal effort during events). This is OBSTRUCTIVE (continued respiratory effort against a closed airway).

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes fatigue and weight gain but not the witnessed apneas, snoring, or polysomnographic findings of airway obstruction.

clues: A 65-year-old man with congestive heart failure presents with progressive dyspnea over two weeks.
The symptoms have worsened over two weeks despite adherence to his prescribed diuretic regimen.
Exam reveals decreased breath sounds with dullness to percussion at both lung bases and decreased tactile fremitus.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral meniscus-shaped opacities blunting both costophrenic angles.
Thoracentesis fluid has a protein ratio below 0.5 and LDH ratio below 0.6 relative to serum values.
explanation: Elevated hydrostatic pressure from heart failure pushes fluid across intact capillary membranes into the pleural space. The fluid is protein-poor (transudate) because the capillaries aren't leaky.
keyFact: Transudative (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic) vs exudative (infection, malignancy, PE, autoimmune). Light's criteria distinguish them: exudate if protein ratio >0.5 OR LDH ratio >0.6 OR pleural LDH >2/3 upper normal. Treat the underlying cause for transudates; investigate further for exudates.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pneumonia can cause an effusion (parapneumonic), but it would be exudative with elevated protein and LDH, and the patient would have fever and focal consolidation.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE can cause a small effusion but it's typically unilateral, exudative, and accompanied by pleuritic pain and hypoxia.

wrongAnswers.name: Mesothelioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mesothelioma causes a unilateral exudative effusion with pleural thickening. This is bilateral and transudative from heart failure.

clues: A 40-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough over several months that has not responded to antibiotics or bronchodilators.
He has a history of heavy occupational silica dust exposure over many years as a sandblaster.
Exam reveals mild hypoxemia at rest that worsens significantly with exertion, but the lungs sound surprisingly clear on auscultation.
High-resolution CT shows a geographic 'crazy-paving' pattern of ground-glass opacities with superimposed interlobular septal thickening.
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid is opaque and milky, and PAS staining reveals the alveoli are filled with granular proteinaceous material.
explanation: Accumulation of surfactant-derived lipoproteins fills the alveoli because alveolar macrophages cannot clear the material normally. This impairs gas exchange without significantly affecting air movement.
keyFact: Crazy-paving pattern on HRCT + milky BAL fluid + PAS-positive proteinaceous material = PAP. Most cases are autoimmune (anti-GM-CSF antibodies). The disconnect between severe hypoxemia and relatively clear lung sounds is a clinical clue. Whole-lung lavage physically removes the accumulated material.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumocystis Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PCP also shows ground-glass opacities with BAL findings, but occurs in immunocompromised patients and has a different clinical context.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IPF shows honeycombing (not crazy-paving) on HRCT and BAL shows neutrophils, not milky PAS-positive proteinaceous material.

wrongAnswers.name: Lipoid Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lipoid pneumonia shows fat-laden macrophages on BAL from aspiration of mineral oil or other lipid substances, not the surfactant-derived proteinaceous material.

clues: A 30-year-old woman presents with a persistent dry cough and fatigue over several months.
She has painful red nodules on her shins, blurred vision in her right eye, and mild joint aches.
Exam reveals bilateral tender erythematous nodules on the anterior shins and anterior uveitis on ophthalmologic exam.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, serum ACE level is elevated, and calcium is high.
Biopsy of a skin lesion shows well-formed noncaseating granulomas with no evidence of organisms on AFB or fungal stains.
explanation: A multi-system granulomatous disease of unknown cause, with noncaseating granulomas forming in the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, eyes, liver, and other organs.
keyFact: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + noncaseating granulomas + elevated ACE + hypercalcemia + uveitis + erythema nodosum in a young African American woman is the classic presentation. The granulomas produce 1-alpha-hydroxylase, converting vitamin D to its active form and causing hypercalcemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB granulomas are CASEATING (with central cheesy necrosis) and AFB stain is positive. Sarcoid granulomas are NONcaseating.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy but biopsy shows malignant lymphoid cells, not noncaseating granulomas.

wrongAnswers.name: Berylliosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Berylliosis is histologically identical to sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas) but requires occupational beryllium exposure and is confirmed by beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test.

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with a persistent cough and progressive facial puffiness over the past several weeks.
He has a 50-pack-year smoking history. He also reports progressive weakness, darkening of his skin, and dilated veins across his chest.
Exam reveals facial plethora, proximal muscle weakness, skin hyperpigmentation, and his serum sodium is 118.
CT shows a large central hilar mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy compressing the superior vena cava.
Biopsy of the mass shows small round blue cells with scant cytoplasm, high mitotic rate, and positive chromogranin and synaptophysin staining.
explanation: This aggressive neuroendocrine tumor arises centrally in the lungs and is strongly associated with heavy smoking. It commonly produces ectopic ACTH (causing the cushingoid features) and ADH (causing the hyponatremia).
keyFact: Central mass + heavy smoker + paraneoplastic syndromes (SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert-Eaton) + SVC syndrome = SCLC. Treated with chemotherapy/radiation (not surgery — nearly always disseminated at diagnosis). Initial response is dramatic but relapse is the rule.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous Cell Lung Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Squamous is also central and associated with smoking, but it produces PTHrP (hypercalcemia), not SIADH or ectopic ACTH, and is not neuroendocrine.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Adenocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adenocarcinoma is typically PERIPHERAL, not central. It doesn't produce ectopic hormones and is not neuroendocrine.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mediastinal lymphoma causes SVC syndrome but with lymphoid markers on biopsy, not a neuroendocrine central lung mass with paraneoplastic syndromes.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with sudden onset of right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath that started at rest without trauma.
He is a smoker with no history of lung disease, and the pain is pleuritic, worsening with deep breaths.
Exam reveals decreased breath sounds on the right with hyperresonance to percussion, and he is hemodynamically stable.
Chest X-ray shows absence of lung markings in the right apex with a visible line parallel to the chest wall.
A visceral pleural line is confirmed on the right with a 2.5-cm rim of air between the lung surface and the chest wall.
explanation: Rupture of a subpleural bleb allows air to escape from the lung into the pleural space, partially collapsing the lung.
keyFact: Tall thin young male + sudden pleuritic chest pain + decreased breath sounds + hyperresonance = primary spontaneous pneumothorax. The tall thin body habitus creates greater mechanical stress on apical blebs. Smoking increases risk 20-fold.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE causes sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, but breath sounds are usually normal and chest X-ray shows wedge-shaped opacity, not a pleural line.
