wrongAnswers.name: Tension Pneumothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tension causes hemodynamic collapse with tracheal deviation. This patient is hemodynamically STABLE with a simple pneumothorax.

wrongAnswers.name: Costochondritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Costochondritis causes pleuritic chest pain but exam and X-ray are normal — no decreased breath sounds or visible pleural line.

clues: A 25-year-old man who was stabbed in the right chest presents with rapidly worsening dyspnea and hypotension.
His oxygen saturation is dropping despite supplemental oxygen, and his neck veins are distended.
Exam reveals absent breath sounds on the right, distended jugular veins, and hypotension with tachycardia.
The trachea is palpably deviated toward the left, away from the side with absent breath sounds.
Percussion over the right hemithorax is hyperresonant, and subcutaneous crepitus is felt along the right chest wall.
explanation: Air enters the pleural space through a one-way valve mechanism (air enters with each breath but cannot escape), progressively collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum to the opposite side.
keyFact: The triad of absent breath sounds + tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side + distended neck veins with hypotension = tension pneumothorax. Do NOT wait for X-ray — decompress immediately. This is distinct from simple pneumothorax where the patient is hemodynamically stable.

wrongAnswers.name: Cardiac Tamponade
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tamponade also causes hypotension with distended neck veins, but breath sounds are bilateral and equal, and trachea is midline.

wrongAnswers.name: Simple Pneumothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Simple pneumothorax causes absent breath sounds on one side but WITHOUT hypotension, tracheal deviation, or hemodynamic collapse.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemothorax after chest trauma causes decreased breath sounds with dullness to percussion (blood is heavy). Tension pneumothorax has hyperresonance (air is light).

clues: A 60-year-old woman develops sudden fever, chills, flank pain, and dark urine during a blood product administration.
The symptoms began within minutes of starting a red cell infusion. She reports a burning sensation at the IV site and a sense of impending doom.
Her temperature spikes from 98.6 to 103°F, blood pressure drops, and the urine in the Foley bag turns dark red-brown.
Direct Coombs test is positive, haptoglobin is undetectable, and free hemoglobin is detected in both plasma and urine.
The blood bank crossmatch reveals ABO incompatibility from a clerical labeling error — the unit was labeled for a different patient.
explanation: Preformed recipient antibodies (anti-A or anti-B IgM) immediately attack the transfused incompatible red cells, causing massive intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria.
keyFact: This is almost always caused by a CLERICAL ERROR — wrong blood given to the wrong patient. Onset within minutes of starting the transfusion. Immediate steps: STOP the transfusion, recheck the labels, send blood bank specimen, aggressive fluids to protect kidneys.

wrongAnswers.name: Febrile Nonhemolytic Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FNHTR causes fever and chills during transfusion but is mild, self-limited, and does NOT cause hemolysis, dark urine, or hemodynamic instability.

wrongAnswers.name: Allergic Transfusion Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Allergic reactions cause urticaria and sometimes anaphylaxis but NOT hemolysis, positive Coombs, or hemoglobinuria.

wrongAnswers.name: Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TRALI causes acute respiratory distress within 6 hours of transfusion but without the hemolysis, dark urine, or ABO incompatibility.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with severe abdominal pain — the surgical team was called but her abdomen is soft and non-tender on exam.
She was recently started on an oral contraceptive and reports tingling in her hands and feet. The pain is out of proportion to exam findings.
Exam reveals tachycardia, hypertension, and diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound.
All routine labs, lipase, and abdominal CT are normal, but her urine turns dark reddish-purple after standing in sunlight.
Urine porphobilinogen is massively elevated, and aminolevulinic acid is also markedly increased.
explanation: A deficiency in the third enzyme of heme synthesis causes accumulation of neurotoxic precursors that damage autonomic, peripheral, and central nerves.
keyFact: Severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and dark urine that changes color on standing is the classic presentation. Many patients get unnecessary surgery.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Abdomen
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The soft abdomen without peritoneal signs, normal imaging, and dark urine redirect away from a surgical emergency.

wrongAnswers.name: Lead Poisoning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lead also blocks heme synthesis and causes abdominal pain, but produces basophilic stippling on smear and the urine doesn't change color.

wrongAnswers.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBS can present with ascending weakness and areflexia, but doesn't cause abdominal pain, hypertension, or color-changing urine.

clues: A 4-year-old boy presents with leg pain that makes him refuse to walk for the past two weeks.
He was previously healthy but has been having nosebleeds and now refuses to play or eat well.
Exam reveals pallor, petechiae, small rubbery cervical and axillary lymph nodes, and hepatosplenomegaly.
White count is 48,000 with 80% uniform blast cells on peripheral smear and a hemoglobin of 6.2.
The blast cells express TdT, CD10, and CD19, and karyotyping reveals 54 chromosomes (hyperdiploidy).
explanation: A lymphoid precursor cell proliferated uncontrollably and overtook the marrow, crowding out normal blood production.
keyFact: TdT marks immature lymphoid cells. CD10/CD19 confirm B-cell lineage. Age 1-10, WBC <50,000, and hyperdiploidy are favorable prognostic factors.

wrongAnswers.name: AML
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AML blasts express myeloid markers and may contain rod-shaped inclusions. These are TdT+ with B-cell markers.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP drops platelets in isolation. Pancytopenia with blasts localizes the problem to the marrow.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious Mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBV causes reactive lymphocytes, not a blast-predominant smear with pancytopenia.

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with two weeks of progressive fatigue and pallor noticed by his wife.
He has 20 years of industrial solvent exposure and noticed his gums becoming swollen and boggy over the past week.
Exam reveals pallor, gingival hypertrophy, and petechiae on his lower extremities without lymphadenopathy.
White count is 42,000 with 70% large cells containing pink rod-shaped crystalline inclusions staining positive for myeloperoxidase.
Bone marrow biopsy shows 65% of these myeloperoxidase-positive blast cells with crystalline inclusions.
explanation: A myeloid precursor stopped maturing and proliferated uncontrollably, crowding out normal blood production.
keyFact: The rod-shaped inclusions (Auer rods) are pathognomonic for myeloid lineage. Gum hypertrophy suggests monocytic subtypes. Benzene exposure is a known risk factor.

wrongAnswers.name: ALL
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ALL blasts express lymphoid markers and never contain the myeloid rod-shaped inclusions seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious Mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBV causes reactive atypical lymphocytes, not myeloperoxidase-positive blasts with crystalline inclusions.

wrongAnswers.name: MDS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDS has <20% blasts. This patient has 65% — above the threshold for acute leukemia.

clues: A 28-year-old previously healthy woman presents with one week of nosebleeds that will not stop.
She has also noticed gum bleeding and spontaneous bruises appearing on her trunk over the past several days.
Exam reveals pallor, oozing from the gum margins, and petechiae scattered across her palate and trunk.
The smear shows abnormal cells packed with bright red-pink granules, and PT/aPTT are prolonged with critically low fibrinogen.
The granule-packed cells carry a translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17 on cytogenetic analysis.
explanation: The translocation freezes myeloid development at one stage, and the granule-packed cells release procoagulant substances triggering widespread coagulation consumption.
keyFact: This is the one leukemia treated on suspicion — the coagulation crisis can kill within hours. The vitamin A derivative plus arsenic trioxide achieves cure rates exceeding 90%.

wrongAnswers.name: DIC from Sepsis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Identical coagulation pattern, but the granule-packed blast cells with the specific translocation identify leukemia as the trigger.

wrongAnswers.name: AML (non-APL)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Other AML subtypes lack the specific translocation, the granule-packed morphology, and the response to the vitamin A derivative.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia with normal coagulation studies and no abnormal cells on smear.

clues: A 25-year-old man presents with lifelong mild anemia and fatigue that worsens during infections.
His hemoglobin has never been above 10 and his red cells have always been small, but iron supplements have never helped.
Exam reveals pallor and mild splenomegaly, and the patient appears thin with mild jaundice.
Hemoglobin is 8.5 with microcytic hypochromic red cells, and brilliant cresyl blue stain reveals golf-ball-like inclusions within red cells.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows a fast-migrating band representing tetramers composed entirely of beta chains.
explanation: With only one functional alpha-globin gene out of the normal four, excess beta chains form unstable tetramers that precipitate and damage red cells.
keyFact: Four alpha genes: loss of 1 = silent carrier, 2 = trait, 3 = HbH disease (this case), 4 = hydrops fetalis (incompatible with life). The inclusions are HbH (β4 tetramers) visible on supravital stain.

wrongAnswers.name: Beta-Thalassemia Major
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Beta-thal shows elevated fetal hemoglobin as the dominant band. This shows a fast-migrating band of beta-chain tetramers — an alpha-chain problem.

wrongAnswers.name: Iron Deficiency Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IDA causes microcytic anemia but with low iron and high TIBC. Iron supplementation failed here because the problem is the globin gene, not iron supply.

wrongAnswers.name: G6PD Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: G6PD causes episodic hemolysis with bite cells triggered by oxidative stress, not chronic microcytic anemia with beta-chain tetramer inclusions.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive swelling in his legs that does not respond to diuretics.
He has noticed his tongue getting larger and has difficulty swallowing solid food.
Exam reveals an enlarged tongue protruding beyond his teeth and periorbital purpura without trauma.
Echocardiogram reveals biventricular thickening with a sparkling myocardial texture and diastolic dysfunction.
Tissue biopsy stained with Congo red and viewed under polarized light shows apple-green birefringence.
explanation: Misfolded immunoglobulin light chains deposit as insoluble fibrils in multiple organs, disrupting their architecture and function.
keyFact: Macroglossia is relatively specific for AL type. Congo red with apple-green birefringence under polarized light is diagnostic for all amyloid types. The sparkling echo pattern suggests infiltrative cardiomyopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Myeloma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myeloma has lytic bone lesions with higher paraprotein levels and more marrow plasma cells. Amyloidosis is about protein misfolding and organ deposition, though they can coexist.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The nephrotic-range proteinuria is one manifestation, but the macroglossia, periorbital purpura, neuropathy, and Congo red birefringence identify a systemic infiltrative disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Heart Failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The cardiac involvement mimics HF, but the restrictive physiology with sparkling myocardium plus extracardiac findings point to an infiltrative process.

clues: A 3-year-old girl is brought in because she has never spoken a single word and has global developmental delay.
She laughs and smiles almost constantly with an inappropriately happy demeanor and hand-flapping movements.
Exam reveals ataxic wide-based gait with arms raised and flexed, tongue thrusting, and microcephaly.
EEG shows high-amplitude slow waves with a characteristic triphasic pattern, and seizures have occurred since age 2.
Genetic testing shows a deletion on the MATERNAL copy of chromosome 15q11-13 affecting the UBE3A gene.
explanation: The maternal copy of UBE3A (the only active copy in the brain due to imprinting) is lost. Without it, the neurologic syndrome develops.
keyFact: Maternal deletion = this syndrome (happy, seizures, no speech, ataxia). Paternal deletion = the other syndrome (hypotonia → obesity, hypogonadism). Genomic imprinting at its most elegant.

wrongAnswers.name: Prader-Willi Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prader-Willi is PATERNAL deletion of 15q causing hypotonia then obesity with hypogonadism — very different phenotype.

wrongAnswers.name: Rett Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rett causes regression in girls with loss of hand skills and stereotypic hand-wringing, but from an X chromosome gene mutation — not a 15q deletion.

wrongAnswers.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD can involve language delay, but the constant laughter, puppet-like gait, seizures, and specific deletion are distinctive.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents after her third pregnancy loss, each occurring during the second trimester.
She had an unexplained leg clot at age 25, and her basic thrombophilia workup was previously negative.
Exam reveals livedo reticularis (a lace-like purplish net-like discoloration) on both lower extremities.
The aPTT is PROLONGED in the lab, yet clinically she has had recurrent CLOTTING events in her veins.
Anticardiolipin antibodies, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I, and lupus anticoagulant are all positive on two tests 12 weeks apart.
explanation: Antiphospholipid antibodies interfere with phospholipid-dependent coagulation assays in vitro (prolonging aPTT) while paradoxically activating endothelium and platelets in vivo (causing thrombosis).
keyFact: The paradox: prolonged aPTT in the LAB but CLOTTING in the PATIENT. The recurrent pregnancy losses occur from placental thrombosis. Can be primary or secondary (associated with SLE). Diagnosis requires both clinical criteria (thrombosis or pregnancy loss) AND persistent positive antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Factor V Leiden
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Factor V Leiden causes venous thrombosis but aPTT is normal, there are no specific antibodies, and it doesn't cause the aPTT prolongation paradox.

wrongAnswers.name: DIC
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DIC causes prolonged aPTT with thrombocytopenia and schistocytes. APS has prolonged aPTT from antibody interference, not from consumption.

wrongAnswers.name: Lupus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE can include antiphospholipid antibodies (secondary APS), but primary APS occurs without lupus. The clotting and pregnancy loss pattern — not the rash and nephritis — define this condition.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with recurrent infections over two months despite no prior immune problems.
He was started on chloramphenicol six weeks ago for a bacterial infection.
Exam shows pallor, petechiae, and a temperature of 101.4°F without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.
All three blood cell lines are low with a reticulocyte count of only 0.2%.
Bone marrow biopsy shows less than 20% cellularity with fat replacing normal blood-forming tissue.
explanation: The bone marrow factory has shut down, either from direct toxicity or autoimmune destruction of stem cells. All cell lines drop because the source is gone.
keyFact: Hypocellular marrow with fat replacement distinguishes this from MDS (which is hypercellular despite low counts). The very low reticulocyte count confirms the marrow isn't responding.

wrongAnswers.name: Myelodysplastic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDS causes pancytopenia but with a HYPERcellular marrow — cells are being made but are defective. This marrow is nearly empty.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Leukemia causes pancytopenia but the marrow is packed with blast cells, not empty with fat.

wrongAnswers.name: B12 Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: B12 causes pancytopenia but with megaloblastic changes, hypersegmented neutrophils, and a cellular marrow.

clues: A 9-month-old infant presents with progressive pallor and irritability that began around 6 months of age.
Both parents are known carriers of a hemoglobin disorder, and the infant was completely healthy at birth.
Exam shows frontal bossing, widened facial bones from marrow expansion, and hepatosplenomegaly.
Hemoglobin is 5.2 with microcytic red cells, target cells, and nucleated red blood cells on smear, but iron studies are completely normal.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows fetal hemoglobin as the overwhelming dominant band with complete absence of normal adult hemoglobin.
explanation: Without beta-globin genes, adult hemoglobin cannot be produced after the fetal-to-adult switch at 6 months. Unpaired alpha chains destroy developing red cells in the marrow.
keyFact: Normal iron studies distinguish this from iron deficiency. The onset at 6 months corresponds to the fetal-to-adult hemoglobin switch. Skull changes reflect massive marrow expansion.

wrongAnswers.name: Iron Deficiency Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IDA causes microcytic anemia but with low iron, high TIBC, and low ferritin. Iron is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Sickle Cell Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCD shows a predominant abnormal variant band, not fetal hemoglobin as the dominant species.

wrongAnswers.name: Lead Poisoning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lead causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling but normal hemoglobin electrophoresis.

clues: A 7-year-old boy presents with a rapidly growing jaw mass that doubled in size within two weeks.
He has positive EBV serology and no systemic symptoms such as fevers, night sweats, or weight loss.
Exam reveals a large firm nontender mass deforming the right mandible with loosened teeth.
Biopsy shows sheets of identical medium-sized blue cells with scattered pale macrophages and a proliferation index approaching 100%.
The cells carry a translocation between chromosomes 8 and 14 placing the c-MYC oncogene under the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter.
explanation: The translocation hijacks the B cell's own gene expression machinery to drive nonstop proliferation, making this the fastest-growing human tumor.
keyFact: Despite the fastest growth rate, it is highly curable with chemotherapy because rapidly dividing cells are extremely chemosensitive.

wrongAnswers.name: Rhabdomyosarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rhabdomyosarcoma causes head/neck masses in children but is a muscle-derived sarcoma, not a lymphoid neoplasm.

wrongAnswers.name: Hodgkin Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hodgkin shows giant binucleated cells in an inflammatory background in young adults, not monomorphic blue cells in a child's jaw.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteosarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteosarcoma produces bone matrix with destructive bone changes, not soft tissue sheets of rapidly dividing lymphoid cells.

clues: A 68-year-old man has a white blood cell count of 68,000 discovered incidentally on routine bloodwork while feeling perfectly well.
He has had more frequent upper respiratory infections this winter but no fevers, night sweats, or weight loss.
Exam reveals painless small lymph nodes in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions bilaterally with normal liver and spleen.
The white cells are 92% small mature-appearing lymphocytes, and the smear shows many fragile cells that ruptured during slide preparation.
Flow cytometry shows a monoclonal B-cell population co-expressing CD5, CD20, and CD23.
explanation: A single mature B lymphocyte became malignant but retained its normal appearance. It cloned into billions of functionally useless cells.
keyFact: The ruptured fragile cells (smudge cells) are characteristic. The CD5/CD20/CD23 immunophenotype is the diagnostic fingerprint. Complications include autoimmune hemolytic anemia and transformation to aggressive lymphoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Lymphocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral infections raise lymphocyte counts but not to 68,000 with a monoclonal population on flow cytometry.

wrongAnswers.name: Mantle Cell Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mantle cell is also CD5+/CD20+ but is CD23 NEGATIVE and has t(11;14). CLL is CD23 positive.

wrongAnswers.name: Hairy Cell Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hairy cell causes LOW white counts with massive spleen and NO lymphadenopathy — the opposite picture.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with a dragging heaviness in his left abdomen that has been worsening for months.
He has unintentional weight loss of 10 pounds and feels full after eating only a few bites.
Exam reveals massive splenomegaly extending 8 cm below the left costal margin without lymphadenopathy.
White count is 128,000 showing every stage of myeloid maturation from blasts to mature neutrophils with disproportionate basophils.
Cytogenetics show a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 creating a constitutively active tyrosine kinase fusion protein.
explanation: A stem cell acquired the translocation and began overproducing myeloid cells at every maturation stage.
keyFact: The full maturation spectrum distinguishes chronic from acute leukemia where maturation arrests. The targeted inhibitor transformed this from fatal to manageable.

wrongAnswers.name: Leukemoid Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Severe infections elevate white counts with a left shift but the specific translocation is absent.

wrongAnswers.name: AML
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AML has >20% blasts with arrested maturation. This shows the full spectrum.

wrongAnswers.name: Polycythemia Vera
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PV primarily elevates red cells with a different mutation.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with a palpable purpuric rash on her lower legs and numbness in her feet.
She has chronic hepatitis C. She reports her fingers turning white and painful in cold weather.
Exam reveals palpable purpura on both legs and peripheral neuropathy in a stocking distribution.
Creatinine is elevated with red cell casts on urinalysis, complement C4 is very low, and rheumatoid factor is positive.
Serum left at 4°C for 72 hours produces a visible precipitate that dissolves when rewarmed to 37°C.
explanation: Hepatitis C triggers production of immunoglobulins that precipitate in cold temperatures, depositing in small vessels and causing vasculitis with purpura, glomerulonephritis, and neuropathy.
keyFact: The hepatitis C association is the highest-yield link. Low C4 (from classical pathway activation) and positive rheumatoid factor are characteristic. Treatment targets the underlying HCV infection.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Vasculitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA vasculitis causes palpable purpura in children with normal complement. This is an adult with HCV, low C4, and cryoprecipitate on cooling.

wrongAnswers.name: Polyarteritis Nodosa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PAN is associated with hepatitis B (not C), is ANCA-negative, involves medium arteries with microaneurysms, and spares glomeruli.

wrongAnswers.name: SLE
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus causes purpura and GN with low complement, but with anti-dsDNA antibodies and multi-system involvement — not the HCV association and cold-precipitable immunoglobulins.

clues: A 3-month-old infant presents with severe pallor and poor feeding that developed over the past month.
The infant was healthy at birth but has become progressively more pale and listless, and has a triphalangeal thumb on the right hand.
Exam reveals marked pallor, a flat nasal bridge, and widely spaced eyes.
Hemoglobin is 4.2 with macrocytic red cells and a reticulocyte count near zero, but white blood cells and platelets are completely NORMAL.
Fetal hemoglobin is elevated, and bone marrow shows absent or severely reduced red cell precursors with normal myeloid and megakaryocyte lines.
explanation: A defect in ribosomal protein synthesis causes selective failure of red blood cell production while sparing the other cell lines. The marrow simply cannot make red cells.
keyFact: Isolated red cell aplasia (not pancytopenia) with macrocytosis and elevated fetal hemoglobin in infancy, plus congenital anomalies (especially thumb malformations), is the classic presentation.

wrongAnswers.name: Fanconi Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fanconi causes PANcytopenia (all lines low) and presents later in childhood. DBA is isolated RED cell aplasia with normal white cells and platelets.

wrongAnswers.name: Transient Erythroblastopenia of Childhood
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TEC also causes isolated red cell aplasia but occurs in toddlers (>1 year), is self-limited, and has normal fetal hemoglobin.

wrongAnswers.name: Iron Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IDA causes microcytic anemia with elevated reticulocytes (the marrow is trying). This infant has macrocytic anemia with near-zero reticulocytes.

clues: A 60-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging neck mass over three weeks with night sweats and 10 pounds of weight loss.
He has no prior lymphoma history and feels generally unwell with intermittent fevers.
Exam reveals a 5-cm firm nontender right cervical mass with hepatomegaly but no other lymphadenopathy.
LDH is markedly elevated, and biopsy shows sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells that are CD20+ with a Ki-67 index exceeding 80%.
CT shows the cervical mass plus hepatic lesions with no intervening lymphadenopathy between the two involved sites.
explanation: This is the most common aggressive lymphoma in adults. Non-contiguous spread — skipping node groups — is typical of non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
keyFact: Aggressive but CURABLE with R-CHOP (~60% durable remission). Can arise de novo or by transformation from follicular lymphoma or CLL.

wrongAnswers.name: Hodgkin Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hodgkin spreads contiguously and has CD15/CD30+ giant cells in an inflammatory background. This spreads non-contiguously with CD20+ large cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Metastatic Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The biopsy shows lymphoid cells (CD20+), not epithelial carcinoma cells (cytokeratin+).

wrongAnswers.name: Follicular Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Follicular is indolent with small cleaved cells in a nodular pattern and low Ki-67. This has large cells in sheets with Ki-67 >80%.

clues: A newborn is noted to have poor muscle tone immediately after delivery, with distinctive facial features recognized by the pediatrician.
The mother is 38 years old, and first-trimester screening had shown increased nuchal translucency.
The infant is hypotonic with a flat facial profile, upslanting eyes, prominent epicanthal folds, small ears, a protruding tongue, and a single deep crease across each palm.
Echocardiography reveals an endocardial cushion defect, and CBC shows circulating blasts consistent with a transient proliferative disorder of newborns.
Karyotype confirms 47 chromosomes with an extra copy of the smallest acrocentric autosome.
explanation: The extra chromosome alters development across multiple organ systems. Most cases result from maternal meiotic nondisjunction, with risk increasing with maternal age.
keyFact: Endocardial cushion defects are the most common cardiac anomaly (~40%). Associated with duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, ALL (15-20x risk), hypothyroidism, and early-onset Alzheimer disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Edwards Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trisomy 18 causes clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and prominent occiput — not the hypotonia and single palmar crease seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Congenital Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes hypotonia and a large tongue but without the characteristic facies, single palmar crease, or cardiac cushion defect.

wrongAnswers.name: Prader-Willi Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prader-Willi causes neonatal hypotonia but with different facial features, no cardiac defect, and no chromosomal trisomy.

clues: A newborn is noted to have persistently clenched fists with an unusual overlapping finger pattern on both hands.
The infant is small for gestational age with a birth weight below the 3rd percentile, and the mother is 37 years old.
Exam reveals a small jaw, prominent occiput, low-set malformed ears, and rocker-bottom feet with a short sternum.
Echocardiography shows a ventricular septal defect with an overriding aorta, and renal ultrasound shows horseshoe kidneys.
Karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, and the fists display the 2nd finger overlapping the 3rd and the 5th overlapping the 4th.
explanation: Three copies of this autosome cause severe developmental abnormalities incompatible with long-term survival in most cases.
keyFact: The clenched fist with overlapping fingers (2nd over 3rd, 5th over 4th) is the visual diagnosis. Second most common autosomal trisomy but much more severe than the most common one.

wrongAnswers.name: Patau Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trisomy 13 causes MIDLINE defects — cleft lip/palate, extra digits, and failure of the forebrain to divide. The overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet point to a different trisomy.

wrongAnswers.name: Down Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trisomy 21 causes hypotonia, upslanting eyes, and single palmar crease with much better survival.

wrongAnswers.name: Turner Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Turner (45,X) causes lymphedema and webbed neck in females, not the clenched fists and rocker-bottom feet.

clues: A 55-year-old woman has a platelet count of 850,000 discovered on routine bloodwork while completely asymptomatic.
She has no recent infections, surgery, iron deficiency, or inflammatory conditions and reports occasional burning red fingertips.
Exam is normal except for erythematous warm fingertips that improve with aspirin.
Hemoglobin, white count, iron studies, and inflammatory markers are all normal, and the smear shows giant platelets.
JAK2 V617F mutation is positive, and bone marrow shows increased large megakaryocytes without overgrowth of red cell or white cell lines.
explanation: The myeloproliferative stem cell primarily drives platelet production without significantly affecting other lineages.
keyFact: Diagnosis of exclusion — must rule out PV (normal Hgb here), CML (no Philadelphia chromosome), and reactive causes (normal CRP and iron).

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Thrombocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Infection, iron deficiency, and inflammation elevate platelets reactively. Normal markers and a JAK2 mutation confirm a primary process.

wrongAnswers.name: Polycythemia Vera
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PV also has JAK2 but hemoglobin is markedly elevated. Hemoglobin is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: CML
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CML elevates platelets but WBC is markedly elevated with the Philadelphia chromosome. WBC is normal here.

clues: A 30-year-old woman presents with easy bruising, petechiae on her legs, and progressive pallor over two weeks.
She has no preceding infections, medications, or family history of blood disorders.
Exam reveals scleral icterus, scattered petechiae on both lower extremities, and a palpable spleen tip.
Hemoglobin is 7.5 with a POSITIVE direct Coombs test, elevated reticulocyte count, and elevated LDH.
Her platelets are simultaneously 18,000, and antiplatelet antibodies are detected on separate platelet testing.
explanation: The immune system attacks both red blood cells and platelets simultaneously, combining features of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and ITP in the same patient.
keyFact: The combination of Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia PLUS immune thrombocytopenia is the definition. Often associated with underlying SLE, CLL, or lymphoma — always look for a secondary cause.

wrongAnswers.name: TTP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP also drops both hemoglobin and platelets, but the red cell destruction is mechanical (schistocytes, negative Coombs) not immune-mediated. Coombs is POSITIVE here.

wrongAnswers.name: DIC
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DIC causes hemolysis and thrombocytopenia but with prolonged coagulation studies and schistocytes. This has a positive Coombs with no schistocytes.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP Alone
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP drops only platelets with normal hemoglobin. This patient has BOTH immune-mediated hemolysis and thrombocytopenia.

clues: A 15-year-old boy presents with episodes of severe burning pain in his hands and feet triggered by exercise or fever.
He has clusters of small dark red raised lesions concentrated in the groin and periumbilical area.
Exam reveals the dark red raised lesions in the bathing trunk distribution and corneal opacities on slit-lamp examination.
Echocardiogram reveals concentric left ventricular hypertrophy without hypertension, and urinalysis shows proteinuria.
Alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity is markedly reduced on leukocyte assay, and the gene is on the X chromosome.
explanation: Without this lysosomal enzyme, globotriaosylceramide deposits in blood vessel walls, heart muscle, kidneys, and cornea, causing progressive multi-organ damage.
keyFact: The painful peripheral neuropathy (acroparesthesias) in a teenage boy with angiokeratomas, corneal whorls, cardiac hypertrophy, and renal disease is the classic constellation. X-linked — primarily affects males, though female carriers can have symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatic Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rheumatic fever causes cardiac involvement after strep infection but not the angiokeratomas, corneal opacities, or acroparesthesias.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM causes cardiac hypertrophy but without the skin lesions, corneal findings, renal disease, or acroparesthesias of a storage disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSP causes purpura and renal disease in children but the lesions are palpable purpura on the legs, not angiokeratomas in the groin, and there are no corneal findings.

clues: A 6-year-old boy presents with progressive pallor, and his parents note he is short for his age.
He was born with absent thumbs bilaterally and has café-au-lait spots on his trunk.
Exam reveals short stature, absent thumbs, café-au-lait macules, and a small head circumference.
CBC shows pancytopenia, and the bone marrow is hypocellular.
Chromosomal breakage testing using diepoxybutane shows markedly increased chromosome fragility.
explanation: An inherited defect in DNA repair leads to progressive bone marrow failure, congenital anomalies, and a markedly increased risk of malignancy, especially AML and squamous cell cancers.
keyFact: The triad: pancytopenia + congenital anomalies (absent thumbs, short stature, café-au-lait spots) + increased chromosomal breakage. The DNA repair defect explains both the marrow failure and cancer predisposition.

wrongAnswers.name: Acquired Aplastic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acquired aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia with hypocellular marrow but without the congenital anomalies or increased chromosomal breakage.

wrongAnswers.name: Diamond-Blackfan Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DBA causes isolated red cell aplasia (not pancytopenia) presenting in infancy with macrocytic anemia and elevated fetal hemoglobin.

wrongAnswers.name: Neurofibromatosis Type 1
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NF1 causes café-au-lait spots but without pancytopenia, absent thumbs, or increased chromosomal breakage.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and poor appetite over several months.
He has a history of chronic alcohol use and eats poorly with virtually no green vegetables or fruits in his diet.
Exam reveals pallor and a smooth red tongue without any neurologic abnormalities.
Hemoglobin is 9.0 with MCV of 108, and the smear shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.
Serum folate is low at 1.2 ng/mL. Homocysteine is elevated but methylmalonic acid is normal.
explanation: Folate is absorbed in the jejunum and depleted within months of poor intake. It is required for DNA synthesis but not for myelin maintenance.
keyFact: Folate stores are depleted in months (vs years for B12). Elevated homocysteine with NORMAL MMA = folate deficiency. Alcoholism and poor diet are the most common causes. No neurologic damage — that's the B12 distinction.

wrongAnswers.name: Vitamin B12 Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: B12 deficiency looks identical on smear but elevates BOTH MMA and homocysteine, and causes neurologic damage. MMA is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Liver Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Liver disease causes macrocytosis from altered lipid composition of red cell membranes, but without hypersegmented neutrophils or megaloblastic changes.

wrongAnswers.name: Myelodysplastic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDS causes macrocytic anemia with dysplastic features, not the hypersegmented neutrophils and normal MMA/elevated homocysteine pattern.

clues: A 58-year-old woman presents with painless lymph nodes she has noticed for several months that wax and wane but never fully resolve.
She has no fevers, night sweats, or weight loss and feels generally well.
Exam reveals multiple small rubbery nontender lymph nodes in cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions bilaterally without hepatosplenomegaly.
Biopsy shows a nodular growth pattern of small cleaved B lymphocytes that are CD20+, CD10+, and strongly BCL-2 positive.
Cytogenetics reveal t(14;18) placing the BCL-2 anti-apoptosis gene under control of the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter.
explanation: The translocation overexpresses BCL-2, preventing normal programmed cell death. The cells accumulate because they refuse to die, not because they divide fast.
keyFact: This is the prototypical indolent lymphoma with median survival of 10-15 years. The major risk is transformation to aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (~3% per year).

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Lymphadenopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive nodes are tender and resolve. Persistent painless nodes with monoclonal BCL-2+ cells and t(14;18) are neoplastic.

wrongAnswers.name: CLL/SLL
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CLL is CD5+/CD23+ with smudge cells. Follicular lymphoma is CD10+/BCL-2+ with t(14;18) and a follicular pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Hodgkin Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hodgkin has giant binucleated cells (CD15/CD30+) with contiguous spread. This has small cleaved cells in follicular pattern with t(14;18).

clues: A 25-year-old man presents with bilateral femoral bone pain that has been worsening over several months.
He has had a palpable spleen since childhood and recurrent nosebleeds with easy bruising.
Exam reveals massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and tenderness on palpation of both distal femurs.
Bone marrow biopsy shows large macrophages with a distinctive crinkled tissue paper-like cytoplasm throughout the specimen.
Glucocerebrosidase enzyme activity is markedly reduced on leukocyte assay, confirming a lysosomal lipid storage defect.
explanation: Without the lysosomal enzyme, glucocerebroside accumulates in macrophages throughout the reticuloendothelial system — spleen, liver, and bone marrow.
keyFact: The crinkled tissue paper macrophages (Gaucher cells) are pathognomonic. Type 1 (most common, non-neuronopathic) presents in adults with hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease. Types 2 and 3 have neurologic involvement and present in childhood.

wrongAnswers.name: Niemann-Pick Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Niemann-Pick also accumulates lipid in macrophages but they appear foamy (not crinkled), and the deficient enzyme is sphingomyelinase, not glucocerebrosidase.

wrongAnswers.name: CML
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CML causes massive splenomegaly but with markedly elevated white count and the Philadelphia chromosome, not tissue paper macrophages in the marrow.

wrongAnswers.name: Hairy Cell Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hairy cell causes splenomegaly with pancytopenia but shows hairy lymphocytes, not the crinkled macrophages of a storage disease.

clues: A 5-year-old boy develops sudden pallor, jaundice, and dark cola-colored urine two days after starting a new antibiotic.
He was previously healthy with no history of anemia, and only males in his family have had similar episodes.
Physical examination reveals pallor, mild scleral icterus, and tachycardia without hepatosplenomegaly.
Hemoglobin dropped from 12 to 7.8, and the smear shows red cells with chunks bitten out of them and denatured hemoglobin inclusions.
Enzyme activity testing drawn during the acute episode returns falsely normal because the most deficient cells have already been destroyed.
explanation: Without this enzyme, red cells cannot regenerate antioxidant protection. Oxidative stressors denature hemoglobin into clumps that the spleen plucks out, leaving bitten-out cells.
keyFact: Common triggers: sulfonamides, antimalarials, fava beans, infections. Testing during crisis gives false negatives because the most deficient cells are already destroyed.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIHA shows spherocytes with a positive Coombs test, not drug-triggered bite cells with denatured hemoglobin inclusions.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary Spherocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Spherocytosis causes chronic hemolysis with spherocytes, not acute drug-triggered episodes with bite cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Aplastic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia with low reticulocytes, not isolated acute hemolysis.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with recurrent bacterial infections requiring three hospitalizations in six months.
He has no weight loss or lymphadenopathy, and his doctor found his spleen is massively enlarged.
Exam reveals massive splenomegaly but notably NO lymphadenopathy.
All blood counts are low, the few abnormal lymphocytes have delicate cytoplasmic projections, and the marrow aspirate is a dry tap due to fibrosis.
The abnormal cells are positive for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase and carry the BRAF V600E mutation.
explanation: The 'hairy' cells infiltrate the marrow and spleen, causing fibrosis in the marrow (dry tap) and massive splenomegaly. Pancytopenia results from both marrow infiltration and splenic sequestration.
keyFact: Massive spleen + pancytopenia + NO lymphadenopathy is the clinical triad. The dry tap and TRAP positivity are diagnostic. Remarkably treatment-responsive.

wrongAnswers.name: CLL
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CLL causes HIGH white count with diffuse lymphadenopathy. This has LOW counts, no lymphadenopathy, and massive splenomegaly.

wrongAnswers.name: Myelofibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myelofibrosis also causes a dry tap with splenomegaly but shows teardrop cells, not hairy lymphocytes with TRAP positivity.

wrongAnswers.name: Splenic Marginal Zone Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SMZL causes splenomegaly with lymphocytosis but cells lack the hair-like projections and BRAF V600E mutation.

clues: A 4-year-old boy presents with bloody diarrhea for three days followed by decreased urine output and progressive pallor.
He ate an undercooked hamburger at a cookout one week ago, and the diarrhea progressed from watery to bloody.
The child is pale and lethargic with petechiae and blood pressure elevated for his age.
Hemoglobin is 7.8, platelets 34,000, creatinine 3.4, and the smear shows fragmented red cells with completely normal coagulation studies.
Stool culture grows E. coli O157:H7, a Shiga toxin-producing strain isolated on sorbitol-MacConkey agar.
explanation: The bacterial toxin directly damages kidney endothelium, triggering microthrombi that consume platelets and shear red cells passing through damaged vessels.
keyFact: No antibiotics — bacterial lysis releases more toxin. Normal coagulation studies distinguish this from DIC. Bloody diarrhea after undercooked meat in a child is the classic history.

wrongAnswers.name: TTP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP occurs in adults without preceding diarrhea, with neurologic symptoms dominating.

wrongAnswers.name: DIC
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DIC would show prolonged PT/aPTT and low fibrinogen — both normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia without hemolysis or renal failure.

clues: A 3-year-old boy presents with a swollen painful right knee after a minor fall, and his mother says his joints swell from trivial injuries.
His maternal uncle had a similar bleeding condition, and the boy bled excessively after circumcision.
The knee has a tense effusion without external bruising and there are no petechiae anywhere.
Platelet count and PT are normal but the aPTT is prolonged at 68 seconds and corrects when mixed 1:1 with normal plasma.
A single intrinsic pathway factor is severely reduced at 2% while all other coagulation factors are normal.
explanation: The missing factor is in the intrinsic pathway. Bleeding occurs in deep spaces — joints, muscles, retroperitoneum — not on skin surfaces.
keyFact: Deep bleeding = factor deficiency. Mucocutaneous bleeding = platelet or adhesion problem. Mixing study correction confirms a missing factor, not an inhibitor.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemophilia B
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Clinically identical but a different intrinsic pathway factor is deficient. Only specific factor assays distinguish them.

wrongAnswers.name: Von Willebrand Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: vWD causes mucocutaneous bleeding with abnormal ristocetin testing, not deep joint bleeding.

wrongAnswers.name: Child Abuse
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Concerning for abuse, but the prolonged aPTT with a specific factor deficiency and X-linked family history confirms a coagulation disorder.

clues: A 5-year-old boy presents with a large expanding thigh hematoma after a playground fall that is disproportionate to the injury.
He bled for a prolonged time after circumcision, and his maternal grandfather had a bleeding disorder.
There is a firm expanding hematoma in the right thigh without petechiae or joint swelling.
PT is normal, aPTT is prolonged at 62 seconds and corrects on mixing study, and the most commonly deficient intrinsic factor is completely normal.
A different intrinsic pathway factor — one that is vitamin K-dependent — is severely reduced at 3%.
explanation: This factor is also in the intrinsic pathway and produces a clinical picture identical to the more common form. Only specific factor assays distinguish them.
keyFact: This factor is vitamin K-dependent so warfarin affects it. The more common deficiency involves a factor that is NOT vitamin K-dependent.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemophilia A
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Identical presentation but the commonly deficient factor is normal here. A different intrinsic factor is reduced.

wrongAnswers.name: Vitamin K Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs BOTH PT and aPTT. PT is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Von Willebrand Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: vWD causes mucocutaneous bleeding, not deep tissue hematomas.

clues: A 65-year-old man being treated with anticoagulation for a leg clot develops a new clot in the opposite leg, and his platelet count has dropped.
His platelets were 220,000 when his blood thinner was started 7 days ago and are now 85,000 — a greater than 50% drop in one week.
There is a new painful swollen left leg with confirmed DVT on duplex ultrasound despite being on therapeutic anticoagulation.
His platelet nadir is 85,000 — a greater than 50% drop. Sepsis workup, medication review, and marrow evaluation are unrevealing.
Anti-PF4/heparin antibodies are strongly positive by ELISA, and a serotonin release assay is confirmatory.
explanation: Heparin binds to platelet factor 4, creating a neoantigen. IgG antibodies against this complex activate platelets, causing both platelet consumption (thrombocytopenia) and massive thrombin generation (thrombosis).
keyFact: The paradox: low platelets but the clinical problem is CLOTTING, not BLEEDING. Typical onset 5-10 days after starting heparin. Do NOT transfuse platelets — they fuel the prothrombotic process. Do NOT switch to warfarin until platelets recover (warfarin can cause limb gangrene in acute HIT).

wrongAnswers.name: DIC
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DIC drops platelets and causes clotting, but coagulation studies are prolonged (PT/aPTT elevated, fibrinogen low). HIT has normal coagulation studies.

wrongAnswers.name: Heparin Overdose
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Heparin overdose causes bleeding from excessive anticoagulation, not new thrombosis with falling platelets.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP drops platelets from autoimmune destruction but causes BLEEDING, not thrombosis, and is not temporally related to heparin exposure.

clues: A 12-year-old boy presents with intermittent jaundice and fatigue and had pigmented gallstones removed at age 10.
His father has a history of anemia and splenomegaly, and the jaundice worsens during viral illnesses.
Exam reveals mild scleral icterus, splenomegaly, and an indirect bilirubin elevated at 3.8 mg/dL.
Hemolysis markers are elevated with a NEGATIVE direct Coombs test, and the smear shows small round densely-staining red cells without central pallor.
The cells lyse prematurely when placed in progressively dilute salt solutions on osmotic fragility testing.
explanation: Defective membrane skeleton proteins cause red cells to lose surface area and round up into spheres that are trapped and destroyed in the spleen.
keyFact: Negative Coombs distinguishes this from autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which also produces spherocytes. Splenectomy cures the anemia but increases infection risk.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIHA produces spherocytes but the Coombs test is POSITIVE. Coombs is negative here.

wrongAnswers.name: G6PD Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: G6PD causes episodic hemolysis with bite cells triggered by drugs, not chronic hemolysis with spherocytes.

wrongAnswers.name: Gilbert Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gilbert causes intermittent jaundice without hemolysis — reticulocytes, LDH, and haptoglobin are normal.

clues: A 24-year-old man presents with painless lumps in his neck that have been growing for six weeks.
He reports drenching night sweats that soak through his sheets and an unusual symptom — his neck aches after drinking alcohol.
Exam reveals firm rubbery nontender matted lymph nodes in the left cervical and supraclavicular regions.
CT shows enlarged nodes extending in a connected chain from left cervical through mediastinal to left para-aortic regions.
Excisional biopsy shows scattered giant cells with mirror-image double nuclei and large red nucleoli that stain CD15+ and CD30+.
explanation: The malignant giant cells are only 1-2% of the tumor mass — the rest is the immune system's reaction. The disease spreads contiguously from one node group to the next adjacent group.
keyFact: Alcohol-induced node pain is rare but essentially diagnostic. Contiguous spread distinguishes this from other lymphomas which jump between non-adjacent groups.

wrongAnswers.name: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NHL spreads non-contiguously and typically expresses CD20 rather than CD15/CD30.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious Mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mono resolves in weeks. Six weeks of progressive matted nodes with B symptoms needs biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervical TB shows caseating granulomas on biopsy, not giant binucleated cells in an inflammatory background.

clues: An 8-year-old boy is referred by his eye doctor after a dislocated lens was found during a routine exam.
He struggles in school with poor academic performance and had an unexplained blood clot in his leg at age 6.
Exam reveals tall thin build, long limbs, pectus excavatum, fair skin, and a lens that has shifted downward and inward.
Serum methionine is elevated, and the urine turns positive on a cyanide-nitroprusside test detecting excess sulfur-containing amino acids.
Serum homocysteine levels are markedly elevated, and cystathionine beta-synthase activity is reduced.
explanation: Without cystathionine beta-synthase, homocysteine accumulates, damaging vascular endothelium (thrombosis), weakening lens zonules (subluxation), and impairing brain development.
keyFact: Lens DOWN and IN = homocystinuria. Lens UP and OUT = Marfan. Both are tall and thin, but Marfan has normal intelligence, no thrombosis, and opposite lens direction.

wrongAnswers.name: Marfan Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Marfan causes tall thin habitus with lens subluxation but the lens goes UP and OUT, intelligence is normal, and there is no thrombotic tendency.

wrongAnswers.name: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EDS causes connective tissue laxity but no lens dislocation, no elevated homocysteine, and no thrombotic risk.

wrongAnswers.name: Cystinuria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cystinuria causes cystine kidney stones from a renal transport defect — completely different despite the similar-sounding name.

clues: A 4-year-old boy presents with progressive hearing loss and behavioral aggression noticed by his teachers.
His maternal uncle died young of a similar condition, and no female family members have been affected.
Exam reveals coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, joint contractures, and pebbly ivory papules on his upper back — but his corneas are CLEAR.
Urine shows elevated dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, and X-rays show dysostosis multiplex.
The deficient enzyme is iduronate-2-sulfatase, and the inheritance pattern is X-linked recessive.
explanation: Without iduronate sulfatase, the same glycosaminoglycans accumulate as in the autosomal recessive form, but the corneas are spared.
keyFact: X-linked = only boys affected. Clear corneas distinguish it from the autosomal recessive form. The pebbly skin papules on the back are distinctive. Severity ranges from mild to severe.

wrongAnswers.name: Hurler Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hurler has CLOUDY corneas, is autosomal recessive (affects both sexes), and involves a different enzyme.

wrongAnswers.name: Sanfilippo Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sanfilippo (MPS III) causes severe behavioral and cognitive decline with less somatic involvement — features are less coarse.

wrongAnswers.name: Morquio Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Morquio (MPS IV) causes severe skeletal abnormalities with normal intelligence and no hepatosplenomegaly.

clues: An 18-month-old presents with coarse facial features that have become more pronounced over recent months.
He was normal at birth but has been losing developmental milestones and had umbilical and inguinal hernias repaired.
Exam reveals a large tongue, cloudy corneas, hepatosplenomegaly, and claw-hand deformities from joint stiffness.
Urine shows elevated dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, and X-rays reveal dysostosis multiplex.
The deficient enzyme is alpha-L-iduronidase, and both males and females are affected in the family.
explanation: Without alpha-L-iduronidase, glycosaminoglycans accumulate in lysosomes throughout every organ, causing progressive organ damage and developmental regression.
keyFact: Hurler vs Hunter: both have coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, and GAG accumulation. Hurler = autosomal recessive + corneal CLOUDING. Hunter = X-linked + clear corneas. Memory aid: Hunters need to see to hunt.

wrongAnswers.name: Hunter Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hunter has similar features but is X-linked (only boys), has CLEAR corneas (not cloudy), and is caused by a different enzyme (iduronate sulfatase).

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Congenital hypothyroidism causes coarse features and developmental delay but without corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, or dysostosis multiplex.

wrongAnswers.name: Down Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Down syndrome has dysmorphic features present from birth that don't worsen progressively, and there is no corneal clouding, dysostosis, or GAG elevation.

clues: A 25-year-old woman presents with easy bruising and small nonblanchable red dots on her legs over the past week.
She had a viral upper respiratory infection two weeks ago and is otherwise healthy with no medications.
Exam shows petechiae on both lower extremities and ecchymoses on her arms without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.
Platelets are 12,000 but hemoglobin, white blood cell count, and coagulation studies are all completely normal.
The peripheral smear confirms decreased but abnormally LARGE platelets with no fragmented red cells or abnormal white cells.
explanation: Autoantibodies coat platelets and mark them for splenic destruction. The marrow compensates by releasing young, large platelets.
keyFact: Isolated thrombocytopenia with large platelets and normal everything else means peripheral destruction, not production failure.

wrongAnswers.name: TTP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP also drops platelets but causes hemolytic anemia with fragmented red cells and neurologic changes. Hemoglobin is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: DIC
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DIC drops platelets with prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, and fragmented red cells. Coagulation is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Leukemia causes thrombocytopenia with abnormal white cells and usually anemia. All other lines are normal here.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with a craving for chewing ice that she cannot explain.
Her menstrual periods are heavy, lasting 8 days with frequent pad changes.
Exam reveals pallor, cracked corners of her mouth, and fingernails that are thin and curve upward like spoons.
Hemoglobin is 8.2 with MCV of 68, iron of 22, TIBC of 480, and ferritin of 6.
The peripheral smear shows small pale red cells with occasional pencil-shaped forms.
explanation: Heavy menstrual blood loss has slowly drained her iron stores. Without iron, hemoglobin synthesis is impaired and the marrow produces smaller, paler red cells.
keyFact: Low iron, high TIBC, low ferritin is the fingerprint. Ferritin is the most sensitive single test but is an acute phase reactant that can be falsely normal during concurrent inflammation. Ice craving (pagophagia) is a specific form of pica.

wrongAnswers.name: Thalassemia Trait
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thalassemia trait causes microcytic anemia but with normal iron studies and elevated HbA2 on electrophoresis.

wrongAnswers.name: Anemia of Chronic Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ACD has low iron but ALSO low TIBC and elevated ferritin — iron is trapped, not depleted.

wrongAnswers.name: Lead Poisoning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lead causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling but normal iron studies.

clues: A 3-year-old boy presents with irritability, decreased appetite, and intermittent abdominal pain over several weeks.
He lives in a house built in the 1920s being renovated, and his parents noticed him eating paint chips from the windowsill.
Exam reveals pallor, a faint blue-gray line along his gum margins, and mild abdominal distension.
Hemoglobin is 9.8 with microcytic red cells showing basophilic stippling on smear, but iron studies are completely NORMAL.
Venous blood lead level returns at 52 mcg/dL, and X-ray of the knees shows dense metaphyseal bands.
explanation: Lead inhibits multiple enzymes in heme synthesis, causing microcytic anemia that mimics iron deficiency but with normal iron stores.
keyFact: Basophilic stippling and dense metaphyseal bands on X-ray are the classic findings. Normal iron studies distinguish this from iron deficiency — the iron is there but cannot be incorporated into heme.

wrongAnswers.name: Iron Deficiency Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IDA causes microcytic anemia but with LOW iron, HIGH TIBC, and LOW ferritin. Iron studies are normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Thalassemia Trait
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thalassemia trait causes microcytic anemia with normal iron but no basophilic stippling, gum line, or metaphyseal bands.

wrongAnswers.name: Sideroblastic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lead poisoning IS a form of sideroblastic anemia, but the clinical context with paint chip ingestion, gum line, and elevated blood lead makes the specific diagnosis.

clues: A 2-year-old boy presents with orange-red sandy crystals noticed in his diapers over the past several months.
He has developmental delay and involuntary writhing movements, and only males in the family have been affected.
Exam reveals lip and finger mutilation from self-biting, dystonia, choreoathetosis, and hyperreflexia.
Uric acid is markedly elevated at 14 mg/dL, and the child has already passed a uric acid kidney stone.
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) enzyme activity is absent on erythrocyte assay.
explanation: Complete deficiency of the purine salvage enzyme causes massive uric acid production and devastating neurologic damage including the compulsive self-mutilation that is essentially pathognomonic.
keyFact: Self-mutilation + hyperuricemia + dystonia + X-linked = this diagnosis. Partial enzyme deficiency causes gout without neurologic symptoms. Allopurinol lowers uric acid but does not improve the neurologic features.

wrongAnswers.name: Gout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gout causes hyperuricemia and joint inflammation in adults without neurologic symptoms or self-mutilation. This is a child with devastating neurologic disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD can involve self-injurious behavior but without hyperuricemia, orange crystals, or dystonia.

wrongAnswers.name: Cerebral Palsy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CP causes motor impairment but is static, doesn't cause hyperuricemia, and the self-mutilation pattern is different.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with a palpable breast mass found on self-exam; biopsy confirms invasive carcinoma.
Her father died of a brain tumor at age 40 and her younger brother was diagnosed with an osteosarcoma at age 14.
She has no BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations on targeted genetic testing for hereditary breast cancer.
Expanded genetic panel reveals a germline mutation in TP53, the gene encoding the p53 tumor suppressor protein.
Multiple family members across three generations have developed different cancer types before age 45.
explanation: Loss of the master tumor suppressor removes the cell's most critical checkpoint for DNA damage, allowing mutations to accumulate unchecked.
keyFact: The classic SBLA cancers: Sarcomas, Breast, Leukemia, Adrenal cortical carcinoma. Multiple different cancers at young ages across generations is the pattern. The gene (TP53) is the most commonly mutated gene in all human cancers.

wrongAnswers.name: BRCA1/2 Mutation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BRCA causes hereditary breast and ovarian cancer but not the diverse spectrum of sarcomas, brain tumors, leukemias, and adrenal cancers at young ages across the family.

wrongAnswers.name: Lynch Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lynch causes colon and endometrial cancer from mismatch repair gene mutations, not the broad multi-organ cancer susceptibility involving sarcomas and brain tumors.

wrongAnswers.name: Cowden Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cowden increases breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancer risk from PTEN mutations, but without the sarcomas, brain tumors, and childhood cancers.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with worsening abdominal discomfort and diarrhea with 12 pounds of weight loss.
Colonoscopy performed for the diarrhea shows multiple small polyp-like nodules throughout the colon.
Exam reveals generalized lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.
Biopsy shows monotonous small-to-medium B lymphocytes that are CD5+, CD20+, and CD23 NEGATIVE with overexpression of cyclin D1.
Cytogenetics show t(11;14) placing cyclin D1 under the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter.
explanation: The translocation overexpresses cyclin D1, pushing cells from G1 into S phase. Despite small cell morphology, this behaves aggressively.
keyFact: CD5+/CD20+ but CD23 NEGATIVE distinguishes this from CLL (which is CD23+). GI involvement with lymphomatous polyposis is characteristic. Median survival 3-5 years.

wrongAnswers.name: CLL/SLL
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CLL is also CD5+/CD20+ but is CD23 POSITIVE and is indolent. This is CD23 negative with aggressive behavior.

wrongAnswers.name: Follicular Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Follicular is CD10+/BCL-2+ with t(14;18). This is CD5+/cyclin D1+ with t(11;14).

wrongAnswers.name: MALT Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MALT lymphoma of the GI tract is very indolent, lacks CD5 expression, and is associated with H. pylori.

clues: A 5-day-old neonate presents with poor feeding and progressive lethargy since day 3 of life.
The nursing staff notices a distinctive sweet caramel-like smell during diaper changes and bathing.
Exam reveals a hypotonic infant with poor suck reflex, decreased spontaneous movement, and sweet-smelling urine.
Blood work shows severe metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap, and the newborn screen is flagged.
Serum amino acid analysis reveals markedly elevated leucine, isoleucine, and valine with elevated alloisoleucine.
explanation: Without the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, the three branched-chain amino acids and their toxic ketoacid derivatives accumulate.
keyFact: The sweet maple syrup odor comes from the branched-chain ketoacids in urine, sweat, and earwax. Presents in the first week of life with encephalopathy. Dietary restriction of leucine, isoleucine, and valine is lifelong.

wrongAnswers.name: Phenylketonuria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PKU causes a musty (not sweet) odor from phenylalanine accumulation and presents later with developmental delay, not neonatal crisis.

wrongAnswers.name: Organic Acidemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Propionic and methylmalonic acidemia cause similar neonatal crisis with metabolic acidosis but without the sweet maple syrup odor or branched-chain amino acid elevation.

wrongAnswers.name: Galactosemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Galactosemia presents in the first week after milk feeding with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and cataracts — not sweet-smelling urine with branched-chain amino acid elevation.

clues: A 20-year-old man presents with severe muscle cramps during a basketball game that forced him to stop playing.
He reports that if he rests briefly and pushes through, his exercise tolerance paradoxically improves — a 'second wind.'
Exam between episodes is completely normal with no muscle weakness or wasting.
His urine after exercise is dark brown and tests positive for blood on dipstick but shows NO red blood cells on microscopy.
An ischemic forearm exercise test shows NO rise in lactate despite a normal rise in ammonia.
explanation: Without myophosphorylase, skeletal muscle cannot access its glycogen stores during exercise. The second wind occurs when the muscle switches to using fatty acids and blood glucose from the liver as fuel.
keyFact: The blood-positive urine without red cells = myoglobinuria from muscle breakdown. The flat lactate curve on ischemic forearm test is diagnostic. The second wind phenomenon occurs from the metabolic switch to alternative fuels.

wrongAnswers.name: Rhabdomyolysis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rhabdomyolysis is a complication that occurs in McArdle disease, not a separate diagnosis. The flat lactate curve and second wind identify the underlying metabolic cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polymyositis causes chronic proximal weakness with elevated CK, but weakness is present at rest (not just with exercise) and there is no second wind phenomenon.

wrongAnswers.name: Fibromyalgia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fibromyalgia causes exercise intolerance and pain but CK is normal, there is no myoglobinuria, and the ischemic forearm test is normal.

clues: A 25-year-old man presents appearing cyanotic with dusky lips and fingertips, but he reports only mild shortness of breath.
He had a topical anesthetic (benzocaine) sprayed in his throat for a dental procedure two hours ago.
The pulse oximeter reads 85% and does not improve with supplemental oxygen at any flow rate.
Arterial blood gas on 100% oxygen shows a PaO2 of 350 mmHg, and the arterial blood is an unusual dark brownish color that does not redden in air.
Co-oximetry on the arterial sample reveals 28% methemoglobin, confirming oxidation of hemoglobin iron.
explanation: The oxidizing drug converted the iron in hemoglobin from the functional ferrous state to the non-functional ferric state, which cannot bind oxygen.
keyFact: The SpO2 gap is the clue — pulse oximetry reads ~85% regardless of true PaO2 because the abnormal hemoglobin absorbs light differently. Chocolate brown blood that doesn't redden with air exposure is diagnostic.

wrongAnswers.name: Cyanotic Heart Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cyanotic lesions cause low SpO2 and low PaO2. This patient's PaO2 is 350 — plenty of oxygen, it just can't be carried properly.

wrongAnswers.name: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CO poisoning causes a falsely HIGH SpO2 with cherry RED blood. This has falsely LOW SpO2 with chocolate BROWN blood — opposite findings.

wrongAnswers.name: ARDS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lung disease causes hypoxia responsive to supplemental oxygen with low PaO2. This patient's PaO2 is 350 — the lungs are fine.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with progressive back pain for three months that does not improve with rest.
He reports increased thirst and urination, recurrent sinus infections, and fatigue without a history of trauma.
Exam reveals pallor and tenderness over multiple vertebral spinous processes without neurologic deficits.
Hemoglobin is 9.2, creatinine 2.4, calcium 12.8, and protein electrophoresis shows a single tall sharp monoclonal peak.
Skull X-rays reveal dozens of perfectly round punched-out lytic lesions, and bone marrow biopsy shows 45% clonal plasma cells.
explanation: A single plasma cell cloned into millions, all producing the same useless antibody that accumulates in blood, clogs kidneys, and activates bone destruction.
keyFact: The protein gap (total protein minus albumin) is a bedside clue. Lytic lesions mean bone scans miss them — use skeletal survey or CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Metastatic Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bone metastases cause pain but without the monoclonal protein peak or 45% marrow plasma cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PHPT causes high calcium but no protein peak, marrow plasma cells, or punched-out lesions.

wrongAnswers.name: MGUS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MGUS has a small protein peak, <10% marrow plasma cells, and no organ damage.

clues: A 72-year-old man who received chemotherapy for lymphoma five years ago presents with progressive fatigue.
His blood counts have been declining despite normal nutrition and no bleeding source.
Exam reveals pallor, scattered petechiae, and no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
The smear reveals hypolobated neutrophils and hypogranular platelets with macrocytic red cells.
Bone marrow biopsy is HYPERCELLULAR despite the peripheral cytopenias, with 8% blasts and ringed sideroblasts on iron stain.
explanation: The marrow is producing cells but they are defective and die before reaching the blood — ineffective hematopoiesis creates the paradox of a packed marrow with empty blood.
keyFact: Hypercellular marrow with peripheral cytopenias is the hallmark paradox. Prior chemotherapy and benzene are risk factors. Transforms to AML in approximately 30%.

wrongAnswers.name: Aplastic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia with a HYPOcellular marrow. This marrow is HYPERcellular — that's the key distinction.

wrongAnswers.name: B12 Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: B12 causes macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, not hypolobated neutrophils with ringed sideroblasts.

wrongAnswers.name: AML
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AML requires ≥20% blasts. This patient has 8% — consistent with MDS, though it may transform over time.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with a dragging sensation in his left abdomen and 15 pounds of weight loss.
He reports night sweats and feels increasingly fatigued over several months.
Exam reveals massive splenomegaly extending to the pelvic brim.
The peripheral smear shows teardrop-shaped red cells with nucleated red blood cells and immature myeloid precursors in the circulation.
Bone marrow aspiration is a dry tap, and the biopsy shows dense reticulin and collagen fibrosis replacing normal tissue.
explanation: Progressive fibrosis replaces the bone marrow, forcing blood production to relocate to the spleen and liver (extramedullary hematopoiesis), which causes the massive splenomegaly.
keyFact: The dry tap (can't aspirate because of fibrosis) plus the teardrop cells and leukoerythroblastic smear (immature red AND white cells in peripheral blood) are the diagnostic triad. JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations are found in >80%.

wrongAnswers.name: CML
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CML causes massive splenomegaly with high white count showing the full maturation spectrum, but marrow is hypercellular (not fibrotic) and the Philadelphia chromosome is present.

wrongAnswers.name: Hairy Cell Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hairy cell also causes a dry tap with splenomegaly, but shows hairy lymphocytes with TRAP positivity, not teardrop cells with leukoerythroblastic picture.

wrongAnswers.name: Metastatic Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastatic cancer to marrow can cause a leukoerythroblastic picture, but there would be a known primary tumor and no JAK2/CALR mutation.

clues: A 4-month-old infant presents with progressive developmental regression first noticed by the parents at home.
The infant was developing normally until about 3 months and is now losing skills and not fixing on faces.
Exam reveals hepatosplenomegaly, hypotonia, and poor visual tracking with roving eye movements.
Fundoscopic exam shows a bright red circular area in the center of the macula surrounded by a pale ring from lipid-laden cells.
Bone marrow biopsy reveals large macrophages with foamy vacuolated cytoplasm, and sphingomyelinase activity is markedly reduced.
explanation: Without sphingomyelinase, sphingomyelin accumulates in macrophages in the liver, spleen, marrow, and brain, causing both organomegaly and neurodegeneration.
keyFact: Cherry red macula WITH hepatosplenomegaly = Niemann-Pick. Cherry red macula WITHOUT hepatosplenomegaly = Tay-Sachs. The foamy macrophages are the pathologic hallmark.

wrongAnswers.name: Tay-Sachs Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tay-Sachs also shows a cherry red macula and neurodegeneration but WITHOUT hepatosplenomegaly — the ganglioside accumulates only in neurons, not systemically.

wrongAnswers.name: Gaucher Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gaucher causes hepatosplenomegaly with tissue-paper macrophages (not foamy), and type 1 does not cause neurodegeneration or cherry red macula.

wrongAnswers.name: Farber Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Farber disease is also a lipid storage disease but presents with painful joint swelling, subcutaneous nodules, and hoarseness — not cherry red macula with foamy macrophages.

clues: A 3-day-old male newborn becomes progressively lethargic after initiation of protein-containing feeds.
His mother mentions a brother who died as a newborn, and no female family members have been severely affected.
The infant is obtunded with irregular breathing and no focal neurologic findings.
Ammonia is critically elevated at 800 mcmol/L, but liver function tests are normal and there is no metabolic acidosis.
Urine organic acid analysis reveals markedly elevated orotic acid alongside the hyperammonemia.
explanation: The most common urea cycle defect prevents the first mitochondrial step of converting ammonia to urea. Ammonia accumulates to neurotoxic levels after protein feeding introduces amino acids.
keyFact: Hyperammonemia + elevated orotic acid + X-linked inheritance is the triad. The elevated orotic acid distinguishes this from other urea cycle defects — the carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis. X-linked = boys severely affected, carrier girls may have milder protein intolerance.

wrongAnswers.name: Maple Syrup Urine Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MSUD causes neonatal crisis with metabolic ACIDOSIS and elevated branched-chain amino acids. This has no acidosis and the crisis is from hyperammonemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Galactosemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Galactosemia causes neonatal illness after milk feeding but with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and cataracts — not isolated hyperammonemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Organic Acidemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Organic acidemias cause neonatal crisis with hyperammonemia AND metabolic acidosis. This has hyperammonemia WITHOUT acidosis — that's a urea cycle defect.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with dark cola-colored urine that is worst in the morning and clears throughout the day.
He had a blood clot in his liver veins six months ago with no family history of clotting disorders and mildly low blood counts.
Exam reveals pallor, mild jaundice, and fatigue without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.
Hemolysis markers are elevated with a negative Coombs test, and LDH is markedly elevated at 1,200 U/L.
Flow cytometry shows red cells, white cells, and monocytes all missing the GPI-anchored proteins CD55 and CD59.
explanation: A stem cell mutation prevents construction of GPI anchors that hold complement-regulatory proteins on cell surfaces, leaving cells vulnerable to complement-mediated destruction.
keyFact: The triad: Coombs-negative hemolysis, pancytopenia, and thrombosis in unusual veins. Dark morning urine is free hemoglobin from overnight destruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIHA has a POSITIVE Coombs test. Coombs is negative here with missing surface proteins on flow cytometry.

wrongAnswers.name: Aplastic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aplastic anemia causes low counts WITHOUT hemolysis markers. This patient has active red cell destruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Factor V Leiden
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Factor V Leiden causes thrombosis but no hemolysis, pancytopenia, or dark urine.

clues: A newborn presents with a bilateral cleft lip and palate and extra fingers on both hands noticed at delivery.
Prenatal ultrasound had shown a failure of the forebrain to divide into two hemispheres.
Exam reveals bilateral cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, microcephaly, and small eyes with a patch of missing scalp skin on the posterior head.
Echocardiography shows a large ventricular septal defect, and head ultrasound confirms a single midline cerebral ventricle.
Karyotype shows 47 chromosomes with three copies of chromosome 13 on G-banding analysis.
explanation: Three copies of this autosome disrupt midline development. The brain may fail to divide into hemispheres, the face develops clefts, and multiple organs are malformed.
keyFact: Midline defects are the theme. The missing scalp patch (cutis aplasia) and polydactyly distinguish this from the trisomy with overlapping fingers. Survival is very poor.

wrongAnswers.name: Edwards Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trisomy 18 has clenched fists with overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet — NOT the midline clefting, extra digits, and absent forebrain division.

wrongAnswers.name: Holoprosencephaly (Isolated)
