wrongAnswers.whyNot: Isolated holoprosencephaly can occur but the combination with polydactyly, cleft lip, and cutis aplasia points to a full chromosomal syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Down Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trisomy 21 causes hypotonia, upslanting eyes, and cardiac cushion defects — not midline clefting or polydactyly.

clues: A 6-month-old infant presents with a musty body odor noticed by the parents during diaper changes.
The newborn screening was reportedly normal but the family missed the follow-up appointment.
The infant has fair skin and light hair compared to both darker-complexioned parents, and has patchy eczema.
Serum phenylalanine is markedly elevated at 25 mg/dL, and MRI of the brain shows delayed myelination.
Serum tyrosine level is low at 0.4 mg/dL, and phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme activity is deficient on liver assay.
explanation: Without the converting enzyme, phenylalanine accumulates to neurotoxic levels while its product tyrosine (needed for melanin and neurotransmitter synthesis) is deficient.
keyFact: Light features (fair skin, blonde hair) occur because tyrosine — the melanin precursor — cannot be produced. The musty/mousy odor is from phenylacetic acid. Maternal PKU (elevated phenylalanine during pregnancy) causes congenital heart defects and microcephaly in the unaffected fetus.

wrongAnswers.name: Maple Syrup Urine Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MSUD causes a different sweet smell (maple syrup, not musty) from accumulation of branched-chain amino acids, not phenylalanine.

wrongAnswers.name: Albinism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Albinism causes light features from melanin deficiency but without elevated phenylalanine, intellectual disability, or musty odor.

wrongAnswers.name: Homocystinuria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Homocystinuria causes light features but with lens dislocation, marfanoid habitus, and thrombosis — not musty odor or elevated phenylalanine.

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with intense itching that occurs specifically after hot showers.
He has burning pain in his hands and feet, lives at sea level with no lung disease, and has had two episodes of gout.
Exam reveals a deeply red flushed face and splenomegaly.
Hemoglobin is 21.2 with hematocrit of 63%, and the erythropoietin level is SUPPRESSED.
JAK2 V617F mutation is positive, and bone marrow is hypercellular with trilineage hyperplasia.
explanation: The kinase mutation makes stem cells hypersensitive to growth signals, causing autonomous overproduction primarily of red cells with suppressed EPO.
keyFact: Suppressed EPO separates primary (autonomous) from secondary (hypoxia-driven, EPO high). The post-shower itching from mast cell degranulation is nearly pathognomonic.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Polycythemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary causes have HIGH EPO driving appropriate red cell production. EPO is suppressed here.

wrongAnswers.name: Dehydration
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dehydration raises hematocrit but white cells, platelets, and EPO are normal with no splenomegaly.

wrongAnswers.name: CML
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CML primarily elevates white cells with the Philadelphia chromosome. The dominant finding here is red cell overproduction.

clues: A 4-month-old infant presents with progressive weakness described by the parents as a 'floppy baby.'
The infant cannot hold up her head, and her tongue appears enlarged and protrudes from the mouth.
Chest X-ray reveals a massively enlarged heart filling most of the chest cavity.
Echocardiogram shows massive biventricular hypertrophy with outflow obstruction, and muscle biopsy shows vacuoles filled with glycogen.
Acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase) enzyme activity is markedly reduced, and the enzyme is located within lysosomes.
explanation: Glycogen that enters lysosomes cannot be broken down and accumulates, destroying cardiac and skeletal muscle cells. This is the only glycogen storage disease caused by a lysosomal rather than cytoplasmic enzyme defect.
keyFact: Massive cardiomegaly + hypotonia + macroglossia in an infant = Pompe until proven otherwise. The lysosomal nature is the board pearl — enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant acid maltase is available.

wrongAnswers.name: Von Gierke Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Von Gierke causes massive hepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycemia. Pompe causes massive cardiomegaly with hypotonia — different organ, different enzyme location.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM causes cardiac hypertrophy but presents in adolescents/young adults with exertional symptoms, not floppy infants with macroglossia and skeletal myopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Spinal Muscular Atrophy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SMA causes severe hypotonia in infants but with a normal heart — no cardiomegaly, no macroglossia, no glycogen-filled vacuoles.

clues: A newborn presents with severe hypotonia and a weak cry requiring nasogastric tube feeds.
He has a narrow forehead, almond-shaped eyes, thin upper lip, and small hands and feet.
As a toddler, he develops an insatiable appetite leading to progressive severe obesity.
He has short stature, hypogonadism with undescended testes, and mild intellectual disability.
Genetic testing shows a deletion on the PATERNAL copy of chromosome 15q11-13 confirmed by methylation analysis.
explanation: The paternal copy of genes in this region are the only active copies due to genomic imprinting. When they are deleted, there is no functional gene expression because the maternal copies are silenced.
keyFact: Paternal deletion of 15q = this syndrome (hypotonia → obesity, hypogonadism). Maternal deletion of 15q = a different syndrome (happy affect, seizures, no speech). Same region, different parent.

wrongAnswers.name: Angelman Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Angelman is deletion of the MATERNAL 15q — causing happy affect, seizures, ataxia, and absent speech. Very different phenotype despite the same chromosomal region.

wrongAnswers.name: Down Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Down syndrome causes hypotonia and intellectual disability but with characteristic facies, cardiac defects, and trisomy 21 — not the obesity and insatiable appetite pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes obesity and developmental delay but without the specific facial features, small hands/feet, or the chromosomal deletion.

clues: A 35-year-old woman with a chronic hemolytic anemia presents with sudden severe worsening of her baseline anemia.
She had a mild viral illness with a 'slapped cheek' facial rash one week ago, and her hemoglobin dropped from 8.0 to 3.5.
Exam reveals severe pallor, tachycardia at 130 bpm, and a systolic flow murmur without splenomegaly.
White blood cells and platelets are normal, but the reticulocyte count is 0% and bone marrow shows absent red cell precursors with giant pronormoblasts.
Serology is positive for parvovirus B19 IgM antibodies, and PCR detects viral DNA in the bone marrow aspirate.
explanation: The virus selectively destroys red cell precursors via the P antigen on their surface. In patients with normal red cell lifespan this causes mild illness, but in those with chronic hemolysis who depend on high red cell production, the sudden production halt is catastrophic.
keyFact: In healthy people, parvovirus B19 causes fifth disease (slapped cheek rash). In patients with shortened red cell lifespan (sickle cell, spherocytosis), the same virus causes aplastic crisis with dangerously severe anemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Sickle Cell Crisis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A vaso-occlusive crisis causes pain with ongoing hemolysis and HIGH reticulocytes. This patient has ZERO reticulocytes — the marrow has stopped making red cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Splenic Sequestration
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sequestration causes rapid hemoglobin drop with a large spleen trapping red cells. The spleen is not enlarged here and reticulocytes are absent.

wrongAnswers.name: Aplastic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aplastic anemia drops ALL three cell lines. This patient has isolated red cell aplasia with normal white cells and platelets.

clues: A newborn develops severe jaundice requiring phototherapy within 48 hours of life without blood group incompatibility.
A sibling has chronic hemolytic anemia inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
The infant has persistent indirect hyperbilirubinemia with elevated reticulocytes and a negative Coombs test.
The smear shows spiculated red cells with multiple small surface projections, and both G6PD activity and osmotic fragility are normal.
Red cell pyruvate kinase enzyme activity is reduced, measured on a washed erythrocyte sample to avoid leukocyte contamination.
explanation: Without adequate ATP from glycolysis, membrane ion pumps fail and red cells become rigid and spiculated.
keyFact: Spiculated cells with normal osmotic fragility distinguish this from spherocytosis. Normal G6PD rules out the more common enzyme deficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: G6PD Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: G6PD causes episodic hemolysis with bite cells. This is chronic hemolysis with echinocytes and normal G6PD.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary Spherocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Spherocytosis shows spherocytes with abnormal osmotic fragility, not echinocytes with normal fragility.

wrongAnswers.name: ABO Hemolytic Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ABO incompatibility causes neonatal jaundice with a positive Coombs test. Coombs is negative here.

clues: An 8-year-old boy presents with sudden severe pain in his arms and legs without any preceding trauma.
He has had identical painful episodes every few months since age 2 and was hospitalized twice last year.
On exam, his spleen is not palpable despite his young age, and there is dactylitis of the right hand.
Peripheral smear shows target cells and small nuclear remnants inside red cells that a functioning spleen would normally remove.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis reveals a single predominant abnormal band with absent normal adult hemoglobin.
explanation: A point mutation causes hemoglobin to polymerize under low oxygen, creating rigid crescent-shaped cells that occlude small vessels. The spleen auto-infarcts by age 5.
keyFact: The nuclear remnants (Howell-Jolly bodies) prove functional asplenia. Any fever is a medical emergency requiring blood cultures and empiric antibiotics.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Leukemia causes bone pain in children but shows blast cells on smear, not target cells with nuclear remnants and an abnormal hemoglobin band.

wrongAnswers.name: Beta-Thalassemia Major
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thalassemia shows fetal hemoglobin as the dominant band (90%+), not a single abnormal variant alongside minor fetal hemoglobin.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteomyelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteomyelitis is focal to one bone with point tenderness, not diffuse multifocal pain without focal findings.

clues: A 70-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and pallor over several months.
He has a history of chronic alcohol use and takes isoniazid for latent tuberculosis.
Exam reveals pallor and mild hepatomegaly without splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.
Hemoglobin is 8.8 with microcytic red cells, elevated serum iron, elevated ferritin, and transferrin saturation of 85%.
Bone marrow iron stain reveals erythroid precursors with a ring of blue iron granules encircling more than one-third of the nucleus.
explanation: Defective heme synthesis within the mitochondria traps iron in a perinuclear ring. The marrow is loaded with iron it cannot use, producing iron-overloaded but hemoglobin-poor red cells.
keyFact: Ringed sideroblasts on marrow iron stain are diagnostic. Causes: alcohol, isoniazid (depletes B6, a cofactor for ALA synthase), lead, and inherited forms. Unlike IDA, iron indices are HIGH — the iron is there but the heme synthesis machinery is broken.

wrongAnswers.name: Iron Deficiency Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IDA has LOW iron, LOW ferritin, and HIGH TIBC — the opposite. Here iron is elevated because the problem is utilization, not supply.

wrongAnswers.name: Thalassemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thalassemia causes microcytic anemia with normal or elevated iron but the bone marrow does not show ringed sideroblasts.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemochromatosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemochromatosis causes iron overload with organ damage but the marrow does not show ringed sideroblasts and the anemia pattern is different.

clues: A 6-month-old infant presents with progressive loss of developmental milestones and an exaggerated startle response to sounds.
The infant was developing normally until about 4 months of age and is now losing the ability to sit and track objects.
Exam reveals a hypotonic infant with poor head control and no hepatosplenomegaly.
Fundoscopic exam reveals a bright red circular area in the center of the macula surrounded by a pale white ring of swollen ganglion cells.
Hexosaminidase A enzyme activity is absent on serum assay, with normal hexosaminidase B levels.
explanation: Without hexosaminidase A, GM2 ganglioside accumulates in neurons, causing progressive neurodegeneration. The ganglion cells around the fovea become swollen and opaque, leaving the fovea's normal red color visible by contrast.
keyFact: Cherry red macula + no hepatosplenomegaly = Tay-Sachs. Cherry red macula WITH hepatosplenomegaly = Niemann-Pick. The lack of organomegaly occurs because the accumulated material is limited to neurons.

wrongAnswers.name: Niemann-Pick Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Niemann-Pick also shows a cherry red macula but WITH hepatosplenomegaly because sphingomyelin accumulates in macrophages throughout the body, not just neurons.

wrongAnswers.name: Gaucher Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gaucher causes hepatosplenomegaly without neurologic involvement in the common type 1 form, and does not produce a cherry red macula.

wrongAnswers.name: Krabbe Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Krabbe causes progressive neurodegeneration in infancy from galactocerebroside accumulation, but does not produce the cherry red macula.

clues: A 35-year-old previously healthy woman presents with confusion developing over two days.
She has no preceding diarrheal illness, no new medications, and no prior bleeding history.
On exam she is disoriented to time and place with scattered petechiae across her trunk.
Platelets are 18,000 with fragmented red cells on smear, but PT and aPTT are completely NORMAL.
The metalloprotease that prevents oversized platelet-adhesion protein multimers from accumulating has less than 5% activity.
explanation: An antibody blocks the enzyme that trims ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers, which snag platelets and shred red cells in the microvasculature.
keyFact: Normal coagulation studies separate this from DIC. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated — it provides fuel for microthrombi. Emergency treatment is plasma exchange.

wrongAnswers.name: DIC
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DIC also fragments red cells and drops platelets but PT/aPTT are PROLONGED and fibrinogen is LOW. Coagulation is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia without hemolysis, fragmented cells, or neurologic symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: HUS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HUS follows bloody diarrhea in children with renal failure dominating. No diarrhea and neurologic symptoms dominate here.

clues: A 20-year-old man with a newly diagnosed blood cancer develops muscle cramps, nausea, and an irregular heartbeat 48 hours after starting chemotherapy.
He has a large tumor burden with bulky lymphadenopathy and markedly elevated LDH at diagnosis.
He becomes oliguric with less than 200 mL of urine output in 12 hours and develops tetanic muscle spasms.
Labs show potassium 7.2, phosphorus 8.5, calcium 6.1, uric acid 15, and creatinine rising rapidly from baseline.
All four electrolyte derangements appeared simultaneously within 48 hours of chemotherapy initiation against a rapidly proliferating tumor.
explanation: Rapid tumor cell death (from chemotherapy or spontaneously in fast-growing tumors) dumps intracellular contents into the blood, overwhelming renal excretory capacity and causing dangerous electrolyte derangements.
keyFact: The lethal electrolyte combination: hyperkalemia (cardiac arrhythmia), hyperphosphatemia (binds calcium → hypocalcemia → seizures, tetany), and hyperuricemia (uric acid nephropathy → renal failure). Prevention with allopurinol or rasburicase and aggressive hydration is critical in high-risk patients.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Kidney Injury from Chemotherapy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chemotherapy nephrotoxicity causes rising creatinine but without the specific pattern of simultaneous hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Sepsis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sepsis causes organ dysfunction post-chemotherapy but with fever, hypotension, and positive cultures — not the specific electrolyte derangement pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Adrenal Crisis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adrenal crisis causes hyperkalemia and hypotension but with hyponatremia and low cortisol, not the hyperphosphatemia and hyperuricemia pattern.

clues: A 62-year-old woman presents with progressive numbness in her feet and increasing difficulty with balance over several months.
She had gastric bypass surgery 5 years ago, has a sore smooth tongue, and reports tingling in both hands.
Exam reveals diminished vibration and position sense in both feet with an unsteady gait that worsens with eyes closed.
Hemoglobin is 9.4 with an MCV of 112, and the peripheral smear shows oval macrocytes and neutrophils with 6-7 nuclear lobes.
Both methylmalonic acid AND homocysteine are elevated on serum testing, and the serum B12 level is critically low.
explanation: Without a stomach to produce intrinsic factor, B12 cannot be absorbed in the terminal ileum. B12 is needed for DNA synthesis (large red cells) and myelin maintenance (neurologic damage).
keyFact: Hypersegmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes) are pathognomonic for megaloblastic anemia. B12 elevates BOTH MMA and homocysteine. Folate elevates ONLY homocysteine. Only B12 deficiency causes neurologic damage.

wrongAnswers.name: Folate Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Folate deficiency produces identical blood findings but methylmalonic acid is NORMAL and there are no neurologic symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Myelodysplastic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDS causes macrocytic anemia but with dysplastic changes like hypolobated neutrophils, not HYPERsegmented neutrophils.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes mild macrocytosis but not to MCV 112 with hypersegmented neutrophils or neurologic damage.

clues: A 6-month-old infant presents with seizures and a protuberant abdomen that has been growing for several weeks.
The infant becomes symptomatic after only a few hours of fasting and has had several emergency visits for low blood sugar.
Exam reveals a doll-like face with fat cheeks, a massively enlarged liver, and short stature.
Fasting glucose is 28, lactate is markedly elevated, uric acid and triglycerides are elevated — but ketones are inappropriately LOW.
Glucagon administration fails to raise blood glucose, and liver biopsy shows absent glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme activity.
explanation: Without the final enzyme in glucose release, glycogen builds up in the liver but cannot be converted to free glucose. Both glycogen breakdown and new glucose production are blocked at the same terminal step.
keyFact: Severe fasting hypoglycemia + massive hepatomegaly + lactic acidosis + hyperuricemia + hyperlipidemia is the metabolic signature. The low ketones are because the liver is shunting metabolites to fatty acid synthesis rather than ketogenesis.

wrongAnswers.name: Pompe Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pompe is also a glycogen storage disease but presents with hypotonia and cardiomegaly from glycogen in cardiac muscle, not fasting hypoglycemia with hepatomegaly.

wrongAnswers.name: Galactosemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Galactosemia causes hepatomegaly in infants but after milk introduction with jaundice, cataracts, and positive reducing substances in urine.

wrongAnswers.name: Medium-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCADD causes fasting hypoglycemia with LOW ketones, but the liver is normal-sized and lactate/uric acid are not elevated.

clues: A 16-year-old girl presents with heavy menstrual periods since menarche and prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction last year.
Her mother has similar bleeding symptoms, and the patient bruises easily with frequent nosebleeds.
Exam shows scattered bruises on her extremities without petechiae, joint swelling, or deep tissue bleeding.
Platelet count and PT are normal, the aPTT is mildly prolonged, and ristocetin cofactor activity is decreased.
The deficient protein carries and stabilizes a coagulation factor in the intrinsic pathway, explaining why that factor's level is also mildly reduced.
explanation: The adhesion protein is deficient, impairing platelet plug formation at sites of vessel injury.
keyFact: Mucocutaneous bleeding (nosebleeds, heavy periods) distinguishes this from hemophilia (deep joint and muscle bleeding). Autosomal dominant inheritance means both sexes are affected.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemophilia A
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemophilia causes deep tissue bleeding with X-linked inheritance, not mucocutaneous bleeding in a girl with an affected mother.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes mucocutaneous bleeding with LOW platelets and normal aPTT. Platelets are normal here with prolonged aPTT.

wrongAnswers.name: Bernard-Soulier Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bernard-Soulier has decreased ristocetin activity but with LOW platelet count and LARGE platelets.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with progressively blurred vision over several weeks that worsens when he bends over.
He reports headaches, frequent nosebleeds, and numbness in his feet over several months.
Exam reveals distended retinal veins with flame hemorrhages and papilledema on fundoscopic examination.
Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal IgM spike, and serum viscosity is markedly elevated.
Bone marrow biopsy shows infiltration by lymphoplasmacytic cells with the MYD88 L265P mutation detected.
explanation: Malignant B cells that are halfway between lymphocytes and plasma cells produce massive amounts of IgM, which is the largest immunoglobulin and dramatically increases blood viscosity.
keyFact: Hyperviscosity symptoms (blurred vision, bleeding, neurologic changes, retinal vessel distension) distinguish this from multiple myeloma, which produces IgG or IgA and rarely causes hyperviscosity. Myeloma has lytic bone lesions; this does not.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Myeloma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myeloma produces IgG or IgA with lytic bone lesions, renal failure, and hypercalcemia. This produces IgM with hyperviscosity and no bone lesions.

wrongAnswers.name: CLL
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CLL causes lymphocytosis with smudge cells but does not produce a monoclonal IgM spike or hyperviscosity symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Cryoglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cryoglobulinemia involves immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold causing purpura and glomerulonephritis, not the warm hyperviscosity syndrome seen here.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with headaches and unsteadiness that have been worsening over months.
His father had kidney cancer at age 35 and his sister had a retinal tumor removed.
MRI of the brain shows a cystic mass with a vascular mural nodule in the cerebellum.
Abdominal imaging reveals bilateral renal cysts and a solid enhancing mass in the left kidney consistent with renal cell carcinoma.
Genetic testing confirms a mutation in a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p that normally regulates the hypoxia-inducible factor pathway.
explanation: Loss of VHL protein prevents proper degradation of HIF (hypoxia-inducible factor), leading to constitutive production of VEGF and other growth factors that drive the highly vascular tumors.
keyFact: The tumor association: hemangioblastomas (brain/retina), clear cell renal carcinomas (bilateral), pheochromocytomas, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. RCC in VHL is bilateral and occurs at young age.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberous Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TSC also causes renal tumors but they are angiomyolipomas (fat-containing), not clear cell carcinomas. TSC has skin findings (ash-leaf spots, angiofibromas) absent here.

wrongAnswers.name: MEN2A
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MEN2A includes pheochromocytoma but with medullary thyroid cancer and parathyroid hyperplasia, not cerebellar hemangioblastomas or renal cell carcinoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Polycystic Kidney Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ADPKD causes bilateral renal cysts but without the solid renal masses, hemangioblastomas, or pheochromocytoma.

clues: A 40-year-old woman presents with worsening difficulty swallowing over two years, along with regurgitation of undigested food.
She reports chest pain with swallowing, nighttime coughing from regurgitation, and 15 pounds of weight loss. Dysphagia affects both solids and liquids equally.
Barium swallow shows a dilated esophageal body that tapers to a smooth narrow point at the gastroesophageal junction, described as a 'bird's beak' appearance.
Esophageal manometry shows absent peristalsis in the esophageal body with incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter during swallowing.
In endemic regions, serologic testing for Trypanosoma cruzi is sent to evaluate for parasitic destruction of the myenteric plexus producing the same motility pattern.
explanation: Loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus prevents the lower esophageal sphincter from relaxing and eliminates normal peristalsis, creating a functional obstruction.
keyFact: Dysphagia to BOTH solids and liquids equally from the onset suggests a motility disorder. Dysphagia to solids progressing to liquids suggests a mechanical obstruction (stricture, cancer). The bird's beak on barium swallow and absent peristalsis on manometry are diagnostic.

wrongAnswers.name: Esophageal Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cancer causes progressive dysphagia to solids THEN liquids with an irregular stricture on barium study, not the smooth bird's beak with absent peristalsis.

wrongAnswers.name: GERD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GERD causes heartburn and regurgitation but with normal peristalsis and a relaxing LES on manometry.

wrongAnswers.name: Diffuse Esophageal Spasm
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DES causes intermittent dysphagia with chest pain but manometry shows simultaneous contractions with NORMAL LES relaxation, and barium shows a 'corkscrew' pattern.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with abdominal pain that started around the umbilicus 12 hours ago and has since moved.
He has nausea, no appetite at all, and the pain worsened over bumps during the car ride.
Exam reveals maximal tenderness two-thirds the distance from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine with involuntary guarding.
White count is 14,000, and CT shows a dilated fluid-filled appendix greater than 7 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding.
The pain is now localized to the right lower quadrant, and the patient winces with passive extension of the right hip.
explanation: Luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia) leads to appendiceal distension, ischemia, bacterial invasion, and eventually perforation if untreated.
keyFact: The pain migration is the most important historical feature. The psoas sign (pain on hip extension) localizes inflammation to the retrocecal area. Anorexia is nearly universal — a hungry patient is unlikely to have appendicitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Mesenteric Lymphadenitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mesenteric lymphadenitis (often viral) causes RLQ pain in children but CT shows enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes with a NORMAL appendix.

wrongAnswers.name: Crohn Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Crohn can cause RLQ pain with terminal ileitis, but the acute presentation with migratory pain and dilated appendix on CT confirms appendicitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Ovarian Torsion
wrongAnswers.whyNot: In females, ovarian torsion enters the differential for RLQ pain but shows an enlarged ovary with absent blood flow, not a dilated appendix.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with severe upper abdominal pain that started after a fatty meal and has been constant for 8 hours.
She is obese. She has had shorter similar episodes that resolved within an hour, but this one has persisted for 8 hours and counting.
Temperature is 101°F with severe right upper quadrant tenderness and guarding — she catches her breath when you palpate deeply under the right costal margin.
White count is 15,000, and ultrasound shows gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening over 4 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and a sonographic Murphy sign.
HIDA scan shows non-visualization of the gallbladder after 4 hours, indicating cystic duct obstruction.
explanation: A gallstone obstructs the cystic duct, and the trapped bile causes gallbladder distension, inflammation, and eventual bacterial superinfection.
keyFact: Biliary colic resolves in <6 hours. Pain lasting >6 hours with fever and elevated WBC = cholecystitis (gallbladder inflammation). The inspiratory arrest during RUQ palpation (Murphy sign) is the classic exam finding.

wrongAnswers.name: Biliary Colic
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Biliary colic from transient stone impaction resolves within 1-6 hours. This pain has persisted 8 hours with fever and elevated WBC — that's inflammation, not simple colic.

wrongAnswers.name: Choledocholithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CBD stone causes pain with elevated bilirubin and dilated CBD on imaging. The focus here is gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid — the stone is in the cystic duct, not the CBD.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Pancreatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with elevated lipase. The RUQ focus with gallbladder wall changes on ultrasound localizes this to the gallbladder.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe upper abdominal pain that is worse when lying flat and better when leaning forward.
He has a history of heavy alcohol use. He has been vomiting and the pain started acutely 12 hours ago after a drinking binge.
Exam reveals epigastric tenderness with guarding, decreased bowel sounds, and low-grade fever.
Lipase is 1,850 (more than 3x normal), white count is 16,000, and CT shows a swollen pancreas with peripancreatic fat stranding.
The pain radiates straight through to his back and improves when he leans forward. Lipase is more than 3 times the upper limit of normal.
explanation: Premature activation of digestive enzymes within the pancreas causes autodigestion of the gland, triggering inflammation, edema, and potentially hemorrhagic necrosis.
keyFact: Lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase. Severity is predicted by clinical scoring systems and presence of organ failure. The two biggest causes: gallstones and alcohol. Ranson criteria at admission and 48 hours predict mortality.

wrongAnswers.name: Peptic Ulcer Perforation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Perforated ulcer causes acute epigastric pain with free air on X-ray and peritoneal signs. This patient has elevated lipase with pancreatic edema on CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Cholecystitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholecystitis causes RUQ pain with gallbladder wall thickening. This is epigastric pain radiating to the back with massively elevated lipase.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocardial Infarction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Inferior MI can cause epigastric pain, but ECG and troponin are normal and lipase is not 1,850 in MI.

clues: A 48-year-old man presents with jaundice, fever, and upper abdominal pain that developed over the past week.
He has been drinking a pint of vodka daily for 15 years. He reports right upper quadrant pain and malaise.
Exam reveals jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, mild ascites, and low-grade fever with no signs of obstruction.
AST is 280, ALT is 120 (ratio greater than 2:1), total bilirubin is 12, and white count is 18,000.
Liver biopsy shows hepatocyte ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies, and neutrophilic infiltration.
explanation: Alcohol directly damages hepatocytes, causing an acute inflammatory response with neutrophil infiltration, hepatocyte ballooning, and Mallory-Denk bodies (damaged intermediate filaments).
keyFact: AST:ALT >2:1 is the alcoholic liver disease signature (alcohol damages mitochondria where AST resides, and B6 deficiency impairs ALT synthesis). AST rarely exceeds 300 in alcoholic hepatitis — if >500, think viral hepatitis. Maddrey score >32 = severe, treat with steroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral hepatitis typically elevates transaminases much higher (>1000) with ALT > AST. The AST:ALT >2:1 pattern with levels <300 is characteristic of alcoholic injury.

wrongAnswers.name: Cholangitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ascending cholangitis causes fever, jaundice, and RUQ pain (Charcot triad) but with biliary dilation on imaging and usually gallstones.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatocellular Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCC causes hepatomegaly and jaundice but with markedly elevated AFP and a mass on imaging, not the acute inflammatory picture with AST:ALT >2:1.

clues: A 25-year-old woman presents with fatigue and yellowing of her skin over several weeks.
She has a history of Hashimoto thyroiditis, takes no medications, drinks no alcohol, and has no risk factors for viral hepatitis.
Exam reveals jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and tiny red vascular lesions on her chest.
AST is 620, ALT is 840, IgG is markedly elevated, ANA is positive at 1:320, and anti-smooth muscle antibodies are positive.
Liver biopsy shows lymphocytes and plasma cells invading from the portal tracts into the hepatocyte plate.
explanation: The immune system attacks hepatocytes, causing interface hepatitis with plasma cell infiltration. The dramatic steroid response is both therapeutic and diagnostic.
keyFact: Type 1 (most common): ANA + and/or anti-smooth muscle antibody +, elevated IgG. Type 2 (children): anti-LKM-1 +. Always rule out viral hepatitis, Wilson, and drug-induced injury first.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: All viral serologies are negative. The positive autoantibodies and steroid response confirm an autoimmune process.

wrongAnswers.name: Wilson Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wilson presents in young women with hepatitis but has low ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings, and elevated urine copper.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-Induced Liver Injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: She takes no medications. The autoantibodies and plasma cell-rich biopsy confirm autoimmune hepatitis.

clues: A 55-year-old man with 20 years of poorly controlled acid reflux presents for a screening endoscopy.
He is obese. His heartburn has actually improved recently without any medication change, which concerns his gastroenterologist.
EGD reveals salmon-colored mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastroesophageal junction replacing the normal pale esophageal lining.
Biopsy of the salmon-colored area shows intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells replacing the normal squamous epithelium.
The biopsy confirms goblet cells within the columnar epithelium, establishing intestinal metaplasia of the esophageal lining.
explanation: Chronic acid reflux damages the squamous lining, which is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium (metaplasia) that is more resistant to acid but carries a premalignant potential.
keyFact: Goblet cells are the defining histologic feature. The paradoxical improvement in symptoms occurs because metaplastic columnar epithelium is less pain-sensitive than squamous epithelium. Progression: GERD → metaplasia → low-grade dysplasia → high-grade dysplasia → adenocarcinoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Squamous cell cancer of the esophagus is associated with alcohol and smoking in the upper/middle esophagus. Barrett progresses to ADENOcarcinoma in the lower esophagus.

wrongAnswers.name: Eosinophilic Esophagitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EoE causes dysphagia with esophageal rings and eosinophilic infiltrate on biopsy, not the salmon-colored columnar metaplasia with goblet cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Esophageal Candidiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Candida causes white plaques on the esophageal mucosa in immunosuppressed patients, not salmon-colored columnar metaplasia.

clues: A 6-week-old infant presents with persistent jaundice that has been worsening since birth.
The stools have been consistently pale and clay-colored since birth, and the urine has become dark.
Exam reveals an enlarged firm liver edge palpable 4 cm below the costal margin and acholic stool in the diaper.
Total bilirubin is 12 with a direct fraction of 8.5, and GGT is markedly elevated.
Hepatobiliary scintigraphy shows tracer uptake by the liver but no excretion into the intestine, and intraoperative cholangiogram confirms absent extrahepatic bile ducts.
explanation: The extrahepatic bile ducts are obliterated, preventing bile from draining to the intestine. Progressive biliary damage leads to cirrhosis if not corrected surgically.
keyFact: DIRECT (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia in an infant is ALWAYS pathologic. Physiologic jaundice and breast milk jaundice cause INDIRECT (unconjugated) elevation. Any direct bilirubin >1 mg/dL in an infant demands workup.

wrongAnswers.name: Breast Milk Jaundice
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Breast milk jaundice causes prolonged UNCONJUGATED hyperbilirubinemia with normal stool color and normal direct bilirubin.

wrongAnswers.name: Neonatal Hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Neonatal hepatitis causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but the nuclear medicine scan typically shows tracer reaching the intestine — the ducts are patent.

wrongAnswers.name: Choledochal Cyst
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A choledochal cyst causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but ultrasound shows a cystic dilation of the bile duct, not atretic ducts.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with sudden severe chest and upper abdominal pain that began after an episode of forceful vomiting.
He was drinking heavily before the episode. The pain worsens with swallowing, and he feels crepitus in his neck.
Exam reveals tachycardia, fever, subcutaneous emphysema in the neck, and decreased breath sounds on the left.
Chest X-ray shows a left-sided pleural effusion with pneumomediastinum and air tracking along the mediastinal contours.
Pleural fluid analysis shows a very low pH with food particles and elevated salivary amylase.
explanation: Forceful vomiting against a closed glottis generates massive intraluminal pressure that ruptures the esophageal wall, usually at its weakest point — the left posterolateral distal esophagus.
keyFact: Subcutaneous emphysema after vomiting is essentially diagnostic. The left-sided pleural effusion (from the left posterolateral tear) with food particles clinches it. This is a surgical emergency — untreated mediastinitis is rapidly fatal.

wrongAnswers.name: Mallory-Weiss Tear
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mallory-Weiss is a PARTIAL thickness mucosal tear that causes hematemesis but NOT perforation, pneumomediastinum, or subcutaneous emphysema.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Pancreatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain after drinking but without subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, or food particles in pleural fluid.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocardial Infarction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MI causes chest pain but without the vomiting trigger, subcutaneous emphysema, or left pleural effusion with food particles.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with episodic facial flushing triggered by alcohol and stress.
She also has watery diarrhea and wheezing that her pulmonologist cannot explain.
Exam during an episode reveals bright red flushing of the face and neck with expiratory wheezes.
24-hour urine 5-HIAA is markedly elevated, and chromogranin A is also above normal.
CT shows a 2-cm enhancing mass in the distal ileum with multiple hypervascular liver metastases.
explanation: The neuroendocrine tumor secretes serotonin and other vasoactive substances. When limited to the gut, portal circulation delivers them to the liver for metabolism. Once liver metastases are present, the substances bypass hepatic metabolism and cause systemic effects.
keyFact: Flushing + diarrhea + wheezing + liver metastases + elevated urinary 5-HIAA = carcinoid syndrome. Right-sided heart valve disease (tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonic stenosis) can develop from chronic serotonin exposure. The ileum is the most common primary site.

wrongAnswers.name: VIPoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VIPoma causes massive watery diarrhea but without flushing, wheezing, or elevated 5-HIAA.

wrongAnswers.name: Pheochromocytoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pheo causes episodic flushing with hypertension and elevated catecholamines, but not diarrhea, wheezing, or elevated 5-HIAA.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic Mastocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mastocytosis causes flushing and diarrhea from histamine release, but tryptase is elevated and 5-HIAA is normal.

clues: A 30-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhea and bloating that have not responded to dietary changes.
She has iron deficiency anemia refractory to oral iron supplementation and an intensely itchy blistering rash on her elbows.
Exam reveals pallor, the vesicular rash on extensor surfaces, and mild abdominal distension.
Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody is strongly positive, and small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.
All symptoms and histologic changes resolve completely on a strict gluten-free diet.
explanation: An immune reaction to gluten (in wheat, barley, rye) causes destruction of small intestinal villi, impairing absorption of nutrients, vitamins, and minerals.
keyFact: The itchy rash (dermatitis herpetiformis) with granular IgA deposits is essentially pathognomonic. Iron deficiency refractory to oral supplementation is a clue — the damaged duodenum can't absorb it. Associated with HLA-DQ2/DQ8.

wrongAnswers.name: Tropical Sprue
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tropical sprue causes similar villous atrophy and malabsorption but occurs in tropical regions and responds to antibiotics, not a gluten-free diet.

wrongAnswers.name: Crohn Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Crohn causes diarrhea with malabsorption but with transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and granulomas — not villous atrophy with anti-tTG antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Lactose Intolerance
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhea with dairy but no villous atrophy, no rash, and no anti-tTG antibodies.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with painless progressive jaundice over 3 weeks and 10 pounds of weight loss.
He has a history of chronic biliary inflammation. His urine is dark, stools are clay-colored, and he has lost 15 pounds.
Exam reveals deep jaundice, a palpable nontender distended gallbladder, and hepatomegaly with a firm liver edge.
Direct bilirubin is markedly elevated with very high alkaline phosphatase, and CT shows a mass at the bile duct bifurcation.
ERCP with brushings from the mass at the hepatic hilum shows malignant cells of biliary epithelial origin.
explanation: Malignant transformation of bile duct epithelium, often in the setting of chronic biliary inflammation from PSC or parasitic infections, obstructs bile flow.
keyFact: PSC is the strongest Western risk factor. Liver fluke infections (Clonorchis, Opisthorchis) are the strongest Asian risk factor. A painless distended gallbladder with jaundice suggests distal malignant obstruction — gallstones cause a scarred contracted gallbladder that cannot distend.

wrongAnswers.name: Pancreatic Head Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pancreatic cancer also causes painless obstructive jaundice, but the mass is at the pancreatic head, not the bile duct bifurcation, and PSC is not a risk factor.

wrongAnswers.name: Gallstone Obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gallstones cause jaundice with PAIN and a contracted (not distended) gallbladder.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatocellular Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCC produces AFP, shows arterial enhancement with washout, and doesn't typically obstruct bile ducts unless very large.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with a progressively distended abdomen and swollen legs over several weeks.
He has a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use. His skin has been turning yellow.
Exam reveals jaundice, red palms, breast tissue enlargement, dilated veins fanning from his navel, and splenomegaly.
AST is 88, ALT is 42 (2:1 ratio), albumin is 2.1, INR is 1.8, and ultrasound shows a shrunken nodular liver.
Paracentesis shows a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.8 g/dL, and FibroScan shows liver stiffness of 42 kPa.
explanation: Decades of alcohol damage replaced functional liver tissue with scar. The distorted architecture increases portal blood flow resistance (portal hypertension) and impairs synthetic function.
keyFact: AST:ALT >2:1 is the alcoholic liver disease signature. Portal hypertension causes ascites, varices, splenomegaly, and dilated abdominal wall veins. Low albumin and prolonged INR reflect failed synthetic function.

wrongAnswers.name: Congestive Heart Failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Right HF causes ascites and edema but with JVD, elevated BNP, and without the stigmata of chronic liver disease (palmar erythema, gynecomastia, spider nevi).

wrongAnswers.name: Budd-Chiari Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Budd-Chiari causes hepatomegaly with ascites acutely, but the liver is typically enlarged (not shrunken) and there is hepatic vein thrombosis on imaging.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nephrotic causes edema from low albumin but without jaundice, portal hypertension, or the stigmata of chronic liver disease.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with crampy abdominal pain and 15 pounds of weight loss over 3 months.
He has had a painful draining area near his anus for several weeks that has been intermittently discharging fluid.
Exam reveals right lower quadrant tenderness, a perianal fistula with drainage, and aphthous ulcers on his buccal mucosa.
Colonoscopy shows patchy areas of deep linear ulcers with normal mucosa between them, and the terminal ileum is inflamed.
Biopsy shows transmural inflammation with noncaseating granulomas extending through the full thickness of the bowel wall.
explanation: This chronic inflammatory bowel disease can affect any portion of the GI tract from mouth to anus, with transmural inflammation that leads to complications unique to its full-thickness nature.
keyFact: Skip lesions + transmural + granulomas + fistulas = Crohn. Continuous + mucosal only + crypt abscesses + bloody diarrhea = UC. The terminal ileum involvement and perianal disease are the classic locations.

wrongAnswers.name: Ulcerative Colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: UC causes CONTINUOUS inflammation starting from the rectum, limited to the MUCOSA, with BLOODY diarrhea and no skip lesions, granulomas, or fistulas.

wrongAnswers.name: Appendicitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Appendicitis causes acute RLQ pain but without the chronic course, perianal fistula, skip lesions, or granulomas.

wrongAnswers.name: Intestinal Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Intestinal TB can mimic Crohn with ileal involvement and granulomas, but the granulomas are CASEATING and AFB stain is positive.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with intermittent chest pain and difficulty swallowing that comes and goes unpredictably.
The chest pain sometimes mimics cardiac pain and has led to two emergency department visits where cardiac workup was negative.
Barium swallow shows a 'corkscrew' or 'rosary bead' appearance of the esophagus during a symptomatic episode.
Esophageal manometry reveals intermittent simultaneous high-amplitude contractions in the esophageal body, but the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes normally.
The contractions are uncoordinated and simultaneous rather than sequential, and they occur intermittently between episodes of normal peristalsis.
explanation: Uncoordinated simultaneous contractions of the esophageal body cause intermittent obstruction and chest pain, but the LES functions normally between the spasms.
keyFact: Normal LES relaxation distinguishes DES from achalasia (failed LES relaxation). The intermittent nature distinguishes it from achalasia (constant). Corkscrew esophagus on barium is the imaging hallmark. Calcium channel blockers and nitrates can relieve spasm.

wrongAnswers.name: Achalasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Achalasia has ABSENT peristalsis with FAILED LES relaxation and a bird's beak appearance. DES has intermittent simultaneous contractions with NORMAL LES relaxation and a corkscrew pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ACS causes chest pain but with ECG changes, troponin elevation, or wall motion abnormalities — all negative here.

wrongAnswers.name: GERD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GERD causes heartburn from acid reflux but manometry shows normal peristalsis, not the simultaneous high-amplitude contractions.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with left lower quadrant pain and fever for two days.
He reports a low-fiber diet and has had mild intermittent discomfort in this area for years, but this episode is much more severe with chills.
Exam reveals fever of 101.5°F and focal left lower quadrant tenderness with guarding.
CT shows sigmoid colon wall thickening, pericolonic fat stranding, and a 2-cm pericolonic abscess.
Multiple outpouchings of the colonic wall are visible on CT in the sigmoid segment surrounding the inflamed area.
explanation: A diverticulum (outpouching of mucosa through the colonic wall at a point of vascular penetration) becomes obstructed and microperforation leads to pericolonic inflammation and infection.
keyFact: Left lower quadrant pain + fever + leukocytosis in an older patient on a low-fiber diet = diverticulitis. Sometimes called 'left-sided appendicitis.' CT is the diagnostic modality of choice. Avoid colonoscopy acutely — perform 6-8 weeks later.

wrongAnswers.name: Colon Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Colon cancer can present with LLQ symptoms and must be excluded — that's why colonoscopy is done after recovery. The acute inflammatory picture with wall thickening and fat stranding suggests diverticulitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic Colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic colitis causes LLQ pain in elderly patients but with bloody diarrhea and mucosal changes on CT, not the pericolonic abscess pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Ulcerative Colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: UC causes LLQ pain but with bloody diarrhea and continuous mucosal inflammation starting from the rectum, not focal pericolonic inflammation from a diverticulum.

clues: A 52-year-old man presents with sudden massive vomiting of bright red blood and hemodynamic instability.
He has known alcoholic cirrhosis. He vomited approximately 500 mL of blood in one episode.
Exam reveals jaundice, spider nevi, ascites, and active blood in the oropharynx with blood pressure of 85/50 and heart rate of 125.
Hemoglobin dropped from 11 to 7.2, and emergent endoscopy reveals large tortuous dilated submucosal veins with active spurting at the GE junction.
Endoscopic band ligation is applied to the actively spurting vessels at the GE junction, and portal venous pressure gradient measures 18 mmHg.
explanation: Portal hypertension from cirrhosis forces blood through collateral pathways including the submucosal esophageal veins, which dilate under the abnormally high pressure and can rupture catastrophically.
keyFact: Variceal bleeding is the most life-threatening complication of portal hypertension. Band ligation is first-line endoscopic therapy. Nonselective beta-blockers (propranolol, nadolol) reduce portal pressure for primary and secondary prophylaxis. TIPS is rescue therapy for refractory bleeding.

wrongAnswers.name: Mallory-Weiss Tear
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mallory-Weiss causes hematemesis from a mucosal tear at the GE junction after vomiting, but the bleeding is typically less massive and the tear is a linear mucosal defect, not dilated submucosal veins.

wrongAnswers.name: Peptic Ulcer Bleeding
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ulcer bleeding is the most common cause of upper GI bleeding overall, but endoscopy shows an ulcer crater (not dilated veins) and the patient typically lacks cirrhosis stigmata.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastric Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gastric cancer can cause upper GI bleeding but with an ulcerated mass on endoscopy, not dilated submucosal veins at the GE junction.

clues: A 15-year-old boy undergoes colonoscopy after his father was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 35.
He has no GI symptoms — the screening colonoscopy was performed solely because of his father's diagnosis.
Colonoscopy reveals hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps carpeting the entire colon.
Genetic testing reveals a germline mutation in the APC tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q.
The father's surgical pathology also showed hundreds of colonic polyps, and additional family members are being tested for the same mutation.
explanation: Loss of the APC gatekeeper gene allows unchecked cell proliferation. With thousands of polyps, at least one will inevitably accumulate enough additional mutations to become cancer.
keyFact: APC mutation is the first hit in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (APC → KRAS → p53). Gardner variant adds osteomas and desmoid tumors. Turcot variant adds brain tumors. Attenuated FAP has fewer polyps with later cancer onset.

wrongAnswers.name: Lynch Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lynch (HNPCC) causes colon cancer from mismatch repair gene mutations but with FEWER polyps (not hundreds) and right-sided predominance. Lynch does not carpet the colon.

wrongAnswers.name: Juvenile Polyposis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Juvenile polyposis involves hamartomatous polyps that are histologically different from the adenomatous polyps in this condition.

wrongAnswers.name: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Peutz-Jeghers causes hamartomatous polyps with mucocutaneous pigmentation, not the carpet of adenomatous polyps seen here.

clues: A 60-year-old man presents with melena, fatigue, and lightheadedness over two weeks, prompting an ER visit.
He has no history of NSAID use, no prior GI disease, and no alcohol use. Hemoglobin is 8.2 with iron deficiency.
EGD shows a submucosal mass with normal overlying mucosa and a central ulcerated area. The mass appears to grow outward from the stomach wall.
Biopsy shows spindle cells on histology. CT confirms a 5-cm well-circumscribed mass arising from the gastric wall.
Immunohistochemistry is positive for CD117 (c-KIT), confirming the tumor cell lineage and guiding targeted therapy selection.
explanation: Mutations in the KIT or PDGFRA tyrosine kinase receptors drive proliferation of the interstitial pacemaker cells of the gut wall.
keyFact: CD117 (c-KIT) positive spindle cell tumor of the GI wall = GIST. Most common in the stomach. Imatinib (the same drug that targets BCR-ABL in CML) targets the mutant KIT protein and has transformed outcomes for metastatic disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastric Adenocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adenocarcinoma arises from the MUCOSA and grows into the lumen. GIST arises from the WALL and grows outward, with normal overlying mucosa.

wrongAnswers.name: Leiomyoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle tumors that are CD117 NEGATIVE. GIST is CD117 POSITIVE and can be malignant.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gastric lymphoma shows lymphoid markers (CD20 for B-cell), not the CD117/c-KIT positivity of GIST.

clues: A 40-year-old woman presents with intermittent severe upper abdominal pain that occurs 30-60 minutes after fatty meals and lasts 1-4 hours before resolving completely.
She is obese and multiparous. The pain radiates to her right shoulder blade and she has had 4 similar episodes over the past 3 months.
Exam between episodes is completely normal — no tenderness, fever, jaundice, or signs of peritonitis.
Ultrasound shows multiple mobile echogenic foci within the gallbladder casting acoustic shadows, with normal wall thickness and bile ducts.
Liver enzymes, bilirubin, and white blood cell count are all normal. Between episodes, she is completely asymptomatic.
explanation: Cholesterol supersaturation of bile leads to crystal formation and stone growth. When a stone temporarily impacts the cystic duct during gallbladder contraction (triggered by fatty meals), the distension causes biliary colic.
keyFact: Risk factors: Female, Forty, Fat, Fertile (the 4 F's). Pain resolves in <6 hours = biliary colic. Pain >6 hours with fever = cholecystitis. Normal labs between episodes distinguishes colic from complications.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Cholecystitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholecystitis causes persistent pain >6 hours with fever, elevated WBC, and gallbladder wall thickening. This patient's pain resolves completely with normal labs between episodes.

wrongAnswers.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PUD causes epigastric pain related to meals but without the right scapular radiation or the mobile echogenic foci on ultrasound.

wrongAnswers.name: Biliary Dyskinesia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Biliary dyskinesia causes similar postprandial RUQ pain but ultrasound shows NO stones — the diagnosis requires a HIDA scan showing reduced ejection fraction.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with early satiety and unintentional 20-pound weight loss over three months.
He has a history of chronic infection with a spiral-shaped bacterium and a diet high in smoked and pickled foods.
Exam reveals a palpable firm left supraclavicular lymph node and a nontender epigastric mass on deep palpation.
EGD shows a large ulcerated mass in the gastric body with heaped-up borders, and biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma with signet ring cells.
CT staging shows the mass invading through the gastric wall with perigastric lymphadenopathy and ascites.
explanation: Chronic H. pylori-driven inflammation progresses through atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and eventually carcinoma over decades.
keyFact: The left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) is a classic site of metastasis from abdominal cancers via the thoracic duct. Signet ring cells with diffuse infiltration (linitis plastica) carries a worse prognosis. Risk factors: H. pylori, smoked/pickled diet, blood type A.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastric Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gastric MALT lymphoma is also associated with H. pylori but biopsy shows lymphoid tissue, not adenocarcinoma with signet ring cells.

wrongAnswers.name: GIST
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GISTs are submucosal spindle cell tumors that are c-KIT positive, not epithelial adenocarcinomas with signet ring cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PUD causes epigastric pain and ulceration, but a large ulcerated mass with signet ring cells and nodal metastases is cancer.

clues: A newborn is delivered with loops of bowel protruding through a defect in the abdominal wall, adjacent to the umbilical cord.
The mother is 19 years old and used tobacco and NSAIDs during pregnancy. Prenatal ultrasound had identified the defect.
The herniated bowel is not covered by any membrane and appears matted, edematous, and inflamed from exposure to amniotic fluid.
The umbilical cord inserts normally into the abdominal wall, separate from the defect, which is located to the right of the cord.
Karyotype is normal, echocardiogram shows no cardiac defects, and no other anomalies are identified on full evaluation.
explanation: A full-thickness defect in the abdominal wall (thought to result from vascular disruption of the right omphalomesenteric artery) allows bowel to herniate without any covering membrane.
keyFact: Gastroschisis: RIGHT of umbilicus, NO membrane, cord inserts normally, usually ISOLATED. Omphalocele: central at umbilicus, COVERED by membrane, cord inserts into sac, associated with OTHER anomalies (cardiac, chromosomal).

wrongAnswers.name: Omphalocele
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Omphalocele is central at the umbilicus, COVERED by a membrane, with the cord inserting into the sac, and is associated with cardiac and chromosomal anomalies.

wrongAnswers.name: Umbilical Hernia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Umbilical hernia protrudes through the umbilical ring UNDER intact skin, not exposed bowel through a full-thickness defect.

wrongAnswers.name: Prune Belly Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prune belly causes a deficient abdominal wall musculature with a wrinkled appearance but the abdominal contents are contained within the abdomen, not herniated.

clues: A 60-year-old woman presents with a painful blistering rash on her groin and legs that heals in one area and appears in another.
She has been diagnosed with new diabetes and has lost significant weight over 4 months.
Exam reveals a scaly erythematous eruption with central clearing and crusting in intertriginous areas, along with a smooth red tongue.
Fasting glucose is 250, and serum glucagon level is markedly elevated at 900 pg/mL.
CT reveals a large hypervascular mass in the pancreatic tail with contrast enhancement on arterial phase imaging.
explanation: Excess glucagon causes hyperglycemia (gluconeogenesis), protein catabolism (weight loss, amino acid depletion), and the characteristic skin rash from hypoaminoacidemia.
keyFact: The rash (necrolytic migratory erythema) is the most recognizable feature — it's painful, blistering, migratory, and concentrated in intertriginous areas. The 4 D's: dermatitis, diabetes, DVT, depression.

wrongAnswers.name: VIPoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VIPoma causes massive watery diarrhea with hypokalemia, not the migratory skin rash with diabetes and weight loss.

wrongAnswers.name: Type 2 Diabetes
wrongAnswers.whyNot: T2DM causes hyperglycemia but not the migratory blistering rash, weight loss, or massively elevated glucagon with a pancreatic mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Pemphigus Vulgaris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pemphigus causes blistering with a positive Nikolsky sign from anti-desmoglein antibodies, not the migratory pattern with glucagon elevation.

clues: A 48-year-old man of Northern European descent presents with joint pain in his second and third knuckles on both hands.
He was recently diagnosed with diabetes despite being lean, and he reports erectile dysfunction.
Exam reveals diffuse bronze-gray skin discoloration, hepatomegaly, and tenderness over the affected knuckle joints.
Ferritin is 2,800 and transferrin saturation is 82%. Liver biopsy shows heavy iron deposition on Prussian blue stain.
HFE gene testing confirms homozygosity for the C282Y mutation. His siblings are referred for genetic testing.
explanation: Excess iron absorption deposits iron in the liver, pancreas, heart, skin, joints, and pituitary, causing progressive organ damage through free radical generation.
keyFact: The joint involvement preferentially affects the second and third MCP joints. Transferrin saturation >45% is the best screening test. Cancer surveillance continues even after iron depletion if cirrhosis has developed.

wrongAnswers.name: Wilson Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wilson involves COPPER overload with corneal rings and low ceruloplasmin — different metal, different gene.

wrongAnswers.name: Type 2 Diabetes
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The diabetes is real but SECONDARY to iron depositing in the pancreas. New diabetes in a lean patient with bronze skin and sky-high ferritin should trigger iron overload workup.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA causes joint disease but with inflammatory markers, symmetric MCP/PIP involvement, and no iron metabolism abnormalities. The second/third MCP pattern with bronze skin and high ferritin is distinctive.

clues: A 58-year-old man with known chronic liver disease presents with upper abdominal pain and unintentional weight loss over the past month.
His liver disease is from hepatitis B cirrhosis. His liver function has deteriorated rapidly after years of stability.
Exam reveals a hard nodular liver edge extending 6 cm below the costal margin with ascites.
AFP is markedly elevated at 850. Ultrasound shows a new 5-cm mass in the right lobe of the liver.
Triple-phase CT shows arterial phase hyperenhancement of the mass followed by portal venous phase washout.
explanation: Chronic liver injury from hepatitis B or C, alcohol, or NASH drives cycles of cell death and regeneration that eventually produce malignant transformation.
keyFact: The arterial enhancement with portal venous washout pattern is diagnostic. AFP >400 ng/mL is highly suggestive. Risk factors: HBV (can cause HCC even without cirrhosis), HCV, alcohol, NASH, hemochromatosis, aflatoxin B1 exposure.

wrongAnswers.name: Liver Metastases
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastases are more common than primary liver cancer but are usually multiple, lack the arterial enhancement-washout pattern, and AFP is normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatic Hemangioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor but shows peripheral nodular enhancement that fills in centripetally — the opposite of HCC's washout pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Cholangiocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from bile duct epithelium with delayed enhancement, produces CA 19-9 (not AFP), and causes biliary obstruction.

clues: A 55-year-old man with advanced liver disease and fluid overload develops rising creatinine from 1.0 to 3.8 over one week despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
He has decompensated cirrhosis with refractory ascites. There is no nephrotoxic drug exposure and no obstruction on imaging.
Exam reveals tense ascites, jaundice, and hypotension with a bland urine sediment.
Urine sodium is less than 10 mEq/L and urine microscopy shows no casts or cells. Kidneys appear structurally normal on imaging.
Creatinine continues to rise despite a 1.5 g/kg albumin challenge and withdrawal of diuretics.
explanation: Severe portal hypertension causes splanchnic vasodilation, which triggers intense renal vasoconstriction to maintain blood pressure. The kidneys are structurally normal but functionally shut down from reduced perfusion.
keyFact: Diagnosis of exclusion: rising creatinine + no structural kidney disease + no nephrotoxins + no response to volume + low urine sodium + bland sediment. Type 1 (rapidly progressive, weeks) has worse prognosis than type 2 (gradual). Midodrine + octreotide + albumin is a temporizing bridge to transplant.

wrongAnswers.name: Prerenal AKI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prerenal AKI also has low urine sodium, but it RESPONDS to fluid resuscitation. HRS persists despite adequate volume.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ATN has high urine sodium (>40) and muddy brown casts on microscopy. This patient has low urine sodium and bland sediment.

wrongAnswers.name: NSAID Nephrotoxicity
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NSAIDs cause renal vasoconstriction in cirrhotics but the patient has no nephrotoxic medications. Medication history was specifically excluded.

clues: A 2-day-old newborn has not passed meconium since birth and has a progressively distended abdomen with bilious vomiting.
The infant was full-term with no prenatal complications, and abdominal X-ray shows dilated loops of bowel with no air in the rectum.
On rectal exam, a gush of stool and air is expelled immediately after the examining finger is withdrawn.
Barium enema shows a narrow distal segment with a dilated proximal segment and a transition zone between them.
Suction rectal biopsy confirms absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal plexus, and acetylcholinesterase staining is markedly elevated in the aganglionic segment.
explanation: Neural crest cells failed to migrate completely to the distal colon during embryonic development, leaving an aganglionic segment that cannot relax, creating a functional obstruction.
keyFact: Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours of birth is the classic presentation. The aganglionic segment is ALWAYS distal and ALWAYS includes the rectum. The explosive stool on rectal exam (squirt sign) is characteristic. Associated with Down syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Meconium Ileus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meconium ileus (associated with cystic fibrosis) causes neonatal bowel obstruction but from thick meconium plugging the ileum, not from an aganglionic segment. Barium shows the obstruction in the small bowel, not a transition zone in the colon.

wrongAnswers.name: Intestinal Atresia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atresia causes neonatal bowel obstruction but from a structural gap in the bowel lumen. Biopsy would show normal ganglion cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Neonatal Sepsis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sepsis can cause ileus with abdominal distension but without the characteristic transition zone, absent ganglion cells, or explosive stool on rectal exam.

clues: A 4-week-old infant presents with forceful vomiting after every feeding that has worsened over the past week.
He is the firstborn male. Despite the vomiting, the infant is hungry and feeds eagerly immediately after emesis. The vomitus has no bile.
Exam reveals visible peristaltic waves moving from left to right across the upper abdomen and a firm olive-shaped mass palpable in the epigastrium.
Blood gas shows hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and abdominal ultrasound shows pyloric muscle thickness greater than 4 mm and length greater than 16 mm.
The vomitus contains only milk curds without any green or yellow bile pigment, and the infant remains hungry afterward.
explanation: Hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter muscle creates a progressive gastric outlet obstruction. The firstborn male predilection and the 2-6 week age of onset are classic demographic features.
keyFact: Nonbilious = obstruction is ABOVE the ampulla of Vater (where bile enters). Bilious vomiting means obstruction is BELOW the ampulla — a much more concerning finding. The hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis results from vomiting pure HCl.

wrongAnswers.name: Midgut Volvulus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Volvulus causes BILIOUS vomiting (obstruction is distal to the ampulla) and is a surgical emergency. This vomiting is NONbilious (pyloric obstruction is proximal to the ampulla).

wrongAnswers.name: GERD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reflux causes spitting up but not the projectile quality, olive mass, or the progressive worsening with metabolic alkalosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Overfeeding
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Overfeeding can cause vomiting but without the palpable olive mass, progressive worsening, or electrolyte derangements.

clues: A 9-month-old infant presents with episodes of inconsolable crying every 15-20 minutes, with calm intervals in between.
He draws his knees to his chest during episodes, has been vomiting, and had a viral illness last week.
The infant is pale and listless between episodes. A sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant.
Abdominal ultrasound shows concentric rings of bowel wall in cross-section. His diaper contains red jelly-like material.
Therapeutic air enema confirms and reduces the abnormality, with bowel returning to normal position under fluoroscopic guidance.
explanation: A segment of bowel telescopes into the adjacent segment, compressing its blood supply. The trapped bowel becomes ischemic, producing the classic bloody mucus stool.
keyFact: Peak age 6-36 months. Preceding viral illness causes lymphoid patch enlargement that acts as a lead point. The red jelly stool (blood and mucus) is a late finding. In children >2 years, always look for a pathologic lead point (polyp, lymphoma).

wrongAnswers.name: Pyloric Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pyloric stenosis causes projectile vomiting in 2-6 week olds with an olive-shaped epigastric mass, not episodic pain with bloody stool in an older infant.

wrongAnswers.name: Meckel Diverticulum
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meckel causes painless rectal bleeding, not the colicky episodic pain with sausage-shaped mass seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Appendicitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Appendicitis is rare in infants and causes continuous RLQ pain, not the intermittent episodes with pain-free intervals.

clues: A 75-year-old woman presents with sudden crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhea.
She has a history of atrial fibrillation and peripheral vascular disease. Bright red blood per rectum appeared within 2 hours of onset.
Exam reveals mild left lower quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs, and the abdomen is soft and nondistended.
CT shows wall thickening of the descending colon and splenic flexure with surrounding fat stranding.
Colonoscopy reveals a well-demarcated segment of hemorrhagic edematous mucosa at the splenic flexure with sharp transition to normal bowel.
explanation: Transient or sustained hypoperfusion of the colonic blood supply causes mucosal ischemia, inflammation, and hemorrhage, predominantly at watershed areas.
keyFact: Elderly patient + vascular risk factors + sudden abdominal pain + bloody diarrhea + involvement at watershed zones (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid) = ischemic colitis. Most cases are nonocclusive and self-limited. Peritoneal signs or pneumatosis indicate transmural necrosis requiring surgery.

wrongAnswers.name: Ulcerative Colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: UC causes bloody diarrhea but in younger patients, starting from the rectum and extending continuously, not a segmental watershed pattern in an elderly patient.

wrongAnswers.name: Diverticulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diverticulitis causes LLQ pain but with fever and pericolonic abscess, not the watershed mucosal hemorrhage pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute mesenteric ischemia affects the small bowel (SMA territory) with severe pain out of proportion to exam. Ischemic colitis affects the COLON and is typically less severe.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with bright red blood in his vomit after a bout of forceful retching earlier today.
The vomiting followed heavy alcohol consumption. He retched several times before noticing blood, and the bleeding was self-limited.
Exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness, stable vital signs, and no signs of chronic liver disease.
Upper endoscopy reveals a linear mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction without active bleeding.
The tear involves only the mucosa and submucosa on endoscopic visualization. There is no pneumomediastinum on imaging.
explanation: Forceful vomiting or retching creates a sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure that tears the mucosa at the GE junction, the weakest point of the esophageal wall.
keyFact: Partial thickness (mucosal) tear = this diagnosis (self-limited, conservative management). Full thickness (transmural) rupture = Boerhaave syndrome (surgical emergency, pneumomediastinum). Most tears stop bleeding spontaneously.

wrongAnswers.name: Boerhaave Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Boerhaave is a FULL-thickness esophageal rupture with pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysema, and sepsis. This is a PARTIAL-thickness mucosal tear that stopped bleeding on its own.

wrongAnswers.name: Esophageal Varices
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Varices cause massive hematemesis in cirrhotics from dilated submucosal veins. This patient has no liver disease and endoscopy shows a linear tear, not varices.

wrongAnswers.name: Peptic Ulcer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ulcer bleeding is related to meals and acid, not to vomiting. Endoscopy shows an ulcer crater, not a GE junction tear.

clues: A 2-year-old boy presents with painless bright red rectal bleeding in large volume.
He is otherwise healthy with no diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal tenderness, and growth and development are normal.
Exam reveals a well-appearing child with bright red blood in the diaper but a soft nontender abdomen and no palpable masses.
Standard abdominal imaging and upper and lower endoscopy are unrevealing for a source of the bleeding.
A nuclear medicine scan using a radiolabeled tracer taken up by gastric mucosa shows ectopic uptake in the right lower quadrant.
explanation: This is a remnant of the embryologic duct connecting the midgut to the yolk sac. When it contains ectopic gastric mucosa, the acid production causes ulceration and painless bleeding.
keyFact: Rule of 2s: 2% of population, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric most common, pancreatic), presents before age 2. Most common cause of painless lower GI bleeding in children.

wrongAnswers.name: Intussusception
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Intussusception causes episodic colicky pain with 'currant jelly' stool. This bleeding is painless and bright red without abdominal pain.

wrongAnswers.name: Juvenile Polyp
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Juvenile polyps cause painless rectal bleeding in children, but the nuclear medicine scan with ectopic gastric uptake identifies the source as the diverticulum.

wrongAnswers.name: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IBD can cause rectal bleeding in young patients but with diarrhea, abdominal pain, and mucosal inflammation on endoscopy — none present here.

clues: A 3-day-old premature infant born at 28 weeks develops abdominal distension and bloody stools after starting feeds.
The infant was started on formula rather than breast milk. Temperature is dropping, and he is becoming lethargic with apnea episodes.
Exam reveals a tense shiny distended abdomen with discolored abdominal wall and absent bowel sounds.
Abdominal X-ray shows distended bowel loops with tiny gas bubbles tracking within the intestinal wall itself.
Gas is also visible in the portal venous system on the X-ray, and a fixed dilated loop persists on serial films.
explanation: The immature intestinal lining in premature infants is vulnerable to bacterial invasion. Formula feeds provide substrate for overgrowth, and bacteria invade the damaged wall producing intramural gas.
keyFact: Gas in the bowel wall (pneumatosis intestinalis) is the pathognomonic radiographic finding. Prematurity is the #1 risk factor. Formula feeding increases risk — breast milk is protective.

wrongAnswers.name: Hirschsprung Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hirschsprung causes abdominal distension and failure to pass meconium from absent ganglion cells, but without bloody stools, pneumatosis, or the septic presentation.

wrongAnswers.name: Midgut Volvulus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Volvulus causes bilious vomiting and distension but shows a 'corkscrew' duodenum on upper GI, not pneumatosis and portal venous gas.

wrongAnswers.name: Meconium Ileus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meconium ileus causes bowel obstruction in neonates (associated with cystic fibrosis) but without bloody stools, pneumatosis, or the septic picture.

clues: A 52-year-old woman is found to have persistently elevated liver enzymes on routine bloodwork despite feeling well.
She is obese with type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia. She drinks no alcohol and has negative viral hepatitis serologies.
Exam reveals a BMI of 36, acanthosis nigricans on her neck, and hepatomegaly with no hepatotoxic medication exposure.
ALT is 68, AST is 52, ultrasound shows a hyperechoic bright liver, and autoimmune markers are negative.
Liver biopsy shows steatosis with hepatocyte ballooning, lobular inflammation, and early fibrosis.
explanation: Insulin resistance drives fat accumulation in hepatocytes (steatosis), which can progress to inflammation (steatohepatitis), fibrosis, and eventually cirrhosis.
