keyFact: ALT > AST in NASH (opposite of alcoholic disease where AST > ALT). The biopsy is histologically indistinguishable from alcoholic hepatitis — only the clinical history separates them. NASH is now the leading indication for liver transplantation in many countries.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcoholic Hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alcoholic hepatitis has AST > ALT (>2:1 ratio) and requires significant alcohol use. This patient drinks no alcohol and has ALT > AST.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemochromatosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemochromatosis causes hepatomegaly with elevated transaminases but with markedly elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation. Iron studies are normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune Hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIH causes elevated transaminases with positive ANA or anti-smooth muscle antibodies. Autoimmune markers are negative here.

clues: A newborn is delivered with a mass protruding from the center of the abdomen, covered by a glistening translucent membrane.
Prenatal ultrasound had shown elevated maternal AFP, and the anomaly was diagnosed before delivery.
The intact membrane covers visible loops of bowel and part of the liver, and the umbilical cord inserts directly into the sac.
Echocardiogram reveals an atrial septal defect, and chromosomal analysis is sent to evaluate for associated syndromes.
The defect is central at the umbilicus with cord insertion into the sac, and associated cardiac and chromosomal anomalies are identified.
explanation: The midgut fails to return to the abdominal cavity during embryonic development, remaining outside covered by a sac of peritoneum and amnion.
keyFact: Covered + central + cord into sac + associated anomalies = omphalocele. Uncovered + lateral (right of umbilicus) + normal cord + usually isolated = gastroschisis. This distinction is a guaranteed board question.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastroschisis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gastroschisis is an uncovered defect to the RIGHT of the umbilicus with normally-inserting cord and is usually an isolated finding without other anomalies.

wrongAnswers.name: Umbilical Hernia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Umbilical hernia has bowel protruding under intact SKIN, not through a peritoneal membrane. It usually closes spontaneously by age 5.

wrongAnswers.name: Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CDH involves bowel herniating into the chest through the diaphragm causing respiratory distress, not a visible abdominal wall mass.

clues: A 70-year-old man presents with painless jaundice that has been deepening for 2 weeks.
He has lost 20 pounds and was diagnosed with diabetes just 3 months ago despite being lean.
Exam reveals cachexia, jaundice, a palpable nontender gallbladder, and a migratory superficial thrombophlebitis on his left leg.
CT shows a hypodense mass in the pancreatic head with upstream dilation of both the pancreatic and bile ducts.
CA 19-9 is markedly elevated, and the mass encases the superior mesenteric artery.
explanation: The tumor arises from ductal epithelium and is notoriously silent until it obstructs the bile duct (jaundice) or invades retroperitoneal nerves (back pain).
keyFact: New-onset diabetes in an older patient without risk factors should raise concern. The migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) is a paraneoplastic phenomenon. The double-duct sign (dilated pancreatic and bile ducts) is characteristic of a pancreatic head mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Cholangiocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholangiocarcinoma causes similar obstructive jaundice but the mass is at the bile duct, not the pancreatic head, and there is no pancreatic duct dilation.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Pancreatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic pancreatitis causes back pain and new diabetes but with pancreatic calcifications and a history of alcohol, not an obstructing mass with jaundice.

wrongAnswers.name: Ampullary Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ampullary cancer causes obstructive jaundice with a better prognosis and is visible on endoscopy at the ampulla, not a large pancreatic mass on CT.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with burning epigastric pain that wakes him at night.
The pain occurs 2-3 hours after meals and is relieved by eating or taking antacids. He has been taking daily NSAIDs for knee pain for a year.
Exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding, and the abdomen is soft and nondistended.
Urea breath test is positive, and EGD reveals a clean-based 1-cm ulcer in the duodenal bulb.
Stool antigen testing also confirms the presence of the same organism detected on breath testing.
explanation: The bacterium colonizes the gastric antrum, increasing acid secretion, while NSAIDs reduce mucosal prostaglandin protection. The combination overwhelms the mucosal defense.
keyFact: Duodenal ulcers: pain 2-3 hours after eating, relieved by food (acid is buffered). Gastric ulcers: pain worsened by food. H. pylori and NSAIDs are the two major causes — eliminating both dramatically reduces recurrence.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastric Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gastric cancer can present as an ulcer, but duodenal ulcers are almost never malignant. Gastric ulcers require biopsy to rule out cancer.

wrongAnswers.name: GERD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GERD causes burning epigastric/substernal pain but it's positional (worse lying down) and related to acid reflux, not meal timing.

wrongAnswers.name: Functional Dyspepsia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Functional dyspepsia causes similar symptoms but EGD is normal — this patient has a visible ulcer.

clues: A 52-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue and intense itching that is worst at night.
She has dry eyes and dry mouth, and her skin has become darker over several months.
Exam reveals hyperpigmentation, excoriations from scratching, hepatomegaly, and cholesterol deposits around her eyes.
Alkaline phosphatase is 420 with GGT of 380, and anti-mitochondrial antibody is positive at 1:640.
Liver biopsy shows granulomatous destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts with portal inflammation.
explanation: Autoimmune destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts impairs bile drainage, causing bile salt accumulation (pruritus), cholesterol elevation (xanthelasma), and progressive liver damage.
keyFact: AMA positive + small ducts + middle-aged woman + associated with Sjogren and hypothyroidism = PBC. AMA negative + large ducts + associated with UC + younger male = PSC.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSC targets LARGE ducts, is AMA NEGATIVE, p-ANCA positive, and is associated with UC — not the AMA-positive small duct disease seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-Induced Cholestasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug cholestasis resolves with drug withdrawal and doesn't produce AMA or the specific granulomatous duct destruction on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Choledocholithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CBD stones cause acute obstructive jaundice with pain, not the chronic progressive cholestatic picture with positive AMA.

clues: A 38-year-old man with a history of inflammatory bowel disease develops fatigue, pruritus, and jaundice.
His colitis has been in remission for years. He has right upper quadrant discomfort and no history of alcohol use or new medications.
Exam reveals mild jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and excoriations on the arms and trunk from scratching.
Alkaline phosphatase is 580 with GGT of 420, AMA is negative, and p-ANCA is positive.
MRCP shows alternating areas of narrowing and dilation creating a 'beaded' appearance of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.
explanation: Chronic inflammation and concentric fibrosis of medium and large bile ducts causes progressive stricturing and impaired bile flow, ultimately leading to cirrhosis.
keyFact: PSC + UC is the classic association (~70-80% of PSC patients have UC). AMA negative distinguishes from PBC. The cholangiocarcinoma risk means any new dominant stricture needs brushings. UDCA does NOT work in PSC (unlike PBC).

wrongAnswers.name: PBC
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PBC targets SMALL ducts, is AMA POSITIVE, affects middle-aged women, and responds to UDCA. PSC targets LARGE ducts, is AMA negative, and doesn't respond to UDCA.

wrongAnswers.name: Cholangiocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholangiocarcinoma is the feared COMPLICATION of PSC. The diffuse beading represents the underlying PSC; a focal dominant stricture would raise concern for superimposed cancer.

wrongAnswers.name: IgG4-Related Cholangitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgG4 disease mimics PSC on imaging but has elevated serum IgG4 and responds dramatically to steroids.

clues: A 60-year-old woman with a history of multiple abdominal surgeries presents with crampy abdominal pain and inability to pass gas for 24 hours.
The vomiting is bilious and becoming feculent, and her abdomen is progressively distending.
Exam reveals a distended tympanitic abdomen with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds and a midline surgical scar.
X-ray shows multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels and absence of gas in the colon.
CT shows a discrete transition point where dilated proximal bowel abruptly changes to collapsed distal bowel.
explanation: Fibrous adhesions from prior surgery create bands that can kink or compress the bowel, blocking the passage of intestinal contents and causing progressive dilation upstream.
keyFact: The most common cause of SBO in developed countries is adhesions from prior surgery. The transition point on CT identifies the site of obstruction. Complete obstruction (no gas in rectum) requires more urgent evaluation for strangulation than partial obstruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Paralytic Ileus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ileus causes distension and absent bowel sounds (not the high-pitched tinkling of mechanical obstruction) and there is no discrete transition point on imaging.

wrongAnswers.name: Large Bowel Obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LBO shows a dilated colon (not small bowel) and the most common cause is colon cancer, not adhesions.

wrongAnswers.name: Volvulus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sigmoid volvulus causes a coffee-bean sign on X-ray from twisted colon. This shows multiple dilated SMALL bowel loops with a transition point from adhesive bands.

clues: A 60-year-old woman presents with new-onset diabetes diagnosed just 3 months ago despite no family history or risk factors.
She has also been found to have gallstones, and her stools have become pale and greasy.
Exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness and steatorrhea confirmed on fecal fat testing.
CT reveals a large mass in the pancreatic head, and serum somatostatin level is markedly elevated.
The triad of new diabetes, gallstones, and steatorrhea occurred simultaneously in the absence of prior risk factors for any of them.
explanation: The tumor floods the body with the inhibitory hormone, shutting down multiple GI functions simultaneously.
keyFact: The triad of diabetes + gallstones + steatorrhea in a patient without prior risk factors should raise suspicion. Often found in the pancreatic head or duodenum. The duodenal location is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1.

wrongAnswers.name: Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pancreatic head cancer causes obstructive jaundice from bile duct compression, not the triad of diabetes + gallstones + steatorrhea with elevated somatostatin.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Pancreatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic pancreatitis causes diabetes and steatorrhea but with calcifications on imaging and a history of alcohol use, not the gallstone component with a pancreatic mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Glucagonoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Glucagonoma causes diabetes but with a distinctive migratory skin rash and weight loss, not gallstones and steatorrhea.

clues: A 58-year-old man with known chronic liver disease and abdominal fluid buildup presents with worsening belly pain and fever over 24 hours.
He has cirrhosis with tense ascites. He has had no abdominal procedures or obvious infection source, and his mental status is declining.
Exam reveals diffuse abdominal tenderness with tense ascites, confusion, and fever without peritoneal signs.
Diagnostic paracentesis shows ascitic fluid with an absolute neutrophil count greater than 250 cells/mm³.
Ascitic fluid culture grows a single organism (E. coli). No secondary source of infection is found on CT imaging.
explanation: Bacteria translocate from the gut lumen through the edematous intestinal wall into the ascitic fluid, which has impaired immune defenses (low complement, low opsonizing capacity).
keyFact: Ascitic fluid neutrophil count >250 cells/mm³ = SBP, treat immediately. SINGLE organism on culture distinguishes SBP from secondary peritonitis (multiple organisms, should prompt imaging for perforation). Prophylaxis with daily fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX after an episode reduces recurrence.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Peritonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary peritonitis from bowel perforation grows MULTIPLE organisms and requires surgery. SBP grows a SINGLE organism and is treated with antibiotics alone.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatic Encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HE causes confusion in cirrhotics but SBP can TRIGGER HE. The fever and elevated ascitic neutrophils identify the infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Perforated Viscus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Perforation causes peritonitis with free air on imaging and MULTIPLE organisms on culture. This has no free air and a single organism.

clues: A newborn presents with excessive drooling and choking with the first attempted feeding.
Attempts to pass a nasogastric tube are unsuccessful — the tube coils in the upper portion and cannot advance.
Chest X-ray shows the NG tube coiled in the upper pouch, and gas is visible in the stomach and bowel.
The presence of gas in the GI tract confirms a connection between the airway and the lower esophageal segment.
Echocardiogram, renal ultrasound, and spinal imaging are ordered to evaluate for vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies.
explanation: Abnormal separation of the foregut into trachea and esophagus during embryonic development creates a blind proximal pouch and a fistulous connection between the distal esophagus and trachea.
keyFact: The most common type (85%) has proximal esophageal atresia with a distal TEF. Gas in the stomach PROVES a distal fistula exists. No gas in the stomach = pure atresia without fistula. The VACTERL association describes commonly co-occurring anomalies.

wrongAnswers.name: Esophageal Web
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Webs cause dysphagia but not complete inability to pass an NG tube with gas in the stomach from an airway connection.

wrongAnswers.name: Choanal Atresia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Choanal atresia causes neonatal respiratory distress relieved by crying (mouth breathing) but without the feeding difficulties and coiled NG tube.

wrongAnswers.name: Laryngomalacia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Laryngomalacia causes stridor in infants but feeding is usually preserved and an NG tube passes normally into the stomach.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with bloody diarrhea containing mucus for 6 weeks.
She has 10-15 bowel movements per day with urgency and crampy lower abdominal pain.
Exam reveals mild left lower quadrant tenderness and blood on rectal exam.
Colonoscopy shows continuous erythematous friable mucosa starting at the rectum and extending to the splenic flexure with a sharp transition to normal.
Biopsy shows inflammation limited to the mucosa with crypt abscesses — the rectum is ALWAYS involved.
explanation: Chronic mucosal inflammation starts at the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous fashion. The inflammation is limited to the mucosal layer, unlike the transmural inflammation of Crohn.
keyFact: Continuous from rectum + mucosal only + crypt abscesses + bloody diarrhea = UC. Always involves rectum. Major long-term risk: colorectal cancer (surveillance colonoscopy starting 8-10 years after diagnosis). Associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Crohn Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Crohn causes skip lesions with transmural inflammation, granulomas, and often spares the rectum. This is continuous inflammation starting at the rectum with mucosal-only involvement.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious Colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Infectious colitis (C. diff, Shigella) causes bloody diarrhea but is acute, not 6 weeks, and biopsy shows acute neutrophilic inflammation without chronic architectural changes.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic Colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic colitis causes bloody diarrhea in elderly patients at watershed areas (splenic flexure), not continuous disease starting from the rectum in a young woman.

clues: A 52-year-old woman presents with massive watery diarrhea producing over 5 liters of stool per day.
The diarrhea persists even when she stops eating entirely. She is severely dehydrated with muscle cramps and tingling in her fingers.
Exam reveals marked dehydration, hypotension, and decreased deep tendon reflexes.
Potassium is 2.4, bicarbonate is 14, and the stool electrolyte pattern shows a secretory process.
Serum VIP level is markedly elevated, and CT shows a large mass in the pancreatic tail.
explanation: The tumor produces vasoactive intestinal peptide, which stimulates massive secretion of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen while inhibiting gastric acid production.
keyFact: Secretory diarrhea persists during fasting — this distinguishes it from osmotic diarrhea which stops when the offending solute is removed. The severe hypokalemia causes muscle weakness and potentially fatal arrhythmias.

wrongAnswers.name: Celiac Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Celiac causes chronic diarrhea related to gluten ingestion that improves on a gluten-free diet. This diarrhea persists during complete fasting.

wrongAnswers.name: Carcinoid Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoid causes diarrhea from serotonin with flushing and bronchospasm, not the massive 5-6 L/day secretory volume with low potassium.

wrongAnswers.name: Cholera
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholera causes massive secretory diarrhea from a toxin but is an acute infectious process with rice-water stools, not a chronic presentation with a pancreatic mass.

clues: An 18-year-old college student presents with a tremor that is getting worse over several months.
His roommate has noticed personality changes including impulsivity and emotional outbursts.
Exam reveals a resting and intention tremor, dysarthria, and a golden-brown ring at the periphery of each cornea visible on slit-lamp exam.
Ceruloplasmin is low at 8 mg/dL, and 24-hour urine copper is markedly elevated at 210 mcg per 24 hours.
Liver biopsy shows elevated hepatic copper content at 380 mcg/g dry weight, with steatohepatitis and early fibrosis.
explanation: Defective copper transport protein causes copper to accumulate in the liver, brain (especially basal ganglia), and cornea, causing hepatic, neurologic, and psychiatric damage.
keyFact: The corneal ring is copper deposited in Descemet's membrane. Presents as liver disease in children or neuropsychiatric disease in young adults. Always check in any young person with unexplained liver disease, movement disorder, or psychiatric symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemochromatosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemochromatosis involves IRON overload, not copper. Different metal, different gene, different organs primarily affected (liver, pancreas, heart, skin).

wrongAnswers.name: Huntington Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Huntington causes chorea and psychiatric changes but from a trinucleotide repeat expansion with caudate atrophy on imaging — no corneal ring or copper abnormality.

wrongAnswers.name: Parkinson Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Parkinson causes tremor but at a much older age (>60), without corneal rings or copper metabolism abnormalities. The tremor here includes intention component suggesting cerebellar involvement.

clues: A 75-year-old man presents with regurgitation of food eaten hours or even days earlier.
He has difficulty swallowing, persistent bad breath, and occasionally finds food particles on his pillow in the morning.
Exam reveals a soft compressible mass on the left side of his neck that gurgles when palpated.
Barium swallow shows a posterior outpouching arising from the pharyngoesophageal junction.
The outpouching is lined only by mucosa and submucosa without a muscular wall, and it fills with retained food debris visible on imaging.
explanation: Increased pharyngeal pressure during swallowing forces the mucosa to herniate through a weak point (Killian's triangle) in the posterior pharyngeal wall, creating a pouch that traps food.
keyFact: Elderly patient + regurgitation of OLD undigested food + halitosis + left-sided neck mass = Zenker diverticulum. It's a FALSE diverticulum (mucosa and submucosa only, no muscular wall). Aspiration pneumonia is a major complication.

wrongAnswers.name: Esophageal Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cancer causes progressive dysphagia but without regurgitation of days-old food, a compressible neck mass, or the posterior pharyngeal outpouching on barium.

wrongAnswers.name: Achalasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Achalasia causes food regurgitation but from esophageal body dilation with failed LES relaxation, not a pharyngeal outpouching.

wrongAnswers.name: Thyroid Nodule
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A thyroid mass can cause a neck lump but is anterior, doesn't gurgle, and doesn't cause regurgitation of old food.

clues: A 48-year-old man presents with recurrent epigastric pain despite maximum-dose acid suppression medication.
H. pylori testing is negative. Prior ulcers have been found in unusual locations including the jejunum, and he has chronic watery diarrhea.
Exam reveals epigastric tenderness, and prior endoscopy showed prominent thickened gastric folds.
Fasting gastrin is 1,200 pg/mL with a gastric pH below 2, confirming endogenous acid hypersecretion is present.
Intravenous secretin causes a paradoxical rise in gastrin, and CT shows a small enhancing mass in the pancreaticoduodenal region.
explanation: A gastrin-secreting tumor drives massive acid production that overwhelms mucosal defenses, causing ulcers even in locations downstream of the usual duodenal bulb.
keyFact: Refractory ulcers + unusual locations + diarrhea + massively elevated gastrin + low gastric pH = ZES. Must confirm pH is low — elevated gastrin with HIGH pH is just compensatory (atrophic gastritis or PPI effect, not ZES). Evaluate for MEN1.

wrongAnswers.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ordinary PUD responds to PPIs and H. pylori treatment. Refractory ulcers in unusual locations with gastrin >1000 suggest a gastrinoma.

wrongAnswers.name: H. pylori Gastritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: H. pylori is negative here. While H. pylori causes most ulcers and mildly elevates gastrin, it doesn't elevate it to 1,200.

wrongAnswers.name: PPI-Induced Hypergastrinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PPIs raise gastrin by suppressing acid, but gastric pH would be HIGH. Here the pH is LOW (<2) despite the elevated gastrin — the tumor is making acid.

clues: A 12-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of blood in his urine noticed during routine checkups.
His mother reports his hearing has been declining. His maternal uncle required dialysis in his 20s, and his maternal grandfather was deaf and died of kidney failure.
Exam reveals bilateral sensorineural hearing loss on audiometry and no skin, joint, or other abnormalities.
Urinalysis shows persistent microscopic hematuria with mild proteinuria, and audiogram confirms bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.
Kidney biopsy on electron microscopy shows lamellation and splitting of the glomerular basement membrane with a 'basket-weave' appearance.
explanation: Mutations in type IV collagen (a key component of basement membranes) affect the kidney, inner ear, and eye because all three organs rely on this collagen for structural integrity.
keyFact: Hematuria + sensorineural hearing loss + family history of renal failure = Alport. X-linked is most common (COL4A5 — males more severely affected). The basket-weave GBM on EM is pathognomonic. Some patients develop anterior lenticonus (eye finding).

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy causes recurrent hematuria but WITHOUT hearing loss, family history of renal failure, or the basket-weave GBM on EM.

wrongAnswers.name: Thin Basement Membrane Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thin BMD causes benign persistent hematuria with a thin (not split) GBM, no hearing loss, and an excellent prognosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Post-Streptococcal GN
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSGN causes hematuria 2-3 weeks after strep infection with low complement. This is RECURRENT hematuria with hearing loss and a family history.

clues: A 40-year-old man presents with flank pain on both sides and blood in his urine over the past several weeks.
His father had organ failure at age 50 requiring dialysis, and his sister had a brain aneurysm diagnosed recently.
Exam reveals bilateral palpable enlarged kidneys, blood pressure of 152/96, and mild costovertebral angle tenderness.
Renal ultrasound shows bilaterally enlarged kidneys filled with innumerable cysts replacing normal parenchyma.
CT also reveals multiple hepatic cysts, and genetic testing confirms a PKD1 mutation on chromosome 16.
explanation: Mutations in PKD1 or PKD2 cause progressive cyst formation that gradually replaces functional kidney tissue, leading to renal failure by age 50-70.
keyFact: Bilateral large cystic kidneys + family history + hypertension + liver cysts + berry aneurysm association = ADPKD. PKD1 (chromosome 16, 85% of cases) has earlier onset than PKD2. The most common hereditary cause of renal failure in adults.

wrongAnswers.name: Simple Renal Cysts
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Simple cysts are common, usually solitary or few, unilateral, and benign. ADPKD has innumerable BILATERAL cysts replacing the kidneys with a family history.

wrongAnswers.name: Autosomal Recessive PKD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ARPKD presents in infancy with bilateral enlarged kidneys and hepatic fibrosis. ADPKD presents in adults with a dominant family history.

wrongAnswers.name: Medullary Sponge Kidney
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Medullary sponge kidney causes medullary cysts with recurrent stones but kidneys are normal-sized, not massively enlarged and replaced by cysts.

clues: A 35-year-old African American man presents with progressive leg swelling and foamy urine over several weeks.
He has HIV and obesity. He was diagnosed 5 years ago and is not on antiretroviral therapy.
Exam reveals bilateral pitting edema to the knees, elevated blood pressure, and periorbital edema in the morning.
Urine protein is 8.4 g/day, albumin is 2.1, cholesterol is elevated, complement is normal, and renal ultrasound shows large echogenic kidneys.
Kidney biopsy shows segmental sclerosis in a subset of glomeruli, with the remaining glomeruli and segments appearing normal.
explanation: Podocyte injury causes segmental sclerosis that starts in some glomeruli and progressively involves more over time.
keyFact: Most common nephrotic syndrome in African Americans and in HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing variant). Looks like minimal change on EM (foot process effacement) but has sclerosis on light microscopy. Steroid RESISTANT — that's the clinical clue.

wrongAnswers.name: Minimal Change Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCD has completely normal light microscopy and responds to steroids in >90%. This shows sclerosis on biopsy and failed steroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Membranous Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Membranous shows diffuse capillary wall thickening with subepithelial deposits. This shows focal segmental scarring pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetic Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diabetic nephropathy shows nodular glomerulosclerosis in long-standing diabetics. This patient has HIV and obesity as the drivers.

clues: A 20-year-old man notices bright red blood in his urine on the same day he develops a sore throat.
He has had 3 similar episodes over 2 years — each time visible blood appears in his urine within a day of catching a cold, then resolves.
Blood pressure is mildly elevated and there is no edema or rash.
Urinalysis shows red blood cells and mild protein, and serum complement C3 and C4 are both completely NORMAL.
Kidney biopsy shows mesangial proliferation, and immunofluorescence reveals bright granular deposits of a single immunoglobulin class concentrated in the central stalk of the filtering units.
explanation: Overproduction of the mucosal immunoglobulin during infections leads to deposition in the glomerular mesangium, triggering inflammation and hematuria synchronous with infection.
keyFact: Hematuria DURING infection (synpharyngitic) with normal complement = this disease. Hematuria WEEKS AFTER infection with low complement = the post-streptococcal type. The mesangial deposits are histologically identical to the renal lesion in the IgA vasculitis of children.

wrongAnswers.name: Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSGN occurs 1-3 weeks AFTER infection with LOW complement. This occurs DURING infection with NORMAL complement.

wrongAnswers.name: Thin Basement Membrane Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thin BMD causes persistent microscopic hematuria (not episodic gross hematuria) with thin GBM on EM and no mesangial immunoglobulin deposits.

wrongAnswers.name: Alport Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alport causes persistent hematuria with hearing loss and eye abnormalities from type IV collagen defects, not episodic hematuria with mesangial deposits.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive lower extremity swelling and darker, foamy urine over the past month.
She has chronic hepatitis C. She noticed her urine becoming darker and foamy over the past month.
Exam reveals bilateral pitting edema and hypertension with her blood pressure elevated on this visit.
Urinalysis shows nephrotic-range proteinuria and active sediment with red blood cell casts. Complement C3 is low.
Kidney biopsy shows thickened capillary walls with a tram-track splitting of the basement membrane from mesangial interposition.
explanation: Immune complexes (often from hepatitis C-related cryoglobulinemia) deposit in the glomerulus, activating complement and stimulating mesangial cell proliferation that splits the basement membrane.
keyFact: Low C3 AND C4 (both complement pathways activated) with mixed nephrotic-nephritic picture. The tram-track (double-contour) appearance on biopsy is characteristic. Strongly associated with hepatitis C and cryoglobulinemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Membranous Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Membranous causes pure nephrotic syndrome with normal complement and subepithelial deposits. This has mixed nephrotic-nephritic features with low complement and a tram-track pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Post-Streptococcal GN
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSGN has low C3 but NORMAL C4 (alternative pathway only) and occurs after strep infection, not with chronic hepatitis C.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy has NORMAL complement with mesangial deposits. This has LOW complement with a tram-track pattern.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with progressive leg swelling and foamy urine for two months.
He has no systemic symptoms, no recent infections, and no medications known to affect the kidneys.
Exam reveals bilateral pitting edema and no rash, joint swelling, or other systemic findings.
Urine protein is 7.8 g/day, albumin is 2.0, cholesterol is elevated, complement is normal, and anti-PLA2R antibody is strongly positive.
Kidney biopsy shows diffuse capillary wall thickening, and electron microscopy reveals subepithelial dense deposits with a spike-and-dome pattern.
explanation: Antibodies target the PLA2R receptor on podocyte foot processes, forming immune complexes that deposit on the subepithelial side of the basement membrane and activate complement locally.
keyFact: Subepithelial deposits with spike-and-dome pattern on silver stain is pathognomonic. Anti-PLA2R in ~70% of primary cases. Always screen for secondary causes: hepatitis B, SLE, solid organ malignancy (especially in older patients), NSAIDs.

wrongAnswers.name: Minimal Change Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCD causes nephrotic syndrome with completely normal light microscopy. This shows diffuse capillary wall thickening with subepithelial deposits.

wrongAnswers.name: FSGS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS shows segmental sclerosis on light microscopy without the subepithelial deposits or spike-and-dome pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA deposits in the MESANGIUM, not the subepithelial space. IgA nephropathy typically presents with hematuria, not pure nephrotic syndrome.

clues: A 4-year-old boy develops puffy eyes and swollen legs one week after a cold, and his mother notices his urine looks foamy.
He has no blood in his urine, no recent sore throat, and he has been eating and drinking normally.
Exam reveals periorbital edema, bilateral pitting edema in the legs, and ascites with normal blood pressure.
Urine shows 4+ protein but NO blood and NO casts, albumin is 1.6, and complement levels are completely normal.

Kidney biopsy shows tissue that looks completely NORMAL under the light microscope and negative on immunofluorescence — the damage is visible ONLY on electron microscopy, which reveals fusion of the foot-like extensions of the cells wrapping the filtering capillaries.
explanation: The podocytes retract their foot processes, creating gaps in the filtration barrier that let albumin pour into the urine. The process is invisible to routine microscopy.
keyFact: Normal light microscopy is THE hallmark. >90% of children respond to steroids within 4 weeks. If steroids fail, the real diagnosis may be FSGS, which can look identical early but shows sclerosis on larger biopsy samples.

wrongAnswers.name: FSGS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS also causes nephrotic syndrome with foot process fusion, but light microscopy shows segmental sclerosis in some glomeruli. Light microscopy is completely normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Post-Streptococcal GN
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSGN causes nephrITIC syndrome — hematuria, red cell casts, hypertension, low complement. This is nephrOTIC — massive protein with no blood and normal complement.

wrongAnswers.name: Membranous Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Membranous is the most common nephrotic syndrome in ADULTS. Light microscopy shows thickened capillary walls. This child has normal light microscopy.

clues: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden severe flank pain that makes him unable to sit still, along with nausea and blood in his urine.
The pain radiates toward his groin. He has a history of recurrent stones and a high-oxalate diet with low fluid intake.
Exam reveals severe left costovertebral angle tenderness with no peritoneal signs.
Urinalysis shows blood with envelope-shaped crystals, and non-contrast CT reveals a 5-mm density in the left ureterovesical junction with proximal dilation.
The envelope-shaped crystals on urine microscopy are calcium oxalate. The 5-mm stone is lodged at the left ureterovesical junction.
explanation: Supersaturation of urine with calcium and oxalate leads to crystal formation and stone growth in the collecting system. When the stone enters the ureter, the obstruction and peristaltic contractions cause excruciating colicky pain.
keyFact: Envelope-shaped (bipyramidal) crystals = calcium oxalate (most common type, 80%). Coffin-lid crystals = struvite (infection stones). Hexagonal crystals = cystine. Rhomboid crystals = uric acid. Non-contrast CT is the imaging modality of choice.

wrongAnswers.name: Appendicitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Appendicitis causes RLQ pain but with peritoneal signs and no flank tenderness, hematuria, or stones on CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RCC causes hematuria but with a renal parenchymal mass, not a calcified density in the ureter with colicky pain.

wrongAnswers.name: Pyelonephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pyelonephritis causes flank pain with fever and pyuria, not the acute colicky pain with hematuria and a stone on CT.

clues: A 7-year-old boy's urine turned the color of cola this morning, and his mother says his face looks puffy.
He had a sore throat treated with antibiotics two weeks ago that has since resolved.
Exam reveals periorbital edema and blood pressure of 134/88, elevated for a 7-year-old.
Urine microscopy shows red blood cell casts, ASO titer is elevated at 640, and C3 is very low with normal C4.
ASO titer is 640, confirming recent streptococcal infection preceding the onset of nephritis by 1-3 weeks.
explanation: Immune complexes of streptococcal antigens and antibodies deposit in glomeruli, activating complement and triggering neutrophil infiltration. The infection is already over — the damage is from the delayed immune response.
keyFact: Low C3 with normal C4 indicates alternative pathway activation. The ASO titer confirms recent streptococcal infection. Antibiotics do NOT prevent this complication (unlike rheumatic fever, which antibiotics DO prevent).

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy causes hematuria DURING the infection (synpharyngitic), not 2 weeks later. Complement is NORMAL in IgA nephropathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HUS causes kidney failure in children but follows BLOODY DIARRHEA with fragmented red cells and low platelets — not sore throat with red cell casts.

wrongAnswers.name: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSP can cause hematuria but requires the classic tetrad: palpable purpura, joint pain, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. None of those are present here.

clues: A 60-year-old man presents with tea-colored urine and sharply declining function of his filtration organs over just two weeks.
He has had general malaise, and his creatinine has jumped from 1.2 to 5.8 in just 14 days.
Exam reveals hypertension, bilateral lower extremity edema, and decreased urine output over the past several days.
Urinalysis shows dysmorphic red blood cells and red cell casts with heavy proteinuria.
Kidney biopsy shows cellular crescents in more than 50% of glomeruli, and immunofluorescence reveals a pauci-immune pattern with positive anti-MPO antibodies.
explanation: The crescents form when the glomerular capillary wall is severely breached, allowing fibrin and inflammatory cells to leak into Bowman's space and trigger a proliferative response. Without treatment, end-stage renal failure develops in weeks to months.
keyFact: RPGN is a clinical syndrome (rapid kidney failure over days to weeks) with a pathologic correlate (crescents on biopsy). Three immune categories: anti-GBM (linear IF), immune complex (granular IF), pauci-immune/ANCA (negative IF). Identifying the category determines treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ATN causes acute kidney injury but with muddy brown granular casts and no red cell casts. The biopsy shows tubular damage, not glomerular crescents.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Kidney Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CKD develops over months to years with small scarred kidneys. This developed in 2 weeks — the tempo defines it as rapidly progressive.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy usually causes episodic hematuria with slow progression. The rapid 2-week decline with crescents on >50% of glomeruli indicates a much more aggressive process.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with blood pressure that remains elevated despite three medications and worsening lab values after a new prescription was added.
He has known coronary artery disease and peripheral vascular disease with claudication. The new prescription was an ACE inhibitor.
Exam reveals an abdominal bruit in the epigastric region and asymmetric kidney sizes on prior imaging.
Starting the ACE inhibitor caused his creatinine to jump from 1.4 to 3.2, which returned to baseline after stopping it.
Duplex ultrasound shows peak systolic velocity exceeding 200 cm/s in the right renal artery with a renal-aortic ratio above 3.5.
explanation: Narrowing of the renal artery reduces perfusion pressure to the kidney, which responds by activating the renin-angiotensin system to maintain filtration — causing secondary hypertension.
keyFact: Resistant hypertension + creatinine rise with ACE inhibitor + abdominal bruit + asymmetric kidney size = suspect RAS. In young women, consider fibromuscular dysplasia (string-of-beads on angiography). In older patients with atherosclerotic risk factors, atherosclerotic RAS is more common.

wrongAnswers.name: Essential Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Essential HTN is a diagnosis of exclusion with equal kidney sizes and no creatinine rise with ACE inhibitors. The resistant HTN with ACE inhibitor-induced renal failure suggests a secondary cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Kidney Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CKD causes hypertension and elevated creatinine, but the dramatic creatinine rise specifically triggered by ACE inhibition and the abdominal bruit point to renovascular disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Aldosteronism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary aldosteronism causes resistant hypertension but with low renin and high aldosterone. RAS has HIGH renin (the kidney is trying to compensate for low perfusion).

clues: A 30-year-old woman presents with recurrent kidney stones and muscle weakness over the past 2 years.
She has had 4 calcium phosphate stones and reports fatigue and proximal muscle cramps.
Labs show a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis with a serum bicarbonate of 14 and potassium of 2.8.
Despite the systemic acidosis, her urine pH is above 5.5 on repeated measurements with no evidence of UTI.
Stone analysis shows calcium phosphate composition, and an ammonium chloride loading test fails to lower urine pH below 5.3.
explanation: The distal tubule's alpha-intercalated cells cannot secrete hydrogen ions into the urine, so acid accumulates in the blood while the urine remains inappropriately alkaline.
keyFact: Non-anion gap acidosis + urine pH >5.5 + hypokalemia + calcium phosphate stones = type 1 (distal) RTA. Type 2 (proximal) also has hypokalemia but urine pH can be <5.5 (the proximal tubule wastes bicarb but the distal can still acidify). Type 4 has HYPERkalemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Tubular Acidosis Type 2
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Type 2 (proximal) causes non-anion gap acidosis from bicarbonate wasting, but the distal tubule CAN acidify urine below 5.5 once the bicarb threshold is exceeded.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Tubular Acidosis Type 4
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Type 4 causes non-anion gap acidosis but with HYPERkalemia (not hypokalemia) from aldosterone deficiency or resistance.

wrongAnswers.name: Diarrhea-Induced Acidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diarrhea causes non-anion gap acidosis from bicarbonate loss, but the kidneys respond normally by acidifying urine to pH <5.5. This patient's urine is inappropriately alkaline.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with severe thigh pain and dark brown urine after an intense exercise session.
He ran a marathon without adequate training or hydration. He reports diffuse muscle tenderness in both thighs.
Exam reveals tender swollen thigh muscles and urine that tests positive for blood on dipstick but shows NO red blood cells on microscopy.
CK is massively elevated at 45,000 IU/L, potassium is 6.2 mEq/L, and creatinine is rising rapidly.
Urine dipstick is positive for blood but microscopy shows zero red blood cells. Urine myoglobin is positive.
explanation: Massive skeletal muscle breakdown releases myoglobin, potassium, phosphorus, and CK into the bloodstream. Myoglobin is filtered by the kidneys and can precipitate in the tubules, causing acute kidney injury.
keyFact: Blood-positive urine dipstick WITHOUT red blood cells = myoglobinuria (or hemoglobinuria). CK >5x normal confirms the diagnosis. The hyperkalemia can be immediately life-threatening. Aggressive IV fluids to force diuresis is the cornerstone of treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Kidney Injury from Dehydration
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dehydration causes prerenal AKI but CK is normal, urine dipstick doesn't show blood, and there's no myoglobinuria.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemolysis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemolysis also causes blood-positive dipstick without RBCs (hemoglobinuria), but CK would be normal and the muscle findings would be absent.

wrongAnswers.name: Urinary Tract Infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: UTI causes positive dipstick for blood with white cells and bacteria, not the massively elevated CK and dark brown urine without RBCs.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents because his wedding ring no longer fits and his shoes are two sizes larger than five years ago.
He has worsening headaches and excessive sweating, and his wife says his face looks different.
Exam reveals enlarged hands and feet, frontal bossing, prognathism, widened tooth spacing, and bitemporal visual field deficits.
An oral glucose tolerance test fails to suppress growth hormone below 1 ng/mL, and IGF-1 is elevated.
MRI of the sella shows a 2.2-cm pituitary macroadenoma with suprasellar extension abutting the optic chiasm.
explanation: A pituitary adenoma secretes excess growth hormone, which stimulates IGF-1 production from the liver, causing progressive enlargement of acral structures and soft tissues in adults.
keyFact: In adults (fused growth plates), excess GH causes acral enlargement. In children (open growth plates), the same excess causes gigantism. The OGTT is the confirmatory test — GH normally suppresses with glucose loading.

wrongAnswers.name: Prolactinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prolactinomas cause galactorrhea and amenorrhea/hypogonadism without the acral enlargement and coarsening of facial features.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes facial puffiness and skin changes but not progressive bony enlargement of hands, feet, and jaw.

wrongAnswers.name: Paget Disease of Bone
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Paget causes bone enlargement (especially skull) but with elevated alkaline phosphatase and characteristic mosaic bone on biopsy, not soft tissue growth with pituitary mass.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue that has been worsening for months despite adequate sleep.
She has lost 15 pounds, feels dizzy and lightheaded when she stands up quickly, and has been craving salty foods.
Exam reveals hypotension that worsens on standing and darkening of the skin in her palmar creases and buccal mucosa.
Sodium is low, potassium is high, and a cosyntropin stimulation test shows cortisol fails to rise above 3 mcg/dL after stimulation.
ACTH level is markedly elevated at 450 pg/mL, and adrenal CT shows bilateral small atrophic adrenal glands.
explanation: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex eliminates cortisol and aldosterone production. The pituitary compensates by dramatically increasing ACTH, which cross-reacts with melanocyte receptors causing hyperpigmentation.
keyFact: Hyperpigmentation distinguishes primary (high ACTH → melanocyte stimulation) from secondary (low ACTH → no pigmentation). Low Na + high K = aldosterone deficiency (only in primary). Adrenal crisis with acute illness is life-threatening — stress-dose steroids are essential.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary (pituitary) insufficiency has LOW ACTH so there is NO hyperpigmentation. Potassium is normal because aldosterone is still produced (controlled by renin, not ACTH).

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes fatigue and weight changes but without hyperpigmentation, hyperkalemia, or hyponatremia from aldosterone deficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: SIADH
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SIADH causes hyponatremia but with LOW potassium (not high) and no hyperpigmentation or cortisol deficiency.

clues: A 75-year-old woman presents with a rapidly enlarging neck mass causing difficulty swallowing and hoarseness over just 4 weeks.
She had a known thyroid nodule for decades that was stable until one month ago when it began growing explosively.
Exam reveals a large fixed hard thyroid mass with vocal cord paralysis and stridor from airway compression.
FNA shows highly pleomorphic undifferentiated cells with bizarre mitotic figures.
Radioactive iodine uptake scan shows no uptake in the mass, and PET-CT reveals intense FDG avidity in the tumor.
explanation: This represents dedifferentiation of a prior well-differentiated thyroid cancer into an anaplastic form that has lost all thyroid-specific functions including iodine uptake.
keyFact: Rapidly enlarging hard fixed mass in an elderly patient with a long-standing goiter/nodule = anaplastic until proven otherwise. No RAI uptake (dedifferentiated). Median survival ~6 months. This is in stark contrast to the excellent prognosis of papillary and follicular thyroid cancers.

wrongAnswers.name: Thyroid Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thyroid lymphoma also presents as a rapidly enlarging mass in elderly patients (usually with Hashimoto), but biopsy shows lymphoid cells and it responds to chemotherapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Papillary has a slow course with excellent prognosis. This explosive growth with undifferentiated cells and no RAI uptake is anaplastic.

wrongAnswers.name: Riedel Thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Riedel causes a rock-hard thyroid from fibrosis but biopsy shows dense collagen, not undifferentiated malignant cells.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with difficulty starting his urine stream and a weak flow over the past year.
He gets up 4-5 times per night to urinate and has the sensation that his bladder never fully empties.
Digital rectal exam reveals a smooth symmetrically enlarged nontender prostate without nodules or irregularity.
PSA is mildly elevated at 5.2, urinalysis is normal, and post-void residual is 180 mL.
Uroflowmetry shows a diminished peak flow rate of 8 mL/sec with a prolonged voiding time.
explanation: The transitional zone of the prostate proliferates under the influence of DHT, compressing the urethra and causing obstructive voiding symptoms.
keyFact: Obstructive symptoms (hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying) + irritative symptoms (frequency, nocturia, urgency). Smooth symmetric enlargement distinguishes from cancer (hard, irregular nodule). PSA can be mildly elevated from size alone.

wrongAnswers.name: Prostate Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prostate cancer presents with a hard, irregular nodule on DRE, often in the posterior lobe (peripheral zone). This prostate is smooth and symmetric.

wrongAnswers.name: Urethral Stricture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stricture causes obstructive voiding symptoms but the prostate exam is normal, and there's usually a history of STI, trauma, or instrumentation.

wrongAnswers.name: Neurogenic Bladder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Neurogenic bladder causes urinary retention but with associated neurologic findings and a normal-sized prostate on exam.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding after intercourse and a foul-smelling watery discharge for 3 months.
She has never had a Pap smear, has had multiple sexual partners beginning at age 15, and smokes one pack daily.
Exam reveals a friable exophytic mass on the cervix that bleeds easily on contact.
Biopsy confirms invasive squamous cell carcinoma, and HPV testing is positive for a high-risk strain.
MRI pelvis shows the tumor extending into the parametria bilaterally with enlarged pelvic lymph nodes.
explanation: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types (16 and 18 account for ~70%) causes progressive cervical dysplasia that can advance to invasive cancer over years to decades.
keyFact: HPV types 16 and 18 are the highest-risk. The E6 protein degrades p53, and E7 inactivates Rb — disabling both major tumor suppressors. Early sexual activity, multiple partners, smoking, and immunosuppression are risk factors. Screening has dramatically reduced incidence in countries with organized programs.

wrongAnswers.name: Endometrial Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Endometrial cancer causes painless postmenopausal bleeding from estrogen excess, not postcoital bleeding with a cervical mass in a premenopausal woman with HPV.

wrongAnswers.name: Cervicitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervicitis causes discharge and cervical inflammation but without an exophytic mass, and biopsy shows inflammation, not invasive carcinoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Cervical Polyp
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervical polyps are benign, smooth, pedunculated growths — not the friable exophytic mass with biopsy-confirmed invasion seen here.

clues: A 10-year-old boy presents with headaches that have been worsening over 6 months.
He has fallen off his growth curve and reports increased thirst and frequent urination.
Exam reveals short stature, delayed puberty for age, and bitemporal visual field deficits.
CT shows a cystic and solid suprasellar mass with calcifications, and the cyst component has high protein content.
MRI confirms the mass is compressing the optic chiasm and pituitary stalk, and the cystic component contains dark oily fluid.
explanation: This benign but locally aggressive tumor arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch in the suprasellar region, compressing the pituitary, hypothalamus, and optic chiasm.
keyFact: The most common suprasellar tumor in children. Calcified cystic suprasellar mass + growth failure + visual field deficits + diabetes insipidus = craniopharyngioma. Despite being benign, its location makes complete resection difficult and recurrence is common.

wrongAnswers.name: Pituitary Adenoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pituitary adenomas are rare in children, are INTRAsellar (not suprasellar), and are usually solid without calcifications.

wrongAnswers.name: Optic Glioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Optic gliomas cause visual loss in children (often associated with NF1) but are solid enhancing masses along the optic pathway without the calcified cystic appearance.

wrongAnswers.name: Germinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Intracranial germinomas occur in the suprasellar region in children but are solid enhancing masses without calcifications, and beta-hCG may be elevated.

clues: A 52-year-old woman presents with a round face that looks different from her photos two years ago.
She has gained weight in her trunk while her arms and legs have gotten thinner, and she bruises from the slightest touch.
Exam reveals wide purple-red streaks on her abdomen wider than 1 cm, central obesity, a fat pad behind her neck, and proximal muscle weakness.
24-hour urine cortisol is 384, and overnight dexamethasone suppression fails to lower cortisol below 1.8.
ACTH is elevated at 88 pg/mL, and MRI sella shows a 6-mm pituitary microadenoma with contrast enhancement.
explanation: A pituitary adenoma produces excess ACTH, driving the adrenal glands to overproduce cortisol, which redistributes fat, breaks down muscle and skin, and deranges glucose metabolism.
keyFact: Wide (>1 cm) violaceous striae are the clinical pearl — purple because cortisol thins the skin until blood vessels show through. Algorithm: confirm excess cortisol → check ACTH → if high, image pituitary. Suppression with high-dose dex = pituitary source.

wrongAnswers.name: Metabolic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metabolic syndrome causes central obesity and diabetes but NOT the violaceous striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, or unsuppressible cortisol.

wrongAnswers.name: Exogenous Steroid Use
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The most common cause of this syndrome overall is prescribed steroids — but ACTH would be LOW (suppressed). Here ACTH is elevated.

wrongAnswers.name: Ectopic ACTH
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCLC can produce ectopic ACTH, but it does NOT suppress with high-dose dexamethasone. This patient's cortisol suppressed, pointing to the pituitary.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with extreme thirst and frequent urination starting 10 days after pituitary surgery.
He produces up to 12 liters of urine per day and wakes 8-10 times per night to urinate.
Exam reveals dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor despite the patient drinking water continuously.
Sodium is 148, serum osmolality is 305, but urine osmolality is only 75 despite concentrated blood.
Administration of desmopressin causes urine osmolality to rise from 75 to 600 within two hours of the dose.
explanation: Pituitary surgery damaged ADH-producing neurons. Without ADH, the collecting ducts remain impermeable to water and the kidneys produce massive amounts of dilute urine.
keyFact: Desmopressin response = central (brain problem). No response = nephrogenic (kidney problem). Central causes: surgery, trauma, tumors. Nephrogenic causes: lithium (#1), hypercalcemia, hypokalemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Psychogenic Polydipsia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polydipsia causes dilute urine but serum sodium is LOW (diluted from excess water). This patient's sodium is HIGH — he's losing free water.

wrongAnswers.name: SIADH
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SIADH causes CONCENTRATED urine with LOW serum sodium — the mirror image. This has DILUTE urine with HIGH sodium.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetes Mellitus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DM causes polyuria from glucose pulling water into the urine (osmotic diuresis) with high blood glucose. This patient's glucose is normal.

clues: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her roommate because she has been vomiting since last night and seems confused.
Her roommate says she takes daily insulin injections but ran out 2 days ago. Her breathing is deep and rapid with a fruity odor on her breath.
Exam reveals dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, and diffuse abdominal tenderness with no peritoneal signs.
Blood glucose is 480, pH is 7.12, bicarbonate is 6, anion gap is 28, and serum ketones are markedly positive.
Urine ketones are strongly positive and beta-hydroxybutyrate level is 8.2 mmol/L.
explanation: Without insulin, the body cannot use glucose and switches to fat metabolism, producing ketone bodies that accumulate and cause metabolic acidosis. The deep rapid breathing is the body's attempt to blow off CO2 to compensate.
keyFact: The anion gap metabolic acidosis from ketone accumulation is the defining feature. Always check potassium — it may be normal or high on presentation (shifting out of cells) but drops rapidly with insulin treatment. The abdominal pain mimics an acute abdomen.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HHS has very high glucose (>600) with high osmolality but WITHOUT significant ketosis or acidosis. This patient has profound ketoacidosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Lactic Acidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lactic acidosis causes an anion gap acidosis but without the hyperglycemia, ketonemia, or fruity breath.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Pancreatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The abdominal pain mimics pancreatitis, but the ketoacidosis with hyperglycemia after missed insulin doses identifies the metabolic cause.

clues: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a hard painless lump in her left chest wall area that she noticed 3 weeks ago.
Her mother had a similar malignancy at age 50. She started menarche at 11 and has never been pregnant.
Exam reveals a 2-cm firm irregular fixed mass in the upper outer quadrant with skin dimpling and a palpable axillary lymph node.
Mammogram shows a spiculated mass with clustered microcalcifications. Ultrasound confirms a solid hypoechoic lesion.
Core needle biopsy confirms invasive ductal carcinoma that is ER-positive, PR-positive, and HER2-negative.
explanation: This is the most common type of breast cancer. Malignant ductal epithelial cells invade through the basement membrane and can metastasize to axillary lymph nodes and distant sites.
keyFact: Upper outer quadrant is the most common location (most breast tissue). Skin dimpling occurs from tumor tethering to Cooper ligaments. ER/PR-positive tumors respond to endocrine therapy. HER2-positive tumors respond to trastuzumab. Triple-negative (ER-/PR-/HER2-) has the worst prognosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Fibroadenoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fibroadenoma is a painless breast mass in YOUNG women that is mobile, well-circumscribed, and rubbery — not fixed, irregular, or spiculated.

wrongAnswers.name: Breast Cyst
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cysts are fluid-filled, round, smooth, and often tender. Ultrasound shows an anechoic lesion, not a solid spiculated mass with calcifications.

wrongAnswers.name: Phyllodes Tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Phyllodes tumor is a large rapidly growing breast mass but is usually smooth and well-circumscribed, not spiculated with microcalcifications.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks of missed periods and lower pelvic pain on one side.
She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease. She has a positive urine pregnancy test and has been having vaginal spotting.
Exam reveals right adnexal tenderness without peritoneal signs and a closed cervical os.
Serum beta-hCG is 2,500, but transvaginal ultrasound shows NO intrauterine pregnancy and a complex mass in the right adnexa.
Serum beta-hCG is above the discriminatory level of 2,000, yet no intrauterine gestational sac is visible on transvaginal ultrasound.
explanation: The fertilized egg implanted in the fallopian tube (most common site) instead of the uterus. As it grows, it stretches the tube, causing pain, and eventual rupture causes life-threatening hemorrhage.
keyFact: Prior PID/tubal damage is the biggest risk factor. The discriminatory zone is critical: above that hCG level, you MUST see an intrauterine pregnancy on TVUS — if you don't, it's ectopic or nonviable until proven otherwise.

wrongAnswers.name: Threatened Abortion
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Threatened abortion causes bleeding with a VISIBLE intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound. No IUP is seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Ovarian Cyst Rupture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ruptured ovarian cyst causes adnexal pain but with a negative pregnancy test.

wrongAnswers.name: Appendicitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Appendicitis causes RLQ pain but with a negative pregnancy test and no adnexal mass.

clues: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with painless vaginal bleeding that has occurred intermittently for 2 months.
She is obese and nulliparous. She took unopposed estrogen for menopausal symptoms for 10 years and has diabetes.
Exam reveals an obese woman with a normal pelvic exam, no palpable masses, and no visible cervical or vaginal lesion.
Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 14 mm — in a postmenopausal woman, normal is less than 4-5 mm.
Endometrial biopsy reveals well-differentiated adenocarcinoma with invasion into the myometrium.
explanation: Chronic estrogen stimulation without progesterone opposition causes endometrial hyperplasia that can progress to carcinoma. Obesity (adipose tissue converts androgens to estrogen), nulliparity (no progesterone from pregnancy), and exogenous estrogen all contribute.
keyFact: ANY postmenopausal bleeding requires workup to exclude endometrial cancer. Risk factors share a theme of excess estrogen: obesity, nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause, unopposed estrogen, tamoxifen (acts as estrogen agonist in the uterus), PCOS.

wrongAnswers.name: Cervical Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervical cancer causes postcoital bleeding in younger women with HPV, not painless postmenopausal bleeding in an obese elderly woman with unopposed estrogen exposure.

wrongAnswers.name: Endometrial Polyp
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polyps cause postmenopausal bleeding with a thickened endometrium, but biopsy shows benign glandular tissue, not adenocarcinoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrophic Vaginitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atrophic vaginitis causes postmenopausal bleeding from thin fragile vaginal mucosa, but endometrial thickness would be thin (not 14 mm) and biopsy would be normal.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with severe cramping pelvic pain that occurs cyclically with her menstrual periods.
She has pain with intercourse, has been trying to conceive for 2 years without success, and has pain with bowel movements during menstruation.
Exam reveals a fixed retroverted uterus, tenderness in the posterior cul-de-sac, and nodularity along the uterosacral ligaments.
Ultrasound shows a 4-cm homogeneous cyst with low-level echoes in the left ovary, and CA-125 is mildly elevated.
Laparoscopy reveals dark 'powder-burn' or blue-black lesions on the peritoneal surfaces and ovaries.
explanation: Endometrial tissue implants outside the uterus and responds to cyclic hormonal changes, proliferating and bleeding with each menstrual cycle. The resulting inflammation causes pain and adhesions.
keyFact: Cyclic pelvic pain + dysmenorrhea + dyspareunia + infertility = endometriosis. The endometrioma ('chocolate cyst') contains old menstrual blood. The only definitive diagnosis is laparoscopy. Treatment: NSAIDs, hormonal suppression (OCPs, GnRH agonists), or surgical excision.

wrongAnswers.name: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PID causes pelvic pain but with fever, cervical motion tenderness, and purulent discharge — not the cyclic pattern with infertility and uterosacral nodularity.

wrongAnswers.name: Ovarian Cyst Rupture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ruptured cyst causes acute pain from a single event, not the chronic cyclic monthly pattern with infertility.

wrongAnswers.name: Adenomyosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adenomyosis causes dysmenorrhea with a diffusely enlarged boggy uterus from endometrial tissue within the myometrium. Endometriosis is endometrial tissue OUTSIDE the uterus.

clues: A 50-year-old woman presents with a slowly enlarging nodule on the front of her neck and new hip pain that prompted an X-ray.
The X-ray shows a lytic lesion in her femur. She has no family history of endocrine tumors and takes iodine supplementation for endemic goiter.
Exam reveals a 3-cm smooth thyroid nodule and tenderness over the right proximal femur.
FNA of the thyroid shows follicular cells with microfollicular architecture, but the pathologist CANNOT distinguish benign from malignant on cytology alone.
Surgical excision reveals capsular and vascular invasion on histopathology that was not visible on fine needle aspiration.
explanation: This carcinoma arises from follicular epithelial cells and preferentially spreads hematogenously to bone and lung, unlike the more common type that spreads through lymphatics.
keyFact: Hematogenous spread (bone, lung) distinguishes this from papillary (lymphatic spread). FNA CANNOT diagnose this cancer — capsular/vascular invasion seen only on surgical pathology is required. Iodine deficiency is a risk factor.

wrongAnswers.name: Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Papillary spreads LYMPHATICALLY (cervical nodes) and has distinctive nuclear features on FNA. Follicular spreads HEMATOGENOUSLY (bone, lung) and requires surgical histology for diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Follicular Adenoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adenoma and follicular carcinoma look identical on FNA. Only the surgical specimen showing capsular/vascular invasion proves malignancy.

wrongAnswers.name: Metastatic Cancer to Thyroid
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastatic cancer to the thyroid could present with a thyroid nodule and bone lesion, but the follicular architecture on biopsy confirms a primary thyroid tumor.

clues: A 20-year-old woman with a positive pregnancy test at 10 weeks presents with vaginal bleeding and severe nausea.
Her uterus is larger than expected for 10 weeks, and she is passing grape-like vesicles through her vagina.
Exam reveals a uterus measuring 16 weeks size, bilateral enlarged cystic ovaries, and blood pressure of 152/98.
Beta-hCG is 250,000 mIU/mL, and ultrasound shows a 'snowstorm' pattern without a visible fetus.
No fetal heart tones are detected, and the tissue passed per vagina shows hydropic chorionic villi on pathology.
explanation: Abnormal fertilization produces a mass of proliferating trophoblastic tissue instead of a viable embryo. The trophoblast produces massive amounts of hCG, which can stimulate the ovaries (theca-lutein cysts) and thyroid.
keyFact: Complete mole: 46,XX (all paternal), no fetus, highest risk of malignant transformation. Partial mole: 69,XXY (triploid), fetal parts present, lower risk. The hypertension before 20 weeks mimics preeclampsia and is a clue to GTD. The ovarian cysts resolve after evacuation as hCG falls.

wrongAnswers.name: Ectopic Pregnancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ectopic causes pain and elevated hCG but without the snowstorm uterine pattern, grape-like vesicles, or massively elevated hCG level.

wrongAnswers.name: Threatened Abortion
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Threatened abortion causes first-trimester bleeding but with a visible embryo on ultrasound and normal hCG trajectory.

wrongAnswers.name: Choriocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Choriocarcinoma is a malignant sequela of GTD, not the initial presentation. It would be diagnosed if hCG rises AFTER molar evacuation.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with unintentional weight loss despite eating more than usual.
She reports heat intolerance, tremor, and her eyes feel gritty and are more prominent than before.
Exam reveals a fine resting tremor, diffuse nontender goiter with an audible bruit, lid retraction, and exophthalmos.
TSH is undetectable, free T4 and T3 are elevated, and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) is positive.
Radioactive iodine uptake is diffusely increased throughout the entire gland at 65% at 24 hours.
explanation: Autoantibodies that mimic TSH bind and activate TSH receptors on thyroid follicular cells, causing unregulated thyroid hormone production. The same antibodies attack retro-orbital tissue causing the eye disease.
keyFact: The eye disease (ophthalmopathy) is specific to this autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism — not seen in other causes. Diffuse uptake on scan distinguishes this from toxic nodule (focal) and thyroiditis (low uptake).

wrongAnswers.name: Toxic Multinodular Goiter
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Toxic MNG causes hyperthyroidism but with PATCHY uptake on scan and no ophthalmopathy or TSH receptor antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Subacute Thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thyroiditis causes transient hyperthyroidism but with LOW uptake on scan (preformed hormone is leaking out, not being newly produced), neck pain, and elevated ESR.

wrongAnswers.name: Factitious Hyperthyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion causes low TSH with high T4, but the thyroid gland is small (not enlarged) and uptake is LOW.

clues: A 32-year-old woman at 36 weeks gestation presents with sudden right upper quadrant pain.
She has a history of preeclampsia this pregnancy. She reports nausea, vomiting, malaise, and dark urine.
Blood pressure is 158/102 with right upper quadrant tenderness, and the patient appears acutely uncomfortable.
LDH is 780, AST is 310, and platelets have dropped from 210,000 last week to 62,000 on today's labs.
Peripheral smear shows fragmented red cells (schistocytes) with undetectable haptoglobin and elevated indirect bilirubin.
explanation: Severe endothelial dysfunction causes microangiopathic hemolysis (shearing red cells), liver inflammation and necrosis (elevated enzymes, RUQ pain), and platelet consumption.
keyFact: HELLP = Hemolysis + Elevated Liver enzymes + Low Platelets. The RUQ pain is from hepatic capsule distension. Can progress to hepatic rupture. This can occur without significant hypertension or proteinuria in some cases.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AFLP causes liver failure in pregnancy but with hypoglycemia, low fibrinogen, and DIC — different from the microangiopathic hemolysis pattern here.

wrongAnswers.name: TTP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP causes microangiopathic hemolysis with thrombocytopenia but occurs outside pregnancy with neurologic symptoms and ADAMTS13 deficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Cholecystitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholecystitis causes RUQ pain but without hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, or the pregnancy-specific context.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue that she attributed to her busy schedule.
She has gained 15 pounds, is constipated, and feels cold when everyone else is comfortable.
Exam reveals a firm nontender goiter, dry coarse skin, periorbital puffiness, and delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes.
TSH is markedly elevated at 45 mIU/L with low free T4, and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are strongly positive.
Thyroid ultrasound shows a diffusely heterogeneous hypoechoic gland with increased vascularity.
explanation: Autoimmune T-cell-mediated destruction of thyroid follicular cells gradually reduces thyroid hormone production. The pituitary compensates by increasing TSH until it can no longer maintain adequate hormone levels.
keyFact: Anti-TPO antibodies are the diagnostic marker. The firm goiter is from lymphocytic infiltration and fibrosis. Increased risk of thyroid lymphoma (MALT type). Levothyroxine replacement is lifelong.

wrongAnswers.name: Subacute Thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis causes a TENDER painful gland with elevated ESR, often following a viral illness. This gland is firm and nontender.

wrongAnswers.name: Iodine Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Iodine deficiency causes hypothyroidism with goiter but anti-TPO antibodies are negative. This is the leading cause worldwide but not in iodine-sufficient countries.

wrongAnswers.name: Riedel Thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Riedel causes a rock-hard 'woody' thyroid from fibrosis that can mimic cancer, but it is rare and typically not associated with high anti-TPO antibodies.

clues: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because he has become progressively less responsive over the past several days.
He has type 2 diabetes managed with oral medications. His family says he stopped drinking fluids and appears severely dehydrated.
Exam reveals dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, and altered mental status. He is not breathing deeply or rapidly.
Blood glucose is 950 and serum osmolality is 385. He is severely dehydrated with poor skin turgor and dry mucous membranes.
pH is 7.32 with minimal ketones on serum and urine testing. C-peptide is detectable, indicating residual insulin production.
explanation: Residual insulin production in type 2 diabetes is sufficient to prevent ketogenesis but not enough to control glucose. The resulting severe hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis and progressive dehydration.
keyFact: HHS vs DKA: HHS has HIGHER glucose (often >600), HIGHER osmolality (>320), MORE dehydration, ALTERED mental status, but MINIMAL ketosis and MILD acidosis. DKA has lower glucose, significant ketosis, severe acidosis (pH <7.3), and Kussmaul breathing. HHS occurs in elderly type 2; DKA in young type 1.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DKA has significant ketosis with pH <7.3, low bicarbonate, anion gap, and the deep rapid breathing pattern. This patient has minimal ketones with pH 7.32 — not acidotic enough for DKA.

wrongAnswers.name: Stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stroke causes acute neurologic deficits but blood glucose would not be 950. The altered mental status here is from hyperosmolality.

wrongAnswers.name: Sepsis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sepsis causes altered mental status with dehydration, but the glucose of 950 with osmolality of 385 and minimal ketones identifies the specific metabolic emergency.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with tingling around her mouth and numbness in her fingertips one day after neck surgery.
She reports a feeling of tightness in her throat and intermittent muscle spasms in her hands.
Exam reveals a positive response when tapping on the facial nerve anterior to the ear — the corner of the mouth twitches.
Calcium is 6.8, phosphorus is 6.2, and PTH is inappropriately low at 4 pg/mL despite severe hypocalcemia.
The surgical report notes that total thyroidectomy was performed, and no parathyroid tissue was identified in the specimen.
explanation: Without PTH, the kidneys cannot reabsorb calcium or excrete phosphorus, and intestinal calcium absorption falls. The resulting hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability.
keyFact: Low calcium + low PTH + high phosphorus = hypoparathyroidism. Low calcium + HIGH PTH = the parathyroid is responding to low calcium from another cause (vitamin D deficiency, CKD). The facial twitch (Chvostek sign) and carpopedal spasm with BP cuff inflation (Trousseau sign) indicate neuromuscular irritability.

wrongAnswers.name: Vitamin D Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vitamin D deficiency causes low calcium but with HIGH PTH (the parathyroids respond appropriately) and low-normal phosphorus. PTH is LOW here.

wrongAnswers.name: Pseudohypoparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pseudo-HPT has low calcium with HIGH PTH (the kidneys are resistant to PTH). This has LOW PTH — the glands aren't making it.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypomagnesemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Severe magnesium deficiency can cause hypocalcemia by impairing PTH secretion, but magnesium is normal here and the post-surgical context makes surgical hypoparathyroidism most likely.

clues: A 32-year-old woman presents with inability to breastfeed following a complicated delivery.
The delivery involved massive hemorrhage requiring transfusion. She has had no menstrual periods since delivery 6 months ago, with progressive fatigue and cold intolerance.
Exam reveals pallor, dry skin, absent axillary and pubic hair, hypotension, and a well-healed cesarean scar.
TSH is low with low free T4, cortisol is low with low ACTH, and FSH/LH are low with low estradiol.
MRI sella shows a partially empty sella with decreased pituitary volume compared to expected size.
explanation: Massive blood loss during delivery caused ischemic necrosis of the enlarged pituitary gland. All anterior pituitary hormones are lost, causing failure of the thyroid, adrenals, and gonads.
keyFact: Low TSH WITH low T4 = central (pituitary) hypothyroidism. High TSH with low T4 = primary (thyroid) hypothyroidism. Failure to lactate postpartum is often the earliest sign because prolactin-producing cells are the most vulnerable to ischemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary hypothyroidism has HIGH TSH (the pituitary is trying). This patient has LOW TSH with low T4 — the pituitary has failed.

wrongAnswers.name: Addison Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Addison has low cortisol with HIGH ACTH (the pituitary is intact and screaming). This has low cortisol with LOW ACTH — the pituitary signal is absent.

wrongAnswers.name: Postpartum Depression
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PPD causes fatigue and mood changes but with normal hormone levels. The combination of multiple hormonal deficiencies after hemorrhagic delivery points to pituitary necrosis.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of confusion that resolve immediately with eating.
The episodes occur most often before meals and in the early morning. She has gained 20 pounds from eating constantly to prevent episodes.
Exam between episodes is unremarkable, but during a supervised fast she becomes confused with a glucose of 38.
At the time of hypoglycemia, insulin and C-peptide are both inappropriately elevated, and a sulfonylurea screen is negative.
CT with pancreatic protocol shows a 1.2-cm enhancing lesion in the pancreatic body.
