explanation: A beta cell tumor autonomously produces insulin regardless of blood glucose, causing fasting hypoglycemia that the patient compensates for by eating constantly.
keyFact: High insulin + high C-peptide = endogenous source (tumor or sulfonylurea). High insulin + LOW C-peptide = exogenous insulin injection. Sulfonylurea screen distinguishes drug-induced from tumor-produced insulin.

wrongAnswers.name: Factitious Hypoglycemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Injected insulin causes high insulin but LOW C-peptide. This patient has HIGH C-peptide — the insulin is coming from her own pancreas.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Hypoglycemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive hypoglycemia occurs 2-4 hours AFTER eating. This patient has FASTING hypoglycemia — worst before meals and overnight.

wrongAnswers.name: Adrenal Insufficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adrenal insufficiency causes hypoglycemia but insulin levels would be appropriately LOW, not elevated.

clues: An 18-year-old male is evaluated for delayed puberty and tall stature with long limbs.
He has noticed breast tissue developing and is struggling in school with language-based tasks.
Exam reveals gynecomastia, sparse facial and body hair, and testes measuring only 2-3 mL bilaterally.
Testosterone is low, FSH and LH are markedly elevated, and semen analysis shows no sperm.
Karyotype shows 47 chromosomes with an extra sex chromosome, confirming the suspected chromosomal aneuploidy.
explanation: The extra X chromosome causes seminiferous tubule fibrosis and Leydig cell dysfunction, resulting in small testes, low testosterone, and infertility.
keyFact: Most common sex chromosome aneuploidy in males. Gynecomastia carries 20-50x increased breast cancer risk. Associated with learning disabilities. Testosterone replacement improves quality of life but not fertility.

wrongAnswers.name: Kallmann Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kallmann causes delayed puberty with LOW FSH/LH (pituitary failure) and anosmia. Here FSH/LH are HIGH — the pituitary is working but the testes can't respond.

wrongAnswers.name: Prolactinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prolactinoma causes gynecomastia and low testosterone but FSH/LH are LOW from prolactin suppression, not HIGH.

wrongAnswers.name: Turner Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Turner affects FEMALES with short stature and 45,X karyotype. This is a tall male with 47,XXY.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with recurrent epigastric pain despite maximum-dose acid suppression.
His father had a pituitary tumor and died of pancreatic cancer. The patient recently had kidney stones from elevated calcium.
Labs show elevated calcium with elevated PTH, massively elevated gastrin, and elevated prolactin.
MRI shows a pituitary macroadenoma, CT shows a pancreatic mass, and sestamibi scan shows a parathyroid adenoma.
Genetic testing reveals a germline mutation in the menin tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13.
explanation: Loss of the menin tumor suppressor protein causes neoplastic transformation in three endocrine organs. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common and often earliest manifestation.
keyFact: The 3 P's: Pituitary + Pancreas + Parathyroid. Primary hyperparathyroidism is present in >95% and is often the first abnormality detected. Pancreatic tumors include gastrinoma (most common functional), insulinoma, glucagonoma. The menin gene is on chromosome 11.

wrongAnswers.name: MEN2A
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MEN2A involves medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia — different tumor spectrum with a RET mutation.

wrongAnswers.name: Sporadic Primary Hyperparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sporadic PHPT is a single parathyroid adenoma without pituitary or pancreatic tumors or family history.

wrongAnswers.name: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ZES can be sporadic or part of MEN1. The combination with pituitary tumor and hyperparathyroidism identifies the familial syndrome.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with a firm thyroid nodule found on routine physical examination during a checkup.
Her mother died of a thyroid malignancy, and her brother was recently diagnosed with an adrenal tumor causing episodic hypertension.
FNA of the thyroid nodule shows medullary thyroid carcinoma, and serum calcitonin is markedly elevated.
She has mildly elevated calcium with elevated PTH suggesting concurrent parathyroid disease.
Genetic testing confirms a RET proto-oncogene mutation, and her brother is found to have the same mutation.
explanation: Gain-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene cause tumor development in the thyroid C cells, adrenal medulla, and parathyroid glands.
keyFact: MEN2A: Medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma + primary hyperparathyroidism. MEN2B: MTC + pheo + mucosal neuromas + marfanoid habitus (NO parathyroid disease). ALWAYS screen for and treat pheo BEFORE any surgery. Prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended for RET mutation carriers.

wrongAnswers.name: MEN1
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MEN1 involves pituitary, pancreatic, and parathyroid tumors with a menin gene mutation. MEN2A involves thyroid, adrenal, and parathyroid with a RET mutation — different organs and different gene.

wrongAnswers.name: Sporadic Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sporadic MTC occurs without the familial pattern. The family history of thyroid and adrenal tumors with RET mutation confirms the hereditary syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Familial Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FMTC is a variant with MTC ONLY (no pheo or PHPT). This patient has concurrent hyperparathyroidism and her brother has a pheo — that's full MEN2A.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with a firm painless nodule on the front of his neck and unexplained chronic watery diarrhea.
His mother died of a pheochromocytoma, and his brother was recently diagnosed with hyperparathyroidism.
Exam reveals a hard fixed 2-cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe with palpable ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.
Serum calcitonin is markedly elevated, and fine needle aspiration shows cells with amyloid deposits that stain positive with Congo red.
Genetic testing confirms a RET proto-oncogene mutation on chromosome 10. His siblings are referred for screening.
explanation: Malignant parafollicular C cells overproduce calcitonin and deposit amyloid in the tumor stroma. The familial form is part of a multi-organ endocrine tumor syndrome.
keyFact: Calcitonin-producing C cells + amyloid on biopsy + RET mutation + family history of pheo and hyperparathyroidism = MEN2A pattern. Always check for pheo BEFORE thyroidectomy — undiagnosed pheochromocytoma during surgery can cause fatal hypertensive crisis.

wrongAnswers.name: Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Papillary is the most common thyroid cancer but arises from follicular cells (not C cells), does not produce calcitonin, and is not associated with RET mutations or MEN syndromes.

wrongAnswers.name: Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anaplastic is a rapidly fatal undifferentiated cancer in elderly patients, not a calcitonin-producing tumor in a young man with a familial syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Thyroid Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thyroid lymphoma presents as a rapidly enlarging mass in patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis, without calcitonin elevation or amyloid.

clues: A 75-year-old woman is brought in obtunded after being found in her unheated home during winter.
Her family reports she stopped taking a daily medication months ago and has been increasingly sluggish, confused, and sleeping excessively for weeks.
Her temperature is 93°F, heart rate 42, blood pressure 88/60, and she has generalized nonpitting edema with delayed deep tendon reflexes.
TSH is greater than 100 mIU/L with undetectable free T4, sodium is 122, and glucose is 55.
ABG shows CO2 retention from hypoventilation, and the medication she discontinued was levothyroxine.
explanation: Severe prolonged hypothyroidism decompensates into coma, usually triggered by cold exposure, infection, or medication noncompliance. Every organ system slows: heart, brain, lungs, kidneys, and thermoregulation.
keyFact: The triad: hypothermia + altered mental status + precipitating event in a hypothyroid patient. Give hydrocortisone WITH levothyroxine — if the patient has coexisting adrenal insufficiency, T4 alone increases cortisol metabolism and can be fatal.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothermia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothermia alone causes bradycardia and confusion but TSH is normal and there is no myxedematous edema or history of hypothyroidism.

wrongAnswers.name: Sepsis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sepsis causes altered mental status and hypotension but typically with fever (not hypothermia) and elevated white count, not TSH >100.

wrongAnswers.name: SIADH
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SIADH causes hyponatremia but severe hypothyroidism also impairs free water excretion. The TSH >100 with obtundation and hypothermia identifies the primary problem.

clues: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with progressive abdominal bloating and early satiety over 3 months.
Her sister had breast cancer at age 45, and her mother died of an ovarian malignancy at age 55.
Exam reveals shifting dullness consistent with ascites and a firm irregular pelvic mass palpable on bimanual exam.
CA-125 is 485, and CT shows bilateral complex adnexal masses with omental caking.
Peritoneal biopsies during surgical staging confirm high-grade serous carcinoma with characteristic psammoma bodies.
explanation: Epithelial ovarian cancer spreads by direct peritoneal seeding, producing ascites and omental involvement early. The deep pelvic location and nonspecific symptoms lead to late diagnosis in the majority of cases.
keyFact: Vague symptoms (bloating, early satiety, pelvic pressure) + postmenopausal + bilateral complex masses + omental caking + elevated CA-125 + ascites = ovarian cancer. BRCA1/2 mutations dramatically increase risk. No effective screening test exists for the general population.

wrongAnswers.name: Ovarian Cystadenoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cystadenomas are benign cystic ovarian tumors that are usually unilocular, unilateral, without solid components or peritoneal disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Meigs Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meigs syndrome is a fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion — benign, resolves after tumor removal. The bilateral complex masses with carcinomatosis here indicate malignancy.

wrongAnswers.name: Peritoneal Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Peritoneal TB causes ascites with peritoneal thickening and elevated CA-125 (a known mimic), but biopsy shows caseating granulomas, not carcinoma.

clues: A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal bloating and early satiety over two months.
She has no fever, weight loss, or menstrual irregularities, and her CA-125 is within normal limits.
Exam reveals a large nontender smooth mobile pelvic mass extending to the umbilicus.
Ultrasound shows a large thin-walled unilocular cystic mass arising from the right ovary without solid components, papillary projections, or ascites.
Surgical pathology shows the cyst is lined by a single layer of columnar epithelium without atypia or stromal invasion.
explanation: These are benign epithelial tumors that can grow very large, especially the mucinous type which can fill the entire abdomen. They are distinguished from their malignant counterparts by the absence of solid components, papillary excrescences, and peritoneal involvement.
keyFact: Serous cystadenoma = most common benign ovarian epithelial tumor. Mucinous can become massive. Features suggesting malignancy: solid components, papillary projections, septations, ascites, elevated CA-125. Bilateral serous tumors raise concern for malignancy.

wrongAnswers.name: Ovarian Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ovarian malignancy shows solid components, papillary projections, ascites, and elevated CA-125. This is a simple thin-walled cyst without worrisome features.

wrongAnswers.name: Mature Cystic Teratoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Teratomas contain fat, calcifications, and teeth from three germ layers. This is a simple cystic mass lined by epithelium without germ layer-derived contents.

wrongAnswers.name: Meigs Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meigs syndrome is a fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion. This is a cystic epithelial tumor without ascites.

clues: A 25-year-old woman presents with mild pelvic pain found during a routine gynecologic exam.
She has no menstrual irregularities, no weight changes, and no systemic symptoms.
Exam reveals a smooth mobile nontender adnexal mass approximately 6 cm in diameter on the right side.
Pelvic ultrasound shows a complex cystic mass with echogenic components including fat, calcifications, and what appears to be a tooth. CA-125 and AFP are normal.
CT confirms fat density within the mass, and the mass contains hair and sebaceous material.
explanation: This benign tumor contains differentiated tissues including skin, hair, teeth, bone, and thyroid tissue, derived from all three germ layers. It is the most common ovarian tumor in young women.
keyFact: Fat + calcification + teeth on imaging = dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma). Mature = benign. Immature = malignant (contains embryonic tissue, elevated AFP). Complications: ovarian torsion (the mass makes the ovary heavy) and rarely malignant transformation of a tissue component (usually squamous cell).

wrongAnswers.name: Ovarian Cystadenoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cystadenomas are cystic ovarian tumors but contain serous or mucinous fluid, not the fat/teeth/hair of a dermoid.

wrongAnswers.name: Endometrioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Endometriomas ('chocolate cysts') contain old blood and are associated with endometriosis symptoms. They don't contain fat, teeth, or calcifications.

wrongAnswers.name: Ovarian Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ovarian cancer causes solid/complex masses with elevated CA-125 in older women. This is a well-circumscribed mass with fat and teeth in a young woman with normal markers.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with sudden severe pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting that began while she was jogging.
She has a known 6-cm ovarian cyst diagnosed two months ago. The pain is constant and progressively worsening.
Exam reveals right lower quadrant tenderness with guarding, a palpable adnexal mass on bimanual exam, and no vaginal bleeding.
Pregnancy test is negative. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 9-cm enlarged right ovary with peripheral follicles pushed to the edges.
Doppler interrogation shows absent arterial and venous flow to the right ovary with a whirlpool sign of the twisted vascular pedicle.
explanation: The ovary rotates on its vascular pedicle, cutting off blood supply. The weight of a cyst or mass increases the risk by making the ovary pendulous.
keyFact: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain + known ovarian mass + absent Doppler flow = torsion until proven otherwise. Surgical emergency — ovarian viability decreases with time. Unlike testicular torsion, there is no 6-hour rule, but earlier intervention is better.

wrongAnswers.name: Ruptured Ovarian Cyst
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ruptured cyst causes sudden pelvic pain but with free fluid in the pelvis and PRESERVED ovarian blood flow on Doppler.

wrongAnswers.name: Ectopic Pregnancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ectopic causes pelvic pain with a positive pregnancy test. This patient's pregnancy test is negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Appendicitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Appendicitis causes RLQ pain but without an adnexal mass or absent ovarian blood flow on Doppler.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with a painless neck lump that her boyfriend noticed.
She has a history of childhood radiation to the neck for a prior malignancy. She has no symptoms of thyroid dysfunction.
Exam reveals a 1.5-cm firm nontender thyroid nodule with a small palpable cervical lymph node.
Thyroid ultrasound shows a hypoechoic solid nodule with microcalcifications and irregular margins.
FNA reveals cells with large, clear, grooved nuclei described as having an 'Orphan Annie eye' appearance, with psammoma bodies.
explanation: This is the most common thyroid malignancy, arising from follicular epithelial cells. It preferentially spreads via lymphatics to cervical lymph nodes.
keyFact: Psammoma bodies (concentric calcified laminations) and the nuclear features (grooves, inclusions, clearing) are pathognomonic. Radiation exposure is the strongest risk factor. Lymphatic spread to cervical nodes is common but prognosis remains excellent.

wrongAnswers.name: Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Follicular carcinoma spreads hematogenously (to lung and bone), not lymphatically. FNA cannot distinguish follicular carcinoma from adenoma — capsular invasion on surgical pathology is required.

wrongAnswers.name: Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Medullary arises from C cells, produces calcitonin, and deposits amyloid. Papillary has Orphan Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies from follicular cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Thyroid Adenoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adenomas are benign with regular architecture. The nuclear features (grooves, clearing, inclusions) and psammoma bodies confirm carcinoma.

clues: A 42-year-old woman presents with paroxysmal episodes of pounding headache lasting 15-20 minutes that resolve spontaneously.
During the episodes she is drenched in sweat with a racing heart, and her blood pressure has been resistant to four medications.
Between episodes her exam is unremarkable, but during one in the office her blood pressure spikes to 242/138.
Plasma free metanephrines are massively elevated at 12 times the upper limit of normal, and 24-hour urine catecholamines are elevated.
CT abdomen shows a 3.2-cm bright enhancing left adrenal mass with areas of central necrosis.
explanation: A catecholamine-producing tumor dumps epinephrine and norepinephrine in unpredictable boluses, causing paroxysmal hypertensive crises.
keyFact: Alpha-before-beta is the survival rule. Rule of 10s: 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, 10% malignant, 10% familial (MEN2A, VHL, NF1, SDH mutations). Plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive screening test.

wrongAnswers.name: Essential Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Essential hypertension is sustained and steady, not paroxysmal with 15-minute episodes of headache and diaphoresis.

wrongAnswers.name: Panic Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Panic attacks cause palpitations and sweating, but BP doesn't reach 242 systolic and metanephrines aren't elevated.

wrongAnswers.name: Thyroid Storm
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thyroid storm causes tachycardia and hypertension but continuously, not in discrete 15-minute paroxysms, and without an adrenal mass.

clues: A 34-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding.
She has had two prior cesarean deliveries and no prenatal complications until now.
Exam reveals a soft nontender uterus with a fetus in breech presentation. Digital cervical exam is specifically avoided.
Transabdominal ultrasound shows the placenta completely covering the internal cervical os.
Fetal heart tracing is reassuring, and the bleeding episode self-resolves with bed rest and observation.
explanation: The placenta implanted over the cervical os instead of in the upper uterus. As the cervix begins to thin and dilate in the third trimester, it shears the overlying placenta, causing painless bleeding.
keyFact: PAINLESS bleeding = previa. PAINFUL bleeding = abruption. Never do a digital cervical exam in previa — you could rupture a vessel in the placenta. Prior cesarean sections increase risk due to lower uterine segment scarring.

wrongAnswers.name: Placental Abruption
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Abruption causes PAINFUL bleeding with a rigid, tender uterus and sometimes fetal distress. This bleeding is PAINLESS with a soft nontender uterus.

wrongAnswers.name: Vasa Previa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vasa previa causes painless bleeding but from fetal vessels crossing the membranes, not the placenta itself covering the os. Fetal distress occurs immediately.

wrongAnswers.name: Bloody Show
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bloody show is scant mucoid blood-tinged discharge at labor onset, not the sudden bright red hemorrhage seen here.

clues: A 30-year-old woman at 35 weeks gestation presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding.
She has poorly controlled hypertension and reports recent cocaine use. The pain is constant and worsening.
Exam reveals a rigid, board-like, tender uterus with dark red vaginal blood and fetal heart tracings showing decelerations.
Ultrasound shows the placenta is NOT covering the cervical os. A retroplacental collection is difficult to visualize.
Emergent delivery reveals a large retroplacental blood clot compressing 40% of the placental surface. Fibrinogen is dropping rapidly.
explanation: The placenta separates prematurely from the uterine wall, causing hemorrhage behind the placenta. Blood may be trapped (concealed) or flow externally. The rigid uterus reflects continuous contraction around the blood collection.
keyFact: PAINFUL bleeding with a rigid tender uterus = abruption. PAINLESS bleeding with a soft uterus = previa. Risk factors: hypertension (#1), cocaine, trauma, prior abruption. DIC is the major maternal complication.

wrongAnswers.name: Placenta Previa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Previa causes PAINLESS bleeding with a soft nontender uterus. This has a rigid PAINFUL uterus with dark blood — classic abruption.

wrongAnswers.name: Uterine Rupture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rupture causes sudden pain and fetal distress (similar presentation) but typically in patients with prior uterine scars during active labor, not in the setting of hypertension and cocaine use.

wrongAnswers.name: Labor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal labor causes intermittent contractions with relaxation between them. The uterus here is continuously rigid and board-like — this is not normal labor.

clues: A 24-year-old woman presents with irregular periods occurring every 2-3 months since menarche.
She is obese. She has progressive dark coarse hair growth on her chin and upper lip and has been unable to conceive for over a year.
Exam reveals acne on her jawline, hirsutism on her face and abdomen, and dark velvety skin on the back of her neck.
Total testosterone is mildly elevated, LH:FSH ratio is greater than 2:1, and fasting insulin is elevated.
Pelvic ultrasound shows bilateral enlarged ovaries with 15 or more small follicles arranged peripherally — the string-of-pearls sign.
explanation: Excess androgens and insulin resistance disrupt normal follicular development, causing anovulation with multiple small arrested follicles, irregular cycles, and clinical signs of androgen excess.
keyFact: Diagnosis requires 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria: oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. The dark neck skin (acanthosis nigricans) signals insulin resistance. Metformin improves insulin sensitivity and may restore ovulation.

wrongAnswers.name: Cushing Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cushing causes weight gain and hirsutism but with central obesity, striae, proximal weakness, and elevated cortisol. This patient has normal cortisol with elevated androgens and LH:FSH imbalance.

wrongAnswers.name: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Late-onset CAH causes hyperandrogenism and irregular cycles, but 17-hydroxyprogesterone is elevated. It must be excluded in the workup of PCOS.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes menstrual irregularity and weight gain but not hirsutism, elevated testosterone, or polycystic ovaries. TSH should be checked.

clues: A 22-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 34 weeks gestation presents with a new headache and seeing flashing lights.
Her hands and face are significantly more swollen than expected for this stage of pregnancy, worsening over the past week.
Blood pressure is 162/104 measured on two occasions 4 hours apart, with 3+ pitting edema of the hands and face.
Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein with a protein-to-creatinine ratio of 1.2, platelets are 98,000, and AST is 142.
Serum uric acid is elevated at 7.8, and the sFlt-1 to PlGF ratio is markedly abnormal at greater than 85.
explanation: Abnormal placental development leads to release of antiangiogenic factors into the maternal circulation, causing widespread endothelial dysfunction with hypertension, proteinuria, and end-organ damage.
keyFact: New hypertension + proteinuria after 20 weeks gestation = preeclampsia. Severe features include: BP ≥160/110, platelets <100K, elevated LFTs, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, or cerebral/visual symptoms. Seizure (eclampsia) is the most feared neurologic complication.

wrongAnswers.name: Gestational Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gestational HTN is new hypertension after 20 weeks but WITHOUT proteinuria or end-organ damage. This patient has proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and elevated LFTs.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic HTN is present before 20 weeks or persists postpartum. This patient had normal pressures until 34 weeks.

wrongAnswers.name: HELLP Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HELLP (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) is a severe variant on the same spectrum — this patient is approaching HELLP territory with low platelets and elevated AST.

clues: A 50-year-old man on three blood pressure medications presents with recurrent muscle weakness and cramping.
His blood pressure remains elevated at 168/102 despite maximal doses. His potassium keeps dropping below 3.0 despite supplementation.
Exam reveals no remarkable findings beyond difficult-to-control hypertension — there is no cushingoid appearance or palpable mass.
Potassium is 2.8, bicarbonate is 30 (metabolic alkalosis), aldosterone is elevated, and renin is suppressed — the ratio is markedly elevated.
CT shows a 1.5-cm adrenal nodule, and adrenal vein sampling confirms lateralized aldosterone overproduction from the right adrenal gland.
explanation: An autonomous aldosterone-producing adenoma retains sodium (raising blood pressure) while excreting potassium and hydrogen ions (causing hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis).
keyFact: High aldosterone + LOW renin = primary (autonomous adrenal). High aldosterone + HIGH renin = secondary (renin-driven, as in renal artery stenosis). Metabolic alkalosis from H+ wasting is a subtle but consistent finding.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Artery Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RAS causes secondary aldosteronism with HIGH renin. This has LOW renin — the aldosterone production is autonomous.

wrongAnswers.name: Diuretic-Induced Hypokalemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thiazides cause hypokalemia, but the suppressed renin with elevated aldosterone and adrenal nodule confirm a primary adrenal process.

wrongAnswers.name: Cushing Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cortisol excess causes hypertension and hypokalemia but with cushingoid features and elevated cortisol — not isolated high aldosterone with low renin.

clues: A 60-year-old woman has an elevated calcium found incidentally on routine bloodwork.
She reports vague fatigue, constipation, and increased urination. She had a calcium-based kidney stone 2 years ago.
Exam is unremarkable without palpable neck masses, and there is no bony tenderness or deformity.
Calcium is 11.8, phosphorus is low at 2.1, PTH is elevated at 125, and 24-hour urine calcium is increased.
Sestamibi scan shows a single focus of increased uptake posterior to the left lower thyroid lobe.
explanation: An autonomous parathyroid adenoma ignores the high calcium feedback signal and continues secreting PTH, which raises calcium by increasing bone resorption, renal reabsorption, and vitamin D activation.
keyFact: 'Stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones' = kidney stones, bone pain, abdominal pain/constipation, and depression/confusion. High Ca + low PO4 + high PTH = primary. High Ca + LOW PTH = non-PTH-mediated (malignancy, granulomatous disease).

wrongAnswers.name: Hypercalcemia of Malignancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malignancy causes high calcium but PTH is LOW (suppressed) because the calcium elevation is from PTHrP, not from the parathyroid glands.

wrongAnswers.name: Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FHH also has high calcium and high PTH but urine calcium is LOW (the kidneys reabsorb it). Surgery doesn't help in FHH. Check urine calcium before surgery.

wrongAnswers.name: Vitamin D Intoxication
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vitamin D excess causes hypercalcemia but PTH is suppressed (LOW) and 25-OH vitamin D levels are markedly elevated.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with amenorrhea for 8 months and milky nipple discharge that occurs spontaneously from both sides.
She has noticed decreased libido and occasional headaches. A pregnancy test is negative.
Exam reveals bilateral galactorrhea expressed on exam with no visual field deficits.
Prolactin level is 220 ng/mL (normal <25), TSH is normal, and pregnancy has been excluded.
MRI shows a 9-mm pituitary microadenoma. The prolactin level of 220 ng/mL correlates with the tumor size.
explanation: The adenoma autonomously secretes prolactin, which suppresses GnRH pulsatility, causing hypogonadism (amenorrhea, decreased libido) and galactorrhea.
keyFact: Prolactinoma is the most common functioning pituitary adenoma. ALWAYS check prolactin before any pituitary surgery — if it's a prolactinoma, surgery is NOT first-line. Dopamine agonists both shrink the tumor and normalize prolactin. The prolactin level generally correlates with tumor size.

wrongAnswers.name: Pregnancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pregnancy elevates prolactin and causes amenorrhea with galactorrhea, but pregnancy test is negative here.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes mild prolactin elevation (TRH stimulates prolactin release), but TSH is normal here and prolactin is far higher than hypothyroidism alone would cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Medication Side Effect
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Antipsychotics and metoclopramide elevate prolactin by blocking dopamine, but this patient is on no medications and has a visible pituitary mass.

clues: A 70-year-old man presents for follow-up after an elevated lab value was found on screening.
He is asymptomatic with no urinary complaints, but his PSA has risen from 4.0 to 8.2 over two years.
Digital rectal exam reveals a hard irregular nodule in the posterior aspect of the prostate.
Transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy shows Gleason 3+4=7 adenocarcinoma involving 4 of 12 cores.
Staging bone scan shows multiple foci of increased uptake in the spine and pelvis, and alkaline phosphatase is elevated.
explanation: Prostate cancer arises from the peripheral zone (unlike BPH which is in the transitional zone), which is why it is palpable on DRE before causing urinary symptoms.
keyFact: Peripheral zone (cancer) vs transitional zone (BPH). Osteoblastic metastases (bone-forming, elevated alkaline phosphatase) vs most other cancers which cause osteolytic metastases. Gleason score predicts aggressiveness. Low-risk disease may be managed with active surveillance.

wrongAnswers.name: BPH
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BPH causes smooth symmetric enlargement of the transitional zone with obstructive urinary symptoms. This is a hard irregular nodule in the peripheral zone found on DRE.

wrongAnswers.name: Prostatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prostatitis causes a tender boggy prostate with urinary symptoms and fever, not a painless hard nodule with rising PSA.

wrongAnswers.name: Bladder Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bladder cancer causes hematuria from a bladder wall mass, not a prostatic nodule detected on DRE with rising PSA.

clues: A 65-year-old man with a known lung mass is brought to the emergency department confused and lethargic.
He has nausea and headache and appears clinically euvolemic — no signs of dehydration or fluid overload.
Exam shows no JVD, no edema, moist mucous membranes, and the only abnormality is altered mental status.
Sodium is 118, serum osmolality is 255, urine osmolality is 550, and urine sodium is 45. TSH and cortisol are both normal.
The lung biopsy report shows small cell carcinoma, and the ADH level is inappropriately elevated.
explanation: The lung tumor produces ADH that the body didn't ask for. Excess ADH causes the kidneys to retain water, diluting the blood and dropping the sodium while the patient appears euvolemic.
keyFact: Low Na + low serum osmolality + inappropriately concentrated urine + high urine Na + euvolemia + normal thyroid/adrenal = SIADH. Rule out hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency first. Rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Cerebral Salt Wasting
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CSW also causes low sodium with high urine sodium, but the patient is HYPOVOLEMIC (dehydrated), not euvolemic.

wrongAnswers.name: Heart Failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HF causes low sodium from dilution but the patient is VOLUME OVERLOADED with JVD and edema, not euvolemic.

wrongAnswers.name: Psychogenic Polydipsia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polydipsia dilutes blood but the urine is maximally DILUTE (osmolality <100). This urine is CONCENTRATED — the kidneys are inappropriately retaining water.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with neck pain radiating to her jaw and ear that started a few days ago.
She had a viral upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago. She feels jittery, has a fast heartbeat, and the neck is exquisitely tender.
Exam reveals an exquisitely tender enlarged firm thyroid gland, tachycardia of 110, and low-grade fever.
Free T4 is elevated at 3.8, TSH is suppressed at 0.02, ESR is 90, and CRP is markedly elevated.
Radioactive iodine uptake is very low at less than 2% at 24 hours despite the elevated hormone levels.
explanation: Viral infection triggers granulomatous destruction of thyroid follicles, releasing preformed thyroid hormone (thyrotoxic phase) followed by hypothyroidism as stores are depleted, then eventual recovery.
keyFact: The triphasic course: hyperthyroid (hormone leak) → hypothyroid (stores depleted) → euthyroid (recovery). LOW radioactive iodine uptake distinguishes this from Graves disease (HIGH uptake). NSAIDs or steroids for pain — NOT antithyroid drugs (the gland isn't making new hormone).

wrongAnswers.name: Graves Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Graves causes hyperthyroidism but with HIGH radioactive iodine uptake (the gland is hyperactive), a painless diffuse goiter, and often eye findings. This has LOW uptake and a painful gland.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Suppurative Thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial thyroiditis causes a tender thyroid but with fluctuance, purulence, and positive cultures. Subacute is post-viral with granulomatous inflammation.

wrongAnswers.name: Hashimoto Thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hashimoto causes a painless goiter with hypothyroidism and positive anti-TPO antibodies. This is an acutely painful gland with hyperthyroidism following a viral illness.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with a painless firm mass in his right testicle that he noticed while showering.
He has a history of an undescended right testicle that was surgically corrected at age 3.
Exam reveals a firm nontender mass within the right testis that does not transilluminate with a penlight.
Testicular ultrasound confirms a solid hypoechoic intratesticular mass. Serum beta-hCG is mildly elevated, AFP is normal, and LDH is elevated.
Radical inguinal orchiectomy pathology shows sheets of uniform large cells with clear cytoplasm separated by fibrous septa containing lymphocytes.
explanation: This is the most common testicular germ cell tumor, occurring in young men with a peak incidence at age 25-35. Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) is the strongest risk factor even after surgical correction.
keyFact: AFP NORMAL = pure seminoma (very radiosensitive, excellent prognosis). AFP ELEVATED = nonseminomatous component (needs chemotherapy, not just radiation). All painless testicular masses are cancer until proven otherwise — never biopsy through the scrotum (risk of tumor seeding).

wrongAnswers.name: Testicular Torsion
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Torsion causes sudden severe PAIN with an absent cremasteric reflex. This mass is painless.

wrongAnswers.name: Epididymitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Epididymitis causes a painful, tender epididymis that improves with elevation (Prehn sign), not a painless solid intratesticular mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Hydrocele
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A hydrocele transilluminates (lights up when a penlight is held behind it). This mass does NOT transilluminate — it's solid.

clues: A 14-year-old boy presents with sudden severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep 3 hours ago.
The pain started abruptly without trauma, and he has nausea and vomiting. He has had one prior episode that resolved spontaneously.
Exam reveals a high-riding left testicle with a horizontal lie, an absent cremasteric reflex on the left, and tenderness that does not improve with elevation.
Color Doppler ultrasound shows absent arterial and venous blood flow to the left testicle compared to normal on the right.
Manual detorsion in the ER restores blood flow, confirmed by repeat Doppler showing return of arterial signal.
explanation: The spermatic cord twists, cutting off arterial blood supply and venous drainage to the testicle. Without rapid detorsion, the testicle becomes ischemic and dies.
keyFact: Absent cremasteric reflex is the most sensitive physical exam finding. The testis must be salvaged within 6 hours for >90% viability — after 24 hours, salvage rate drops below 10%. The contralateral testis is ALSO fixed during surgery (bilateral orchiopexy) to prevent future torsion on the other side.

wrongAnswers.name: Epididymitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Epididymitis causes gradual onset of scrotal pain with fever, dysuria, and RELIEF with elevation (positive Prehn sign). This is sudden onset WITHOUT relief on elevation and no cremasteric reflex.

wrongAnswers.name: Testicular Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cancer causes a painless firm mass within the testicle, not sudden severe pain with absent blood flow.

wrongAnswers.name: Inguinal Hernia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: An incarcerated hernia causes groin pain with a palpable mass in the inguinal canal. Ultrasound shows bowel in the inguinal canal, not absent testicular blood flow.

clues: A 35-year-old woman who recently stopped her methimazole presents to the emergency department with a fever of 104°F, severe agitation, and confusion.
She recently underwent emergency surgery for appendicitis, which appears to have triggered the decompensation. She had been on methimazole.
Exam reveals a delirious diaphoretic woman with heart rate of 160 (irregularly irregular), fine tremor, and a diffuse goiter with an audible bruit.
Free T4 is markedly elevated and TSH is undetectable. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated and calcium is high.
The Burch-Wartofsky score exceeds 45 based on fever over 104, heart rate over 140, atrial fibrillation, delirium, and a precipitating surgical event.
explanation: This is a life-threatening decompensation of hyperthyroidism, typically precipitated by surgery, infection, or medication noncompliance. Every organ system is in overdrive from catecholamine hypersensitivity.
keyFact: This is a CLINICAL diagnosis — there is no lab threshold that defines it. The Burch-Wartofsky score uses clinical criteria (fever, tachycardia, CNS dysfunction, GI symptoms). The treatment ORDER matters: beta-blocker → thionamide → iodine (after thionamide). Adding corticosteroids blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.

wrongAnswers.name: Sepsis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sepsis causes fever and tachycardia, but without the goiter, lid lag, tremor, or markedly elevated thyroid hormones with undetectable TSH.

wrongAnswers.name: Pheochromocytoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pheo causes hypertension and tachycardia from catecholamine excess, but without elevated thyroid hormones, goiter, or lid lag.

wrongAnswers.name: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NMS causes high fever with rigidity from dopamine blockade, not the fine tremor and goiter with elevated thyroid hormones.

clues: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated because she has never had a menstrual period and is much shorter than her peers despite average-height parents.
She was born with puffy hands and feet as a newborn, and breast development has not begun.
Exam reveals short stature, a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, a low posterior hairline, a webbed neck, and no signs of puberty.
FSH and LH are markedly elevated while estradiol is undetectable, renal ultrasound shows a horseshoe kidney, and echocardiogram reveals a bicuspid aortic valve.
Karyotype shows only 45 chromosomes with a single sex chromosome.
explanation: With only one X chromosome, the ovaries develop initially but degenerate before birth, leaving nonfunctional streaks. Without ovarian estrogen, puberty cannot occur.
keyFact: Bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation are the classic cardiac associations — aortic dissection is a leading cause of death. Intelligence is normal. Neonatal lymphedema and cystic hygroma on prenatal ultrasound are early clues.

wrongAnswers.name: Klinefelter Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Klinefelter (47,XXY) affects MALES with tall stature, small testes, and gynecomastia — not a short female with primary amenorrhea.

wrongAnswers.name: Kallmann Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kallmann causes amenorrhea but with LOW FSH/LH (the pituitary isn't signaling) and anosmia. Here FSH/LH are HIGH — the pituitary is trying but the ovaries can't respond.

wrongAnswers.name: Constitutional Growth Delay
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Constitutional delay causes short stature and delayed puberty but FSH/LH are low (prepubertal), and there are no associated anomalies.

clues: A 12-year-old boy presents with excessive thirst that has been worsening over three weeks.
He has been urinating frequently including bedwetting at night, and has lost 10 pounds.
Exam reveals a thin dehydrated boy with dry mucous membranes and fruity-smelling breath.
Blood glucose is 420, pH is 7.22, bicarbonate is 10, and serum ketones are markedly positive.
Anti-GAD65 and anti-islet cell antibodies are positive, and C-peptide is undetectable.
explanation: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells creates absolute insulin deficiency. Without insulin, glucose cannot enter cells and the body switches to fat metabolism, producing ketones.
keyFact: Low C-peptide (no insulin production) with positive autoantibodies distinguishes this from type 2 (where C-peptide is high from insulin resistance). DKA is often the presenting event. Associated with HLA-DR3 and DR4.

wrongAnswers.name: Type 2 Diabetes
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Type 2 occurs in obese adults with high C-peptide (insulin resistance), no autoantibodies, and rarely presents with ketoacidosis.

wrongAnswers.name: DKA from Type 2
wrongAnswers.whyNot: While type 2 can rarely cause DKA, the thin child with autoantibodies and undetectable C-peptide confirms autoimmune type 1.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetes Insipidus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DI causes polyuria and polydipsia but with dilute urine and normal glucose — not the hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis.

clues: A 52-year-old man presents with increased thirst and frequent urination noticed over the past few months.
He is obese with a BMI of 34. He has a non-healing wound on his foot that has been present for 6 weeks despite local care.
Exam reveals dark velvety thickened skin on the back of his neck and a 2-cm neuropathic ulcer on his plantar surface.
Fasting glucose is 210, hemoglobin A1c is 9.2%, and fasting insulin is elevated.
C-peptide level is elevated, confirming endogenous insulin production. Anti-GAD and anti-islet cell antibodies are both negative.
explanation: Peripheral tissues resist the action of insulin, and the pancreas initially compensates by producing more. Eventually the beta cells cannot keep up with the demand.
keyFact: Elevated C-peptide = the pancreas IS making insulin but the body isn't responding. Acanthosis nigricans is a marker of insulin resistance. Metformin is first-line. SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists have cardiovascular and renal benefits.

wrongAnswers.name: Type 1 Diabetes
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Type 1 has LOW C-peptide (no insulin production), positive autoantibodies, and presents in thin young patients with ketoacidosis. This patient is obese with high C-peptide.

wrongAnswers.name: MODY
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MODY is monogenic diabetes presenting in thin young patients with autosomal dominant inheritance. This is a classic metabolic syndrome presentation.

wrongAnswers.name: Cushing Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cushing causes secondary diabetes with central obesity, but the acanthosis nigricans, family history, and lack of classic cushingoid features favor primary type 2 diabetes.

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with heavy prolonged menstrual periods requiring frequent pad changes.
She has pelvic pressure and urinary frequency, and her periods have been getting heavier over 2 years.
Exam reveals an irregularly enlarged nontender uterus palpable at the level of the umbilicus.
Hemoglobin is 9.2 from chronic blood loss, and pelvic ultrasound shows multiple well-circumscribed solid masses within the myometrium.
MRI pelvis confirms the masses are T2-hypointense well-defined intramural lesions without evidence of necrosis or rapid growth.
explanation: Benign monoclonal smooth muscle tumors arise within the myometrium and grow under hormonal influence, causing heavy bleeding (submucosal location), bulk symptoms (intramural), or pain (pedunculated with torsion).
keyFact: Most common benign tumor in women. Higher prevalence in African American women. Submucosal fibroids cause the most bleeding. Subserosal cause bulk symptoms. They SHRINK after menopause. Rapid growth in postmenopausal women raises concern for leiomyosarcoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Endometrial Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Endometrial cancer causes abnormal uterine bleeding but with a thickened endometrium on imaging, not well-circumscribed myometrial masses.

wrongAnswers.name: Adenomyosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adenomyosis causes heavy bleeding with a diffusely enlarged boggy uterus, not the focal well-circumscribed masses seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Ovarian Tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ovarian tumors are adnexal masses separate from the uterus. These are clearly within the myometrium on ultrasound.

clues: A 7-year-old girl is referred by her teacher for frequent brief episodes of staring and unresponsiveness throughout the school day.
Episodes start and stop abruptly, lasting 5-10 seconds, and she resumes her activity immediately with no memory of what happened.
During an observed episode, she stares with subtle eyelid fluttering, is unresponsive to her name, then returns to normal within seconds.
The episodes are reliably provoked by 3 minutes of hyperventilation, and there is no post-event confusion or drowsiness.
EEG shows generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges that begin and end abruptly, corresponding to the observed clinical episodes.
explanation: Generalized thalamocortical circuits produce synchronous rhythmic discharges that briefly impair consciousness without causing convulsive movements.
keyFact: Brief staring spells (5-15 seconds) + no post-ictal state + provoked by hyperventilation + 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave = absence seizures. Ethosuximide is first-line for absence-only epilepsy. Valproate if generalized tonic-clonic seizures coexist. Most children outgrow them by adolescence.

wrongAnswers.name: Complex Partial Seizures
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Complex partial seizures cause staring but with automatisms (lip-smacking, fumbling), post-ictal confusion, and focal EEG discharges — not generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave.

wrongAnswers.name: ADHD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ADHD causes inattention but the child is still responsive when spoken to and there are no EEG abnormalities.

wrongAnswers.name: Daydreaming
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Daydreaming children respond to external stimulation and don't have the abrupt onset/offset, eyelid fluttering, or EEG changes.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with hearing loss on the right side that has worsened gradually over two years.
She has persistent tinnitus in the right ear and occasional unsteadiness when walking.
Tuning fork tests confirm sensorineural hearing loss on the right; the rest of the neurologic exam is normal.
Audiometry shows asymmetric high-frequency sensorineural loss on the right with poor word discrimination.
MRI with gadolinium shows a 2.5-cm enhancing mass in the right cerebellopontine angle arising from the vestibular nerve.
explanation: Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve proliferate to form a benign tumor that compresses the cochlear nerve (hearing loss), vestibular nerve (unsteadiness), and potentially the facial nerve (CN VII) and trigeminal nerve (CN V) as it enlarges.
keyFact: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + CPA mass on MRI = schwannoma. Bilateral tumors = NF2. The cerebellopontine angle location can also compress CN V (facial numbness) and CN VII (facial weakness).

wrongAnswers.name: Meniere Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meniere causes episodic vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness, but MRI is normal — no mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Otosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Otosclerosis causes CONDUCTIVE hearing loss (bone > air on Rinne) from stapes fixation, not sensorineural loss with a CPA mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningiomas can occur at the CPA and look similar on imaging, but they arise from meninges and have a dural tail on MRI, while schwannomas arise from the nerve itself.

clues: A 72-year-old woman is brought by her family for gradually worsening memory over the past 2 years.
She has gotten lost driving to familiar places, left the stove on multiple times, and cannot remember how to operate the microwave.
She cannot recall three objects after 5 minutes, cannot copy interlocking pentagons, and has word-finding difficulty, but motor function and reflexes are normal.
MRI shows bilateral hippocampal atrophy with temporoparietal cortical thinning, without focal lesions or white matter disease.
CSF biomarkers show decreased amyloid-beta-42 and elevated phosphorylated tau protein levels.
explanation: Progressive accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles destroys neurons in the hippocampus and association cortex, causing the gradual memory and cognitive decline.
keyFact: Insidious onset with gradual progression, early memory loss (hippocampus), then language, visuospatial, and executive function decline. Motor and sensory function are preserved until late stages. The most common cause of dementia.

wrongAnswers.name: Vascular Dementia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vascular dementia has a stepwise decline with focal neurologic deficits and white matter changes on MRI. This is gradual with hippocampal atrophy and no vascular lesions.

wrongAnswers.name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NPH causes the triad of dementia + gait disturbance + urinary incontinence with enlarged ventricles. This has hippocampal atrophy without gait or urinary symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Lewy Body Dementia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LBD has fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. This patient has gradual decline without fluctuations, hallucinations, or motor findings.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with 6 months of progressive hand weakness and difficulty gripping a pen.
The weakness has spread to his left hand and he is tripping more frequently, with mildly slurred speech and no numbness anywhere.
Exam shows severe wasting of the small hand muscles with visible spontaneous twitching, yet reflexes are brisk throughout with upgoing toes bilaterally and intact sensation.
MRI of the brain and spine is normal, and EMG shows widespread denervation across multiple body regions with normal nerve conduction velocities.
Upper motor neuron signs (brisk reflexes, upgoing toes) and lower motor neuron signs (wasting, twitching, denervation) are present simultaneously in the same limbs, with no sensory loss.
explanation: Both upper and lower motor neurons degenerate simultaneously. Upper neuron death causes hyperreflexia; lower neuron death causes atrophy and fasciculations. Sensation is spared because sensory neurons are not affected.
keyFact: Mixed UMN + LMN signs in the same territory without sensory loss is pathognomonic. Most die of respiratory failure within 3-5 years. Riluzole extends survival modestly. Normal MRI excludes structural causes.

wrongAnswers.name: Cervical Myelopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cord compression causes UMN signs in legs and LMN signs in arms at ONE level. ALS causes mixed signs at MULTIPLE levels with normal MRI.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS causes UMN signs with sensory changes and MRI lesions. ALS has NO sensory loss and NORMAL MRI. The LMN signs (atrophy, fasciculations) don't occur in MS.

wrongAnswers.name: Myasthenia Gravis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MG causes fatigable weakness starting in the eyes with normal reflexes and no atrophy. ALS has hyperactive reflexes and visible wasting.

clues: A 35-year-old man woke up this morning with the right side of his face drooping and food falling from his mouth.
He had pain behind his right ear yesterday and noticed everything tasted metallic on the right side of his tongue.
Exam shows complete right-sided facial weakness affecting both the forehead and the lower face -- he cannot wrinkle his forehead, close his eye, or smile on the right.
There are no other cranial nerve deficits, no limb weakness, and hearing and vestibular function are normal.
MRI shows enhancement and swelling of the right facial nerve within the temporal bone canal, with no intracranial mass or stroke.
explanation: Inflammation and swelling of the facial nerve within the narrow bony canal in the temporal bone causes compression and dysfunction of the entire nerve.
keyFact: Upper AND lower face = peripheral (LMN) lesion. Lower face ONLY with forehead sparing = central (UMN) lesion (stroke). The forehead receives bilateral cortical input, so a unilateral stroke spares it. Most cases recover completely. Eye protection is critical to prevent corneal damage.

wrongAnswers.name: Stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A stroke affecting the facial nerve nucleus causes lower face weakness ONLY — the forehead is spared because it receives bilateral cortical innervation. This patient's forehead is involved.

wrongAnswers.name: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ramsay Hunt is VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion causing facial paralysis WITH vesicles in the ear canal and severe ear pain. No vesicles are described here.

wrongAnswers.name: Acoustic Neuroma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acoustic neuromas primarily cause hearing loss and tinnitus, with facial nerve involvement occurring late as the tumor grows. Isolated acute facial palsy without hearing loss is not the typical presentation.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with brief intense spinning episodes triggered by rolling over in bed or looking up.
Each episode lasts less than 60 seconds and resolves on its own; she has no hearing loss or tinnitus.
Dix-Hallpike testing with the right ear down provokes upbeating torsional nystagmus after a 2-3 second delay that fatigues with repetition and resolves in 30 seconds.
Hearing is normal on formal testing, and there are no cerebellar or brainstem signs.
A canalith repositioning maneuver (Epley) resolves the nystagmus and vertigo completely within one session.
explanation: Small calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia) from the utricle become dislodged and float into a semicircular canal (usually posterior), where they stimulate the hair cells with positional changes.
keyFact: Brief episodes (<60 seconds) triggered by specific head positions + latent fatigable nystagmus on positional testing + normal hearing = BPPV. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver both diagnoses and (via the Epley maneuver) treats it. No medication needed — just repositioning.

wrongAnswers.name: Meniere Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meniere causes episodes lasting HOURS (not seconds) with hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness. BPPV episodes last <60 seconds with normal hearing.

wrongAnswers.name: Vestibular Neuritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vestibular neuritis causes constant vertigo lasting DAYS from viral inflammation, not brief positional episodes.

wrongAnswers.name: Central Vertigo
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Central causes (brainstem stroke, posterior fossa tumor) cause non-fatigable nystagmus, non-positional vertigo, and associated cerebellar or brainstem signs. BPPV nystagmus is latent and fatigable.

clues: A 28-year-old man presents with leg weakness on one side and numbness to pain on the opposite side after a penetrating neck injury.
He cannot feel a pinprick on his left leg but can feel it normally on his right leg, which is the weak side.
Exam shows right-sided weakness below the injury with an upgoing toe, loss of vibration and position sense on the right, but loss of pain and temperature on the left.
Light touch and proprioception are lost on the same side as the injury and motor deficit; pain and temperature are lost on the opposite side.
MRI of the cervical spine shows a hemicord lesion on the right at the level of the stab wound, with sparing of the left hemicord.
explanation: Hemisection of the cord disrupts ipsilateral motor fibers (corticospinal tract) and ipsilateral position/vibration fibers (dorsal columns) while disrupting contralateral pain/temperature fibers (spinothalamic tract, which has already crossed).
keyFact: Ipsilateral motor loss + ipsilateral proprioception/vibration loss + CONTRALATERAL pain/temperature loss = cord hemisection. The reason: spinothalamic crosses within 1-2 levels, dorsal columns and corticospinal cross in the brainstem.

wrongAnswers.name: Central Cord Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Central cord syndrome causes bilateral upper extremity weakness greater than lower with dissociated sensory loss. Brown-Séquard is distinctly unilateral with contralateral pain loss.

wrongAnswers.name: Anterior Cord Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anterior cord syndrome causes bilateral motor and pain/temperature loss below the level with preserved proprioception. Brown-Séquard is hemisection with ipsilateral/contralateral split.

wrongAnswers.name: Cauda Equina Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cauda equina causes bilateral lower motor neuron signs with saddle anesthesia. This is an upper motor neuron hemisection pattern with dissociated sensory findings.

clues: A 45-year-old man with chronic back pain presents with new-onset inability to urinate that developed over 24 hours.
He noticed he could not feel the toilet seat when sitting down, and he has bilateral leg weakness.
Exam reveals decreased perianal sensation, absent anal wink reflex, decreased rectal tone, and bilateral ankle areflexia.
Post-void residual is 600 mL, and lower extremity reflexes are absent bilaterally.
MRI shows a large central disc herniation at L4-L5 compressing the nerve roots below the conus medullaris.
explanation: A large central disc compresses the bundle of nerve roots that continue below the spinal cord terminus (which ends at L1-L2), causing bilateral lower motor neuron signs and sphincter dysfunction.
keyFact: The 'red flags': urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg weakness, and decreased rectal tone. This is a LOWER motor neuron pattern (flaccid, areflexic) because it compresses roots, not the cord itself. Surgical emergency.

wrongAnswers.name: Conus Medullaris Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Conus involves the spinal cord terminus (L1-L2) and causes UPPER and lower motor neuron mixed signs with early sphincter involvement. Cauda equina is pure LOWER motor neuron.

wrongAnswers.name: Lumbar Disc Herniation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A typical lateral disc herniation compresses a SINGLE nerve root causing unilateral radiculopathy. Cauda equina is a CENTRAL herniation compressing MULTIPLE roots bilaterally.

wrongAnswers.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBS causes ascending bilateral weakness with areflexia, but onset is over days-weeks after an infection, not acute with a disc herniation and saddle anesthesia.

clues: A 25-year-old woman presents with headaches at the back of her skull that worsen with coughing and straining.
She has neck pain and numbness in her hands with difficulty performing fine motor tasks.
Exam reveals downbeat nystagmus on downgaze and decreased pain sensation across both shoulders in a cape-like distribution.
MRI of the cervical spine shows a fluid-filled cavity within the central cord extending from C3 to C7.
MRI of the craniocervical junction shows the cerebellar tonsils extending more than 5 mm below the foramen magnum.
explanation: The cerebellar tonsils herniate through the foramen magnum, compressing the brainstem and upper cord and obstructing CSF flow, which can produce a secondary syrinx.
keyFact: Occipital headaches worsened by Valsalva + downbeat nystagmus + cape-distribution sensory loss + tonsillar herniation >5mm on MRI = Chiari I. Type I is acquired/congenital. Type II (with myelomeningocele) presents in infancy. The secondary syrinx explains the dissociated sensory findings.

wrongAnswers.name: Tension Headache
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tension headache is bilateral and pressing but not worsened specifically by coughing/straining and does not cause downbeat nystagmus or sensory loss.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS causes varied neurologic deficits but with periventricular white matter lesions, not tonsillar herniation on MRI.

wrongAnswers.name: Posterior Fossa Tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A posterior fossa tumor can cause similar symptoms but MRI shows a mass lesion, not tonsillar herniation.

clues: A 65-year-old woman presents with rapidly progressive cognitive decline developing over just 8 weeks.
She went from fully functional to unable to care for herself in under two months, with visual disturbances and involuntary jerking.
Exam reveals myoclonus, cerebellar ataxia, and akinetic mutism.
EEG shows periodic sharp wave complexes at regular intervals, and MRI DWI shows high signal in the cortex and caudate.
CSF RT-QuIC assay is positive, and CSF 14-3-3 protein is elevated.
explanation: A misfolded prion protein (PrPSc) catalyzes normal PrPC to refold into the abnormal form, creating a chain reaction that produces spongiform vacuolation in the brain.
keyFact: Rapidly progressive dementia (weeks to months) with myoclonus + periodic sharp waves on EEG + cortical ribboning on DWI-MRI is the classic triad. No treatment exists. The prion resists standard sterilization — instruments require special decontamination.

wrongAnswers.name: Alzheimer Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alzheimer progresses over YEARS, not weeks. The extremely rapid decline with myoclonus and periodic sharp waves on EEG is not Alzheimer.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Encephalitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Encephalitis causes acute confusion with fever and CSF pleocytosis. CJD has no fever, no CSF pleocytosis, and a distinctive EEG pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune Encephalitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Autoimmune encephalitis causes subacute cognitive decline with seizures and specific antibodies, but it is treatable and doesn't show the periodic sharp wave EEG pattern.

clues: A 4-year-old boy presents with difficulty climbing stairs and frequent falls during play.
He uses a characteristic maneuver to stand from the floor, walking his hands up his thighs to push himself upright.
Exam reveals pseudohypertrophy of the calves that feel firm and rubbery, proximal weakness, and a waddling gait.
CK is massively elevated at 15,000, and genetic testing confirms a deletion in the dystrophin gene on the X chromosome.
Muscle biopsy immunostaining shows complete absence of dystrophin protein at the sarcolemma.
explanation: Without the anchoring protein, the muscle cell membrane tears during contraction, allowing calcium influx that destroys the fiber. Progressive replacement with fat and fibrosis produces the pseudohypertrophy.
keyFact: X-linked recessive — only boys. The maneuver of climbing up the legs (Gowers sign) reflects proximal weakness. CK is massively elevated (10,000-50,000). Death typically from respiratory failure or cardiomyopathy by age 20-30. The milder form (Becker) has partial protein present.

wrongAnswers.name: Becker Muscular Dystrophy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Becker involves the same gene but with REDUCED (not absent) protein, later onset, and slower progression — ambulation is preserved into adulthood.

wrongAnswers.name: Spinal Muscular Atrophy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SMA causes proximal weakness in children but from anterior horn cell degeneration with NORMAL CK and no pseudohypertrophy.

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polymyositis causes proximal weakness with elevated CK but in adults with inflammatory infiltrate on biopsy, not a genetic protein deficiency in a young boy.

clues: A 20-year-old man presents after being hit in the head with a baseball, followed by a brief loss of consciousness.
After appearing lucid for about an hour, he rapidly becomes confused and then unresponsive.
GCS has dropped from 14 to 7, the left pupil is fixed and dilated, and he has right-sided weakness.
CT shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection between the skull and dura on the left temporal region with midline shift.
A skull fracture is visible crossing the groove of the middle meningeal artery on the left temporal bone.
explanation: Trauma ruptures the middle meningeal artery (the temporal bone is thin and the artery runs in a groove along its inner surface). Arterial pressure rapidly expands the collection between skull and dura.
keyFact: The lucid interval is classic but not universal. Biconvex (lens-shaped) on CT = epidural (arterial, doesn't cross suture lines). Crescent-shaped on CT = subdural (venous, crosses suture lines). This is a neurosurgical emergency.

wrongAnswers.name: Subdural Hematoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Subdural is crescent-shaped on CT from torn bridging veins, with slower onset (often in elderly on anticoagulants). This is biconvex with the classic lucid interval after temporal trauma.

wrongAnswers.name: Concussion
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Concussion causes brief LOC with full recovery. The deterioration with pupil dilation and hemiparesis after a lucid interval indicates an expanding intracranial mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SAH shows blood in the cisterns and subarachnoid space, not a biconvex extra-axial collection.

clues: An 18-month-old child has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes during a febrile illness.
The child was developmentally normal, has no seizure history, and the seizure was symmetric and brief.
After the seizure the child cries briefly then returns to normal neurologic baseline within 15 minutes.
CBC, electrolytes, and glucose are normal; the child is alert and back to baseline.
Temperature is 103.8 F from otitis media, and the fever rose rapidly just before the event occurred.
explanation: The immature brain has a lower threshold for seizure activity during rapid temperature changes. The seizure is provoked by fever, not by an underlying neurologic disorder.
keyFact: Simple febrile seizure: generalized, <15 minutes, single occurrence in 24 hours, normal development = benign, no workup beyond identifying the fever source. Complex febrile seizure: focal, >15 minutes, or recurrent in 24 hours = needs further evaluation.

wrongAnswers.name: Epilepsy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Epilepsy causes unprovoked seizures. This seizure was provoked by fever in the typical age range and was simple — no increased epilepsy risk.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningitis causes seizures with fever but with persistent altered mental status, neck stiffness, and abnormal CSF. This child returns to normal baseline quickly.

wrongAnswers.name: Shaken Baby Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Abusive head trauma causes seizures in infants but with retinal hemorrhages, subdural hematoma, and encephalopathy — not a brief generalized seizure with rapid return to baseline during a febrile illness.

clues: A 12-year-old boy presents with progressive difficulty walking and clumsiness that began around age 8.
He stumbles frequently and his handwriting has deteriorated; a sister has similar symptoms.
Exam reveals a wide-based gait, absent deep tendon reflexes at the ankles and knees, positive Romberg sign, and bilateral upgoing toes.
Echocardiogram reveals concentric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and scoliosis is present on spine examination.
Genetic testing reveals a homozygous GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin gene.
explanation: The expanded GAA repeat silences production of frataxin, a mitochondrial protein needed for iron-sulfur cluster assembly. Iron accumulates in mitochondria, generating free radicals that damage the heart, dorsal root ganglia, spinocerebellar tracts, and corticospinal tracts.
keyFact: The combination of areflexia (peripheral nerve/dorsal column damage — lower motor neuron sign) with upgoing toes (corticospinal tract damage — upper motor neuron sign) is unusual and characteristic. Autosomal RECESSIVE — unlike most trinucleotide repeat disorders which are autosomal dominant.

wrongAnswers.name: Ataxia-Telangiectasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AT causes progressive ataxia too but with telangiectasias, IgA deficiency, and elevated AFP — none present here. AT involves a DNA repair gene, not mitochondrial iron.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS can cause ataxia with mixed upper/lower motor neuron findings, but presents in adults with relapsing episodes and white matter lesions on MRI — not progressive childhood ataxia with cardiomyopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Vitamin E Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vitamin E deficiency causes spinocerebellar ataxia that mimics Friedreich ataxia, and should always be checked — but it doesn't cause cardiomyopathy or have a trinucleotide repeat.

clues: A 58-year-old man is brought by his wife for personality changes over the past year, including disinhibited behavior and shoplifting.
He was previously a reserved accountant; he now overeats compulsively and seems to lack empathy for others' feelings.
He is unconcerned about his behavior, makes inappropriate jokes during the exam, and has poor insight, but his memory is relatively preserved for recent events.
Neuropsychological testing shows severe deficits in executive function and social cognition with relatively spared episodic memory.
MRI shows marked bilateral atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes with relative sparing of the parietal and occipital lobes.
explanation: Degeneration of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes causes progressive deterioration of personality, social conduct, and executive function before memory is significantly affected.
keyFact: Behavioral changes BEFORE memory loss distinguishes this from Alzheimer (memory loss first). Onset typically age 45-65 (younger than Alzheimer). Subtypes include behavioral variant, semantic dementia, and progressive nonfluent aphasia.

wrongAnswers.name: Alzheimer Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alzheimer presents with MEMORY loss first with relative preservation of personality early. This patient has personality and behavioral changes with preserved memory.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mania can cause disinhibition, but it's episodic with a return to baseline. This is progressive and unrelenting with frontal lobe atrophy on imaging.

wrongAnswers.name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NPH causes dementia with gait disturbance and urinary incontinence with enlarged ventricles, not focal frontal-temporal atrophy with behavioral disinhibition.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with progressive weakness starting in his feet and climbing upward over 4 days.
He had watery diarrhea 2 weeks ago that resolved on its own, and he reports tingling in his hands and feet.
Lower extremity strength is severely reduced, upper extremity grip is mildly weak, and deep tendon reflexes are absent at every level tested.
Lumbar puncture shows protein of 186 mg/dL with only 3 white cells.
Forced vital capacity is 33% of predicted, and nerve conduction studies show prolonged distal latencies with conduction block in multiple nerves.
explanation: Post-infectious molecular mimicry triggers autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin, causing ascending weakness with areflexia. The ascending pattern threatens the phrenic nerve and respiratory muscles.
keyFact: High protein with normal cells in the spinal fluid is the classic laboratory finding. Respiratory monitoring every 4-6 hours is essential — the breathing muscles are peripheral nerve targets. IVIG or plasmapheresis works; steroids do NOT.

wrongAnswers.name: Spinal Cord Compression
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cord compression causes UPPER motor neuron signs — brisk reflexes, upgoing toes, a sensory level, and early bladder dysfunction. This has absent reflexes with no bladder symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Myasthenia Gravis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MG starts in the eyes, worsens with repeated use, and has normal reflexes. This started in the feet, is progressively worsening regardless of rest, and reflexes are absent.

wrongAnswers.name: Poliomyelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polio causes asymmetric lower motor neuron weakness without sensory involvement. This is symmetric ascending weakness with sensory changes and elevated CSF protein.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with a droopy right eyelid that his wife noticed recently.
He also has right shoulder and arm pain radiating down the inside of his arm.
Exam reveals right-sided ptosis, a constricted right pupil, and decreased sweating on the right face.
The pupillary asymmetry increases in darkness -- the affected pupil fails to dilate while the normal pupil does.
CT chest shows a mass at the apex of the right lung invading the adjacent bony and neurovascular structures.
explanation: Disruption of the sympathetic chain at any point from the hypothalamus to the eye causes loss of pupil dilation (miosis), loss of lid elevation by Mueller's muscle (ptosis), and loss of facial sweating (anhidrosis).
keyFact: Ptosis + miosis + anhidrosis = sympathetic disruption. Causes vary by location: central (stroke, tumor), preganglionic (Pancoast tumor, trauma), postganglionic (carotid dissection, cluster headache). The apical lung tumor (Pancoast) is the classic board association.

wrongAnswers.name: Third Nerve Palsy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CN III palsy causes ptosis but with a DILATED pupil (the opposite — parasympathetic disruption) and an eye that is 'down and out.'

wrongAnswers.name: Myasthenia Gravis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MG causes ptosis that WORSENS with sustained upgaze and may be bilateral, but pupils are NORMAL and there's no anhidrosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Cluster Headache
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cluster headaches can cause a temporary Horner-like picture (ptosis, miosis) during attacks, but the symptoms resolve between episodes and there's no lung mass.

clues: A 42-year-old man presents with involuntary jerky movements of his arms and face that he cannot suppress.
His wife reports progressive personality changes including irritability and poor judgment over the past year.
Exam reveals chorea, impaired saccadic eye movements, and executive dysfunction on cognitive testing.
MRI shows bilateral caudate nucleus atrophy with compensatory enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles.
Genetic testing reveals an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat beyond the pathologic threshold in a gene on chromosome 4.
explanation: The expanded CAG repeat produces an abnormal protein with a toxic polyglutamine stretch that accumulates in and destroys neurons, particularly in the caudate nucleus.
keyFact: Chorea + psychiatric symptoms + dementia with caudate atrophy in a middle-aged adult with autosomal dominant inheritance is the classic presentation. Anticipation can occur (earlier onset in successive generations). There is no cure — treatment is symptomatic.

wrongAnswers.name: Wilson Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wilson causes movement disorder and psychiatric symptoms in young adults but with corneal copper rings and low ceruloplasmin — treatable with chelation.

wrongAnswers.name: Sydenham Chorea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sydenham causes chorea in children after streptococcal infection as part of rheumatic fever — not the progressive adult-onset chorea with caudate atrophy.

wrongAnswers.name: Parkinson Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Parkinson causes a resting tremor with rigidity and bradykinesia. The rapid flowing involuntary movements (chorea) here are a different movement disorder.

clues: A 72-year-old man presents with sudden right-sided weakness and inability to speak that began 90 minutes ago.
His wife witnessed the onset -- one moment he was fine, then his face drooped and his right arm went limp.
Exam reveals right facial droop (lower face only), right arm flaccid with no movement, right leg weakness, and inability to produce speech despite apparently understanding commands.
Non-contrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage; his medical history includes atrial fibrillation and he recently stopped his anticoagulation.
CT angiography reveals an abrupt cutoff of the left middle cerebral artery with no distal flow.
explanation: A blood clot formed in the fibrillating atrium, embolized to the brain, and lodged in the MCA. The left MCA territory supplies motor cortex for the right body and Broca's area for speech production.
keyFact: Face and arm weaker than leg = MCA territory. Leg weaker than arm = ACA territory. CT first to rule out hemorrhage — tPA in hemorrhagic stroke is fatal. Thrombectomy can be done up to 24 hours if there's salvageable tissue.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemorrhagic Stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CT shows NO blood. This must be confirmed before giving tPA.

wrongAnswers.name: Todd Paralysis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Todd paralysis is transient weakness after a seizure. No seizure was witnessed and CTA shows an actual clot.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypoglycemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke perfectly. Always check glucose immediately — but the CTA finding of an MCA occlusion confirms vascular etiology.

clues: A 5-day-old newborn develops high-pitched crying, arching of the back, and poor feeding.
Total bilirubin is 32 mg/dL (unconjugated), far above the exchange transfusion threshold, and phototherapy was delayed.
The infant is hypertonic with opisthotonus (severe back arching), a shrill high-pitched cry, and a bulging fontanelle.
Direct Coombs test is positive, and blood type incompatibility is identified between mother and infant.
MRI of the brain shows bilateral high signal in the globus pallidus on T1-weighted sequences.
explanation: Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin is lipid-soluble and freely crosses the blood-brain barrier, depositing in the basal ganglia (especially the globus pallidus) and causing irreversible neuronal damage.
keyFact: UNCONJUGATED bilirubin is neurotoxic (lipid-soluble, crosses BBB). CONJUGATED bilirubin is NOT neurotoxic (water-soluble).
