This is why physiologic jaundice and breastfeeding jaundice (unconjugated) are monitored carefully — they can progress if severe. Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to a water-soluble isomer that can be excreted.

wrongAnswers.name: Neonatal Sepsis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sepsis can cause neonatal jaundice with irritability, but the markedly elevated unconjugated bilirubin with globus pallidus signal and opisthotonus point to bilirubin toxicity.

wrongAnswers.name: Intraventricular Hemorrhage
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IVH causes bulging fontanelle in premature infants but with germinal matrix hemorrhage on imaging, not the bilateral globus pallidus signal.

wrongAnswers.name: Neonatal Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningitis causes irritability and high-pitched cry but with CSF pleocytosis and positive cultures, not the specific biliary deposition pattern on MRI.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with inability to remember what happened 5 minutes ago despite being alert and conversational.
He has a history of severe chronic alcohol use. He makes up elaborate stories to fill memory gaps without realizing he is doing it.
His eye movement problems and gait instability from a recent hospitalization have improved, but the memory impairment persists.
He can recall remote events from years ago with accuracy but cannot form any new memories or recall recent conversations.
MRI shows bilateral mammillary body atrophy with abnormal signal intensity in the medial thalami.
explanation: This is the chronic irreversible sequel to the acute thiamine deficiency encephalopathy. The acute triad (confusion, ataxia, eye movement abnormalities) partially resolves with thiamine, but the memory circuit damage persists.
keyFact: The acute phase (confusion + ataxia + ophthalmoplegia) is reversible with immediate IV thiamine. The chronic phase (anterograde amnesia + confabulation) is largely irreversible. Always give thiamine BEFORE glucose in alcoholic patients — glucose without thiamine can precipitate the acute phase.

wrongAnswers.name: Alzheimer Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alzheimer causes gradual memory loss but with cortical deficits (aphasia, agnosia, apraxia) and hippocampal atrophy, not the selective mammillary body destruction with confabulation.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatic Encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hepatic encephalopathy causes confusion in alcoholics but is reversible with lactulose, has asterixis, and does not cause isolated anterograde amnesia with confabulation.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcohol Intoxication
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Intoxication causes acute confusion that resolves with sobriety. This patient has a persistent structural memory deficit that does not improve.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with difficulty rising from a chair due to proximal leg weakness that has developed over the past few months.
He is a heavy smoker. His strength actually IMPROVES briefly with repeated use, which is the opposite of what he expected.
Exam reveals proximal weakness that improves with sustained effort, hyporeflexia that normalizes after exercising the muscle, and dry mouth.
Repetitive nerve stimulation shows an incremental response — the muscle response gets LARGER with repeated stimulation.
Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels are detected, and CT chest reveals a lung mass — this is a paraneoplastic syndrome.
explanation: Antibodies block calcium channels on the presynaptic motor nerve terminal, reducing acetylcholine release. Repeated stimulation allows calcium to accumulate and partially overcome the blockade.
keyFact: IMPROVES with use (Lambert-Eaton) vs WORSENS with use (myasthenia gravis). Incremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation (LE) vs decremental (MG). Strong association with small cell lung cancer — always image the chest.

wrongAnswers.name: Myasthenia Gravis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MG causes weakness that WORSENS with repeated use, has a decremental response on nerve stimulation, and involves antibodies against postsynaptic receptors — the opposite pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polymyositis causes proximal weakness but without the improvement with use, incremental nerve response, or presynaptic antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Botulism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Botulism blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release but presents acutely with descending paralysis after food exposure, not chronic proximal weakness with a lung mass.

clues: A 75-year-old man is brought to clinic for progressively worsening memory problems over the past year.
His family reports episodes of confusion that fluctuate in severity throughout the day, and he sometimes acts out dreams during sleep.
He reports seeing small animals running around his home that no one else can see.
Physical exam reveals mild rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor.
Cognitive testing shows impaired attention and visuospatial deficits that fluctuate between visits; a DaTscan shows reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the striatum.
explanation: Alpha-synuclein protein deposits (Lewy bodies) form in cortical and brainstem neurons, causing the combination of dementia, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder.
keyFact: The core features: fluctuating cognition, detailed formed visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. REM sleep behavior disorder (acting out dreams) is a strong supporting feature. Neuroleptic sensitivity is a critical management pearl.

wrongAnswers.name: Alzheimer Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alzheimer causes progressive memory loss but without the fluctuating cognition, formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, or dream enactment.

wrongAnswers.name: Parkinson Disease Dementia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The distinction is timing — if parkinsonism precedes dementia by >1 year, it's PD dementia. If cognitive symptoms appear within 1 year of motor symptoms, it's Lewy body dementia.

wrongAnswers.name: Delirium
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Delirium causes fluctuating confusion but is acute, has an identifiable trigger (infection, medication), and resolves with treatment. This is a chronic progressive illness.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with 3 days of worsening vision in her left eye with pain on eye movement.
Eight months ago her legs went numb below the knees for 3 weeks, and she never saw a doctor because it resolved on its own.
Exam reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect in the left eye, increased lower extremity reflexes, and an upgoing toe on the right.
MRI brain shows multiple bright lesions clustered around the ventricles oriented perpendicular to them, and MRI cervical spine shows a short-segment lesion.
Lumbar puncture reveals bands of antibody in the spinal fluid that are NOT present in a paired blood sample, confirming intrathecal immune activation.
explanation: The immune system attacks myelin sheaths at different locations in the CNS at different times. Each attack causes a new symptom that may partially or fully recover.
keyFact: The pupil that dilates to light means the optic nerve is sending a weaker signal. The electric shock with neck flexion indicates cervical cord demyelination. Lesions in multiple locations at multiple times satisfies the diagnostic criteria.

wrongAnswers.name: Neuromyelitis Optica
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NMO attacks optic nerves and spinal cord with long cord lesions (≥3 segments) and a specific antibody (aquaporin-4). Brain MRI is usually NORMAL — this patient has multiple brain lesions.

wrongAnswers.name: Isolated Optic Neuritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Isolated optic neuritis can occur without MS, but the prior leg numbness plus brain and cord lesions establish dissemination in space and time.

wrongAnswers.name: B12 Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: B12 damages posterior columns and corticospinal tracts but doesn't cause optic neuritis, pupillary defects, or periventricular brain lesions.

clues: A 29-year-old woman presents with drooping eyelids and double vision that are minimal in the morning but worsen progressively through the day.
She reports difficulty swallowing that is worse at dinner than at breakfast, and her voice becomes nasal-sounding by evening.
Her eyelid droops more after 60 seconds of sustained upward gaze, and arm strength declines measurably after 10 repetitive movements.
An antibody targeting the acetylcholine receptor is strongly positive, and CT chest reveals a mass in the front of the chest behind the sternum.
Administration of a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor produces dramatic transient improvement in her eyelid droop and strength within 30 seconds.
explanation: Autoantibodies block, destroy, and cross-link acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, reducing the number available for synaptic transmission. Repetitive use depletes the remaining acetylcholine faster than it can be replenished.
keyFact: Worsens with USE, improves with REST — opposite of Lambert-Eaton (which IMPROVES with use). The anterior mediastinal mass is the thymus — thymoma occurs in ~15% and thymectomy is recommended. Aminoglycosides, beta-blockers, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate crisis.

wrongAnswers.name: Lambert-Eaton Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lambert-Eaton causes proximal weakness that IMPROVES with use (opposite of this disease) and is associated with small cell lung cancer, not thymic masses.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS causes neurologic deficits but they are CNS-based (optic neuritis, myelitis), don't worsen with repetitive use, and have characteristic MRI lesions.

wrongAnswers.name: Botulism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Botulism causes descending paralysis starting with cranial nerves but from presynaptic acetylcholine release blockade, not postsynaptic receptor antibodies.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with difficulty releasing his grip after handshakes and progressive facial and distal limb weakness.
His father has similar but milder symptoms that began in his 50s, and the patient's 2-year-old son has severe hypotonia from birth.
Exam reveals a thin face with temporal wasting, frontal balding, ptosis, and weakness of the hands and feet.
When the thenar eminence is tapped with a reflex hammer, the thumb contracts and remains contracted for several seconds before slowly relaxing.
ECG shows first-degree heart block, and genetic testing reveals an expanded CTG trinucleotide repeat that is larger in the patient than in his father.
explanation: The expanded CTG repeat in the DMPK gene produces toxic RNA that sequesters RNA-binding proteins, disrupting splicing of multiple genes and causing multi-system disease.
keyFact: The sustained muscle contraction after percussion (percussion myotonia) and grip myotonia are characteristic. Multisystem: cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, diabetes, testicular atrophy, cognitive impairment. Anticipation = worsening severity in successive generations as the repeat expands.

wrongAnswers.name: Myasthenia Gravis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MG causes ptosis and weakness but it IMPROVES with rest and worsens with repetition — opposite of the sustained contraction (myotonia) seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Muscular Dystrophy (Duchenne/Becker)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DMD/BMD causes proximal weakness in boys from dystrophin mutations, not distal weakness with myotonia and multi-system involvement in adults.

wrongAnswers.name: ALS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ALS causes progressive weakness but with upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia). Myotonic dystrophy has myotonia and a distinctive pattern of distal and facial weakness with multi-organ involvement.

clues: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for multiple tan flat spots on his skin that his parents have noticed increasing in number since birth.
He has learning difficulties in school and has freckling in both armpits that appeared around age 5.
Exam reveals more than six café-au-lait macules each greater than 1.5 cm, axillary freckling, and multiple small soft fleshy bumps on his skin.
Slit-lamp examination reveals pigmented hamartomas on both irises.
An MRI of the brain shows bright spots on T2-weighted images in the basal ganglia and brainstem — the gene involved normally encodes a protein that regulates a key cell growth signaling pathway.
explanation: Loss of the tumor suppressor neurofibromin (which normally inhibits the RAS signaling pathway) leads to uncontrolled growth of neural crest-derived cells.
keyFact: Diagnostic criteria: ≥2 of: >6 café-au-lait spots, axillary/inguinal freckling, ≥2 neurofibromas, optic glioma, ≥2 iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), bone dysplasia, first-degree relative. Increased risk of optic gliomas, pheochromocytoma, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors.

wrongAnswers.name: Neurofibromatosis Type 2
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NF2 primarily causes bilateral vestibular schwannomas (hearing loss) and is on a different chromosome. Café-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules are features of NF1, not NF2.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberous Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TSC causes skin lesions too but different types — ash-leaf spots (hypopigmented), facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches. Not café-au-lait spots with axillary freckling.

wrongAnswers.name: McCune-Albright Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: McCune-Albright causes café-au-lait spots but with coast-of-Maine (irregular) borders, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and precocious puberty — a different triad.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with progressive hearing loss and ringing in both ears over the past year.
He has a family history of brain tumors. He also reports occasional balance problems and dizziness.
Exam reveals bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with decreased corneal reflexes.
MRI shows bilateral enhancing masses at the cerebellopontine angles compressing the vestibulocochlear nerves.
Genetic testing confirms a mutation in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22 encoding the tumor suppressor merlin.
explanation: Loss of the tumor suppressor merlin leads to bilateral vestibular schwannomas, which is virtually diagnostic. The acoustic nerves are compressed bilaterally.
keyFact: BILATERAL vestibular schwannomas are pathognomonic for NF2. NF1 = peripheral (skin neurofibromas, café-au-lait spots, Lisch nodules). NF2 = central (bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas). 'NF2 = 2 tumors on CN 2x4 (VIII).'

wrongAnswers.name: NF1
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NF1 causes peripheral neurofibromas and café-au-lait spots. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark of NF2.

wrongAnswers.name: Acoustic Neuroma (Sporadic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sporadic vestibular schwannoma is UNILATERAL. BILATERAL schwannomas are diagnostic of NF2.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningiomas CAN occur in NF2, but the bilateral cerebellopontine angle masses compressing CN VIII bilaterally are schwannomas, not meningiomas.

clues: A 72-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty walking described as 'magnetic' — his feet seem stuck to the floor.
He has developed urinary incontinence and his wife notices he is slower in his thinking.
Exam reveals a wide-based shuffling gait with short steps and cognitive slowing primarily affecting attention and executive function.
MRI shows markedly enlarged ventricles that are out of proportion to the degree of cortical atrophy.
A large-volume lumbar puncture produces dramatic temporary improvement in his gait within hours.
explanation: Impaired CSF absorption leads to ventricular enlargement that stretches the periventricular white matter fibers controlling gait, bladder, and cognition — in that order of involvement.
keyFact: The triad: wet (incontinence), wacky (dementia), wobbly (gait apraxia). Gait is the first to appear and the most likely to improve with shunting. The ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy distinguishes this from ex vacuo dilation in Alzheimer.

wrongAnswers.name: Alzheimer Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alzheimer causes memory loss with hippocampal atrophy and ventricles enlarged IN PROPORTION to cortical atrophy. NPH ventricles are disproportionately large.

wrongAnswers.name: Parkinson Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Parkinson causes shuffling gait but with resting tremor, rigidity, and asymmetric onset — no incontinence or ventriculomegaly.

wrongAnswers.name: Vascular Dementia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vascular dementia causes gait problems and cognitive decline but with stepwise progression and white matter ischemic changes, not disproportionate ventriculomegaly.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with a tremor in his right hand that is most noticeable when his hand is resting in his lap.
His wife says he moves slowly, his handwriting has gotten smaller, and his face seems expressionless.
Exam reveals a pill-rolling resting tremor of the right hand, cogwheel rigidity of the right arm, bradykinesia with decreased arm swing on the right, and a shuffling gait.
The symptoms are notably asymmetric, predominantly affecting the right side, and MRI of the brain is normal.
DaTscan shows asymmetrically reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the left putamen.
explanation: Dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta degenerate, depleting dopamine in the striatum and causing the characteristic motor symptoms.
keyFact: The four cardinal features: resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability (TRAP). Asymmetric onset is characteristic. Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra with Lewy body inclusions (alpha-synuclein) is the pathologic hallmark.

wrongAnswers.name: Essential Tremor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Essential tremor is an ACTION tremor (worse with movement) that is bilateral and symmetric, often affecting the voice and head. This is a RESTING tremor that is asymmetric.

wrongAnswers.name: Lewy Body Dementia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LBD has parkinsonism plus early cognitive decline with visual hallucinations. In Parkinson disease, motor symptoms precede any cognitive changes by years.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple System Atrophy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MSA causes parkinsonism with early autonomic failure and cerebellar signs, with POOR response to levodopa. This patient has excellent levodopa response.

clues: A 65-year-old man with a history of prostate cancer presents with 2 weeks of progressive back pain followed by difficulty walking.
The back pain is severe, worse at night and when lying down, and not relieved by rest.
Exam reveals a sensory level at T10, bilateral lower extremity weakness with hyperreflexia, upgoing toes, and a distended bladder.
PSA is markedly elevated and a bone scan shows multiple areas of uptake throughout the spine.
MRI of the spine shows a mass in the T10 vertebral body extending into the epidural space and compressing the spinal cord.
explanation: Tumor in the vertebral body grows posteriorly into the epidural space, compressing the spinal cord and causing progressive myelopathy that becomes irreversible without urgent treatment.
keyFact: Back pain that is worse at night and with recumbency + known cancer + progressive neurologic deficits = cord compression until MRI proves otherwise. The ambulatory status at the time of treatment is the strongest predictor of outcome — once they can't walk, recovery is unlikely.

wrongAnswers.name: Cauda Equina Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cauda equina causes LOWER motor neuron signs (areflexia, flaccidity) below L1-L2. This has UPPER motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, upgoing toes) from cord compression at T10.

wrongAnswers.name: Degenerative Disc Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Degenerative back pain improves with rest and lying down. This pain is WORSE at night and with recumbency — that's a red flag for malignancy.

wrongAnswers.name: Transverse Myelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Transverse myelitis causes a similar clinical picture but MRI shows an intrinsic cord lesion, not an extrinsic compressive mass from tumor.

clues: A 35-year-old man with epilepsy is brought to the ED in continuous generalized tonic-clonic convulsive activity that has lasted 15 minutes.
He ran out of his antiepileptic medications 3 days ago, and paramedics administered one dose of a benzodiazepine en route without effect.
He is cyanotic with clenched jaw, generalized rhythmic jerking, and is unresponsive, with tachycardia, hypertension, and temperature of 102 F.
Point-of-care labs show glucose of 65, lactate of 8.2, and CK is rising from ongoing muscle breakdown.
Continuous EEG shows unrelenting generalized spike-and-wave activity without any interictal baseline between discharges.
explanation: Continuous or rapidly recurrent seizure activity without recovery of consciousness between events causes progressive neuronal injury, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and metabolic acidosis.
keyFact: Defined as seizure lasting >5 minutes or recurrent seizures without return to baseline. Treatment escalation: benzodiazepine → antiepileptic load (fosphenytoin or levalbuterol) → continuous infusion. Most common cause in known epileptics: medication noncompliance. Always check glucose first.

wrongAnswers.name: Pseudoseizure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psychogenic nonepileptic events mimic seizures but lack the cyanosis, elevated lactate, rising CK, and post-ictal metabolic derangements of true status epilepticus.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningitis can cause seizures but with fever, neck stiffness, and CSF pleocytosis as the primary findings. This is a known epileptic who stopped medications.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypoglycemic Seizure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypoglycemia causes seizures but glucose here is 65 (low-normal), and the patient is a known epileptic off medications.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with an explosive headache that she describes as the worst of her life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds.
She was exercising when it started and briefly lost consciousness; she has a history of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
Exam reveals neck stiffness with resistance to flexion, blood pressure of 192/108, photophobia, and confusion.
Non-contrast CT shows bright white blood filling the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures.
CT angiography identifies a saccular aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery.
explanation: A berry aneurysm at a branch point of the Circle of Willis ruptured, flooding the subarachnoid space with blood that irritates the meninges and can trigger devastating delayed vasospasm.
keyFact: Thunderclap headache (maximal in seconds) = SAH until proven otherwise. ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos are associated with berry aneurysms. If CT is negative (misses ~5% within 6 hours), LP is mandatory looking for xanthochromia.

wrongAnswers.name: Migraine
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Migraines build over minutes to hours. This peaked in SECONDS with loss of consciousness and blood on CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningitis causes neck stiffness with headache but develops over hours-days with fever, not seconds.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertensive Emergency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Severe hypertension can cause headache, but the thunderclap onset with blood in the subarachnoid space and a berry aneurysm confirm rupture.

clues: A 78-year-old man on warfarin presents with progressive confusion developing over two weeks.
His family reports a fall three weeks ago where he bumped his head but seemed fine afterward.
Exam reveals fluctuating level of consciousness, bilateral papilledema, and a drift of the left arm when both are held outstretched.
INR is 3.8, and there are no focal findings other than the left arm drift.
CT shows a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection over the right cerebral convexity that crosses suture lines with mild midline shift.
explanation: Bridging veins between the brain surface and dural sinuses tear during head acceleration-deceleration. The slow venous ooze gradually accumulates and compresses the brain over days to weeks.
keyFact: Crescent-shaped = subdural. Biconvex = epidural. Chronic subdural is common in elderly (brain atrophy stretches bridging veins) and anticoagulated patients. Presentation is often insidious with fluctuating mental status, not acute.

wrongAnswers.name: Epidural Hematoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Epidural is biconvex, acute (hours), arterial, and typically in young patients after temporal trauma. This is crescent-shaped, chronic (weeks), venous, and in an elderly patient.

wrongAnswers.name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NPH causes dementia, gait disturbance, and incontinence with enlarged ventricles but no extra-axial collection on CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Brain Tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A tumor would appear as an intra-axial mass with enhancement. This is an extra-axial crescent-shaped collection crossing sutures.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with painless burns on his hands that he didn't feel, and he notices he cannot tell hot from cold water in the shower.
He has had progressive hand weakness and atrophy but his ability to feel light touch and vibration in his hands is completely preserved.
Exam reveals bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation across the shoulders and upper extremities in a cape-like distribution with preserved light touch and proprioception in the same areas.
There is atrophy and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles with absent biceps and triceps reflexes but hyperreflexia in the lower extremities.
MRI of the cervical spine shows a fluid-filled cavity within the central spinal cord that is often associated with a hindbrain malformation at the foramen magnum.
explanation: The expanding cavity in the central cord first destroys the crossing pain and temperature fibers in the anterior commissure, then expands to damage the anterior horn cells and eventually the lateral corticospinal tracts.
keyFact: Dissociated sensory loss (pain/temperature gone but touch/proprioception preserved) in a cape distribution = central cord lesion. The hand atrophy is from anterior horn cell destruction (LMN). Lower extremity hyperreflexia is from lateral corticospinal tract compression (UMN).

wrongAnswers.name: Cervical Myelopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervical myelopathy from disc compression causes upper and lower extremity signs but without the dissociated sensory loss or fluid-filled cavity within the cord.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS causes white matter lesions with variable sensory and motor findings but does not produce the characteristic cape-distribution dissociated sensory loss with a central cord cavity.

wrongAnswers.name: ALS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ALS causes hand atrophy with upper and lower motor neuron signs but NEVER causes sensory loss. The dissociated sensory deficit rules out ALS.

clues: A 30-year-old woman presents with leg weakness developing over 48 hours that is making it hard for her to walk.
She reports a band-like tightness around her torso and had a viral upper respiratory infection two weeks ago.
Exam reveals a sensory level at T8 below which pinprick is absent, with bilateral lower extremity weakness, hyperreflexia, and upgoing toes.
MRI of the thoracic spine shows a T2-hyperintense lesion spanning 3 vertebral segments within the central cord.
CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein. No compressive lesion is seen on imaging.
explanation: Inflammation within the spinal cord destroys both motor and sensory pathways at the affected level, causing bilateral deficits below that point with upper motor neuron signs.
keyFact: Sensory level + bilateral UMN signs below + bladder dysfunction = myelopathy. If the lesion spans >3 segments (longitudinally extensive), consider neuromyelitis optica (anti-AQP4 antibodies). If shorter, consider MS as the first presentation.

wrongAnswers.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBS causes ascending weakness but with AREFLEXIA (lower motor neuron), no sensory level, and normal MRI. This has hyperreflexia and a cord lesion on MRI.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS can present with myelitis, but MS lesions are typically short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies) and partial. This is longitudinally extensive — raising concern for NMO.

wrongAnswers.name: Spinal Cord Compression
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Compression from tumor or disc causes similar findings but MRI shows an extrinsic mass compressing the cord, not an intrinsic T2-hyperintense inflammatory lesion.

clues: A 60-year-old woman presents with episodes of excruciating face pain that last only seconds and feel like electric shocks.
The pain is triggered by chewing, brushing her teeth, or a light breeze on her cheek.
Between episodes she has no pain and her neurologic exam is completely normal with no sensory loss.
The pain is localized to the right maxillary and mandibular divisions of cranial nerve V.
MRI shows a blood vessel loop compressing the trigeminal nerve root as it exits the brainstem.
explanation: A blood vessel (usually the superior cerebellar artery) pulsates against the nerve root entry zone, causing demyelination and aberrant firing that produces the characteristic lancinating pain.
keyFact: Brief lancinating pain in the distribution of CN V2 or V3, triggered by light touch, with NORMAL neurologic exam between attacks = classic trigeminal neuralgia. Sensory loss or abnormal exam should raise concern for a secondary cause (tumor, MS).

wrongAnswers.name: Cluster Headache
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cluster headaches cause severe unilateral facial pain but last 15-180 MINUTES (not seconds), occur in clusters with autonomic symptoms (tearing, nasal congestion), and are not triggered by light touch.

wrongAnswers.name: Temporal Arteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GCA causes temporal pain in older patients but with constant aching (not lancinating), elevated ESR, and jaw claudication — not seconds-long electric shocks triggered by touch.

wrongAnswers.name: Dental Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dental pain can be severe and triggered by chewing, but it is constant, localizes to a specific tooth, and doesn't produce the seconds-long electric shock quality triggered by non-dental stimuli.

clues: A 2-year-old child presents with seizures that began as infantile spasms.
The child has developmental delay, and the seizures have been difficult to control.
Exam reveals hypopigmented ash-leaf-shaped macules on Wood lamp exam, small red papules across the nose and cheeks, and a rough elevated patch on the lower back.
Renal ultrasound reveals bilateral angiomyolipomas, and echocardiogram shows a cardiac rhabdomyoma.
CT of the brain shows calcified subependymal nodules lining the lateral ventricles.
explanation: Loss of TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin), which normally suppress the mTOR growth pathway, leads to hamartomas in the brain, skin, kidneys, heart, and lungs.
keyFact: Classic triad: seizures, intellectual disability, facial angiofibromas. The ash-leaf spots (best seen with Wood lamp), cardiac rhabdomyomas (most common cardiac tumor in infants), and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas are characteristic. mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) are used therapeutically.

wrongAnswers.name: Neurofibromatosis Type 1
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NF1 causes café-au-lait spots (hyperpigmented), not ash-leaf spots (hypopigmented). The facial lesions in NF1 are neurofibromas, not angiofibromas.

wrongAnswers.name: Sturge-Weber Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sturge-Weber causes seizures and a port-wine stain on the face following a trigeminal nerve distribution, not ash-leaf spots with bilateral renal masses.

wrongAnswers.name: von Hippel-Lindau Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VHL causes renal masses too but these are clear cell renal carcinomas, not angiomyolipomas, and there are no skin findings or brain calcifications.

clues: A 70-year-old man presents with cognitive decline that has worsened in a stepwise pattern over the past 2 years.
He has poorly controlled hypertension and diabetes. His wife says he was stable for weeks then suddenly got worse, in distinct steps.
Exam reveals bilateral hyperreflexia, a wide-based gait, and focal signs including a mild left-sided pronator drift.
MRI shows multiple lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and extensive periventricular white matter hyperintensities.
Neuropsychological testing shows executive dysfunction with relatively preserved memory, and the stepwise decline correlates temporally with the imaging findings.
explanation: Repeated small strokes and chronic ischemic white matter damage progressively destroy brain tissue, causing cognitive decline that worsens in sudden steps corresponding to each new vascular event.
keyFact: Stepwise decline (not gradual) + focal neurologic signs + vascular risk factors + white matter disease on MRI = vascular dementia. Executive dysfunction (planning, organizing) is often more prominent than memory loss early on.

wrongAnswers.name: Alzheimer Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alzheimer has a gradual progressive decline without sudden steps, no focal neurologic signs, and hippocampal atrophy rather than multiple infarcts.

wrongAnswers.name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NPH causes dementia with gait and urinary symptoms but with dilated ventricles, not multiple lacunar infarcts and white matter disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Lewy Body Dementia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LBD has fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. The stepwise decline with focal signs and vascular lesions point to vascular dementia.

clues: A 50-year-old man is brought to the ED confused, unsteady on his feet, and unable to move his eyes properly.
He has severe chronic alcohol use. He was recently hospitalized for pancreatitis and received IV dextrose without vitamin supplementation.
Exam reveals confusion, bilateral lateral gaze palsy with nystagmus, and a wide-based ataxic gait.
Serum thiamine level is critically low. Red cell transketolase activity is reduced.
MRI shows symmetric signal abnormalities in the mammillary bodies, medial thalami, and periaqueductal gray matter.
explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is a cofactor for essential enzymes in glucose metabolism. Depletion causes neuronal damage in the mammillary bodies, medial thalamus, periaqueductal gray, and cerebellar vermis.
keyFact: The triad: confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia. ALWAYS give thiamine BEFORE glucose. The acute phase is potentially reversible with immediate thiamine. If untreated, it progresses to the chronic irreversible amnestic state.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatic Encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hepatic encephalopathy causes confusion in alcoholics but with asterixis, elevated ammonia, and no ophthalmoplegia or the specific triad.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcohol Intoxication
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Intoxication causes confusion and ataxia but resolves with sobriety and does not cause the specific eye movement abnormalities.

wrongAnswers.name: Delirium Tremens
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DT causes agitation, tremor, and hallucinations during alcohol withdrawal, not the specific triad of ophthalmoplegia, confusion, and ataxia.

clues: A 16-year-old girl is brought by her parents for progressive weight loss over 6 months.
She exercises excessively, counts every calorie, insists she is still overweight at 82 pounds, and has not had a menstrual period in 5 months.
Exam reveals BMI of 14, fine downy hair on her face and arms, bradycardia at 48 bpm, hypotension, and hypothermia.
Labs show leukopenia, elevated BUN from dehydration, low estrogen, low LH and FSH, and elevated cortisol.
ECG shows a prolonged QTc interval, potassium is 2.9 mEq/L, and phosphate is low at 1.8 mg/dL.
explanation: Intense fear of weight gain and distorted body image drive severe caloric restriction. The body enters a starvation state, suppressing reproductive hormones and slowing metabolic rate to conserve energy.
keyFact: The fine body hair (lanugo) is the body's attempt to conserve heat. The amenorrhea results from hypothalamic suppression of GnRH. Refeeding syndrome (hypophosphatemia) is the most dangerous complication of treatment — electrolytes must be monitored closely during nutritional rehabilitation.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperthyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss but with tachycardia, heat intolerance, and elevated thyroid hormones — not bradycardia and hypothermia with body image distortion.

wrongAnswers.name: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IBD causes weight loss with GI symptoms (diarrhea, pain). This patient restricts intake voluntarily with body image distortion.

wrongAnswers.name: Addison Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Addison causes weight loss with hypotension but from cortisol deficiency. This patient has ELEVATED cortisol from physiologic stress response to starvation.

clues: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after being found running through traffic at 3 AM.
His family says he has not slept for 4 days, has been talking nonstop, and spent $15,000 on a business venture overnight.
He is hyperverbal, making rhyming associations between unrelated words, has flight of ideas, and is grandiose and irritable when interrupted.
Urine drug screen is negative and TSH is normal. He believes he has been chosen to lead the United Nations.
This is his second such episode; between episodes he functions normally at work for months at a time.
explanation: Mania is defined by a distinct period of persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy lasting at least 7 days, with at least 3 additional symptoms (decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, or risky behavior).
keyFact: A single manic episode defines Bipolar I (even without a depressive episode). The episodic nature with return to baseline distinguishes from schizophrenia (continuous). Lithium is the classic mood stabilizer but requires renal and thyroid monitoring. Valproate is an alternative.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia causes continuous psychotic symptoms without full return to baseline between episodes. This patient functions normally between episodes.

wrongAnswers.name: Substance-Induced Mania
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stimulants cause manic-like symptoms, but the drug screen is negative and this is his second episode.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperthyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thyrotoxicosis can mimic mania with hyperactivity and insomnia, but TSH is normal.

clues: A 24-year-old woman presents to the ED after a superficial wrist laceration following an argument with her boyfriend.
She says she 'absolutely hates' him after 'absolutely adoring' him yesterday, and this is her fifth ED visit this year.
She reports chronic emptiness, intense fear of abandonment, and a pattern of unstable relationships cycling between idealization and devaluation.
Her mood shifts rapidly in response to interpersonal stressors, and she has a history of impulsive binge drinking and reckless driving.
She describes a persistent feeling that she does not know who she really is, and her self-image changes depending on whom she is around.
explanation: A pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and emotions, combined with marked impulsivity, defines this personality disorder. Intense fear of abandonment drives much of the interpersonal dysfunction.
keyFact: The hallmark is splitting — rapidly oscillating between idealization and devaluation of the same person. Chronic emptiness, identity disturbance, and frantic efforts to avoid abandonment are core features. DBT is the gold standard therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bipolar mood episodes last days-weeks and are not specifically triggered by interpersonal events. BPD mood shifts are rapid (hours) and triggered by relationship conflicts.

wrongAnswers.name: Major Depressive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDD causes sustained depressed mood for ≥2 weeks. BPD has chronic emptiness with rapid mood shifts, not sustained depression.

wrongAnswers.name: Histrionic Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Histrionic involves excessive emotionality and attention-seeking but without the self-harm, abandonment fear, identity disturbance, and splitting seen in BPD.

clues: A 22-year-old college woman presents with her dentist's referral after severe erosion of the enamel on the inner surfaces of her upper front teeth.
She admits to episodes of eating large amounts of food in short periods followed by self-induced vomiting, occurring at least twice weekly for the past year.
Exam reveals a normal BMI, bilateral painless parotid gland enlargement, and calluses on the dorsal surface of her knuckles.
Labs show hypokalemia at 2.6 mEq/L, metabolic alkalosis with bicarbonate of 34, and elevated serum amylase.
Her weight is within normal range, and she acknowledges that the binge-purge behavior is abnormal but feels unable to stop.
explanation: Cycles of binge eating followed by compensatory purging (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics) cause characteristic physical findings from repeated exposure to gastric acid.
keyFact: The knuckle calluses (Russell sign) are from teeth scraping the hand during self-induced vomiting. The dental erosion is on the LINGUAL surfaces (inner) from acid bathing the teeth. Parotid hypertrophy is from repeated stimulation. The hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting can cause dangerous arrhythmias.

wrongAnswers.name: Anorexia Nervosa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anorexia causes severe weight loss with BMI <18.5. This patient has NORMAL weight with binge-purge cycles.

wrongAnswers.name: GERD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GERD causes acid erosion of teeth but without binge eating, knuckle calluses, or parotid enlargement.

wrongAnswers.name: Sjogren Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sjogren causes parotid enlargement but with dry eyes and mouth from autoimmune gland destruction, not the binge-purge history with dental erosion.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with sudden inability to walk after witnessing a car accident.
She has complete paralysis of both legs when tested directly but is observed moving her legs normally when she does not know she is being watched.
When lying supine and asked to lift her 'paralyzed' leg, her other leg pushes downward into the bed; when asked to lift the 'good' leg, the 'paralyzed' leg does not push down.
MRI of brain and spine is completely normal, as are nerve conduction studies and routine labs.
The neurologic examination is internally inconsistent, with strength varying depending on the method of testing and the patient's awareness of observation.
explanation: Genuine neurologic symptoms are produced by altered brain processing of motor or sensory signals, not by conscious fabrication. The symptoms are real to the patient and cause genuine distress.
keyFact: Positive examination signs (Hoover sign, give-way weakness, inconsistency) MAKE the diagnosis — it is not just 'normal workup therefore functional.' The patient is not faking. A precipitating psychological stressor is common but not required.

wrongAnswers.name: Malingering
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malingering is intentional fabrication for external gain (lawsuit, disability). Conversion disorder is involuntary and causes genuine distress without external motivation.

wrongAnswers.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBS causes ascending paralysis with areflexia and abnormal nerve conduction studies. Exam is internally consistent and NCS is abnormal — the opposite of this case.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS causes neurologic deficits but with consistent exam findings and MRI lesions. The internal inconsistency and normal imaging exclude MS.

clues: An 82-year-old man who was cognitively normal at baseline becomes acutely confused and agitated after hip surgery.
He is picking at his IV lines, appears frightened, sees people in his room who are not there, and is worse at night.
His attention is severely impaired; he cannot recite the months of the year backwards or spell 'world' backwards.
His symptoms fluctuate throughout the day, with lucid intervals alternating with periods of confusion and agitation.
Workup reveals a urinary tract infection, and his medication list includes a newly started anticholinergic drug for bladder spasms.
explanation: An acute medical insult (infection, medications, metabolic derangements) disrupts global brain function, causing fluctuating inattention, disorientation, and often perceptual disturbances.
keyFact: ACUTE onset + FLUCTUATING course + INATTENTION = delirium. INSIDIOUS onset + PROGRESSIVE course + MEMORY loss = dementia. Delirium is REVERSIBLE when the underlying cause is treated. Anticholinergic medications are the most common drug cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Dementia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dementia develops gradually over months-years and does not fluctuate acutely. This patient was normal at baseline and became confused acutely after surgery.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia causes hallucinations and disorganized thinking but onset is in young adults, is chronic, and does not resolve with treating a UTI.

wrongAnswers.name: Sundowning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sundowning is worsening confusion at night in dementia patients. This patient had no prior cognitive decline — the acute onset after surgery identifies delirium.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with severe agitation, confusion, and seeing things that aren't there, starting 72 hours after abruptly stopping a substance he used daily.
He has a history of heavy daily alcohol use for 20 years. He was admitted for pneumonia and the substance was stopped without prophylaxis.
He is diaphoretic, tremulous, and confused with heart rate of 140, blood pressure of 190/110, and temperature of 102.5°F.
He is seeing and swatting at insects that are not there and is pulling at his IV lines in agitation.
He is seeing and swatting at insects that are not there. CIWA score is 28. The onset is 72 hours after his last drink.
explanation: Chronic alcohol use causes compensatory upregulation of excitatory NMDA receptors and downregulation of inhibitory GABA receptors. When alcohol is abruptly removed, the brain is left in a hyperexcitable state.
keyFact: Timeline: 6-24 hours = tremor, anxiety, insomnia. 24-48 hours = hallucinations, seizures. 48-96 hours = delirium tremens (the most dangerous stage). Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are the treatment of choice. CIWA protocol guides dosing.

wrongAnswers.name: Sepsis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sepsis causes confusion, tachycardia, and fever, but the temporal relationship to alcohol cessation with visual hallucinations and severe agitation points to withdrawal.

wrongAnswers.name: Wernicke Encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wernicke causes confusion with ophthalmoplegia and ataxia from thiamine deficiency. DTs cause confusion with severe agitation, hallucinations, and autonomic instability from withdrawal.

wrongAnswers.name: Serotonin Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Serotonin syndrome causes agitation, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability but requires serotonergic medications and features clonus and hyperreflexia.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with 8 months of persistent uncontrollable worrying.
She has difficulty sleeping and constant muscle tension in her neck and shoulders.
Exam reveals an anxious woman with tense neck muscles and mild tachycardia but no tremor or exophthalmos.
TSH and metabolic panel are normal, and the anxiety is not limited to specific situations or triggers.
She reports worrying about her job, her children's safety, finances, and her health on most days, and the worry has persisted for more than 6 months.
explanation: Persistent excessive worry across multiple domains with associated physical symptoms represents the most common anxiety disorder in primary care.
keyFact: GAD = diffuse worry about EVERYTHING for ≥6 months. Panic disorder = discrete sudden attacks. Social anxiety = specific to social situations. OCD = intrusive thoughts with compulsive rituals. SSRIs and buspirone are first-line. Benzodiazepines are short-term only.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperthyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thyrotoxicosis causes anxiety, tachycardia, and insomnia but with tremor, weight loss, and abnormal TSH. TSH is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Panic Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Panic disorder causes discrete intense attacks of sudden terror with physical symptoms, not the chronic diffuse worry about multiple life domains.

wrongAnswers.name: Social Anxiety Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Social anxiety is limited to social or performance situations. This patient worries about work, health, and children — multiple domains.

clues: A 40-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks of persistent sadness and loss of interest in activities she used to enjoy.
She has trouble concentrating at work, has lost 10 pounds without trying, and wakes at 4 AM unable to fall back asleep.
She moves and speaks slowly, makes poor eye contact, and cries during the interview.
TSH, CBC, and metabolic panel are all normal with no medical cause for her symptoms identified.
She reports persistent feelings of worthlessness and guilt, with diminished energy and recurrent thoughts that her family would be better off without her.
explanation: A neurobiological disorder involving dysregulation of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine pathways causes sustained depressed mood with neurovegetative symptoms.
keyFact: The SIG E CAPS mnemonic: Sleep, Interest (anhedonia), Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor changes, Suicidal ideation. Need depressed mood or anhedonia PLUS ≥5 total for ≥2 weeks. SSRIs are first-line treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes fatigue, weight gain, and depressed mood, but TSH is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Normal Grief
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Grief causes sadness but typically with preserved self-esteem, some positive moments, and duration <2 months. This is 6 weeks of persistent anhedonia with neurovegetative symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Adjustment Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adjustment disorder is an identifiable stressor-triggered response that doesn't meet the full criteria for MDD. This patient meets full criteria with 5+ symptoms for 2+ weeks.

clues: A 20-year-old college student presents because he spends 4 hours daily washing his hands until they are raw and bleeding.
He has an overwhelming fear of contamination. He recognizes the behavior is excessive and irrational but cannot stop.
His hands are red, cracked, and excoriated from constant washing, and he is failing his courses because the rituals consume his day.
He has no psychotic symptoms, and the intrusive thoughts are experienced as unwanted products of his own mind.
The anxiety becomes unbearable if he tries to resist the handwashing, and performing the ritual provides only temporary relief before the urge returns.
explanation: Intrusive unwanted thoughts (obsessions) cause intense anxiety that is temporarily relieved by repetitive behaviors (compulsions), creating a self-reinforcing cycle.
keyFact: Ego-dystonic = patient knows it's irrational but can't stop. This distinguishes OCD from psychosis (where the patient doesn't recognize delusions as irrational). First-line: SSRIs (often at higher doses than for depression) + exposure and response prevention (ERP) therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia involves delusions that the patient BELIEVES are real (ego-syntonic). This patient recognizes his thoughts are irrational (ego-dystonic).

wrongAnswers.name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GAD causes diffuse worry but without the specific obsession-compulsion cycle and ritualistic behaviors.

wrongAnswers.name: Body Dysmorphic Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BDD involves obsessive preoccupation with perceived physical flaws. This patient's obsessions center on contamination with compulsive hand-washing.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of sudden overwhelming terror with chest tightness and pounding heart.
The episodes peak within 10 minutes and resolve within 30, occurring unpredictably several times per week.
Between episodes she lives in constant fear of the next attack and has started avoiding public places.
Cardiac workup including ECG and echocardiogram, thyroid function, and drug screen are all completely normal.
During a witnessed episode in the ED, she develops tachycardia, diaphoresis, trembling, and reports a sensation of choking and fear of dying that peaks and resolves within minutes.
explanation: Sudden surges of sympathetic activation produce intense physical symptoms that the patient interprets as a medical emergency, creating a cycle of fear and avoidance.
keyFact: Discrete sudden attacks (minutes) vs chronic diffuse worry (months) is the key distinction from GAD. Agoraphobia (avoiding places where escape is difficult) commonly develops. SSRIs are first-line long-term; benzodiazepines for acute rescue only.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ACS causes chest pain and shortness of breath, but cardiac workup is completely normal here with recurrent stereotyped episodes.

wrongAnswers.name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GAD causes chronic persistent worry about multiple domains. Panic is discrete sudden attacks with symptom-free intervals.

wrongAnswers.name: Pheochromocytoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pheo causes episodic sympathetic symptoms but with markedly elevated blood pressure and catecholamines. BP is normal here and workup is negative.

clues: A 28-year-old military veteran presents with recurrent nightmares about combat persisting for 6 months since returning from deployment.
He avoids fireworks and crowds, feels emotionally numb, and is unable to experience positive emotions.
He is hypervigilant in the waiting room, sitting with his back to the wall and scanning all exits.
He has difficulty sleeping, poor concentration, and an exaggerated startle response to unexpected loud sounds.
He describes flashbacks where he re-experiences the traumatic event as if it is happening in the present moment.
explanation: Exposure to a traumatic event causes persistent re-experiencing, avoidance, negative mood changes, and hyperarousal that significantly impair daily functioning.
keyFact: Duration >1 month distinguishes PTSD from acute stress disorder (<1 month). Trauma-focused CBT and prolonged exposure therapy are first-line. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are first-line pharmacotherapy. Benzodiazepines should be AVOIDED — they interfere with trauma processing.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Stress Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD has similar symptoms but lasts 3 days to 1 month after trauma. At 6 months, this is PTSD.

wrongAnswers.name: Adjustment Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adjustment disorder is a disproportionate response to a stressor but without the specific re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal clusters of PTSD.

wrongAnswers.name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GAD causes chronic diffuse worry but without a specific traumatic trigger, flashbacks, or the four symptom clusters.

clues: A 20-year-old college sophomore is brought by his parents because his behavior has changed dramatically over the past year.
His grades dropped, he stopped showering, withdrew from friends, and his emotional expression has become flat.
He sits motionless, speaks in monotone, and reports hearing two voices commenting on his actions.
He believes his thoughts are being broadcast on television and that the government is monitoring his mind.
Urine drug screen is negative, TSH, B12, RPR, and brain MRI are all normal, and his symptoms have been continuous for 8 months.
explanation: This disorder of thought content, perception, and motivation typically emerges in late adolescence/early adulthood. Positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) and negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition) reflect distinct pathophysiology.
keyFact: Duration distinguishes it from brief psychotic disorder (<1 month) and schizophreniform disorder (1-6 months). This patient has 8 months of symptoms. Negative drug screen rules out substance-induced psychosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Substance-Induced Psychosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cannabis and stimulants can cause identical psychotic symptoms. The negative drug screen and 8-month continuous course without substance use support a primary psychiatric diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar Disorder with Psychotic Features
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bipolar can include psychosis during mood episodes, but the psychosis resolves between episodes. This patient has continuous psychosis without prominent mood episodes.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophreniform Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophreniform has identical symptoms but lasts 1-6 months. At 8 months, this exceeds the threshold.

clues: A newborn is noted to have disproportionately short limbs with a normal-sized trunk and a large head.
Both parents are of normal height, and prenatal ultrasound had shown shortened long bones in the third trimester.
Exam reveals rhizomelic shortening (proximal limbs shorter than distal), frontal bossing, depressed nasal bridge, and a trident hand.
Skeletal survey shows shortened long bones with flared metaphyses and a narrowed spinal canal at the lumbar level.
Genetic testing reveals a gain-of-function mutation in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) on chromosome 4p.
explanation: FGFR3 normally acts as a brake on long bone growth. The activating mutation makes the brake permanently on, preventing normal endochondral ossification at the growth plates. Intramembranous ossification (skull, facial bones) is unaffected, causing the characteristic disproportion.
keyFact: Most common cause of dwarfism. Autosomal dominant but ~80% are new mutations in the paternal FGFR3 gene (associated with advanced paternal age). Intelligence is normal. Major complication is spinal stenosis from the narrowed canal.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteogenesis Imperfecta
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OI causes fragile bones that fracture easily but does not cause short stature with rhizomelic limb shortening. OI involves type I collagen, not FGFR3.

wrongAnswers.name: Turner Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Turner causes short stature but with normal body proportions, webbed neck, and 45,X karyotype — not rhizomelic limb shortening.

wrongAnswers.name: Rickets
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rickets causes bowing and short stature but with widened frayed metaphyses and metabolic abnormalities. The flared metaphyses here are from a growth plate signaling defect.

clues: A 25-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain and morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes each day.
His symptoms started gradually in his late teens, and he has also had episodes of a painful red eye and heel pain.
Exam reveals limited lumbar spine flexion, reduced chest expansion measured at the nipple line, and tenderness over both sacroiliac joints.
HLA-B27 is positive, ESR is elevated, and X-ray of the pelvis shows bilateral sacroiliac joint sclerosis, erosion, and early fusion.
Lateral spine X-ray shows squaring of the vertebral bodies with syndesmophytes bridging adjacent vertebrae.
explanation: Chronic inflammation at the entheses (where tendons and ligaments attach to bone) leads to progressive bony fusion of the sacroiliac joints and spine.
keyFact: Inflammatory back pain (young man, insidious onset, morning stiffness >30 min, improves with exercise, worsens with rest) is the opposite of mechanical back pain (worse with activity, better with rest). Bilateral sacroiliitis is the hallmark. Extra-articular: uveitis, aortitis, apical pulmonary fibrosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Mechanical Low Back Pain
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mechanical pain is WORSE with activity and BETTER with rest. This pain IMPROVES with exercise and is WORST in the morning — the inflammatory pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Lumbar Disc Herniation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Disc herniation causes radicular pain down a leg with positive straight-leg raise. This is bilateral axial back pain with sacroiliac inflammation.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis causes asymmetric oligoarthritis after GI/GU infections. This is bilateral sacroiliitis with progressive spinal fusion.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with painful recurrent oral ulcers that have been occurring for over a year.
He has also developed painful ulcers on his scrotum and episodes of painful red eyes with blurred vision.
Exam reveals deep aphthous ulcers on the buccal mucosa, scrotal ulceration scars, and anterior uveitis.
A skin prick test at the IV insertion site produces a sterile pustule within 48 hours of the needle stick.
Biopsy of an affected vessel shows neutrophilic vasculitis, and the pathergy test result is positive.
explanation: A neutrophilic vasculitis causes recurrent ulceration and inflammation at mucocutaneous surfaces, in the eyes, and in blood vessels.
keyFact: Oral ulcers + genital ulcers + uveitis is the classic triad. The pathergy test (pustule forming at needle prick site) is relatively specific. Most common along the ancient Silk Road (Turkey, Middle East, East Asia). Treat with colchicine, steroids, or biologics.

wrongAnswers.name: SLE
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus causes oral ulcers but they are painless, and lupus doesn't cause genital ulcers or positive pathergy test.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis causes oral ulcers, urethritis, and eye inflammation but following an infection, with oligoarthritis as the dominant feature.

wrongAnswers.name: Herpes Simplex
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV causes painful oral and genital ulcers but they are vesicular, recur in the same location, and don't have uveitis or positive pathergy.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with painless gross hematuria that appeared suddenly without any urinary symptoms.
He smoked a pack per day for 40 years, and the blood was present throughout the entire urinary stream.
Exam is unremarkable including a normal prostate on digital rectal exam and no costovertebral angle tenderness.
Urine cytology shows atypical cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, and CT urogram reveals a mass arising from the bladder wall.
Cystoscopy with biopsy confirms a high-grade papillary tumor arising from the urothelial lining.
explanation: The transitional epithelium lining the urinary tract undergoes malignant transformation, most commonly from carcinogen exposure through smoking or occupational chemicals excreted in urine.
keyFact: Painless hematuria in an older smoker = bladder cancer until proven otherwise. Smoking is the #1 risk factor. Occupational exposure (aniline dyes, aromatic amines, rubber, leather) is #2. BCG immunotherapy for superficial disease is one of the oldest successful cancer immunotherapies.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RCC causes hematuria but typically with a renal mass on imaging, not a bladder wall mass on cystoscopy.

wrongAnswers.name: Kidney Stone
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stones cause hematuria but with severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin. This hematuria is PAINLESS.

wrongAnswers.name: Urinary Tract Infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: UTI causes hematuria with dysuria, frequency, and pyuria. This patient has no urinary symptoms and cytology shows atypical cells.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging painful mass in his pelvis and upper thigh over one year.
He has no constitutional symptoms, and the growth has been gradual but relentless.
Exam reveals a large deep fixed mass in the proximal thigh with limited hip range of motion.
X-ray shows a destructive lesion in the pelvic bone with stippled 'popcorn' calcifications within the tumor matrix on CT.
Biopsy shows malignant chondrocytes in a hyaline cartilage matrix with lobular architecture and myxoid changes.
explanation: Malignant chondrocytes produce cartilage matrix that calcifies in a characteristic stippled or ring-and-arc pattern visible on imaging. The tumor grows slowly but inexorably.
keyFact: Older adult + axial skeleton (pelvis, proximal femur) + stippled/popcorn calcifications + resistant to chemo and radiation = chondrosarcoma. Treatment is surgical — there's no effective adjuvant therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteosarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteosarcoma occurs in adolescents in the metaphysis of long bones with osteoid production. This is a middle-aged adult with a pelvic tumor producing cartilage matrix.

wrongAnswers.name: Enchondroma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Enchondroma is a BENIGN cartilage tumor in the hand with similar stippled calcifications. Chondrosarcoma is the malignant counterpart, typically in the pelvis or proximal bones.

wrongAnswers.name: Metastatic Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastatic cancer to bone is more common than primary bone tumors in adults, but the stippled cartilage matrix calcifications identify a primary cartilage-producing tumor.

clues: A 40-year-old woman with a long history of severe asthma presents with numbness in her right foot.
She has had worsening asthma with nasal polyps and now has a purpuric rash on her legs.
Exam reveals a foot drop on the right from peroneal nerve involvement, palpable purpura on both legs, and wheezing.
Eosinophil count is 8,500, p-ANCA is positive, and chest imaging shows transient pulmonary infiltrates.
Biopsy of the skin lesion shows eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation centered on small vessel walls.
explanation: This vasculitis evolves through three phases: allergic (asthma, rhinitis), eosinophilic (tissue infiltration), and vasculitic (small vessel damage with purpura and neuropathy).
keyFact: Asthma + eosinophilia + vasculitis is the triad. The asthma typically PRECEDES the vasculitis by years and then paradoxically worsens. p-ANCA positive in ~40%. Distinguished from GPA by the asthma, eosinophilia, and rarity of renal involvement.

wrongAnswers.name: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ABPA causes asthma with eosinophilia but from an Aspergillus hypersensitivity reaction — no vasculitis, purpura, or neuropathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GPA causes a lung-kidney syndrome but WITHOUT asthma, without peripheral eosinophilia, and with c-ANCA/PR3 rather than p-ANCA.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypereosinophilic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HES causes persistent eosinophilia with organ damage but is a primary eosinophilic disorder, not a vasculitis with granulomas and p-ANCA.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with severe worsening leg pain 6 hours after a tibial fracture, despite adequate pain medication.
The pain is out of proportion to the injury and is worst when someone passively dorsiflexes his toes.
The affected leg is tense and firm to palpation, and he reports numbness between his first and second toes.
Compartment pressure is measured at 42 mmHg using an intracompartmental needle device, and distal pulses remain palpable.
The anterior compartment is bulging and taut, and the cast is immediately bivalved with no improvement in pressure.
explanation: Swelling within a rigid fascial compartment raises pressure above capillary perfusion pressure, causing ischemia of muscle and nerves trapped within the compartment.
keyFact: Pain out of proportion + pain with passive stretch + paresthesias = compartment syndrome until proven otherwise. The 5 P's (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paralysis, poikilothermia) are LATE findings — don't wait for them. Pulses may be present because arterial pressure exceeds compartment pressure even when capillary flow is compromised.

wrongAnswers.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DVT causes calf pain and swelling but without the tense compartment, pain with passive stretch, or elevated compartment pressures.

wrongAnswers.name: Fracture Pain
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fracture pain is expected but should improve with immobilization and analgesia. WORSENING pain despite treatment with pain on passive stretch is the red flag.

wrongAnswers.name: Arterial Injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Arterial injury causes limb ischemia with absent pulses. Compartment syndrome has PRESERVED pulses because the pressure is below arterial but above capillary.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive difficulty climbing stairs and rising from chairs over the past 3 months.
She has noticed a violaceous discoloration of her upper eyelids and a scaly rash over her knuckles.
Exam reveals symmetric proximal weakness in deltoids and hip flexors, periorbital edema, and erythematous scaly papules over her MCP and PIP joints.
CK is 4,200, aldolase is elevated, and EMG shows myopathic changes with fibrillations — anti-Mi-2 antibodies are positive.
Muscle biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy with perimysial inflammation and complement deposition on capillaries.
explanation: An autoimmune process attacks skeletal muscle and skin simultaneously, causing proximal weakness with characteristic cutaneous findings. The malignancy association makes cancer screening mandatory.
keyFact: The violet eyelid rash and the knuckle papules (Gottron papules) are pathognomonic skin findings. The rash can PRECEDE the weakness (amyopathic form). Cancer screening: ovarian, lung, GI, breast, and lymphoma are the most common associated malignancies.

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polymyositis causes identical proximal weakness with elevated CK but WITHOUT the skin findings. The heliotrope rash and Gottron papules distinguish dermatomyositis.

wrongAnswers.name: SLE
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus causes a facial rash but the malar rash spares the nasolabial folds and is NOT associated with severe proximal weakness and CK elevation.

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PMR causes proximal pain but with NORMAL strength and NORMAL CK. This patient has TRUE weakness with CK of 4,200.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with a history of recurrent joint dislocations and skin that bruises extremely easily.
Her shoulder has dislocated 4 times and her kneecap subluxes regularly, and she has a wound that healed with a wide papery scar.
Exam reveals hyperextensible velvety skin that can be stretched well beyond normal, joint hypermobility at multiple sites, and wide atrophic scars.
Beighton hypermobility score is 8/9, and she has a positive thumb-to-forearm sign and elbow hyperextension beyond 10 degrees.
Genetic testing reveals a collagen type V mutation, and echocardiogram shows no aortic root dilation.
explanation: Defective collagen makes connective tissues too stretchy and fragile. Joints dislocate because ligaments can't hold them, and skin tears easily and heals poorly.
keyFact: The vascular type (type III collagen) kills — arterial dissection, bowel perforation, uterine rupture. The hypermobile type is most common and least dangerous. Always determine the subtype.

wrongAnswers.name: Marfan Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Marfan involves elastic fiber scaffolding (fibrillin) and causes lens subluxation and aortic root dilation. EDS involves collagen and causes skin hyperextensibility and joint hypermobility.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteogenesis Imperfecta
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OI is a type I collagen defect that primarily weakens BONE (fractures, blue sclerae), not skin and joints.

wrongAnswers.name: Benign Joint Hypermobility
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Benign hypermobility is common but without the skin fragility, abnormal scarring, or collagen gene mutation.

clues: A 12-year-old boy presents with progressive thigh pain and fever that have been worsening for 6 weeks.
He has lost 5 pounds and has a soft tissue mass overlying his mid-femur.
Exam reveals a warm tender mass overlying the mid-femoral shaft.
X-ray shows a permeative lytic lesion in the DIAPHYSIS with a layered 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction.
Biopsy reveals sheets of uniform small round blue cells with a characteristic translocation t(11;22).
explanation: A primitive neuroectodermal tumor arises in the bone diaphysis, producing fever and elevated inflammatory markers that can mimic osteomyelitis.
keyFact: DIAPHYSEAL location + onion-skin periosteal reaction + small round blue cells + t(11;22) + fever in a child/adolescent = Ewing. The fever and elevated WBC mimic infection — always biopsy before treating as osteomyelitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteosarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteosarcoma occurs in the METAPHYSIS with a sunburst periosteal reaction and produces osteoid. Ewing is DIAPHYSEAL with onion-skin and small round blue cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteomyelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteomyelitis mimics Ewing with bone pain, fever, and elevated WBC. But the onion-skin periosteal reaction and small round blue cells on biopsy confirm malignancy.

wrongAnswers.name: Neuroblastoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Neuroblastoma causes bone metastases in children with small round blue cells, but the primary is an adrenal/sympathetic chain mass with elevated urine catecholamines.

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with widespread body pain and unrefreshing sleep for over a year despite normal sleep duration.
She reports pain 'everywhere' along with cognitive difficulties she describes as 'brain fog.'
Exam reveals tenderness at multiple bilateral symmetric points but NORMAL joints with no swelling, warmth, or deformity.
ESR, CRP, CK, CBC, TSH, and ANA are all completely NORMAL with no objective abnormalities found.
Widespread pain index and symptom severity scores meet diagnostic criteria with no alternative explanation identified on workup.
explanation: Central sensitization amplifies normal sensory signals into pain signals, producing widespread pain without peripheral tissue damage or inflammation.
keyFact: Completely NORMAL labs and NORMAL exam (except tenderness) is the pattern. If ESR, CRP, CK, or ANA are abnormal, look for another diagnosis. Exercise is the most effective nonpharmacologic treatment. Duloxetine, pregabalin, and milnacipran are FDA-approved medications.

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PMR has markedly elevated ESR and CRP with girdle pain. Fibromyalgia has NORMAL inflammatory markers with widespread pain.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes fatigue and diffuse achiness but TSH is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA causes joint pain but with SWOLLEN joints, elevated inflammatory markers, and positive autoantibodies. Joints are normal on exam here.

clues: A 74-year-old woman presents with a new severe headache localized over her left temple for two weeks.
She has jaw pain that forces her to stop chewing during meals, aching shoulders and hips, and brief vision loss in one eye yesterday.
The artery at her left temple is tender, thickened, and nodular with a reduced pulse, and her scalp is tender when she brushes her hair.
ESR is 98, CRP is markedly elevated, and duplex ultrasound of the temporal artery shows a hypoechoic halo sign.
Temporal artery biopsy shows transmural granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and intimal thickening.
explanation: Granulomatous inflammation of cranial artery branches narrows the lumen, threatening the blood supply to the optic nerve.
keyFact: Jaw claudication (chewing fatigue) is highly specific. Transient vision loss is the WARNING — permanent loss follows. Treat immediately on suspicion. 40-60% have concurrent polymyalgia rheumatica. Never occurs under age 50.

wrongAnswers.name: Tension Headache
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tension headache is bilateral pressing pain without temporal artery abnormalities, jaw claudication, vision symptoms, or elevated ESR.

wrongAnswers.name: Migraine
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Migraine is unilateral with aura and photophobia but not temporal artery thickening, jaw claudication, or ESR of 98.

wrongAnswers.name: Takayasu Arteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Takayasu involves the aorta and great vessels in women UNDER 40. This involves cranial arteries in a woman OVER 50.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with progressive knee pain and swelling that has been worsening over two months.
The pain is activity-related and she recently felt the knee 'give way' while walking down stairs.
Exam reveals a palpable firm mass at the distal femur just above the knee joint with full but painful range of motion.
X-ray shows a lytic, expansile, 'soap bubble' lesion in the epiphysis of the distal femur extending to the subchondral bone without sclerotic rim.
Biopsy shows numerous multinucleated giant cells with 20-50 nuclei evenly distributed in a background of mononuclear stromal cells.
explanation: This locally aggressive benign tumor has a strong predilection for the epiphysis of long bones around the knee (distal femur, proximal tibia) in patients with closed growth plates.
keyFact: Epiphyseal + soap bubble lytic + skeletally mature young adult + around the knee = GCT. Most bone tumors are metaphyseal — the epiphyseal location is distinctive. Despite being benign, it is locally aggressive with a significant recurrence rate.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteosarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteosarcoma occurs in the METAPHYSIS of young patients with a sunburst periosteal reaction, not an epiphyseal soap bubble lesion.

wrongAnswers.name: Aneurysmal Bone Cyst
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ABC causes an expansile lytic lesion but is eccentric and metaphyseal, not centered in the epiphysis with giant cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Chondroblastoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chondroblastoma is also epiphyseal but occurs in skeletally IMMATURE patients (open growth plates) and has a characteristic chondroid matrix.

clues: A 54-year-old man is woken from sleep at 3 AM by excruciating pain in his right great toe.
He attended a dinner with steak, shellfish, and beer the night before, and he takes hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure.
The first joint of the right great toe is swollen, red, hot, and exquisitely tender to even light touch.
Joint aspiration reveals turbid fluid with 42,000 white cells, and serum uric acid is elevated at 9.8 mg/dL.
Under polarized light with a red compensator, the fluid contains needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent.
explanation: Chronic hyperuricemia deposits monosodium urate crystals in joints. The crystals trigger a massive neutrophil-driven inflammatory response, classically in the first MTP joint.
keyFact: Negative birefringence + needle-shaped = gout. Positive birefringence + rhomboid-shaped = pseudogout (CPPD). Thiazides increase uric acid. The first MTP (podagra) is classic because it's the coolest, most dependent joint.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic joint also produces a hot swollen painful joint with high WBC in fluid. Always rule it out — but the negatively birefringent needle crystals identify gout.

wrongAnswers.name: Pseudogout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CPPD involves the knee or wrist more often, and crystals are RHOMBOID and POSITIVELY birefringent — not needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The overlying redness mimics cellulitis, but joint aspiration with crystal-laden fluid confirms crystal arthropathy.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with chronic bloody nasal crusting that has not responded to multiple rounds of antibiotics.
