He has developed a cough with blood-tinged sputum, and his urine has become dark over the past month.
Exam reveals a collapsed nasal bridge and bilateral lung crackles.
Creatinine is 3.8, urine shows red blood cell casts, chest X-ray shows bilateral cavitating nodules, and c-ANCA with PR3 antibodies is positive.
Kidney biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with NO immune deposits on immunofluorescence — a 'pauci-immune' pattern.
explanation: The vasculitis attacks small and medium vessels in three classic locations: upper airway (sinuses, nose), lungs (nodules, hemorrhage), and kidneys (crescentic GN).
keyFact: c-ANCA/PR3 = this disease. p-ANCA/MPO = microscopic polyangiitis (no upper airway disease, no granulomas). The pauci-immune (no deposits) biopsy pattern distinguishes both from immune complex diseases and from anti-GBM disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Goodpasture Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Goodpasture causes a lung-kidney syndrome but with LINEAR IgG on biopsy and no upper airway destruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Microscopic Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MPA causes pauci-immune crescentic GN with pulmonary hemorrhage but has NO upper airway disease and is p-ANCA/MPO positive.

wrongAnswers.name: Cocaine Use
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cocaine can destroy the nasal septum and even cause positive ANCA tests, but doesn't produce pulmonary nodules or crescentic GN.

clues: A 16-year-old boy presents after his eye doctor discovered a dislocated lens during a routine vision screening.
His father has a similar build, and a paternal uncle died suddenly at age 35 from a cardiovascular event.
Exam reveals arm span exceeding height, long fingers, high-arched palate, pectus excavatum, and the dislocated lens has shifted upward and outward.
Echocardiogram shows aortic root dilation to 4.5 cm (Z-score >3) with mitral valve prolapse.
Genetic testing confirms a pathogenic mutation in FBN1, encoding fibrillin-1, the scaffold for elastic fibers.
explanation: Defective elastic fiber scaffolding weakens the aortic wall, lens suspensory ligaments, and other connective tissues.
keyFact: Lens UP and OUT = this syndrome. Lens DOWN and IN = homocystinuria. Both are tall and thin but this has normal intelligence and no thrombosis. Prophylactic aortic surgery at root diameter of 5.0 cm.

wrongAnswers.name: Homocystinuria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Also tall and thin with lens subluxation, but the lens goes DOWN and IN, there is intellectual disability, and thrombosis risk. Opposite lens direction.

wrongAnswers.name: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EDS causes joint hypermobility from collagen defects but no lens subluxation, no marfanoid habitus, and the vascular type involves collagen rather than elastic fiber scaffolding.

wrongAnswers.name: Loeys-Dietz Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Loeys-Dietz causes aortic aneurysm with some similar features but has bifid uvula and hypertelorism, and no lens subluxation.

clues: A 68-year-old woman presents with knee pain that has worsened over several years and is worst at the end of the day after prolonged activity.
Morning stiffness lasts about 15 minutes then loosens up. The pain gets WORSE with activity and BETTER with rest.
Exam reveals hard bony enlargements at the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints and crepitus on knee flexion and extension.
X-rays show asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts, and osteophytes — ESR and CRP are normal.
Synovial fluid analysis shows a non-inflammatory pattern with a white cell count below 2,000 and no crystals under polarized light.
explanation: Articular cartilage wears away over decades. Without cushioning, bone grinds on bone. The body compensates by growing new bone at margins (osteophytes) and thickening subchondral bone (sclerosis).
keyFact: DIP involvement (Heberden nodes) + PIP (Bouchard nodes) = OA. MCPs spared. Brief morning stiffness (<30 min) worsening with activity = mechanical. Prolonged stiffness (>1 hour) improving with activity = inflammatory (RA). Normal inflammatory markers confirm degenerative process.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA is symmetric MCP/PIP inflammation with >1 hour morning stiffness IMPROVING with use, elevated ESR/CRP, and erosions. RA SPARES the DIPs.

wrongAnswers.name: Pseudogout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CPPD causes acute flares with joint inflammation and chondrocalcinosis on X-ray, not the chronic progressive mechanical pain pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Gout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gout causes acute hot red joint attacks, not chronic progressive bilateral knee pain with bony enlargements and normal inflammatory markers.

clues: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with a femur fracture after a minor fall from standing height.
The parents report multiple previous fractures from minimal trauma, and there is a family history of similar fractures in the mother.
Exam reveals blue-tinged sclerae, mild joint hypermobility, and evidence of a healing rib fracture on incidental chest X-ray.
Skeletal survey shows diffuse osteopenia with thin cortices and old fractures in various stages of healing — but metaphyses are normal.
Genetic testing reveals a pathogenic variant in COL1A1, the gene encoding the alpha-1 chain of type I collagen.
explanation: Defective type I collagen weakens bone matrix, causing fractures from forces that would not injure normal bone. The severity ranges from mild to lethal depending on the mutation.
keyFact: Blue sclerae + hearing loss + multiple fractures with minimal trauma = OI. Type I (mild, autosomal dominant) is the most common. Type II (lethal in utero) is the most severe. Must be distinguished from child abuse — the normal metaphyses help (abuse often damages the metaphysis).

wrongAnswers.name: Child Abuse
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Non-accidental trauma is appropriately considered with multiple fractures, but the blue sclerae, family history, osteopenia, and normal metaphyses support a collagen disorder.

wrongAnswers.name: Rickets
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rickets causes fractures and bowing but with widened frayed metaphyses and lab abnormalities (low calcium, low phosphorus, elevated ALP). Metaphyses are normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EDS involves type V (or III in vascular type) collagen causing joint hypermobility and skin fragility, not the bone fragility from type I collagen defect.

clues: A 10-year-old boy presents with refusal to bear weight on his right leg for three days and low-grade fevers.
He scraped his shin on a rock one week ago, and the area has become progressively more painful.
Exam reveals warmth, erythema, and exquisite point tenderness over the right tibial metaphysis.
ESR and CRP are elevated, and MRI shows marrow edema with a subperiosteal fluid collection and periosteal reaction.
Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus, the most common pathogen identified in this condition.
explanation: Bacteria seeded the bone via hematogenous spread or direct inoculation from the skin wound, establishing infection in the metaphysis where sluggish blood flow allows bacterial colonization.
keyFact: S. aureus is the most common organism at all ages. The metaphysis is the classic location in children due to its rich blood supply and sluggish flow. MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality. In sickle cell patients, Salmonella is disproportionately common.

wrongAnswers.name: Ewing Sarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ewing causes bone pain and fever in children with an 'onion skin' periosteal reaction, but cultures are negative and biopsy shows small round blue cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic arthritis causes joint pain and fever but the infection is in the joint space (effusion), not in the bone marrow. MRI localizes this to the bone.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis causes skin warmth and erythema but without the deep bone tenderness, marrow edema on MRI, or periosteal reaction.

clues: A 16-year-old boy presents with progressive knee pain that is worse at night and no longer relieved by ibuprofen.
The pain has been present for 3 months, and his parents noticed the area looks larger than the other side.
Exam reveals a firm fixed tender mass at the distal femur above the knee with restricted range of motion.
X-ray shows a destructive lesion in the metaphysis of the distal femur with a 'sunburst' periosteal reaction and soft tissue mass.
Biopsy shows malignant spindle cells producing osteoid matrix, and serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated.
explanation: The most common primary malignant bone tumor in adolescents arises from mesenchymal cells that produce osteoid. It preferentially occurs in the metaphysis of rapidly growing long bones.
keyFact: Metaphyseal + around the knee (distal femur > proximal tibia) + sunburst periosteal reaction + osteoid production + adolescent = osteosarcoma. Elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects bone formation. Associated with Rb gene mutations, Li-Fraumeni, and Paget disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Ewing Sarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ewing occurs in the DIAPHYSIS (not metaphysis) with an 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction (not sunburst) and does NOT produce osteoid.

wrongAnswers.name: Giant Cell Tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GCT occurs in the EPIPHYSIS of young adults (closed growth plates), not the metaphysis of an adolescent.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteomyelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteomyelitis causes metaphyseal bone destruction with periosteal reaction in children, but cultures grow bacteria and there is no osteoid-producing malignant tissue.

clues: A 70-year-old man presents because his hat size has increased and he has progressive hearing loss in both ears.
He has been having lower back and hip pain, and his wife says his posture is more stooped.
Exam reveals skull enlargement, mild bowing of the left tibia, and warmth over the affected bones.
Alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated at 650 with normal calcium, phosphorus, and PTH — X-ray shows cortical thickening and coarsened trabeculae.
Bone biopsy shows a 'mosaic' pattern of disorganized lamellar bone from chaotic cycles of resorption and formation.
explanation: Overactive osteoclasts drive excessive bone resorption, followed by exuberant but disorganized osteoblastic new bone formation. The result is expanded, weakened, structurally chaotic bone.
keyFact: Markedly elevated ALP with NORMAL calcium = Paget (ALP reflects osteoblastic activity). Skull enlargement, hearing loss (CN VIII compression), bowing of long bones, and warmth (increased vascularity) are classic. Rare complication: transformation to osteosarcoma (<1%).

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PHPT elevates BOTH ALP and calcium. Paget has elevated ALP with NORMAL calcium.

wrongAnswers.name: Metastatic Cancer to Bone
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bone metastases cause lytic or blastic lesions but without the characteristic mosaic pattern, skull enlargement, or isolated ALP elevation with normal calcium.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteoporosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteoporosis causes decreased bone density with fractures but ALP is normal and there's no mosaic pattern or bone expansion.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with unexplained fevers, weight loss, and diffuse muscle aches over several weeks.
He has chronic hepatitis B. He has developed pain in seemingly unconnected areas — his belly, his right foot, and his left testicle.
Exam reveals hypertension, a mottled net-like skin discoloration on his legs, and weakness of right foot dorsiflexion.
ANCA is NEGATIVE, and mesenteric and renal angiography shows multiple microaneurysms along the arteries with segmental narrowing.
Biopsy shows transmural inflammation of medium-sized arteries with fibrinoid necrosis — the disease spares the lungs and does NOT involve glomeruli.
explanation: Immune complex-mediated vasculitis attacks medium-sized muscular arteries, weakening vessel walls to form aneurysms and narrowing lumens to cause downstream ischemia.
keyFact: ANCA negative + lung sparing + no glomerulonephritis = this disease. The hepatitis B association is high-yield. Mononeuritis multiplex (individual named nerves dying sequentially) is very characteristic.

wrongAnswers.name: GPA
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GPA is c-ANCA positive, involves lungs and glomeruli, and has upper airway destruction. This is ANCA negative, spares lungs and glomeruli.

wrongAnswers.name: Microscopic Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MPA is p-ANCA positive and involves small vessels (capillaries/venules) causing GN and pulmonary hemorrhage. This involves medium arteries with no GN.

wrongAnswers.name: Fibromuscular Dysplasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FMD causes a beaded appearance on angiography but is non-inflammatory in young women — no fevers, no weight loss, no hepatitis.

clues: A 72-year-old woman presents with shoulder and hip pain and stiffness that takes over an hour to loosen each morning.
She has difficulty raising her arms to brush her hair and getting out of a chair, and has lost 8 pounds unintentionally.
Exam reveals painful limited active range of motion at both shoulders but FULL passive range and NORMAL muscle strength.
ESR is 85 and CRP is 6.2, but CK is completely normal. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are negative.
Low-dose prednisone (15 mg daily) produces dramatic improvement in pain and stiffness within 48 hours.
explanation: An inflammatory condition of unclear etiology causes pain and stiffness in the shoulder and hip girdles without true muscle weakness or damage — the CK is normal because muscle fibers are not being destroyed.
keyFact: Bilateral shoulder/hip girdle PAIN with NORMAL strength and NORMAL CK distinguishes PMR from inflammatory myopathy (which has TRUE weakness and elevated CK). The dramatic response to low-dose prednisone is a hallmark. Always screen for GCA (present in 15-20%).

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polymyositis causes proximal weakness with ELEVATED CK from muscle destruction. PMR has proximal PAIN but NORMAL strength and NORMAL CK.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA causes morning stiffness with elevated inflammatory markers, but involves small joints (MCPs, PIPs), not the shoulder/hip girdle pattern with normal CK.

wrongAnswers.name: Fibromyalgia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain but ESR and CRP are NORMAL. This patient has markedly elevated inflammatory markers.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive difficulty climbing stairs and rising from chairs over 3 months.
She has no rash, no joint pain, and no sensory complaints — the weakness is purely motor and purely proximal.
Exam reveals symmetric proximal weakness (4/5 in deltoids and hip flexors) with NORMAL sensation, NORMAL reflexes, and no skin findings.
CK is 6,800, aldolase is elevated, and EMG shows myopathic changes with fibrillations — anti-Jo-1 antibodies are positive.
Muscle biopsy shows endomysial CD8+ T-cell infiltrate surrounding and invading individual non-necrotic muscle fibers.
explanation: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells directly invade and destroy skeletal muscle fibers, causing symmetric proximal weakness without skin involvement.
keyFact: Proximal weakness + elevated CK + NO skin findings = polymyositis. ADD skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules) = dermatomyositis. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with interstitial lung disease (antisynthetase syndrome).

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatomyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatomyositis has identical muscle findings but WITH characteristic skin changes. This patient has NO rash.

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PMR causes proximal PAIN but with NORMAL strength and NORMAL CK. This patient has TRUE weakness with CK of 6,800.

wrongAnswers.name: Inclusion Body Myositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IBM causes asymmetric distal AND proximal weakness in older men with poor treatment response. This is symmetric proximal weakness in a middle-aged woman.

clues: A 72-year-old woman presents with acute onset of a swollen, red, painful right knee that began this morning.
She has a history of osteoarthritis and hemochromatosis, and had no preceding trauma or dietary triggers.
Exam reveals a warm erythematous right knee with a large effusion and painful range of motion.

Joint aspiration shows inflammatory fluid with white cells, and under polarized light the crystals are rhomboid-shaped and weakly POSITIVELY birefringent — appearing blue when parallel to the compensator axis.
Knee X-ray shows a thin white line of calcification within the meniscal cartilage, confirming calcium crystal deposition.
explanation: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals deposit in cartilage (chondrocalcinosis) and can periodically shed into the joint space, triggering an acute inflammatory attack.
keyFact: Positive birefringence + rhomboid = CPPD (pseudogout). Negative birefringence + needle = gout. Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray is a supportive finding. Associated with hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and hypomagnesemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Gout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gout crystals are NEEDLE-shaped and NEGATIVELY birefringent, and the first MTP is the classic joint. This has RHOMBOID, POSITIVELY birefringent crystals in the knee.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic joint causes similar acute monoarthritis but gram stain and culture would be positive, and no crystals are seen.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteoarthritis Flare
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OA causes chronic knee pain but the acute inflammatory presentation with positively birefringent crystals identifies crystal disease, not mechanical wear.

clues: A 40-year-old man presents with swelling of his entire right third finger that resembles a sausage.
He has a 10-year history of a chronic scaly skin condition, back pain, and tenderness at his left Achilles tendon insertion.
Exam reveals the diffusely swollen 'sausage digit,' asymmetric DIP joint swelling, and nail pitting with onycholysis.
Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are NEGATIVE, and X-rays show 'pencil-in-cup' deformity at the DIP joints.
On closer skin inspection, silvery scaly plaques are present on the extensor surfaces of his elbows, knees, and gluteal cleft.
explanation: The same autoimmune process that drives skin psoriasis attacks the joints, entheses, and nails. The pattern is characteristically different from rheumatoid arthritis.
keyFact: Five patterns: DIP predominant, asymmetric oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis (RA mimic), spondylitis, and arthritis mutilans (severely destructive). Dactylitis (sausage digit) and enthesitis (tendon insertion inflammation) are characteristic. RF and anti-CCP are NEGATIVE.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA involves MCPs and PIPs symmetrically, SPARES the DIPs, is RF/anti-CCP positive, and causes erosions — not pencil-in-cup deformity.

wrongAnswers.name: Gout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gout causes acute monoarthritis with urate crystals. Dactylitis with nail changes and DIP involvement in a psoriasis patient is PsA.

wrongAnswers.name: Ankylosing Spondylitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AS causes axial spondylitis but without peripheral DIP arthritis, dactylitis, nail changes, or skin psoriasis.

clues: A 25-year-old man presents with a swollen painful right knee that began 3 weeks after an episode of bloody diarrhea.
He also has pain on urination and bilateral red irritated eyes that developed around the same time.
Exam reveals a warm swollen right knee effusion, bilateral conjunctival injection, and painless shallow ulcers on his glans.
Joint aspiration is STERILE — no organisms are identified despite the inflammatory fluid — and HLA-B27 is positive.
Synovial biopsy shows nonspecific inflammation, and stool cultures from the initial diarrheal episode grew Campylobacter.
explanation: A preceding GI or GU infection triggers an immune-mediated inflammatory response that targets joints, eyes, and the genitourinary tract in genetically susceptible (HLA-B27+) individuals.
keyFact: The classic triad: can't see (conjunctivitis), can't pee (urethritis), can't climb a tree (arthritis). The joint is STERILE — this is immune-mediated, not infectious. Common triggers: Chlamydia (GU), Salmonella/Shigella/Campylobacter/Yersinia (GI).

wrongAnswers.name: Septic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic arthritis grows organisms from the joint fluid. This joint fluid is STERILE — the inflammation is immune-mediated, not from direct infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Gonococcal Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Disseminated gonococcal infection causes septic arthritis with urethritis, but joint fluid cultures or NAAT would be positive. The joint fluid here is sterile.

wrongAnswers.name: Gout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gout causes acute monoarthritis but with urate crystals on polarized microscopy and no preceding GI infection or conjunctivitis.

clues: A 60-year-old man presents with painless blood in his urine that appeared without any other urinary symptoms.
He is a smoker. He has had unexplained fevers, night sweats, and an elevated red blood cell count despite chronic disease.
Exam reveals a palpable left flank mass and a new left-sided varicocele that does not decompress when he lies flat.
CT shows a 7-cm enhancing mass arising from the left kidney with extension into the left renal vein.
Biopsy shows clear cells arranged in nests with prominent vascular channels. Hemoglobin is 18.2 g/dL.
explanation: Arising from proximal tubular epithelial cells, this tumor invades the renal vein (and sometimes the IVC) and produces a variety of hormones and cytokines as paraneoplastic phenomena.
keyFact: Classic triad: hematuria + flank pain + palpable mass (seen in only ~10% but highly suggestive). Left-sided varicocele that doesn't decompress supine = left renal vein obstruction. The diverse paraneoplastic syndromes make it the 'internist's tumor.'

wrongAnswers.name: Wilms Tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wilms is the renal malignancy of CHILDREN (age 2-5). RCC occurs in ADULTS.

wrongAnswers.name: Transitional Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TCC causes hematuria from the collecting system/ureter/bladder, not a solid enhancing parenchymal mass with renal vein invasion.

wrongAnswers.name: Polycythemia Vera
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PV causes elevated hemoglobin from a JAK2 mutation with suppressed EPO. This patient's polycythemia is from ectopic EPO production by the tumor — EPO would be elevated.

clues: A 4-year-old boy presents with a rapidly growing mass protruding from his nasal cavity and recurrent nosebleeds.
The mass has grown noticeably over just 3 weeks and is now causing nasal obstruction and proptosis of the right eye.
Exam reveals a polypoid mass visible in the right naris with proptosis and periorbital swelling.
CT shows an aggressive soft tissue mass arising from the nasopharynx, eroding through the nasal wall into the right orbit.
Biopsy shows small round blue cells, and immunohistochemistry is positive for desmin and myogenin confirming skeletal muscle lineage.
explanation: Malignant cells with skeletal muscle differentiation arise in areas where striated muscle is present or where mesenchymal cells can differentiate toward skeletal muscle lineage.
keyFact: Small round blue cells + desmin/myogenin positivity = rhabdomyosarcoma. Embryonal type (head/neck, GU tract) is most common in young children. Alveolar type (extremities) in adolescents carries worse prognosis with t(2;13).

wrongAnswers.name: Neuroblastoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Neuroblastoma causes facial swelling in children from orbital metastases, but the primary is an adrenal mass with elevated urine catecholamines, not a nasal mass with muscle markers.

wrongAnswers.name: Nasal Polyp
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nasal polyps are benign and slow-growing. A rapidly growing nasal mass in a child with proptosis is malignant until proven otherwise.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma can cause nasal masses but biopsy shows lymphoid markers, not the desmin and myogenin muscle markers.

clues: A 40-year-old woman presents with hand pain and stiffness that is worst in the morning, takes over an hour to improve, and gets better as she uses her hands.
The symptoms have been present for 4 months and are symmetric, affecting both hands equally.
Exam reveals boggy swelling of the MCP and PIP joints bilaterally with tender wrists — the DIP joints are completely SPARED.
RF is positive and ESR is 62. Hand X-rays show periarticular osteopenia at the MCP joints.
Anti-CCP antibodies are strongly positive at 340 U/mL, and follow-up X-rays show new marginal erosions at the second and third MCP joints.
explanation: Autoimmune inflammation of the synovial lining creates an invasive tissue (pannus) that erodes cartilage and bone from the joint margins.
keyFact: Sparing of the end finger joints (DIPs) distinguishes this from osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthritis. Morning stiffness >1 hour that improves with use is inflammatory. Anti-CCP is more specific than rheumatoid factor.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteoarthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OA involves the DIP joints with brief morning stiffness (<30 min) that WORSENS with use and normal inflammatory markers.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriatic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PsA CAN involve DIPs (unlike RA), causes sausage digits (dactylitis), is RF/anti-CCP negative, and associates with skin psoriasis.

wrongAnswers.name: SLE
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus arthritis is non-erosive with reducible deformities, unlike the erosive destruction seen on X-ray here.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with an acutely swollen, hot, painful knee that developed over 24 hours.
He has diabetes. He has a fever of 102.5°F and cannot bend or straighten the knee without severe pain.
Exam reveals a tense warm erythematous knee effusion with severe pain on any attempt at passive range of motion.
Joint aspiration reveals purulent fluid with 85,000 white cells, and gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters.
Synovial fluid white count is 85,000 with gram-positive cocci in clusters. Crystal analysis under polarized light is negative.
explanation: Bacteria seeded the joint hematogenously, triggering a massive neutrophilic response. The enzymes released by neutrophils and bacteria rapidly degrade cartilage, making drainage urgent.
keyFact: S. aureus is the most common organism overall. N. gonorrhoeae is most common in sexually active young adults. Joint fluid WBC >50,000 with >75% PMNs is highly suggestive. Must be distinguished from crystal arthropathy — check polarized microscopy for crystals.

wrongAnswers.name: Gout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gout causes an acute hot swollen joint but with negatively birefringent needle crystals on aspiration and a lower WBC count. Always rule out septic arthritis — they can coexist.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis causes joint inflammation but is sterile (gram stain and cultures are negative) and occurs after GI or GU infections.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemarthrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemarthrosis (as in hemophilia) causes a tense joint effusion but the fluid is bloody, not purulent, and there's no fever.

clues: A 48-year-old woman presents with persistently dry eyes and dry mouth for over a year, requiring constant water to swallow dry food.
She has a gritty sandy sensation in her eyes and her dentist found 6 new cavities at her last visit despite good hygiene.
Both parotid glands are mildly enlarged, and a filter paper strip placed inside her lower eyelid barely wets in 5 minutes.
Anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La) antibodies are positive, and RF is also elevated.
Minor salivary gland biopsy from the inner lip shows dense focal lymphocytic infiltrates with more than 50 lymphocytes per focus.
explanation: Lymphocytes infiltrate and destroy the moisture-producing glands. Without tears the eyes dry and scar; without saliva the teeth decay rapidly.
keyFact: Anti-SSA (Ro) antibodies cross the placenta → neonatal lupus with congenital heart block. MALT lymphoma risk is 40x general population. Can be primary or secondary (with RA, lupus, or scleroderma).

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis can enlarge parotid glands but shows non-caseating granulomas on biopsy, not lymphocytic infiltration. Autoantibodies are negative.

wrongAnswers.name: IgG4-Related Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgG4-RD mimics this with gland enlargement but has IgG4-positive plasma cells on biopsy and elevated serum IgG4 — responds dramatically to steroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Medication Side Effect
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anticholinergic drugs commonly cause dry mouth and eyes but without autoantibodies, parotid enlargement, or positive lip biopsy.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressively tight skin on her hands and face and increasing difficulty swallowing solid foods.
Her fingers turn white then blue then red in cold temperatures, and she has chronic worsening heartburn.
Exam reveals thickened shiny taut skin on the hands, forearms, and face that cannot be pinched, pitted scars at the fingertips, and telangiectasias.
ANA is positive with a nucleolar pattern, and anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibodies are positive.
CT chest shows ground-glass opacities with early fibrosis at the lung bases, and skin thickening extends proximal to the elbows.
explanation: The immune system activates fibroblasts to deposit excessive collagen in skin and internal organs, with concurrent vascular damage causing the color changes in the fingers.
keyFact: Diffuse form: anti-topoisomerase (anti-Scl-70), rapid skin progression, lung fibrosis, renal crisis. Limited form (CREST): anti-centromere, slow skin progression limited to hands/face, pulmonary arterial hypertension.

wrongAnswers.name: SLE
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus causes a facial rash and joint disease but not the skin fibrosis, sclerodactyly, and anti-topoisomerase antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: CREST Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CREST is the limited form with skin changes only distal to elbows/knees, anti-centromere antibodies, and less visceral involvement. This has proximal skin involvement with anti-topoisomerase.

wrongAnswers.name: Eosinophilic Fasciitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eosinophilic fasciitis causes skin tightening but spares the hands and face and involves the fascia rather than the dermis.

clues: A 25-year-old woman presents with exertional arm pain and fatigue that worsen with overhead activities.
She has had fevers and unintentional weight loss, and her doctor noticed a blood pressure difference between her arms.
Exam reveals absent radial pulse on the left, a blood pressure discrepancy of 30 mmHg between arms, and arterial bruits over the carotids.
ESR is markedly elevated, and CT angiography shows concentric wall thickening and narrowing of the aortic arch and its major branches.
Biopsy of the vessel wall shows granulomatous inflammation with giant cells affecting the aorta and its primary branches.
explanation: Large vessel granulomatous vasculitis narrows the aorta and its major branches, reducing blood flow to the arms (pulse deficits) and causing ischemic symptoms.
keyFact: Age <40, female, Asian = classic demographics. The pulse deficits give it the name 'pulseless disease.' Histologically identical to the elderly cranial artery vasculitis — age and vessel distribution differentiate them.

wrongAnswers.name: Giant Cell Arteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GCA affects patients >50 and involves temporal and cranial arteries. This affects a 25-year-old and involves the aorta and great vessels.

wrongAnswers.name: Subclavian Steal Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Subclavian steal causes arm claudication but from atherosclerotic stenosis in older patients — not inflammatory wall thickening in a young woman.

wrongAnswers.name: Coarctation of the Aorta
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Coarctation causes arm-leg blood pressure differences, not arm-to-arm differences. It's congenital, not inflammatory.

clues: A 3-year-old girl is brought in after her mother noticed a large smooth mass in the child's abdomen while bathing her.
The child is otherwise healthy and playful, with no pain, blood in the urine, or weight loss.
Exam reveals a large smooth firm nontender flank mass that does NOT cross the midline, and blood pressure is mildly elevated for age.
Abdominal CT shows a large intrarenal mass with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis arising from the left kidney, displacing surrounding structures.
Biopsy shows triphasic histology with blastemal, stromal, and epithelial components representing embryonic kidney tissue.
explanation: Persistent embryonic renal tissue (metanephric blastema) undergoes malignant transformation, forming a large renal mass. The tumor is remarkable for its excellent response to multimodal therapy.
keyFact: Abdominal mass + child aged 2-5 + does NOT cross midline + intrarenal on imaging = Wilms. CROSSES the midline = neuroblastoma (adrenal origin). Wilms has excellent prognosis (~90% cure). Associated with WAGR syndrome (Wilms, Aniridia, GU anomalies, intellectual disability) and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Neuroblastoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Neuroblastoma arises from the adrenal gland and CROSSES the midline with elevated urine catecholamines. Wilms is intrarenal and does NOT cross the midline.

wrongAnswers.name: Polycystic Kidney Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ADPKD causes enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts, not a solid intrarenal mass with hemorrhage and necrosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RCC is the renal malignancy of ADULTS (peak age 50-70), not a 3-year-old. Wilms is the renal malignancy of childhood.

clues: A 20-year-old woman develops throat tightness, diffuse hives, and difficulty breathing within 5 minutes of eating at a restaurant.
She has a known shellfish allergy and was told the dish did not contain shellfish.
She is wheezing with stridor, diffuse urticaria, and her blood pressure has dropped to 78/42 with a heart rate of 128.
Serum tryptase drawn within 1 hour of the episode is markedly elevated at 85 ng/mL, confirming mast cell degranulation.
The allergen is identified as shrimp protein cross-contamination in the kitchen.
explanation: Massive mast cell and basophil degranulation releases histamine and other mediators that cause widespread vasodilation (hypotension), bronchospasm (wheezing), laryngeal edema (stridor), and urticaria.
keyFact: Epinephrine IM is FIRST — it reverses all the pathophysiology (vasoconstriction, bronchodilation, decreased mediator release). Antihistamines and steroids are SECOND. Observe for 4-6 hours for biphasic reaction. Prescribe an epinephrine auto-injector at discharge.

wrongAnswers.name: Severe Allergic Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Allergic reactions without hemodynamic compromise (just urticaria or angioedema) can be treated with antihistamines. Once hypotension, airway compromise, or multisystem involvement occurs, it's anaphylaxis requiring epinephrine.

wrongAnswers.name: Vasovagal Syncope
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vasovagal reaction causes hypotension and bradycardia but without urticaria, wheezing, or stridor.

wrongAnswers.name: Panic Attack
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Panic causes throat tightness and dyspnea but without urticaria, wheezing, or true hypotension.

clues: A 5-year-old child presents with progressive difficulty walking and recurrent sinopulmonary infections.
The ataxia began when the child started walking and has progressively worsened. The parents noticed red lesions on the eyes and face.
Exam reveals cerebellar ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, and dilated small blood vessels on the conjunctivae and face.
IgA levels are low, serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated, and lymphocyte karyotyping shows increased chromosomal breakage.
Chromosomal breakage studies show markedly increased sensitivity to ionizing radiation, and the gene involved encodes a DNA damage-sensing kinase.
explanation: The ATM kinase normally detects double-strand DNA breaks and coordinates cell cycle arrest for repair. Without it, DNA damage accumulates in neurons (causing ataxia) and the immune system (causing immunodeficiency), with markedly increased cancer risk.
keyFact: Cerebellar ataxia + oculocutaneous telangiectasias + IgA deficiency + elevated AFP is the classic tetrad. Increased sensitivity to ionizing radiation means CT scans should be avoided when possible. High risk of lymphoma and leukemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Friedreich Ataxia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Friedreich causes ataxia too but from a trinucleotide repeat expansion affecting iron metabolism in mitochondria — no telangiectasias, no immunodeficiency, no elevated AFP.

wrongAnswers.name: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: WAS causes immunodeficiency with eczema and small platelets, but no ataxia or telangiectasias.

wrongAnswers.name: Common Variable Immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID causes low immunoglobulins and recurrent infections but without the ataxia, telangiectasias, or elevated AFP.

clues: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent deep-seated infections including liver abscesses and pneumonia caused by catalase-positive organisms.
His infections include Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, and Nocardia — organisms that share a specific biochemical feature.
Exam reveals hepatomegaly and surgical scars from prior abscess drainage.
Neutrophil function testing shows markedly reduced oxidative burst on dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry.
The nitroblue tetrazolium test is negative — neutrophils cannot generate the oxidative burst needed to kill catalase-positive organisms.
explanation: Without the NADPH oxidase complex, phagocytes cannot generate the reactive oxygen species needed to kill ingested bacteria and fungi. Catalase-negative organisms produce hydrogen peroxide that even defective cells can use, so they are still killed.
keyFact: Catalase-positive organisms are the key: S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia, Burkholderia. Granulomas form because organisms can't be killed, triggering chronic inflammation. X-linked (most common) or autosomal recessive.

wrongAnswers.name: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LAD causes recurrent infections with very high white counts but without pus formation — neutrophils can't migrate to the site. CGD neutrophils migrate fine but can't kill.

wrongAnswers.name: SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCID causes susceptibility to all organisms from absent adaptive immunity. CGD specifically targets catalase-positive organisms because the innate killing mechanism is defective.

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked Agammaglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLA causes recurrent bacterial infections from absent antibodies, but neutrophil function is normal — no liver abscesses from catalase-positive organisms.

clues: A 25-year-old woman presents with her fourth episode of bacterial pneumonia in two years.
She has had chronic sinusitis and persistent diarrhea that started in her late teens.
Exam reveals a thin woman with crackles at the left lung base and no lymphadenopathy.
Quantitative immunoglobulins show markedly reduced IgG, IgA, and IgM levels despite normal B cell numbers.
Flow cytometry confirms B cells are present but fail to differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells in vitro.
explanation: B cells are present but cannot mature into effective plasma cells, resulting in pan-hypogammaglobulinemia. Unlike XLA where B cells are absent, here they are present but dysfunctional.
keyFact: B cells PRESENT but dysfunctional (vs XLA where B cells are absent). Onset in teens/adults (vs XLA which presents at 6 months). Affects both sexes (vs XLA which is X-linked). Increased risk of lymphoma, autoimmune disease, and granulomatous inflammation.

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked Agammaglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLA has ABSENT B cells, presents at 6 months, and only affects males. This patient has present B cells, presented at 18, and is female.

wrongAnswers.name: Selective IgA Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA deficiency has only low IgA with normal IgG/IgM and is usually mild. Here ALL immunoglobulin classes are low.

wrongAnswers.name: HIV/AIDS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HIV causes immunodeficiency from T-cell depletion, not B-cell dysfunction with pan-hypogammaglobulinemia and normal T cells.

clues: A newborn develops seizures on day 2 of life, and a cardiac murmur is detected on the initial examination.
A cleft palate is noted at delivery, and the ionized calcium level returns critically low at 0.7 mmol/L.
Exam reveals low-set ears, a small mandible, hypertelorism, and the chest X-ray shows an absent thymic shadow.
Flow cytometry shows profoundly decreased T cells with normal B cell numbers, and echocardiography reveals an interrupted aortic arch.
Genetic testing confirms a microdeletion on chromosome 22q11.2, involving the region encoding pharyngeal pouch development.
explanation: The microdeletion impairs development of structures derived from the pharyngeal pouches: the thymus (T-cell deficiency), parathyroids (hypocalcemia), and conotruncal cardiac structures.
keyFact: CATCH-22 mnemonic: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia — from 22q11.2 deletion. The cardiac defects are conotruncal: tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch, truncus arteriosus.

wrongAnswers.name: SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCID has profound T AND B cell deficiency but without the cardiac defects, cleft palate, or hypocalcemia. SCID is a purely immune defect.

wrongAnswers.name: Neonatal Hypocalcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Neonatal hypocalcemia can occur from many causes, but the combination with absent thymus, T-cell deficiency, cardiac defect, and cleft palate identifies a specific developmental syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: CHARGE Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CHARGE also causes conotruncal heart defects and immune issues but with colobomas, choanal atresia, and ear anomalies — from CHD7 mutations, not 22q11.2 deletion.

clues: A 25-year-old man presents with two weeks of coughing up blood followed by dark urine and rising creatinine.
He is a pack-a-day smoker. His creatinine was normal 3 months ago and is now 4.2.
Exam reveals bilateral lung crackles, pallor, and trace lower extremity edema with elevated blood pressure.
Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts, chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody is positive with negative ANCA.
Kidney biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with a smooth linear pattern of IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence.
explanation: Antibodies target a specific collagen component present in both kidney and lung basement membranes, explaining why both organs are attacked simultaneously.
keyFact: LINEAR immunofluorescence is the hallmark — antibodies binding in a continuous line along the membrane. Treatment is plasmapheresis to physically remove the pathogenic antibodies plus immunosuppression.

wrongAnswers.name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GPA causes a lung-kidney syndrome but the biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic GN (no deposits at all) with ANCA positivity. This has LINEAR deposits with negative ANCA.

wrongAnswers.name: SLE Nephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus nephritis has a granular (lumpy) immunofluorescence pattern with five immune components. This has a LINEAR single-antibody pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA deposits in the mesangium (center of the filtering unit), not along the basement membrane in a linear pattern. And IgA nephropathy doesn't cause lung hemorrhage.

clues: A 6-year-old boy presents with a rash on his buttocks and legs that does not blanch with pressure.
He has abdominal pain and joint swelling that started 2 weeks after a sore throat.
Exam reveals nontender palpable purpura on both legs and buttocks, swollen tender ankles, and periumbilical tenderness.
Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria with mild proteinuria, and platelet count and coagulation studies are normal.
Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposition — the same immunoglobulin deposits in the kidneys.
explanation: IgA immune complexes deposit in small vessels throughout the body — skin (purpura), joints (arthritis), GI tract (abdominal pain, bleeding), and kidneys (glomerulonephritis).
keyFact: Palpable purpura (legs/buttocks) + arthritis + abdominal pain + renal involvement + normal platelets in a child after URI = HSP. The IgA deposits are histologically identical to IgA nephropathy — HSP is essentially the systemic form. Self-limited in most children.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes purpura from LOW platelets that are NOT palpable (flat petechiae). HSP has NORMAL platelets with PALPABLE purpura from vasculitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningococcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningococcemia causes purpura with sepsis and DIC. This child is well with normal platelets and coagulation studies.

wrongAnswers.name: Child Abuse
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bruising in a child raises concern, but the palpable quality, gravity-dependent distribution, and associated arthritis/nephritis/abdominal pain confirm vasculitis.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of severe facial and lip swelling that last 2-3 days and resolve spontaneously.
The episodes occur without hives and do not respond to antihistamines or epinephrine.
Exam during an episode reveals nonpitting edema of the lips and periorbital area without urticaria.
C4 level is persistently low even between episodes, and C1 inhibitor level is undetectable.
Her father has the same condition, and family members carry emergency medication for laryngeal episodes.
explanation: C1 inhibitor normally blocks kallikrein, which generates bradykinin. Without the inhibitor, bradykinin accumulates and causes edema. This is NOT histamine-mediated, which is why antihistamines and epinephrine don't work.
keyFact: No urticaria + no response to epinephrine/antihistamines distinguishes this from allergic angioedema. Low C4 is the screening test (even between attacks). ACE inhibitors are contraindicated because ACE also degrades bradykinin. Treat acute attacks with C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant (bradykinin receptor antagonist).

wrongAnswers.name: Allergic Angioedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Allergic angioedema is histamine-mediated with urticaria, responds to epinephrine, and has normal complement. This has no urticaria, doesn't respond to epinephrine, and has low C4.

wrongAnswers.name: ACE Inhibitor Angioedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ACE inhibitor angioedema is also bradykinin-mediated and doesn't respond to antihistamines, but it requires ACE inhibitor use and complement levels are normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Anaphylaxis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anaphylaxis causes swelling with urticaria, bronchospasm, and hypotension — all responding to epinephrine. This swelling has no urticaria and doesn't respond to epinephrine.

clues: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent bacterial pneumonias and chronic diarrhea.
Stool testing identifies Cryptosporidium as the cause of the diarrhea. His brother had similar infections.
Exam reveals bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, mild hepatomegaly, and scattered oral ulcers on the buccal mucosa.
IgM is markedly elevated at 650 mg/dL while IgG is 45 and IgA is undetectable, with normal B cell numbers.
Flow cytometry shows absent CD40 ligand (CD154) expression on activated T cells, confirming the class-switching defect.
explanation: Without the class-switching signal, B cells produce only IgM. They cannot switch to IgG (needed for opsonization), IgA (needed for mucosal immunity), or IgE. The Cryptosporidium susceptibility reflects impaired T-cell cooperation.
keyFact: High IgM + low IgG/IgA = class-switching defect. The T-cell molecule involved (CD40 ligand) is X-linked, so primarily males are affected. Cryptosporidium and Pneumocystis susceptibility reflects the T-cell component of the defect.

wrongAnswers.name: CVID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID has low levels of ALL immunoglobulin classes including IgM. Here IgM is elevated — only class switching is defective.

wrongAnswers.name: XLA
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLA has absent B cells and all immunoglobulins low. Here B cells are present and IgM is actually elevated — they can make antibody but can't switch classes.

wrongAnswers.name: Selective IgA Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA deficiency has isolated low IgA with normal IgG and IgM. This has HIGH IgM with low IgG AND low IgA — a broader switching defect.

clues: A 20-year-old woman presents with recurrent sinusitis and one episode of a parasitic diarrheal illness.
She is otherwise healthy and functions normally. Stool testing identified Giardia in the previous episode.
Exam is unremarkable except for mild nasal congestion and post-nasal drip from chronic sinus inflammation.
Serum IgA is undetectable at less than 5 mg/dL while IgG and IgM are completely within normal limits.
She is advised that blood products containing IgA could trigger a severe transfusion reaction because of anti-IgA antibodies.
explanation: This is the most common primary immunodeficiency. Most patients are asymptomatic, but some have increased sinopulmonary and GI infections, particularly Giardia.
keyFact: Associated with celiac disease and autoimmune conditions. The transfusion reaction risk from anti-IgA antibodies is high-yield. If blood products are needed, use washed RBCs or products from IgA-deficient donors.

wrongAnswers.name: CVID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID involves low levels of multiple immunoglobulin classes with more severe infection susceptibility. Here only IgA is low with IgG and IgM normal.

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked Agammaglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLA has ALL immunoglobulins profoundly low with absent B cells. This patient has absent IgA with normal IgG and IgM.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyper-IgM Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyper-IgM has elevated IgM with low IgG and IgA from a class-switching defect. This has isolated absent IgA with normal IgM.

clues: A 4-month-old infant presents with persistent oral thrush that has not responded to topical antifungals.
He has had chronic diarrhea and two pneumonias since birth despite no known exposures.
Exam reveals an emaciated infant with absent tonsils and no palpable lymph nodes.
Absolute lymphocyte count is critically low, and immunoglobulin levels for all classes are undetectable.
Newborn screening TREC assay shows absent T-cell receptor excision circles, confirming failed thymic T-cell development.
explanation: Defective T-cell development leaves the infant with virtually no adaptive immunity. Without T-cell help, B cells cannot produce effective antibodies even if present.
keyFact: The most common X-linked form involves the common gamma chain shared by multiple interleukin receptors. ADA deficiency is the most common autosomal recessive form. Bone marrow transplant is curative. Gene therapy is available for some forms.

wrongAnswers.name: DiGeorge Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DiGeorge causes T-cell deficiency from absent thymus but WITH cardiac defects, hypocalcemia, and characteristic facial features from pharyngeal pouch maldevelopment.

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked Agammaglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLA has absent B cells but normal T cells, presenting AFTER 6 months when maternal antibodies wane — not the profound combined deficiency seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: HIV/AIDS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HIV causes acquired T-cell deficiency but is not present at birth in this manner. Maternal antibodies would be positive in vertically transmitted HIV.

clues: A 24-year-old woman presents with joint pain in her hands and wrists that has been worsening for 3 months.
She has noticed a rash spreading across both cheeks and the bridge of her nose that worsens with sun exposure.
Exam reveals a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash sparing the nasolabial folds and swollen metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally.
ANA is positive at 1:640, anti-dsDNA antibodies are elevated, and complement C3 and C4 are both low.
Urinalysis reveals proteinuria with red blood cell casts, and a 24-hour urine protein is elevated at 2.8 grams.
explanation: Autoantibodies against nuclear components form immune complexes that deposit in joints, skin, kidneys, heart, and blood vessels. Low complement means it's being consumed clearing these complexes.
keyFact: Anti-dsDNA tracks with disease activity and nephritis. Anti-Smith is the most specific antibody. The unique five-component immunofluorescence pattern on renal biopsy is diagnostic.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA causes joint disease but not facial rash, nephritis with immune complex deposition, or anti-dsDNA antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-Induced Lupus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug-induced lupus has anti-histone antibodies, does NOT cause nephritis, and resolves when the drug is stopped.

wrongAnswers.name: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCTD has overlapping features with anti-U1 RNP antibodies but typically mild renal involvement and negative anti-dsDNA.

clues: A 6-month-old boy presents with bloody diarrhea and petechiae since the first weeks of life.
He has severe eczema on his face and arms, and only males in his family have been affected.
Exam reveals eczematous patches on the face and extremities, diffuse petechiae, ecchymoses, and hepatosplenomegaly.
Platelets are low at 38,000 and the mean platelet volume is abnormally small at 5.2 fL on the complete blood count.
Flow cytometry shows absent WASP protein expression in lymphocytes, and genetic testing confirms an X-linked mutation.
explanation: Defective cytoskeletal organization impairs both immune cell signaling and platelet production, creating the triad of thrombocytopenia with small platelets, eczema, and immunodeficiency.
keyFact: SMALL platelets are the giveaway — in ITP the platelets are LARGE. X-linked. Increased lymphoma risk. Bone marrow transplant is curative.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP drops platelets but they are LARGE (young, compensatory). Here they are SMALL — an intrinsic production defect, not peripheral destruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Atopic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atopic dermatitis causes eczema and elevated IgE but without thrombocytopenia, immunodeficiency, or small platelets.

wrongAnswers.name: SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCID causes severe immunodeficiency but without the eczema, small platelets, or thrombocytopenia.

clues: A 9-month-old boy presents with his third episode of bacterial pneumonia since age 6 months.
He also has recurrent otitis media and a history of septic arthritis. His older sister is completely healthy.
Exam reveals absent tonsils, no palpable lymph nodes anywhere, and bilateral crackles at the lung bases.
All immunoglobulin classes (IgG, IgA, IgM) are profoundly low, and flow cytometry shows absent CD19+ B cells with normal T cell numbers.
Genetic testing identifies a mutation in Bruton tyrosine kinase, arresting B cell development at the pre-B cell stage.
explanation: Without the signaling kinase, B cell development arrests at the pre-B cell stage. No mature B cells means no antibody production. T cells are completely normal.
keyFact: Onset at ~6 months when maternal IgG wanes. Absent B cells with normal T cells. The absent tonsils and lymph nodes reflect the lack of B-cell-containing lymphoid tissue. Treat with lifelong IVIG replacement.

wrongAnswers.name: SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCID affects BOTH T and B cells, presenting earlier with opportunistic infections. This patient has normal T cells — only the B-cell compartment is empty.

wrongAnswers.name: CVID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID also causes low immunoglobulins and recurrent infections, but B cells are PRESENT (just dysfunctional), onset is later (teens/adults), and it affects both sexes.

wrongAnswers.name: Transient Hypogammaglobulinemia of Infancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Transient hypogammaglobulinemia causes temporary low IgG after maternal antibodies wane but B cells are present and the condition resolves spontaneously.

clues: A 55-year-old man with poor dentition presents with a slowly growing firm mass at the angle of his jaw that has been draining for months.
He recently had a dental extraction, and the mass has not responded to short courses of antibiotics.
Exam reveals a woody firm mass with multiple sinus tracts draining to the skin, and the drainage contains tiny yellow granules visible to the naked eye.
Biopsy shows granulation tissue with characteristic sulfur granules surrounded by a chronic inflammatory infiltrate.
Gram stain shows filamentous branching gram-positive rods, and the organism grows slowly on anaerobic culture.
explanation: A normal oral commensal becomes pathogenic when tissue integrity is disrupted. It forms chronic invasive abscesses that cross tissue planes and create sinus tracts, closely mimicking malignancy.
keyFact: The yellow granules in the drainage are colonies of the organism, not actual sulfur. The organism is a BACTERIUM despite its filamentous appearance. Three locations: cervicofacial (after dental work), thoracic (aspiration), abdominal (after appendectomy or IUD use).

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Oral SCC causes a firm jaw mass but it's ulcerative without draining sinus tracts or yellow granules.

wrongAnswers.name: Nocardia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nocardia is also filamentous and gram-positive, but it's PARTIALLY ACID-FAST (this organism is not), affects immunocompromised patients, and primarily causes pulmonary disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervical TB (scrofula) causes matted lymph nodes with caseating granulomas, not the firm mass with sinus tracts and yellow granules.

clues: A 28-year-old man presents with dark urine that has looked like cola for the past three days.
He had unprotected sex with a new partner approximately 3 months ago and now feels nauseated with no appetite.
Exam reveals jaundice, scleral icterus, and tender hepatomegaly without signs of chronic liver damage.
AST is 1,180 and ALT is 1,420, and HBsAg is detected in serum.
IgM anti-HBc is positive, while IgG anti-HBc is negative.
explanation: The virus reached the liver via sexual transmission. The liver damage is from the immune response attacking infected hepatocytes, not from the virus itself.
keyFact: IgM anti-core is the marker of acute infection — the only marker positive during the 'window period.' Surface antigen = infected. Surface antibody = immune. If surface antigen persists >6 months = chronic carrier.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatitis A
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HAV is transmitted fecal-orally with shorter incubation. The 3-month incubation after sexual contact and positive surface antigen/IgM core antibody confirm HBV.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatitis C
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCV is transmitted parenterally and rarely presents with acute symptomatic hepatitis — it silently becomes chronic in ~80%. The HBV serologies confirm the diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune Hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIH causes elevated transaminases with ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibodies. The positive viral serologies confirm an infectious etiology.

clues: A 45-year-old postal worker presents with a painless skin lesion on his forearm surrounded by marked swelling.
He handled suspicious packages at work one week ago and initially noticed a small pruritic papule that progressed to a vesicle then developed a dark eschar.
Exam reveals a 2-cm painless necrotic eschar with striking surrounding nonpitting edema and mild regional lymphadenopathy.
Gram stain of fluid beneath the eschar shows large gram-positive rods in chains with no hemolysis on blood agar and a ground-glass colony appearance.
Blood cultures grow the same large gram-positive rod, and a gamma phage lysis test is positive.
explanation: Spores enter through broken skin, germinate, and produce toxins that cause the characteristic painless necrotic eschar with gelatinous edema.
keyFact: Cutaneous (most common, painless black eschar), inhalational (widened mediastinum, hemorrhagic mediastinitis), and GI are the three forms. The painless nature of the eschar distinguishes it from other skin infections.

wrongAnswers.name: Brown Recluse Spider Bite
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Brown recluse causes a necrotic skin lesion but is PAINFUL, lacks the gelatinous edema, and has no gram-positive rods on culture.

wrongAnswers.name: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Leishmaniasis causes chronic painless ulcers in tropical areas but without the rapid eschar formation, gelatinous edema, or gram-positive rods.

wrongAnswers.name: Ecthyma Gangrenosum
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ecthyma gangrenosum from Pseudomonas causes necrotic skin lesions in immunocompromised patients but grows gram-negative rods, not gram-positive rods in chains.

clues: A 55-year-old man with acute leukemia develops fever and pleuritic chest pain during prolonged neutropenia despite broad-spectrum antibiotics.
His absolute neutrophil count has been below 100 for 12 days, and his fever persists despite antipseudomonal and anti-gram-positive coverage.
Exam reveals pleuritic chest pain and decreased breath sounds at the right base.
CT chest shows a nodular lesion surrounded by a halo of ground-glass opacity, and serum galactomannan antigen is positive.
Tissue biopsy shows septate hyphae branching at acute 45-degree angles invading blood vessel walls.
explanation: The mold invades blood vessel walls (angioinvasion), causing thrombosis and tissue infarction. The halo of hemorrhage around the nodule on CT reflects this vascular invasion.
keyFact: Septate hyphae, acute-angle (45°) branching. The halo sign on CT = hemorrhage around infarcted lung from angioinvasion. Galactomannan antigen aids diagnosis. Prolonged neutropenia is the major risk factor. Treat with voriconazole.

wrongAnswers.name: Mucormycosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mucor has NON-septate hyphae branching at 90-degree WIDE angles and preferentially infects patients in DKA or with iron overload, not neutropenic leukemia patients.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumocystis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PJP causes bilateral ground-glass opacities in HIV/AIDS patients, not focal nodular lesions with halo sign in neutropenic patients.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacterial Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial pneumonia causes consolidation, not the nodule-with-halo pattern. The persistent fever despite broad-spectrum antibiotics and positive galactomannan point to fungal infection.

clues: A 65-year-old man from coastal New England presents with high fevers and dark urine during the summer months.
He enjoys hiking and recently found an engorged tick on his leg.
Exam reveals splenomegaly, jaundice, and a temperature of 103 F.
Peripheral blood smear shows ring forms inside red blood cells, and labs show hemolytic anemia with elevated LDH and low haptoglobin.
Some infected red cells show a distinctive tetrad arrangement of organisms resembling a Maltese cross pattern.
explanation: The parasite is transmitted by the Ixodes tick (same vector as Lyme and Ehrlichia). It infects red cells and causes hemolytic anemia. Severe disease occurs in asplenic, elderly, and immunocompromised patients.
keyFact: Maltese cross (tetrad) formation inside red cells distinguishes this from malaria. Same tick vector as Lyme disease — co-infection is possible. Northeastern US (Cape Cod, Nantucket, coastal New England). Treat with atovaquone + azithromycin (mild) or clindamycin + quinine (severe).

wrongAnswers.name: Plasmodium falciparum
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malaria shows ring forms but with banana-shaped gametocytes and requires travel to endemic areas. The Maltese cross tetrads, domestic tick exposure, and northeastern US location point to Babesia.

wrongAnswers.name: Lyme Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Same tick vector but Lyme causes a rash, arthritis, and nerve palsies — not hemolytic anemia with intraerythrocytic parasites.

wrongAnswers.name: Ehrlichiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ehrlichia is also tick-borne but infects WHITE blood cells (intracytoplasmic morulae), not red cells.

clues: A 10-year-old girl presents with a tender enlarged lymph node in her left armpit that appeared about 2 weeks after getting a new kitten.
She has a small healing bump on her left forearm where the kitten broke her skin. The papule appeared a few days after the injury.
Exam reveals a 3-cm tender left axillary lymph node and a healing papule on the left forearm with no other lymphadenopathy.
Blood cultures are negative. Serologic testing for Bartonella henselae IgM is positive.
Lymph node biopsy shows stellate necrotizing granulomas with surrounding palisading histiocytes and scattered microabscesses.
explanation: The bacteria inoculated by the scratch travel to regional lymph nodes and cause granulomatous lymphadenitis. In immunocompromised patients, the organism causes bacillary angiomatosis and peliosis hepatis.
keyFact: Regional lymphadenopathy proximal to a cat scratch is the classic presentation. Self-limited in immunocompetent. In HIV/AIDS, the same organism causes bacillary angiomatosis (vascular skin lesions that can mimic Kaposi sarcoma). Biopsy shows stellate (star-shaped) granulomas.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphadenopathy from lymphoma is painless and progressive without a clear inoculation site or cat exposure history.

wrongAnswers.name: Sporotrichosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sporotrichosis causes ascending lymphangitic nodules after a thorn prick, not isolated regional lymphadenopathy after a cat scratch.

wrongAnswers.name: Tularemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tularemia causes ulceroglandular disease from contact with rabbits or ticks, not cats. The organism and exposure are different.

clues: A 40-year-old man from the Great Lakes region presents with a cough that has persisted for 3 weeks despite antibiotics.
He has also developed a raised crusted skin lesion on his face that has been growing.
Exam reveals a verrucous (wart-like) skin lesion on the nose with raised irregular borders and bilateral lung crackles.
Chest X-ray shows a mass-like consolidation in the right upper lobe.
KOH preparation of material from the skin lesion shows large broad-based budding yeast cells.
explanation: Inhaled spores convert to yeast in the lungs and can disseminate to skin and bone. The characteristic verrucous (wart-like) skin lesions are often misdiagnosed initially.
keyFact: Great Lakes and Ohio/Mississippi River Valleys. Broad-based budding yeast is pathognomonic. Skin and bone are the most common extrapulmonary sites. Can mimic squamous cell carcinoma, TB, or bacterial infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Histoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Histoplasma is a small yeast INSIDE macrophages. This shows LARGE yeast with broad-based budding — completely different morphology.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The verrucous skin lesion mimics cancer, but KOH prep reveals fungal yeast — always consider infectious etiology for non-healing skin lesions.

wrongAnswers.name: Coccidioidomycosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Coccidioides is found in the southwestern US and forms spherules with endospores, not the broad-based budding seen here.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with blurred vision and drooping eyelids that started 24 hours ago.
She ate home-canned vegetables from a bulging jar 36 hours before symptom onset.
Her weakness is progressing downward -- it started with cranial nerves (vision, swallowing) and is now affecting her arms.
Pupils are dilated and sluggishly reactive, deep tendon reflexes are diminished, and she has no sensory deficits.
EMG shows incremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation at high frequency, and stool assay detects the toxin.
explanation: The toxin irreversibly blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release, causing descending flaccid paralysis starting with cranial nerves because they have the shortest distance for the toxin to travel.
keyFact: DESCENDING paralysis = this disease. ASCENDING paralysis = Guillain-Barré. Both cause flaccid weakness but in opposite directions. The dilated unreactive pupils distinguish this from myasthenia gravis (which has normal pupils).

wrongAnswers.name: Myasthenia Gravis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MG causes ptosis and bulbar weakness but pupils are NORMAL, weakness is fatigable (worsens with use), and there's no food exposure history with multiple victims.

wrongAnswers.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBS causes ASCENDING paralysis from feet upward with areflexia. This is DESCENDING from cranial nerves downward.

wrongAnswers.name: Organophosphate Poisoning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OP poisoning causes a cholinergic EXCESS crisis (salivation, lacrimation, miosis, bradycardia). This causes cholinergic DEFICIENCY (dry mouth, mydriasis, weakness).

clues: A 40-year-old farmer presents with waves of fever that come and go over several weeks.
He works with cattle and frequently drinks unpasteurized milk and fresh cheese.
Exam reveals hepatosplenomegaly and tenderness over the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints.
Blood cultures are positive after prolonged incubation, growing small gram-negative coccobacilli.
Serum agglutination titer is greater than 1:160, and the organism is identified as an intracellular pathogen on culture.
explanation: The intracellular organism causes chronic granulomatous infection with undulating fevers (recurring waves of high temperature) and osteoarticular involvement, especially spondylitis and sacroiliitis.
keyFact: Transmission: unpasteurized dairy products (most common worldwide), direct animal contact, or laboratory exposure. The undulating fever pattern and osteoarticular complaints in a livestock worker are classic.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB causes chronic fever with weight loss but primarily pulmonary disease, and cultures show acid-fast bacilli, not gram-negative coccobacilli.

wrongAnswers.name: Infective Endocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Endocarditis causes prolonged fever and positive blood cultures but with valvular findings and embolic phenomena, not the undulating pattern with sacroiliitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma causes fever and hepatosplenomegaly but without the undulating pattern, positive blood cultures, or occupational exposure.

clues: A 40-year-old man presents with painful swallowing and the sensation of food getting stuck in his chest over the past two weeks.
He has a severely weakened immune system with a CD4 count of 75. He has white patches in his mouth that scrape off to a raw red surface.
Exam reveals white plaques on the buccal mucosa and palate that scrape off to reveal an erythematous base.
Upper endoscopy shows white raised plaques adhering to the esophageal mucosa, and brushings reveal pseudohyphae and budding yeast.
Brushings from the esophageal plaques reveal pseudohyphae and budding yeast forms on KOH preparation.
explanation: Severe immunosuppression allows the normally commensal yeast to overgrow and invade the esophageal mucosa.
keyFact: Most common esophageal infection in HIV/AIDS. The oral thrush is a clue but esophageal involvement can occur without it. If fluconazole fails: CMV (large shallow ulcers, biopsy shows intranuclear inclusions) or HSV (multiple small deep ulcers, biopsy shows multinucleated giant cells).

wrongAnswers.name: CMV Esophagitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CMV causes large shallow linear ulcers in the distal esophagus, not adherent white plaques. Biopsy shows intranuclear owl-eye inclusions.

wrongAnswers.name: HSV Esophagitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV causes multiple small deep 'punched-out' ulcers, often in the distal esophagus. Biopsy shows multinucleated giant cells with Cowdry type A inclusions.

wrongAnswers.name: Pill Esophagitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pill esophagitis causes a discrete ulcer at the point where the pill lodged, typically mid-esophagus. This is diffuse white plaques with pseudohyphae.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy and a low-grade fever 3 weeks after unprotected sexual contact.
He recalls a small painless genital papule that ulcerated and healed quickly before the lymph nodes appeared.
Exam reveals large matted tender inguinal lymph nodes on the left with erythematous overlying skin, bulging above and below the inguinal ligament.
The enlarged nodes above and below the inguinal ligament create a visible groove between them along the ligament.
Nucleic acid testing confirms Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3.
explanation: Unlike the common genital serovars (D-K) that infect epithelium, the L serovars invade lymphatic tissue, causing destructive lymphadenopathy that can fistulize and scar.
keyFact: Three stages: painless papule/ulcer → painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) → chronic scarring with fistulas and strictures. The groove sign from bulging nodes above and below the inguinal ligament is classic.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Syphilitic chancre is painless with nontender rubbery lymphadenopathy. LGV has a transient ulcer followed by PAINFUL tender suppurative nodes.

wrongAnswers.name: Genital Herpes
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV causes painful vesicles with tender lymphadenopathy, but the nodes are bilateral and don't suppurate or form the groove sign.

wrongAnswers.name: Cat Scratch Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bartonella causes regional lymphadenopathy but after a cat scratch, not sexual exposure. No genital lesion precedes it.

clues: A 72-year-old woman presents with profuse watery diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain 5 days after completing a course of clindamycin.
She was recently discharged from a nursing facility and is having 6-8 watery stools per day.
Exam reveals diffuse abdominal tenderness, dehydration, and low-grade fever.
White blood cell count is 18,000, and CT abdomen shows diffuse colonic wall thickening.
Stool PCR for the organism's toxin gene and enzyme immunoassay for toxin B are both positive.
explanation: Antibiotic disruption of normal gut flora allows the toxin-producing anaerobe to proliferate. Toxins A and B damage the colonic mucosa.
keyFact: Most implicated antibiotics: fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, broad-spectrum cephalosporins. Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are first-line — IV vancomycin doesn't reach the colon. For recurrent disease: fidaxomicin or fecal microbiota transplant.

wrongAnswers.name: Ulcerative Colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: UC causes bloody diarrhea with continuous mucosal inflammation. The temporal relationship to antibiotics and positive toxin test confirm the infectious etiology.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Gastroenteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral GI is self-limited in days. This developed after antibiotics with positive toxin testing — a specific pathogen is identified.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic Colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic colitis causes bloody diarrhea in elderly patients at watershed areas. This is watery (not bloody) diarrhea after antibiotic exposure.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with a cough and fever 2 weeks after moving to Arizona from the East Coast.
He also reports joint pain and has noticed painful red bumps on his shins.
Exam reveals tender erythematous nodules on both shins and bilateral pulmonary crackles.
Chest X-ray shows a thin-walled cavity in the right upper lobe, and serologic testing shows positive IgM antibodies against the organism.
Tissue biopsy reveals large spherules filled with endospores — a morphology unique to this dimorphic fungus found in the desert Southwest.
explanation: Inhaled arthroconidia from desert soil convert to the characteristic tissue form in the lungs. Most infections are self-limited, but dissemination occurs in immunocompromised patients and certain ethnic groups.
keyFact: Southwestern US (Arizona, Central Valley of California). Desert soil disrupted by construction, earthquakes, or wind. Spherules with endospores are pathognomonic. Erythema nodosum is a good prognostic sign (robust immune response). Disseminated disease: meningitis, skin, bone.

wrongAnswers.name: Histoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Histoplasma is endemic to the Ohio/Mississippi River Valley (not the Southwest) and shows small yeast inside macrophages, not spherules with endospores.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes bilateral hilar LAD with erythema nodosum, but the cavitary disease, southwestern geography, and spherules with endospores confirm infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Blastomycosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Blastomyces is endemic to the Great Lakes region and shows large yeast with broad-based budding, not spherules.

clues: A 2-year-old boy presents with a barking cough and noisy breathing that worsened overnight.
He had a runny nose and mild cough for 2 days before the barking cough developed.
He has mild stridor at rest that worsens with agitation; the barking cough is recognizable from across the room.
Temperature is 100.8 F, oxygen saturation is 95%, and there is no drooling or toxic appearance.
AP neck X-ray shows symmetrical subglottic narrowing creating a steeple-shaped appearance of the upper airway.
explanation: Parainfluenza virus (most common cause) infects the subglottic region, causing edema that narrows the already small pediatric airway and produces the characteristic barking cough and stridor.
keyFact: Barking cough + steeple sign + gradual onset with viral prodrome + 6 months to 3 years age = croup. The subglottis is the narrowest part of a child's airway (cricoid cartilage is a complete ring). Cool mist, dexamethasone, and nebulized epinephrine are the treatments.

wrongAnswers.name: Epiglottitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Epiglottitis is acute onset, toxic child, NO cough, drooling, thumbprint sign. Croup is gradual onset, barking cough, steeple sign.

wrongAnswers.name: Foreign Body
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Foreign body causes sudden onset without viral prodrome and usually has unilateral findings. Croup has bilateral subglottic narrowing after a viral illness.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacterial Tracheitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial tracheitis causes high fever with toxic appearance and purulent secretions, not responding to croup treatment. Croup responds to dexamethasone.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with a gradually worsening headache over 3 weeks that is not responding to over-the-counter pain relievers.
He has a severely weakened immune system with a CD4 count of 45. He has low-grade fevers and neck stiffness.
Exam reveals mild meningismus without cranial nerve palsies or lateralizing signs.
CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated opening pressure, and India ink reveals round organisms surrounded by a clear halo.
Serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen tests are both strongly positive with high titers.
explanation: The encapsulated yeast causes meningitis in severely immunocompromised patients. The thick polysaccharide capsule is visible as a clear halo on India ink stain and is detected by the antigen test.
keyFact: Subacute meningitis in HIV with CD4 <100. The polysaccharide capsule gives the large halo on India ink and is the basis of the highly sensitive antigen test. Elevated ICP management with serial LPs is critical — the pressure kills, not just the infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacterial Meningitis
