wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial meningitis presents explosively over hours with neutrophilic CSF and gram-positive or gram-negative organisms. This is subacute with encapsulated yeast.

wrongAnswers.name: TB Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB meningitis is also subacute with lymphocytic CSF, but AFB stain is positive and India ink/antigen tests are negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Toxoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Toxoplasma causes focal ring-enhancing brain lesions with neurologic deficits. Cryptococcus causes meningitis with elevated pressure and no focal lesions.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with high fever and severe pain behind his eyes after returning from Southeast Asia one week ago.
He describes the bone and joint pain as the worst he has ever experienced.
Exam reveals a blanching maculopapular rash on his trunk and a positive tourniquet test showing petechiae after cuff inflation.
Platelet count is 62,000 and hematocrit is rising on serial measurements.
NS1 antigen test is positive, and IgM serology confirms acute flavivirus infection transmitted by the Aedes mosquito.
explanation: The Aedes mosquito-transmitted flavivirus causes a spectrum from mild fever to hemorrhagic fever and shock. Second infections with a different serotype carry a higher risk of severe disease through antibody-dependent enhancement.
keyFact: High fever + retro-orbital pain + severe myalgias/arthralgias ('breakbone fever') + thrombocytopenia + rising hematocrit after tropical travel = dengue. Warning signs for severe dengue: persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, mucosal bleeding, and rising hematocrit with falling platelets.

wrongAnswers.name: Malaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malaria causes fever after tropical travel but with cyclic fevers, anemia from hemolysis, and parasites on blood smear — not the severe myalgias with thrombocytopenia and rising hematocrit pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Chikungunya
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chikungunya causes fever and severe joint pain after mosquito exposure but with prominent polyarthralgia/arthritis and usually NORMAL platelets.

wrongAnswers.name: Zika
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Zika causes mild fever with rash and conjunctivitis but symptoms are much milder — not the severe 'breakbone' pain and significant thrombocytopenia.

clues: A 5-year-old unvaccinated child presents with sore throat, hoarse voice, and low-grade fever for 3 days.
His parents noticed a grayish membrane in the back of his throat.
Exam reveals a thick gray-white adherent membrane covering the tonsils and posterior pharynx that bleeds when removal is attempted.
Neck swelling gives a 'bull neck' appearance from cervical lymphadenopathy and soft tissue edema.
Culture on tellurite agar grows gray-black colonies of a gram-positive rod, and an Elek test confirms toxin production.
explanation: The gram-positive rod produces a potent exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis in host cells, damaging the heart (myocarditis), nerves (polyneuropathy), and kidneys.
keyFact: The adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds on removal is the clinical hallmark. Antitoxin administration takes priority over antibiotics. Complications: myocarditis (arrhythmias, heart failure) and demyelinating polyneuropathy. Prevention by vaccination has made this rare in developed countries.

wrongAnswers.name: Streptococcal Pharyngitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Strep pharyngitis causes tonsillar exudate but it is easily removed without bleeding. The tough adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds is specific to this disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious Mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBV causes tonsillar exudate but with generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and atypical lymphocytes — not the adherent pseudomembrane.

wrongAnswers.name: Peritonsillar Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PTA causes unilateral tonsillar swelling with deviation of the uvula, not a bilateral adherent pseudomembrane.

clues: A 22-year-old sexually active woman presents with fever and joint pain that has been migrating from one joint to another.
She has a scattered rash on her hands consisting of a few painless papulopustules; symptom onset corresponded with her menstrual period.
Exam reveals a swollen hot right wrist, two pustular skin lesions on her fingers, and tenosynovitis of the left hand.
Cervical, rectal, and pharyngeal NAAT swabs are all obtained for testing.
Blood cultures grow a gram-negative diplococcus, and cervical NAAT is positive for the same organism.
explanation: The organism disseminates from the genital tract during bacteremia, seeding skin (pustular dermatitis), tendons (tenosynovitis), and joints.
keyFact: Migratory polyarthralgia + tenosynovitis + pustular skin lesions in a young sexually active person = this diagnosis. Menstruation and terminal complement deficiency increase dissemination risk. Must always co-treat for Chlamydia.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis causes oligoarthritis after infection but the joint involvement is NON-migratory and there are no hemorrhagic pustules or positive blood cultures.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningococcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningococcemia also involves gram-negative diplococci with skin lesions, but the clinical context (purpura, meningitis, shock) and organism species are different.

wrongAnswers.name: SLE
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE causes arthritis with rash but without the tenosynovitis, hemorrhagic pustules in this distribution, or positive cultures for gram-negative diplococci.

clues: A 60-year-old man from the southeastern US presents with fever and malaise one week after a tick bite while deer hunting.
He reports the tick was attached for at least 24 hours before he noticed and removed it.
Exam reveals fever and mild hepatomegaly but notably no rash.
CBC shows leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, and liver transaminases are mildly elevated.
Peripheral smear shows clusters of bacteria (morulae) within the cytoplasm of monocytes.
explanation: The organism is transmitted by the lone star tick and infects monocytes, forming the characteristic morulae (mulberry-like inclusion bodies) visible on blood smear.
keyFact: Tick-borne + leukopenia + thrombocytopenia + elevated LFTs + no rash = ehrlichiosis. RMSF is tick-borne WITH rash. The morulae in monocytes are the diagnostic finding on smear.

wrongAnswers.name: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RMSF causes a rash (starting on wrists/ankles) with similar fever and tick bite history. This patient has NO rash and morulae in monocytes.

wrongAnswers.name: Lyme Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lyme disease presents with the erythema migrans rash, not leukopenia with morulae in monocytes.

wrongAnswers.name: Babesiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Babesiosis causes tick-borne hemolytic anemia with parasites INSIDE red blood cells, not morulae inside monocytes.

clues: A 3-year-old unvaccinated child presents with acute-onset high fever and drooling that developed over just a few hours.
He is sitting upright with his neck extended and chin thrust forward, and refuses to lie down.
The child appears toxic with stridor but is not coughing; his voice is muffled and he cannot swallow his secretions.
Lateral neck X-ray shows swelling of the epiglottis at the base of the tongue.
Laryngoscopy in the operating room reveals a swollen, cherry-red epiglottis, and blood cultures grow a gram-negative coccobacillus.
explanation: Bacterial infection (historically H. influenzae type b, now reduced by vaccination) causes rapid swelling of the supraglottic structures that can completely obstruct the airway within hours.
keyFact: Acute onset, toxic-appearing, drooling, tripod position, NO cough = epiglottitis. Gradual onset, barking cough, steeple sign = croup. The H. influenzae type b vaccine has dramatically reduced the incidence. Do NOT examine the throat or lay the child flat.

wrongAnswers.name: Croup
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Croup has a barking cough with steeple sign on X-ray and gradual onset over days. Epiglottitis has NO cough, acute toxic onset, and thumbprint sign.

wrongAnswers.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Foreign body causes sudden choking with unilateral decreased breath sounds. This is a toxic child with fever, drooling, and the thumbprint sign — an infectious process.

wrongAnswers.name: Retropharyngeal Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Retropharyngeal abscess causes neck stiffness and drooling but with a widened prevertebral space on X-ray, not the thumbprint sign of supraglottic swelling.

clues: A 40-year-old man presents with severe pain and swelling in his right thigh 2 days after a deep penetrating wound from a farming accident.
The pain is rapidly worsening and the skin has developed a bronze discoloration with large hemorrhagic bullae.
There is crepitus palpable in the thigh, and a thin watery brownish discharge with a sweet foul odor; the muscle beneath is dark and non-contractile.
X-ray shows extensive gas within the muscle compartments.
Gram stain of the discharge shows large gram-positive rods with no spores visible, and anaerobic culture confirms the organism.
explanation: The anaerobic spore-forming rod produces a lecithinase that dissolves cell membranes. Gas production from fermentation and rapid toxin-mediated tissue destruction create the characteristic clinical picture.
keyFact: This involves MUSCLE (myonecrosis), while necrotizing fasciitis involves FASCIA. Both are surgical emergencies. The bronze skin, crepitus, and dishwater-brown discharge are classic. The alpha-toxin (phospholipase C) is the key virulence factor.

wrongAnswers.name: Necrotizing Fasciitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Necrotizing fasciitis involves the FASCIA, not muscle. Both cause crepitus and are surgical emergencies, but the deep muscle involvement with non-contractile tissue here indicates myonecrosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis causes spreading erythema but without gas in tissues, muscle necrosis, or the rapid life-threatening course.

wrongAnswers.name: Compartment Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Compartment syndrome causes severe pain with tense compartments but from pressure (not gas), without crepitus, skin discoloration, or gram-positive rods on stain.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with a two-week illness of fever and sore throat after recent unprotected sexual contact.
He has a diffuse macular rash on his trunk and painful oral ulcers.
Exam reveals generalized nontender lymphadenopathy, a maculopapular rash, and pharyngeal erythema.
The initial screening antibody test is negative, but a 4th-generation combo assay detects p24 antigen.
Viral RNA level is detectable at 850,000 copies/mL, confirming acute infection before antibody seroconversion.
explanation: The retrovirus targets CD4+ T cells. The acute presentation mimics mononucleosis and occurs 2-4 weeks after exposure. Antibodies may not yet be detectable — the 4th-generation test catches the viral protein first.
keyFact: Acute retroviral syndrome mimics mono. The 4th-gen test detects p24 antigen before antibodies appear (window period). Opportunistic infection thresholds: <200 = PJP, <100 = toxoplasma/crypto, <50 = MAC/CMV.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious Mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBV mono looks nearly identical but has positive heterophile antibodies and atypical lymphocytes. HIV testing is mandatory in any mono-like syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary syphilis causes rash with lymphadenopathy but with positive RPR/VDRL. Both should be tested for simultaneously.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug reactions cause fever and rash but the sexual exposure history, oral ulcers, and positive viral testing confirm acute retroviral syndrome.

clues: A 25-year-old man presents with dark urine and jaundice after returning from a trip to Mexico where he ate street food.
He has fatigue, nausea, and lost his appetite 5 days ago.
Exam reveals jaundice, mild hepatomegaly, and a low-grade fever.
AST is 2,400 and ALT is 2,800 with total bilirubin of 8.5; HBsAg and anti-HCV are both negative.
IgM anti-HAV antibody is positive.
explanation: The virus is transmitted fecal-orally through contaminated food or water. Unlike hepatitis B and C, it never causes chronic infection.
keyFact: IgM anti-HAV = acute infection. IgG anti-HAV = prior infection or vaccination (immune). NO chronic carrier state — this distinguishes it from HBV (5% chronic in adults) and HCV (80% chronic). Transaminases can be extremely high (>1000) in acute hepatitis but this does NOT predict severity.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatitis B
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HBV can present identically with acute hepatitis but is diagnosed by HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc. HAV is diagnosed by IgM anti-HAV.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatitis E
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HEV is also fecal-oral and presents similarly, especially after travel. It's important in pregnant women where it can cause fulminant hepatitis. Testing distinguishes them.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune Hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIH causes elevated transaminases with positive ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibodies. Viral serologies are negative in AIH.

clues: A 52-year-old man has elevated liver enzymes found incidentally on routine bloodwork.
He has a history of IV drug use in his 20s and has been completely asymptomatic.
Exam reveals a slightly firm liver edge on palpation without jaundice or stigmata of cirrhosis.
Anti-HCV antibody is positive, and noninvasive fibrosis assessment shows moderate fibrosis.
HCV RNA viral load is 2.8 million IU/mL, and genotype testing identifies genotype 1a.
explanation: This RNA virus causes chronic infection in approximately 80% of those infected. It is the most common chronic blood-borne infection and a leading cause of liver transplant.
keyFact: Chronicity in ~80% (vs ~5% for HBV). No vaccine exists (high mutation rate of RNA virus). Cryoglobulinemia and membranoproliferative GN are extrahepatic associations. DAAs have revolutionized treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatitis B
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HBV would show positive surface antigen. The positive anti-HCV with detectable RNA confirms hepatitis C.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcoholic Hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alcoholic hepatitis has AST:ALT ratio >2:1 with heavy alcohol use. The positive viral serologies and IV drug use history confirm HCV.

wrongAnswers.name: NAFLD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NAFLD is common and causes elevated enzymes but does not produce positive anti-HCV or detectable viral RNA.

clues: A 72-year-old man presents with 3 days of burning pain along a band on the left side of his chest, followed by blisters in the same area.
He had chickenpox as a child and has not received the newer vaccine against reactivation.
Exam reveals grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution from the left mid-back to the left nipple, stopping sharply at the midline.
The rash strictly follows a single dermatome (T5) and does not cross the midline.
PCR of vesicle fluid is positive for varicella-zoster virus.
explanation: The virus establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia after primary infection and reactivates when T-cell immunity wanes, traveling down the nerve to cause the characteristic dermatomal vesicular eruption.
keyFact: Does NOT cross midline (follows one dermatome). Thoracic dermatomes most common. Ophthalmic division involvement (forehead vesicles, nasal tip = nasociliary branch) threatens the eye. Postherpetic neuralgia is the most common complication.

wrongAnswers.name: HSV Reactivation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV reactivation occurs in the same area repeatedly (usually oral or genital), not in a single dermatomal band. HSV affects a small cluster, not a full dermatome.

wrongAnswers.name: Contact Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Contact dermatitis follows exposure patterns, can be bilateral, and doesn't stop sharply at the midline with grouped vesicles.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis causes spreading erythema without the grouped vesicles in a strict dermatomal pattern.

clues: A 45-year-old man from the Ohio River Valley presents with a cough and low-grade fever for two weeks.
He recently explored a cave that was home to a large bat colony.
Exam reveals a few scattered crackles at both lung bases but is otherwise unremarkable.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with scattered small pulmonary nodules.
Urine antigen test is positive, and sputum silver stain shows small oval yeast forms within macrophages.
explanation: Inhaled spores from soil enriched by bird or bat droppings (caves, chicken coops) convert to yeast in the lungs. In immunocompromised patients, the infection disseminates to liver, spleen, adrenals, and mucous membranes.
keyFact: Ohio and Mississippi River Valleys. Caves and chicken coops (bat/bird droppings). Small yeast INSIDE macrophages is the morphologic hallmark. Can mimic TB and sarcoidosis. Disseminated form causes oral ulcers and adrenal involvement.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB causes similar imaging with granulomas and hilar lymphadenopathy, but AFB stain is positive and the organisms are not intracellular within macrophages.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis shows bilateral hilar LAD with non-caseating granulomas, but the granulomas are sterile — no organisms on stain. The cave exposure and positive antigen distinguish infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Blastomycosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Blastomycosis causes pulmonary and skin disease but the yeast forms are LARGE with broad-based budding, not the small intramacrophage forms seen here.

clues: An 18-year-old college student presents with a severe sore throat that has not improved after 10 days.
He has high fevers, profound fatigue, and his girlfriend had similar symptoms last month.
Exam reveals exudative tonsillar pharyngitis, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
CBC shows atypical lymphocytes comprising 30% of the differential.
A heterophile antibody (Monospot) test is positive, and EBV-specific IgM (VCA) antibody is positive.
explanation: The virus infects B cells, and the atypical lymphocytes on smear are reactive CD8+ T cells mounting a response against the infected B cells.
keyFact: The amoxicillin rash occurs in almost all patients given amoxicillin during acute infection — it is NOT a true allergy and does not contraindicate future penicillin use. Heterophile antibodies may be negative in the first week and in young children.

wrongAnswers.name: Streptococcal Pharyngitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Strep pharyngitis causes exudative tonsillitis but without splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes, or positive heterophile antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute HIV
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute HIV causes a mono-like syndrome but heterophile antibodies are negative. HIV testing should always be performed in mono-like illness with negative heterophile.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma causes persistent lymphadenopathy, but the acute febrile illness with atypical lymphocytes, positive heterophile, and self-limited course confirms infection.

clues: A 32-year-old man who injects drugs presents with three weeks of fevers that he cannot shake.
He has lost 8 pounds and notices blood spots in his urine.
Exam reveals a new murmur not previously documented and small painless red spots on his palms.
Blood cultures drawn from separate sites both grow the same gram-positive organism in clusters.
Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a mobile vegetation on the tricuspid valve.
explanation: IV drug use seeded bacteria onto the tricuspid valve. The vegetation showers septic emboli to the lungs (right-sided) and the back pain represents a septic embolus to the spine.
keyFact: New murmur + positive blood cultures + embolic phenomena = endocarditis. Right-sided sends emboli to lungs. Left-sided sends emboli to brain, kidneys, spleen. The back pain was the clue that tied everything together.

wrongAnswers.name: Vertebral Osteomyelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The spine infection is real but it's a downstream complication. The valvular vegetation with lung emboli and positive cultures make endocarditis the unifying diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Bilateral Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Multiple round densities in both lungs aren't pneumonia — they're septic emboli raining from the valve.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fevers and weight loss suggest lymphoma, but positive blood cultures, a valvular mass, and embolic lesions point to infection.

clues: A 3-year-old boy presents with 6 days of high fever that has not responded to antibiotics.
He has red eyes without discharge, cracked red lips, a red bumpy tongue, and a rash on his trunk.
His hands and feet are red and swollen, and there is a single enlarged lymph node greater than 1.5 cm in the right cervical chain.
CRP is markedly elevated, platelet count is 650,000, and ESR is 85.
Echocardiography shows dilation of the left main coronary artery to a z-score of 3.2.
explanation: An acute self-limited vasculitis of medium-sized arteries primarily affecting young children. Coronary artery involvement can lead to aneurysms, stenosis, and myocardial infarction.
keyFact: Diagnosis requires ≥5 days fever plus ≥4 of 5 criteria: bilateral conjunctival injection, oral changes, rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy. Aspirin is used in children here — one of the few pediatric indications.

wrongAnswers.name: Scarlet Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue after streptococcal pharyngitis, responds to antibiotics, and doesn't cause coronary artery damage.

wrongAnswers.name: Measles
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Measles causes fever, conjunctivitis, and rash with Koplik spots, cough, and coryza — but no coronary involvement and the rash spreads cephalocaudally.

wrongAnswers.name: Toxic Shock Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TSS causes fever and rash but with hypotension and multiorgan failure, not the mucocutaneous findings and coronary artery disease.

clues: A 60-year-old man presents with high fever, confusion, and a cough 5 days after staying at a hotel.
He is a smoker. The hotel had a large cooling tower system, his cough produces very little sputum, and he has had watery diarrhea.
Exam reveals a temperature of 104°F, confusion, and crackles at the right lung base.
Sodium is 128 (hyponatremia), and sputum gram stain shows many neutrophils but NO organisms — the bacteria do not stain with standard gram stain.
Urine antigen test is positive, and the organism grows only on charcoal yeast extract agar supplemented with iron and cysteine.
explanation: The gram-negative rod lives in warm water systems (cooling towers, hot tubs, hospital water). It is a facultative intracellular pathogen that infects alveolar macrophages.
keyFact: Pneumonia + GI symptoms (diarrhea) + hyponatremia + confusion = this pathogen until proven otherwise. Hotel/hospital water systems are the classic source. Doesn't grow on standard media — requires charcoal yeast extract agar.

wrongAnswers.name: Mycoplasma Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mycoplasma also causes atypical pneumonia with no organisms on gram stain, but occurs in young adults with dry cough and doesn't cause diarrhea or hyponatremia.

wrongAnswers.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pneumococcal pneumonia shows gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci on stain. This gram stain shows no organisms — the bacteria don't take up gram stain.

wrongAnswers.name: Influenza
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Influenza causes fever and cough but with myalgias, no diarrhea, normal sodium, and visible organisms are absent because it's viral.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with sudden high fever and severe headache three days after swimming in a tropical freshwater lake.
He had a small cut on his leg at the time of exposure, and the lake is frequented by stray dogs.
Exam reveals conjunctival redness without discharge, jaundice, and calf muscle tenderness.
Creatinine is elevated with thrombocytopenia, and transaminases are elevated but less than 200.
Microscopic agglutination test is positive for antibodies against a spirochetal organism.
explanation: The spirochete is shed in animal urine and enters through cuts or mucous membranes during freshwater exposure. It causes vasculitis affecting kidneys, liver, and other organs.
keyFact: Conjunctival suffusion (red eyes without discharge) is an important early clue that distinguishes this from other causes of tropical febrile illness. The severe icteric form with renal failure and hemorrhage is called Weil disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatitis A
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HAV causes jaundice with very elevated transaminases (>1000) and no renal failure or conjunctival suffusion.

wrongAnswers.name: Dengue Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dengue causes fever and thrombocytopenia in tropical settings but with retro-orbital pain and rash, not jaundice with renal failure.

wrongAnswers.name: Malaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malaria causes fever with jaundice in tropical areas but has cyclic fevers with parasites visible on blood smear.

clues: A 35-year-old hiker presents with an expanding red rash on his right thigh that appeared one week after a tick bite.
He reports fatigue, headache, and mild joint aches but is otherwise functional.
Exam reveals a 12-cm erythematous annular plaque with central clearing on the right thigh.
The rash has expanded from a small red papule at the bite site to its current size over 5 days.
ELISA screening is positive, and Western blot confirms IgM antibodies against the Borrelia spirochete.
explanation: The spirochete is transmitted by the Ixodes tick. The expanding ring with central clearing is the hallmark early localized lesion, and recognition at this stage prevents disseminated disease.
keyFact: The rash is diagnostic — treat empirically without waiting for serology. Early disseminated: facial nerve palsy (most common CN), AV block, meningitis. Late: large joint oligoarthritis (especially knee). Two-tier serologic testing: ELISA then Western blot.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis causes warm erythematous skin without central clearing. The expanding ring with clearing is pathognomonic for the tick-borne spirochetal infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Corporis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ringworm produces annular lesions with central clearing but they are smaller, scaly, and pruritic — not the large expanding erythematous plaque.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug reactions can cause erythematous rashes but not the annular expanding pattern with central clearing and tick exposure history.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with cyclical fevers every 48 hours with chills and sweats 2 weeks after returning from Central America.
She took chloroquine prophylaxis while traveling and completed the full course.
Exam reveals splenomegaly and mild anemia.
Peripheral smear shows enlarged red cells with multiple dots of staining (Schuffner dots), and parasitemia is 1.5%.
PCR confirms the species, and G6PD testing is ordered before starting the drug needed to eliminate dormant liver-stage forms.
explanation: This species and P. ovale form hypnozoites — dormant liver stages that can reactivate months to years later causing relapsing malaria. Eliminating these requires an additional drug.
keyFact: Primaquine kills liver hypnozoites to prevent relapse. MUST check G6PD status first because primaquine causes oxidative hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients. The enlarged, stippled red cells distinguish this from the dangerous species which infects normal-sized red cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Plasmodium falciparum
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Falciparum infects ALL-age red cells causing high parasitemia (>5%), banana-shaped gametocytes, and does NOT form liver dormant stages. This has low parasitemia with enlarged stippled cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Babesiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Babesia is transmitted by Ixodes tick in northeastern US with Maltese cross tetrads, not the cyclical fevers after Central American travel with stippled enlarged red cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Typhoid Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Typhoid causes sustained fever after travel but no organisms in red cells on smear.

clues: A 5-year-old unvaccinated child presents with high fever and cough for 3 days.
He has cough, runny nose, and red watery eyes (the three C's: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis).
The rash is maculopapular and has spread from behind his ears and face to his trunk over 2 days.
Small white-blue spots on a red base are noted on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars (Koplik spots).
Measles IgM antibody is positive, and viral PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab confirms the paramyxovirus.
explanation: The paramyxovirus causes a highly contagious respiratory illness with the characteristic prodrome of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis followed by the rash spreading cephalocaudally.
keyFact: The three C's (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) + the white mucosal spots (Koplik spots) + cephalocaudal maculopapular rash = measles. Complications: pneumonia (most common cause of death), encephalitis, and the rare progressive fatal encephalitis (SSPE) years later.

wrongAnswers.name: Rubella
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rubella causes a milder illness with postauricular lymphadenopathy and a finer rash. No mucosal spots. The concern is congenital rubella if pregnant.

wrongAnswers.name: Roseola
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Roseola (HHV-6) causes high fever FOLLOWED by rash as fever breaks — the rash appears when the child improves. In measles, rash appears while the child is still ill.

wrongAnswers.name: Kawasaki Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kawasaki causes fever with rash, conjunctivitis, and oral changes in children, but the oral changes are strawberry tongue and cracked lips — not the white mucosal spots.

clues: A 55-year-old man admitted for a metabolic emergency develops severe facial pain, dark nasal discharge, and periorbital swelling on hospital day 3.
He is diabetic and was admitted for ketoacidosis. He has fever and the nasal discharge has turned black.
Nasal endoscopy reveals black necrotic tissue on the turbinates and hard palate — the tissue is dying.
CT shows sinus opacification with bony erosion toward the orbit, and biopsy shows wide ribbon-like hyphae branching at 90-degree angles WITHOUT septations.
Biopsy shows wide ribbon-like nonseptate hyphae branching at 90-degree angles that are invading blood vessel walls.
explanation: The organism thrives in the acidotic, iron-rich environment of DKA. It invades blood vessel walls, causing thrombosis and infarction of surrounding tissue — explaining the characteristic black necrotic eschar.
keyFact: NON-septate hyphae, 90-degree WIDE-angle branching (vs Aspergillus: septate, 45-degree acute-angle). DKA and iron overload (deferoxamine use) are the classic risk factors. Angioinvasive like Aspergillus but different morphology and clinical context.

wrongAnswers.name: Aspergillosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aspergillus has SEPTATE hyphae branching at 45-degree acute angles and primarily infects neutropenic patients. This has non-septate hyphae at 90 degrees in a patient with DKA.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacterial Sinusitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial sinusitis causes facial pain and fever but NOT black necrotic tissue, bony erosion, or fungal hyphae on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Orbital Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Orbital cellulitis causes periorbital swelling from sinusitis spread but without the tissue necrosis and wide-angle non-septate hyphae.

clues: A 42-year-old man from Southeast Asia presents with a persistent productive cough for three months.
He has drenching night sweats, evening fevers, and has lost 20 pounds without trying.
Exam reveals a cachectic man with crackles and hollow-sounding breath sounds over the right upper back.
Chest X-ray shows a thick-walled cavity in the right upper lobe with surrounding infiltrate.
Three sputum samples collected early morning all show red-staining rod-shaped organisms on acid-fast stain.
explanation: The organism's waxy cell wall resists decolorization with acid-alcohol after staining, making it 'acid-fast.' Upper lobe cavities form because the organism thrives in high-oxygen environments.
keyFact: Upper lobe cavitary disease = reactivation (secondary) TB. Primary TB causes a lower lobe infiltrate with hilar lymphadenopathy. The cavities contain the highest bacterial load and are most infectious.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cancer can cause hemoptysis with a cavitary lesion, but the acid-fast positive sputum confirms infection. Always rule out TB before biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with non-caseating granulomas. TB has caseating granulomas with acid-fast organisms.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Abscess shows a cavity with air-fluid level in dependent lung segments from aspiration. TB cavities are in the upper lobes without air-fluid levels.

clues: A 20-year-old college student presents with a dry nonproductive cough that has persisted for 3 weeks.
He has a low-grade fever and malaise but feels well enough to attend classes.
Exam reveals scattered bilateral crackles; the patient appears more well than the lung findings suggest.
Chest X-ray shows patchy bilateral interstitial infiltrates that appear worse than the clinical exam suggests.
Cold agglutinins are positive, and PCR of sputum identifies an organism that lacks a cell wall.
explanation: This is the smallest free-living organism and lacks a cell wall. The interstitial pattern on X-ray with a relatively well-appearing patient who keeps functioning creates the classic clinical-radiologic dissociation.
keyFact: The patient looks better than the X-ray (clinical-radiologic dissociation). No cell wall = beta-lactams (which target cell wall synthesis) don't work. Treat with macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. Cold agglutinins (IgM against red cell I antigen) are positive in ~50%.

wrongAnswers.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pneumococcal pneumonia causes lobar consolidation with high fever, productive cough, and the patient looks very sick — matching their X-ray findings.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral URI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A URI doesn't produce the bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Legionella Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Legionella causes atypical pneumonia with high fever, diarrhea, hyponatremia, and confusion in older patients exposed to water systems — not the mild illness in a college student.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with rapidly worsening pain in his right leg that began as a small wound yesterday.
He is diabetic. The pain is severe and out of proportion to the visible skin findings, and he has developed high fevers.
Exam reveals dusky discolored skin with tense edema, hemorrhagic bullae, and crepitus on palpation from gas in the tissue.
CT shows gas tracking along the fascial planes, white count is 28,000, and lactate is 6.2.
Intraoperatively, the subcutaneous tissue is gray and necrotic with dishwater-colored fluid, and the fascia separates easily with blunt dissection.
explanation: Bacteria (often mixed flora or Group A Strep) rapidly spread along fascial planes, producing toxins and gas that destroy tissue and cut off blood supply, creating a self-propagating cycle of necrosis.
keyFact: Pain out of proportion to exam findings is the earliest and most important clue. Crepitus = gas in soft tissue. The hallmark is rapid progression — hours, not days. Delay in surgical debridement dramatically increases mortality.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis causes spreading erythema but the pain is proportional to the visible findings, there is no crepitus or gas on imaging, and it responds to antibiotics without surgery.

wrongAnswers.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DVT causes leg swelling and pain but without skin changes, crepitus, or gas on imaging.

wrongAnswers.name: Gas Gangrene
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is related but specifically involves MUSCLE, not fascia, and classically follows traumatic wounds with Clostridium perfringens.

clues: A 20-year-old college student living in a dormitory presents with severe headache that developed rapidly over 6 hours.
He has a high fever, vomiting, and photophobia, and his roommate noticed he seemed confused.
Exam reveals neck stiffness with resistance to flexion and a rapidly spreading petechial rash on his trunk and extremities.
CSF shows WBC of 2,500 (mostly neutrophils), glucose of 20, and protein of 250.
CSF Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci, and CSF latex agglutination confirms the organism.
explanation: Gram-negative diplococci invade the meninges via the bloodstream. The petechial rash indicates meningococcemia. Rapid deterioration to fulminant sepsis with DIC and adrenal hemorrhage is the feared complication.
keyFact: CSF pattern: HIGH WBC (neutrophils), HIGH protein, LOW glucose = bacterial. Dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality. Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts is mandatory.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral meningitis has lymphocytic CSF with mildly elevated protein and NORMAL glucose. The neutrophilic pleocytosis with very low glucose here is bacterial.

wrongAnswers.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SAH causes sudden headache with neck stiffness but has blood on CT or xanthochromic CSF, not purulent fluid with gram-negative diplococci.

wrongAnswers.name: HSV Encephalitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV encephalitis causes fever and confusion but with temporal lobe involvement on MRI and lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose, not the neutrophilic CSF with low glucose.

clues: A 6-month-old incompletely vaccinated infant is brought in with paroxysms of rapid coughing followed by a high-pitched gasping sound on inspiration.
The coughing spells are so severe that the infant turns red, vomits after each spell, and appears exhausted between episodes.
Between paroxysms, the infant appears surprisingly well.
White blood cell count is 45,000 with 80% lymphocytes.
Nasopharyngeal PCR is positive for a gram-negative coccobacillus; DFA staining of the nasopharyngeal specimen is also positive.
explanation: The organism attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium and releases toxins that cause intense inflammation. The toxin also prevents lymphocytes from migrating out of the bloodstream, causing the characteristic lymphocytosis.
keyFact: Three stages: catarrhal (URI-like, most infectious), paroxysmal (characteristic cough with whoop), convalescent (gradual resolution over weeks). The marked lymphocytosis is a classic lab clue. Antibiotics reduce transmission but don't significantly shorten the paroxysmal phase.

wrongAnswers.name: RSV Bronchiolitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RSV causes wheezing and respiratory distress in infants but with continuous symptoms — not the episodic paroxysms with well intervals and marked lymphocytosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Croup
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Croup causes a barking cough with stridor from subglottic swelling. The inspiratory whoop here is from forceful inspiration after a prolonged coughing spell.

wrongAnswers.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aspiration causes sudden choking with unilateral findings, not the paroxysmal pattern with lymphocytosis and positive PCR.

clues: A 25-year-old man from rural New Mexico presents with sudden high fever and chills over 24 hours.
He works as a park ranger and recalls flea bites about a week ago while handling a dead prairie dog.
Exam reveals an exquisitely tender 4-cm fluctuant mass in the left inguinal region with overlying erythema.
Aspirate Gram stain shows gram-negative coccobacilli, and a Wayson stain shows bipolar 'safety pin' staining.
Blood cultures grow the organism, and fluorescent antibody testing confirms identification.
explanation: Yersinia pestis is transmitted from rodents via flea bites. The bacteria travel to regional lymph nodes, which swell into the characteristic painful bubo.
keyFact: Three forms: bubonic (most common, bubo), septicemic (bloodstream without bubo), pneumonic (person-to-person via respiratory droplets — the most dangerous form requiring strict isolation).

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphogranuloma Venereum
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LGV causes inguinal lymphadenopathy but is sexually transmitted, less acutely toxic, and caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.

wrongAnswers.name: Cat Scratch Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CSD causes regional lymphadenopathy from Bartonella but is less acutely ill with a more indolent course.

wrongAnswers.name: Tularemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tularemia causes ulceroglandular disease with lymphadenopathy after animal exposure but the organism is Francisella, not the bipolar-staining coccobacillus.

clues: A 32-year-old man presents with cyclical high fevers and drenching sweats one week after returning from sub-Saharan Africa.
His fevers spike every 48 hours with rigors followed by drenching diaphoresis; he did not take prophylaxis during travel.
Exam reveals splenomegaly, jaundice, and a temperature of 104 F during a febrile paroxysm.
Thick smear is positive for malaria, and thin smear shows ring-shaped organisms inside red blood cells with some cells containing multiple rings.
Parasitemia is 8%, and banana-shaped gametocytes are identified on the thin smear.
explanation: The most dangerous malaria species because it infects red blood cells of all ages (not just young or old ones), allowing parasitemia to reach levels that cause organ failure.
keyFact: Multiple rings per cell and banana-shaped gametocytes identify the species. Complications: cerebral malaria, severe anemia, ARDS, renal failure. The other species form liver dormant stages (hypnozoites) requiring primaquine — check G6PD first.

wrongAnswers.name: Babesiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Babesia also shows ring forms in red cells but transmitted by Ixodes tick in northeastern US, with Maltese cross tetrads and no banana-shaped gametocytes.

wrongAnswers.name: Typhoid Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Typhoid causes sustained fever with relative bradycardia and rose spots but no organisms visible on blood smear.

wrongAnswers.name: Dengue
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dengue causes fever with thrombocytopenia but no organisms in red cells on blood smear.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with gradually worsening shortness of breath and a dry cough over several weeks.
He has advanced immunosuppression with a CD4 count of 85 and has not been taking prophylactic medications.
Exam reveals tachypnea with oxygen saturation of 88% on room air but surprisingly few findings on lung auscultation.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities, and LDH is markedly elevated.
Induced sputum with silver stain reveals disc-shaped cysts with a characteristic central dot.
explanation: This fungus causes pneumonia almost exclusively in severely immunocompromised patients. The subacute onset with exertional dyspnea, bilateral ground-glass opacities, and elevated LDH is characteristic.
keyFact: Prophylaxis with TMP-SMX when CD4 <200. Corticosteroids are added when PaO2 <70 or A-a gradient >35 (to reduce inflammation-mediated respiratory failure). The organism cannot be cultured — diagnosis requires staining of respiratory samples.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacterial Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial pneumonia presents acutely with productive cough, focal consolidation, and leukocytosis — not the subacute dry cough with bilateral ground-glass opacities.

wrongAnswers.name: CMV Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CMV pneumonia occurs at CD4 <50 and shows similar bilateral infiltrates but diagnosis requires tissue biopsy showing intranuclear inclusions — not disc-shaped cysts.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB causes upper lobe disease with cavitation and acid-fast organisms, not bilateral ground-glass opacities with disc-shaped cysts.

clues: A 45-year-old farmer presents with high fever and severe headache one week after lambing season.
Several of his sheep had stillbirths recently, and he assisted with the deliveries without respiratory protection.
Exam reveals a temperature of 104 F, bibasilar crackles, and hepatomegaly.
Routine blood cultures are negative, liver transaminases are elevated, and chest X-ray shows rounded opacities.
Phase II IgM and IgG antibodies are elevated on serologic testing, identifying an obligate intracellular organism; notably, there is no rash.
explanation: The obligate intracellular organism is shed in massive quantities in birth products of infected livestock. Inhalation of contaminated aerosols causes pneumonia, hepatitis, or both.
keyFact: No rash distinguishes this from all other rickettsial diseases. The three classic presentations are pneumonia, hepatitis, and culture-negative endocarditis (chronic form). Livestock exposure, especially during birthing, is the key history.

wrongAnswers.name: Mycoplasma Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia but without hepatomegaly, high fever to 104°F, or the livestock birthing exposure.

wrongAnswers.name: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RMSF is rickettsial but DOES cause a rash (starts on wrists/ankles and spreads centrally), unlike Q fever which is the rickettsial exception.

wrongAnswers.name: Psittacosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psittacosis causes atypical pneumonia from bird exposure, not sheep. Q fever is specifically linked to livestock birth products.

clues: A 30-year-old man from rural India presents with violent involuntary spasms of the throat triggered by attempts to swallow water.
He was bitten by a stray dog 6 weeks ago and did not receive any post-exposure treatment.
He is agitated, intermittently lucid, and has excessive salivation with inability to swallow his own secretions.
He also has spasms triggered by air drafts on the skin (aerophobia).
Nuchal skin biopsy analyzed by fluorescent antibody testing at the hair follicle is positive for viral antigen.
explanation: The neurotropic virus travels from the bite wound up peripheral nerves to the CNS over weeks to months. Once it reaches the brain, the encephalitis is almost universally fatal.
keyFact: The incubation period (weeks to months) provides the window for post-exposure prophylaxis. Hydrophobia and aerophobia (spasms triggered by air drafts) are pathognomonic. Once symptomatic, there is no effective treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Tetanus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tetanus causes muscle spasms from a toxin but with trismus (lockjaw) and opisthotonus, not hydrophobia with salivation.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Encephalitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Other viral encephalitides cause confusion and seizures but not the specific hydrophobia, aerophobia, and salivation pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Psychogenic Water Phobia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The violent involuntary diaphragmatic spasms on attempted swallowing, positive viral antigen on biopsy, and exposure history confirm an organic cause.

clues: A 10-year-old boy presents with fever and joint pain that moves from one large joint to another.
Two weeks ago he had a sore throat that resolved without antibiotics.
Exam reveals a new holosystolic murmur at the apex and painless subcutaneous nodules on the extensor surfaces of his elbows.
ASO titer is elevated, ESR is markedly elevated, and CRP is positive.
Echocardiogram shows mitral valve regurgitation with leaflet thickening and restricted motion.
explanation: Antibodies against the streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve tissue, causing a pancarditis that can permanently damage the valves.
keyFact: Migratory polyarthritis + carditis + subcutaneous nodules + ring-shaped rash + chorea = major Jones criteria. Only follows pharyngitis (not skin infections). Mitral valve most commonly affected. The key is PREVENTION — treat strep pharyngitis with antibiotics.

wrongAnswers.name: Infective Endocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IE has positive blood cultures and valvular vegetations. Rheumatic fever has sterile blood cultures — the valve damage is immune-mediated, not infectious.

wrongAnswers.name: Kawasaki Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kawasaki affects children <5 with mucocutaneous findings and coronary involvement, not the migratory arthritis with cardiac valve disease after strep pharyngitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis causes non-migratory oligoarthritis with urethritis and conjunctivitis. Rheumatic fever has MIGRATORY polyarthritis with cardiac involvement.

clues: A 10-year-old boy presents with high fever and severe headache 5 days after playing in a wooded area.
His parents found a tick attached to his scalp that they removed, and he now has a rash.
Exam reveals a maculopapular rash on the wrists and ankles that has begun spreading toward the trunk, with petechial components.
Labs show thrombocytopenia, elevated LFTs, and hyponatremia.
The rash started on the wrists and ankles and is spreading centripetally (toward the trunk), including the palms and soles.
explanation: The obligate intracellular bacterium infects vascular endothelial cells, causing a vasculitis that manifests as the spreading petechial rash with potential for multiorgan dysfunction.
keyFact: The rash starts at the EXTREMITIES (wrists, ankles) and spreads CENTRIPETALLY — opposite of most rashes. Palms and soles involved. Despite the name, most cases occur in southeastern US. Doxycycline is used even in children — the risk of untreated disease far exceeds the minimal risk of dental staining.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningococcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningococcemia causes petechial rash with fever and shock but the rash is TRUNCAL (centrifugal from center outward), not starting at the extremities moving inward.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Syphilis involves palms and soles but the rash is maculopapular (not petechial), painless, and associated with a prior chancre — not an acute febrile illness after tick exposure.

wrongAnswers.name: ITP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes petechiae but without fever, headache, or the centripetal spreading rash from extremities. The thrombocytopenia here is from the vasculitis, not immune-mediated platelet destruction.

clues: A 6-year-old boy presents with fever and sore throat for 2 days.
He has a red swollen tongue with prominent papillae and flushed cheeks with pallor around his mouth.
Exam reveals tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymph nodes, and a diffuse rough-textured rash with accentuation in skin folds.
Rapid antigen test is positive for group A streptococcus.
The rash feels like sandpaper on palpation and blanches with pressure; desquamation of the fingertips is noted beginning at day 7.
explanation: The erythrogenic exotoxin produced by certain group A streptococcal strains causes the diffuse sandpaper-textured rash in the setting of streptococcal pharyngitis.
keyFact: Sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue + circumoral pallor + strep pharyngitis = scarlet fever. The linear red streaks in skin folds (Pastia lines) are characteristic. Desquamation of the fingertips occurs during recovery.

wrongAnswers.name: Kawasaki Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kawasaki causes fever with rash and strawberry tongue in children, but requires 5 days of fever plus 4 of 5 criteria, and strep test is negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Measles
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Measles rash starts on the face and spreads down, with the three C's and mucosal spots. Scarlet fever rash is sandpaper-textured with strep pharyngitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Staphylococcal Toxic Shock
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TSS causes a diffuse erythematous rash but with hypotension, multiorgan involvement, and negative throat culture for strep.

clues: A 28-year-old man presents with a diffuse rash that involves his palms and soles.
He had a painless genital ulcer 6 weeks ago that healed on its own without treatment.
Exam reveals a diffuse maculopapular rash including palms and soles, flat moist patches on his tongue, and painless generalized lymphadenopathy.
RPR is reactive at 1:64.
Confirmatory FTA-ABS is positive, and darkfield microscopy of a mucosal lesion shows motile spirochetes.
explanation: The spirochete has disseminated hematogenously from the healed primary chancre. The rash on the palms and soles is a high-yield clinical clue that narrows the differential dramatically.
keyFact: Rash involving palms and soles = think of this disease, RMSF, and endocarditis. The reaction after treatment (Jarisch-Herxheimer) is self-limited. If untreated, tertiary disease follows years later with gummas, aortitis, and tabes dorsalis.

wrongAnswers.name: Pityriasis Rosea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pityriasis rosea causes a herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree rash on the trunk, but SPARES the palms and soles and has no mucosal lesions.

wrongAnswers.name: HIV Acute Retroviral Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute HIV causes rash with lymphadenopathy but without the palm/sole involvement, condylomata, or positive treponemal serologies. Both should be tested simultaneously.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug reactions can cause widespread rash but rarely involve palms/soles with the specific mucosal and perianal lesions, healed chancre history, and positive RPR.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with sudden high fever and a rash that looks like a severe sunburn covering her entire body.
She is on day 4 of her menstrual period and has been using super-absorbent tampons.
Exam reveals diffuse erythematous rash including palms and soles, strawberry tongue, conjunctival injection, and blood pressure of 72/44.
Blood cultures are negative; creatinine, AST, and bilirubin are all elevated indicating multiorgan involvement.
A retained tampon is found and removed; vaginal cultures grow coagulase-positive gram-positive cocci.
explanation: The superantigen bypasses normal antigen processing, causing massive nonspecific T-cell activation and cytokine release — a cytokine storm causing shock and multiorgan dysfunction.
keyFact: NEGATIVE blood cultures because this is toxin-mediated, not bacteremic. The sunburn-like rash (not petechial) with desquamation of palms and soles 1-2 weeks later during recovery is characteristic.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningococcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningococcemia causes shock with a PETECHIAL/purpuric rash and POSITIVE blood cultures. This has a sunburn-like (macular) rash with negative cultures.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic Shock
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic shock has positive blood cultures from bloodstream infection. This has negative cultures because the damage is from circulating toxin.

wrongAnswers.name: Kawasaki Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kawasaki affects children <5 with mucocutaneous findings and coronary involvement but NOT shock or multiorgan failure.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with abrupt onset of high fever, shaking chills, and a productive cough that started earlier today.
He has diabetes. His sputum is rust-colored and he has sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breathing.
Exam reveals decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right lower lung base with bronchial breath sounds.
Chest X-ray shows dense lobar consolidation of the right lower lobe with air bronchograms.
Gram stain of sputum shows lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci, and a urine antigen test confirms the organism.
explanation: The most common cause of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia. The capsule prevents phagocytosis, making vaccination critical especially in asplenic patients, elderly, and immunocompromised.
keyFact: Rust-colored sputum, lobar consolidation, and lancet-shaped diplococci with capsular halos are classic. The sound change (egophony) occurs because solid lung transmits higher frequencies. Asplenic patients are at extreme risk.

wrongAnswers.name: Klebsiella Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Klebsiella causes lobar pneumonia with 'currant jelly' sputum in alcoholics, often upper lobe with bulging fissure — not the rust-colored sputum and lancet-shaped diplococci.

wrongAnswers.name: Mycoplasma Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mycoplasma causes 'walking pneumonia' with dry cough and diffuse interstitial infiltrates in young adults — not lobar consolidation with high fever and rust sputum.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Abscess causes a cavitary lesion with air-fluid level, often from aspiration. This is a non-cavitary lobar consolidation.

clues: A 45-year-old farmworker presents with jaw stiffness that has progressed to difficulty opening his mouth, followed by painful muscle spasms.
He had a deep puncture wound from a rusty nail one week ago that he cleaned and bandaged at home.
Exam reveals masseter rigidity preventing mouth opening, a fixed grimacing facial expression, and rigid arching of the back triggered by any noise or touch.
The diagnosis is entirely clinical -- there is no confirmatory laboratory test; vaccination records show no history of immunization.
The wound is deep and necrotic on inspection, and anaerobic culture of wound tissue grows gram-positive spore-forming rods.
explanation: The anaerobic spore-forming bacterium produces a neurotoxin that travels retrograde along peripheral nerves to the spinal cord, where it blocks inhibitory neurotransmission.
keyFact: The jaw stiffness (trismus/lockjaw) and back arching (opisthotonus) are classic. The toxin is the second most potent known (after botulinum). Treatment: human tetanus immunoglobulin, wound debridement, metronidazole, and muscle relaxants. Prevention by vaccination.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningitis causes neck stiffness but with fever, headache, and altered mental status from infection of the meninges — not the jaw rigidity and full-body spasms with clear sensorium.

wrongAnswers.name: Strychnine Poisoning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Strychnine also blocks glycine receptors causing similar spasms, but from ingestion rather than a wound — always consider in the differential.

wrongAnswers.name: Dystonic Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug-induced dystonia causes jaw and neck stiffness but is acute, related to dopamine antagonists, and responds to anticholinergics — not wound-associated with progressive total-body rigidity.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with a worsening headache over 2 weeks and new difficulty using his left hand.
He has a severely weakened immune system with a CD4 count of 60. He has developed confusion and left-sided body weakness.
Exam reveals left-sided hemiparesis, hyperreflexia, and an upgoing toe on the left.
MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia and cortex with surrounding edema.
Anti-Toxoplasma IgG is positive. Empiric treatment produces clinical and radiographic improvement within 2 weeks.
explanation: The intracellular parasite reactivates from tissue cysts when cellular immunity wanes. It preferentially causes necrotizing encephalitis in HIV patients with CD4 <100.
keyFact: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in an HIV patient with CD4 <100 = toxoplasmosis until proven otherwise. Treat empirically first — if no response in 2 weeks, biopsy for primary CNS lymphoma (the main differential, which typically shows a single lesion and is EBV-associated).

wrongAnswers.name: Primary CNS Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CNS lymphoma is the main differential — it also causes ring-enhancing lesions in HIV patients but is typically a single periventricular lesion, EBV-positive, and doesn't respond to anti-Toxoplasma therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Brain Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial brain abscess causes ring-enhancing lesions but with a different clinical context — usually from contiguous spread (sinusitis, otitis) or endocarditis, not CD4 <100.

wrongAnswers.name: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PML causes white matter lesions without ring enhancement or mass effect, from JC virus reactivation — a different imaging pattern.

clues: A 35-year-old hunter presents with fever and a painful ulcerated lesion on his right hand.
He skinned several rabbits with bare hands while hunting one week ago.
Exam reveals a punched-out ulcer at the base of the right thumb with tender right axillary lymphadenopathy.
Labs show elevated inflammatory markers, and the laboratory is notified of the suspected organism before cultures are processed due to biosafety concerns.
Serum agglutination titer is 1:256, and PCR from the ulcer base confirms Francisella tularensis.
explanation: This highly infectious gram-negative coccobacillus is transmitted through direct animal contact (especially rabbits), tick bites, or inhalation of contaminated aerosols.
keyFact: The ulceroglandular form (ulcer at entry site + painful regional lymphadenopathy) is most common. Extremely infectious — only 10-50 organisms needed. Lab workers are at high risk. Treatment: streptomycin or gentamicin.

wrongAnswers.name: Cat Scratch Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CSD causes regional lymphadenopathy after cat scratch/bite but with an indolent course and a papule (not punched-out ulcer) at the inoculation site.

wrongAnswers.name: Sporotrichosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sporotrichosis causes an ulcer with nodular lymphangitic spread up the arm after plant/soil exposure, not rabbit contact with axillary lymphadenopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Plague
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Plague causes a bubo (tender lymphadenopathy) but without the primary skin ulcer, and is associated with flea bites from rodents rather than rabbit handling.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with chronic watery diarrhea and 25 pounds of weight loss over one year.
He has migratory joint pain that predated his GI symptoms by several years and has been increasingly forgetful.
Exam reveals cachexia, diffuse lymphadenopathy, and hyperpigmented skin patches.
Small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy with lamina propria stuffed with foamy macrophages that are PAS-positive.
PCR of the biopsy tissue identifies Tropheryma whipplei DNA.
explanation: The gram-positive actinobacterium infects macrophages throughout the body. The macrophages ingest the bacteria but cannot destroy them, accumulating PAS-positive material.
keyFact: The triad of diarrhea/malabsorption + arthritis + neurologic symptoms (dementia, oculomasticatory myorhythmia) in a middle-aged man is classic. The synchronous jaw and eye movements are virtually pathognomonic. Treat with long-term antibiotics — relapses are common.

wrongAnswers.name: Celiac Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Celiac causes malabsorption with villous blunting but the macrophages are not PAS-positive, there's no arthralgias or dementia, and it responds to gluten withdrawal.

wrongAnswers.name: Crohn Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Crohn causes chronic diarrhea with weight loss and joint involvement, but biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas — not PAS-positive foamy macrophages.

wrongAnswers.name: Tropical Sprue
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tropical sprue causes malabsorption with villous blunting but without the joint and neurologic manifestations or PAS-positive macrophages.

clues: A 60-year-old man presents for evaluation of rough scaly patches on his face and forearms that have accumulated over years.
He spent decades working outdoors as a construction worker without regular sunscreen use.
Exam reveals multiple small erythematous scaly macules on sun-exposed areas that feel like sandpaper when palpated.
Dermoscopy shows a strawberry pattern with white-to-yellow scale and prominent follicular openings.
Biopsy shows dysplastic keratinocytes confined to the lower epidermis with solar elastosis in the underlying dermis.
explanation: Chronic UV exposure induces keratinocyte dysplasia that is confined to the epidermis. Without treatment, a small percentage (~1-10%) progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma over years.
keyFact: Sandpaper texture + sun-exposed distribution + fair skin + chronic UV exposure = AK. These are premalignant — NOT yet cancer. The dysplasia is confined to the epidermis. Once it invades through the basement membrane into the dermis, it becomes SCC.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCC is invasive through the basement membrane with dermal invasion. AK is confined to the epidermis — the precursor but not yet cancer.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriasis causes scaly plaques but they are thick, silvery, symmetric, and on extensor surfaces — not the thin rough sandpaper patches limited to sun-exposed areas.

wrongAnswers.name: Seborrheic Keratosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SK is a benign waxy 'stuck-on' lesion that is well-circumscribed and easily peeled off, not the rough sandpaper texture of AK.

clues: An 8-month-old infant presents with itchy red patches on her cheeks and scalp that appeared at 3 months of age.
She has a family history of asthma and allergic rhinitis, and the rash worsens in winter when the air is dry.
Exam reveals red weeping crusted patches on both cheeks and forehead with dry rough skin on the arms and legs; the diaper area is spared.
Serum IgE is elevated, and a culture from a weeping area grows Staphylococcus aureus.
The rash distribution spares the diaper area and is concentrated on the face and extensor surfaces, with xerosis of uninvolved skin.
explanation: A defective skin barrier (often from filaggrin mutations) allows allergen penetration, triggering a Th2-dominant immune response with elevated IgE. The inflamed skin is easily colonized by bacteria.
keyFact: Distribution varies by age: infants = face and extensors; children = flexural surfaces (antecubital, popliteal); adults = hands and flexures. Diaper area is SPARED (moisture-protected). Eczema herpeticum (HSV superinfection) is a medical emergency.

wrongAnswers.name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Infant seborrheic dermatitis (cradle cap) causes greasy yellowish scales, not the dry red weeping patches. It's also not particularly itchy.

wrongAnswers.name: Scabies
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scabies causes intense itching with burrows in web spaces and involvement of palms/soles. In infants, the diaper area IS involved — opposite of atopic dermatitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Contact Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Contact dermatitis has sharp borders matching the irritant exposure pattern, not the diffuse symmetric distribution with family atopic history.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with a slowly growing bump on his nose that has been present for over a year.
He has a history of chronic sun exposure and multiple blistering sunburns as a farmer.
Exam reveals a 1-cm translucent papule with rolled borders, visible telangiectatic vessels on the surface, and a central depression.
Dermoscopy shows arborizing tree-like blood vessels and a blue-gray ovoid nest within the lesion.
Biopsy shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact at the tumor-stroma interface.
explanation: UV radiation damages DNA in basal keratinocytes, causing them to proliferate into a slow-growing locally invasive tumor that virtually never spreads to distant sites.
keyFact: Pearly, translucent, telangiectatic, rolled borders = BCC. Most common on the face (nose is the #1 specific site). UV exposure is the major risk factor. Despite being a 'cancer,' metastasis is exceedingly rare — the issue is local tissue destruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCC presents as a firm keratotic or ulcerated nodule, not pearly and translucent. SCC can metastasize; BCC almost never does.

wrongAnswers.name: Melanoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Melanoma is a pigmented asymmetric lesion with color variation. This is a non-pigmented pearly papule with telangiectasia.

wrongAnswers.name: Sebaceous Hyperplasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sebaceous hyperplasia causes yellowish papules with a central dell but they lack the pearly quality, rolled borders, and telangiectasia of BCC.

clues: An 80-year-old man presents with intensely itchy tense blisters on his trunk and limbs over several weeks.
The blisters are firm and dome-shaped, difficult to rupture, and arise on both normal and erythematous skin.
Oral examination is completely normal with no mucosal blisters, erosions, or involvement.
Biopsy shows a subepidermal split with eosinophils in the blister cavity and perivascular infiltrate.
Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone.
explanation: IgG antibodies attack hemidesmosomal proteins that anchor the epidermis to the basement membrane. The deeper split (below the epidermis) keeps blisters intact longer than in pemphigus.
keyFact: TENSE blisters + SUBepidermal split + LINEAR basement membrane IgG + spared mouth + older patient = pemphigoid. FLACCID blisters + INTRAepidermal split + fishnet IgG + oral involvement + middle-aged = pemphigus.

wrongAnswers.name: Pemphigus Vulgaris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pemphigus has FLACCID blisters with INTRAepidermal split, fishnet IgG, and prominent oral involvement. This has TENSE blisters with SUBepidermal split and LINEAR IgG.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatitis Herpetiformis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DH causes intensely itchy grouped vesicles on extensors with granular IgA deposits, not tense blisters with linear IgG and eosinophils.

wrongAnswers.name: Bullous Drug Eruption
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug eruptions can cause blisters but without the specific hemidesmosomal antibodies or linear IgG pattern on immunofluorescence.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with intensely itchy clusters of small blisters on his elbows and knees recurring for months.
The itching is so severe he scratches the blisters open before they can be seen intact.
Exam reveals grouped excoriated papulovesicles symmetrically distributed on extensor surfaces and buttocks.
He also reports intermittent bloating and loose stools, and serum anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies are elevated.
Direct immunofluorescence of uninvolved perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of the dermal papillae.
explanation: IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase deposit in the dermal papillae, causing the intensely pruritic vesicular eruption. Nearly all patients have underlying celiac disease on biopsy even if asymptomatic.
keyFact: Granular IgA at dermal papillae = DH. Linear IgA at basement membrane = linear IgA bullous dermatosis (different entity). The extensor distribution (elbows, knees, buttocks) is characteristic. Responds to both dapsone (rapid) and gluten-free diet (slower but treats the underlying cause).

wrongAnswers.name: Bullous Pemphigoid
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BP has LINEAR IgG at the basement membrane with tense blisters on the trunk. DH has GRANULAR IgA at dermal papillae with grouped vesicles on extensors.

wrongAnswers.name: Eczema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eczema causes itchy patches in flexural areas without the grouped vesicular pattern on extensors or the granular IgA deposits.

wrongAnswers.name: Herpes Simplex
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV causes grouped vesicles but at ONE location (typically perioral or genital), not the symmetric extensor distribution with IgA deposits.

clues: A 25-year-old man develops a rash on his hands and forearms 10 days after a cold sore on his lip.
He has had similar episodes in the past, each preceded by a recurrence of his oral herpes.
Exam reveals multiple lesions on the hands, forearms, and feet with minimal mucosal involvement.
Each lesion has three distinct zones: a central dark area, a pale ring, and an outer red ring creating a true target pattern.
The lesions are fixed (do not migrate), are acral-predominant, and the three-zone target morphology is confirmed on dermoscopy.
explanation: HSV triggers an immune-complex mediated reaction in the skin, producing the characteristic three-zone target lesions predominantly on acral surfaces.
keyFact: True three-zone targets + acral distribution + triggered by HSV = erythema multiforme minor. The key distinction from SJS: EM is HSV-triggered with true targets and minimal mucosal disease. SJS is drug-triggered with atypical targets and prominent mucosal involvement.

wrongAnswers.name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SJS is drug-triggered with widespread atypical targetoid lesions, prominent mucosal involvement, and skin detachment. EM is HSV-triggered with true targets and minimal mucosa.

wrongAnswers.name: Urticaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Urticaria causes raised wheals that migrate and resolve within 24 hours. Target lesions are fixed and persist for days.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Syphilis causes targetoid lesions on palms but with a generalized rash, condylomata, and positive treponemal serology.

clues: A 25-year-old woman presents with painful red lumps on both shins that appeared suddenly about a week ago.
She was recently started on an oral contraceptive. The nodules are tender and warm but there are no skin breaks or drainage.
Exam reveals bilateral tender erythematous nodules on the anterior shins that are firm and deep — they feel like they are within the fat layer, not the skin surface.
The nodules evolve through color changes like a bruise (red to purple to yellow-green) over 2-6 weeks and resolve without scarring or ulceration.
Biopsy shows septal panniculitis without vasculitis. The inflammation is confined to the connective tissue septa between fat lobules.
explanation: This is a reactive process (not a specific disease) where immune complexes deposit in the subcutaneous fat, causing inflammation of the connective tissue septa between fat lobules.
keyFact: Bilateral pretibial tender nodules + septal panniculitis WITHOUT vasculitis or ulceration = EN. It's a nonspecific reaction pattern — the underlying trigger must be identified. Common triggers: strep infection, sarcoidosis, IBD, OCPs, pregnancy.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis is typically unilateral, spreading, with warmth and fever. EN is bilateral, symmetric, with discrete nodules.

wrongAnswers.name: DVT
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DVT causes unilateral leg swelling and pain, not bilateral discrete tender nodules on the shins.

wrongAnswers.name: Polyarteritis Nodosa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PAN can cause subcutaneous nodules but they are along arterial paths with vasculitis on biopsy. EN shows septal panniculitis WITHOUT vasculitis.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with intensely itchy bumps on her wrists and ankles, plus painful streaks inside her cheeks.
The skin lesions have a shiny surface with fine white lines visible on close inspection.
Exam reveals polygonal flat-topped violaceous papules on the flexor wrists and ankles with a fine lacy white network on the surface.
White reticular streaks (Wickham striae) are present bilaterally on the buccal mucosa on oral exam.
Biopsy shows a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction with destruction of the basal layer and pointed rete ridges with a 'sawtooth' appearance.
explanation: T-cell mediated destruction of the basal layer of the epidermis produces the characteristic flat-topped purple papules with the fine white surface lines.
keyFact: The 5 P's: Pruritic, Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped), Purple Papules. The fine white lines on the surface (Wickham striae) are characteristic. Oral involvement with white reticular streaks is common. Associated with HCV.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriasis causes silvery scaly plaques on EXTENSORS. Lichen planus causes flat-topped purple papules on FLEXORS with white surface lines.

wrongAnswers.name: Eczema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eczema causes itchy patches without the flat-topped purple polygonal morphology or white surface lines.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Syphilis can cause papular lesions but they're widespread including palms/soles, with positive serology and no white mucosal streaks.

clues: A 52-year-old man presents because his wife noticed a changing mole on his upper back.
It has been getting darker, larger, and more irregular over several months. He has more than 50 moles on his body.
The lesion is asymmetric with an irregular jagged border, contains multiple colors including brown, black, and blue-gray, and measures 9 mm.
Dermoscopy shows an atypical pigment network, blue-white veil, and irregular dots and globules.
Excisional biopsy shows atypical melanocytes extending into the dermis to a depth of 1.8 mm without ulceration.
explanation: A melanocyte became malignant and is growing both outward and downward through the skin. The deeper the invasion, the closer to blood and lymph vessels, and the more likely to metastasize.
keyFact: ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6mm, Evolution. Breslow depth determines management: <1mm = excellent prognosis, >4mm = poor. Acral lentiginous type is the most common in dark-skinned patients.

wrongAnswers.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BCC is a pearly translucent papule with telangiectasia — not a pigmented asymmetric lesion with color variation.

wrongAnswers.name: Dysplastic Nevus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dysplastic nevi have irregular features but atypical melanocytes remain in the epidermis. Once they invade the dermis (1.8mm here), it's melanoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Seborrheic Keratosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SK is a well-circumscribed waxy 'stuck-on' lesion without the irregular border, color variation, or dermal invasion.

clues: A 50-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions that have made eating difficult for weeks.
Fragile blisters then appeared on her trunk that rupture easily, leaving raw painful erosions that are slow to heal.
Exam reveals multiple flaccid blisters and shallow erosions on her trunk, and lateral pressure on uninvolved skin causes it to separate.
Biopsy shows an intraepidermal split with separation of keratinocytes just above the basal layer.
Direct immunofluorescence reveals a 'fishnet' pattern of IgG surrounding individual keratinocytes throughout the epidermis.
explanation: IgG antibodies attack desmoglein proteins that hold keratinocytes together. The cells detach from each other (acantholysis), forming flaccid blisters within the epidermis that rupture easily.
keyFact: Intraepidermal split + acantholysis + fishnet IgG pattern = pemphigus. SUBepidermal split + linear IgG at the basement membrane = bullous pemphigoid. Pemphigus starts in the mouth (mucosal-dominant). Pemphigoid rarely involves the mouth.

wrongAnswers.name: Bullous Pemphigoid
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BP causes TENSE blisters (subepidermal split keeps them intact longer) with LINEAR IgG at the basement membrane and minimal oral involvement.

wrongAnswers.name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SJS is drug-triggered with targetoid lesions and full-thickness epidermal necrosis, not the acantholytic intraepidermal split with fishnet IgG.

wrongAnswers.name: Herpes Simplex
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV causes grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that resolve in 7-10 days. Pemphigus causes persistent non-healing erosions with acantholysis.

clues: A 20-year-old woman noticed a single oval scaly pink patch on her trunk one week ago, followed by many smaller similar patches.
