The initial lesion was larger than the subsequent ones and had a collarette of scale at its periphery.
Exam reveals multiple oval salmon-colored patches arranged along the skin cleavage lines on the trunk in a pattern resembling the branches of a Christmas tree.
The patient is otherwise well with no systemic symptoms, and RPR testing for syphilis is negative.
The eruption began with a solitary herald patch followed 1-2 weeks later by the generalized secondary eruption of smaller lesions.
explanation: A viral exanthem (possibly HHV-6 or HHV-7) causes the characteristic herald patch followed by the generalized eruption along skin lines.
keyFact: Herald patch (large initial lesion) → Christmas tree pattern (smaller lesions along skin lines) → self-limited resolution = pityriasis rosea. MUST check RPR because secondary syphilis can produce an identical-appearing rash.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Syphilis can mimic the rash perfectly but with positive RPR/VDRL, condylomata, and systemic symptoms. RPR is negative here.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Corporis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ringworm causes scaly annular patches but they have raised active borders with central clearing and positive KOH prep.

wrongAnswers.name: Guttate Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Guttate psoriasis causes small scaly papules on the trunk (often after strep), but they are thicker, more scaly, and not arranged in a Christmas tree pattern.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents to a dermatology clinic with a persistent, itchy rash on both arms that has not responded to over-the-counter moisturizers.
The rash has been recurring for years, and new lesions appear at sites of skin injury. He has joint stiffness in his fingers.
Exam reveals well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick silvery scale on extensor surfaces — removing the scale produces pinpoint bleeding.
He also has pitting of his fingernails and asymmetric swelling of two distal interphalangeal joints.
Biopsy shows regular rete ridge elongation, parakeratosis, and neutrophil collections (Munro microabscesses) in the stratum corneum.
explanation: A T-cell mediated autoimmune process accelerates keratinocyte turnover from the normal 28 days to 3-5 days, producing the thick scaly plaques.
keyFact: The pinpoint bleeding upon scale removal (Auspitz sign) reflects elongated dermal papillae. Koebner phenomenon = new lesions at trauma sites. The nail pitting and DIP joint involvement (psoriatic arthritis) distinguish this from other papulosquamous diseases.

wrongAnswers.name: Eczema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eczema causes itchy patches but in flexural areas (not extensors) without the thick silvery scale, nail pitting, or joint involvement.

wrongAnswers.name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Seborrheic dermatitis causes greasy yellowish scales on the scalp and face, not the thick silvery plaques on extensors with joint disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatophyte Infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea causes scaly patches but with a raised active border and central clearing, not the well-demarcated silvery plaques.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with persistent facial redness and intermittent pustular lesions on her cheeks.
She reports that her face flushes easily after hot beverages, spicy food, and sun exposure.
She specifically denies any clogged pores, blackheads, or whiteheads on her face at any time.
Exam reveals central facial erythema and telangiectasias on the nose and cheeks.
Inflammatory papulopustules are present on the central face with no comedones identified on close inspection.
explanation: Chronic inflammation of facial blood vessels and pilosebaceous units causes persistent erythema with inflammatory papulopustules in the central face.
keyFact: Central facial erythema + papulopustules + telangiectasias + NO comedones = rosacea. The ABSENCE of comedones distinguishes it from acne vulgaris. Triggers: sun, heat, alcohol, spicy food. Untreated, can progress to rhinophyma (bulbous nose enlargement).

wrongAnswers.name: Acne Vulgaris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acne has comedones (blackheads and whiteheads) as the primary lesion. Rosacea specifically LACKS comedones.

wrongAnswers.name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Seborrheic causes greasy yellowish scales in nasolabial folds, eyebrows, and scalp. Rosacea causes erythema with papulopustules on the cheeks and nose.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic Lupus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus malar rash causes butterfly erythema that spares the nasolabial folds, without papulopustules or telangiectasias.

clues: A 25-year-old college student presents with intensely itchy bumps that are worst at night.
His roommate has developed the same symptoms. The itching started 3 weeks after moving into the dormitory.
Exam reveals excoriated papules and short wavy lines in the web spaces between fingers, wrists, axillary folds, and waistband area.
Dermoscopy of a burrow shows a dark triangular structure at the leading edge ('delta wing jet' sign).
Skin scraping from one of the wavy lines examined under the microscope reveals a mite, eggs, and fecal pellets.
explanation: The female mite burrows into the superficial epidermis to lay eggs. The intense itching is an immune reaction to the mite, its eggs, and fecal material, which is why it takes 2-4 weeks to develop after initial infestation.
keyFact: Nocturnal pruritus + interweb space burrows + close contacts affected = scabies. The 2-4 week delay before itching begins means the patient is contagious before symptomatic. Treat ALL contacts simultaneously to prevent re-infestation.

wrongAnswers.name: Atopic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eczema causes itching but is not contagious, occurs in flexural areas, and does not show burrows or mites on scraping.

wrongAnswers.name: Contact Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Contact dermatitis is localized to the area of exposure with geometric borders. Scabies is in characteristic locations (web spaces, waist, axillae) with burrows.

wrongAnswers.name: Body Lice
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Body lice cause pruritus but the lice live in CLOTHING seams, not burrowed into the skin. Web space burrows with mites on scraping confirm scabies.

clues: A 70-year-old man presents with a firm nodule on his lower lip that has been growing over 3 months.
He has a history of heavy sun exposure, smokes cigarettes, and has multiple scaly rough patches on his sun-exposed skin.
Exam reveals the nodule on the lower lip vermilion border with a hard keratotic center, plus multiple scattered rough scaly macules on his face and forearms.
The nodule is indurated with poorly defined borders, and a palpable submandibular lymph node is noted on the ipsilateral side.
Biopsy shows nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearl formation invading through the basement membrane into the dermis.
explanation: UV radiation and other carcinogens (smoking for lip lesions) cause malignant transformation of keratinocytes, producing an invasive tumor that can metastasize to regional lymph nodes.
keyFact: The rough scaly patches (actinic keratoses) are the precursor lesions. The lower lip is a classic high-risk site due to combined UV and tobacco exposure. Immunosuppression (especially organ transplant recipients) dramatically increases risk and aggressiveness.

wrongAnswers.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BCC is pearly and translucent with rolled borders and telangiectasia. This is a keratotic firm nodule with keratin pearls — a different cell of origin.

wrongAnswers.name: Keratoacanthoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Keratoacanthoma is a well-differentiated SCC variant that grows rapidly then may regress, with a characteristic central keratin crater. The distinction matters for management.

wrongAnswers.name: Actinic Keratosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AK is the precursor — flat, scaly, and sandpaper-textured. Once it becomes a nodule with dermal invasion and keratin pearls, it has progressed to invasive SCC.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with fever and a painful rash that began on her face and spread to her trunk over several days.
She reports painful skin sensitivity and difficulty eating due to oral discomfort. Two weeks ago she started trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI.
Exam reveals diffuse erythematous macules with targetoid lesions, flaccid blisters, and erosions on her lips, oral mucosa, and conjunctivae.
Nikolsky sign is positive, and involved skin peels off with gentle lateral pressure.
Total body surface area of skin detachment is approximately 6%, measured by the rule of nines.
explanation: This is a severe drug hypersensitivity reaction where the immune system attacks the epidermis and mucous membranes, causing widespread keratinocyte death and skin detachment.
keyFact: <10% BSA = SJS. 10-30% = SJS/TEN overlap. >30% = TEN. Mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital) is required. Common culprits: sulfonamides, allopurinol, carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine. Stop the drug immediately.

wrongAnswers.name: Erythema Multiforme
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EM causes target lesions but is usually HSV-triggered, limited to the skin, and lacks significant mucosal involvement or widespread skin detachment.

wrongAnswers.name: Pemphigus Vulgaris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pemphigus causes oral erosions and Nikolsky-positive skin from anti-desmoglein antibodies — an autoimmune, not drug-triggered, mechanism.

wrongAnswers.name: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SSSS causes skin peeling from staphylococcal toxin but has NO mucosal involvement and the split is superficial within the epidermis.

clues: A 48-year-old woman presents with rapidly spreading skin blistering and sloughing.
She started allopurinol for gout two weeks ago. She had fever and malaise for three days before large sheets of skin began peeling off.
She appears like a burn patient with large confluent areas of denuded skin, and Nikolsky sign is strongly positive over uninvolved skin.
Her eyes and mouth are severely involved with oral, ocular, and genital mucosal erosions.
Total detached body surface area is approximately 42%, and biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis.
explanation: This is the severe end of the same drug-induced spectrum, differing only in the extent of skin detachment. The entire epidermis is dying from T-cell mediated keratinocyte apoptosis.
keyFact: SJS (<10%) → overlap (10-30%) → TEN (>30%). HLA-B*5801 screening before starting allopurinol is recommended in high-risk populations (Southeast Asian, African American) to prevent this reaction.

wrongAnswers.name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SJS is the same disease with <10% BSA involvement. At 42% detachment, this is TEN. Management principles are similar but mortality is much higher.

wrongAnswers.name: Burn Injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The patient looks like a burn victim but there was no thermal exposure. The drug history, mucosal involvement, and Nikolsky sign confirm a drug-induced process.

wrongAnswers.name: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SSSS causes skin peeling but has NO mucosal involvement and the split is superficial. TEN has severe mucosal involvement and full-thickness necrosis.

clues: A 4-year-old child presents with severe sunburn after minimal sun exposure and has already developed multiple pigmented skin lesions.
The parents report extreme sensitivity to sunlight since infancy, and the child has freckle-like lesions on sun-exposed areas far beyond what is normal for age.
Exam reveals numerous lentigines and atrophic patches on the face, arms, and hands with several suspicious-looking pigmented lesions.
Skin biopsy of one lesion shows malignant melanoma, and two other biopsies show squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma — all in a 4-year-old.
The defect is in nucleotide excision repair, the pathway that normally corrects UV-induced thymine dimers in DNA.
explanation: Without the ability to repair UV-induced DNA damage, every sun exposure causes permanent mutations that accumulate and drive cancer formation at an enormously accelerated rate.
keyFact: Over 1000x increased risk of skin cancers before age 10. Strict lifelong sun avoidance is required. Also at risk for neurologic degeneration. Autosomal recessive inheritance.

wrongAnswers.name: Albinism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Albinism increases sun sensitivity and skin cancer risk from lack of protective melanin, but DNA repair is intact and cancer doesn't appear in early childhood.

wrongAnswers.name: Ataxia-Telangiectasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AT has a DNA repair defect too but involves double-strand break repair, presents with ataxia and telangiectasias, and primarily increases lymphoma risk — not UV-induced skin cancers.

wrongAnswers.name: Fanconi Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fanconi has a DNA repair defect but affects DNA crosslink repair, causing bone marrow failure and congenital anomalies — not UV sensitivity and early skin cancers.

clues: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sharp chest pain that worsens when he takes a deep breath and lies flat.
He had a viral upper respiratory infection about two weeks ago with fevers, body aches, and a sore throat that resolved on its own.
On exam, a scratchy, high-pitched three-component sound is heard over the left sternal border that varies with the cardiac cycle.
ECG shows diffuse concave-upward ST elevation across multiple leads with PR depression in leads II, III, and aVF.
Echocardiogram reveals a small circumferential pericardial effusion with diffusely thickened, hyperechoic pericardial layers.
explanation: Inflammation of the pericardium, often following a viral illness, causes fibrinous or serous exudate between the visceral and parietal layers. The inflamed surfaces rubbing together produce the friction rub, and irritation of the pericardium generates the characteristic pleuritic, positional chest pain.
keyFact: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression is the classic ECG pattern; unlike MI, the ST changes are concave-up and present in nearly all leads without reciprocal changes. Most cases are idiopathic or viral.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocardial Infarction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MI causes ST elevation in a territorial distribution with reciprocal ST depression, not diffuse ST elevation with PR depression across multiple leads.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE produces pleuritic pain with dyspnea and tachycardia, but does not cause a friction rub or diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myocarditis presents with heart failure symptoms and troponin elevation, not a friction rub, and ECG changes are typically focal ST-T changes rather than diffuse elevation with PR depression.

clues: A 24-year-old woman presents with progressive exercise intolerance and bluish discoloration of her lips and fingertips over the past year.
She was born with a heart defect repaired incompletely in infancy and has had gradually worsening shortness of breath since adolescence.
Exam shows central cyanosis, digital clubbing, a loud single S2, and a right ventricular heave. The previously documented murmur is now quieter.
Chest X-ray shows prominent central pulmonary arteries with peripheral pruning. Echocardiogram reveals right ventricular hypertrophy and a reversed shunt across the interventricular septum.
Right heart catheterization demonstrates a pulmonary vascular resistance of 14 Wood units with systemic-level pulmonary artery pressures and bidirectional-to-right-to-left shunting.
explanation: A long-standing left-to-right cardiac shunt causes progressive pulmonary vascular remodeling and irreversible pulmonary hypertension. When pulmonary pressures exceed systemic pressures, the shunt reverses direction (right-to-left), mixing deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation and producing cyanosis.
keyFact: Reversal of a left-to-right shunt due to irreversible pulmonary hypertension defines Eisenmenger physiology. Once established, surgical repair of the defect is contraindicated because the right ventricle depends on the shunt as a pressure relief valve.

wrongAnswers.name: Tetralogy of Fallot
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TOF causes cyanosis from birth due to a fixed right-to-left shunt through right ventricular outflow obstruction, not from acquired reversal of a left-to-right shunt.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Pulmonary Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary pulmonary hypertension occurs without an underlying cardiac shunt; this patient has a known congenital defect with documented shunt reversal.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrial Septal Defect
wrongAnswers.whyNot: An uncomplicated ASD produces a left-to-right shunt with a fixed split S2 and no cyanosis; cyanosis with shunt reversal indicates progression to Eisenmenger physiology.

clues: A 29-year-old woman presents with joint pain, fatigue, and an episode of right-arm weakness that resolved spontaneously after thirty minutes.
She has a history of recurrent oral ulcers, a photosensitive facial rash, and two prior first-trimester miscarriages.
Exam reveals a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, small painless erythematous lesions on the palms, and a soft systolic murmur at the apex.
Labs show positive ANA, anti-dsDNA antibodies, low complement C3 and C4, and prolonged aPTT with positive anticardiolipin antibodies.
Transesophageal echocardiogram reveals small, irregular, wart-like vegetations on both surfaces of the mitral valve leaflets with mild regurgitation.
explanation: Immune complex deposition on valve endocardium in systemic lupus erythematosus causes sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations. These verrucous lesions characteristically appear on both surfaces of the valve, unlike the single-surface vegetations of infective or rheumatic disease.
keyFact: Libman-Sacks vegetations are sterile, occur on both sides of the valve (unique finding), and are associated with SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome. They can embolize causing stroke but rarely cause significant valve destruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Infective Endocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Infective endocarditis presents with positive blood cultures, high fevers, and large oscillating vegetations on one surface of the valve, not sterile vegetations on both surfaces with negative cultures.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatic Heart Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rheumatic valvular disease follows streptococcal pharyngitis and produces commissural fusion of the mitral valve, not bilateral verrucous vegetations in a patient with lupus serology.

wrongAnswers.name: Antiphospholipid Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: APS explains the miscarriages and prolonged aPTT, but the valvular vegetations with underlying SLE serology specifically indicate Libman-Sacks endocarditis as the cardiac manifestation.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with intermittent palpitations and a sensation of her heart skipping beats, particularly during stressful situations.
She is tall and thin with a low BMI, has joint hypermobility, and reports occasional lightheadedness on standing quickly.
Auscultation reveals a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the cardiac apex. The click moves earlier with standing.
Standing from squatting causes the click to occur earlier in systole with a longer murmur. Squatting delays the click and shortens the murmur.
Echocardiogram demonstrates posterior displacement of the mitral leaflet by 4 mm beyond the annular plane into the left atrium during systole with mild regurgitation.
explanation: Redundant mitral valve leaflet tissue prolapses into the left atrium during systole. The click occurs when the chordae tendineae reach maximum tension as the leaflet billows back. Maneuvers that reduce left ventricular volume cause earlier prolapse, moving the click closer to S1.
keyFact: The click-murmur moves EARLIER with maneuvers that DECREASE preload (standing, Valsalva) because the smaller ventricle allows the leaflet to prolapse sooner. Squatting INCREASES preload and delays the click. MVP is the most common valvular abnormality.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary mitral regurgitation produces a holosystolic murmur without the characteristic mid-systolic click. The click-to-murmur relationship with positional changes is unique to prolapse.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aortic stenosis causes a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, not a mid-systolic click with late systolic murmur at the apex.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM has a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva and standing, but it is a crescendo-decrescendo murmur without a mid-systolic click, and echocardiography shows septal hypertrophy rather than leaflet prolapse.

clues: A 19-year-old male college student presents with progressive fatigue, chest discomfort, and difficulty breathing while walking to class over the past five days.
He had a febrile illness with diarrhea and sore throat about ten days ago that he attributed to a stomach bug and treated with rest.
Exam reveals tachycardia to 112, a low-grade fever, an S3 gallop, bilateral lower extremity edema, and jugular venous distension.
ECG shows sinus tachycardia with diffuse low-voltage QRS complexes and nonspecific ST-T wave changes. Troponin I is elevated at 3.4 ng/mL.
Cardiac MRI shows patchy late gadolinium enhancement in a mid-wall and epicardial distribution with diffuse myocardial edema on T2-weighted sequences.
explanation: Viral infection triggers direct myocyte injury and an immune-mediated inflammatory response in the myocardium. The inflammation impairs contractility and disrupts the conduction system, leading to heart failure and arrhythmias, particularly in young patients following a viral prodrome.
keyFact: Coxsackievirus B is the most common viral cause. Cardiac MRI showing mid-wall or epicardial late gadolinium enhancement (not subendocardial, which suggests ischemia) with myocardial edema is the key noninvasive diagnostic pattern. Endomyocardial biopsy with Dallas criteria is the gold standard but rarely performed.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pericarditis causes pleuritic positional chest pain with a friction rub and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, not heart failure with troponin elevation and mid-wall gadolinium enhancement.

wrongAnswers.name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DCM presents with chronic heart failure and a dilated ventricle but without the acute viral prodrome, elevated troponin, or active myocardial edema on MRI.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Myocardial Infarction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MI causes troponin elevation but in a coronary territory distribution with subendocardial enhancement on MRI, not the mid-wall and epicardial pattern seen here in a young patient without coronary risk factors.

clues: A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department at 4 AM with severe substernal chest pressure that woke her from sleep, along with diaphoresis and nausea.
She smokes one pack of cigarettes per day but has no other cardiac risk factors. She reports similar episodes occurring at rest in the early morning hours over the past month.
Exam during the episode shows blood pressure of 148/92, diaphoresis, and no murmurs or extra heart sounds. Between episodes she appears well.
ECG obtained during the episode shows transient ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. A repeat ECG thirty minutes later after symptom resolution shows completely normal ST segments.

Coronary angiography shows no obstructive lesions. Provocative testing with intracoronary ergonovine reproduces focal spasm of the right coronary artery with ST elevation that resolves with intracoronary nitroglycerin.
explanation: Transient focal spasm of an epicardial coronary artery causes transmural ischemia, producing ST elevation that resolves completely when the spasm relaxes. Unlike atherosclerotic angina, the coronary arteries are structurally normal or minimally diseased.
keyFact: Prinzmetal angina occurs at rest (often early morning), causes transient ST ELEVATION (not depression), and has normal coronary arteries on angiography. Calcium channel blockers and nitrates are the treatment; beta-blockers are contraindicated as they allow unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction.

wrongAnswers.name: STEMI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: STEMI causes persistent ST elevation due to complete thrombotic coronary occlusion visible on angiography, not transient ST elevation with clean coronary arteries that resolves spontaneously.

wrongAnswers.name: Unstable Angina
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Unstable angina causes ST depression or T-wave inversions from partial coronary obstruction, not transient ST elevation with entirely normal coronary anatomy on angiography.

wrongAnswers.name: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Takotsubo causes ST elevation with apical ballooning on ventriculography after emotional stress, not recurrent early-morning episodes with focal coronary spasm on provocative testing.

clues: A 58-year-old man in the ICU develops rapidly worsening shortness of breath and low oxygen levels over the past twelve hours despite supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula.
He was admitted three days ago for severe pancreatitis and has been receiving IV fluids, pain management, and bowel rest.
Exam reveals tachypnea to 34, diffuse bilateral crackles, accessory muscle use, and oxygen saturation of 82% on 15L non-rebreather mask.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse opacities that are not fully explained by effusions. Echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function with no elevated filling pressures.
Arterial blood gas on mechanical ventilation with FiO2 of 1.0 and PEEP of 10 shows PaO2 of 88 mmHg, yielding a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 88.
explanation: An inciting inflammatory event causes diffuse alveolar damage with protein-rich edema flooding the alveoli and inactivating surfactant. This creates widespread atelectasis and intrapulmonary shunting that is refractory to supplemental oxygen, distinguishing it from cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
keyFact: ARDS is defined by the Berlin criteria: acute onset within 1 week, bilateral opacities not explained by effusions, respiratory failure not explained by heart failure, and PaO2/FiO2 ratio classification (mild 200-300, moderate 100-200, severe <100). The PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 88 here indicates severe ARDS.

wrongAnswers.name: Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cardiogenic edema shows elevated left ventricular filling pressures and responds to diuresis; this patient has normal cardiac function on echocardiogram with noncardiogenic bilateral opacities.

wrongAnswers.name: Bilateral Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bilateral pneumonia can trigger ARDS but alone does not explain the refractory hypoxemia with a PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 100 and normal cardiac function meeting Berlin criteria.

wrongAnswers.name: Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DAH presents with hemoptysis, dropping hemoglobin, and increasingly bloody bronchoalveolar lavage returns, none of which are described in this case.

clues: A 67-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry nonproductive cough that has worsened over the past two years.
He worked in shipbuilding and pipe insulation for over thirty years and retired a decade ago.
Exam reveals bilateral inspiratory crackles at the lung bases, digital clubbing, and decreased chest expansion. No wheezing is heard.
Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern with reduced FVC, reduced DLCO, and a normal FEV1/FVC ratio. Chest X-ray shows bilateral lower lobe reticular opacities.
High-resolution CT shows bilateral subpleural honeycombing and reticular opacities in the lower lobes with calcified pleural plaques along the diaphragmatic surfaces.
explanation: Inhaled asbestos fibers deposit in the lung parenchyma and trigger a chronic fibrotic response, particularly in the lower lobes. The fibers are too long for macrophages to completely engulf, causing persistent inflammation that leads to progressive interstitial fibrosis and restrictive lung disease.
keyFact: Asbestosis causes lower-lobe predominant fibrosis with pleural plaques (pathognomonic of asbestos exposure). It is associated with increased risk of bronchogenic carcinoma (most common malignancy) and mesothelioma (most specific malignancy). The latency period is typically 15-20 years.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IPF also shows lower-lobe honeycombing, but the occupational history and calcified pleural plaques are specific to asbestos exposure and distinguish asbestosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Silicosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Silicosis causes upper-lobe predominant nodular opacities with eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes, not lower-lobe fibrosis with pleural plaques.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes an obstructive pattern on PFTs with increased FRC and hyperinflation, not the restrictive pattern with lower-lobe fibrosis seen here.

clues: A 56-year-old man presents with severe pain in his right shoulder radiating down the inner aspect of his right arm that has not responded to physical therapy over three months.
He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and has noticed weakness and tingling in his right hand, particularly the ring and little fingers.
Exam reveals ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis of the right face. There is atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the right hand with decreased grip strength.
Chest X-ray shows asymmetric opacification at the right lung apex with destruction of the posterior first and second ribs.
CT-guided biopsy of the apical mass reveals non-small cell lung carcinoma invading the brachial plexus and adjacent chest wall.
explanation: A lung carcinoma arising in the superior sulcus invades the adjacent brachial plexus (C8-T1), causing arm and shoulder pain with hand weakness, and compresses the ipsilateral sympathetic chain ganglia, producing Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).
keyFact: Pancoast tumors are defined by their apical location and local invasion, not histology. The triad is shoulder/arm pain from brachial plexus invasion (C8-T1 distribution), Horner syndrome from sympathetic chain involvement, and apical lung mass. Most are non-small cell carcinomas.

wrongAnswers.name: Cervical Radiculopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervical radiculopathy causes arm pain and weakness but does not produce Horner syndrome or an apical lung opacity with rib destruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thoracic outlet syndrome can compress the brachial plexus causing similar hand symptoms, but does not cause Horner syndrome or a destructive apical lung mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Brachial Plexus Neuritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Brachial plexus neuritis causes acute shoulder pain with weakness but is self-limited, does not include Horner syndrome, and imaging is negative for apical mass or rib destruction.

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with chronic cough productive of black-tinged sputum and progressive shortness of breath over the past several years.
He spent 28 years working in underground coal mines in West Virginia and has been retired for five years.
Exam reveals decreased breath sounds bilaterally with scattered rhonchi. No clubbing is present. Oxygen saturation is 91% on room air.
Chest X-ray shows multiple small rounded opacities predominantly in the upper lung zones bilaterally.
CT chest confirms diffuse small centrilobular nodules in the upper lobes with several nodules coalescing into a large mass in the right upper lobe surrounded by emphysematous change.
explanation: Chronic inhalation of coal dust leads to accumulation of carbon-laden macrophages around respiratory bronchioles, forming coal macules. Progressive massive fibrosis occurs when these macules coalesce into large fibrotic masses, typically in the upper lobes, with surrounding emphysematous destruction.
keyFact: Simple CWP shows small rounded opacities on chest X-ray. Complicated CWP (progressive massive fibrosis) is defined by coalescent opacities greater than 1 cm. Coal dust itself causes macule formation; coexisting silica exposure drives the fibrotic progression to PMF.

wrongAnswers.name: Silicosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Silicosis also produces upper-lobe nodules but characteristically shows eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes and occurs in sandblasters, miners of silica-containing rock, or stone cutters rather than coal miners.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis can cause upper-lobe predominant disease but presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and noncaseating granulomas in a younger patient, not an older coal miner with occupational exposure.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB causes upper-lobe cavitary disease with caseating granulomas and positive AFB testing, not progressive coalescent nodules with coal dust-laden macrophages in a coal miner.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough over the past three years without fever or weight loss.
He has worked as a sandblaster in a foundry for over twenty years. He does not smoke and has no other significant medical history.
Exam reveals decreased breath sounds in the upper lung fields bilaterally. Pulmonary function tests show a mixed obstructive and restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral upper-lobe predominant small rounded opacities with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy showing peripheral rim calcification.
CT chest confirms multiple small nodules in the upper lobes with hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes demonstrating eggshell calcification and early coalescence of nodules bilaterally.
explanation: Inhaled crystalline silica particles are engulfed by alveolar macrophages but cannot be degraded, causing macrophage death and release of inflammatory cytokines and fibrogenic factors. This leads to formation of silicotic nodules composed of concentric layers of collagen, predominantly in the upper lobes.
keyFact: Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes is the radiographic hallmark. Silicosis increases susceptibility to tuberculosis (silico-tuberculosis) because silica impairs macrophage bactericidal function. Occupations at risk include sandblasters, stone cutters, and tunnel drillers.

wrongAnswers.name: Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CWP produces similar upper-lobe nodules but occurs in coal miners and does not characteristically show eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy but the nodes show homogeneous enhancement rather than eggshell calcification, and the condition occurs without occupational silica exposure.

wrongAnswers.name: Berylliosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Berylliosis presents similarly to sarcoidosis with noncaseating granulomas but occurs in aerospace or electronics workers exposed to beryllium, not sandblasters, and lacks eggshell calcification.

clues: A 24-year-old man presents with dark cola-colored urine, decreased urine output, and swelling of his legs and face that has developed over the past week.
He works as a painter and has smoked cigarettes for eight years. He had an episode of blood-streaked sputum two weeks ago that he attributed to a cold.
Exam reveals periorbital edema, bilateral lower extremity pitting edema, and blood pressure of 162/98. Urinalysis shows heavy proteinuria, hematuria, and red blood cell casts.
Serum creatinine is 5.2 mg/dL, up from 0.9 three months ago. Serum anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are strongly positive. Complement levels C3 and C4 are normal.
Renal biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG staining along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence microscopy.
explanation: Autoantibodies directed against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane cause a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. The same antigen is present in the pulmonary alveolar basement membrane, which explains the pulmonary hemorrhage that can accompany the renal disease.
keyFact: Linear IgG deposition along the GBM on immunofluorescence is the pathognomonic finding. The target is the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, shared between glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Smoking is a risk factor for pulmonary involvement. Treatment requires plasmapheresis to remove circulating antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy causes episodic hematuria with mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence, not linear IgG staining along the GBM, and does not cause rapidly progressive renal failure.

wrongAnswers.name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GPA causes pulmonary-renal syndrome but shows pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis (no immune deposits) with positive c-ANCA, not the linear IgG deposition seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Lupus Nephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus nephritis shows 'full house' immunofluorescence (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q) with a granular pattern and low complement levels, not linear IgG staining with normal complement.

clues: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of poor weight gain, excessive thirst, and frequent urination since infancy.
His mother reports he drinks large volumes of water throughout the day and produces copious dilute urine. He was born prematurely at 32 weeks with polyhydramnios.
Exam shows a small, thin child below the 5th percentile for weight and height. Blood pressure is 78/50, which is low for his age. He appears mildly dehydrated.

Labs show serum potassium of 2.6 mEq/L, serum chloride of 88 mEq/L, bicarbonate of 32 mEq/L, and metabolic alkalosis on blood gas. Urine calcium is elevated. Renin and aldosterone levels are markedly elevated.
Urine studies show inappropriately high urinary potassium and chloride excretion despite hypokalemia and hypochloremia, with a pattern mimicking chronic loop diuretic use.
explanation: A genetic defect in ion transporters in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (NKCC2, ROMK, or ClC-Kb channels) impairs sodium chloride reabsorption. This causes salt wasting, volume contraction, and compensatory activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, leading to hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
keyFact: Bartter syndrome mimics chronic loop diuretic use: hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypercalciuria and normal-to-low blood pressure despite elevated renin and aldosterone. It presents in infancy/early childhood, unlike Gitelman which presents later and mimics thiazide use.

wrongAnswers.name: Gitelman Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gitelman syndrome also causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis but presents in older children or adults, causes hypocalciuria (not hypercalciuria), and mimics thiazide rather than loop diuretic use.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis but with hypertension and suppressed renin, not the hypotension and elevated renin seen in Bartter syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetes Insipidus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia but with dilute urine and hypernatremia, not the salt wasting and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis seen here.

clues: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of bowed legs, difficulty walking, and poor growth since he began walking at 18 months.
His parents note he drinks and urinates excessively. He has had two episodes of unexplained dehydration requiring IV fluids in the past year.
Exam shows short stature below the 3rd percentile, frontal bossing, widened wrists, and genu varum. He has a waddling gait and diffuse muscle weakness.
Labs show a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, serum phosphate of 1.8 mg/dL, serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L, and serum bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L. Wrist X-ray shows widened and frayed metaphyses.
Urinalysis reveals simultaneous glucosuria with normal serum glucose, generalized aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, bicarbonaturia, and low-molecular-weight proteinuria.
explanation: Global dysfunction of the proximal convoluted tubule causes failure to reabsorb glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, uric acid, and low-molecular-weight proteins. Phosphate wasting leads to hypophosphatemic rickets, and bicarbonate wasting produces a Type 2 proximal renal tubular acidosis.
keyFact: Fanconi syndrome is a proximal tubular defect causing loss of everything normally reabsorbed proximally: glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, uric acid. In children, the most common cause is cystinosis. The rickets is hypophosphatemic (not vitamin D deficient), caused by renal phosphate wasting.

wrongAnswers.name: Vitamin D Deficiency Rickets
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vitamin D deficiency rickets causes similar bone findings but with low calcium and elevated phosphate, not the low phosphate with glucosuria and aminoaciduria indicating generalized proximal tubular dysfunction.

wrongAnswers.name: Type 1 Renal Tubular Acidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Type 1 RTA causes non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis but from distal tubular dysfunction without the proximal losses of glucose, amino acids, and phosphate seen in Fanconi syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: X-Linked Hypophosphatemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: X-linked hypophosphatemia causes phosphate wasting and rickets but through isolated FGF23-mediated phosphaturia, not through generalized proximal tubule dysfunction with glucosuria and aminoaciduria.

clues: A 17-year-old girl presents with muscle cramps, intermittent tingling in her hands and feet, and fatigue that has been worsening over the past year.
She is otherwise healthy with no medications and has normal blood pressure. She reports occasional muscle spasms and a craving for salty foods.
Exam reveals a blood pressure of 105/62, positive Chvostek sign with facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve, and carpopedal spasm with blood pressure cuff inflation.
Labs show serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L, serum magnesium of 1.1 mg/dL, bicarbonate of 30 mEq/L, and metabolic alkalosis. Urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio is very low.
Urine electrolytes show elevated fractional excretion of potassium and magnesium with low urinary calcium excretion, mimicking chronic thiazide diuretic administration.
explanation: A loss-of-function mutation in the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule impairs sodium and chloride reabsorption. This causes volume contraction with compensatory aldosterone activation, potassium and magnesium wasting, and paradoxically enhanced calcium reabsorption.
keyFact: Gitelman mimics chronic thiazide diuretic use: hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria. The hypocalciuria distinguishes it from Bartter syndrome (which has hypercalciuria and mimics loop diuretics). Gitelman is generally milder and presents in adolescence or adulthood.

wrongAnswers.name: Bartter Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bartter syndrome also causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis but presents in infancy with hypercalciuria and mimics loop diuretic use, unlike the hypocalciuria and adolescent presentation here.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis but with hypertension, not the normal-to-low blood pressure and hypomagnesemia seen in Gitelman syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypomagnesemia from Malnutrition
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nutritional hypomagnesemia does not cause the full pattern of hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypocalciuria and elevated urinary magnesium wasting seen here.

clues: A 16-year-old boy is found to have blood pressure of 168/102 on a routine sports physical. He is asymptomatic and has no other medical history.
His mother was diagnosed with hypertension at age 20 and his maternal grandfather had a stroke at age 42. There is no obesity or kidney disease in the family.
Exam shows blood pressure elevated in both arms, no abdominal bruits, and no cushingoid features. BMI is 22. Fundoscopic exam shows early arteriolar narrowing.
Labs show serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L, bicarbonate of 31 mEq/L, and metabolic alkalosis. Both serum renin and aldosterone levels are markedly suppressed.
Genetic testing reveals a gain-of-function mutation in the SCNN1B gene encoding the beta subunit of the epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct.
explanation: A gain-of-function mutation in the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting duct causes constitutive sodium reabsorption independent of aldosterone. The excess sodium retention expands intravascular volume, causing hypertension, while enhanced electrochemical gradient drives potassium secretion causing hypokalemia.
keyFact: Liddle syndrome has hypertension with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and LOW renin AND LOW aldosterone. This distinguishes it from primary hyperaldosteronism (low renin, high aldosterone) and renovascular hypertension (high renin, high aldosterone). Treatment is amiloride or triamterene (ENaC blockers), not spironolactone.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension with hypokalemia but has low renin with HIGH aldosterone, whereas Liddle syndrome has both renin and aldosterone suppressed.

wrongAnswers.name: Cushing Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cushing syndrome can cause hypertension with hypokalemia but presents with cushingoid features (moon facies, central obesity, striae) and elevated cortisol, none of which are present here.

wrongAnswers.name: Renovascular Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Renovascular hypertension in a young patient causes high renin and high aldosterone with an abdominal bruit, not the suppressed renin and aldosterone seen here.

clues: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician because his parents noticed progressive swelling of his face and legs over the past two weeks.
He recently recovered from an upper respiratory infection. His mother reports his urine has been foamy and his shoes no longer fit due to swollen feet.
Exam shows significant periorbital edema, tense ascites, and 3+ pitting edema of the lower extremities. Blood pressure is 98/60. No rash or joint swelling is noted.

Labs show serum albumin of 1.4 g/dL, total cholesterol of 380 mg/dL, and 24-hour urine protein of 5.2 g. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein with oval fat bodies but no red blood cell casts. C3 and C4 are normal.
Renal biopsy shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy and immunofluorescence. Electron microscopy reveals diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes without immune deposits.
explanation: Loss of the podocyte charge barrier allows massive protein leak into the urine. The resulting hypoalbuminemia decreases plasma oncotic pressure, causing diffuse edema. The liver compensates by increasing lipoprotein synthesis, producing hyperlipidemia. Urinary loss of antithrombin III and immunoglobulins increases risk of thrombosis and infection.
keyFact: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and edema. In children, minimal change disease is the most common cause (~80%) and shows foot process effacement on EM with normal light microscopy and IF. It is highly responsive to corticosteroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephritic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nephritic syndrome presents with hematuria, red blood cell casts, hypertension, and mild-to-moderate proteinuria, not the massive proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and bland sediment seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS also causes nephrotic syndrome but shows segmental sclerosis of some glomeruli on light microscopy, not the completely normal light microscopy with isolated foot process effacement.

wrongAnswers.name: Membranous Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome in adults but shows thickened capillary walls on light microscopy with subepithelial immune deposits, not normal light microscopy and IF.

clues: A 20-year-old woman is found to have microscopic hematuria on a routine urinalysis performed during a college health screening. She is completely asymptomatic.
Her mother and maternal aunt were also told they had blood in their urine but have never had kidney problems. There is no family history of kidney failure or deafness.
Exam is entirely normal. Blood pressure is 112/68. There is no edema, rash, or joint swelling.

Labs show serum creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL, normal complement levels, negative ANA, and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.1. Urinalysis confirms dysmorphic red blood cells without red blood cell casts.
Renal biopsy shows a uniformly thinned glomerular basement membrane measuring 180 nm on electron microscopy with no immune deposits on immunofluorescence and normal light microscopy.
explanation: A heterozygous mutation in type IV collagen genes (COL4A3 or COL4A4) produces a uniformly thin glomerular basement membrane that allows red blood cells to pass into the urine. Unlike Alport syndrome (which involves mutations in the same collagen genes but with progressive GBM disruption), thin basement membrane disease has an excellent prognosis with persistent hematuria but preserved renal function.
keyFact: Thin basement membrane disease is the most common cause of persistent isolated microscopic hematuria with a benign prognosis. GBM thickness is uniformly less than 250 nm (normal ~300-400 nm). Heterozygous COL4A3/A4 mutations cause TBMD; homozygous or X-linked COL4A5 mutations cause Alport syndrome with progressive renal failure and sensorineural deafness.

wrongAnswers.name: Alport Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alport syndrome causes hematuria with progressive renal failure, sensorineural hearing loss, and GBM splitting/lamellation on EM, not the uniformly thin but structurally normal GBM with preserved function seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy is a common cause of hematuria but shows mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence, not the negative immunofluorescence and thin GBM found on this biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Minimal Change Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Minimal change disease presents with heavy proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome, not isolated microscopic hematuria with negligible proteinuria and a thinned basement membrane.

clues: A newborn is brought to the nursery for evaluation of atypical-appearing external genitalia noted immediately after delivery.
The infant has been feeding poorly, is increasingly lethargic over the first week of life, and has lost more weight than expected.
Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L, potassium is 7.2 mEq/L, and the infant appears dehydrated with poor skin turgor and sunken fontanelles.
Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated at 15,000 ng/dL on newborn screening confirmation.
Karyotype returns 46,XX, and pelvic ultrasound reveals normal ovaries and a uterus, confirming virilization of a genetic female.
explanation: Deficiency of 21-hydroxylase blocks cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, shunting steroid precursors into the androgen pathway. Excess androgens virilize female genitalia in utero, while aldosterone deficiency causes life-threatening salt wasting.
keyFact: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of CAH cases. Elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the key lab marker. The salt-wasting form presents with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and ambiguous genitalia in 46,XX newborns.

wrongAnswers.name: Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIS presents with female external genitalia in a 46,XY individual and does not cause salt wasting or elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

wrongAnswers.name: Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison Disease)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary adrenal insufficiency can cause salt wasting but is acquired, does not present at birth, and does not cause genital ambiguity.

wrongAnswers.name: Pyloric Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pyloric stenosis causes vomiting and dehydration but produces hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, not hyperkalemia, and does not affect genitalia.

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with persistent headaches and intermittent muscle cramps that have worsened over several months.
She was recently diagnosed with hypertension at age 36 and has been refractory to three antihypertensive medications at adequate doses.
Blood pressure is 162/104 despite triple therapy. Serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L on two separate occasions without diuretic use. Bicarbonate is 32 mEq/L.
Plasma aldosterone concentration is 28 ng/dL with a suppressed plasma renin activity of 0.2 ng/mL/hr, yielding an aldosterone-to-renin ratio of 140.
Adrenal CT reveals a 1.8-cm solitary, well-circumscribed, lipid-rich left adrenal nodule with a normal contralateral gland.
explanation: An aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma secretes aldosterone autonomously, causing sodium retention and potassium excretion. The resulting hypertension and hypokalemia are independent of the renin-angiotensin system, which becomes suppressed.
keyFact: Conn syndrome (aldosterone-producing adenoma) is distinguished from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia by adrenal venous sampling. Unilateral adenoma is treated with adrenalectomy; bilateral hyperplasia is managed with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.

wrongAnswers.name: Renovascular Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Renal artery stenosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism with elevated renin, not the suppressed renin seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Cushing Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cushing syndrome can cause hypertension and hypokalemia, but would also present with weight gain, striae, and elevated cortisol rather than isolated aldosterone elevation.

wrongAnswers.name: Pheochromocytoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pheochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension with palpitations, diaphoresis, and headache, but does not produce hypokalemia or elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with anterior neck pain radiating to her jaw and ears, along with palpitations and tremor over the past two weeks.
She had an upper respiratory infection about three weeks ago that resolved on its own before the neck pain began.
The thyroid gland is exquisitely tender to palpation and feels firm. Heart rate is 108. TSH is suppressed at 0.05 mIU/L with elevated free T4.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 85 mm/hr. White blood cell count is normal. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are negative.
Radioactive iodine uptake is markedly decreased at 1%, showing virtually no tracer accumulation despite the hyperthyroid labs.
explanation: A viral infection triggers granulomatous inflammation of the thyroid, destroying follicular cells and releasing preformed thyroid hormone into circulation. The gland cannot trap iodine during the destructive phase, producing low radioactive iodine uptake despite biochemical hyperthyroidism.
keyFact: Low radioactive iodine uptake in the setting of hyperthyroidism distinguishes destructive thyroiditis (De Quervain, painless thyroiditis) from Graves disease (high uptake). De Quervain is painful and self-limited, typically following a viral illness.

wrongAnswers.name: Graves Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Graves disease causes diffuse, non-tender thyroid enlargement with elevated radioactive iodine uptake, not the tender gland and near-zero uptake seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Hashimoto Thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hashimoto typically presents with hypothyroidism, positive TPO antibodies, and a painless goiter, unlike the painful gland with negative antibodies here.

wrongAnswers.name: Suppurative Thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial thyroiditis causes unilateral tenderness with fever, leukocytosis, and abscess formation, not the bilateral tenderness with normal WBC seen here.

clues: A 12-year-old boy is brought in after his father suffered a myocardial infarction at age 38. The boy is otherwise healthy with no complaints.
The father and paternal grandfather both had documented coronary artery disease before age 45. The boy's mother has normal cholesterol.
Yellowish nodular deposits are noted on the Achilles tendons bilaterally. A grayish-white ring is visible at the corneal periphery.
Fasting lipid panel shows total cholesterol of 410 mg/dL and LDL of 335 mg/dL. HDL and triglycerides are within normal limits.
Genetic testing reveals a pathogenic loss-of-function mutation in the LDL receptor gene on chromosome 19.
explanation: Mutations in the LDL receptor impair hepatic clearance of LDL cholesterol from the blood, resulting in markedly elevated LDL from birth. Chronic exposure to high LDL leads to premature atherosclerosis, tendon xanthomas, and corneal arcus.
keyFact: Heterozygous FH (1 in 250) causes LDL 200-400 mg/dL with coronary disease by age 40-50. Homozygous FH (1 in 1,000,000) causes LDL >500 mg/dL with coronary disease in childhood. LDL receptor mutations are the most common cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Familial Hypertriglyceridemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: This condition elevates triglycerides, not LDL, and does not cause tendon xanthomas or corneal arcus at a young age.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nephrotic syndrome causes secondary hyperlipidemia but presents with proteinuria, edema, and hypoalbuminemia, none of which are present here.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism raises LDL secondarily but presents with fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance, and does not cause tendon xanthomas in a child.

clues: A 58-year-old woman presents with fatigue, constipation, and vague abdominal discomfort that she attributes to stress over the past few months.
She passed a kidney stone six months ago and has noticed increased thirst and frequent urination over the past several weeks.
Serum calcium is 11.8 mg/dL on two separate draws. Phosphorus is 2.1 mg/dL. Creatinine is normal.
Intact PTH level is 128 pg/mL, which is inappropriately elevated in the setting of hypercalcemia. 24-hour urine calcium excretion is elevated.
Sestamibi scan reveals a single focus of increased uptake posterior to the left lower pole of the thyroid gland, consistent with a parathyroid adenoma.
explanation: A parathyroid adenoma secretes PTH autonomously, increasing bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption while decreasing phosphorus reabsorption. The resulting hypercalcemia causes the classic constellation of stones, bones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric moans.
keyFact: Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in outpatients. Elevated calcium with an inappropriately normal or elevated PTH confirms the diagnosis. A single adenoma accounts for 80-85% of cases.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypercalcemia of Malignancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malignancy-related hypercalcemia presents with suppressed PTH due to PTHrP or osteolytic metastases, not the elevated PTH seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FHH causes mild hypercalcemia with low urinary calcium excretion, unlike the elevated urine calcium found in this patient.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes hypercalcemia through excess 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production by granulomas, resulting in suppressed PTH.

clues: A 16-year-old boy is brought in by his parents because he has not yet shown any signs of puberty. His peers have all developed secondary sexual characteristics.
He has never been able to smell and was excused from a chemistry lab safety exercise involving odor identification. His younger brother is developing normally.
Tanner stage 1 bilaterally. Bilateral cryptorchidism is noted. Arm span exceeds height by 7 cm. Testicular volume is 2 mL bilaterally.
Serum testosterone is 35 ng/dL. LH is 0.4 mIU/mL and FSH is 0.6 mIU/mL, both well below the normal adult male range.
MRI of the brain reveals absent olfactory bulbs and sulci bilaterally, with otherwise normal pituitary size and morphology.
explanation: GnRH-producing neurons fail to migrate from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus during embryonic development. Without GnRH signaling, the pituitary does not secrete LH and FSH, resulting in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism paired with anosmia due to shared developmental origin.
keyFact: Kallmann syndrome is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism plus anosmia. The shared embryologic origin of GnRH neurons and olfactory neurons from the olfactory placode explains both findings. KAL1 (X-linked) and FGFR1 are commonly mutated genes.

wrongAnswers.name: Klinefelter Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Klinefelter (47,XXY) causes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with elevated LH/FSH due to primary gonadal failure, and does not affect olfaction.

wrongAnswers.name: Constitutional Growth Delay
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Constitutional delay produces transiently low gonadotropins but does not cause anosmia, absent olfactory bulbs, or cryptorchidism.

wrongAnswers.name: Pituitary Adenoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A pituitary mass could suppress gonadotropins but would show an abnormal pituitary on MRI and does not explain anosmia or absent olfactory bulbs.

clues: A 5-year-old girl is brought in after her mother noticed vaginal bleeding and breast development over the past three months.
She has had recurrent fractures of the left femur after minimal trauma starting at age 3, with persistent left leg pain between episodes.
Large, flat, irregularly bordered hyperpigmented skin patches are present on the left trunk and thigh. They do not cross the midline.
Estradiol is elevated at 48 pg/mL with suppressed LH and FSH. Skeletal survey shows expansile ground-glass lesions in the left femur and pelvis.
Bone biopsy of the femoral lesion reveals fibrous tissue replacing normal bone with irregularly shaped trabeculae in a 'Chinese letter' pattern.
explanation: A postzygotic activating mutation in the GNAS gene causes constitutive activation of Gs-alpha protein in affected tissues. This produces a mosaic pattern of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, cafe-au-lait spots with irregular borders, and autonomous endocrine hyperfunction including GnRH-independent precocious puberty.
keyFact: The triad is polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, cafe-au-lait spots with irregular ('coast of Maine') borders, and precocious puberty. The GNAS mutation is somatic and mosaic, which is why it affects tissues unilaterally and variably.

wrongAnswers.name: Neurofibromatosis Type 1
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NF1 cafe-au-lait spots have smooth ('coast of California') borders and are bilateral, and NF1 does not cause fibrous dysplasia or precocious puberty.

wrongAnswers.name: Central Precocious Puberty
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Central precocious puberty shows elevated LH and FSH from premature hypothalamic activation, not the suppressed gonadotropins seen in this peripheral form.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteogenesis Imperfecta
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OI causes recurrent fractures but from abnormal collagen, not fibrous replacement of bone, and does not cause skin pigmentation or precocious puberty.

clues: A 42-year-old man presents with recurrent epigastric pain, diarrhea, and a 10-pound weight loss over four months despite a good appetite.
His father had surgery for a parathyroid adenoma at age 40, and his paternal aunt had a pituitary tumor removed at age 35.
Serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL with elevated intact PTH. A visual field exam reveals bitemporal hemianopia.
Fasting serum gastrin is 1,200 pg/mL. Secretin stimulation test shows a paradoxical rise in gastrin to 1,850 pg/mL. Prolactin is elevated at 180 ng/mL.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen reveals multiple small hypervascular lesions in the pancreatic head and body, and MRI of the sella shows a 1.5-cm pituitary macroadenoma.
explanation: Loss-of-function mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin) on chromosome 11q13 cause tumors in the parathyroids, anterior pituitary, and pancreatic islet cells. Gastrinomas in MEN1 are often multiple and located in the duodenum or pancreas.
keyFact: MEN1 = the 3 P's: Parathyroid (primary hyperparathyroidism, most common and earliest manifestation), Pituitary (prolactinoma most common), and Pancreas (gastrinoma most common functional tumor). Autosomal dominant, menin gene on 11q13.

wrongAnswers.name: MEN2A
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MEN2A involves medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia from RET mutations, not pituitary or pancreatic tumors.

wrongAnswers.name: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (Sporadic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sporadic ZES explains the gastrinoma but not the concurrent hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumor, which together indicate MEN1.

wrongAnswers.name: Prolactinoma (Sporadic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: An isolated prolactinoma does not account for the elevated gastrin, pancreatic lesions, hyperparathyroidism, or family history of endocrine tumors.

clues: A 32-year-old woman presents with persistent fatigue, dizziness, and inability to breastfeed her 6-week-old infant due to absent milk production.
Her delivery was complicated by severe postpartum hemorrhage requiring transfusion of four units of packed red blood cells.
Blood pressure is 88/56. Skin is dry and pale. She has not had a menstrual period since delivery. Axillary and pubic hair appear thinned.
Morning cortisol is 1.8 mcg/dL, TSH is 0.3 mIU/L with free T4 of 0.4 ng/dL, prolactin is undetectable, and LH and FSH are both low.
MRI of the sella turcica shows a partially empty sella with a small, atrophic pituitary remnant.
explanation: The pituitary gland enlarges during pregnancy due to lactotroph hyperplasia but does not receive a proportional increase in blood supply. Severe postpartum hemorrhage causes hypotension and ischemic necrosis of the enlarged gland, leading to panhypopituitarism.
keyFact: Agalactia (failure to lactate) is the earliest and most specific sign of Sheehan syndrome because prolactin-producing lactotrophs are the most vulnerable cells. Loss of all anterior pituitary hormones follows with low TSH, low cortisol, and amenorrhea.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphocytic Hypophysitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphocytic hypophysitis can occur peripartum but typically causes headache with an enlarged, contrast-enhancing pituitary, not the empty sella seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Postpartum Thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Postpartum thyroiditis causes transient thyroid dysfunction but does not affect cortisol, prolactin, or gonadotropins, and TSH would be elevated in the hypothyroid phase.

wrongAnswers.name: Postpartum Depression
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Postpartum depression can cause fatigue but does not explain hypotension, agalactia, panhypopituitarism, or the empty sella on imaging.

clues: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with high fever, irritability, and a rapidly spreading rash that began two hours ago.
He attends daycare and was well yesterday. A classmate was recently hospitalized for a serious infection. The boy's immunizations are up to date except for one missed booster.
Temperature is 40.1C, heart rate is 180, blood pressure is 62/38. Diffuse non-blanching purpuric patches are coalescing across the trunk and extremities.
Blood cultures are drawn. Coagulation studies show DIC with elevated D-dimer, prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen, and thrombocytopenia.
Random serum cortisol is critically low at 1.2 mcg/dL despite severe physiologic stress, and CT of the abdomen shows bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.
explanation: Fulminant meningococcemia triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation, which causes hemorrhagic infarction of the adrenal glands bilaterally. The resulting acute adrenal insufficiency compounds the septic shock, creating a rapidly fatal positive feedback loop without emergent intervention.
keyFact: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal hemorrhagic necrosis most commonly caused by Neisseria meningitidis septicemia. The hallmark is purpura fulminans with DIC leading to acute adrenal crisis. Treatment is immediate IV corticosteroids and antibiotics.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningococcemia Without Adrenal Involvement
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningococcemia can cause purpura and DIC, but the critically low cortisol and bilateral adrenal hemorrhage specifically indicate Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes petechiae from isolated thrombocytopenia but does not cause fever, DIC, hemodynamic collapse, or adrenal hemorrhage.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HUS causes thrombocytopenia and purpura but presents with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and renal failure, not fulminant DIC with adrenal destruction.

clues: A 34-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal swelling, dull right upper quadrant pain, and lower extremity edema over the past three weeks.
She has a history of a myeloproliferative disorder diagnosed two years ago and takes oral contraceptive pills. She does not drink alcohol.
The liver is enlarged and tender, extending 6 cm below the costal margin. Ascitic fluid analysis shows a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 2.1 and a high total protein of 3.8 g/dL.
Doppler ultrasound of the abdomen shows absent flow in two of three hepatic veins with intraluminal echogenic material. The portal vein is patent.
Hepatic venography confirms occlusion of the right and middle hepatic veins with a characteristic spider-web pattern of collateral vessels.
explanation: Thrombosis of the hepatic veins impairs blood outflow from the liver, causing sinusoidal congestion, hepatocellular necrosis, and portal hypertension. The high protein ascites results from direct transudation of protein-rich fluid from the congested hepatic sinusoids.
keyFact: Budd-Chiari presents with the triad of hepatomegaly, ascites, and abdominal pain. High-protein ascites with a high SAAG (>1.1) is characteristic. Most common causes are myeloproliferative disorders, hypercoagulable states, and oral contraceptives.

wrongAnswers.name: Cirrhosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cirrhotic ascites has a high SAAG but low total protein (<2.5 g/dL), unlike the high-protein ascites seen here with acute hepatomegaly.

wrongAnswers.name: Portal Vein Thrombosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Portal vein thrombosis causes portal hypertension but the Doppler showed a patent portal vein; the occlusion here is in the hepatic veins.

wrongAnswers.name: Right Heart Failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Right heart failure causes hepatic congestion and high-protein ascites, but would show elevated JVP, peripheral edema, and cardiac abnormalities rather than isolated hepatic vein thrombosis.

clues: A 72-year-old man in the surgical ICU develops progressive abdominal distension and absent bowel sounds on postoperative day 3 after hip replacement surgery.
He has been receiving IV opioids for pain management and has not passed stool or flatus since surgery. He has a history of chronic kidney disease.
The abdomen is tympanitic and diffusely distended but soft, with no peritoneal signs. No hernias are palpable. Rectal exam reveals an empty vault.
Abdominal X-ray shows massive dilation of the cecum to 11 cm and ascending colon with gas extending to the splenic flexure but no gas in the rectum. No transition point is identified.
Water-soluble contrast enema flows freely to the splenic flexure without encountering a mechanical obstruction, confirming the absence of a physical blockage.
explanation: Disruption of the autonomic nervous system balance in the colon, often in hospitalized patients after surgery or critical illness, causes functional colonic dilation without mechanical obstruction. Medications like opioids and electrolyte imbalances exacerbate the dysmotility.
keyFact: Ogilvie syndrome is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction with cecal dilation >10-12 cm posing a risk of perforation. First-line treatment is neostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor), which restores parasympathetic tone. Correct electrolytes and discontinue offending medications.

wrongAnswers.name: Sigmoid Volvulus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sigmoid volvulus shows a characteristic bent inner tube or coffee bean sign on X-ray with a transition point at the sigmoid, not diffuse colonic dilation without a transition point.

wrongAnswers.name: Mechanical Large Bowel Obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mechanical obstruction would show a transition point on imaging, and contrast enema would not pass freely through the entire colon.

wrongAnswers.name: Toxic Megacolon
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Toxic megacolon presents with systemic toxicity, fever, and signs of colitis, typically in the setting of inflammatory bowel disease or C. difficile infection.

clues: A 4-week-old firstborn male infant is brought in for forceful vomiting after every feeding that has worsened over the past five days.
The vomiting is non-bilious and has become increasingly projectile. The infant appears hungry immediately after vomiting and eagerly tries to feed again.
The infant appears dehydrated with sunken fontanelles and decreased skin turgor. A firm, mobile, olive-sized mass is palpated in the right upper quadrant during a feeding.
Serum electrolytes reveal sodium of 132, potassium of 2.9, chloride of 88, and bicarbonate of 34 mEq/L. Venous blood gas shows pH of 7.52.
Abdominal ultrasound shows pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and pyloric channel length of 20 mm with no passage of gastric contents into the duodenum.
explanation: Hypertrophy of the pyloric circular muscle layer progressively obstructs gastric outflow. Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid through vomiting produces hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis as the kidneys compensate by retaining hydrogen ions and excreting potassium.
keyFact: Pyloric stenosis classically presents at 2-6 weeks in firstborn males with non-bilious projectile vomiting and a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Ultrasound criteria: muscle thickness >3 mm, channel length >15 mm. Treatment is Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.

wrongAnswers.name: Malrotation with Midgut Volvulus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Midgut volvulus causes bilious vomiting due to obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater, unlike the non-bilious vomiting seen in pyloric stenosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastroesophageal Reflux
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GER causes effortless regurgitation, not projectile vomiting, and does not produce a palpable pyloric mass or metabolic alkalosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Milk Protein Allergy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Milk protein allergy can cause vomiting but typically presents with bloody stools, and does not cause a palpable olive mass or metabolic alkalosis.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with chronic watery diarrhea, bloating, and a 15-pound unintentional weight loss over four months.
He recently returned from a two-year stint working in Southeast Asia. His symptoms began insidiously during his last few months abroad.
He appears thin and pale. Glossitis is noted with a smooth, beefy red tongue. Peripheral blood smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils and macrocytic red cells.
Serum folate is critically low. Vitamin B12 is also low. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies are negative. D-xylose absorption test is abnormal.
Small bowel biopsy shows villous blunting with crypt hyperplasia and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate affecting the jejunum and ileum diffusely.
explanation: Chronic enteric infection in tropical regions causes inflammation and villous atrophy throughout the small bowel, impairing absorption of nutrients including folate and B12. Unlike celiac disease, tropical sprue responds to antibiotics and folate supplementation.
keyFact: Tropical sprue affects the entire small bowel (jejunum and ileum), causing both folate and B12 deficiency. Celiac disease primarily affects the proximal small bowel and is serologically positive. Tropical sprue responds to tetracycline and folic acid.

wrongAnswers.name: Celiac Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Celiac disease causes similar villous atrophy but is identified by positive anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, which are negative here, and primarily affects the proximal bowel.

wrongAnswers.name: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SIBO can cause malabsorption and B12 deficiency but typically shows an abnormal breath test rather than diffuse villous atrophy on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Whipple Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Whipple disease causes malabsorption with PAS-positive macrophages on biopsy and joint symptoms, not the diffuse villous blunting with mixed infiltrate seen here.

clues: A 78-year-old nursing home resident with a history of chronic constipation presents with acute abdominal pain, distension, and obstipation over the past 18 hours.
He has a history of Parkinson disease and takes multiple anticholinergic medications. He has had two prior episodes of similar symptoms that resolved spontaneously.
The abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic. Bowel sounds are high-pitched. The rectum is empty on digital examination.
Abdominal X-ray shows a massively dilated loop of colon extending from the pelvis toward the right upper quadrant with loss of haustra, resembling a bent inner tube.
Contrast enema shows a smooth, tapered narrowing at the rectosigmoid junction with a bird's beak appearance, and the contrast column does not advance past this point.
explanation: The redundant sigmoid colon twists on its mesentery, creating a closed-loop obstruction. The torsion compromises venous return and then arterial supply, leading to ischemia, necrosis, and perforation if not relieved. Chronic constipation and a redundant sigmoid are key risk factors.
keyFact: Sigmoid volvulus is the most common type of colonic volvulus. The coffee bean sign on X-ray and bird's beak sign on contrast enema are classic. Initial treatment is endoscopic detorsion with a rectal tube; recurrence is common (>50%), so elective sigmoid resection is recommended.

wrongAnswers.name: Cecal Volvulus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cecal volvulus shows a dilated cecum displaced to the left upper quadrant, not the bent inner tube arising from the pelvis seen in sigmoid volvulus.

wrongAnswers.name: Ogilvie Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ogilvie syndrome causes diffuse colonic dilation without a transition point, whereas the bird's beak sign here indicates a mechanical twist at the rectosigmoid.

wrongAnswers.name: Obstructing Colon Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Colon cancer would show an irregular apple-core lesion on contrast enema, not the smooth tapered bird's beak narrowing of a volvulus.

clues: A 9-month-old boy is brought in for his third episode of bacterial pneumonia. He was previously hospitalized for otitis media at 6 months.
He was healthy for the first five months of life. No maternal history of immunodeficiency is known. He has a maternal uncle who died of pneumonia as a toddler.
Tonsils are absent on oropharyngeal examination. No lymph nodes are palpable in the cervical, axillary, or inguinal regions despite active infection.
Quantitative immunoglobulins show IgG of 45 mg/dL, IgA undetectable, and IgM of 12 mg/dL. All classes are profoundly decreased. T cell counts and function are normal.
