Flow cytometry of peripheral blood reveals fewer than 1% CD19+ and CD20+ B cells. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in the BTK gene on the X chromosome.
explanation: Mutations in Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) arrest B cell development at the pre-B cell stage in the bone marrow, preventing maturation into circulating B cells. Without B cells, the patient cannot produce immunoglobulins, leading to recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections after maternal antibody wanes around 6 months.
keyFact: Bruton agammaglobulinemia is X-linked, affecting males. Infections begin after 6 months when maternal IgG wanes. Absent B cells and all immunoglobulin classes are reduced. T cells are normal. Treatment is lifelong IV immunoglobulin replacement.

wrongAnswers.name: Common Variable Immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID also causes hypogammaglobulinemia but presents later in life (teens to 30s), has normal or low B cell numbers (not absent), and is not X-linked.

wrongAnswers.name: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCID causes both T and B cell dysfunction with failure to thrive and opportunistic infections in early infancy, but T cells are normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Transient Hypogammaglobulinemia of Infancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Transient hypogammaglobulinemia causes mildly low IgG that self-resolves, with normal B cell counts and no BTK mutation.

clues: A 2-year-old boy is brought in for recurrent skin and respiratory infections that have required multiple courses of antibiotics since infancy.
His parents report that he has always been very fair-skinned despite both parents having medium-dark complexions. They also note his eyes seem to reflect light unusually.
Partial oculocutaneous albinism is noted with silvery-gray hair and light irides that transilluminate. Hepatosplenomegaly is present on abdominal examination.
Peripheral blood smear shows giant cytoplasmic granules within neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes. Neutrophil function testing shows impaired chemotaxis and delayed bacterial killing.
Genetic testing reveals a homozygous mutation in the LYST (CHS1) gene, which encodes a lysosomal trafficking regulator protein.
explanation: Mutations in the LYST gene impair lysosomal trafficking, causing fusion of granules into giant, dysfunctional aggregates. Defective neutrophil degranulation leads to recurrent pyogenic infections, while abnormal melanin distribution within melanosomes causes partial albinism.
keyFact: Chediak-Higashi is autosomal recessive with the triad of recurrent pyogenic infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism, and giant granules in leukocytes. An accelerated lymphoproliferative phase (hemophagocytic syndrome) is often fatal without bone marrow transplant.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Granulomatous Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CGD causes recurrent infections from defective NADPH oxidase but does not produce albinism or giant granules on peripheral smear.

wrongAnswers.name: Oculocutaneous Albinism (Isolated)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Isolated OCA causes albinism but does not impair immune function, cause giant granules, or lead to hepatosplenomegaly.

wrongAnswers.name: Hermansky-Pudlak Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hermansky-Pudlak causes albinism with a bleeding diathesis from platelet storage pool deficiency, but does not produce giant granules in leukocytes or recurrent infections.

clues: A 5-year-old boy is brought in for a large abscess on his right arm that appeared without preceding trauma. He has had multiple similar skin abscesses since infancy.
He has a history of recurrent pneumonias with formation of lung cavities. His primary teeth have not fallen out despite eruption of permanent teeth behind them.

He has a broad nose, prominent forehead, and deep-set eyes. Multiple healed scars from prior abscesses are visible. The current abscess is fluctuant but notably non-tender and lacks surrounding erythema.
Serum IgE is markedly elevated at 4,800 IU/mL. Eosinophil count is 1,200/mcL. Cultures from the abscess grow Staphylococcus aureus.
Genetic testing identifies a dominant-negative mutation in STAT3, and skeletal survey shows pathologic fractures with decreased bone density.
explanation: STAT3 mutations impair Th17 cell differentiation, reducing IL-17 production needed for neutrophil recruitment to sites of infection. This explains the 'cold' abscesses that lack the expected warmth and tenderness. Defective STAT3 signaling also affects bone remodeling, dental root resorption, and connective tissue development.
keyFact: Job syndrome features the triad of recurrent 'cold' staphylococcal abscesses (non-inflamed), extremely elevated IgE (>2000 IU/mL), and eczema. Additional features include retained primary teeth, pathologic fractures, and characteristic facies. STAT3 loss-of-function mutation is the cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Atopic Dermatitis (Severe)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Severe atopic dermatitis elevates IgE and causes skin infections but does not produce cold abscesses, retained primary teeth, or skeletal abnormalities.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Granulomatous Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CGD causes recurrent abscesses with catalase-positive organisms but has normal IgE, warm inflammatory abscesses, and no skeletal or dental anomalies.

wrongAnswers.name: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: WAS causes eczema and elevated IgE but classically presents with thrombocytopenia and small platelets, not cold abscesses or retained teeth.

clues: A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents after prolonged bleeding from a small cut on his lip that has not stopped after two hours.
He has had recurrent nosebleeds lasting over 30 minutes since infancy and excessive bruising with minor trauma throughout early childhood.
Platelet count is 68,000/uL. Peripheral blood smear shows abnormally large platelets approaching the size of red blood cells.
Bleeding time is markedly prolonged. Platelet aggregation studies show absent response to ristocetin that does not correct with addition of normal plasma.
Flow cytometry of platelets reveals absent glycoprotein Ib/IX/V complex on the platelet surface membrane.
explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from a deficiency or dysfunction of the glycoprotein Ib/IX/V complex, which is the receptor for von Willebrand factor on the platelet surface. Without this receptor, platelets cannot adhere to exposed subendothelial collagen at sites of vascular injury, causing mucocutaneous bleeding.
keyFact: Bernard-Soulier syndrome shows absent ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation that does NOT correct with normal plasma (unlike von Willebrand disease, which does correct). The hallmark peripheral smear finding is giant platelets with mild thrombocytopenia.

wrongAnswers.name: Von Willebrand Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: vWD also shows decreased ristocetin aggregation, but it corrects with addition of normal plasma (which supplies vWF). Platelet size is normal in vWD.

wrongAnswers.name: Glanzmann Thrombasthenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Glanzmann shows absent aggregation to ADP, collagen, and epinephrine, but normal ristocetin response. Platelet count and size are normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes thrombocytopenia with normal-sized or slightly large platelets, but platelet aggregation studies and ristocetin response are normal.

clues: A 62-year-old man in the ICU develops oozing from IV sites, blood in his urine, and spreading bruises across his trunk over several hours.
He was admitted two days ago for sepsis secondary to a perforated bowel and has been on broad-spectrum antibiotics and vasopressors.
Petechiae cover the extremities. Blood oozes from venipuncture sites and the surgical wound. Fingers appear dusky with mottled discoloration.
Platelet count has dropped from 180,000 to 32,000/uL. PT and aPTT are both prolonged. Fibrinogen is 65 mg/dL. D-dimer is markedly elevated.
Peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes and fragmented red blood cells consistent with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia from fibrin strand deposition.
explanation: Systemic activation of the coagulation cascade leads to widespread microvascular fibrin deposition, consuming platelets and clotting factors. Simultaneous clot formation and fibrinolysis produce both thrombotic organ damage and hemorrhagic bleeding, with fibrin strands shearing red blood cells in small vessels.
keyFact: DIC is distinguished by the combination of thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer, and schistocytes on smear. It is always secondary to an underlying trigger (sepsis, malignancy, obstetric complications, trauma).

wrongAnswers.name: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP causes thrombocytopenia and schistocytes but PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen are typically normal because coagulation factors are not consumed.

wrongAnswers.name: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HIT causes thrombocytopenia with thrombosis but does not produce prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, or diffuse bleeding from multiple sites.

wrongAnswers.name: Liver Failure Coagulopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hepatic failure prolongs PT/aPTT and reduces fibrinogen, but platelet count drops less acutely, D-dimer is less dramatically elevated, and schistocytes are absent.

clues: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with dark-colored urine, fatigue, and yellowing of his eyes that started yesterday.
His mother reports he was prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole three days ago for a urinary tract infection. He had no prior history of anemia.
Scleral icterus is present. Conjunctivae are pale. Spleen tip is palpable. Hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL, down from 12.1 two months ago. Reticulocyte count is elevated.
Peripheral blood smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies on supravital staining. Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Haptoglobin is undetectable.
Quantitative G6PD enzyme assay performed eight weeks after the acute episode reveals activity at 12% of normal, confirming the enzyme deficiency.
explanation: G6PD is required to generate NADPH, which maintains glutathione in its reduced form to protect red blood cells from oxidative damage. Exposure to oxidant stressors causes denatured hemoglobin to precipitate as Heinz bodies, leading to splenic removal of damaged membrane (bite cells) and acute intravascular hemolysis.
keyFact: G6PD enzyme levels can be falsely normal during an acute hemolytic episode because older deficient cells have been destroyed and reticulocytes have higher enzyme activity. Testing should be repeated 8-12 weeks after the episode for accurate diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIHA causes hemolysis with spherocytes and a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, not bite cells and Heinz bodies with a negative DAT.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary Spherocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hereditary spherocytosis produces chronic hemolysis with spherocytes on smear and a positive osmotic fragility test, not episodic hemolysis triggered by medications.

wrongAnswers.name: Sickle Cell Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sickle cell causes vaso-occlusive crises with sickle-shaped cells on smear, not bite cells and Heinz bodies precipitated by drug exposure.

clues: A 3-year-old girl is brought in for recurrent, heavy nosebleeds and easy bruising that her parents have noticed since she was an infant.
Her parents are first cousins. She required a blood transfusion at 18 months after prolonged bleeding following a minor fall in which she cut her tongue.
Platelet count is 245,000/uL with normal platelet morphology and size on peripheral smear. Bleeding time is markedly prolonged at 22 minutes.
Platelet aggregation studies show absent response to ADP, collagen, epinephrine, and thrombin, but a normal response to ristocetin.
Flow cytometry demonstrates absent glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (integrin alphaIIb-beta3) on the platelet surface.
explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, the fibrinogen receptor on platelets that mediates platelet-to-platelet aggregation. Platelets can still adhere to the vessel wall via vWF-GPIb interaction but cannot crosslink with each other through fibrinogen bridges.
keyFact: Glanzmann thrombasthenia shows absent aggregation to all agonists (ADP, collagen, epinephrine, thrombin) but NORMAL ristocetin-induced aggregation, because GPIb (adhesion receptor) is intact. This is the opposite pattern of Bernard-Soulier syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Bernard-Soulier Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bernard-Soulier shows absent ristocetin aggregation with giant platelets and thrombocytopenia, whereas this case has normal ristocetin response, normal platelet count, and normal platelet size.

wrongAnswers.name: Von Willebrand Disease Type 1
wrongAnswers.whyNot: vWD type 1 shows decreased ristocetin response and mildly prolonged aPTT, but aggregation to ADP, collagen, and epinephrine is normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Platelet Storage Pool Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Storage pool defects cause reduced secondary aggregation waves but do not produce complete absence of aggregation to multiple agonists.

clues: A 2-year-old boy is brought in with a growing bump on the side of his head and a persistent scaly rash on his scalp that has not responded to antifungal shampoo.
His parents report excessive thirst and frequent wet diapers over the past month. He has also had recurrent ear drainage despite multiple antibiotic courses.
A 3-cm soft, non-tender mass is palpable over the right parietal bone. Skull X-ray reveals a well-defined, punched-out lytic lesion with no sclerotic border.
Urine specific gravity is 1.002 despite overnight fluid restriction. Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L. Serum osmolality is elevated with inappropriately dilute urine.
Biopsy of the skull lesion shows large cells with folded, kidney-shaped nuclei that stain positive for CD1a and S-100, with rod-shaped Birbeck granules on electron microscopy.
explanation: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involves clonal proliferation of pathologic Langerhans-type cells that infiltrate bone, skin, and other organs. Infiltration of the posterior pituitary stalk causes central diabetes insipidus, while bony involvement produces characteristic lytic skull lesions.
keyFact: Birbeck granules (tennis racket-shaped on EM) and CD1a positivity are pathognomonic for Langerhans cell histiocytosis. The classic triad of lytic bone lesions, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos (Hand-Schuller-Christian disease) represents multifocal disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Ewing Sarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ewing sarcoma causes lytic bone lesions with an onion-skin periosteal reaction, typically in the diaphysis of long bones, not punched-out skull lesions with CD1a-positive cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteomyelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteomyelitis presents with fever, tenderness, and surrounding soft tissue inflammation, and imaging shows periosteal elevation rather than clean punched-out lesions without sclerosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Neuroblastoma with Skull Metastases
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Neuroblastoma metastases to the skull cause irregular permeative destruction and periorbital ecchymoses, and biopsy shows small round blue cells rather than CD1a-positive histiocytes.

clues: A 68-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue, difficulty walking due to unsteadiness, and tingling in her hands and feet over the past six months.
She has a history of autoimmune thyroid disease and follows a diet with adequate meat and dairy intake. She reports a sore, smooth tongue.
Conjunctivae are pale with a slight lemon-yellow tint to the skin. Vibration and proprioception are diminished in both feet. Romberg sign is positive.
Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL with MCV 118 fL. Peripheral smear shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes. LDH and indirect bilirubin are elevated.
Serum vitamin B12 is 78 pg/mL. Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are both markedly elevated. Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are positive.
explanation: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells eliminates intrinsic factor production, preventing B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells, producing megaloblastic changes in the bone marrow, while demyelination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts causes subacute combined degeneration.
keyFact: Hypersegmented neutrophils (>=5 lobes) on peripheral smear are the earliest and most specific finding of megaloblastic anemia. Both B12 and folate deficiency elevate homocysteine, but only B12 deficiency elevates methylmalonic acid.

wrongAnswers.name: Folate Deficiency Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Folate deficiency produces identical hematologic findings but does not cause neurologic symptoms (no subacute combined degeneration) and methylmalonic acid remains normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Myelodysplastic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDS can cause macrocytic anemia with dysplastic changes, but hypersegmented neutrophils, elevated methylmalonic acid, and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies point to B12 deficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism can cause mild macrocytic anemia, but MCV rarely exceeds 105, and it does not produce hypersegmented neutrophils, elevated MMA, or neurologic findings of dorsal column dysfunction.

clues: A 2-year-old boy is brought in by his parents after they noticed a firm mass in his abdomen while bathing him. He has been increasingly irritable and not eating well.
His parents report intermittent episodes of watery diarrhea over the past several weeks and dark circles around both of his eyes that appeared without any trauma.
A firm, irregular, non-tender mass crosses the midline in the upper abdomen. Bilateral periorbital ecchymoses are present. Blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg.
Urine catecholamine metabolites (vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid) are markedly elevated. CT shows a suprarenal calcified mass encasing the aorta and crossing the midline.
Bone marrow biopsy shows clusters of small round blue cells forming Homer-Wright pseudorosettes. MYCN gene amplification is detected on fluorescence in situ hybridization.
explanation: Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest cells, most commonly in the adrenal medulla. The tumor secretes catecholamines and their metabolites, causing hypertension and diarrhea, while metastatic spread to the periorbital bones produces characteristic raccoon eyes.
keyFact: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood. MYCN amplification is the most important adverse prognostic marker. Unlike Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma crosses the midline, is irregular, and encases (rather than displaces) blood vessels.

wrongAnswers.name: Wilms Tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wilms tumor is a smooth, well-encapsulated renal mass that does not cross the midline, does not calcify frequently, and does not elevate urine catecholamine metabolites.

wrongAnswers.name: Pheochromocytoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pheochromocytoma also elevates catecholamines but occurs in adults, presents with episodic hypertension and palpitations, and does not show Homer-Wright rosettes or midline-crossing abdominal mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatoblastoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hepatoblastoma arises from the liver with elevated alpha-fetoprotein, does not produce catecholamines, and does not show periorbital ecchymoses or pseudorosettes on biopsy.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging, painless neck mass over the past three weeks along with progressive fatigue and unintentional weight loss.
He reports drenching night sweats requiring sheet changes and intermittent fevers over the past month. He has no history of infection or autoimmune disease.
Multiple firm, rubbery, non-tender lymph nodes are palpable in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions bilaterally. The spleen is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin.
CT shows widespread lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm with an 8-cm retroperitoneal mass. LDH is markedly elevated at 650 U/L. PET scan shows intense FDG uptake in all nodal sites.
Excisional lymph node biopsy shows effacement of nodal architecture by large atypical lymphoid cells positive for CD20 and CD19, with a high Ki-67 proliferative index of 85%.
explanation: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, the most common aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, arises from clonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes that efface normal lymph node architecture. Rapid proliferation leads to bulky disease, elevated LDH from high cell turnover, and constitutional B symptoms.
keyFact: Non-Hodgkin lymphomas spread noncontiguously (unlike Hodgkin lymphoma, which spreads contiguously). DLBCL is the most common subtype in adults. CD20 positivity makes it targetable with rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) in combination with CHOP chemotherapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Hodgkin Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hodgkin lymphoma typically presents in younger patients with contiguous nodal spread, and biopsy shows Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15/CD30 positive) in a reactive background, not sheets of CD20-positive large cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CLL presents with lymphocytosis of small mature lymphocytes, smudge cells on smear, and indolent course, not rapidly enlarging masses with large atypical cells and high Ki-67.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Lymphadenopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive lymph nodes preserve normal architecture, are often tender, and do not show monoclonal B-cell populations, effacement, or markedly elevated LDH.

clues: An 18-month-old girl is brought in by her mother who noticed something unusual about the appearance of her daughter's left eye in photographs taken over the past month.
The child's maternal uncle had an eye removed as an infant. The mother recalls being told it was due to a tumor but does not know the specific diagnosis.
The left pupil shows a whitish reflex when illuminated. The right pupil has a normal red reflex. The left eye appears to have a slight inward deviation.
Fundoscopic examination under anesthesia reveals a white-yellow endophytic mass arising from the retina in the left eye. A smaller lesion is also found in the right eye.
MRI of the orbits shows an enhancing intraocular mass with foci of calcification. Genetic testing reveals a germline mutation in the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13q14.
explanation: Retinoblastoma arises from loss of both alleles of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene, which normally inhibits the cell cycle by restraining the G1 to S phase transition. Germline mutations follow the two-hit hypothesis: one inherited inactivated allele requires only a single somatic hit in the other, leading to bilateral and multifocal disease.
keyFact: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) is the most common presenting sign. Germline RB1 mutations cause bilateral disease (heritable form, ~40% of cases) and carry increased risk of secondary malignancies, especially osteosarcoma. The RB protein is a key regulator of the G1/S cell cycle checkpoint.

wrongAnswers.name: Congenital Cataract
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Congenital cataracts produce leukocoria but show lens opacification on exam, not a retinal mass. They are not associated with calcification or RB1 mutations.

wrongAnswers.name: Persistent Fetal Vasculature
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Persistent fetal vasculature causes unilateral leukocoria with a retrolental membrane, but it is non-hereditary, does not form a calcified retinal mass, and is always unilateral.

wrongAnswers.name: Coats Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Coats disease causes leukocoria from retinal telangiectasia and exudative detachment, but it is unilateral, occurs in older boys, and does not show a solid calcified mass or RB1 mutations.

clues: A 9-month-old boy of Mediterranean descent is brought in for increasing pallor, poor feeding, and irritability that have worsened progressively since he was about six months old.
He was born full-term and appeared healthy at birth. His growth has slowed, and his parents note that his abdomen seems to be getting bigger over the past two months.
The infant is pale and listless. Hepatosplenomegaly is prominent. Frontal bossing and maxillary prominence give the face a chipmunk-like appearance.

Hemoglobin is 4.2 g/dL with MCV 62 fL. Peripheral smear shows severe microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, nucleated red blood cells, and marked anisopoikilocytosis. Iron studies are normal.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows hemoglobin F at 90%, hemoglobin A2 at 8%, and absent hemoglobin A, confirming complete lack of beta-globin chain production.
explanation: Beta thalassemia major results from homozygous mutations in the beta-globin gene, eliminating beta-chain production. Without beta chains, excess unpaired alpha chains precipitate in erythroid precursors, causing massive ineffective erythropoiesis. Compensatory marrow expansion produces skeletal deformities, while extramedullary hematopoiesis causes hepatosplenomegaly.
keyFact: Beta thalassemia major presents after 6 months of age when fetal hemoglobin (alpha2-gamma2) should transition to adult hemoglobin A (alpha2-beta2). Hemoglobin electrophoresis showing absent HbA with elevated HbF is diagnostic. Crew-cut appearance on skull X-ray reflects marrow expansion.

wrongAnswers.name: Iron Deficiency Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia but presents with low ferritin and high TIBC, not normal iron studies and absent hemoglobin A on electrophoresis.

wrongAnswers.name: Sickle Cell Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sickle cell also presents after 6 months but shows sickle cells on smear and hemoglobin S on electrophoresis, not absent HbA with 90% HbF.

wrongAnswers.name: Alpha Thalassemia (Hemoglobin H Disease)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HbH disease shows Heinz bodies and hemoglobin H (beta-4 tetramers) on electrophoresis, not absent HbA with elevated HbF from failed beta-chain synthesis.

clues: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive pain deep in his left groin and thigh that has worsened over the past three months, especially with weight-bearing.
He has systemic lupus erythematosus and has been on high-dose prednisone for the past year. He also reports moderate alcohol consumption of four to five drinks daily.
Range of motion at the left hip is restricted, particularly internal rotation and abduction. There is an antalgic gait favoring the left side. No warmth or effusion is noted.
Plain radiographs of the left hip show a crescent-shaped subchondral lucency (crescent sign) at the superior aspect of the femoral head with subtle flattening of the articular surface.
MRI reveals a serpiginous line of low signal intensity in the femoral head on T1 sequences with a double-line sign on T2 (low-signal outer line with high-signal inner line), confirming the diagnosis.
explanation: Disruption of blood supply to the femoral head causes ischemic death of bone and marrow, most commonly from chronic corticosteroid use or alcohol. The subchondral bone weakens and collapses, producing the crescent sign on X-ray, while the MRI double-line sign represents the interface between necrotic and viable bone.
keyFact: The double-line sign on T2-weighted MRI is pathognomonic for avascular necrosis. The most common site is the femoral head. Major risk factors include corticosteroid use, alcohol abuse, sickle cell disease, and lupus. MRI detects disease before X-ray changes appear.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteoarthritis of the Hip
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteoarthritis shows joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis, not a crescent sign or double-line sign on MRI suggesting bone infarction.

wrongAnswers.name: Femoral Neck Stress Fracture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stress fractures show a linear fracture line on MRI with surrounding edema, not the serpiginous low-signal band with a double-line sign seen in avascular necrosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Transient Osteoporosis of the Hip
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Transient osteoporosis shows diffuse bone marrow edema on MRI without the focal serpiginous necrotic boundary or crescent sign that characterize avascular necrosis.

clues: A 52-year-old woman presents with difficulty swallowing solid foods, heartburn, and color changes in her fingers turning white then blue in cold weather over the past two years.
She has noticed small red spots appearing on her face and hands over the past year. Her fingers feel stiff and appear puffy, making it hard to fully open her hands.
Skin thickening is limited to the fingers and face. Small telangiectasias are visible on the cheeks, lips, and palms. Hard, white subcutaneous nodules are palpable on the finger pads.
Barium swallow shows decreased peristalsis in the lower two-thirds of the esophagus with a dilated, atonic distal segment. ANA is positive in a centromere pattern.
Anti-centromere antibodies are detected at high titer. Echocardiogram shows estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 55 mmHg, consistent with pulmonary hypertension.
explanation: CREST syndrome is the limited cutaneous form of systemic sclerosis, characterized by calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias. Fibrosis and vascular damage are confined primarily to distal extremities and the GI tract, with pulmonary arterial hypertension as the leading cause of disease-related mortality.
keyFact: Anti-centromere antibodies are highly specific for limited systemic sclerosis (CREST). The major life-threatening complication is pulmonary arterial hypertension. This contrasts with diffuse scleroderma, which is associated with anti-Scl-70 antibodies and interstitial lung disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Diffuse Systemic Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diffuse scleroderma causes widespread skin thickening extending proximal to the elbows and knees, is associated with anti-Scl-70 (not anti-centromere), and primarily causes interstitial lung disease rather than isolated pulmonary hypertension.

wrongAnswers.name: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCTD has overlapping features of SLE, polymyositis, and scleroderma with anti-U1 RNP antibodies, not the isolated anti-centromere pattern and classic pentad of CREST seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Raynaud Phenomenon
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary Raynaud is isolated vasospasm without skin thickening, esophageal dysmotility, calcinosis, or positive autoantibodies.

clues: A 72-year-old postmenopausal woman presents after tripping on a rug and falling on her outstretched hand, resulting in immediate pain and swelling of her wrist.
She went through menopause at age 48, has a BMI of 19, smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily, and takes no calcium or vitamin D supplementation.
X-ray reveals a displaced distal radius fracture (Colles fracture). Incidentally, the bones appear diffusely radiolucent with thinned cortices throughout. No lytic or blastic lesions are seen.
Serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are all within normal limits. CBC and serum protein electrophoresis are also normal.
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan reveals a T-score of -3.1 at the lumbar spine and -2.8 at the femoral neck.
explanation: Estrogen deficiency after menopause accelerates osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, leading to decreased bone mineral density and microarchitectural deterioration. The resulting fragile bone is susceptible to low-energy fractures, particularly of the distal radius, vertebrae, and proximal femur.
keyFact: Osteoporosis is defined by a DEXA T-score of -2.5 or below. Unlike osteomalacia, laboratory values (calcium, phosphorus, ALP, vitamin D) are normal because the bone that is present is normally mineralized; there is simply less of it.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteomalacia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteomalacia causes undermineralized bone with low calcium or phosphorus, elevated ALP, low vitamin D, and Looser zones on imaging, not the normal labs seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Myeloma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myeloma can cause diffuse osteopenia and fractures, but it presents with elevated protein on SPEP, anemia, and lytic lesions, all of which are absent here.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyperparathyroidism causes bone loss but presents with elevated calcium and PTH, subperiosteal resorption, and brown tumors, not the normal labs found in this case.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive tightening of the skin on her arms, chest, and face over the past six months, along with increasing shortness of breath on exertion.
She has noticed her fingers turning white in cold weather for the past two years. She reports worsening difficulty bending her elbows and knees due to skin stiffness.
Skin is diffusely thickened and taut over the forearms, upper arms, trunk, and face with loss of wrinkles. Finger flexion contractures and digital pitting scars are present bilaterally.

Pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern with reduced FVC and markedly reduced DLCO. High-resolution CT of the chest reveals bilateral ground-glass opacities and reticular changes at the lung bases.
Anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibodies are positive at high titer. Skin biopsy shows dense dermal collagen deposition replacing subcutaneous fat with perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates.
explanation: Diffuse systemic sclerosis involves widespread fibroblast activation and excessive collagen deposition in the skin and internal organs, driven by vascular damage and immune dysregulation. Progressive interstitial lung disease from pulmonary fibrosis and scleroderma renal crisis are the major life-threatening complications.
keyFact: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are specific for diffuse systemic sclerosis and are associated with interstitial lung disease. This contrasts with limited scleroderma (CREST), which has anti-centromere antibodies and pulmonary arterial hypertension as the primary pulmonary complication.

wrongAnswers.name: CREST Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Limited scleroderma (CREST) confines skin thickening to distal extremities and face, is associated with anti-centromere (not anti-Scl-70) antibodies, and causes pulmonary hypertension rather than interstitial lung disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Eosinophilic Fasciitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eosinophilic fasciitis causes limb skin thickening with a peau d'orange appearance and peripheral eosinophilia, but spares the fingers and face and does not cause Raynaud phenomenon or anti-Scl-70 positivity.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatomyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatomyositis causes proximal muscle weakness with heliotrope rash and Gottron papules, not diffuse skin thickening with contractures and anti-Scl-70 antibodies.

clues: A 74-year-old woman presents with a new, severe headache over her right temple and pain in her jaw when chewing food that forces her to stop eating and rest.
She has had aching and stiffness in her shoulders and hips for the past three months, making it difficult to get out of bed in the morning.
The right temporal artery is tender, thickened, and nodular on palpation with a diminished pulse. Scalp tenderness is present over the temporal region.
ESR is 105 mm/hr and CRP is 8.4 mg/dL. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL with elevated platelet count. Liver function tests show an isolated elevated alkaline phosphatase.
Temporal artery biopsy shows transmural granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells, fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, and intimal hyperplasia with luminal narrowing.
explanation: Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium-sized arteries, particularly the branches of the external carotid artery. Inflammatory infiltrates destroy the internal elastic lamina and narrow the vessel lumen, causing ischemic symptoms including headache, jaw claudication, and potentially irreversible vision loss from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy.
keyFact: Jaw claudication is the most specific symptom of GCA. The most feared complication is irreversible vision loss from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. High-dose glucocorticoids must be started immediately upon clinical suspicion, before biopsy results, to prevent blindness.

wrongAnswers.name: Tension-Type Headache
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tension headache causes bilateral, band-like pressure without temporal artery abnormalities, jaw claudication, or markedly elevated inflammatory markers.

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PMR causes shoulder and hip girdle stiffness with elevated ESR but does not produce headache, jaw claudication, temporal artery tenderness, or granulomatous arteritis on biopsy. PMR coexists with GCA in ~50% of cases but is a distinct entity.

wrongAnswers.name: Takayasu Arteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis but typically affects young women, involves the aorta and its major branches, and presents with limb claudication and blood pressure discrepancies, not temporal headache and jaw claudication.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with a patch of hair loss on the top of her head that she first noticed while brushing her hair two weeks ago.
She has a personal history of Hashimoto thyroiditis and a family history of vitiligo. She reports significant emotional stress from a recent job loss.
A 4-cm round, completely smooth, well-demarcated patch of total hair loss is present on the vertex of the scalp. The exposed skin appears normal without scarring, scaling, or erythema.

At the margins of the patch, several short hairs are seen that taper to a narrow point at the scalp surface and widen toward the distal end (exclamation point hairs). A pull test at the border is positive.
Dermoscopy reveals yellow dots (empty follicular ostia with keratinous plugs), black dots (broken hairs at the surface), and exclamation mark hairs, confirming a non-scarring immune-mediated process.
explanation: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition in which CD8+ T lymphocytes attack the hair follicle bulb during the anagen (growth) phase, causing abrupt cessation of hair production. The follicular stem cells in the bulge region are spared, preserving the potential for hair regrowth.
keyFact: Exclamation point hairs (narrow base, wider distal end, 3-4 mm long) at the periphery of a patch are pathognomonic for alopecia areata. The condition is associated with other autoimmune diseases (thyroiditis, vitiligo, pernicious anemia). Unlike scarring alopecias, follicular ostia are preserved.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Capitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea capitis causes patches of hair loss with scaling, broken hair stubs, and sometimes kerion formation, and KOH prep shows fungal hyphae. The smooth, non-scaling patch without inflammation here is inconsistent.

wrongAnswers.name: Trichotillomania
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trichotillomania shows irregularly shaped patches with broken hairs of varying lengths and no exclamation point hairs. Biopsy shows traumatic follicular changes, not peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate.

wrongAnswers.name: Discoid Lupus Erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Discoid lupus causes scarring alopecia with follicular plugging, atrophy, and dyspigmentation, leading to permanent hair loss with destroyed follicular ostia, unlike the preserved follicles seen here.

clues: A 34-year-old man presents with multiple painless purple-red patches on his legs and face that have been slowly growing and spreading over the past two months.
He was recently found to be HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 85 cells/uL. He has not started antiretroviral therapy and reports progressive fatigue and unintentional weight loss.

Multiple violaceous, non-blanching, indurated papules and plaques are distributed on the lower extremities, trunk, and hard palate. Some lesions follow skin tension lines. Non-tender lymphedema of the left leg is present.
CT chest incidentally shows bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates with flame-shaped opacities and pleural effusions. Bronchoscopy reveals violaceous endobronchial lesions.
Skin biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation forming slit-like vascular channels with extravasated red blood cells. Immunohistochemistry is positive for HHV-8 (LANA-1) in the spindle cell nuclei.
explanation: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm driven by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) infection, which induces endothelial cell proliferation and angiogenesis. In the setting of HIV-associated immunosuppression, loss of immune control over HHV-8 allows unregulated viral oncogene expression and tumor development.
keyFact: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is necessary for all forms of Kaposi sarcoma. The AIDS-associated form occurs with CD4 counts typically below 200. The most important treatment is immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy, which can cause tumor regression without direct chemotherapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacillary Angiomatosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacillary angiomatosis also produces vascular papules in immunocompromised patients, but it is caused by Bartonella species, responds to antibiotics, and biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltration with bacterial clumps rather than HHV-8-positive spindle cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Angiosarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that can produce violaceous skin lesions, but it is not associated with HHV-8, occurs more commonly in elderly patients on the scalp, and biopsy shows atypical endothelial cells without the characteristic slit-like channels.

wrongAnswers.name: Pyogenic Granuloma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pyogenic granulomas are solitary, rapidly growing, friable red nodules that bleed easily, not multifocal violaceous plaques. They show lobular capillary proliferation without spindle cells or HHV-8.

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with persistent itchy skin patches on his trunk and buttocks that have been present for several years and have not responded to topical steroids or antifungals.
The patches have slowly progressed from flat discolorations to raised, thickened areas. Some areas have developed into firm nodules over the past several months.

Multiple well-demarcated, erythematous patches and plaques of varying sizes are distributed on the trunk, buttocks, and proximal extremities in a bathing-suit distribution. Some areas show fine wrinkling and poikiloderma.

Skin biopsy shows atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform (convoluted) nuclei infiltrating the epidermis, forming small collections within the epidermis (Pautrier microabscesses). The surrounding dermis shows a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate.
Immunohistochemistry confirms the atypical cells are CD4-positive, CD3-positive T lymphocytes. T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies demonstrate a monoclonal T-cell population.
explanation: Mycosis fungoides is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, arising from malignant CD4+ skin-homing T lymphocytes. It progresses slowly through patch, plaque, and tumor stages over years to decades. Epidermotropism, where malignant lymphocytes migrate into the epidermis, is the histologic hallmark.
keyFact: Pautrier microabscesses (collections of atypical lymphocytes within the epidermis) are pathognomonic for mycosis fungoides. The leukemic variant, Sezary syndrome, presents with erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and circulating atypical T cells (Sezary cells) with cerebriform nuclei in the blood.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriasis produces well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale and Munro microabscesses of neutrophils, not the lymphocytic epidermotropism and Pautrier microabscesses of atypical T cells seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atopic dermatitis causes itchy patches but involves spongiosis on biopsy with polyclonal lymphocytes, not the monoclonal cerebriform T cells and epidermotropism seen in mycosis fungoides.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Corporis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea corporis produces annular erythematous patches with central clearing and active scaly border. KOH prep shows fungal hyphae, and biopsy does not reveal atypical lymphocytic infiltration of the epidermis.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with progressively enlarging white patches on her hands, around her eyes, and near her mouth that she first noticed about four months ago.
She has a family history of type 1 diabetes and was recently diagnosed with autoimmune thyroid disease herself. She denies any prior skin injury, rash, or chemical exposure in the affected areas.

Well-demarcated, completely depigmented, chalk-white macules and patches are symmetrically distributed on the dorsal hands, periorbital region, and perioral area. The skin surface is otherwise normal with no scaling, atrophy, or scarring.

Wood lamp examination reveals bright blue-white fluorescence of the depigmented patches with sharply defined borders that are more apparent than under natural light. Several subclinical lesions not visible to the naked eye are also detected.

Skin biopsy from the edge of a lesion shows complete absence of melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis on Melan-A and HMB-45 immunostaining, with a sparse perivascular and perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate at the lesion margin.
explanation: Vitiligo is an autoimmune disorder in which CD8+ cytotoxic T cells selectively destroy melanocytes in the epidermis, resulting in complete depigmentation. The predilection for acral and periorificial sites may relate to the density of melanocytes and increased mechanical stress at these locations.
keyFact: Vitiligo is strongly associated with other autoimmune conditions (thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, Addison disease). Depigmented patches fluoresce bright blue-white under Wood lamp. Unlike post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, vitiligo causes complete melanocyte loss, not just reduced melanin production.

wrongAnswers.name: Pityriasis Alba
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pityriasis alba causes hypopigmented (not completely depigmented) patches with fine scaling, typically on the face in children, and melanocytes are present but have reduced melanin transfer.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Versicolor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea versicolor produces hypopigmented patches with fine scale and KOH-positive spaghetti-and-meatball appearance. Lesions are on the trunk, not acral or periorificial, and melanocytes are intact.

wrongAnswers.name: Piebaldism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Piebaldism is a congenital, stable depigmentation with a white forelock present from birth, caused by KIT gene mutations. It does not progress, is not autoimmune, and lacks the lymphocytic infiltrate seen in vitiligo.

clues: A newborn is evaluated in the NICU for difficulty feeding and episodes of noisy, high-pitched breathing that worsen during sleep.
Prenatal ultrasound had revealed an open lumbosacral spinal defect, and the infant was delivered via planned cesarean section at 37 weeks.
The infant has a large head circumference tracking above the 98th percentile, a tense anterior fontanelle, and downward deviation of both eyes.
Cranial ultrasound shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with apparent obstruction at the level of the posterior fossa.
MRI of the brain demonstrates elongation and caudal displacement of the cerebellar vermis, brainstem, and fourth ventricle through the foramen magnum.
explanation: In Chiari II malformation, the posterior fossa is abnormally small, causing the cerebellar vermis and brainstem to herniate downward through the foramen magnum. This is nearly always associated with open myelomeningocele. Obstruction of CSF flow leads to hydrocephalus, and brainstem compression produces cranial nerve dysfunction including stridor and feeding difficulty.
keyFact: Chiari II malformation is defined by caudal herniation of the cerebellar vermis and brainstem through the foramen magnum and is virtually always associated with myelomeningocele. Chiari I involves only tonsillar herniation and is usually not associated with myelomeningocele.

wrongAnswers.name: Dandy-Walker Malformation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dandy-Walker involves an enlarged posterior fossa with absent or hypoplastic cerebellar vermis and cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle, not downward herniation of posterior fossa contents.

wrongAnswers.name: Aqueductal Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aqueductal stenosis causes obstructive hydrocephalus but is not associated with myelomeningocele or cerebellar herniation through the foramen magnum.

wrongAnswers.name: Holoprosencephaly
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Holoprosencephaly involves failure of the forebrain to divide into hemispheres and presents with midline facial defects, not posterior fossa herniation or spinal defects.

clues: A 34-year-old man presents with worsening headache, fever, and swelling around his left eye that has progressed rapidly over two days.
He had been squeezing and manipulating a painful pustule on the left side of his nose approximately five days ago.
The left eye is proptotic with chemosis and restricted movement in all directions. A similar but milder process is now developing on the right side.
CT with contrast shows filling defects within an expanded left cavernous sinus. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus.
MR venography demonstrates absent flow signal in the left cavernous sinus with thrombus extending into the right cavernous sinus via the intercavernous sinuses.
explanation: Infection from the facial danger triangle drains via the valveless ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus, producing septic thrombosis. The cavernous sinus contains cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI along with the internal carotid artery. Bilateral involvement occurs because the two cavernous sinuses communicate through intercavernous sinuses.
keyFact: The facial danger triangle (nose and upper lip) drains via valveless veins to the cavernous sinus. Bilateral cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, VI) with proptosis after facial infection is classic for cavernous sinus thrombosis. S. aureus is the most common causative organism.

wrongAnswers.name: Orbital Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Orbital cellulitis causes unilateral proptosis and ophthalmoplegia but does not produce bilateral involvement or filling defects within the cavernous sinus.

wrongAnswers.name: Mucormycosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis can involve the cavernous sinus but typically occurs in diabetic ketoacidosis or immunocompromised patients, with necrotic black eschar on the palate or nasal mucosa.

wrongAnswers.name: Graves Ophthalmopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Graves disease causes bilateral proptosis and extraocular muscle enlargement but is not associated with fever, acute infection, or venous sinus thrombosis.

clues: A 52-year-old woman with a history of heavy alcohol use is brought in for confusion and difficulty speaking that developed over the past day.
She was hospitalized three days ago for severe hyponatremia of 108 mEq/L and received aggressive intravenous saline correction to 132 mEq/L within the first 24 hours.
She initially improved on day two but then acutely developed dysarthria, dysphagia, and progressive quadriparesis on day three.
Serum sodium is now 136 mEq/L. CT head is unremarkable. Pupillary reflexes and vertical eye movements are preserved despite inability to move the extremities.
MRI of the brain shows a symmetric, well-demarcated T2-hyperintense lesion in the central basis pontis without enhancement or mass effect.
explanation: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia causes osmotic stress on oligodendrocytes that had adapted to the hypotonic environment. The central pons is particularly vulnerable due to its unique vascular architecture and arrangement of gray and white matter, resulting in demyelination that manifests as quadriparesis, pseudobulbar palsy, and locked-in syndrome.
keyFact: Sodium correction in chronic hyponatremia should not exceed 8-10 mEq/L per 24 hours. Risk factors for osmotic demyelination include alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease, and hypokalemia. The classic MRI finding is a trident-shaped T2 hyperintensity in the central pons.

wrongAnswers.name: Basilar Artery Occlusion
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Basilar artery stroke causes acute brainstem symptoms but would show restricted diffusion on DWI and typically presents with sudden onset rather than delayed deterioration after sodium correction.

wrongAnswers.name: Wernicke Encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wernicke encephalopathy in alcoholics causes confusion and ophthalmoplegia but affects the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray, not the central pons, and does not cause quadriparesis.

wrongAnswers.name: Pontine Glioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A brainstem glioma causes progressive pontine symptoms but develops over weeks to months, shows mass effect and enhancement, and is unrelated to sodium correction.

clues: A 4-month-old infant is brought in because the parents noticed the baby's head has been growing faster than expected over the past two months.
The infant has delayed motor milestones and has not yet achieved head control. There is no history of birth trauma or perinatal complications.
Head circumference is above the 99th percentile with a bulging anterior fontanelle. The occiput appears unusually prominent and rounded.
Cranial ultrasound reveals marked dilation of the lateral ventricles and a large fluid-filled cystic structure in the posterior fossa communicating with the fourth ventricle.
MRI confirms complete agenesis of the cerebellar vermis with a massively dilated fourth ventricle that expands the posterior fossa and elevates the tentorium and torcula.
explanation: Dandy-Walker malformation results from failure of the cerebellar vermis to develop, leaving the fourth ventricle to expand as a large posterior fossa cyst. The enlarged posterior fossa elevates the transverse sinuses and torcula. Obstruction of CSF outflow leads to hydrocephalus in the majority of affected infants.
keyFact: The classic triad of Dandy-Walker malformation is: (1) complete or partial agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, (2) cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle, and (3) enlargement of the posterior fossa with upward displacement of the torcula. It is associated with hydrocephalus in ~80% of cases.

wrongAnswers.name: Arnold-Chiari Malformation (Type II)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chiari II involves a small posterior fossa with downward herniation of the cerebellar vermis through the foramen magnum and is associated with myelomeningocele, not an enlarged posterior fossa with absent vermis.

wrongAnswers.name: Arachnoid Cyst
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A posterior fossa arachnoid cyst is a benign extra-axial fluid collection that displaces but does not replace the cerebellar vermis, and the fourth ventricle remains normal in size.

wrongAnswers.name: Mega Cisterna Magna
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mega cisterna magna is an enlarged cisterna magna with a normal cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle, considered a normal variant that does not cause hydrocephalus.

clues: A 22-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed episode of staring and unresponsiveness lasting about 90 seconds during class.
He reports a history of recurrent episodes preceded by an intense feeling of having experienced the current moment before, along with a rising sensation in his abdomen.
During a monitored episode, he stares blankly, smacks his lips repetitively, and fumbles with his shirt buttons. He is confused and unable to recall the event afterward.
Routine EEG shows intermittent sharp waves and spike discharges arising from the left anterior temporal region during drowsiness.
MRI of the brain reveals increased T2 signal and volume loss in the left hippocampus consistent with mesial temporal sclerosis.
explanation: Temporal lobe epilepsy is the most common form of focal epilepsy in adults. Seizures arise from the mesial temporal structures, particularly the hippocampus and amygdala. The aura (deja vu, epigastric rising) reflects early ictal activation of these structures, followed by impaired awareness and automatisms as the seizure spreads.
keyFact: Mesial temporal sclerosis (hippocampal sclerosis) is the most common structural cause of temporal lobe epilepsy. The classic aura triad is deja vu, epigastric rising sensation, and fear. Oroalimentary automatisms (lip smacking, chewing) with postictal confusion distinguish temporal lobe seizures from absence seizures.

wrongAnswers.name: Absence Epilepsy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Absence seizures cause brief staring spells with 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave on EEG but lack auras, automatisms, and postictal confusion, and typically onset in childhood.

wrongAnswers.name: Transient Ischemic Attack
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TIAs cause focal neurological deficits from vascular insufficiency but do not produce stereotyped automatisms, EEG epileptiform discharges, or hippocampal sclerosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Psychogenic Non-Epileptic Seizures
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psychogenic episodes do not produce epileptiform discharges on EEG during events and are not associated with structural hippocampal abnormalities on MRI.

clues: A 58-year-old woman presents with gradually worsening headaches and a subtle change in personality noticed by her family over the past year.
She has a history of prior breast cancer treated with radiation therapy. Her family notes she has become uncharacteristically apathetic and disinhibited.
Neurological examination reveals anosmia on the left, mild papilledema bilaterally, and subtle weakness of the right lower extremity with hyperreflexia.
CT head with contrast shows a well-circumscribed, densely enhancing extra-axial mass at the left frontal convexity with a broad dural attachment and adjacent hyperostosis.
Histopathology of the resected specimen reveals whorls of meningothelial cells with psammoma bodies and positive staining for epithelial membrane antigen.
explanation: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells of the meninges and are the most common primary intracranial tumor. They are extra-axial, typically benign (WHO grade I), and compress rather than invade brain parenchyma. Prior radiation and female sex are risk factors, as many express progesterone receptors.
keyFact: Meningiomas are the most common primary intracranial tumor. Key histological features are whorls of meningothelial cells and psammoma bodies. They are extra-axial with a dural tail on contrast imaging. Risk factors include prior radiation, female sex, and neurofibromatosis type 2.

wrongAnswers.name: Glioblastoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Glioblastoma is an intra-axial tumor with irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis, and crossing of the corpus callosum, unlike this well-circumscribed extra-axial mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Brain Metastasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastatic lesions are typically intra-axial, multiple, and at the gray-white junction with surrounding edema, not extra-axial with a broad dural base and hyperostosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Schwannoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Intracranial schwannomas most commonly arise at the cerebellopontine angle from CN VIII, not at the frontal convexity, and show Antoni A and B patterns rather than psammoma bodies.

clues: A 19-year-old man presents with irresistible daytime sleepiness for the past eight months that occurs despite sleeping nine or more hours each night.
He reports episodes of sudden bilateral knee buckling and jaw dropping triggered by laughing hard with friends, lasting several seconds without loss of consciousness.
He describes vivid, frightening dream-like imagery occurring as he falls asleep and occasional inability to move for up to a minute upon waking.
A multiple sleep latency test shows a mean sleep latency of 3.2 minutes with REM sleep occurring within 4 minutes on four of five nap opportunities.
Cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 (orexin-A) level is measured at 28 pg/mL, well below the 110 pg/mL diagnostic threshold.
explanation: Narcolepsy type 1 results from autoimmune destruction of hypocretin (orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. Loss of hypocretin destabilizes boundaries between wakefulness, NREM, and REM sleep, causing intrusion of REM-associated phenomena (muscle atonia, dreaming) into wakefulness and sleep transitions.
keyFact: Narcolepsy type 1 is defined by cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion) and/or low CSF hypocretin-1 (<110 pg/mL). It is strongly associated with HLA-DQB1*0602. MSLT criteria require mean sleep latency <=8 minutes with >=2 sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs).

wrongAnswers.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OSA causes excessive daytime sleepiness from fragmented sleep but does not produce cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, or sleep-onset REM periods on MSLT.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic Hypersomnia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Idiopathic hypersomnia causes excessive sleepiness with prolonged unrefreshing naps but lacks cataplexy, does not show SOREMPs on MSLT, and has normal CSF hypocretin.

wrongAnswers.name: Kleine-Levin Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kleine-Levin syndrome causes episodic hypersomnia with cognitive and behavioral changes during episodes but is not persistent and lacks cataplexy and low CSF hypocretin.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with daily headaches that are worse in the morning and a whooshing sound in her ears that pulses with her heartbeat.
Her BMI is 38. She started an oral contraceptive pill and gained 15 pounds over the past four months, during which time her headaches began.
Visual acuity is 20/30 bilaterally. Fundoscopic examination reveals bilateral disc swelling with obscuration of the disc margins. Visual field testing shows enlarged blind spots.
MRI of the brain with and without contrast is normal, with no mass lesion, hydrocephalus, or venous sinus thrombosis on MR venography.
Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position reveals an opening pressure of 34 cm H2O with normal CSF cell count, protein, and glucose.
explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension involves elevated CSF pressure without a structural cause. It predominantly affects obese women of childbearing age. The elevated pressure is transmitted to the optic nerve sheaths, causing papilledema that can lead to progressive vision loss if untreated.
keyFact: Diagnostic criteria require elevated opening pressure (>25 cm H2O in adults), normal CSF composition, normal neuroimaging, and papilledema. Risk factors include obesity, female sex, and medications (tetracyclines, vitamin A, OCPs). The major morbidity is permanent vision loss from untreated papilledema.

wrongAnswers.name: Migraine
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Migraines cause recurrent headaches but do not produce papilledema, elevated CSF pressure, or pulsatile tinnitus.

wrongAnswers.name: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Venous sinus thrombosis can mimic IIH with headache and papilledema but would show filling defects on MR venography, which was normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: An intracranial mass lesion could raise ICP and cause papilledema, but MRI was normal without any mass, hydrocephalus, or structural abnormality.

clues: A 63-year-old man with a history of high blood pressure and smoking presents with sudden-onset vertigo, difficulty swallowing, and hoarseness that began one hour ago.
He also reports persistent hiccups since onset and numbness on the left side of his face along with a clumsy, unsteady gait veering to the left.
Examination shows left ptosis and miosis, absent left gag reflex, left-sided cerebellar ataxia, and decreased pain and temperature sensation on the left face and right body.
CT head without contrast is negative for hemorrhage. CT angiography shows irregular narrowing of the left vertebral artery near its intracranial segment.
MRI diffusion-weighted imaging reveals a wedge-shaped area of restricted diffusion in the left lateral medulla.
explanation: Wallenberg syndrome results from infarction of the lateral medulla, most commonly due to occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery or the vertebral artery. The lateral medulla contains the nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei, spinal trigeminal nucleus, spinothalamic tract, sympathetic fibers, and inferior cerebellar peduncle, producing the characteristic crossed sensory findings.
keyFact: The hallmark of Wallenberg syndrome is crossed sensory loss: ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain/temperature loss. Ipsilateral Horner syndrome, cerebellar ataxia, dysphagia, hoarseness, and vertigo complete the picture. It is the most common posterior circulation stroke syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Medial Medullary Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome affects the medial medulla, causing contralateral hemiparesis (corticospinal tract), contralateral proprioceptive loss (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue deviation, not the crossed pain/temperature loss or Horner syndrome seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Cerebellar Infarction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Isolated cerebellar infarction causes ataxia and vertigo but does not produce crossed sensory deficits, Horner syndrome, or cranial nerve palsies affecting swallowing and phonation.

wrongAnswers.name: Vestibular Neuritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vestibular neuritis causes acute vertigo and nystagmus but is a peripheral vestibular disorder that does not produce dysphagia, Horner syndrome, or crossed sensory findings.

clues: A 26-year-old man is evaluated after being mandated for psychiatric assessment following his third arrest for assault in two years.
Records show multiple school suspensions beginning at age 11 for fighting, fire-setting, and cruelty to animals, with a juvenile arrest for theft at age 14.
He shows no remorse when discussing the incidents, blaming others for provoking him. He has a pattern of unstable employment due to conflicts with supervisors and coworkers.
Psychological testing reveals a pervasive pattern of disregard for the rights of others since age 15, with deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability, and failure to conform to social norms.
Review of childhood records confirms a documented diagnosis of conduct disorder before age 15, meeting the prerequisite criterion for the current diagnosis.
explanation: Antisocial personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of others' rights, beginning in childhood or early adolescence and continuing into adulthood. A prerequisite is evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15. The individual must be at least 18 years old for the diagnosis.
keyFact: ASPD requires evidence of conduct disorder before age 15 and a pervasive pattern of disregard for others' rights since age 15. Key features include deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability/aggressiveness, reckless disregard for safety, irresponsibility, and lack of remorse. The individual must be at least 18 for diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Narcissistic Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NPD involves grandiosity, need for admiration, and lack of empathy but does not require conduct disorder before age 15 or a pattern of criminal behavior and violating others' rights.

wrongAnswers.name: Borderline Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BPD features emotional instability, fear of abandonment, and self-harm, but the aggression is typically reactive and self-directed rather than the calculated, predatory pattern seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Intermittent Explosive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IED involves discrete episodes of disproportionate aggressive outbursts but does not encompass the pervasive pattern of deceitfulness, irresponsibility, and lack of remorse that defines this presentation.

clues: A 24-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is brought to the emergency department by her roommate for sudden onset of disorganized speech and bizarre behavior.
Her roommate reports that the patient's fiance unexpectedly ended their engagement two days ago, and she has been inconsolable and sleepless since.
She is agitated, speaks in tangential and loosely associated sentences, and insists that the television is sending her coded messages about her fiance's whereabouts.
Urine drug screen, thyroid function, CBC, CMP, and head CT are all within normal limits. There is no prior history of mood episodes or psychotic symptoms.
The psychotic symptoms resolve completely within 10 days with supportive care and low-dose antipsychotics, with full return to her previous level of functioning.
explanation: Brief psychotic disorder is characterized by sudden onset of at least one psychotic symptom (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or grossly disorganized behavior) lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with eventual full return to premorbid functioning. It may occur with or without a marked stressor.
keyFact: Brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month with full return to baseline. If psychotic symptoms persist beyond 1 month but less than 6 months, the diagnosis becomes schizophreniform disorder. Beyond 6 months with functional decline, schizophrenia is diagnosed.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophreniform Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophreniform disorder requires symptoms lasting 1-6 months. This patient's symptoms resolved completely within 10 days, falling within the brief psychotic disorder timeframe.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of disturbance with active-phase symptoms for at least 1 month and functional decline, none of which apply to this acute, self-limited presentation.

wrongAnswers.name: Delusional Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Delusional disorder involves non-bizarre delusions lasting at least 1 month without the disorganized speech, agitation, and rapid full resolution seen here.

clues: A 47-year-old man is brought in by his wife because he has been increasingly convinced for the past three months that she is having an affair, despite no evidence.
He has installed cameras in their home, follows her to work, and checks her phone multiple times daily. He functions normally at work and maintains his hygiene and social obligations.

Mental status examination reveals a well-groomed, articulate man with organized thought processes. His beliefs about infidelity are fixed and unshakeable, but he has no hallucinations or formal thought disorder.
Comprehensive medical workup including brain MRI, thyroid function, RPR, and urine drug screen are all unremarkable. Neuropsychological testing shows intact cognition.
Psychiatric evaluation over several weeks confirms a single, encapsulated, non-bizarre delusion persisting for over one month with no other psychotic symptoms and preserved overall functioning.
explanation: Delusional disorder involves one or more non-bizarre delusions lasting at least one month in the absence of other prominent psychotic features. Functioning is not markedly impaired, and behavior apart from the delusion is not obviously odd. Subtypes include persecutory, jealous, erotomanic, grandiose, and somatic.
keyFact: Delusional disorder features non-bizarre delusions (situations that could occur in real life) lasting at least 1 month. Functioning is relatively preserved, and criteria for schizophrenia have never been met. The jealous subtype involves the fixed belief that one's partner is unfaithful.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia requires at least two active-phase symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms) with functional decline. This patient has only delusions with preserved functioning.

wrongAnswers.name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OCD involves intrusive, ego-dystonic thoughts recognized as excessive, whereas this patient's beliefs are ego-syntonic and held with delusional conviction without insight.

wrongAnswers.name: Paranoid Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Paranoid personality disorder involves pervasive distrust and suspicion without fixed delusional beliefs. This patient has a specific, fixed, false belief about his wife's infidelity that meets criteria for a delusion.

clues: A 33-year-old woman presents to a new hospital with a dramatic story of recurrent fevers and abdominal pain, requesting admission for further workup.
Review of outside records reveals 14 hospitalizations at 8 different hospitals over the past two years for similar complaints, with multiple unrevealing extensive workups.
She displays detailed medical knowledge, seems eager for invasive procedures, and becomes hostile when staff suggests her symptoms may not have a medical cause. No visitors come during her stay.

Repeated blood cultures grow polymicrobial organisms, and nursing staff observe her manipulating her IV line without gloves. She has a markedly elevated WBC without corresponding clinical deterioration.
A search of her belongings reveals syringes containing fecal material, and surveillance footage confirms self-injection of contaminated material into her IV line.
explanation: Factitious disorder imposed on self involves deliberate falsification or induction of physical or psychological symptoms in oneself, motivated by the desire to assume the sick role rather than for external rewards. Patients often have medical knowledge, present with dramatic histories, and engage in hospital-hopping to avoid detection.
keyFact: Factitious disorder is distinguished from malingering by motivation: factitious disorder is driven by the psychological need to assume the sick role, while malingering is motivated by external incentives (disability payments, avoiding work). Polymicrobial bacteremia in the absence of an obvious source should raise suspicion.

wrongAnswers.name: Malingering
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malingering involves intentional symptom production for external gain (financial compensation, avoiding legal consequences). This patient has no identifiable external incentive and appears motivated by the sick role itself.

wrongAnswers.name: Somatic Symptom Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Somatic symptom disorder involves genuine distress about physical symptoms with excessive health-related behaviors, but symptoms are not intentionally produced or falsified.

wrongAnswers.name: Conversion Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Conversion disorder produces neurological symptoms incompatible with recognized conditions but is not intentional. This patient is deliberately inducing infections by self-injection.

clues: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by family for talking to unseen people and expressing grandiose plans to save the world over the past three weeks.
She has been sleeping only two hours per night, spending excessively, speaking rapidly, and is euphoric and highly energized during this same period.
She reports hearing a running commentary from two voices discussing her actions. She believes the government has chosen her for a special mission and has placed transmitters in her teeth.
Her mood episode resolves with treatment after four weeks, but the auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions persist unchanged for an additional three weeks without any mood symptoms.

Review of her longitudinal history confirms at least two weeks of delusions and hallucinations in the absence of mood episodes, while psychotic and mood symptoms were concurrent for the majority of the illness.
explanation: Schizoaffective disorder requires an uninterrupted period of illness during which a major mood episode (manic or depressive) co-occurs with symptoms meeting Criterion A of schizophrenia. Crucially, delusions or hallucinations must also be present for at least two weeks in the absence of a mood episode during the lifetime duration of illness.
keyFact: The key distinguishing feature of schizoaffective disorder is psychotic symptoms occurring for at least 2 weeks WITHOUT a concurrent mood episode, while mood episodes are present for the majority of the total illness duration. This separates it from schizophrenia (mood is minor) and bipolar/MDD with psychotic features (psychosis only during mood episodes).

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
wrongAnswers.whyNot: In bipolar I with psychotic features, hallucinations and delusions occur only during mood episodes and resolve when the mood episode resolves. This patient's psychosis persisted for weeks after the mood episode ended.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia can have mood symptoms, but they are brief relative to the total duration of psychosis. This patient had prominent manic symptoms concurrent with psychosis for the majority of her illness.

wrongAnswers.name: Brief Psychotic Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than one month and fully resolves. This patient has a prolonged course with persistent psychosis beyond one month and a clear mood component.

accept: somatic symptom disorder with predominant pain
clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with chronic pain in her back, head, and abdomen and reports frequent nausea, all of which have been present for over two years.
She has seen numerous specialists and undergone extensive imaging, blood work, and endoscopic studies, all of which have been unremarkable or showed only minor incidental findings.

She spends several hours daily researching her symptoms online, frequently calls her physician's office about her health concerns, and has missed significant work due to her preoccupation with these symptoms.

Psychological assessment reveals excessive and disproportionate thoughts, feelings, and behaviors related to her somatic symptoms, with persistent high anxiety about health that is out of proportion to any objective findings.

Longitudinal psychiatric evaluation over six months confirms persistent somatic symptoms with excessive associated thoughts, feelings, or behaviors lasting well beyond six months, without evidence of intentional symptom production.
explanation: Somatic symptom disorder is characterized by one or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or result in significant disruption of daily life, accompanied by excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to the symptoms. Unlike factitious disorder or malingering, the symptoms and distress are not intentionally produced.
keyFact: Somatic symptom disorder requires somatic symptoms PLUS excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to those symptoms. The diagnosis does not require that symptoms be medically unexplained. It replaces the older DSM-IV somatization disorder. Duration must be at least 6 months.

wrongAnswers.name: Illness Anxiety Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Illness anxiety disorder involves preoccupation with having a serious illness with minimal or no somatic symptoms. This patient has prominent, persistent somatic symptoms driving her distress.

wrongAnswers.name: Factitious Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Factitious disorder involves intentional falsification or induction of symptoms. This patient's symptoms and distress are genuine, not deliberately produced.

wrongAnswers.name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
