wrongAnswers.whyNot: GAD features excessive worry across multiple domains, not the specific, persistent focus on somatic symptoms and health-related behaviors that dominate this presentation.

clues: A 7-year-old boy from a rural farming community is brought in for intermittent abdominal pain, bloating, and poor appetite over the past several weeks.
His family uses untreated human waste as fertilizer in their vegetable garden, and the child frequently plays in the soil and eats unwashed produce.

He has a distended abdomen and appears malnourished. A peripheral blood smear shows eosinophilia at 18%. A recent chest radiograph showed transient bilateral patchy infiltrates that have since resolved.
Abdominal radiograph reveals multiple tubular filling defects within loops of dilated small bowel, and ultrasound shows linear echogenic structures within the biliary tree.
Stool microscopy reveals large, oval, bile-stained eggs with a mammillated outer shell, measuring approximately 60 by 45 micrometers.
explanation: Ascaris lumbricoides is the most common helminthic infection worldwide. Eggs are ingested from contaminated soil, hatch in the intestine, and larvae penetrate the gut wall to migrate through the liver and lungs (causing transient pulmonary infiltrates and eosinophilia known as Loeffler syndrome) before being swallowed back into the intestine to mature into adult worms.
keyFact: Ascaris follows a hepatopulmonary migration cycle. Loeffler syndrome (transient pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia) occurs during larval lung migration. Intestinal obstruction is the most common complication in heavy infections. Diagnosis is by identifying the characteristic mammillated eggs on stool microscopy.

wrongAnswers.name: Hookworm Infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hookworm enters through the skin (not oral ingestion), causes iron-deficiency anemia from intestinal blood loss, and produces thin-shelled ovoid eggs without mammillation.

wrongAnswers.name: Strongyloides
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Strongyloides causes eosinophilia and pulmonary symptoms but enters through the skin, and stool examination shows larvae rather than eggs.

wrongAnswers.name: Giardia lamblia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Giardiasis causes bloating and malabsorption but does not produce eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, or visible filling defects on abdominal imaging.

clues: A 34-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids over the past two weeks, along with pain behind his breastbone when eating.
He was recently diagnosed with HIV infection with a CD4 count of 62 cells/microL and has not yet started antiretroviral therapy.
Oral examination reveals whitish, curd-like plaques on the buccal mucosa and palate that can be scraped off to reveal an erythematous base underneath.
Barium swallow shows a shaggy, irregular esophageal mucosa with multiple linear and plaque-like filling defects throughout the length of the esophagus.
Upper endoscopy reveals raised, white-yellow adherent plaques on the esophageal mucosa, and brushings show pseudohyphae and budding yeast cells on KOH preparation.
explanation: Esophageal candidiasis is an AIDS-defining illness that typically occurs when CD4 counts fall below 100 cells/microL. Candida albicans, a commensal organism, overgrows in the setting of severe immunosuppression, forming pseudomembranes on the esophageal mucosa that cause odynophagia and dysphagia.
keyFact: Esophageal candidiasis is an AIDS-defining condition occurring at CD4 <100. Oral thrush with dysphagia/odynophagia in an HIV patient can be treated empirically with fluconazole. Endoscopy with biopsy is performed if symptoms fail to respond. Pseudohyphae on KOH prep confirm the diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: CMV Esophagitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CMV esophagitis in immunocompromised patients produces large, deep, linear ulcers on endoscopy with intranuclear owl-eye inclusions on biopsy, not the diffuse white plaques and pseudohyphae seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Herpes Simplex Esophagitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV esophagitis causes small, discrete, well-circumscribed shallow ulcers often with raised edges, with multinucleated giant cells on biopsy, not diffuse pseudomembranous plaques.

wrongAnswers.name: Pill Esophagitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pill esophagitis causes discrete ulceration typically at a single level of the esophagus, often the aortic arch region, and is not associated with oral thrush or immunosuppression.

clues: An 8-year-old girl is brought in by her parents for a painless swelling in her left armpit that has been slowly growing over the past two weeks.
The family recently adopted a kitten, and the child plays with it daily. She had a small scratch on her left hand about three weeks ago that developed a red bump.
She has a low-grade fever of 38.2 C. Examination reveals a 3-cm warm, fluctuant lymph node in the left axilla. A small papule is noted on the dorsum of the left hand.
Serologic testing returns positive IgM and IgG antibodies against Bartonella henselae. CBC shows a mild leukocytosis. PPD is negative.
Lymph node biopsy shows stellate (star-shaped) necrotizing granulomas with surrounding palisading histiocytes and Warthin-Starry silver stain revealing clusters of small pleomorphic bacilli.
explanation: Cat scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae, a gram-negative bacterium transmitted through a cat scratch or bite, particularly from kittens. The organism drains to regional lymph nodes, causing granulomatous lymphadenitis. The disease is typically self-limited in immunocompetent patients.
keyFact: Cat scratch disease presents with regional lymphadenopathy proximal to a scratch/bite inoculation site, most commonly in children. Histology shows stellate necrotizing granulomas. In immunocompromised patients, Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis (vascular skin lesions) and peliosis hepatis.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma can present with painless lymphadenopathy but typically involves multiple nodal groups, and biopsy would show malignant lymphocytes rather than necrotizing granulomas with bacilli.

wrongAnswers.name: Mycobacterial Lymphadenitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Non-tuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis causes cervical lymphadenopathy with caseating granulomas but is not associated with cat exposure, inoculation papules, or positive Bartonella serology.

wrongAnswers.name: Toxoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Toxoplasmosis can cause lymphadenopathy but is acquired from cat feces (not scratches), and biopsy shows non-necrotizing granulomas without the stellate pattern or Warthin-Starry-positive organisms.

clues: A 42-year-old man originally from rural Bolivia presents with progressive exertional shortness of breath, palpitations, and lower extremity swelling over the past several months.
He recalls a prolonged febrile illness as a child in Bolivia after being bitten by an insect while sleeping in an adobe house, with unilateral swelling around one eye that lasted weeks.
Examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse, elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasilar crackles, and pitting edema of both legs. A chest radiograph shows marked cardiomegaly.

ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation with right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block. Echocardiogram reveals a dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm and ejection fraction of 25%.
Serologic testing with two different assays (ELISA and IFA) returns positive for anti-Trypanosoma cruzi IgG antibodies, confirming chronic infection.
explanation: Chagas disease is caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by triatomine (reduviid or kissing) bugs that deposit infected feces near the bite wound. The acute phase may feature Romana sign (periorbital edema at the inoculation site). Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy develops decades later through progressive myocardial fibrosis and destruction of the cardiac conduction system.
keyFact: Chagas disease is the leading cause of cardiomyopathy in Latin America. Classic findings include dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm and right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block. Megaesophagus and megacolon from autonomic nerve destruction are other chronic manifestations. Romana sign is pathognomonic of acute infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic Dilated Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Idiopathic DCM causes heart failure but lacks the specific conduction abnormalities, apical aneurysm, epidemiologic exposure, and positive T. cruzi serology seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatic Heart Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rheumatic heart disease causes valvular pathology (especially mitral stenosis) from prior streptococcal infection, not a dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm and conduction abnormalities.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alcoholic cardiomyopathy produces dilated cardiomyopathy but is associated with heavy alcohol use, not the specific conduction pattern, apical aneurysm, and parasitic serology seen here.

clues: A 35-year-old shepherd from rural Turkey presents with a dull ache in his right upper abdomen and a sensation of fullness that has been gradually worsening over the past year.
He has been raising sheep and working closely with sheepdogs his entire life. He has never traveled outside his home province.
Examination reveals a palpable, smooth, non-tender mass in the right upper quadrant. Liver function tests show mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase. Eosinophil count is 8%.
Abdominal ultrasound reveals a 10-cm well-defined, unilocular hepatic cyst with floating echogenic debris and separation of the inner germinal membrane from the outer pericyst (water lily sign).
Serology returns positive for anti-Echinococcus IgG antibodies, and CT confirms a calcified rim surrounding the hepatic cyst with internal daughter cysts.
explanation: Echinococcus granulosus is a cestode whose definitive host is the dog. Humans are accidental intermediate hosts who ingest eggs from dog feces. Oncospheres penetrate the intestinal wall, reach the liver via portal circulation, and develop into slow-growing hydatid cysts with an outer laminated membrane and inner germinal layer that produces daughter cysts and brood capsules.
keyFact: Echinococcus granulosus causes cystic echinococcosis, most commonly in the liver (65%) and lungs (25%). The dog-sheep cycle is classic. Cyst rupture can cause fatal anaphylaxis and peritoneal dissemination. Percutaneous aspiration without pre-treatment with albendazole risks anaphylaxis and seeding.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatic Abscess (Amoebic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Amoebic liver abscess presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and a single hypoechoic lesion, but contains liquefied necrotic material (anchovy paste), not daughter cysts, membranes, or calcification.

wrongAnswers.name: Simple Hepatic Cyst
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Simple hepatic cysts are thin-walled, anechoic, and asymptomatic. They lack internal debris, floating membranes, daughter cysts, wall calcification, and positive Echinococcus serology.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatocellular Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCC presents as a solid, vascular mass with arterial phase enhancement in patients with chronic liver disease, not a well-defined cystic lesion with daughter cysts in a young patient with normal liver parenchyma.

clues: A 14-year-old boy from a rural village in sub-Saharan Africa presents with fatigue, weakness, and a craving to eat dirt and clay over the past several months.
He frequently walks barefoot in soil contaminated with human waste. He recalls an itchy rash on the soles of his feet several weeks ago that resolved on its own.
He appears pale with conjunctival pallor. Heart rate is 110. A stool sample is noted to have a dark, tarry appearance. Mild epigastric tenderness is present.
CBC reveals hemoglobin of 5.8 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 62 fL, serum ferritin of 4 ng/mL, and peripheral eosinophilia at 12%.
Stool microscopy shows numerous thin-shelled, oval, colorless eggs measuring approximately 60 by 40 micrometers, each containing a developing morula of 4-8 cells.
explanation: Hookworm larvae in contaminated soil penetrate the skin of bare feet, causing ground itch. They migrate to the lungs, are swallowed, and attach to the duodenal and jejunal mucosa, where they feed on blood. Chronic blood loss leads to severe iron-deficiency anemia. Pica (geophagia) is a clinical manifestation of iron deficiency.
keyFact: Hookworm is the leading infectious cause of iron-deficiency anemia worldwide. Larvae penetrate skin (ground itch), migrate through lungs, and attach to small bowel mucosa to feed on blood. Necator americanus is the predominant species. Treatment is albendazole or mebendazole plus iron supplementation.

wrongAnswers.name: Ascariasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ascaris causes intestinal obstruction and malnutrition but is transmitted by oral ingestion (not skin penetration), does not cause significant blood loss or iron-deficiency anemia, and produces large mammillated eggs.

wrongAnswers.name: Strongyloides
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Strongyloides also enters through the skin and causes eosinophilia, but stool shows larvae (not eggs), and it does not typically cause severe iron-deficiency anemia from intestinal blood loss.

wrongAnswers.name: Iron-Deficiency Anemia from Malnutrition
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nutritional iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia but does not produce eosinophilia, tarry stools from intestinal blood loss, or helminth eggs on stool microscopy.

clues: A 5-year-old boy from eastern India presents with persistent fever, progressive abdominal distension, and weight loss over the past two months.
The family lives near marshy land, and the child sleeps without bed nets. Several neighbors have had similar illnesses in the past year.
The child appears cachectic and has darkened skin on his hands and face. The spleen is massively enlarged, extending to the right iliac fossa. The liver is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin.

CBC reveals pancytopenia with hemoglobin 5.2 g/dL, WBC 1,800, and platelets 45,000. Serum protein electrophoresis shows marked polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia with an albumin-to-globulin ratio reversal.
Bone marrow aspirate stained with Giemsa reveals numerous intracellular amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) within macrophages, each showing a nucleus and a rod-shaped kinetoplast.
explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is caused by Leishmania donovani, transmitted by the sandfly. The protozoan parasitizes macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system, leading to massive hepatosplenomegaly. Bone marrow infiltration causes pancytopenia. Polyclonal B-cell activation produces hypergammaglobulinemia. The name kala-azar means black fever, referring to skin darkening.
keyFact: Visceral leishmaniasis classically presents with fever, massive splenomegaly (often the largest spleen in medicine), pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia. Transmitted by sandflies. Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) with kinetoplasts in macrophages on bone marrow, splenic, or liver biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Malaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malaria causes fever and splenomegaly but produces hemolytic anemia with parasites visible inside red blood cells (not macrophages), and does not cause the degree of splenomegaly or hypergammaglobulinemia seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CML causes massive splenomegaly and leukocytosis but shows the Philadelphia chromosome and elevated WBC rather than pancytopenia and intracellular amastigotes in macrophages.

wrongAnswers.name: Schistosomiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis causes splenomegaly from portal hypertension but presents with periportal fibrosis, not pancytopenia from bone marrow infiltration or intracellular amastigotes.

clues: A 19-year-old college football player presents with a painful, swollen, red area on his right thigh that has been worsening over the past four days despite warm compresses.
He shares towels and razors in the team locker room. Two of his teammates were recently treated for similar skin infections in the past month.
Examination reveals a 5-cm fluctuant, erythematous, tender abscess on the anterior right thigh with surrounding induration and a central area of necrosis draining purulent material.
Gram stain of the aspirated pus shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. The organism grows on mannitol salt agar and is coagulase-positive. It is resistant to oxacillin on susceptibility testing.
PCR testing of the isolate detects the mecA gene encoding an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a), and Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL) toxin gene is also detected.
explanation: Community-associated MRSA strains commonly produce Panton-Valentine leukocidin, a pore-forming toxin that destroys neutrophils and contributes to abscess formation and skin necrosis. Resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics is mediated by the mecA gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for beta-lactams.
keyFact: MRSA resistance is conferred by the mecA gene encoding PBP2a with reduced beta-lactam affinity. Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) typically produces PVL toxin and causes skin/soft tissue infections. Treatment of abscesses is incision and drainage. If antibiotics are needed, use TMP-SMX, doxycycline, or clindamycin.

wrongAnswers.name: Methicillin-Sensitive S. aureus Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MSSA causes identical-appearing abscesses but is susceptible to oxacillin on sensitivity testing and lacks the mecA gene, which was detected in this isolate.

wrongAnswers.name: Streptococcal Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Group A Streptococcus causes spreading cellulitis and erysipelas but typically presents as diffuse erythema without a central fluctuant abscess, and Gram stain shows cocci in chains, not clusters.

wrongAnswers.name: Sporotrichosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sporotrichosis causes nodular lymphocutaneous lesions ascending along lymphatic channels from an inoculation site, not a single fluctuant abscess with gram-positive cocci in clusters.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with high fevers, chills, drenching sweats, headache, and body aches that began five days after returning from a two-week trip to Nigeria.
She did not take any prophylactic medications before or during her travel. She visited rural areas and recalls numerous mosquito bites despite using repellent intermittently.
Temperature is 40.1 C with rigors. She appears jaundiced and ill. Spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Heart rate is 120 and blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg.
CBC shows hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 42,000, and WBC 4,200. Total bilirubin is 4.8 mg/dL (indirect predominant). LDH is elevated. Haptoglobin is undetectable.
Giemsa-stained thick and thin peripheral blood smears reveal ring-form trophozoites (some with multiple rings per red cell and applique forms), with a parasitemia of 8% and banana-shaped gametocytes.
explanation: Plasmodium falciparum is the most lethal malaria species, transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. It infects red blood cells of all ages (producing high parasitemia), causes infected cells to adhere to vascular endothelium (sequestration), and leads to hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and end-organ damage. Banana-shaped gametocytes are pathognomonic for P. falciparum.
keyFact: P. falciparum is distinguished by multiple ring forms per RBC, applique (accolle) forms, high parasitemia (>5%), banana-shaped gametocytes, and absence of schizonts on peripheral smear (due to sequestration). It is the only species that causes cerebral malaria. Severe malaria is treated with IV artesunate.

wrongAnswers.name: Plasmodium vivax Malaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: P. vivax produces enlarged RBCs with Schuffner stippling and ameboid trophozoites, infects only reticulocytes (limiting parasitemia), and produces round gametocytes rather than banana-shaped ones.

wrongAnswers.name: Dengue Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dengue causes fever and thrombocytopenia after tropical travel but is a viral infection transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, does not produce hemolytic anemia or splenomegaly, and no parasites are seen on blood smear.

wrongAnswers.name: Typhoid Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Typhoid causes prolonged fever after travel to endemic areas but produces relative bradycardia, rose spots, and leukopenia without hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, or parasites on blood smear.

clues: A 36-year-old man presents with a dry cough, progressive shortness of breath on exertion, and low-grade fevers that have developed insidiously over the past three weeks.
He was diagnosed with HIV two years ago but has not been adherent to antiretroviral therapy. His most recent CD4 count was 45 cells/microL.
Oxygen saturation drops from 94% at rest to 82% after walking across the room. Lung auscultation is remarkably clear despite his dyspnea. Oral thrush is present.
Chest radiograph shows bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates in a ground-glass pattern. Serum LDH is markedly elevated at 580 U/L. Beta-D-glucan is positive.
Bronchoalveolar lavage with Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain reveals cup-shaped or crushed ping-pong ball cysts of Pneumocystis jirovecii.
explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungus that causes pneumonia in severely immunocompromised patients, particularly those with HIV and CD4 counts below 200. The organism fills the alveoli, impairing gas exchange and producing the characteristic exertional desaturation. The disproportionately clear lung exam relative to the degree of hypoxia is a hallmark clinical feature.
keyFact: PCP prophylaxis with TMP-SMX is indicated when CD4 <200 in HIV patients. Elevated LDH and positive beta-D-glucan support the diagnosis. Bilateral ground-glass opacities are classic. If PaO2 <70 mmHg or A-a gradient >35, adjunctive corticosteroids are added to TMP-SMX treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pulmonary TB in HIV patients can present with diffuse infiltrates at low CD4 counts, but TB causes productive cough with cavitary or miliary patterns and is diagnosed by AFB smear/culture, not GMS-positive cysts.

wrongAnswers.name: CMV Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CMV pneumonitis in immunocompromised patients causes interstitial infiltrates but is diagnosed by BAL showing intranuclear owl-eye inclusions, not the cup-shaped cysts of Pneumocystis.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphocytic Interstitial Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LIP can occur in HIV patients with diffuse infiltrates but has a chronic course, is more common in children, and biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltration rather than Pneumocystis organisms.

clues: A 30-year-old man from rural Egypt presents with increasing abdominal distension, fatigue, and episodes of vomiting blood over the past several months.
He has a history of regular swimming and bathing in freshwater canals since childhood. He recalls episodes of itchy skin after water exposure as a child.
Examination reveals a firm, non-tender, enlarged liver with a nodular surface. The spleen is massively enlarged. Ascites is present. There are dilated veins visible on the abdominal wall.
Abdominal ultrasound shows characteristic thickening and fibrosis of the portal vein walls (pipe-stem pattern). Upper endoscopy reveals large esophageal varices with red wale signs.
Stool microscopy reveals large, yellow-brown eggs with a prominent lateral spine, and rectal biopsy shows granulomas surrounding deposited eggs within the portal venules.
explanation: Schistosoma mansoni cercariae released by freshwater snails penetrate human skin during water contact. Adult worms reside in the mesenteric venous plexus, depositing eggs that embolize to the liver via the portal system. The granulomatous immune response to trapped eggs causes periportal (Symmers pipe-stem) fibrosis, leading to portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and esophageal varices.
keyFact: S. mansoni and S. japonicum cause hepatosplenic disease with portal hypertension (pipe-stem fibrosis). S. haematobium affects the bladder (hematuria, squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder). Egg morphology distinguishes species: S. mansoni has a lateral spine, S. japonicum has a small lateral knob, S. haematobium has a terminal spine.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcoholic Cirrhosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alcoholic cirrhosis causes portal hypertension and varices but shows diffuse hepatocyte damage with micronodular cirrhosis on biopsy, not periportal granulomas around helminth eggs.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatitis B Cirrhosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic hepatitis B causes cirrhosis and portal hypertension in endemic areas but shows hepatocyte necrosis with ground-glass hepatocytes on biopsy, not pipe-stem periportal fibrosis with ova.

wrongAnswers.name: Budd-Chiari Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Budd-Chiari syndrome causes hepatomegaly and ascites from hepatic vein thrombosis but presents acutely with tender hepatomegaly, caudate lobe hypertrophy, and absent hepatic vein flow on Doppler, not periportal fibrosis.

clues: A 55-year-old man from Southeast Asia who recently started high-dose corticosteroids for an autoimmune condition presents with worsening abdominal pain, diarrhea, and a new cough.
He has a history of intermittent urticarial rashes and loose stools over the past decade. He walked barefoot in rice paddies during his childhood and young adult life.

He appears acutely ill with temperature 39.5 C, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and wheezing bilaterally. A serpiginous, rapidly migrating urticarial track is visible on his lower abdomen (larva currens).
Peripheral eosinophilia is 25%. Chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates. Sputum Gram stain grows enteric gram-negative bacteria, suggesting bacterial translocation from the gut.
Stool examination and sputum both reveal filariform (L3) larvae of Strongyloides stercoralis, and duodenal aspirate shows rhabditiform larvae.
explanation: Strongyloides stercoralis is unique among helminths in its ability to complete its life cycle within the human host through internal autoinfection. Rhabditiform larvae in the gut can mature into infective filariform larvae that penetrate intestinal mucosa or perianal skin. Immunosuppression (especially corticosteroids) can trigger hyperinfection syndrome with massive larval burden, bacterial translocation, and disseminated disease.
keyFact: Strongyloides is unique for its autoinfection cycle, which can persist for decades. Hyperinfection syndrome occurs with immunosuppression (corticosteroids, HTLV-1). Eosinophilia may paradoxically decrease during hyperinfection. Larvae (not eggs) are found in stool. Screen and treat before immunosuppression in patients from endemic areas.

wrongAnswers.name: Hookworm
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hookworm enters through the skin and causes eosinophilia but cannot autoinfect, does not cause hyperinfection syndrome with immunosuppression, and stool shows eggs rather than larvae.

wrongAnswers.name: Ascariasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ascaris undergoes pulmonary migration causing eosinophilia and cough, but is acquired by oral ingestion, cannot autoinfect, and stool shows characteristic mammillated eggs rather than larvae.

wrongAnswers.name: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EGPA causes eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, and abdominal symptoms but is a vasculitis with no larvae on stool or sputum examination and presents with different systemic features.

clues: A 22-year-old college student originally from rural Guatemala presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure with no prior seizure history.
He immigrated to the United States three years ago and lived in a household where a family member worked as a pig farmer. He has no significant past medical history.
Neurological examination is non-focal after the postictal period resolves. He has a mild headache but no fever, nuchal rigidity, or papilledema.
CT head reveals multiple scattered, small, round, hypodense cystic lesions in the brain parenchyma, some with eccentric hyperdense dots inside and others with ring-like calcifications.

MRI with contrast shows multiple cysts in various stages: some with a visible scolex (bright dot within the cyst), surrounding edema around degenerating cysts, and punctate calcified remnants of prior resolved cysts.
explanation: Neurocysticercosis occurs when humans ingest Taenia solium eggs (from fecal-oral transmission, not from eating pork) and oncospheres penetrate the intestinal wall, disseminating hematogenously to the brain. The larvae encyst and can remain viable for years. Seizures typically occur during cyst degeneration, when the dying larva triggers a host inflammatory response.
keyFact: Neurocysticercosis is the most common cause of acquired epilepsy worldwide. It results from ingesting T. solium eggs (fecal-oral route), NOT from eating undercooked pork (which causes intestinal tapeworm). The scolex within a cyst on imaging is pathognomonic. Treatment depends on cyst stage, viability, and number.

wrongAnswers.name: Brain Metastases
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastatic lesions are typically solid, ring-enhancing masses at the gray-white junction with surrounding edema but lack the cystic morphology with internal scolex and the characteristic multi-stage evolution seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Toxoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CNS toxoplasmosis causes ring-enhancing lesions in immunocompromised (HIV) patients, typically in the basal ganglia, but this immunocompetent patient has cystic lesions with scolices rather than solid ring-enhancing masses.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculomas
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CNS tuberculomas are solid, ring-enhancing granulomas associated with systemic TB symptoms and basilar meningitis, not multi-stage cystic lesions with visible scolices in an otherwise well patient.

clues: A 45-year-old man recently released from a correctional facility presents with a persistent productive cough, intermittent fevers, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss of 10 kg over three months.
He was incarcerated in an overcrowded facility for two years. He has a history of injection drug use and is HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 310 cells/microL.
He appears cachectic and ill. Auscultation reveals diminished breath sounds and crackles at the right apex. Dullness to percussion is present over the right upper lung field.
Chest radiograph shows a right upper lobe cavitary lesion with surrounding infiltrate and possible tree-in-bud opacities. Interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON) is positive.
Three sputum samples show acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining, and nucleic acid amplification test confirms Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex.
explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is transmitted via inhaled droplet nuclei and establishes primary infection in the lungs. Cell-mediated immunity walls off organisms in granulomas, but reactivation occurs with immunosuppression. The predilection for the upper lobes in reactivation TB reflects higher oxygen tension. Cavitation results from caseous necrosis and liquefaction, making patients highly infectious.
keyFact: Reactivation TB classically involves the upper lobes (apical and posterior segments) with cavitary lesions. HIV is the strongest risk factor for reactivation. Diagnosis requires acid-fast bacilli on sputum smear and culture. RIPE therapy (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) is standard initial treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A cavitary lung mass can represent squamous cell carcinoma, but the acute infectious symptoms, upper lobe location with tree-in-bud opacities, positive IGRA, and AFB-positive sputum confirm an infectious rather than neoplastic etiology.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lung abscesses cause cavitary lesions with air-fluid levels, typically in dependent segments after aspiration, and grow polymicrobial anaerobic organisms rather than acid-fast bacilli.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumocystis Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PCP in HIV patients causes bilateral diffuse ground-glass infiltrates with dry cough and exertional hypoxia, not an upper lobe cavitary lesion with productive cough and AFB on smear.

clues: A 24-year-old woman presents with a progressively worsening fever, headache, and abdominal discomfort that have been escalating in a stepwise pattern over the past 10 days after returning from visiting family in South Asia.
She ate street food and drank unbottled water frequently during her trip. She did not receive any travel vaccinations before departure.
Temperature is 40.2 C with a paradoxical heart rate of 68 bpm. Abdomen is mildly distended with hepatosplenomegaly. Faint, blanching, salmon-colored macules are visible on the trunk.
WBC count is 3,200 with relative lymphocytosis. Liver transaminases are mildly elevated. Widal test shows elevated O and H antibody titers.
Blood cultures grow a gram-negative, non-lactose-fermenting bacillus identified as Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi on biochemical and serologic testing.
explanation: Salmonella Typhi is ingested through contaminated food or water, penetrates the intestinal mucosa, and is phagocytosed by macrophages. It survives intracellularly and disseminates via the reticuloendothelial system to the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. The stepwise fever pattern, relative bradycardia, and rose spots are classic clinical features of the bacteremic phase.
keyFact: Typhoid fever classically presents with stepwise fever, relative bradycardia (pulse-temperature dissociation), rose spots on the trunk, and hepatosplenomegaly. Intestinal perforation of Peyer patches is the most serious complication, typically in the third week. Blood culture is the gold standard for diagnosis during the first week.

wrongAnswers.name: Malaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malaria causes high fevers with rigors after tropical travel but produces cyclical fevers with chills and sweats, hemolytic anemia, and parasites on blood smear, not relative bradycardia, rose spots, or gram-negative bacilli on blood culture.

wrongAnswers.name: Dengue Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dengue causes fever and leukopenia after travel to endemic areas but presents with severe myalgia, retro-orbital pain, and thrombocytopenia, without the stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, or rose spots seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious Mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBV causes fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphocytosis but presents with prominent pharyngitis, atypical lymphocytes, and positive heterophile antibodies, not stepwise fever, rose spots, or gram-negative bacteremia.

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset fever, malaise, and a rapidly spreading skin eruption that developed over hours.
She has a longstanding history of plaque-type skin disease and recently stopped oral prednisone abruptly.
Examination reveals hundreds of small yellow-white pustules on a background of diffuse erythema involving the trunk and extremities; pustules appear sterile on bedside assessment.
CBC shows leukocytosis with neutrophilia; pustule cultures are negative; liver enzymes are mildly elevated.
Skin biopsy shows intraepidermal spongiform pustules of Kogoj — subcorneal neutrophilic collections without bacterial organisms.
explanation: Pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch type) is a severe, potentially life-threatening form of psoriasis characterized by sterile neutrophilic pustules on erythematous skin, often triggered by abrupt corticosteroid withdrawal. Biopsy showing spongiform pustules of Kogoj confirms the diagnosis.
keyFact: Abrupt systemic corticosteroid withdrawal is a classic trigger for generalized pustular psoriasis; pustules are always sterile.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AGEP is drug-induced and resolves spontaneously within 2 weeks; lacks prior psoriasis history and is not triggered by steroid withdrawal.

wrongAnswers.name: Impetigo
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Impetigo pustules yield positive bacterial cultures (Staph/Strep) and lack systemic toxicity or background diffuse erythema.

wrongAnswers.name: Disseminated gonococcal infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DGI pustules are acral, sparse, and occur with migratory arthritis and positive gonorrhea cultures, not confluent erythema with hundreds of pustules.

clues: A 7-year-old boy is brought in for multiple bumps on his trunk that his parents first noticed 3 months ago; some have become inflamed.
He regularly swims at a public pool, and a sibling developed similar lesions 2 months ago.
Examination reveals 15–20 flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules ranging 2–5 mm on the trunk and axillae, each with a central umbilication; no surrounding erythema or tenderness.
Dermatoscopy shows a central white amorphous structure surrounded by a crown of vessels in each papule.
Histologic section shows large intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusion bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies) within keratinocytes.
explanation: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus and presents as umbilicated flesh-colored papules transmitted by direct contact or fomites. The pathognomonic finding is Henderson-Paterson (molluscum) bodies on histology, representing large intracytoplasmic viral inclusion bodies.
keyFact: Central umbilication is the clinical hallmark; Henderson-Paterson bodies (intracytoplasmic inclusions) confirm the diagnosis histologically.

wrongAnswers.name: Verruca vulgaris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Warts are hyperkeratotic with black thrombosed capillary dots, lack central umbilication, and have a rough rather than smooth surface.

wrongAnswers.name: Folliculitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Folliculitis papules are centered on hair follicles, often tender and erythematous, and lack central umbilication.

wrongAnswers.name: Basal cell carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BCC occurs in adults with sun-damaged skin and has rolled pearly borders with telangiectasias, not multiple small umbilicated lesions in a child.

clues: A 67-year-old man presents with 3 days of sharp, intermittent pain along his right trunk; he has no visible lesions and denies trauma.
He has never received a varicella vaccine and had chickenpox as a child.

Examination reveals a unilateral band of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base from the right midback to the anterior chest, strictly following the T6 dermatome and not crossing the midline; mild fever is present.
Tzanck smear of a vesicle base shows multinucleated giant cells.
PCR of vesicle fluid is positive for varicella-zoster virus DNA.
explanation: Herpes zoster results from reactivation of latent VZV in a dorsal root ganglion, producing a painful dermatomal vesicular eruption that does not cross the midline. Multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear and VZV PCR confirm the diagnosis.
keyFact: Prodromal dermatomal pain preceding the rash by 1-5 days and strict unilateral dermatomal distribution are hallmarks of herpes zoster.

wrongAnswers.name: Contact dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Contact dermatitis is pruritic rather than burning/painful, is not dermatomal, and has no prodrome of lancinating pain before rash onset.

wrongAnswers.name: Herpes simplex virus infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV produces recurrent grouped vesicles but is not dermatomal and does not cause unilateral chest-to-back distribution in an older immunocompetent adult.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis causes non-vesicular confluent erythema and warmth without the dermatomal pattern or prodromal neuralgia.

clues: A 5-year-old girl presents with spreading crusted lesions on her face that started 4 days ago after a minor scratch.
A classmate at kindergarten had similar lesions recently.
Examination reveals honey-colored crusted plaques with shallow erosions beneath the crust around the nose and mouth; no fever or lymphadenopathy; lesions are mildly pruritic.
Gram stain of crust fluid shows gram-positive cocci in clusters.
Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus from the crusted lesion fluid.
explanation: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection most commonly caused by S. aureus or group A Streptococcus, presenting with honey-colored crusted lesions typically around the nose and mouth in children. Gram stain and culture confirm the causative organism.
keyFact: Honey-colored crusting around the nose and mouth in a school-age child is the classic presentation of non-bullous impetigo caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes.

wrongAnswers.name: Herpes labialis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Herpes labialis produces grouped clear vesicles on erythematous base at the vermilion border with burning/tingling prodrome, not honey-colored crusting.

wrongAnswers.name: Eczema herpeticum
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eczema herpeticum involves punched-out erosions on eczematous skin with systemic illness and requires antiviral treatment, not topical antibiotics.

wrongAnswers.name: Angular cheilitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Angular cheilitis is limited to the oral commissures, is associated with nutritional deficiency or Candida, and lacks the crusting and contagious spread pattern.

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with joint pain, fatigue, low-grade fevers, and a new rash on his chest that has been worsening over the past month.
He has no prior history of autoimmune disease; symptoms began approximately six months after starting a new cardiac medication for his arrhythmia.

Examination shows bilateral symmetric swelling and tenderness of the wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints; a pleural friction rub is heard at the left lung base; there is no malar rash, oral ulcers, or alopecia.
ANA is positive at 1:320 with a homogeneous pattern; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are negative; complement C3 and C4 levels are normal; CBC shows mild leukopenia.

Anti-histone antibody titer is strongly positive at greater than five times the upper limit of normal, and all symptoms and serologic abnormalities resolve completely within eight weeks of stopping the cardiac medication.
explanation: Drug-induced lupus is caused by medications such as hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, and minocycline, producing ANA positivity (typically anti-histone) with lupus-like symptoms that resolve upon drug discontinuation. Anti-dsDNA is typically absent and complement is usually normal, distinguishing it from idiopathic SLE.
keyFact: Anti-histone antibodies are the hallmark of drug-induced lupus; anti-dsDNA and hypocomplementemia are characteristically absent (unlike idiopathic SLE).

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Idiopathic SLE typically has positive anti-dsDNA antibodies, low complement levels, and does not resolve upon stopping a medication.

wrongAnswers.name: Rosacea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rosacea causes facial flushing and papulopustules but does not cause joint pain, positive ANA, or anti-histone antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatomyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatomyositis causes heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and proximal muscle weakness with elevated CK, not a malar rash with anti-histone antibodies.

clues: A 29-year-old man presents with a recurrent well-demarcated lesion on his lower lip; he has had 3 similar episodes over the past year, each resolving with residual discoloration.
He recalls a nearly identical lesion in the exact same location 6 months ago, also occurring shortly after taking an NSAID.
Examination reveals a hyperpigmented oval plaque 2 cm in diameter with a dusky center on the lower lip; mild burning sensation; no other lesions elsewhere; no Nikolsky sign.
Complete blood count, liver function tests, and ANA are all normal; biopsy of the lesion edge shows interface dermatitis with melanin incontinence and eosinophilic infiltrate.
Patch testing with the suspected NSAID applied to the lesion site produces a flare reaction at that site only, with no reaction at uninvolved skin.
explanation: Fixed drug eruption is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction that recurs at the same skin site(s) each time the offending drug is taken, leaving residual post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. NSAIDs, sulfonamides, and tetracyclines are common culprits.
keyFact: Recurrence at the identical anatomic site with each drug re-exposure and residual hyperpigmentation between episodes are pathognomonic of fixed drug eruption.

wrongAnswers.name: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SJS involves widespread blistering, mucosal sloughing, systemic toxicity, and Nikolsky sign — not a single recurrent lesion at a fixed location.

wrongAnswers.name: Erythema multiforme
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Erythema multiforme produces target lesions at multiple sites (acral predominance), not a single recurring hyperpigmented patch at one location.

wrongAnswers.name: Melanoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Melanoma does not appear acutely after drug ingestion, does not resolve between episodes, and does not have a temporal drug relationship.

clues: A 34-year-old woman with longstanding type 1 diabetes presents with slowly enlarging, painless skin changes on her shins noticed 1 year ago; she is concerned about cosmetic appearance.
The lesions have not changed despite improved glucose control over the past 6 months.
Examination reveals bilateral pretibial plaques with a waxy yellow-brown center, atrophic shiny surface, and violaceous borders; telangiectasias are visible within the plaques; no ulceration.
HbA1c is 9.2%; skin biopsy shows palisading granulomas with areas of collagen necrobiosis surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes and plasma cells in the dermis.
Elastic fiber staining shows marked loss of elastic fibers within the necrobiotic zones.
explanation: Necrobiosis lipoidica is a granulomatous skin condition strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, presenting as waxy atrophic yellow-brown pretibial plaques with violaceous borders. Biopsy shows palisading granulomas with collagen necrobiosis and loss of elastic fibers.
keyFact: Waxy atrophic yellow-brown pretibial plaques with violaceous borders in a patient with diabetes — NLD does not reliably improve with glucose control.

wrongAnswers.name: Pretibial myxedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pretibial myxedema occurs in Graves disease and produces non-pitting waxy induration but lacks the yellow atrophic center and diabetic association.

wrongAnswers.name: Granuloma annulare
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Granuloma annulare forms ring-shaped dermal papules, typically on dorsal hands and feet, without the waxy atrophy or yellow coloration of NLD.

wrongAnswers.name: Erythema nodosum
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Erythema nodosum is tender subcutaneous nodules on the shins that resolve within weeks; it lacks the atrophic waxy surface and chronic indolent course.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing nodule on his cheek that appeared 6 weeks ago; he is concerned it could be cancer.
He has a long history of sun exposure and works outdoors.
Examination shows a firm, flesh-colored to pink dome-shaped nodule 1.8 cm with a central keratin-filled crater on sun-exposed skin; no regional lymphadenopathy.
Dermoscopy reveals a central keratin mass surrounded by radially arranged vessels.
Excisional biopsy shows a crateriform architecture with a central keratin plug and atypical squamous epithelium with glassy pink cytoplasm at the shoulder; overall architecture remains symmetric.
explanation: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing crateriform squamous proliferation that classically develops over weeks on sun-exposed skin of older adults, with a central keratin-filled crater. Though often considered a variant of well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, its rapid growth followed by potential spontaneous involution and symmetric crateriform architecture help distinguish it histologically.
keyFact: Rapid growth over weeks to months followed by potential spontaneous regression, with a central keratin plug and crateriform architecture on biopsy, characterizes keratoacanthoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous cell carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCC grows more slowly, lacks the symmetric crateriform architecture, and does not spontaneously regress; however, KA is often treated as SCC due to histologic overlap.

wrongAnswers.name: Basal cell carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BCC grows slowly over years with rolled pearly borders and telangiectasias, lacks a central keratin crater, and does not show the rapid growth kinetics of KA.

wrongAnswers.name: Sebaceous cyst
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sebaceous cysts grow slowly, have a punctum but not a central keratin crater on pathology, and lack the atypical squamous epithelium on biopsy.

clues: A 26-year-old man presents with an intensely pruritic, erythematous lesion on his foot that has been slowly advancing for 5 days.
He recalls walking barefoot on a tropical beach during a recent trip abroad.
Examination reveals a serpiginous, erythematous, raised track 3 mm wide and 8 cm long on the dorsum of the right foot, advancing a few millimeters per day; no systemic symptoms.
CBC shows peripheral eosinophilia (12%); no larvae visible on skin scraping.
Dermoscopy reveals a serpiginous, thread-like larval track within the epidermis, and skin biopsy shows an eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate along a migratory tunnel.
explanation: Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by hookworm larvae (Ancylostoma braziliense or caninum) that penetrate human skin but cannot complete their life cycle, migrating through the epidermis and producing a characteristic advancing serpiginous track. Diagnosis is clinical; oral ivermectin or albendazole is curative.
keyFact: A serpiginous, migratory, pruritic epidermal track following tropical beach exposure is pathognomonic of cutaneous larva migrans (dog/cat hookworm).

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea pedis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea pedis produces scaling between toes or on the sole, is not serpiginous or migratory, and responds to antifungals rather than antiparasitics.

wrongAnswers.name: Scabies
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scabies burrows are in finger webs, wrists, and genitals; they do not produce a single advancing linear track and are caused by Sarcoptes scabiei, not nematode larvae.

wrongAnswers.name: Myiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myiasis causes a furuncular nodule with a central breathing pore from a fly larva, not a serpiginous epidermal track.

clues: A 45-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use presents with fragile skin and recurrent blistering on sun-exposed areas over the past several months.
He takes no photosensitizing medications; he was recently diagnosed with hepatitis C.
Examination shows tense bullae and erosions on the dorsal hands and forearms, skin fragility with minor trauma, milia, hyperpigmentation, and facial hypertrichosis.
Urine is brown and fluoresces coral-pink under Wood lamp examination; AST and ALT are elevated.
Urine uroporphyrin levels are markedly elevated; plasma fluorescence emission peak at 619 nm.
explanation: Porphyria cutanea tarda is caused by deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase leading to accumulation of uroporphyrins, presenting with photosensitive blistering on sun-exposed skin, skin fragility, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation. Triggers include alcohol, hepatitis C, iron overload, and estrogens; coral-pink urine fluorescence and elevated urine uroporphyrins are diagnostic.
keyFact: Coral-pink fluorescence of urine under Wood lamp and elevated urine uroporphyrins are the key diagnostic findings in PCT; hepatitis C and alcohol are the most common triggers.

wrongAnswers.name: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBA is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease with anti-type VII collagen antibodies; it is not triggered by sunlight and lacks porphyrin elevation.

wrongAnswers.name: Pseudoporphyria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pseudoporphyria (e.g., from NSAIDs or tanning beds) has identical clinical appearance but normal porphyrin levels — distinguishable only by urine porphyrin testing.

wrongAnswers.name: Bullous pemphigoid
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bullous pemphigoid occurs in elderly patients with tense bullae on an urticarial base, is not sun-distributed, and is associated with anti-BP180/BP230 antibodies, not porphyrins.

clues: A 22-year-old college student is brought in by his parents after a significant decline in functioning over the past 8 months; he has become increasingly isolated and his academic performance has deteriorated.
He has had no substance use and no prior psychiatric history.
He reports hearing two voices that comment on his actions; he shows flat affect, poverty of speech, and marked social withdrawal; he believes his thoughts are being broadcast on television.
Brain MRI is unremarkable; TSH and metabolic panel are normal; urine toxicology is negative.
Structured interview shows continuous auditory hallucinations and thought broadcasting coexisting with flat affect and avolition for over 6 months, with no mood episodes explaining the full picture.
explanation: Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of continuous disturbance including at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms) with significant functional decline. The diagnosis requires exclusion of mood disorders, substances, and medical conditions.
keyFact: Schizophrenia requires symptoms for at least 6 months (vs. schizophreniform at 1-6 months); negative symptoms (flat affect, alogia, avolition) and functional decline are hallmarks.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophreniform disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophreniform disorder is identical in symptoms but lasts 1-6 months; this patient's 8-month course meets criteria for schizophrenia.

wrongAnswers.name: Brief psychotic disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than 1 month and resolves completely; the 8-month continuous course rules this out.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar disorder with psychotic features
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bipolar psychosis occurs exclusively during mood episodes (manic or depressive); this patient has no current or past mood episodes to account for the full duration.

clues: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the ED after 5 weeks of bizarre behavior including talking to unseen people and refusing to eat because she believes the food is poisoned.
Her prior functioning was good and onset was abrupt with no prodrome; she has no prior psychiatric history.
She has auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, and disorganized thinking on mental status exam.
MRI brain is normal; urine drug screen is negative; there is no history of sustained mood episodes; physical exam and labs are unremarkable.
Structured assessment shows active psychotic symptoms present for 5 weeks with good premorbid functioning and no mood disorder accounting for the presentation.
explanation: Schizophreniform disorder presents with the same symptoms as schizophrenia but lasts between 1 and 6 months. Good prognostic features include rapid onset, good premorbid functioning, and confusion/perplexity at the height of symptoms. If symptoms persist beyond 6 months, the diagnosis is revised to schizophrenia.
keyFact: Schizophreniform disorder = schizophrenia symptoms lasting 1-6 months; good prognosis features include abrupt onset and preserved premorbid function.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia requires a minimum of 6 months of continuous symptoms; this patient's 5-week course does not yet meet that threshold.

wrongAnswers.name: Brief psychotic disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Brief psychotic disorder resolves within 1 month; this patient has had symptoms for 5 weeks with no sign of resolution.

wrongAnswers.name: Delusional disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Delusional disorder involves non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations or disorganization; this patient has florid hallucinations and thought disorganization.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents describing chronic low mood and decreased energy that have affected her work and relationships; she is not sure when it started but thinks it has been "years."
She has never had a 2-month period free of these symptoms.
Mental status exam shows a dysphoric, tearful affect with psychomotor slowing; speech is soft and monotone; she is oriented and alert with no suicidal ideation; cognition is intact.
PHQ-9 score is 11 (moderate); TSH is normal; CBC is unremarkable.

Structured interview reveals depressed mood present more days than not for over 2 years, with poor appetite, insomnia, low energy, and hopelessness — never symptom-free for more than 2 months during that period.
explanation: Persistent depressive disorder (formerly dysthymia) is characterized by chronically depressed mood lasting at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children) with at least 2 of: poor appetite/overeating, insomnia/hypersomnia, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, or hopelessness. It differs from MDD by chronicity rather than severity.
keyFact: PDD requires depressed mood for at least 2 years with no 2-month symptom-free period; 'double depression' occurs when MDD episodes are superimposed on PDD.

wrongAnswers.name: Major depressive disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDD requires at least 5 symptoms for 2 weeks including anhedonia or depressed mood; this patient has subthreshold chronic symptoms without meeting the full MDD 5-symptom threshold.

wrongAnswers.name: Cyclothymic disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cyclothymic disorder involves alternating hypomanic and depressive symptoms (neither meeting full criteria) over 2 years; this patient has no hypomanic periods.

wrongAnswers.name: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adjustment disorder requires an identifiable stressor and does not persist beyond 6 months after the stressor ends; this patient has chronic symptoms without a precipitating stressor.

clues: A 31-year-old woman presents with marked irritability, depressed mood, and emotional outbursts that have been disrupting her work and relationships for the past six months.
She notes the symptoms reliably begin five to seven days before her period and resolve completely within two to three days of menstrual onset; she feels entirely normal for the rest of the cycle.
Mental status exam during the symptomatic phase shows irritable and labile affect with tearfulness and psychomotor agitation; she is oriented and denies suicidal ideation.
Prospective daily symptom ratings over two consecutive menstrual cycles document symptoms exclusively in the luteal phase with complete remission in the follicular phase.
Serum progesterone levels confirm ovulation timing, and symptom onset correlates precisely with the post-ovulatory progesterone rise in each tracked cycle.
explanation: PMDD is characterized by luteal-phase mood and physical symptoms that reliably remit within days of menstrual onset, confirmed by prospective symptom tracking over at least 2 cycles. It requires at least 5 symptoms including at least one of: marked mood swings, irritability, depressed mood, or anxiety/tension.
keyFact: PMDD requires prospective confirmation of luteal-phase symptoms over 2 cycles; complete symptom remission in the follicular phase distinguishes it from premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying mood disorder.

wrongAnswers.name: Premenstrual syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PMS involves milder symptoms that do not meet the 5-symptom threshold or cause significant functional impairment required for PMDD.

wrongAnswers.name: Major depressive disorder with premenstrual exacerbation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: In MDD, depressive symptoms are present throughout the cycle and worsen premenstrually; PMDD has complete symptom absence in the follicular phase.

wrongAnswers.name: Generalized anxiety disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GAD involves persistent, pervasive anxiety not confined to the luteal phase; PMDD symptoms are strictly cyclic and resolve with menstruation.

clues: A 19-year-old man presents with significant distress about his appearance that has led to social isolation and multiple medical consultations for a concern that physicians have found minimal.
He has withdrawn from school to avoid being seen by others.
He spends 3–4 hours per day examining his face in mirrors, picking at his skin, and comparing his appearance to others; he is certain others stare at his 'disfigured' face; his insight is poor.
Y-BOCS modified scale score is 32 (severe); he has had no response to two dermatological interventions.

Structured psychiatric evaluation shows preoccupation with a perceived defect that is not observable or appears minimal to others, with repetitive checking behaviors causing marked distress and functional impairment.
explanation: Body dysmorphic disorder involves persistent preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in physical appearance that are not observable or appear minimal to others, driving repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, skin picking, reassurance seeking) and causing significant distress and functional impairment. It has high rates of social avoidance and poor insight.
keyFact: BDD is classified with OCD-related disorders; poor insight or delusional beliefs about the perceived defect do not preclude the diagnosis — SSRIs and CBT are first-line treatments.

wrongAnswers.name: Social anxiety disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Social anxiety involves fear of negative evaluation in social situations broadly, not a specific preoccupation with a perceived physical flaw and associated repetitive checking behaviors.

wrongAnswers.name: OCD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OCD obsessions are not restricted to appearance preoccupation; BDD is a distinct diagnosis in the OCD spectrum with appearance-specific obsessions and compulsions.

wrongAnswers.name: Delusional disorder, somatic type
wrongAnswers.whyNot: When BDD beliefs are held with delusional intensity, DSM-5 specifies poor insight/delusional BDD rather than a separate delusional disorder diagnosis, avoiding double diagnosis.

clues: A 33-year-old healthcare worker presents with recurrent episodes of unexplained hypoglycemia over 2 years requiring multiple hospitalizations; extensive endocrine workup has been unremarkable.
She has vascular access and detailed medical knowledge; her symptoms resolve promptly once hospitalized and she seeks further workup.
Exam during episodes shows diaphoresis and confusion that resolve with glucose administration; she appears well between episodes.
Serum during episodes shows insulin levels >1000 µU/mL with suppressed C-peptide; no insulinoma is found on imaging; an insulin pen is found in her belongings.
Psychiatric evaluation reveals a pattern of falsifying symptoms and inducing illness in herself without external incentive; she derives psychological benefit from assuming the sick role.
explanation: Factitious disorder imposed on self (Munchausen syndrome) involves deliberately falsifying or inducing physical symptoms to assume the sick role, without external incentives. The combination of exogenous insulin use with suppressed C-peptide, medical knowledge, and repeated hospitalizations at multiple facilities is classic. Distinguishing from malingering requires no identifiable external gain.
keyFact: Suppressed C-peptide with very high insulin in recurrent hypoglycemia indicates exogenous insulin; factitious disorder is diagnosed when there is no external incentive (unlike malingering).

wrongAnswers.name: Insulinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Insulinoma produces high insulin AND high C-peptide during hypoglycemia (both endogenous); suppressed C-peptide with high insulin confirms exogenous insulin source.

wrongAnswers.name: Malingering
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malingering involves intentional symptom production for identifiable external gain (financial, legal); factitious disorder is driven by psychological need to assume the sick role.

wrongAnswers.name: Somatic symptom disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Somatic symptom disorder involves genuine perceived distress about real or minor symptoms without deliberate induction; the lab evidence here confirms intentional insulin self-administration.

clues: A 48-year-old man admitted for pneumonia becomes acutely agitated and confused on hospital day 3; he has a history of heavy daily alcohol use.
He last drank alcohol 72 hours ago on admission.
Vital signs show HR 128, BP 168/96, temperature 38.4°C, diaphoresis; he has visual hallucinations of insects on the walls, is disoriented to place and time, and his hands are tremulous.
CIWA-Ar score is 24; electrolytes show hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia; blood alcohol level is 0.

Continuous EEG monitoring shows generalized fast beta activity with intermittent delta slowing, and benzodiazepine administration produces immediate reduction in CIWA-Ar score and autonomic parameters.
explanation: Delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal delirium) is the most severe manifestation of alcohol withdrawal, typically appearing 48-96 hours after the last drink, with global confusion, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, fever), tremor, and hallucinations. It carries a mortality rate of up to 5% if untreated; benzodiazepines are the cornerstone of treatment.
keyFact: Delirium tremens peaks at 48-96 hours after last drink; it is distinguished from milder withdrawal by global confusion/delirium (not just autonomic symptoms) and requires aggressive benzodiazepine treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcohol hallucinosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alcohol hallucinosis produces auditory (not visual) hallucinations within 12-24 hours of cessation with clear sensorium — no delirium or autonomic instability.

wrongAnswers.name: Wernicke encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wernicke's triad is ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion from thiamine deficiency — not autonomic hyperactivity; onset is not temporally tied to alcohol cessation.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic delirium
wrongAnswers.whyNot: While infection can trigger delirium, the temporal relationship to alcohol cessation at 72 hours, tremor, and CIWA score of 24 point to withdrawal as the primary etiology.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with anxiety, tremor, insomnia, and perceptual disturbances 5 days after an abrupt medication change; she has a history of chronic anxiety managed pharmacologically for years.
Her long-acting anxiolytic was stopped abruptly without a taper.
Vital signs: HR 112, BP 154/92, temperature 37.8°C; she has severe anxiety, sweating, tremor, and one witnessed generalized seizure.
EEG performed post-seizure shows diffuse slowing without focal abnormality; electrolytes and glucose are normal; urine toxicology is negative for other substances.

Urine benzodiazepine metabolite levels are undetectable at presentation, and EEG during the seizure shows generalized epileptiform discharges without focal abnormality, in a patient with documented chronic benzodiazepine use who abruptly stopped.
explanation: Benzodiazepine withdrawal resembles alcohol withdrawal (both act on GABA-A receptors) and can produce life-threatening seizures, delirium, and autonomic instability, particularly with abrupt discontinuation of long-acting agents after prolonged use. Treatment involves reinstitution of a benzodiazepine followed by gradual taper.
keyFact: Benzodiazepine withdrawal can be fatal (seizures, delirium) and is treated similarly to alcohol withdrawal — with benzodiazepines (GABA-A agonism); abrupt cessation of long-term use is high-risk.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcohol withdrawal
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alcohol withdrawal has an identical clinical picture but requires recent alcohol use/cessation; urine toxicology and history confirm benzodiazepine, not alcohol, as the agent.

wrongAnswers.name: Opioid withdrawal
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Opioid withdrawal causes yawning, lacrimation, piloerection, and GI symptoms but is not life-threatening and does not cause seizures.

wrongAnswers.name: Panic disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Panic disorder causes episodic anxiety without the temporal relationship to drug cessation, autonomic instability, or seizures.

clues: A 16-year-old girl is brought in by her mother for patchy hair loss noticed over the past 4 months.
She subsequently discloses she pulls her hair compulsively while doing homework, often without awareness, and has tried to stop without success.
Examination shows irregular, non-scarring patches of hair loss on the vertex and temporal scalp; hairs within the patches are of varying lengths with broken hairs; no scaling or erythema.
Hair pull test is negative; dermoscopy shows broken hairs of differing lengths and 'tulip hairs' without exclamation mark hairs.
Structured interview using a validated hair-pulling scale shows recurrent hair pulling with repeated failed attempts to stop, causing clinically significant distress.
explanation: Trichotillomania is characterized by recurrent, compulsive pulling of one's own hair resulting in noticeable hair loss, with repeated failed attempts to stop, causing distress or functional impairment. The irregular non-scarring alopecia with broken hairs of varying lengths and absence of exclamation mark hairs (seen in alopecia areata) are key clinical clues.
keyFact: Hairs of varying broken lengths within alopecic patches without scaling, exclamation mark hairs, or positive pull test in a distressed adolescent — trichotillomania; N-acetylcysteine and habit reversal training are treatments.

wrongAnswers.name: Alopecia areata
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alopecia areata produces sharply demarcated round patches with exclamation mark hairs at the periphery and a positive pull test; it is autoimmune and not related to behavior.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea capitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea capitis causes scaling, broken 'black dot' hairs (endothrix), and KOH-positive fungal elements; it is infectious and not behavior-related.

wrongAnswers.name: Telogen effluvium
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Telogen effluvium produces diffuse non-patchy shedding following physiologic stress (illness, surgery, delivery), not focal irregular patches with broken hairs.

clues: A 24-year-old woman presents with multiple chronic wounds on her face and arms that have not responded to typical wound care; she describes an irresistible urge preceding each episode.
She spends 1–2 hours per day picking at real or perceived skin irregularities and has tried to stop multiple times without success.
Examination reveals numerous excoriations in various stages of healing, some crusted and some fresh, over the cheeks, chin, forearms, and upper arms; a few lesions show signs of secondary infection.
Toxicology is negative for stimulants; she has no tactile hallucinations or delusional infestation; no primary dermatological condition explains the lesions.
Structured interview using a validated skin-picking impact scale shows recurrent skin picking causing tissue damage, with repeated failed cessation attempts and significant psychosocial impairment.
explanation: Excoriation disorder (skin picking disorder) is an OCD-spectrum disorder characterized by recurrent picking of skin causing tissue damage, repeated failed attempts to stop, and significant distress or functional impairment. It must be distinguished from picking secondary to substances, delusional parasitosis, or primary dermatological disease.
keyFact: Excoriation disorder is classified in the OCD spectrum; negative toxicology (ruling out stimulant-induced picking) and absent tactile hallucinations/delusions are key to diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Delusional parasitosis (Ekbom syndrome)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Delusional parasitosis involves a fixed false belief of infestation with parasites; these patients pick because they believe they are removing bugs, not due to compulsion around skin texture.

wrongAnswers.name: Stimulant-induced skin picking
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Amphetamine and cocaine use can cause intense skin picking and formication; negative urine toxicology excludes this cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatitis artefacta
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatitis artefacta involves deliberate self-infliction with denial of self-causation; excoriation disorder patients acknowledge picking but cannot stop, and the behavior is compulsive rather than intentionally deceptive.

clues: A 6-year-old boy is brought in by his parents because he has had multiple episodes of bacterial pneumonia and meningitis since infancy despite being fully vaccinated.
His older sibling died in infancy from overwhelming bacterial sepsis; his parents are consanguineous.
Physical examination between infections is entirely normal with no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or skin findings; growth parameters are at the 50th percentile.
CH50 is undetectable and AH50 is severely reduced; immunoglobulin levels and lymphocyte subsets are normal.

Quantitative assay of the complement protein at the convergence point of all three activation pathways returns undetectable, and gene sequencing reveals a homozygous loss-of-function variant in the corresponding gene.
explanation: C3 deficiency is the most severe complement deficiency because C3 is the central convergence point of all complement pathways; affected patients suffer recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae, meningococcus) despite vaccination. Both CH50 and AH50 are undetectable, and specific C3 quantification confirms the diagnosis.
keyFact: C3 deficiency causes susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria via all three pathways; both CH50 and AH50 are undetectable (vs. terminal complement deficiencies where only CH50 is low).

wrongAnswers.name: Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Terminal complement (MAC) deficiency causes susceptibility specifically to Neisseria species (meningococcus, gonococcus), not recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia; CH50 is low but AH50 is normal.

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked agammaglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLA causes absent B cells and very low immunoglobulins; this patient has normal immunoglobulin levels, pointing to complement rather than antibody deficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: Common variable immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID features low immunoglobulins and poor vaccine responses; normal Ig levels and absent CH50/AH50 distinguish C3 deficiency.

clues: A 9-year-old girl presents with severe eczematous dermatitis since infancy, recurrent skin infections, and unusually widespread viral skin infections despite no known immunodeficiency.
She has also had recurrent sinopulmonary infections and food allergies; her parents are non-consanguineous and no family members have a similar condition.
Examination shows eczematous changes with widespread flat viral papules; serum IgE is markedly elevated (>2000 IU/mL); IgM is low; eosinophil count is elevated.
Lymphocyte subset analysis shows severely reduced CD8+ T cells and NK cells; B cell numbers are low with poor switched memory B cells.
Gene sequencing reveals a large homozygous deletion in the responsible gene; protein expression is absent on flow cytometry.
explanation: DOCK8 deficiency is an autosomal recessive combined immunodeficiency presenting with severe eczema, recurrent bacterial and viral skin infections (particularly cutaneous viral dissemination), elevated IgE, and low IgM, with reduced CD8+ T cells and NK cells. It mimics hyper-IgE syndrome but lacks the skeletal and dental abnormalities and has distinct genetic and cellular features.
keyFact: DOCK8 deficiency: severe eczema + cutaneous viral dissemination (molluscum, HSV) + elevated IgE + low CD8/NK cells — distinguish from Job syndrome by absent bone/dental anomalies and homozygous DOCK8 deletion.

wrongAnswers.name: Job syndrome (STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome (Job) features coarse facies, retained primary teeth, skeletal abnormalities, and 'cold' abscesses — absent in DOCK8 deficiency, which also has low CD8 T cells not seen in Job.

wrongAnswers.name: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: WAS causes eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections in males; thrombocytopenia and absence of viral susceptibility pattern distinguish it from DOCK8.

wrongAnswers.name: Atopic dermatitis without immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atopic dermatitis alone does not cause invasive bacterial infections, markedly elevated IgE >2000, or severely reduced CD8/NK cell counts.

clues: A 2-month-old infant presents with diffuse skin changes, failure to thrive, and diarrhea since birth; he has been hospitalized for two serious infections.
Family history reveals consanguinity in the parents.
Examination reveals generalized scaling erythroderma, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy; the infant appears cachectic.
CBC shows severe lymphopenia with absence of B cells; the few T cells present are oligoclonal with a Th2 skew; IgG, IgA, IgM are very low, but IgE is paradoxically markedly elevated.
Genetic testing reveals compound heterozygous hypomorphic mutations in RAG1, and bone marrow biopsy shows absent lymphoid precursors.
explanation: Omenn syndrome is a leaky SCID variant caused by hypomorphic mutations in RAG1/RAG2 (or other V(D)J recombination genes), resulting in partial lymphocyte development with oligoclonal, autoreactive T cells causing an erythrodermatous, inflammatory phenotype. It presents in infancy with erythroderma, hepatosplenomegaly, elevated IgE, absent B cells, and oligoclonal T cells — a paradoxically inflammatory form of SCID.
keyFact: Omenn syndrome = leaky SCID with erythroderma, hepatosplenomegaly, elevated IgE, absent B cells, and oligoclonal T cells — caused by hypomorphic RAG1/2 mutations; requires HSCT.

wrongAnswers.name: Severe combined immunodeficiency (classic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Classic SCID presents with infections and lymphopenia but lacks the inflammatory erythroderma and paradoxically elevated IgE, which reflect the partial (leaky) lymphocyte development of Omenn syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Graft-versus-host disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GvHD presents similarly with erythroderma and hepatitis but follows transfusion or transplant exposure; this infant has no such history and has RAG mutations.

wrongAnswers.name: Netherton syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Netherton syndrome (SPINK5 mutation) causes ichthyosis linearis circumflexa and trichorrhexis invaginata but no immunodeficiency, absent B cells, or lymphopenia.

clues: A 10-year-old boy has recurrent skin and lung infections since infancy along with chronic eczema; the infections have unusual characteristics that prompted immunologic evaluation.
He has had multiple fractures with minimal trauma, and several primary teeth persist alongside permanent teeth.

Physical examination reveals coarse facial features, a broad nasal bridge, retained primary teeth, hyperextensible joints, and eczematous skin with scarring from prior 'cold' abscesses that lacked warmth or erythema.
Serum IgE is 4,500 IU/mL (normal <100); peripheral eosinophilia is present; NIH scoring tool yields >40; chest CT shows bilateral pneumatoceles from prior staphylococcal pneumonias.
Gene sequencing reveals a dominant negative heterozygous mutation in STAT3; functional assay shows absent STAT3 phosphorylation.
