explanation: Job syndrome (autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome) is caused by dominant-negative STAT3 mutations and presents with the triad of recurrent 'cold' (non-inflammatory) skin abscesses, pneumonias with pneumatoceles, and markedly elevated IgE, along with coarse facies, retained primary teeth, and skeletal abnormalities. STAT3 signaling defects impair Th17 differentiation, reducing IL-17-mediated neutrophil recruitment.
keyFact: Job syndrome: 'cold' abscesses + pneumatoceles + eczema + IgE >2000 + coarse facies + retained primary teeth — caused by dominant-negative STAT3 mutations impairing Th17/IL-17 axis.

wrongAnswers.name: DOCK8 deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DOCK8 deficiency also causes elevated IgE and eczema but lacks coarse facies, retained teeth, skeletal abnormalities, and pneumatoceles; it has prominent cutaneous viral dissemination instead.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic granulomatous disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CGD causes catalase-positive organism infections and granuloma formation without elevated IgE, coarse facies, or retained teeth.

wrongAnswers.name: Atopic dermatitis with secondary infections
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atopic dermatitis does not cause cold abscesses, pneumatoceles, coarse facies, or retained teeth; IgE elevation in atopy is not as extreme as in Job syndrome.

clues: A 12-year-old previously healthy boy becomes severely ill with high fevers, abdominal pain, and profound fatigue shortly after contracting mononucleosis.
Two maternal uncles died in childhood following mononucleosis-like illnesses.
He appears acutely ill with hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and diffuse petechiae on examination.

CBC shows pancytopenia; ferritin is 48,000 ng/mL; triglycerides are elevated; LFTs are in the thousands; NK cell cytotoxicity assay is severely impaired; bone marrow biopsy shows hemophagocytosis; EBV viral load is 2 million copies/mL.
SH2D1A (SAP) gene sequencing reveals a hemizygous nonsense mutation; SAP protein expression is absent on flow cytometry of T and NK cells.
explanation: X-linked lymphoproliferative disease is caused by mutations in SH2D1A (encoding SAP), an adapter protein critical for cytotoxic T and NK cell responses to EBV-infected B cells. Patients are well until primary EBV infection triggers fulminant hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, aplastic anemia, or dysgammaglobulinemia. SAP-deficient cytotoxic lymphocytes cannot control EBV, leading to uncontrolled lymphoproliferation.
keyFact: XLP (SAP deficiency): healthy boy who develops fatal EBV-triggered hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis — absent SAP protein on T/NK cells confirms diagnosis; HSCT is curative.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary (familial) HLH is caused by perforin/granzyme pathway mutations and presents in infants without a specific EBV trigger; XLP is specifically EBV-triggered in previously healthy older boys.

wrongAnswers.name: Severe EBV mononucleosis in an immunocompetent host
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Immunocompetent mononucleosis is self-limited; bone marrow failure, extreme ferritin, and family history of male deaths from mono indicate an underlying immunodeficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: Common variable immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID causes antibody deficiency and can include EBV complications but does not present with fulminant HLH from primary EBV infection and does not show absent SAP protein.

clues: A 4-year-old girl presents with 10 days of high spiking fevers and irritability.
She has had no recent travel, no sick contacts, and no known immunodeficiency.
Examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and diffuse petechiae; she has developed encephalopathy.
CBC shows pancytopenia; ferritin is 28,000 ng/mL; triglycerides are 480 mg/dL; fibrinogen is low; LFTs are markedly elevated; NK cell cytotoxicity is severely impaired.
Bone marrow aspirate shows macrophages engulfing red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets; soluble IL-2 receptor (CD25) is markedly elevated.
explanation: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of cytotoxic T cells and macrophages, resulting in a cytokine storm with characteristic findings of fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hemophagocytosis on biopsy. Diagnosis requires 5 of 8 HLH-2004 criteria; dexamethasone and etoposide are the cornerstone of treatment.
keyFact: HLH diagnosis requires 5/8 criteria: fever, splenomegaly, bicytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia/hypofibrinogenemia, hemophagocytosis, low NK activity, ferritin >500, elevated soluble CD25; ferritin >10,000 is highly suggestive.

wrongAnswers.name: Sepsis with DIC
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sepsis-associated DIC has elevated fibrinogen initially (acute phase reactant), not low fibrinogen, and lacks hemophagocytosis on marrow biopsy and severely impaired NK cytotoxicity.

wrongAnswers.name: Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Leukemia can cause cytopenias and hepatosplenomegaly but does not produce ferritin in the tens of thousands, hemophagocytosis, or hypertriglyceridemia as primary features.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Systemic JIA can trigger macrophage activation syndrome (secondary HLH) but would have quotidian fevers and arthritis as preceding features; this case lacks those and is primary HLH.

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with recurrent 30- to 90-minute episodes of flushing, abdominal cramping, wheezing, and palpitations occurring monthly for the past two years.
She has identified multiple food triggers but has no known allergies and no prior atopic history.
Between episodes, exam is entirely normal; during a witnessed episode in clinic, she develops diffuse urticaria, tachycardia, and mild hypotension.
Baseline serum tryptase is 7 ng/mL; during an acute episode, serum tryptase rises to 28 ng/mL, exceeding the threshold of baseline x 1.2 + 2; twenty-four-hour urine N-methylhistamine is elevated.
Bone marrow biopsy shows no mast cell aggregates, no aberrant CD25 expression on mast cells, and KIT D816V mutation is negative.
explanation: Mast cell activation syndrome is characterized by recurrent episodes of symptoms involving 2+ organ systems consistent with mast cell mediator release, elevation of a validated urinary or serum mast cell mediator during episodes, and response to anti-mediator therapy — without meeting criteria for systemic mastocytosis (no KIT D816V, <25% mast cell aggregates on biopsy).
keyFact: MCAS diagnosis requires: (1) recurrent multisystem symptoms, (2) elevated mast cell mediator during episode (tryptase >2+20% above baseline), and (3) response to anti-mediator therapy; distinguish from systemic mastocytosis by negative KIT D816V and normal marrow.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic mastocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Systemic mastocytosis requires KIT D816V mutation, mast cell aggregates >25% on marrow biopsy, and Darier sign; negative mutation and normal marrow in this case distinguish MCAS.

wrongAnswers.name: Carcinoid syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoid syndrome causes flushing and diarrhea via serotonin and is diagnosed by elevated 24-hour urine 5-HIAA, not elevated tryptase/n-methylhistamine.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary angioedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HAE causes recurrent angioedema via bradykinin (not histamine), does not cause urticaria or flushing, and is associated with low C4 and C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency.

clues: A 22-year-old woman develops hives and localized swelling on her hands within minutes of certain environmental exposures; she has had this for 8 months and it resolves spontaneously.
The hives resolve within 30–60 minutes of rewarming; she had a similar episode of generalized hives and near-syncope while swimming in a cold lake.
Exam between episodes is entirely normal; skin dermographism testing is negative; ANA, CBC, and thyroid function are normal; no family history of similar symptoms.
An ice cube wrapped in thin plastic is applied to the forearm for 5 minutes and removed; a wheal forms at the contact site within 10 minutes of rewarming.
A cold stimulation threshold test shows wheal formation at temperatures below 18°C with no wheal at warmer temperatures.
explanation: Cold urticaria is a physical urticaria in which IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation is triggered by skin cooling, producing wheals at rewarmed sites. The ice cube test (wheal within 10 minutes of removing the ice) is the standard diagnostic test. Swimming in cold water is dangerous as full-body exposure can trigger systemic anaphylaxis.
keyFact: Cold urticaria: positive ice cube test (wheal on rewarming, not during cold exposure); swimming in cold water can cause fatal anaphylaxis — patients should carry epinephrine.

wrongAnswers.name: Cholinergic urticaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholinergic urticaria is triggered by elevated body temperature (exercise, hot showers) producing small 1-3 mm wheals with surrounding flare, not cold-contact wheals.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary angioedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HAE causes non-pruritic swelling without urticaria and does not respond to antihistamines; it is not triggered by cold contact and has no wheal response on ice cube testing.

wrongAnswers.name: Familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FCAS causes delayed (1-3 hours) urticarial-appearing papules, arthralgias, and fever after generalized cold air exposure (not contact) and is caused by NLRP3 mutations.

clues: A 28-year-old woman has had four episodes of urticaria, throat tightening, and near-syncope over the past year; each episode occurs during physical activity.
Two of the four episodes occurred after eating wheat within 2–4 hours before running; episodes do not occur when she exercises without eating beforehand or eats wheat without exercising.
Examination between episodes is unremarkable; skin is clear with no urticaria, angioedema, or dermatographism; lungs are clear and cardiovascular exam is normal.
A supervised exercise challenge performed 2 hours after eating wheat reproduces urticaria, bronchospasm, and hypotension; exercise alone (fasting) produces no reaction.
Neither the suspected food nor exercise alone triggers a reaction — only the combination within a specific time window reproduces the full anaphylactic syndrome.
explanation: Exercise-induced anaphylaxis, particularly the food-dependent variant, occurs when exercise is performed after ingesting a specific food (most commonly wheat via omega-5 gliadin, or shellfish); neither the food nor exercise alone triggers a reaction. Elevated specific IgE to omega-5 gliadin and a positive provocation test confirm wheat-dependent EIAn.
keyFact: Food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis: neither food nor exercise alone triggers reaction — only the combination does; omega-5 gliadin (Tri a 19) IgE is the key sensitizer for wheat-associated EIAn.

wrongAnswers.name: IgE-mediated wheat allergy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Classic wheat allergy would cause anaphylaxis upon wheat ingestion alone, without requiring the exercise cofactor; this patient tolerates wheat at rest without reaction.

wrongAnswers.name: Cholinergic urticaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholinergic urticaria produces small punctate wheals triggered by any heat/sweat and is not food-dependent; it does not cause anaphylaxis with angioedema and hypotension.

wrongAnswers.name: Exercise-induced asthma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Exercise-induced bronchospasm is isolated to the airway without urticaria, angioedema, or hypotension, and is not food-dependent.

clues: A 28-year-old woman mentions to her doctor that she occasionally notices a pink tinge to her urine, though she feels entirely well otherwise.
Her father and brother have had similar urinary findings; none of them have hearing loss or visual problems.
Exam is unremarkable; blood pressure is 110/68 mmHg; there is no peripheral edema, rash, or joint findings; abdominal and cardiovascular exams are normal.
Kidney biopsy shows normal light microscopy and immunofluorescence; electron microscopy reveals diffusely thin glomerular basement membranes (mean 140 nm; normal >250 nm) without lamellation.
Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous COL4A3 variant; audiometry and ophthalmologic exam are normal.
explanation: Thin basement membrane disease (benign familial hematuria) is the most common cause of persistent glomerular hematuria, caused by heterozygous mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4, producing diffusely thin GBM on electron microscopy without the multilamellated basket-weave appearance of Alport syndrome. Most patients have isolated hematuria with preserved renal function.
keyFact: TBMD: diffusely thin GBM on EM (no basket-weave), persistent glomerular hematuria, normal proteinuria and renal function, family history — heterozygous COL4A3/A4 mutation; Alport has multilamellated GBM and hearing/vision loss.

wrongAnswers.name: Alport syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alport syndrome shows multilamellated basket-weave GBM on EM, and presents with sensorineural hearing loss and lens abnormalities (anterior lenticonus); TBMD has thin but not lamellated GBM and no extrarenal features.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence; TBMD has negative immunofluorescence; IgA nephropathy typically has episodes of gross hematuria with URIs.

wrongAnswers.name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS presents with significant proteinuria (often nephrotic range) and progressing renal insufficiency; TBMD has minimal proteinuria and stable renal function.

clues: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes presents with fever, flank pain, and gross hematuria.
She has a history of heavy NSAID use and recurrent urinary tract infections.
Exam reveals costovertebral angle tenderness on the right; she passes visible tissue fragments in her urine; no suprapubic tenderness or abdominal guarding.

CT of the abdomen shows irregular medullary calcifications in a 'ring' pattern and filling defects in the renal pelvis; intravenous pyelogram shows the 'lobster claw' or 'signet ring' sign in the collecting system.
Histology of the passed tissue shows necrotic renal medullary papillae.
explanation: Renal papillary necrosis results from ischemic infarction of the renal medullary papillae, classically associated with diabetes mellitus, analgesic nephropathy (NSAIDs), sickle cell disease, and obstructive uropathy. IVP or CT urogram demonstrates the 'signet ring' or 'lobster claw' sign as sloughed papillae create filling defects in the collecting system.
keyFact: RPN mnemonic — DANSE: Diabetes, Analgesics (NSAIDs), Nephrolithiasis/obstruction, Sickle cell, Extra (TB, alcohol); 'signet ring' sign on IVP is classic.

wrongAnswers.name: Transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TCC of the renal pelvis also causes filling defects on urogram but lacks the bilaterality, tissue sloughing, ring calcifications, and underlying risk factors of papillary necrosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Complicated pyelonephritis alone
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pyelonephritis can coexist with RPN but does not explain the ring calcifications, filling defects, or tissue passage; RPN is a separate complication with distinct imaging findings.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal infarction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Renal infarction causes cortical (not medullary papillary) ischemia and presents with flank pain and elevated LDH but does not produce the medullary calcifications or signet ring sign.

clues: A 72-year-old man develops livedo reticularis, acute kidney injury, and distal extremity changes 2 weeks after a vascular procedure.
He has a history of extensive atherosclerotic disease and was recently anticoagulated.

Exam shows livedo reticularis on the lower extremities, cyanotic toes ('blue toes') with palpable pedal pulses, and Hollenhorst plaques (yellow refractile deposits) at retinal arteriolar bifurcations on fundoscopy.
Creatinine rises from 1.4 to 3.8 mg/dL over 4 weeks; urinalysis shows mild proteinuria but no active sediment; eosinophilia is present (14%).
Kidney biopsy shows needle-shaped clefts within arterioles (dissolved cholesterol crystals) surrounded by a foreign-body giant cell reaction and concentric fibrosis.
explanation: Cholesterol embolization syndrome occurs when atherosclerotic plaque ruptures (spontaneously or after arterial instrumentation/anticoagulation), releasing cholesterol crystals that lodge in small arteries, causing ischemia, inflammation, and organ dysfunction. Classic findings include livedo reticularis, blue toes, renal insufficiency with a subacute course, eosinophilia, and needle-shaped clefts on biopsy.
keyFact: Cholesterol embolization: subacute renal failure + livedo reticularis + blue toes after arterial procedure + eosinophilia + needle clefts on biopsy — no specific treatment; prognosis is poor.

wrongAnswers.name: Contrast nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Contrast nephropathy peaks at 48-72 hours post-procedure and resolves within 2 weeks; it does not cause livedo reticularis, blue toes, or eosinophilia.

wrongAnswers.name: Polyarteritis nodosa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PAN involves medium-vessel necrotizing arteritis with aneurysms on angiography; it does not follow arterial instrumentation and lacks needle-shaped cholesterol clefts on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute interstitial nephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIN causes eosinophiluria, white cell casts, and rash in the setting of drug exposure; it lacks livedo reticularis, blue toes, and cholesterol crystal emboli on biopsy.

clues: A 58-year-old woman with osteoporosis presents with nausea, confusion, and weakness; she has been taking over-the-counter antacids very frequently for chronic GI complaints.
She also takes calcium carbonate supplements several times daily beyond the recommended dose.
Exam reveals mild dehydration and diffuse abdominal tenderness; no palpable masses.
Labs show calcium 14.2 mg/dL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), bicarbonate 32 mEq/L, PTH <5 pg/mL; PTH-related peptide is negative; 25-OH vitamin D is normal.
Serum PTH-related peptide is negative, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is normal, ACE level is normal, and all calcium and alkalosis resolve after cessation of calcium carbonate and IV hydration.
explanation: Milk-alkali syndrome (calcium-alkali syndrome) is caused by excessive ingestion of calcium and absorbable alkali (commonly calcium carbonate), producing the triad of hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and renal insufficiency. Low PTH distinguishes it from hyperparathyroidism; the syndrome is now the third most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients due to widespread calcium supplement use.
keyFact: Milk-alkali triad: hypercalcemia + metabolic alkalosis + renal failure from excess calcium carbonate — PTH is suppressed (distinguishing it from hyperparathyroidism); resolves with stopping supplements and IV hydration.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary hyperparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary hyperparathyroidism has elevated or inappropriately normal PTH with hypercalcemia; in milk-alkali syndrome, PTH is suppressed due to the direct calcium load suppressing parathyroid glands.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypercalcemia of malignancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malignancy-related hypercalcemia is driven by PTHrP or osteolysis; PTHrP is negative here, no malignancy is found, and direct calcium supplement history explains the syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes hypercalcemia via elevated 1,25-OH2 vitamin D (calcitriol) from granuloma macrophages; 25-OH vitamin D is normal and 1,25-OH2 would be elevated, not consistent with this presentation.

clues: A 45-year-old man with Crohn disease and a history of ileal resection presents with rapidly progressive renal failure; he has not had kidney stones previously.
His fat malabsorption has been poorly controlled since his ileal resection, and he reports a recent diet high in leafy greens and nuts.
Exam reveals mild flank tenderness and peripheral edema; no costovertebral angle tenderness.
Urinalysis shows numerous envelope-shaped and dumbbell-shaped crystals; 24-hour urine oxalate is markedly elevated at 180 mg/day (normal <40); urine calcium is low.
Kidney biopsy shows birefringent crystals in tubular lumens with surrounding tubular injury and interstitial fibrosis; polarized light microscopy shows fan-shaped birefringence.
explanation: Oxalate nephropathy results from hyperoxaluria — in this case enteric hyperoxaluria from ileal disease/resection causing fat malabsorption. Unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium in the gut, leaving free oxalate available for colonic absorption. Birefringent calcium oxalate crystals in tubules on biopsy with polarized light microscopy are diagnostic.
keyFact: Enteric hyperoxaluria: ileal disease/resection → fat malabsorption → intraluminal calcium bound to fatty acids → free oxalate absorbed → oxalate nephropathy; low urine calcium + high urine oxalate.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary hyperoxaluria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary hyperoxaluria is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder (AGXT mutation) presenting in childhood with recurrent stones and progressive renal failure; this adult with ileal resection has secondary (enteric) hyperoxaluria.

wrongAnswers.name: Uric acid nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Uric acid nephropathy produces amorphous or needle-shaped (not birefringent envelope) crystals and is associated with tumor lysis syndrome or gout, not fat malabsorption.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-induced crystalline nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug crystals (acyclovir, indinavir) produce different crystal morphologies in a drug-exposure context; the ileal resection history and fat malabsorption clearly indicate enteric oxalate as the cause.

clues: A 9-year-old boy presents with a purpuric rash on his lower body, abdominal pain, and joint swelling following a recent upper respiratory illness.
The rash appeared first on the buttocks and lower extremities and is non-blanching.
Examination reveals palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, swollen ankles and knees, and mild abdominal tenderness; blood pressure is 118/78 mmHg.
Urinalysis shows 3+ hematuria and 2+ proteinuria; creatinine is mildly elevated at 0.9 mg/dL; serum IgA is elevated; complement levels (C3, C4) are normal; ANA and ANCA are negative.
Kidney biopsy shows mesangial proliferation on light microscopy with dominant mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence and mesangial electron-dense deposits on electron microscopy.
explanation: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is a small-vessel vasculitis mediated by IgA1 immune complexes, presenting with the tetrad of palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and nephritis. Renal involvement (present in ~50%) is the primary determinant of long-term outcome; biopsy shows mesangial IgA deposits identical to IgA nephropathy.
keyFact: IgA vasculitis nephritis = HSP nephritis: mesangial IgA deposits on IF (identical to IgA nephropathy) with normal complement; the systemic tetrad (purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, nephritis) distinguishes it from isolated IgA nephropathy.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy has identical renal biopsy findings but presents as isolated renal disease (gross hematuria with URIs) without the systemic purpura, abdominal pain, and arthritis of IgA vasculitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSGN occurs 1-3 weeks after strep infection with low C3, subepithelial 'humps' on EM, and granular IgG/C3 on IF — not mesangial IgA; it lacks the purpura and arthritis.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningococcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningococcemia causes petechiae/purpura but with septic shock, CSF findings, and no nephritis with IgA deposits; it would not present with arthritis and abdominal pain in this pattern.

clues: A 34-year-old woman presents with bilateral leg edema, hypertension, and frothy urine; she was found to have microscopic hematuria on a routine check 3 years ago.
She has a known chronic viral hepatitis infection.
Exam reveals 2+ pitting edema bilaterally, blood pressure 148/92, and no rash or joint findings.
Urinalysis shows nephrotic-range proteinuria (4.8 g/day) and hematuria with red cell casts; creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL; C3 and C4 are low; cryoglobulins are detected.

Kidney biopsy shows mesangial and endocapillary hypercellularity with 'tram-track' double-contour GBM duplication on silver stain; immunofluorescence shows granular IgG, IgM, and C3 deposits; EM shows subendothelial electron-dense deposits.
explanation: Membranoproliferative GN pattern (now classified by immune complex vs. complement-mediated) presents with mixed nephrotic-nephritic features, low complement, and tram-track GBM on silver stain. Secondary MPGN from hepatitis C and cryoglobulinemia is the most common cause, with subendothelial immune complex deposits on EM.
keyFact: MPGN tram-track sign (double contour GBM) on silver stain = mesangial interposition; HCV + low C3 + low C4 + cryoglobulins = secondary immune complex MPGN.

wrongAnswers.name: Lupus nephritis class IV
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus nephritis can mimic MPGN but requires positive ANA, anti-dsDNA, and low complement from immune complex deposition; the patient has no SLE clinical features and has HCV.

wrongAnswers.name: Dense deposit disease (C3 GN)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dense deposit disease is complement-mediated (not immune complex), with isolated C3 deposits on IF (no IgG/IgM) and intramembranous 'sausage-shaped' dense deposits on EM.

wrongAnswers.name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS shows segmental sclerosis on light microscopy without mesangial hypercellularity, tram-track duplication, or immune complex deposits on IF.

clues: A 61-year-old man presents with progressive leg swelling, fatigue, and foamy urine over the past three months.
He has no history of diabetes and reports unintentional weight loss of 10 pounds.
Exam reveals 2+ pitting edema bilaterally, blood pressure 148/92, and no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.

Serum free kappa/lambda ratio is markedly elevated at 480; urine immunofixation reveals free kappa light chains; kidney biopsy light microscopy shows nodular mesangial sclerosis resembling diabetic nephropathy, but Congo red stain is negative.

Immunofluorescence shows linear staining of glomerular and tubular basement membranes with anti-kappa antibody only; electron microscopy shows granular electron-dense deposits along basement membranes.
explanation: Light chain deposition disease is caused by non-fibrillar monoclonal light chain deposition (usually kappa) in the kidney, producing nodular glomerulosclerosis resembling diabetic nephropathy on light microscopy. Congo red negativity (no amyloid fibrils), linear light chain staining on IF, and granular deposits on EM distinguish it from AL amyloidosis.
keyFact: LCDD vs. AL amyloidosis: both cause nodular glomerulosclerosis from monoclonal light chains — LCDD is Congo red negative with linear kappa IF staining; amyloidosis is Congo red positive with apple-green birefringence.

wrongAnswers.name: AL amyloidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AL amyloidosis also deposits light chains in kidney but forms fibrils: Congo red positive with apple-green birefringence; LCDD deposits are non-fibrillar (Congo red negative).

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetic nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diabetic nephropathy produces Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules with similar light microscopy but has IgG/C3/albumin 'leaky' trapping on IF and no monoclonal light chain staining.

wrongAnswers.name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS does not produce nodular mesangial sclerosis, PAS-positive nodules, or monoclonal light chain linear staining on immunofluorescence.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with 4 days of fatigue, oliguria, and confusion after a gastrointestinal illness with bloody diarrhea one week ago.
The diarrhea was associated with undercooked beef consumption at a barbecue.
Exam reveals pallor, petechiae, and mild confusion; she appears volume-depleted.

Labs show hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 38,000/µL, creatinine 4.6 mg/dL, LDH 1,840 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable; peripheral smear shows numerous schistocytes; Coombs test negative; PT/PTT and fibrinogen normal; stool Shiga toxin assay is positive.
ADAMTS13 activity is >10%, and peripheral smear shows fragmented red cells with normal coagulation studies.
explanation: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is the pathophysiologic process underlying HUS and TTP, characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), thrombocytopenia, and end-organ damage from platelet-fibrin thrombi in small vessels. STEC-HUS (the most common TMA in children) follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection; ADAMTS13 >10% distinguishes it from TTP.
keyFact: STEC-HUS triad: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI after bloody diarrhea; ADAMTS13 activity >10% distinguishes HUS from TTP (<10%); schistocytes + negative Coombs confirm MAHA.

wrongAnswers.name: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP has severely reduced ADAMTS13 activity (<10%) causing systemic platelet microthrombi; it predominantly causes neurologic symptoms and fever rather than AKI, and lacks the diarrheal prodrome.

wrongAnswers.name: DIC
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DIC causes consumption coagulopathy with elevated PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimer; TMA/HUS has normal coagulation studies despite thrombocytopenia.

wrongAnswers.name: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia without hemolytic anemia or AKI; no schistocytes are present and LDH/haptoglobin are normal.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with severe fatigue, diffuse bone pain, and markedly decreased urine output over the past week.
He was recently hospitalized for a cardiac catheterization and received IV contrast; he has been mildly volume-depleted.
Exam reveals pallor, mild costovertebral angle tenderness, and trace peripheral edema; he appears euvolemic now after IV fluids, but urine output remains low.

Serum creatinine is 6.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.4); urine dipstick shows only 1+ protein, but sulfosalicylic acid test shows 8 g/day of proteinuria; urine immunofixation reveals massive free kappa light chains.
Kidney biopsy shows tubules obstructed by large, fractured, eosinophilic casts with surrounding giant cell reaction; anti-kappa staining is positive within the casts.
explanation: Cast nephropathy (myeloma kidney) results from free monoclonal light chains coprecipitating with Tamm-Horsfall protein in the distal tubule, forming obstructive casts with a surrounding giant cell reaction. It is the most common cause of renal failure in multiple myeloma and is exacerbated by dehydration, IV contrast, hypercalcemia, and NSAIDs.
keyFact: Myeloma cast nephropathy: fractured eosinophilic casts with giant cell reaction + anti-light chain positive staining on IF + massive free light chains on urine IFE; dipstick underestimates because it detects albumin, not light chains.

wrongAnswers.name: Light chain deposition disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LCDD causes nodular glomerulosclerosis from non-fibrillar light chain deposition in GBM/TBM without tubular cast obstruction or giant cell reaction — presents with chronic proteinuria rather than acute tubular obstruction.

wrongAnswers.name: AL amyloidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AL amyloidosis deposits fibrillar light chains as amyloid (Congo red positive) causing nodular GN, not obstructive tubular casts with giant cell reaction.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute tubular necrosis from IV contrast
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Contrast nephropathy causes ATN with granular casts but not the large fractured eosinophilic casts with giant cell reaction and anti-kappa positivity characteristic of myeloma kidney.

clues: A 48-year-old man presents with months of diarrhea, weight loss, and diffuse joint pain.
He also reports episodic low-grade fever and darkening of sun-exposed skin.
Exam reveals hyperpigmented skin patches, a distended abdomen with mild diffuse tenderness, and peripheral lymphadenopathy.
Labs show iron-deficiency anemia, low albumin, elevated ESR, and steatorrhea on stool fat testing; small-bowel biopsy shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria.
PCR of biopsy tissue is positive for Tropheryma whipplei DNA.
explanation: Whipple disease is a rare systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, classically presenting with the tetrad of diarrhea, weight loss, arthralgias, and fever. Diagnosis requires small-bowel biopsy demonstrating PAS-positive macrophages, confirmed by PCR.
keyFact: PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the small-bowel lamina propria are the hallmark of Whipple disease; CNS involvement can occur and is treated with long-term TMP-SMX.

wrongAnswers.name: Celiac disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Celiac causes malabsorption and villous atrophy but does not produce PAS-positive macrophages, fever, hyperpigmentation, or lymphadenopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Crohn disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Crohn can cause diarrhea and arthralgias but does not produce PAS-positive macrophages on biopsy and would show granulomatous transmural inflammation.

wrongAnswers.name: Intestinal lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma can cause weight loss and lymphadenopathy but biopsy would show malignant lymphoid cells, not PAS-positive macrophages.

clues: A 42-year-old man presents with recurrent severe heartburn and epigastric pain that has not improved despite multiple courses of standard acid-suppressive therapy.
He has had three duodenal ulcers in the past two years and describes persistent watery diarrhea that worsens with meals.
Exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness; no palpable abdominal masses; rectal exam is guaiac-positive.
Fasting serum gastrin is markedly elevated at 900 pg/mL (normal <100); secretin stimulation test causes a paradoxical rise in gastrin exceeding 200 pg/mL above baseline.
CT scan identifies a 1.5 cm enhancing mass in the gastrinoma triangle (pancreatic head region).
explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) that produces massive gastric acid hypersecretion, leading to refractory peptic ulcers and diarrhea. The secretin stimulation test is diagnostic when fasting gastrin is elevated.
keyFact: ZES should be suspected when ulcers are refractory, multiple, or distal; 25% of cases are associated with MEN1 syndrome, so screen for hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumors.

wrongAnswers.name: H. pylori-related peptic ulcer disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: H. pylori causes peptic ulcers but does not produce markedly elevated gastrin levels or respond paradoxically to secretin stimulation.

wrongAnswers.name: NSAID-induced ulcers
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NSAID ulcers occur in the setting of NSAID use and resolve with cessation; they do not cause diarrhea or hypergastrinemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic mastocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mastocytosis can cause acid hypersecretion via histamine but would show urticaria pigmentosa, elevated tryptase, and mast cell infiltration on biopsy—not elevated gastrin.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids equally over the past 18 months, along with regurgitation of undigested food.
She reports nighttime regurgitation causing coughing episodes and has lost 8 kg; she denies heartburn or acid taste.
Examination reveals mild cachexia; auscultation of the chest reveals a succussion splash in the left lower chest; no neck masses or lymphadenopathy are present.
Timed barium esophagram shows a persistent barium column at five minutes with smooth bird-beak tapering at the gastroesophageal junction and no contrast passage into the stomach.
High-resolution manometry demonstrates an elevated integrated relaxation pressure of 22 mmHg and 100 percent failed peristalsis across all ten test swallows in the esophageal body.
explanation: Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, resulting in absent peristalsis and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax. High-resolution manometry is the gold standard for diagnosis.
keyFact: Achalasia presents with dysphagia to both solids AND liquids from the outset, which distinguishes it from mechanical obstruction (solids first). The bird-beak sign on barium swallow is classic.

wrongAnswers.name: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Esophageal cancer causes progressive dysphagia typically starting with solids and would show an irregular mucosal lesion on endoscopy, not a smooth bird-beak narrowing.

wrongAnswers.name: Diffuse esophageal spasm
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diffuse esophageal spasm causes intermittent chest pain and dysphagia with preserved peristalsis on some swallows; manometry would show premature contractions, not absent peristalsis.

wrongAnswers.name: Scleroderma esophagopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scleroderma causes hypomotility of the distal esophagus and a patulous LES (low pressure), not the elevated LES pressure and failed relaxation seen in achalasia.

clues: A 55-year-old obese man presents for evaluation of chronic heartburn and acid regurgitation that he has managed with over-the-counter antacids for over 20 years.
He is a white male with a BMI of 34 and a strong family history of esophageal cancer; he has smoked a half pack per day for 15 years.
Examination shows an obese man with mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation; no lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or abdominal masses are appreciated.
Upper endoscopy reveals a salmon-colored mucosal tongue extending 4 cm above the gastroesophageal junction, distinct from the surrounding pale squamous epithelium.
Biopsies from the salmon-colored segment show goblet cells interspersed among columnar epithelium on H&E staining, with Alcian blue highlighting the acidic mucin within the goblet cells.
explanation: Barrett esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD in which the normal squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells. It carries a risk of progression to esophageal adenocarcinoma.
keyFact: Barrett esophagus requires both endoscopic evidence of columnar-lined esophagus AND histologic confirmation of intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells). Surveillance intervals depend on the presence and grade of dysplasia.

wrongAnswers.name: Erosive esophagitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Erosive esophagitis shows mucosal breaks or ulcerations on endoscopy without intestinal metaplasia on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Esophageal adenocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adenocarcinoma would show a discrete mucosal irregularity or mass with malignant glandular cells on biopsy, not metaplasia without dysplasia.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastric inlet patch
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A gastric inlet patch is a congenital ectopic gastric mucosa patch in the proximal esophagus, not salmon-colored mucosa at the GEJ with goblet cells.

clues: A 38-year-old man with known inflammatory bowel disease presents with fatigue, pruritus, and right upper quadrant discomfort.
He has ulcerative colitis diagnosed 10 years ago, currently in remission.
Exam reveals jaundice and mild hepatomegaly; no stigmata of chronic liver disease; there are no spider angiomata, palmar erythema, or ascites.
MRCP shows multifocal beaded strictures and dilatations of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.
Liver biopsy shows periductal 'onion-skin' fibrosis around bile ducts.
explanation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic progressive cholestatic liver disease characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the bile ducts, strongly associated with ulcerative colitis. MRCP showing multifocal biliary strictures is diagnostic.
keyFact: PSC is strongly associated with IBD (especially UC) and carries an elevated risk of cholangiocarcinoma; patients require surveillance colonoscopy due to increased colorectal cancer risk even when UC is quiescent.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary biliary cholangitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary biliary cholangitis predominantly affects middle-aged women, involves small intrahepatic ducts, shows anti-mitochondrial antibodies, and is not associated with IBD.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Autoimmune hepatitis presents with predominantly hepatocellular (elevated AST/ALT) rather than cholestatic pattern and shows plasma cell infiltration on biopsy, not periductal fibrosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary sclerosing cholangitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary sclerosing cholangitis results from an identifiable cause (e.g., choledocholithiasis, ischemia) and lacks the association with IBD or the diffuse beaded bile duct appearance.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue, jaundice, and diffuse arthralgias for 3 months.
She has a history of autoimmune thyroiditis and no prior liver disease.
Exam shows jaundice, spider angiomata, and tender hepatomegaly; no Kayser-Fleischer rings are visible.
Labs show ALT 680 U/L, AST 590 U/L, elevated total bilirubin; ANA titer is 1:320, anti-smooth muscle antibody is positive, serum IgG is 2,800 mg/dL; ceruloplasmin is normal.
Liver biopsy shows interface hepatitis with a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and rosette formation of hepatocytes.
explanation: Autoimmune hepatitis is an immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that predominantly affects young women and is associated with other autoimmune conditions. Diagnosis is based on characteristic autoantibodies, elevated IgG, and interface hepatitis on biopsy.
keyFact: Autoimmune hepatitis Type 1 is characterized by ANA and ASMA positivity; Type 2 by anti-LKM1 antibody. First-line treatment is prednisone plus azathioprine.

wrongAnswers.name: Wilson disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wilson disease presents in young patients but would show Kayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin, elevated urine copper, and neuropsychiatric features—autoantibodies would be absent.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic hepatitis C
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hepatitis C can cause elevated transaminases but would be identified by anti-HCV antibody and HCV RNA, without the high-titer ANA/ASMA or elevated IgG characteristic of AIH.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-induced liver injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DILI typically has a temporal relationship to a causative drug and resolves with discontinuation; positive autoantibodies and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate on biopsy favor AIH over DILI.

clues: A 32-year-old woman on oral contraceptives presents with sudden-onset severe right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and abdominal distension.
She has a history of polycythemia vera.
Exam shows an enlarged, tender liver, ascites, prominent dilated abdominal wall veins, and pedal edema.

Liver function tests show mildly elevated transaminases and elevated bilirubin; Doppler ultrasound of the liver shows absent flow in the hepatic veins with a characteristic 'spider-web' collateral pattern.
CT with contrast shows thrombosis of all three hepatic veins with caudate lobe hypertrophy (spared because it drains directly into the IVC via separate veins).
explanation: Budd-Chiari syndrome results from hepatic venous outflow obstruction, most commonly due to thrombosis of the hepatic veins. It classically presents with the triad of abdominal pain, ascites, and hepatomegaly, and is associated with prothrombotic states.
keyFact: The caudate lobe hypertrophies in Budd-Chiari syndrome because it drains directly into the IVC via separate veins and is spared from venous obstruction. Always evaluate for underlying thrombophilia (JAK2 mutation, antiphospholipid syndrome).

wrongAnswers.name: Right heart failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Right heart failure causes hepatic congestion but would present with JVD, peripheral edema, and signs of cardiac disease without isolated hepatic vein thrombosis on imaging.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute viral hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute hepatitis causes transaminase elevation and jaundice but does not produce ascites acutely or show hepatic vein thrombosis on Doppler ultrasound.

wrongAnswers.name: Portal vein thrombosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Portal vein thrombosis causes portal hypertension with ascites but spares hepatic venous outflow; Doppler would show thrombosis in the portal vein, not the hepatic veins.

clues: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe periumbilical abdominal pain that began 4 hours ago.
He was on warfarin but had a supratherapeutic INR managed by holding doses for several days; he has a history of peripheral vascular disease.

Examination shows a soft, non-distended abdomen with only mild diffuse tenderness and no peritoneal signs; the pain appears disproportionately severe relative to the benign abdominal findings; heart rhythm is irregularly irregular.
CT angiography of the abdomen reveals an abrupt filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery with absent distal flow; serum lactate is 5.8 mmol/L.
Surgical exploration reveals hemorrhagic, non-viable jejunal segments with absent mesenteric arterial pulsation, and histology of the resected bowel shows transmural coagulative necrosis.
explanation: Acute mesenteric ischemia due to SMA embolism most commonly arises from a cardiac source (atrial fibrillation). The hallmark is severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical exam; lactic acidosis and CT angiography confirm the diagnosis.
keyFact: Pain out of proportion to physical exam findings is the classic teaching point for acute mesenteric ischemia. Elevated lactate is a late sign indicating bowel infarction; early diagnosis before lactate rises is critical for survival.

wrongAnswers.name: Small bowel obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SBO causes crampy pain with distension, high-pitched bowel sounds, and dilated loops with air-fluid levels on imaging—not a vascular filling defect on CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic dissection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aortic dissection causes tearing back pain radiating to the chest and would show a dissection flap on CT, not an isolated SMA occlusion.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic colitis affects the watershed areas of the colon (splenic flexure, sigmoid) and presents with bloody diarrhea, not sudden severe periumbilical pain from SMA territory ischemia.

clues: A 30-year-old Peace Corps volunteer who spent 18 months in Southeast Asia presents with chronic diarrhea, bloating, and weight loss for 6 months since returning.
He has had no improvement despite a gluten-free diet trial.
Exam shows glossitis, pallor, and diffuse abdominal distension.
Labs show folate and B12 deficiency with macrocytic anemia; small-bowel biopsy shows partial villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes; anti-tTG IgA is negative.
Biopsy shows villous blunting with chronic inflammatory infiltrate throughout the entire small intestine — both proximal and distal — rather than isolated to the proximal duodenum.
explanation: Tropical sprue is a malabsorption syndrome affecting long-term residents of or travelers to tropical regions, caused by colonization of the small intestine with enteric bacteria. It presents with chronic diarrhea, folate/B12 deficiency, and partial villous atrophy on biopsy.
keyFact: Unlike celiac disease, tropical sprue is negative for anti-tTG antibodies and improves with tetracycline plus folate. The geographic exposure history is key to diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Celiac disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Celiac disease presents with similar biopsy findings but requires positive serologic markers (anti-tTG, anti-endomysial IgA) and improvement with a gluten-free diet, not antibiotics.

wrongAnswers.name: Giardiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Giardia causes malabsorptive diarrhea but is identified by stool antigen testing or biopsy showing trophozoites; stool studies were negative in this case.

wrongAnswers.name: Whipple disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Whipple disease presents with PAS-positive macrophages on biopsy and systemic features (arthritis, fever, CNS involvement), not the geographic history and response to tetracycline seen in tropical sprue.

clues: A 24-year-old man with a history of asthma and seasonal allergies presents with intermittent solid food dysphagia and two episodes of food impaction requiring endoscopic removal.
Symptoms have been present for 3 years; he takes a daily PPI with only partial relief.
Physical exam reveals mild eczematous patches on the antecubital fossae; oropharynx is clear; there is no cervical lymphadenopathy; abdomen is soft and nontender.
Esophageal biopsies from the proximal and distal esophagus show a peak eosinophil count of 22 eosinophils per high-power field after a 2-month PPI trial.
Skin prick testing shows multiple food and environmental allergen sensitivities; the eosinophilic infiltration persists despite adequate acid suppression.
explanation: Eosinophilic esophagitis is an immune-mediated esophageal disease driven by food allergens, presenting with dysphagia and food impaction in young atopic males. Diagnosis requires ≥15 eosinophils/HPF on biopsy after a PPI trial to exclude GERD-related eosinophilia.
keyFact: EoE diagnosis requires ≥15 eosinophils/HPF on esophageal biopsy AFTER a PPI trial. The endoscopic triad of rings, furrows, and white exudates is characteristic but not universally present.

wrongAnswers.name: Peptic stricture from GERD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GERD-related strictures are smooth, tapered, and located at the GEJ; biopsy would not show eosinophilic infiltration, and PPI therapy would provide significant relief.

wrongAnswers.name: Schatzki ring
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A Schatzki ring is a thin mucosal ring at the GEJ causing intermittent dysphagia but lacks the endoscopic features of rings/furrows throughout the esophagus or eosinophilic infiltration on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Achalasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Achalasia causes dysphagia to both solids and liquids with manometric evidence of aperistalsis and incomplete LES relaxation—it would not show eosinophilic infiltration on biopsy.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with fatigue, blurred vision, and epistaxis over several months.
He also notes peripheral neuropathy and Raynaud-like symptoms in his fingers.
Exam reveals dilated, tortuous retinal veins on fundoscopy ('sausage-link' appearance) and hepatosplenomegaly.
Serum immunofixation identifies a monoclonal IgM protein; serum viscosity is elevated at 5.8 centipoise; bone marrow biopsy shows lymphoplasmacytic infiltration.
MYD88 L265P mutation is detected on bone marrow molecular testing.
explanation: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma producing monoclonal IgM that causes hyperviscosity syndrome. The MYD88 L265P mutation is present in >90% of cases and supports the diagnosis.
keyFact: The MYD88 L265P mutation is present in >90% of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia cases and helps distinguish it from IgM multiple myeloma or marginal zone lymphoma. Plasmapheresis is used for acute hyperviscosity.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple myeloma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Multiple myeloma typically produces IgG or IgA (not IgM) monoclonal protein, causes lytic bone lesions and hypercalcemia, and shows plasma cell (not lymphoplasmacytic) infiltration on marrow biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: MGUS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MGUS has a monoclonal protein <3 g/dL, <10% clonal cells in marrow, and no end-organ damage—this patient has symptomatic hyperviscosity, neuropathy, and organomegaly.

wrongAnswers.name: CLL
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CLL is a lymphocytic leukemia that does not typically produce significant monoclonal IgM protein or cause hyperviscosity syndrome; marrow would show mature lymphocytic infiltration.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with headaches, burning pain in her hands and feet, and one episode of transient vision loss.
She has no prior hematologic history and takes no medications that could cause a reactive elevation.
Exam shows facial plethora and bilateral erythema with warmth of the distal lower extremities consistent with erythromelalgia.
CBC reveals isolated thrombocytosis at 1,100,000/µL with normal hemoglobin and white cell count. Peripheral smear shows large hypogranular platelets.
Bone marrow biopsy shows proliferation of enlarged, mature megakaryocytes with hyperlobulated nuclei, no significant reticulin fibrosis, and JAK2 V617F mutation is detected.
explanation: Essential thrombocythemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal megakaryocyte proliferation and sustained thrombocytosis, causing thrombotic and vasomotor complications. JAK2 V617F is present in ~60% of cases.
keyFact: Erythromelalgia (burning pain and redness of extremities that responds to aspirin) is a characteristic vasomotor symptom of ET. JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations are found in 85-90% of cases.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive thrombocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive thrombocytosis occurs secondary to infection, iron deficiency, or inflammation; platelets are usually normal-sized, JAK2 is negative, and no vasomotor or thrombotic symptoms occur.

wrongAnswers.name: Polycythemia vera
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PV causes erythrocytosis (elevated Hgb/Hct/RBC mass) in addition to thrombocytosis; this patient has an isolated platelet elevation with normal hemoglobin.

wrongAnswers.name: CML
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CML causes leukocytosis with a left shift and basophilia, and BCR-ABL1 translocation on cytogenetics—not isolated megakaryocyte proliferation with JAK2 mutation.

clues: A 64-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, early satiety, and significant left-sided abdominal fullness over the past year.
He reports drenching night sweats, unintentional 10 kg weight loss, and diffuse bone pain.
Exam reveals massive splenomegaly with the spleen palpable 12 cm below the left costal margin and mild hepatomegaly.
Peripheral smear shows teardrop-shaped red cells, nucleated red blood cells, and immature myeloid precursors in a leukoerythroblastic pattern. LDH and uric acid are elevated.
Bone marrow aspirate yields a dry tap. Biopsy shows hypercellular marrow with atypical megakaryocytes and grade 3/3 reticulin fibrosis. JAK2 V617F mutation is identified.
explanation: Primary myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal proliferation of abnormal hematopoietic stem cells leading to progressive marrow fibrosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, and massive splenomegaly. Teardrop cells and a leukoerythroblastic smear are characteristic.
keyFact: Teardrop-shaped red cells (dacryocytes) on peripheral smear are a hallmark of myelofibrosis, caused by red cells being squeezed through a fibrotic marrow. The 'dry tap' on marrow aspiration is classic.

wrongAnswers.name: CML
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CML causes leukocytosis with a left shift and is defined by BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia chromosome); it does not show marrow fibrosis or teardrop cells early in its course.

wrongAnswers.name: Splenic lymphoma with villous lymphocytes
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Splenic lymphoma causes splenomegaly but would show villous lymphocytes on smear, lymphoid infiltration on biopsy, and would not produce the leukoerythroblastic picture with teardrop cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Hairy cell leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hairy cell leukemia causes splenomegaly and pancytopenia but presents with monocytopenia, TRAP-positive cells on smear, and a marrow showing hairy cell infiltration without the fibrosis pattern.

clues: A 35-year-old woman develops diffuse bleeding from multiple sites, petechiae, and blood-tinged urine 12 hours after an emergency cesarean section complicated by placental abruption.
She has simultaneous signs of bleeding and organ ischemia, with declining urine output and worsening mental status since surgery.
Exam shows diffuse petechiae, purpura, and persistent oozing from all venipuncture and surgical sites.
Platelet count is 28,000, PT and aPTT are both prolonged, fibrinogen is critically low at 80 mg/dL, and D-dimer is markedly elevated above 20 µg/mL. Peripheral smear shows schistocytes.
Repeat peripheral smear at 24 hours shows worsening schistocyte count with progressive fibrinogen depletion despite transfusion, and ISTH DIC score is 7.
explanation: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a syndrome of simultaneous widespread microvascular thrombosis and consumption of clotting factors and platelets, leading to paradoxical bleeding. Common triggers include sepsis, obstetric emergencies, and malignancy.
keyFact: The ISTH DIC score uses platelet count, PT prolongation, fibrinogen level, and D-dimer to diagnose DIC. Low fibrinogen with elevated D-dimer plus thrombocytopenia and prolonged coagulation times is the laboratory hallmark.

wrongAnswers.name: TTP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP causes thrombocytopenia and schistocytes via ADAMTS13 deficiency but typically shows normal or mildly elevated PT/PTT and fibrinogen—it does not produce the profound coagulopathy seen in DIC.

wrongAnswers.name: Liver failure coagulopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Liver failure impairs synthesis of clotting factors causing coagulopathy, but there would be evidence of hepatic dysfunction (elevated transaminases, hyperbilirubinemia) and fibrinogen is often normal or elevated early.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemophilia A
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemophilia A causes isolated factor VIII deficiency with prolonged PTT but normal PT; it does not cause thrombocytopenia, elevated D-dimer, or the consumptive picture following an acute trigger.

clues: A 58-year-old man who had cardiac surgery eight days ago develops sudden pain, swelling, and discoloration in his left leg.
He has been receiving unfractionated heparin since the operation and has no prior history of heparin use.
Exam reveals a swollen, tense left calf with pitting edema, erythema, and positive Homan sign on dorsiflexion.
Platelet count has dropped from 220,000 preoperatively to 78,000 on postoperative day 8, a greater than 50% decline. Anti-PF4/heparin antibody ELISA is strongly positive.
Serotonin release assay confirms heparin-dependent platelet-activating antibodies in a patient with new thrombosis and a >50% platelet drop 5–10 days after heparin initiation.
explanation: HIT is an immune-mediated reaction to heparin in which antibodies against PF4-heparin complexes activate platelets, causing thrombocytopenia and paradoxical thrombosis. All forms of heparin must be stopped immediately and an alternative anticoagulant (e.g., argatroban) started.
keyFact: In HIT, thrombocytopenia is typically moderate (rarely <20,000) and THROMBOSIS (not bleeding) is the major complication. Never give platelet transfusions in HIT—this can worsen thrombosis. Use a direct thrombin inhibitor as alternative anticoagulation.

wrongAnswers.name: TTP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP causes severe thrombocytopenia with MAHA (schistocytes), fever, renal failure, and neurologic symptoms; it is not temporally related to heparin use and would not show PF4 antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Sepsis-related thrombocytopenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sepsis can cause thrombocytopenia but would present with fever, leukocytosis, hemodynamic instability, and positive cultures—not a new thrombotic event on heparin with a positive PF4 antibody.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Other drug-induced thrombocytopenias cause isolated platelet destruction with bleeding risk, not thrombosis, and would not test positive on the PF4-heparin ELISA or serotonin release assay.

clues: A 19-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue, easy bruising, and frequent infections over three months.
She has no prior medical history and takes no medications. There is no identifiable toxic exposure or recent viral illness.
Exam shows pallor and scattered petechiae. There is no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.
CBC shows pancytopenia with hemoglobin 6.8, WBC 1,800, ANC 400, and platelets 18,000. Reticulocyte count is critically low at 0.1%. Flow cytometry shows no PNH clone.

Bone marrow biopsy reveals a markedly hypocellular marrow with less than 10% cellularity, replaced almost entirely by fat with scant residual hematopoietic elements and no clonal cytogenetic abnormalities.
explanation: Aplastic anemia is a bone marrow failure syndrome caused by immune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells, resulting in pancytopenia and a hypocellular marrow. Treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in eligible patients or immunosuppression with ATG and cyclosporine.
keyFact: Aplastic anemia is diagnosed by pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow on biopsy. It must be distinguished from PNH (which can co-exist and evolve) and hypocellular MDS; all newly diagnosed patients should have flow cytometry for GPI-deficient cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute leukemia presents with pancytopenia but marrow biopsy would show hypercellular marrow packed with blasts, not a hypocellular marrow replaced by fat cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PNH can cause pancytopenia and cytopenias but is identified by flow cytometric detection of GPI-deficient blood cell populations; PNH is closely related to AA but is a distinct entity.

wrongAnswers.name: Myelodysplastic syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypocellular MDS can mimic AA but is distinguished by dysplastic cell morphology on smear/biopsy and clonal cytogenetic abnormalities—this patient had normal cytogenetics.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with intermittent dark-colored morning urine, fatigue, and episodic abdominal pain.
He has had two prior episodes of venous thrombosis at unusual sites, including the splenic and portal veins.
Exam shows pallor and mild icterus. There is no splenomegaly.
Labs show hemolytic anemia with LDH elevated at 2,400 U/L, undetectable haptoglobin, elevated indirect bilirubin, and hemoglobinuria. Direct Coombs test is negative.
Flow cytometry of peripheral blood demonstrates a large population of CD55-deficient and CD59-deficient red blood cells and granulocytes, showing absence of GPI-anchored proteins.
explanation: PNH is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder caused by somatic PIGA mutation, resulting in absence of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins (CD55, CD59), leading to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, thrombosis, and cytopenias.
keyFact: Flow cytometry showing GPI-deficient blood cells (absent CD55/CD59) is diagnostic of PNH. The triad of hemolysis, thrombosis at unusual sites, and cytopenias in a young adult should prompt flow cytometry. Eculizumab (anti-C5) is a targeted therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIHA causes hemolysis with a positive direct Coombs test; it does not cause thrombosis at unusual sites or show GPI-deficient cells on flow cytometry.

wrongAnswers.name: Aplastic anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aplastic anemia causes marrow failure with pancytopenia but does not produce hemoglobinuria or the GPI-deficient clone—though AA and PNH can co-exist.

wrongAnswers.name: G6PD deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: G6PD deficiency causes episodic hemolysis triggered by oxidant stress (drugs, infections, fava beans); it does not cause thrombosis, cytopenias, or GPI-deficient cells on flow cytometry.

clues: A 70-year-old woman presents with episodic blue-purple discoloration of her fingers and toes, fatigue, and jaundice that worsens in winter months.
She was treated for a Mycoplasma pneumoniae respiratory infection six weeks ago. Her symptoms intensify with cold exposure.
Exam shows pallor, mild jaundice, and blue-purple discoloration of the fingertips and ears that developed in the cold examination room.
Labs confirm hemolytic anemia with elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, and elevated indirect bilirubin. Direct Coombs test is positive for complement C3d only, with negative IgG.
Cold agglutinin titer is markedly elevated at 1:2048, and thermal amplitude testing shows the antibodies are reactive at temperatures up to 30°C.
explanation: Cold agglutinin disease is an autoimmune hemolytic anemia caused by IgM antibodies (cold agglutinins) that bind red cells at low temperatures, activating complement and causing hemolysis. It may be idiopathic or secondary to Mycoplasma, EBV, or lymphoproliferative disease.
keyFact: Cold agglutinin disease shows IgM-mediated complement activation; the direct Coombs test is positive for C3d but negative for IgG (unlike warm AIHA which is IgG-positive). Avoid cold exposure; secondary causes (especially lymphoma) should be sought in chronic cases.

wrongAnswers.name: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Warm AIHA is caused by IgG antibodies reactive at body temperature; the direct Coombs is positive for IgG, not isolated C3d, and symptoms do not have a cold-triggered pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Cryoglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cryoglobulinemia causes vasculitis and purpura with cold exposure and is associated with HCV; it does not produce high-titer cold agglutinins or complement-coated red cells on Coombs.

wrongAnswers.name: Raynaud phenomenon
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Raynaud causes digital color changes with cold but does not cause hemolytic anemia, jaundice, or a positive Coombs test.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with fatigue, recurrent infections, and a sensation of fullness in his left upper abdomen.
He has had three bacterial infections requiring hospitalization in the past year. No prior hematologic problems.
Exam reveals massive splenomegaly without palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy.

CBC shows pancytopenia with monocytopenia. Peripheral smear shows rare lymphocytes with irregular cytoplasmic projections. Bone marrow aspirate yields a dry tap. Cells are TRAP-positive on cytochemistry.
Flow cytometry shows a CD19+, CD20+, CD11c+, CD25+, CD103+, CD123+ B-cell population. BRAF V600E mutation is detected on molecular testing.
explanation: Hairy cell leukemia is a rare indolent B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by pancytopenia, massive splenomegaly, monocytopenia, and a marrow dry tap. The BRAF V600E mutation is present in virtually all cases and is diagnostically useful.
keyFact: BRAF V600E mutation is present in >95% of hairy cell leukemia cases. Monocytopenia is an underappreciated hallmark. First-line treatment is cladribine (2-CdA), which achieves durable complete remissions in >85% of patients.

wrongAnswers.name: CLL
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CLL causes lymphocytosis (not pancytopenia), peripheral lymphadenopathy, and characteristic CD5+/CD23+ immunophenotype—it does not cause monocytopenia or a marrow dry tap.

wrongAnswers.name: Myelofibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myelofibrosis causes splenomegaly and a dry tap but shows a leukoerythroblastic smear with teardrop cells and megakaryocytic fibrosis on biopsy, not hairy B-cell infiltration.

wrongAnswers.name: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SMZL also causes splenomegaly and is a B-cell disorder, but cells lack the CD103/CD123/CD25 co-expression of HCL and do not harbor BRAF V600E.

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and a sensation of fullness in his neck and abdomen over four months.
He has lost 6 kg and reports early satiety. He has no history of immunosuppression or prior malignancy.
Exam reveals generalized lymphadenopathy involving cervical, axillary, and inguinal chains, along with palpable splenomegaly.

Colonoscopy shows multiple small polyps throughout the colon consistent with lymphomatous polyposis. Lymph node biopsy shows a monotonous population of atypical lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours.
Immunohistochemistry shows CD5+, CD20+, CD23-negative, cyclin D1-positive B cells. FISH confirms t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation.
explanation: Mantle cell lymphoma is an aggressive B-cell NHL driven by t(11;14) translocation causing cyclin D1 overexpression. It typically presents in older men with widespread nodal disease, splenomegaly, and gastrointestinal involvement.
keyFact: The t(11;14) translocation juxtaposes the CCND1 (cyclin D1) gene to the IgH enhancer, driving cyclin D1 overexpression. MCL is CD5+ but CD23- (unlike CLL which is CD5+/CD23+). GI involvement with lymphomatous polyposis is characteristic.

wrongAnswers.name: CLL/SLL
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CLL/SLL is also CD5+ but is CD23+, does not overexpress cyclin D1, lacks t(11;14), and follows a more indolent course without the GI polyposis of MCL.

wrongAnswers.name: Follicular lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Follicular lymphoma carries t(14;18) with BCL2 overexpression, is CD10+ and BCL6+, and does not show cyclin D1 positivity or the characteristic GI polyposis.

wrongAnswers.name: DLBCL
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DLBCL is a more aggressive large B-cell lymphoma with larger cells on biopsy; it does not have the cyclin D1 overexpression or t(11;14) that defines MCL.

clues: A 28-year-old aid worker returning from rural Bihar, India presents with three months of intermittent fever, weight loss, and progressive abdominal distension.
He reports drenching night sweats and profound fatigue. He lived in a rural village with endemic sandfly exposure.
Exam reveals massive splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. The skin appears diffusely dark and hyperpigmented.
CBC shows pancytopenia. Serology with the rK39 rapid antigen test is strongly positive. Liver enzymes are markedly elevated.
Bone marrow biopsy reveals intracellular amastigotes within macrophages, and PCR confirms Leishmania donovani.
explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is caused by Leishmania donovani complex transmitted by sandfly bites, endemic in India, East Africa, and Brazil. It presents with prolonged fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and hyperpigmentation; treatment is liposomal amphotericin B.
keyFact: The rK39 rapid antigen test has high sensitivity and specificity in endemic regions for visceral leishmaniasis. The organism invades reticuloendothelial cells; Leishman-Donovan bodies in marrow macrophages are diagnostic on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Malaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malaria causes cyclical fevers with rigors and can cause splenomegaly, but would show malaria parasites on thick/thin blood smear and does not cause the progressive pancytopenia and hyperpigmentation of VL.

wrongAnswers.name: Disseminated tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Miliary TB can cause fever, night sweats, and organomegaly, but would show granulomas on tissue biopsy and evidence on CT/chest X-ray—not intracellular amastigotes in macrophages.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma causes splenomegaly and systemic symptoms but would show malignant lymphoid cells on biopsy, not Leishmania amastigotes, and would not test positive on rK39 antigen testing.

clues: A 35-year-old recent immigrant from Central America presents with a new-onset generalized seizure and no prior neurologic history.
He has had occasional mild headaches over the past year but was otherwise healthy. He has no family history of seizure disorders.
Neurologic exam is normal between seizures. There is no fever or meningismus.
MRI brain shows multiple ring-enhancing cystic lesions with surrounding edema, several containing an eccentric hyperdense dot. CSF shows mild eosinophilic pleocytosis.

The cystic brain lesions each contain a visible scolex (the characteristic 'dot-in-hole' sign). Serum and CSF anti-cysticercal antibody (EITB assay) are positive. CT also shows calcified lesions representing prior resolved cysts.
explanation: Neurocysticercosis is caused by larval cysts of Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) lodging in the CNS, typically acquired via fecal-oral ingestion of T. solium eggs. It is the most common cause of adult-onset epilepsy in endemic regions.
keyFact: The pathognomonic finding is a cystic lesion with an eccentric scolex on MRI (the 'dot-in-hole' sign). Treatment is antiparasitic (albendazole ± praziquantel) plus corticosteroids and antiepileptics. Calcified lesions represent dead cysts.

wrongAnswers.name: Brain abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial brain abscess presents with fever, headache, and focal deficits; MRI shows a ring-enhancing lesion with restricted diffusion on DWI and no scolex—the patient is afebrile with multiple cysts.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary brain tumor (GBM)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBM shows an irregular ring-enhancing mass with necrosis on MRI; it does not produce multiple cystic lesions with a scolex or CSF eosinophilia.

wrongAnswers.name: Toxoplasma encephalitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Toxoplasma causes ring-enhancing lesions in immunocompromised hosts (typically HIV with CD4 <100), preferentially in the basal ganglia; lesions do not contain a scolex and serology would show Toxoplasma antibodies.

clues: A 40-year-old dairy farmer presents with six weeks of intermittent fever, profuse sweating, and low back pain.
He regularly consumes unpasteurized goat cheese from his farm. The fevers follow an undulating pattern, rising and falling over days.
Exam shows hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse lumbar spine tenderness. Testes are mildly tender bilaterally.
CBC shows mild leukopenia. Blood cultures grow slow-growing gram-negative coccobacilli after prolonged incubation. Brucella agglutination titer is elevated at 1:320.
MRI of the lumbar spine shows spondylodiscitis at L4-L5. The organism is identified as Brucella melitensis on final culture speciation.
explanation: Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by Brucella species, transmitted through contact with infected animals or consumption of unpasteurized dairy. It causes an undulating fever with musculoskeletal, hepatic, and reproductive involvement; doxycycline plus rifampin is first-line treatment.
keyFact: Brucella requires prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (doxycycline + rifampin for 6 weeks) because monotherapy has a high relapse rate. Spondylodiscitis and orchitis are characteristic complications.

wrongAnswers.name: Q fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) also causes undulating fever in livestock workers but is transmitted by aerosols, not unpasteurized dairy; it causes pneumonia or hepatitis more commonly than spondylodiscitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Vertebral osteomyelitis from Staphylococcus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Staph spondylodiscitis causes more acute severe back pain and fever with rapid progression on imaging; it lacks the zoonotic exposure, undulating fever pattern, and orchitis seen in brucellosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Typhoid fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Typhoid causes step-ladder fever pattern, relative bradycardia, rose spots, and diarrhea—it is transmitted via contaminated water/food from humans, not animal products, and Widal test/blood culture would grow S. typhi.

clues: A 45-year-old man who works with livestock presents with acute-onset high fever, severe headache, non-productive cough, and myalgias for ten days.
He spent extensive time during lambing season when many ewes were giving birth. He has no prior pulmonary disease.
Exam shows fever of 39.8°C with relative bradycardia and decreased breath sounds at the right base. No rash is present.
Standard respiratory cultures and viral panels are negative. LFTs are elevated. Chest X-ray shows multiple rounded opacities in the right lower lobe.
Phase II IgG antibody titer against Coxiella burnetii is elevated at 1:256 on acute serology, with a fourfold rise confirmed on convalescent sample two weeks later.
explanation: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular organism transmitted by inhaling aerosols from infected animal placentas, amniotic fluid, or birth products. Acute Q fever presents with a flu-like illness, atypical pneumonia, and hepatitis; doxycycline is the treatment of choice.
keyFact: Q fever is one of the most infectious diseases known—a single organism can cause infection. In pregnant women, Q fever can reactivate and cause obstetric complications; chronic Q fever (endocarditis) occurs in those with valvular heart disease. Serologically, Phase I antibodies dominate in chronic infection, Phase II in acute.

wrongAnswers.name: Brucellosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Brucellosis also affects livestock workers but is transmitted via direct contact or unpasteurized dairy; it causes undulating fever, spondylodiscitis, and orchitis—not acute pneumonia with rounded chest infiltrates.

wrongAnswers.name: Legionella pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Legionella causes atypical pneumonia but is transmitted via contaminated water aerosols (cooling towers, water systems), not animal parturition; Legionella urinary antigen would be positive.

wrongAnswers.name: Psittacosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psittacosis (Chlamydia psittaci) causes atypical pneumonia in bird handlers (parrots, pigeons), not sheep/cattle farmers; serology would show Chlamydophila psittaci antibodies.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with a slowly progressive indurated mass along his right jaw that has developed draining sinuses over four months.
He had a dental extraction five months ago and has poor dentition. The mass has been unresponsive to short courses of oral antibiotics.
Exam reveals hard, woody induration of the right jaw extending to the neck with a sinus tract draining yellowish granular discharge.
Gram stain of the discharge shows gram-positive branching filamentous rods. Yellow macroscopic granules are visible in the purulent material.
Culture under anaerobic conditions grows Actinomyces israelii. Histologic examination of the granules shows the characteristic sulfur granule morphology with surrounding neutrophilic inflammation.
explanation: Actinomycosis is a chronic suppurative infection caused by Actinomyces species (normal oral/GI flora), typically following mucosal disruption (dental procedures). The cervicofacial form is most common, characterized by indurated 'woody' swelling, sinus tracts, and sulfur granules.
keyFact: Sulfur granules are the hallmark of actinomycosis—they are macroscopic aggregates of filamentous bacteria, not actual sulfur. Actinomyces crosses tissue planes without respecting fascial barriers. Treatment requires prolonged high-dose penicillin (6-12 months).

wrongAnswers.name: Nocardiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nocardia also causes sulfur granule-like discharge and branching filamentous rods but is aerobic (not anaerobic), tends to affect immunocompromised hosts, and more commonly causes pulmonary or disseminated disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Ludwig angina
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ludwig angina is an acute, rapidly spreading bilateral submandibular cellulitis causing airway compromise—not a slow, woody, chronic mass with a sinus tract over months.

wrongAnswers.name: Scrofula (cervical TB lymphadenitis)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scrofula causes cervical lymph node swelling with possible sinus tract but is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis; acid-fast bacilli would be identified, not gram-positive branching rods with sulfur granules.

clues: A 52-year-old man on chronic immunosuppressive therapy presents with three weeks of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath.
He takes long-term prednisone for sarcoidosis. Over the past week, he has also developed a tender draining lump on his left forearm.
