Exam reveals decreased breath sounds at the right base with dullness to percussion. A fluctuant subcutaneous nodule is present on the left forearm with purulent drainage.
Sputum Gram stain shows gram-positive branching filamentous rods that are weakly acid-fast on modified Kinyoun stain. The organism grows only under aerobic conditions.
Culture of both sputum and forearm wound drainage grows the same organism, identified as Nocardia brasiliensis, showing disseminated pulmonary and cutaneous involvement.
explanation: Nocardiosis is an opportunistic infection caused by aerobic, gram-positive, branching filamentous, weakly acid-fast bacteria (Nocardia spp.). It typically affects immunocompromised hosts, causing pulmonary disease with a propensity for dissemination to the brain and skin.
keyFact: Nocardia is distinguished from Actinomyces by being aerobic and weakly acid-fast (positive on modified Kinyoun stain). TMP-SMX is first-line; always check for CNS dissemination with brain MRI when pulmonary or disseminated nocardiosis is diagnosed.

wrongAnswers.name: Aspergillosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aspergillus also causes cavitary pulmonary disease in immunocompromised patients but is a mold identified by branching septate hyphae at 45° angles on culture/biopsy—not gram-positive weakly acid-fast rods.

wrongAnswers.name: Actinomycosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Actinomyces causes similar morphology (branching filaments) but is anaerobic, not weakly acid-fast, and typically causes cervicofacial or abdominal disease—not cavitary pneumonia in an immunocompromised host.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB is strongly acid-fast, not weakly acid-fast, grows on specific media (Lowenstein-Jensen), and the clinical scenario lacks the typical TB exposure history; branching filamentous morphology is not seen in TB.

clues: A 40-year-old woman who works as a gardener presents with a painless nodule on her right hand followed by similar nodules ascending up her forearm over several weeks.
She recalls pricking her right hand on a rose thorn about five weeks ago. She has no fever or systemic symptoms.
Exam shows a primary ulcerated nodule at the inoculation site on the dorsal hand and four secondary nodules tracking proximally along the lymphatic channels of the forearm.
Biopsy of a nodule shows granulomatous inflammation. Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 25°C grows a mold with characteristic rosette-arranged conidia along hyphae.
The organism demonstrates thermal dimorphism, converting from a mold form at 25°C to a cigar-shaped yeast form at 37°C.
explanation: Sporotrichosis is a subcutaneous fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii, typically acquired via traumatic inoculation with plant material. The lymphocutaneous form with ascending nodules along lymphatic channels is classic.
keyFact: The 'rose gardener's disease' presents with a primary inoculation nodule and ascending lymphangitic spread. Sporothrix is dimorphic: mold at room temperature, yeast at 37°C. First-line treatment is itraconazole for lymphocutaneous form.

wrongAnswers.name: Mycobacterium marinum infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: M. marinum also causes lymphocutaneous spread following skin inoculation but is associated with fish tank exposure or water-related injury—not rose thorn puncture; AFB stain would be positive.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacterial lymphangitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial lymphangitis (typically Streptococcal) presents acutely with red streaks, pain, tenderness, and systemic fever—not the chronic, painless nodular progression along lymphatics seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Tularemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tularemia's ulceroglandular form causes skin ulcer and regional lymphadenopathy but follows contact with rabbits or tick bites—not a gardening injury—and is caused by Francisella tularensis (bacterium, not fungus).

clues: A 14-year-old girl presents with a painless, enlarging lump in her right armpit that has been growing for three weeks.
She has two kittens at home and recalls being scratched on her right hand about four weeks ago.
Exam shows a 3 cm tender, warm right axillary lymph node and a small healing papule on the dorsum of the right hand.
Bartonella henselae serology (IgG) is elevated at 1:512. Lymph node biopsy shows stellate granulomas with central necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes.
Warthin-Starry silver stain of the biopsy material reveals clumps of small bacilli within the granulomas.
explanation: Cat scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae, transmitted via scratch or bite from infected cats (especially kittens). It presents with regional lymphadenopathy following a scratch, and is usually self-limited in immunocompetent patients.
keyFact: The primary inoculation papule appears 3-10 days after the scratch, followed by regional lymphadenopathy 1-3 weeks later. In immunocompromised hosts, Bartonella henselae can cause bacillary angiomatosis and peliosis hepatis—very different presentations.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma causes painless, rubbery, progressive lymphadenopathy but lacks the scratch history and primary inoculation papule; biopsy would show malignant lymphoid cells, not stellate granulomas.

wrongAnswers.name: Atypical mycobacterial lymphadenitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MAC lymphadenitis typically affects children under 5, involves submandibular or cervical nodes, lacks a scratch history, and shows caseating granulomas with AFB-positive organisms on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Toxoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Toxoplasma can cause cervical lymphadenopathy with granulomas but is associated with undercooked meat or cat feces exposure; serology would show Toxoplasma IgG/IgM rather than Bartonella antibodies.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with sudden-onset fever, severe headache, and myalgias ten days after outdoor recreational activity in the southeastern United States.
He recalls removing an attached tick two weeks prior. No rash has appeared at any point during his illness.
Exam shows fever of 39.5°C and mild meningismus. Skin exam reveals no rash anywhere on the body.
Labs show leukopenia with WBC 2,800, thrombocytopenia with platelets 68,000, and elevated AST and ALT. Peripheral smear shows mulberry-like intracytoplasmic inclusions within monocytes.
PCR of peripheral blood is positive for Ehrlichia chaffeensis. Convalescent serology confirms seroconversion.
explanation: Human monocytic ehrlichiosis is caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, transmitted by the Lone Star tick (Amblyomma americanum) in the south-central and eastern US. It presents with fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and transaminase elevation; morulae in monocytes are diagnostic.
keyFact: Ehrlichiosis classically lacks a rash (unlike RMSF), and shows leukopenia + thrombocytopenia + elevated LFTs. Morulae in monocytes on smear are pathognomonic but infrequently seen. Doxycycline is curative and should not be delayed pending confirmation.

wrongAnswers.name: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RMSF also presents with tick-related fever in the eastern US but characteristically causes a maculopapular rash starting on wrists/ankles and spreading centrally; Rickettsia rickettsii infects endothelial cells, not monocytes.

wrongAnswers.name: Anaplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) causes an identical clinical syndrome but shows morulae in NEUTROPHILS (not monocytes) and is transmitted by the deer tick (Ixodes) in the northeastern US.

wrongAnswers.name: Influenza
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Influenza causes fever and myalgias but is transmitted by respiratory droplets, not tick bites; leukopenia in influenza is not accompanied by thrombocytopenia, transaminase elevation, or morulae on smear.

clues: A 70-year-old asplenic man presents in summer with high spiking fevers, rigors, fatigue, and dark urine after spending time outdoors on Nantucket Island.
He underwent splenectomy years ago for trauma. He has noticed his urine is the color of dark cola.
Exam reveals a temperature of 40.1°C, jaundice, and a well-healed left upper quadrant surgical scar. There is no palpable spleen.
Labs confirm intravascular hemolysis with elevated LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, and hemoglobinuria. Thick and thin peripheral blood smears show intraerythrocytic ring-form parasites.
The peripheral smear demonstrates the pathognomonic tetrad form ('Maltese cross') of intraerythrocytic parasites. PCR and serology confirm Babesia microti.
explanation: Babesiosis is a tick-borne intraerythrocytic protozoan infection caused by Babesia microti, transmitted by Ixodes scapularis in the northeastern US. Asplenic and immunocompromised patients develop severe hemolytic disease. The Maltese cross (tetrad) on smear is pathognomonic.
keyFact: The Maltese cross (tetrad form) is pathognomonic for Babesia. Asplenia is the major risk factor for severe babesiosis. Treatment is atovaquone + azithromycin for mild disease; clindamycin + quinine for severe disease. Co-infection with Lyme disease and anaplasmosis is common in endemic areas.

wrongAnswers.name: Plasmodium falciparum malaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Falciparum malaria causes severe hemolytic disease with ring-form parasites, but does not produce the Maltese cross tetrad form; travel to tropical endemic regions (not New England) would be required.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIHA causes hemolysis with positive direct Coombs test but is not transmitted by ticks, lacks intraerythrocytic parasites on smear, and does not cause the febrile illness with rigors seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Ehrlichiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ehrlichiosis causes fever and leukopenia after tick exposure but does not cause hemolytic anemia or show intraerythrocytic parasites on blood smear.

clues: A 28-year-old man with a 15 pack-year smoking history presents with progressive dyspnea, non-productive cough, and two episodes of spontaneous pneumothorax over the past year.
He is an active smoker with no occupational exposures or connective tissue disease. His symptoms began insidiously about 18 months ago.
Exam shows no clubbing. Chest auscultation reveals diffuse crackles bilaterally.
HRCT of the chest shows a combination of irregular-walled cysts and nodules in the upper and mid lung zones with striking lower lobe sparing. PFTs show a mixed pattern with reduced DLCO.
Bronchoscopic biopsy reveals clusters of cells with characteristic grooved nuclei expressing CD1a and S-100. Electron microscopy shows pentalaminar Birbeck granules.
explanation: Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a smoking-related interstitial lung disease characterized by clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells causing nodules that cavitate into irregular cysts. Upper lobe predominance, recurrent pneumothorax, and a young smoker are characteristic.
keyFact: PLCH is almost exclusively seen in smokers; smoking cessation is the primary treatment and can lead to disease stabilization or regression. BRAF V600E mutation is present in ~50% of PLCH cases. Recurrent pneumothorax distinguishes it from sarcoidosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LAM also causes diffuse cystic lung disease with recurrent pneumothorax but occurs almost exclusively in women of childbearing age and shows round, thin-walled cysts distributed uniformly without nodules; CD1a staining is negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis shows upper lobe nodules and fibrosis on HRCT but does not cause irregular cysts, is not smoking-related, and biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas—not CD1a+ Langerhans cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Emphysema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Emphysema in a young smoker could be considered but shows lower lobe centriacinar emphysema on HRCT without the nodule-to-cyst evolution or Langerhans cell histology.

clues: A 22-year-old man suddenly develops severe left-sided chest pain and rapidly worsening difficulty breathing during physical activity.
Over the next ten minutes, he becomes increasingly agitated and lightheaded. He has no prior lung disease or trauma history.
Exam shows tracheal deviation to the right, completely absent breath sounds over the entire left hemithorax, distended neck veins, and cyanosis. Heart rate is 128 and blood pressure is 78/50.
Bedside point-of-care ultrasound of the left hemithorax shows absent lung sliding with a 'stratosphere sign' (barcode sign) on M-mode, and no B-lines are visible.
Chest X-ray obtained emergently shows complete opacification of the left hemithorax with contralateral mediastinal shift and flattening of the left hemidiaphragm.
explanation: Tension pneumothorax occurs when air accumulates in the pleural space under positive pressure, causing progressive mediastinal shift, impaired venous return, and cardiovascular collapse. It is a clinical diagnosis that requires immediate needle decompression without waiting for imaging.
keyFact: Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed CLINICALLY—do not wait for a chest X-ray if hemodynamically unstable. The triad of absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side, and JVD with hypotension requires immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS, MCL) followed by chest tube.

wrongAnswers.name: Simple spontaneous pneumothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Simple pneumothorax causes chest pain and dyspnea but does NOT cause hemodynamic instability, tracheal deviation, or JVD—these features indicate tension physiology.

wrongAnswers.name: Massive pulmonary embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Massive PE causes hemodynamic collapse and JVD but would show bilateral breath sounds, no tracheal deviation, and would not respond to needle decompression.

wrongAnswers.name: Cardiac tamponade
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tamponade causes Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds) but breath sounds are bilateral and equal; no tracheal deviation; treatment is pericardiocentesis, not needle decompression.

clues: A 16-year-old competitive swimmer reports chest tightness, wheezing, and coughing that consistently develops five to ten minutes into intense exercise.
She has no symptoms at rest and a family history of atopy. She is otherwise healthy with no daily medication use.
Exam at rest is entirely normal. Auscultation reveals clear lung fields with no wheeze at baseline.
Baseline spirometry is normal. Eucapnic voluntary hyperventilation challenge test provokes a 15% fall in FEV1 from baseline after six minutes of hyperventilation.
Repeat spirometry 30 minutes after the bronchoprovocation challenge shows spontaneous return of FEV1 to within 5% of baseline without bronchodilator administration.
explanation: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is airway narrowing triggered by high-ventilation exercise, caused by loss of airway heat and water. It is common in elite athletes and atopic individuals; diagnosis is confirmed by exercise or surrogate challenge tests showing ≥10% FEV1 fall.
keyFact: A ≥10% fall in FEV1 following standardized exercise or EVH challenge confirms EIB. Pre-exercise SABA is the primary treatment. Swimming is often better tolerated than cold-weather sports due to warm, humidified air, but can still trigger EIB.

wrongAnswers.name: Vocal cord dysfunction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VCD causes inspiratory stridor and throat tightness during exercise; flow-volume loop shows inspiratory flattening; the FEV1 on challenge testing is typically normal and SABA pre-treatment does not prevent symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Deconditioning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Deconditioning causes dyspnea with exertion but would not show a reproducible ≥15% FEV1 drop on challenge testing or response to bronchodilator pre-treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Persistent asthma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Persistent asthma causes symptoms at baseline with abnormal resting spirometry showing bronchodilator reversibility—this patient has entirely normal baseline lung function with only exercise-provoked symptoms.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, episodic hemoptysis, and two unexplained strokes over the past three years.
Her father had lifelong recurrent nosebleeds and was found to have a brain lesion. She has noticed small red spots on her lips and fingertips.

Exam shows clubbing, cyanosis that does not fully improve with supplemental oxygen, and a continuous bruit audible over the right lower lung field. Multiple telangiectasias are visible on the lips and tongue.

Arterial blood gas on 100% oxygen shows persistent hypoxemia consistent with a right-to-left shunt. CT chest reveals a 2 cm vascular nidus with a feeding artery and draining vein in the right lower lobe.
Contrast bubble echocardiography demonstrates right-to-left shunt with bubbles appearing in the left atrium after a three-beat delay. Genetic testing identifies a pathogenic ENG (endoglin) mutation.
explanation: Pulmonary AVMs are abnormal direct communications between pulmonary arteries and veins, causing right-to-left shunting, hypoxemia, and paradoxical embolism (stroke, brain abscess). Up to 50% are associated with HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome).
keyFact: Pulmonary AVMs cause shunt-type hypoxemia that does NOT correct with 100% O2 (shunt fraction >30% refractory to O2). HHT should be suspected when AVMs are found with mucocutaneous telangiectasias and family history. Percutaneous embolotherapy is the treatment of choice.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pulmonary hypertension causes dyspnea and hypoxemia but would show RV enlargement and elevated PA pressures on echo without the focal nidus of an AVM, paradoxical embolism, or response to 100% O2 failure from fixed shunt.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia without pulmonary AVM
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HHT without pulmonary AVM would not explain the shunt physiology, hypoxemia refractory to oxygen, or the auscultated bruit over the lung field.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes V/Q mismatch hypoxemia that typically improves with supplemental oxygen, does not cause telangiectasias or paradoxical embolism, and would show obstructive spirometry.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with six weeks of progressive cough, dyspnea, low-grade fevers, and malaise that began like a typical pneumonia.
She has completed two full courses of appropriate antibiotics with no improvement. She has no toxic exposures or connective tissue disease.
Exam shows diffuse bilateral crackles on auscultation; no clubbing, cyanosis, or lymphadenopathy; oxygen saturation is 93% on room air.
BAL shows lymphocytosis with a mixed cellular pattern. Transbronchial biopsy reveals plugs of granulation tissue filling alveolar ducts and alveoli with preserved underlying lung architecture.
Histopathology confirms intraluminal organizing fibroblastic plugs (Masson bodies) within the distal airspaces, with preserved underlying lung architecture and no fibroblastic foci.
explanation: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia is an idiopathic interstitial pneumonia characterized by plugs of granulation tissue in the distal airways. It presents with a subacute pneumonia-like illness that fails to respond to antibiotics; the reverse halo sign on CT is characteristic, and it responds dramatically to corticosteroids.
keyFact: The 'reverse halo' or 'atoll' sign on CT (central ground-glass opacity surrounded by denser consolidation) is highly characteristic of COP. The dramatic response to corticosteroids (often within days) is both therapeutic and diagnostically supportive.

wrongAnswers.name: Community-acquired pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CAP responds to appropriate antibiotics and does not produce the migratory peripheral consolidations with Masson bodies on biopsy—failure to respond to two antibiotic courses strongly argues against bacterial CAP.

wrongAnswers.name: Eosinophilic pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia also shows peripheral consolidations and responds to steroids, but BAL would show markedly elevated eosinophils (>25%) and blood eosinophilia—not the granulation tissue plugs of COP.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HP shows upper lobe predominant ground-glass opacities and mosaic attenuation with a relevant antigen exposure history; biopsy shows poorly formed granulomas and peribronchiolar inflammation, not Masson bodies.

clues: A 22-year-old military recruit presents with acute-onset fever, severe dyspnea, and rapidly progressive hypoxemia over 48 hours.
He started smoking cigarettes for the first time two weeks ago. He has no prior lung disease or allergies.
Exam shows fever, diffuse bilateral crackles, and oxygen saturation of 88% on room air.
Chest imaging shows bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities and interstitial infiltrates. Peripheral blood eosinophil count is initially normal. All infectious cultures and serologies are negative.
Bronchoalveolar lavage reveals markedly elevated eosinophils comprising greater than 25% of the cellular differential, with no organisms seen on special stains.
explanation: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia is an idiopathic eosinophilic lung disease often triggered by new cigarette smoking, presenting with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. Unlike chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, blood eosinophilia may be absent early; BAL eosinophilia is diagnostic.
keyFact: In AEP, blood eosinophilia is often ABSENT initially (unlike chronic EP), making BAL essential for diagnosis. New cigarette smoking is the most common identified trigger. AEP responds rapidly to corticosteroids and does not recur after treatment (unlike CEP).

wrongAnswers.name: ARDS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ARDS is a clinical syndrome of bilateral infiltrates with hypoxemia in the setting of an identifiable cause (sepsis, trauma); it does not show eosinophils on BAL and would not respond dramatically to corticosteroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CEP has a subacute to chronic course (weeks to months), peripheral blood eosinophilia, and a 'photographic negative of pulmonary edema' on chest imaging—not the acute respiratory failure presentation of AEP.

wrongAnswers.name: Community-acquired pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CAP does not produce eosinophils on BAL, would have a bacterial or atypical organism identified on cultures, and would not respond to corticosteroids without antibiotics.

clues: A 58-year-old man with a history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis presents with recurrent hemoptysis over the past several months.
His TB was treated and cured ten years ago. He has a known residual upper lobe cavity on prior imaging.
Exam shows no fever. Breath sounds are decreased over the right upper lung field.

Chest X-ray shows a rounded opacity sitting within a pre-existing right upper lobe cavity with a crescent of air above it. The opacity shifts position on decubitus films. Serum Aspergillus IgG precipitins are elevated.
CT confirms a mobile intracavitary mass displaying the air crescent sign (Monod sign). Bronchoscopy lavage culture grows Aspergillus fumigatus.
explanation: Aspergilloma is a fungal ball (mycetoma) formed by Aspergillus hyphae colonizing a pre-existing pulmonary cavity (from TB, sarcoidosis, or bronchiectasis). It presents with hemoptysis as the major complication; the air crescent sign on imaging is characteristic.
keyFact: The air crescent sign (Monod sign) on chest X-ray or CT—a mobile mass within a cavity with a crescent of air—is the radiographic hallmark of aspergilloma. Massive hemoptysis is the most feared complication; surgical resection or bronchial artery embolization may be required.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactivation pulmonary tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactivation TB can cause hemoptysis and cavitary upper lobe lesions, but negative AFB smears and the imaging appearance of a mobile mass within an existing cavity point to a secondary fungal colonization rather than active TB.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung squamous cell carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cavitating lung cancer can cause hemoptysis and cavitary masses but the lesion would not be mobile within the cavity, and biopsy would show malignant squamous cells rather than Aspergillus hyphae.

wrongAnswers.name: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Invasive aspergillosis occurs in profoundly immunocompromised patients, causes vascular invasion with infarction (halo sign on CT), and presents with fever and rapidly progressive pneumonia—not a mobile fungus ball in an immunocompetent host.

clues: A 12-year-old boy presents with chronic productive cough, recurrent sinusitis and ear infections, and progressive hearing loss since early childhood.
He has had multiple hospitalizations for lower respiratory infections. He was diagnosed with bronchiectasis on CT at age 9.
Exam shows nasal polyps, bilateral tympanic membrane scarring, mild digital clubbing, and the cardiac apex beat is palpated on the right side of the chest.
Sweat chloride test is normal. Nasal nitric oxide measurement is very low at less than 77 nL/min. High-speed video microscopy of a nasal brush biopsy shows immotile cilia.
Transmission electron microscopy of ciliary cross-sections reveals absent inner dynein arms. Genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in DNAI1.
explanation: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of ciliary structure and function causing defective mucociliary clearance. Kartagener syndrome is the subtype with situs inversus. Diagnosis is by nasal NO, ciliary biopsy with high-speed video microscopy, and genetic testing.
keyFact: Kartagener syndrome = PCD + situs inversus (50% of PCD cases). Nasal nitric oxide is low in PCD (contrast with normal/high nNO in other causes of bronchiectasis). Male infertility due to immotile sperm is common.

wrongAnswers.name: Cystic fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CF causes chronic sinopulmonary infections and bronchiectasis but has a markedly elevated sweat chloride test, is caused by CFTR mutations, and does not cause situs inversus or immotile cilia.

wrongAnswers.name: Common variable immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID causes recurrent sinopulmonary infections from impaired antibody production, but immunoglobulin levels would be low and the condition is not associated with situs inversus or ciliary ultrastructural defects.

wrongAnswers.name: Young syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Young syndrome features bronchiectasis, sinusitis, and obstructive azoospermia but ciliary ultrastructure is normal and nasal NO is not reduced—it is distinct from PCD.

clues: A 52-year-old man with severe obesity presents with excessive daytime sleepiness, morning headaches, and progressive lower extremity swelling.
He has not been previously evaluated for sleep disorders. His wife reports loud snoring and witnessed apneas nightly for years.
Exam shows BMI 48, plethoric face, jugular venous distension, bilateral basal crackles, and 3+ pitting edema to the knees.
Arterial blood gas on room air while awake shows pH 7.34, PaCO2 58 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg, and HCO3 30 mEq/L. ECG shows right axis deviation and P-pulmonale. Echo reveals pulmonary hypertension.
Polysomnography confirms severe obstructive sleep apnea with an AHI of 72 per hour. Daytime arterial blood gas with the patient fully awake confirms persistent hypercapnia with PaCO2 of 58 mmHg.
explanation: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is defined by obesity (BMI ≥30), daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg), and sleep-disordered breathing in the absence of other causes of hypoventilation. It leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale if untreated.
keyFact: OHS requires DAYTIME hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg) to distinguish it from OSA alone—OSA causes hypoxemia and intermittent nocturnal hypercapnia but PaCO2 normalizes during the day. Treatment is weight loss and positive airway pressure (CPAP or BiPAP).

wrongAnswers.name: Obstructive sleep apnea alone
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OSA causes nocturnal hypoxemia and fragmented sleep but does not cause persistent daytime hypercapnia or elevated bicarbonate—a normal daytime PaCO2 distinguishes OSA from OHS.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism can cause weight gain, fatigue, and hypoventilation but would show low T4/elevated TSH; TSH was normal in this patient.

wrongAnswers.name: Congestive heart failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CHF causes dyspnea, edema, and orthopnea but is characterized by pulmonary edema on imaging and does not cause daytime hypercapnia; echo would show reduced EF rather than isolated right heart disease.

clues: A 45-year-old lifelong non-smoker presents with chronic productive cough, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections since his thirties, and hoarseness.
Physicians have repeatedly noted an unusually wide trachea on his prior chest imaging. He has no connective tissue disorder or history of prolonged intubation.
Exam shows a barrel chest. The trachea appears visibly widened on neck inspection. Expiratory wheeze is prominent on auscultation.
CT chest shows a tracheal diameter exceeding 3 cm, bilateral main bronchi greater than 2.4 cm, widespread bronchiectasis, and posterior tracheal wall diverticula.
Bronchoscopy demonstrates dynamic collapse of the posterior tracheal wall on expiration and a corrugated mucosal appearance from redundant tissue, with no evidence of cartilage destruction.
explanation: Mounier-Kuhn syndrome (tracheobronchomegaly) is a rare congenital condition caused by atrophy of elastic and smooth muscle fibers in the tracheal and bronchial walls, resulting in massively dilated airways, tracheobronchomalacia, and recurrent infections.
keyFact: Mounier-Kuhn syndrome is defined by tracheal diameter >3 cm on CT. The key distinguishing feature from acquired causes of tracheal widening is the tracheal diverticula (posterior wall outpouchings) and congenital onset. It must be distinguished from relapsing polychondritis (which destroys cartilage) and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Relapsing polychondritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Relapsing polychondritis causes tracheal narrowing and collapse from cartilage destruction with systemic inflammation (saddle-nose deformity, ear chondritis)—not tracheal dilation with posterior wall diverticula.

wrongAnswers.name: Bronchiectasis from cystic fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CF bronchiectasis shows markedly elevated sweat chloride, CFTR mutations, and predilection for upper lobes; the trachea is not dilated and tracheal diverticula are not seen.

wrongAnswers.name: Williams-Campbell syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Williams-Campbell syndrome is another congenital cause of bronchiectasis but results from absence of bronchial cartilage in 4th-6th generation bronchi—the trachea and main bronchi are not dilated as in Mounier-Kuhn.

clues: A 28-year-old man presents with acute pain and swelling in his right knee and left ankle, along with eye irritation and burning with urination that developed over the past two weeks.
He had a urethral discharge following unprotected sexual intercourse three weeks ago; the joint symptoms began about one week after the discharge.

Examination reveals bilateral conjunctival injection, a warm swollen right knee with a palpable effusion, shallow painless oral ulcers on the buccal mucosa, and hyperkeratotic papules on the soles of both feet.
Synovial fluid from the right knee shows 18,000 WBC per microliter with no crystals on polarized microscopy; Gram stain and culture are negative; ESR is 68 mm/hr.
HLA-B27 typing is positive, and biopsy of the sole lesions shows psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia indistinguishable from pustular psoriasis.
explanation: Reactive arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy triggered by a prior genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection, classically presenting with the triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. Chlamydia trachomatis and enteric pathogens (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia) are the most common triggers.
keyFact: The classic triad is 'can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree' — conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis; keratoderma blennorrhagica (hyperkeratotic lesions on soles) and circinate balanitis are pathognomonic skin findings.

wrongAnswers.name: Gonococcal septic arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gonococcal arthritis typically presents with migratory polyarthritis, tenosynovitis, and pustular skin lesions, and joint fluid cultures would be positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

wrongAnswers.name: Ankylosing spondylitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ankylosing spondylitis primarily affects the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints in young men and does not follow a triggering infection or present with urethritis.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriatic arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriatic arthritis is associated with psoriatic skin plaques and nail pitting, not urethritis or a preceding infectious trigger.

clues: A 68-year-old woman presents with six weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip pain and stiffness that is worst in the morning, making it difficult to get out of bed.
She reports difficulty raising her arms above her head and rising from a chair. She has also had fatigue, low-grade fevers, and a 5-pound weight loss.

Musculoskeletal exam shows painful and restricted active range of motion at both shoulders and hip girdles, but formal strength testing reveals no true muscle weakness. No peripheral joint synovitis is detected.
ESR is 85 mm/hr and CRP is elevated. CBC shows normocytic anemia. Rheumatoid factor and ANA are negative. CK and aldolase are normal.
FDG-PET scan shows symmetric uptake in the bilateral shoulder and hip bursae, and ultrasound of the shoulders reveals bilateral subdeltoid bursitis and biceps tenosynovitis without joint erosions.
explanation: Polymyalgia rheumatica is a clinical diagnosis in patients over 50 characterized by bilateral proximal muscle girdle aching and stiffness, markedly elevated ESR/CRP, and rapid response to low-dose corticosteroids. Normal muscle enzymes distinguish it from inflammatory myopathies.
keyFact: PMR is strongly associated with giant cell arteritis (GCA) — up to 50% of GCA patients have PMR, and 15–20% of PMR patients develop GCA; always screen for GCA symptoms (headache, jaw claudication, visual changes).

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polymyositis causes true proximal muscle weakness with elevated CK and aldolase, and does not present with morning stiffness as the dominant feature.

wrongAnswers.name: Fibromyalgia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fibromyalgia does not cause elevated ESR/CRP, anemia, or constitutional symptoms, and does not respond dramatically to low-dose steroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA typically presents with symmetric small joint synovitis in the hands and feet; while elderly-onset RA can mimic PMR, the absence of RF and peripheral synovitis and the rapid steroid response favor PMR.

clues: A 72-year-old woman presents with three weeks of new-onset severe headache localized to her right temple, jaw discomfort while chewing, and scalp tenderness.
She has experienced two episodes of transient blurring in her right eye lasting several minutes each. She has had bilateral shoulder and hip stiffness for two months.
Exam reveals a tender, nodular, non-pulsatile right temporal artery. Fundoscopy shows pallor of the right optic disc. Visual acuity is mildly reduced in the right eye.
ESR is 110 mm/hr and CRP is markedly elevated. Platelet count is elevated. Color Doppler ultrasound of the temporal arteries shows the 'halo sign' of circumferential vessel wall thickening.
Temporal artery biopsy reveals transmural granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina.
explanation: Giant cell arteritis is the most common primary vasculitis in adults over 50, affecting medium and large vessels, most notably the temporal arteries. The most feared complication is irreversible vision loss from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy; high-dose corticosteroids must be started immediately upon clinical suspicion, before biopsy results.
keyFact: Jaw claudication (pain with chewing due to masseter ischemia) is the most specific symptom for GCA; temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard but must be at least 2–3 cm long given skip lesions.

wrongAnswers.name: Migraine
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Migraine typically begins before age 50, does not cause an elevated ESR or a tender palpable temporal artery, and is not associated with jaw claudication or visual loss from optic disc ischemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Trigeminal neuralgia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock facial pain triggered by light touch and does not cause scalp tenderness, constitutional symptoms, or elevated inflammatory markers.

wrongAnswers.name: Takayasu arteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Takayasu arteritis affects large vessels in young women (under 40) and primarily causes limb claudication and absent pulses rather than temporal headache and jaw claudication in an elderly patient.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive weakness in her upper arms and thighs over two months, along with changes in her skin around her eyes, hands, and chest.
She describes a violaceous discoloration around her eyes that appeared before the weakness. The rash on her chest worsens with sun exposure.

Exam reveals symmetric proximal muscle weakness graded 3/5 in the shoulder and hip girdles, a violaceous heliotrope rash on the upper eyelids, raised violaceous papules over the MCP and PIP joints, and V-sign erythema on the anterior chest.
CK is 4,500 U/L with elevated aldolase. Anti-Jo-1 antibody is positive. EMG shows a myopathic pattern. MRI of the thighs shows diffuse muscle edema.
Muscle biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy with perivascular CD4+ T-cell infiltrates and complement deposition on intramuscular capillaries.
explanation: Dermatomyositis is an inflammatory myopathy distinguished from polymyositis by its characteristic skin findings: heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, V-sign, and shawl sign. It carries a significant association with underlying malignancy (especially ovarian, lung, and colorectal cancer) and interstitial lung disease.
keyFact: Gottron's papules (violaceous papules over the dorsal knuckles) are pathognomonic for dermatomyositis; all adult patients require age-appropriate cancer screening at diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Polymyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polymyositis has identical muscle findings but lacks the characteristic skin manifestations (heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules); biopsy shows endomysial CD8+ infiltrates without perifascicular atrophy.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE can cause a malar rash but it spares the knuckles, whereas dermatomyositis specifically involves the knuckles (Gottron's); SLE muscle involvement is mild without the degree of CK elevation seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroid myopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroid myopathy causes proximal weakness and elevated CK but is not associated with characteristic skin findings, anti-Jo-1 antibodies, or perifascicular atrophy on biopsy.

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with three months of progressive weakness in her arms and legs, difficulty swallowing, and shortness of breath on exertion.
She has difficulty lifting objects above her head, rising from a seated position, and climbing stairs. She has no skin rash or joint swelling.

Exam reveals symmetric proximal muscle weakness graded 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs without sensory deficits. No skin abnormalities are found. Mild bibasilar crackles are present on auscultation.

CK is 8,000 U/L with elevated LDH and aldolase. Anti-Jo-1 antibody is positive. PFTs show a restrictive pattern. CT chest reveals bibasilar ground-glass opacities consistent with interstitial lung disease.
Muscle biopsy shows endomysial inflammation with CD8+ T lymphocytes directly invading non-necrotic muscle fibers.
explanation: Polymyositis is an inflammatory myopathy presenting with symmetric proximal muscle weakness, markedly elevated CK, and endomysial CD8+ T-cell infiltration on biopsy. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are associated with antisynthetase syndrome, which includes interstitial lung disease, arthritis, and mechanic's hands.
keyFact: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase) antibody is the most common myositis-specific antibody and is associated with the antisynthetase syndrome: myositis + ILD + arthritis + mechanic's hands + Raynaud's phenomenon.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatomyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatomyositis has identical muscle pathology but requires characteristic skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules) which are absent in this case.

wrongAnswers.name: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Duchenne MD presents in young boys, is X-linked, and shows dystrophin deficiency on biopsy without inflammatory infiltrates; it does not present de novo in adult women.

wrongAnswers.name: Inclusion body myositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Inclusion body myositis typically affects men over 50, causes distal and asymmetric weakness (especially finger flexors and knee extensors), and shows rimmed vacuoles on biopsy.

clues: A 42-year-old woman presents with progressive tightening of the skin on her arms, legs, and face, along with difficulty swallowing and color changes in her fingers with cold exposure.
She has had worsening shortness of breath on exertion, heartburn, and hand and wrist pain over the past year. Her fingers turn white, then blue, then red in the cold.

Exam reveals diffuse skin thickening extending proximal to the elbows and onto the trunk, reduced oral aperture from facial tightening, digital pitting scars on the fingertips, and bibasilar crackles.

ANA is positive at 1:1280 with a nucleolar pattern. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody is positive. PFTs show a restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO. Echo shows elevated right heart pressures.
Skin biopsy shows dense dermal fibrosis with replacement of subcutaneous fat by thickened collagen bundles, loss of adnexal structures, and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates.
explanation: Diffuse systemic sclerosis is characterized by widespread skin fibrosis involving the trunk and proximal extremities, along with internal organ involvement (lungs, heart, kidneys, GI tract). Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are associated with diffuse disease and interstitial lung disease, which is the leading cause of death.
keyFact: Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibody is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis and ILD; anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome) and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

wrongAnswers.name: Limited systemic sclerosis (CREST)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Limited scleroderma (CREST) has skin involvement restricted to the distal extremities and face, is associated with anti-centromere antibody, and has a better prognosis with less aggressive internal organ involvement.

wrongAnswers.name: Mixed connective tissue disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCTD features overlapping elements of SLE, myositis, and scleroderma with high-titer anti-U1-RNP antibodies; it does not typically cause the diffuse proximal skin fibrosis seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Eosinophilic fasciitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eosinophilic fasciitis causes skin thickening with a 'peau d'orange' appearance but spares the hands and face, shows peripheral eosinophilia, and lacks Raynaud's phenomenon and anti-Scl-70 positivity.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with joint pain in her hands and wrists, puffy swollen fingers, muscle weakness, difficulty swallowing, and color changes in her fingers with cold exposure.
She has had joint pain and puffy fingers for over a year; a prior rheumatology evaluation was inconclusive.
Exam reveals swollen sausage-like fingers with early sclerodactyly, mild proximal muscle weakness, synovitis of the wrists and MCPs, and Raynaud phenomenon.

ANA is strongly positive at 1:2560 with a speckled pattern. Anti-U1-RNP antibody is positive at very high titer. Anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, and anti-Scl-70 antibodies are all negative. Complement levels are normal.
Nailfold capillaroscopy shows dilated and disorganized capillary loops with avascular areas, and muscle biopsy shows perivascular inflammatory infiltrates with perifascicular atrophy.
explanation: Mixed connective tissue disease is defined by overlapping features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis in the setting of high-titer anti-U1-RNP antibodies. Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the leading cause of mortality.
keyFact: The hallmark of MCTD is a very high titer of anti-U1-RNP antibodies; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm (which are SLE-specific) are typically absent, distinguishing MCTD from SLE.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE would be expected to have anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm antibodies, complement consumption, and renal or hematologic involvement; the isolated very high anti-U1-RNP with overlapping sclerotic features points away from pure SLE.

wrongAnswers.name: Diffuse systemic sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diffuse scleroderma causes prominent proximal skin thickening and anti-Scl-70 positivity; it does not typically cause the SLE-like or myositis-like features seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Undifferentiated connective tissue disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: UCTD lacks the specific serologic marker (anti-U1-RNP) at very high titers and the characteristic clinical overlap syndrome that defines MCTD.

clues: A 30-year-old man from Turkey presents with recurrent painful oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and episodes of blurred vision with eye pain.
He has had at least three separate episodes of oral ulceration in the past year. He also reports intermittent knee and ankle swelling and a recent episode of painful leg swelling.

Exam reveals two active deep aphthous ulcers in the oral cavity, a healing ulcer on the scrotum, and hypopyon visible on slit-lamp examination of the right eye. Erythema nodosum-like lesions are present on both shins.
Doppler ultrasound of the right lower extremity reveals a deep vein thrombosis. ESR is elevated; CRP is elevated; HLA-B51 is positive.

A pathergy test is performed: intradermal needle prick produces a sterile papulopustular reaction at 48 hours, in a patient with recurrent oral aphthae, genital ulceration, and anterior uveitis with hypopyon.
explanation: Behcet disease is a systemic vasculitis of unknown etiology affecting vessels of all sizes, most prevalent along the ancient Silk Road countries. The diagnosis is clinical, based on recurrent oral ulcers (mandatory) plus genital ulcers, ocular inflammation, skin lesions, or a positive pathergy test.
keyFact: Behcet disease is the only vasculitis that involves both arteries and veins of all sizes; it is the most common cause of hypopyon uveitis in endemic regions, and the pathergy phenomenon (skin hyperreactivity to minor trauma) is highly specific.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis follows a triggering infection and features urethritis with conjunctivitis (not uveitis with hypopyon); oral ulcers are shallow and painless, not the deep recurrent painful aphthous ulcers of Behcet disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Herpes simplex virus infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV can cause oral and genital ulcers but does not cause uveitis with hypopyon, erythema nodosum, pathergy, or recurrent sterile DVT; HSV testing would be positive in HSV disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Inflammatory bowel disease with extraintestinal manifestations
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IBD can cause oral ulcers, uveitis, and erythema nodosum but does not cause genital ulcers or a positive pathergy test, and GI symptoms would be prominent.

clues: A 24-year-old woman presents with fatigue, malaise, left arm weakness during activity, and recurrent episodes of lightheadedness over six months.
She reports that her left arm tires faster than her right and that she has had occasional visual disturbances. New hypertension was discovered at a recent checkup.

Exam reveals an absent left radial pulse with blood pressure 40 mmHg lower in the left arm than the right. Bruits are audible over both subclavian arteries and the abdominal aorta. Fundoscopy shows arteriovenous anastomoses.

ESR and CRP are markedly elevated. MR angiography shows segmental stenosis and concentric wall thickening of the aortic arch and its major branches, with aneurysmal dilation of the descending thoracic aorta.
FDG-PET scan shows intense circumferential uptake in the walls of the aortic arch, left subclavian artery, and left common carotid artery, indicating active large-vessel inflammation.
explanation: Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis predominantly affecting the aorta and its primary branches in young women (under 40), most prevalent in Asia. The inflammatory phase causes constitutional symptoms, followed by the occlusive phase with absent pulses, limb claudication, and renovascular hypertension.
keyFact: Takayasu arteritis is differentiated from GCA by age: Takayasu affects patients under 40 (classically young Asian women), while GCA affects patients over 50; both are granulomatous large-vessel vasculitides.

wrongAnswers.name: Giant cell arteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GCA occurs in patients over 50 and primarily involves the temporal arteries causing headache and jaw claudication; Takayasu affects young women with aortic branch involvement and absent peripheral pulses.

wrongAnswers.name: Atherosclerotic peripheral artery disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atherosclerotic PAD affects older patients with cardiovascular risk factors and does not cause elevated inflammatory markers, constitutional symptoms, or aortic wall thickening on imaging.

wrongAnswers.name: Coarctation of the aorta
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Coarctation causes discrepant upper vs. lower extremity blood pressures (not arm-to-arm), is congenital, does not cause elevated inflammatory markers, and would show a fixed discrete narrowing on imaging rather than segmental wall inflammation.

clues: A 70-year-old man presents with progressive bowing of his right leg, deep aching bone pain, and gradual hearing loss over the past two years.
He reports that his hat size has increased and that his right leg has been progressively bowing.
Exam reveals a warm, visibly bowed right tibia, an enlarged cranium with prominent frontal bossing, and bilateral conductive hearing loss. No joint swelling is present.

Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated at 1,200 U/L with normal calcium, phosphate, and aminotransferases. X-rays show cortical thickening with a 'blade of grass' lytic front in the right tibia and 'cotton wool' densities in the skull.
Technetium bone scan shows intense focal radiotracer uptake in the right tibia, skull, and pelvis, corresponding to areas of disorganized bone remodeling on radiographs.
explanation: Paget disease of bone is a focal disorder of bone remodeling characterized by increased osteoclast activity followed by disorganized osteoblastic repair, resulting in enlarged, structurally weak bone. Alkaline phosphatase is the primary biochemical marker; complications include bone deformity, pathologic fractures, high-output heart failure, and osteosarcoma transformation (1%).
keyFact: Markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium in an elderly patient with bone pain and deformity is the classic lab pattern of Paget disease; serum calcium and phosphate are normal unless the patient is immobilized.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteosarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteosarcoma causes bone pain and destruction but typically in younger patients (peak 10–20 years); alkaline phosphatase elevation alone with the characteristic X-ray pattern of cortical thickening favors Paget disease, though sarcomatous transformation in Paget disease is a rare complication.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyperparathyroidism causes elevated calcium and PTH with subperiosteal bone resorption; it does not cause the focal, markedly enlarged bone changes, cranial enlargement, and 'cotton wool' skull X-ray of Paget disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Bone metastases
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastatic bone disease causes lytic or sclerotic lesions but does not cause the enlargement and cortical thickening characteristic of Paget disease; the markedly elevated isolated ALP with normal calcium and the specific X-ray pattern help distinguish.

clues: A 22-year-old male competitive athlete presents with palpitations and near-syncope that occur during intense exercise.
His older brother died suddenly during a soccer match at age 25; the patient's episodes have been increasing in frequency over the past year.
Examination at rest is unremarkable; heart sounds are regular with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs; there is no jugular venous distension or peripheral edema.

ECG shows T-wave inversions in leads V1 through V3 and small deflections following the QRS complex in right precordial leads; echocardiogram shows a dilated right ventricle with regional wall motion abnormalities.

Cardiac MRI reveals fibrofatty infiltration of the right ventricular free wall, and endomyocardial biopsy shows residual myocyte islands surrounded by fibroadipose tissue replacing more than 60 percent of the myocardium.
explanation: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is a hereditary desmosomal cardiomyopathy characterized by fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium, leading to ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, particularly in young athletes. It is caused by mutations in desmosomal proteins (most commonly desmoplakin, plakophilin-2).
keyFact: The epsilon wave (a small deflection after the QRS in V1–V3) is the most specific ECG finding in ARVC; LBBB morphology of the VT indicates a right ventricular origin.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM causes exercise-related syncope and sudden death but features LV hypertrophy (not RV) on imaging, a systolic murmur, and VT with RBBB (not LBBB) morphology.

wrongAnswers.name: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: WPW causes delta waves and a short PR interval at rest with SVT (not VT); it does not cause RV structural abnormalities or epsilon waves, though it can also cause sudden death.

wrongAnswers.name: Brugada syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Brugada syndrome shows a coved ST-segment elevation in V1–V3 and causes VF (not LBBB-morphology VT); structural heart disease is absent, and arrhythmias typically occur at rest or during sleep.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, intermittent near-syncope when she changes position, and low-grade fever with unexplained weight loss over four months.
She has had two episodes of transient left arm weakness and visual loss lasting 30 minutes each. Her symptoms seem to fluctuate with body position.
Exam reveals a low-pitched diastolic sound that varies with position, a murmur mimicking mitral stenosis that changes intensity when the patient sits up, and digital clubbing.

ESR is elevated. Echocardiography reveals a mobile, pedunculated, 4 cm heterogeneous mass attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis, prolapsing through the mitral valve during diastole.
Surgical excision yields a gelatinous mass. Histopathology shows stellate and polygonal cells embedded in an abundant myxoid stroma.
explanation: Cardiac myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor, most frequently found in the left atrium attached to the interatrial septum. It produces a triad of obstructive symptoms (mimicking mitral stenosis), embolic phenomena (strokes, peripheral emboli), and constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, elevated ESR).
keyFact: The 'tumor plop' is a low-pitched sound in early diastole caused by the myxoma prolapsing through the mitral valve; symptoms classically change with changes in body position — a key distinguishing feature from structural mitral valve disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mitral stenosis causes a fixed diastolic rumble that does not change with position; it does not cause fever, constitutional symptoms, or embolic strokes, and echocardiography would show a thickened, calcified valve rather than a mobile mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Infective endocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Endocarditis causes fever and embolic phenomena but involves valve leaflets (not an intra-atrial mass), shows vegetations on the valve, and would have positive blood cultures.

wrongAnswers.name: Left atrial thrombus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LA thrombus typically forms in the left atrial appendage in the setting of AF or mitral stenosis, is non-mobile and sessile, and would not cause a tumor plop or constitutional symptoms.

clues: A 75-year-old man with a history of prior anterior myocardial infarction presents with episodes of sudden loss of consciousness without warning, fatigue, and exercise intolerance over three months.
He reports several witnessed syncopal episodes with spontaneous recovery. Home heart rate monitoring consistently shows rates around 35 beats per minute.
Exam reveals a regular bradycardic pulse at 36 bpm. Cannon A waves are visible in the jugular venous pulsation. The intensity of S1 varies from beat to beat. Blood pressure is 100/70.
ECG shows P waves marching at 75 bpm and QRS complexes occurring independently at 36 bpm with wide QRS morphology. There is no consistent relationship between P waves and QRS complexes.

Complete atrioventricular dissociation is confirmed on electrophysiology study, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular rate, no conducted P waves, and an infra-Hisian escape rhythm with prolonged HV interval.
explanation: Complete heart block (third-degree AV block) is characterized by complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular conduction; the ventricles are driven by an escape rhythm. Common causes include ischemic heart disease, calcific valve disease, congenital heart disease (neonatal lupus), Lyme disease, and drugs.
keyFact: Cannon A waves (large JVP waves from right atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve) and variable S1 intensity are clinical signs of AV dissociation; Stokes-Adams attacks (sudden loss of consciousness from asystole or VF) are the classic presentation.

wrongAnswers.name: Second-degree AV block (Mobitz II)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mobitz II shows intermittent non-conducted P waves without PR prolongation, with a ratio like 2:1 or 3:1; there is still some relationship between P waves and conducted QRS complexes, unlike the complete dissociation of third-degree block.

wrongAnswers.name: Sick sinus syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sick sinus syndrome involves dysfunction of the SA node with bradycardia, pauses, and tachycardia-bradycardia; the ECG would show sinus bradycardia or arrest, not AV dissociation with an independent ventricular escape rhythm.

wrongAnswers.name: Ventricular tachycardia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VT causes wide-complex tachycardia, not a regular bradycardia with P wave and QRS dissociation; the rate here is too slow for VT.

clues: A 68-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of palpitations followed by lightheadedness, fatigue, and one near-syncopal episode over the past six months.
She notes that periods of rapid heart pounding are followed by prolonged pauses that make her feel faint. She was recently prescribed diltiazem for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
Exam reveals a resting heart rate of 48 bpm. Blood pressure is normal. Heart sounds are regular with no murmurs or gallops; no peripheral edema.

48-hour Holter monitor captures multiple episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, each followed by prolonged sinus pauses up to 4.8 seconds before sinus rhythm resumes, temporally correlated with symptoms.
Electrophysiology study reveals a markedly prolonged sinus node recovery time after atrial pacing, showing intrinsic sinus node dysfunction with the tachycardia-bradycardia pattern.
explanation: Sick sinus syndrome encompasses a spectrum of SA node disorders including sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, sinoatrial exit block, and chronotropic incompetence. The tachycardia-bradycardia variant involves paroxysmal SVT (often AF) followed by prolonged sinus pauses upon termination, causing pre-syncope or syncope.
keyFact: In tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome, the prolonged sinus pause occurs at the termination of the tachyarrhythmia (not during it); rate-controlling drugs for AF must be used cautiously as they can worsen the bradycardia, often necessitating pacemaker implantation before pharmacologic therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Complete heart block
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Complete heart block shows persistent complete AV dissociation with an independent ventricular escape rhythm; it does not show alternating tachyarrhythmias and bradyarrhythmias originating from SA node dysfunction.

wrongAnswers.name: Vasovagal syncope
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vasovagal syncope is triggered by specific situational stimuli (pain, prolonged standing), is accompanied by prodromal symptoms, and does not show the Holter pattern of tachyarrhythmia followed by sinus pauses.

wrongAnswers.name: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity causes syncope triggered specifically by carotid sinus stimulation (tight collar, head turning) and produces asystole or hypotension on carotid sinus massage, not the spontaneous alternating pattern seen on Holter.

clues: A 16-year-old boy presents with gradually worsening exercise intolerance and shortness of breath during sports over the past year.
A murmur was noted in infancy but never further evaluated. His parents report he occasionally appears slightly blue during intense exertion.

Exam reveals a harsh systolic ejection murmur loudest at the upper left sternal border radiating to the back, widely split S2 with a soft P2, a palpable right ventricular heave, and a prominent jugular venous A wave.

ECG shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy. Chest X-ray shows post-stenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery. Echocardiography reveals a thickened, domed valve with a peak transvalvular gradient of 65 mmHg.

Cardiac catheterization confirms a transvalvular pressure gradient of 68 mmHg across the pulmonary valve, with right ventricular systolic pressure of 85 mmHg and a normal pulmonary artery pressure beyond the valve.
explanation: Pulmonary valve stenosis is the most common congenital right-sided valvular lesion, characterized by a domed or dysplastic pulmonary valve obstructing RV outflow. Symptoms (exercise intolerance, RV failure, cyanosis) develop with severe stenosis; balloon valvuloplasty is curative for valvular stenosis.
keyFact: The key auscultatory findings of pulmonic stenosis are: an ejection click that decreases with inspiration (opposite of all other right-sided sounds), a systolic ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border, and a widely split S2 with a soft P2.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrial septal defect
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD causes a fixed split S2 and a soft systolic flow murmur from increased pulmonary blood flow, not a harsh ejection murmur with post-stenotic PA dilation; RV overload is from volume, not pressure.

wrongAnswers.name: Tetralogy of Fallot
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TOF includes pulmonary stenosis but also VSD, RV hypertrophy, and overriding aorta; TOF causes more prominent cyanosis from right-to-left shunting, and the chest X-ray would show a boot-shaped heart.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM causes a systolic ejection murmur that increases with Valsalva and standing (decreased preload), involves the left ventricle, and would not cause post-stenotic pulmonary artery dilation or a soft P2.

clues: A 19-year-old woman presents with worsening palpitations, exercise intolerance, and occasional bluish discoloration of her lips during exertion.
She has always had reduced exercise capacity compared to peers. She reports episodes of sudden rapid heart racing that stop on their own.
Exam reveals mild central cyanosis, a widely split first heart sound, a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, a right-sided S3 and S4, and hepatomegaly with elevated JVP.

ECG shows right bundle branch block, tall peaked P waves, and a short PR interval with a delta wave. Chest X-ray shows massive cardiomegaly with a box-shaped cardiac silhouette from right atrial enlargement.

Echocardiography demonstrates apical displacement of the septal and posterior tricuspid valve leaflets greater than 8 mm/m² below the annular plane, with atrialization of the proximal right ventricle and an associated patent foramen ovale.
explanation: Ebstein anomaly is a congenital malformation of the tricuspid valve where the septal and posterior leaflets are displaced apically into the right ventricle, causing tricuspid regurgitation, right atrial enlargement, and a small functional RV. It is associated with maternal lithium exposure and frequently co-exists with WPW syndrome (right-sided accessory pathway).
keyFact: Ebstein anomaly is the most common congenital heart defect associated with WPW syndrome (up to 25% of cases); the 'box-shaped' heart on chest X-ray from massive right atrial dilation is a characteristic radiographic finding.

wrongAnswers.name: Tricuspid regurgitation from other causes
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary TR (from pulmonary hypertension or RV dilation) would not show the characteristic apical displacement of the tricuspid leaflets on echo, the Himalayan P waves, or the WPW pattern on ECG.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrial septal defect
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD causes right heart volume overload with fixed split S2 and a soft pulmonary flow murmur; it does not produce the massive right atrial enlargement, tricuspid valve displacement, or WPW association seen in Ebstein anomaly.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary atresia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pulmonary atresia causes severe cyanosis from birth with duct-dependent pulmonary circulation; it does not present with the specific tricuspid valve anatomy, WPW, or box-shaped heart of Ebstein anomaly.

clues: A 32-year-old woman presents with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral lower extremity swelling that began several weeks after her recent delivery.
She had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and no prior cardiac history. Her symptoms have worsened over the past week to the point she cannot walk one block.
Exam reveals tachycardia at 112 bpm, elevated JVP, bilateral basal crackles, a displaced and diffuse apical impulse, an S3 gallop, and 3+ pitting edema to both knees.
BNP is markedly elevated at 1,850 pg/mL. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with bilateral pulmonary vascular congestion. ECG shows sinus tachycardia.
Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25%, in a patient whose prenatal echocardiogram at 20 weeks gestation was structurally and functionally normal.
explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a dilated cardiomyopathy presenting in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum, with no prior history of cardiac disease. Risk factors include multiparity, advanced maternal age, African descent, twin pregnancies, and pre-eclampsia. Recovery occurs in approximately 50% of cases.
keyFact: Subsequent pregnancy in a woman with prior PPCM carries significant risk of recurrence and decompensation, even if LV function has normalized; bromocriptine (inhibiting prolactin) has shown benefit in some trials.

wrongAnswers.name: Pre-eclampsia with pulmonary edema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pre-eclampsia presents before delivery or within 24–48 hours postpartum with hypertension and proteinuria; it does not cause a dilated cardiomyopathy with reduced EF persisting weeks after delivery.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE postpartum causes acute dyspnea and hypoxia but would show right heart strain on echo (not dilated LV), elevated D-dimer, and a CT-PA would show filling defects; it does not cause the bilateral edema and S3 gallop.

wrongAnswers.name: Pre-existing dilated cardiomyopathy unmasked by pregnancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pre-existing DCM would have shown LV dysfunction on the mid-pregnancy echocardiogram; by definition, PPCM requires no prior structural heart disease.

clues: A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a severe headache, blurred vision, and chest tightness that developed over the past several hours.
He ran out of his antihypertensive medications two weeks ago. He reports minimal urine output all day.
Blood pressure is 220/140 mmHg confirmed in both arms. He is confused with a GCS of 13. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilledema with flame hemorrhages. An S4 gallop is auscultated.
Creatinine is 3.8 mg/dL from a baseline of 1.0. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts and proteinuria. Troponin is mildly elevated. CT head shows no hemorrhage.
MRI brain shows bilateral posterior white matter edema without restricted diffusion on DWI, consistent with vasogenic edema in the parieto-occipital regions.
explanation: Hypertensive emergency is defined by severely elevated blood pressure (typically >180/120) with acute end-organ damage including encephalopathy, retinopathy, AKI, aortic dissection, or acute MI. Treatment requires IV antihypertensives (nicardipine, labetalol, or nitroprusside) with controlled BP reduction to avoid ischemia from overcorrection.
keyFact: In hypertensive emergency, the MAP should be reduced by no more than 20–25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over the next 2–6 hours; overcorrection can cause watershed ischemic strokes due to impaired cerebral autoregulation.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertensive urgency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypertensive urgency has severely elevated BP without acute end-organ damage; it is managed with oral antihypertensives and does not require ICU admission or IV medications.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic stroke can cause hypertension reactively, but the bilateral papilledema, AKI with casts, and diffuse presentation without a focal deficit points to hypertensive emergency rather than a focal vascular event.

wrongAnswers.name: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PRES is a consequence of hypertensive emergency (the two overlap), but the underlying diagnosis driving the acute presentation is hypertensive emergency; PRES would be a radiographic finding (posterior white matter edema on MRI) in this context.

clues: A 58-year-old male smoker presents with progressive swelling of his face, neck, and both arms along with worsening dyspnea over three weeks.
He reports hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, and headaches that worsen when bending forward. He has lost 15 pounds over the past two months.

Exam reveals facial and neck plethora, non-pulsatile distension of the jugular veins and anterior chest wall collateral veins, periorbital edema, and cyanosis limited to the face and upper extremities. Lower extremities are normal.
CT chest with contrast shows a large right hilar mass encasing mediastinal structures and partially occluding the superior vena cava, with intraluminal filling defects consistent with thrombus.
Bronchoscopy with biopsy of the mediastinal mass reveals small cell carcinoma compressing and invading the superior vena cava.
explanation: SVC syndrome results from obstruction of venous drainage from the head, neck, and upper extremities, most commonly caused by malignancy (lung cancer — especially SCLC — and lymphoma). Features include facial and arm swelling, dilated collateral chest wall veins, and headache worsening with the supine position.
keyFact: The most common cause of SVC syndrome is malignancy (lung cancer accounts for ~65–80%, with SCLC and squamous cell being most common); non-malignant causes include thrombosis from indwelling central venous catheters.

wrongAnswers.name: Cardiac tamponade
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tamponade causes JVP elevation, hypotension, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) with equalization of diastolic pressures; it does not cause the facial plethora, collateral vein dilation, or mediastinal mass seen in SVC syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrotic syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nephrotic syndrome causes generalized dependent edema with hypoalbuminemia and proteinuria; facial edema is periorbital and pitting, not plethoric, and does not cause dilated neck veins or upper extremity predominance.

wrongAnswers.name: Constrictive pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Constrictive pericarditis causes elevated JVP with Kussmaul's sign and pericardial knock; it does not cause facial plethora, differential upper vs. lower extremity venous congestion, or a mediastinal mass.

clues: A 3-year-old boy presents with five days of high fever unresponsive to antipyretics, irritability, and decreased oral intake.
His mother says he has been pulling at his ears and refusing to eat for three days. No one in his daycare has been sick with similar symptoms.

Exam shows a temperature of 39.8°C, bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection, erythema and induration of the palms and soles, a polymorphous truncal rash, and a 2 cm right anterior cervical lymph node.
CBC shows leukocytosis at 22,000 and thrombocytosis at 640,000. ESR is 90 mm/hr with markedly elevated CRP. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria.
Echocardiogram performed on illness day 8 reveals coronary artery dilation with a z-score greater than 2.5 in the left anterior descending artery.
explanation: Kawasaki disease is the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries, characterized by fever lasting ≥5 days plus at least 4 of 5 clinical criteria. The most serious complication is coronary artery aneurysm development; IVIG given within the first 10 days significantly reduces this risk.
keyFact: Coronary artery aneurysms are the most feared complication of Kawasaki disease; periungual desquamation (peeling of skin around the fingernails and toenails) typically occurs in the subacute phase (days 10–25) and is a helpful retrospective clue.

wrongAnswers.name: Scarlet fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scarlet fever (Group A Strep) causes a sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, and pharyngitis, but does not cause conjunctival injection, extremity edema, or coronary artery dilation; it responds to antibiotics.

wrongAnswers.name: Measles
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Measles causes Koplik spots, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis followed by a descending maculopapular rash; it does not cause the extremity changes, prolonged high fever, or coronary artery involvement of Kawasaki disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (systemic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Systemic JIA (Still's disease) causes a characteristic evanescent salmon-pink rash, quotidian fever spikes, and arthritis; it does not cause the specific mucocutaneous changes (lip cracking, conjunctivitis, palm erythema) or coronary artery involvement of Kawasaki disease.

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with anterior neck pain radiating to her jaw and hyperthyroid symptoms following a recent upper respiratory infection.
She reports the pain worsens with swallowing and turning her head. She has also had tremor, excessive sweating, and insomnia for the past two weeks.
Exam reveals an exquisitely tender, firm, mildly enlarged thyroid gland. She is tachycardic at 108 bpm. There is no exophthalmos or pretibial myxedema.
TSH is suppressed below 0.01, free T4 is elevated, and ESR is markedly elevated at 85 mm/hr. CBC shows mild leukocytosis.
Radioactive iodine uptake scan shows near-absent thyroidal uptake at less than 1% at 24 hours.
explanation: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis is a self-limited inflammatory thyroid condition triggered by a viral infection, presenting with a painful tender thyroid, elevated ESR, and a transient hyperthyroid phase (from stored hormone release) followed by hypothyroidism and then recovery. Suppressed radioiodine uptake distinguishes it from Graves disease.
keyFact: The pathognomonic finding is a painful tender thyroid with suppressed RAIU (<5%) in the setting of elevated thyroid hormones — unlike Graves disease where RAIU is elevated (>35%); NSAIDs or corticosteroids treat the pain.

wrongAnswers.name: Graves disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism with elevated RAIU (not suppressed), diffusely enlarged painless goiter, and autoimmune features (exophthalmos, pretibial myxedema, TSI antibodies); there is no preceding viral illness or thyroid tenderness.

wrongAnswers.name: Hashimoto thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hashimoto thyroiditis is typically painless, presents with hypothyroidism or a euthyroid goiter, and is characterized by anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies; ESR is not markedly elevated.

wrongAnswers.name: Suppurative thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Suppurative (infectious) thyroiditis causes severe pain with high fever, fluctuance, and systemic sepsis; it is bacterial (not viral), requires antibiotics and drainage, and is far rarer than subacute thyroiditis.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with agitation, feeling extremely hot, palpitations, and confusion that developed over several hours.
She has a history of Graves disease and stopped taking her antithyroid medication two weeks ago after running out of refills.
Examination reveals a temperature of 40.2 degrees Celsius, heart rate 152 bpm, a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland with an audible bruit, proptosis, lid lag, fine tremor, and warm moist skin.
TSH is undetectable at less than 0.01 mIU/L and free T4 is markedly elevated at 6.8 ng/dL; liver enzymes are mildly elevated; ECG shows atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response.
A clinical severity scoring system incorporating fever above 40 degrees, heart rate above 150, atrial fibrillation, altered mental status, and a precipitating event yields a total of 75 points.
explanation: Thyroid storm is a life-threatening hypermetabolic crisis in severe thyrotoxicosis, most commonly precipitated by surgery, infection, trauma, or iodine load in a patient with uncontrolled hyperthyroidism. The Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale aids diagnosis; treatment targets all steps of thyroid hormone production and action simultaneously.
keyFact: In thyroid storm, PTU is preferred over methimazole because it blocks both new hormone synthesis AND peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 (via inhibition of deiodinase); iodine (Lugol's solution) must be given at least 1 hour AFTER PTU to prevent using the iodine for new hormone synthesis.

wrongAnswers.name: Malignant hyperthermia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malignant hyperthermia occurs intraoperatively from volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine, causing muscle rigidity and rhabdomyolysis; it does not cause hyperthyroid labs, goiter, or exophthalmos, and is treated with dantrolene.

wrongAnswers.name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NMS occurs from dopamine antagonist use, causing hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, and elevated CK; it is not associated with thyroid hormone excess.

wrongAnswers.name: Pheochromocytoma crisis
