wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pheo crisis causes paroxysmal hypertension, headache, diaphoresis, and tachycardia but does not cause the goiter, exophthalmos, elevated thyroid hormones, or the specific precipitation by surgery in a Graves patient.

clues: A 78-year-old woman is found unresponsive at home during the winter by a neighbor who noticed she had not picked up her mail in two days.
She has a history of hypothyroidism and ran out of her levothyroxine refills several months ago.

Examination reveals a core temperature of 32 degrees Celsius, heart rate 48 bpm, blood pressure 88/60 mmHg, obtundation with response only to painful stimuli, periorbital and facial puffiness, doughy non-pitting edema of the extremities, and markedly delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes.
ABG shows CO2 retention at 62 mmHg with hypoxia; sodium is 118 mEq/L; chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with a small pericardial effusion; ECG shows sinus bradycardia with low-voltage QRS complexes.
TSH is greater than 100 mIU/L with undetectable free T4, and bedside echocardiography reveals a moderate pericardial effusion without tamponade.
explanation: Myxedema coma is a rare, life-threatening decompensation of severe hypothyroidism, triggered by cold exposure, infection, or drugs in a patient with untreated or undertreated hypothyroidism. The hallmarks are altered consciousness, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation (CO2 retention), and hyponatremia.
keyFact: Hydrocortisone must be given empirically before or with levothyroxine in myxedema coma because the stress of the condition may unmask coexisting adrenal insufficiency; giving thyroid hormone alone to a cortisol-deficient patient can precipitate an adrenal crisis.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothermia from environmental exposure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Environmental hypothermia causes low temperature but not the doughy non-pitting edema, markedly elevated TSH, hyponatremia, and absent DTRs seen in myxedema coma; thyroid labs would be normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic shock
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic shock causes hypotension and altered mental status but typically with fever (or normal temperature) and elevated WBC; the doughy edema, coarse features, and markedly suppressed thyroid function distinguish myxedema coma.

wrongAnswers.name: Adrenal crisis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adrenal crisis causes hypotension, hyponatremia, and altered consciousness but would show low cortisol and is not associated with the hypothermia, non-pitting edema, and markedly elevated TSH of myxedema coma (though the two can coexist).

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of severe epigastric pain and refractory heartburn over the past two years despite maximum-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy.
His father had a pituitary tumor removed in his forties, and the patient himself has had two episodes of kidney stones.
Exam reveals bitemporal visual field cuts on confrontation testing; a sestamibi scan localizes a right inferior parathyroid adenoma; palpation of the abdomen reveals mild epigastric tenderness.
Calcium is 11.8 mg/dL with elevated PTH; fasting gastrin is greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal; prolactin is elevated; CT abdomen shows a 1.8 cm pancreatic head mass.
Genetic testing reveals a germline loss-of-function mutation on chromosome 11q13 in a patient with concurrent parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors.
explanation: MEN1 (Wermer syndrome) is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin), characterized by the '3 P's': parathyroid (hyperparathyroidism, most common — >90%), pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma most common), and pituitary adenomas (prolactinoma most common).
keyFact: Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common initial manifestation of MEN1, occurring in >90% of patients; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma causing recurrent peptic ulcers with very high gastrin) in a young patient should always prompt evaluation for MEN1.

wrongAnswers.name: MEN2A
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MEN2A involves medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia due to RET mutations; it does not include pituitary adenomas or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

wrongAnswers.name: Sporadic primary hyperparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sporadic HPT is isolated and would not explain the concurrent pituitary adenoma, gastrinoma, and family history; the pattern of multiple endocrine tumors in multiple family members mandates evaluation for MEN1.

wrongAnswers.name: VIPoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VIPoma (Verner-Morrison syndrome) causes watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome) — not peptic ulcers; it can occur in MEN1 but is not the primary pancreatic lesion here (gastrinoma is), given the recurrent ulcers and elevated gastrin.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with episodic headaches, palpitations, and profuse sweating triggered by exercise over the past six months.
She noticed a slowly growing lump in her neck three months ago, and her mother underwent thyroid surgery in her thirties.
Exam reveals a firm, fixed 3 cm right thyroid nodule with palpable right cervical lymphadenopathy; blood pressure is 165/95 mmHg; no marfanoid habitus or mucosal neuromas are noted.

Serum calcitonin is markedly elevated at greater than 2,000 pg/mL; 24-hour urine metanephrines are elevated; CT abdomen shows a 3.5 cm right adrenal mass; PTH is mildly elevated with serum calcium of 11.2 mg/dL.
Genetic testing reveals a gain-of-function mutation at codon 634 of the RET proto-oncogene in a patient with concurrent thyroid, adrenal, and parathyroid disease.
explanation: MEN2A (Sipple syndrome) is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by activating RET proto-oncogene mutations, characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma (100% penetrance), pheochromocytoma (50%), and primary hyperparathyroidism (20–30%). MTC is the most common cause of death; pheochromocytoma must be resected BEFORE thyroidectomy to avoid hypertensive crisis.
keyFact: Pheochromocytoma in MEN2A must always be evaluated and surgically removed BEFORE thyroidectomy to prevent an intraoperative hypertensive crisis from catecholamine release during manipulation of the thyroid; serum calcitonin is the tumor marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma.

wrongAnswers.name: MEN1
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MEN1 features parathyroid hyperplasia, pancreatic NETs, and pituitary adenomas caused by MEN1 gene mutations; it does not include medullary thyroid carcinoma or pheochromocytoma.

wrongAnswers.name: MEN2B
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MEN2B also involves MTC and pheochromocytoma (RET mutations) but includes marfanoid habitus, mucosal neuromas, and ganglioneuromatosis of the GI tract instead of parathyroid disease; it does not cause hyperparathyroidism.

wrongAnswers.name: Papillary thyroid carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Papillary thyroid carcinoma does not secrete calcitonin (calcitonin is secreted by parafollicular C cells in MTC), does not associate with pheochromocytoma or RET mutations in the same way, and has a different pathologic appearance.

clues: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with fatigue, constipation, depressed mood, and difficulty concentrating that have been gradually worsening over several months.
She has had two episodes of calcium-containing kidney stones in the past three years.
Exam reveals mild hypertension at 148/90 mmHg, diffuse proximal muscle weakness, and no palpable neck masses; there is no band keratopathy on slit-lamp examination.
Serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL with normal albumin; intact PTH is 145 pg/mL; phosphate is 2.0 mg/dL; 24-hour urine calcium excretion is 380 mg/day; DEXA shows osteoporosis at the lumbar spine.

Sestamibi scan shows a single focus of increased uptake in the right inferior position that persists on delayed imaging, with 4D-CT localizing a 1.2 cm hypervascular nodule posterior to the right thyroid lobe.
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in the outpatient setting, most commonly caused by a solitary parathyroid adenoma (80–85%). The classic presentation is 'bones, stones, groans, and psychic moans' — but most patients today are asymptomatic and detected incidentally.
keyFact: The key biochemical finding is hypercalcemia with an inappropriately elevated PTH (not suppressed as expected with hypercalcemia from any other cause); hypophosphatemia is also characteristic, distinguishing it from familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) where urine calcium is low.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypercalcemia of malignancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia (from PTHrP or bony metastases) causes elevated calcium but SUPPRESSED PTH (not elevated); it is more common in hospitalized patients and is not associated with longstanding nephrolithiasis and osteoporosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FHH causes mild hypercalcemia with elevated PTH but characteristically LOW urine calcium excretion (unlike the elevated urine calcium in primary HPT); it is benign and requires no surgical intervention.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes hypercalcemia via vitamin D overproduction (elevated 1,25-OH vitamin D) with SUPPRESSED PTH; serum ACE may be elevated and chest imaging shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

clues: A 6-year-old girl is brought in by her parents because she has been growing much faster than her classmates and has developed body odor and early pubic hair.
Her parents are consanguineous, and a sibling died in the neonatal period from an unknown cause involving vomiting and dehydration.
Examination reveals clitoromegaly, increased skin pigmentation in the axillary and inguinal creases, blood pressure at the 5th percentile for age and height, and Tanner stage 2 pubic hair.
Sodium is 118 mEq/L, potassium is 7.4 mEq/L, blood glucose is 38 mg/dL; ACTH is markedly elevated and cortisol is low; bone age X-ray shows skeletal maturation advanced by three years.
Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly elevated at greater than 10,000 ng/dL, and genetic testing reveals a homozygous mutation in the CYP21A2 gene.
explanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is most commonly caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency, leading to impaired cortisol (and aldosterone in severe forms) synthesis with ACTH-driven androgen excess. The classic salt-wasting form presents in the first weeks of life with adrenal crisis; females present with ambiguous genitalia (virilization) at birth.
keyFact: The diagnostic test for 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH is markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone (the substrate that accumulates proximal to the enzyme block); the salt-wasting form is the most severe and presents with life-threatening hyponatremia and hyperkalemia in the neonatal period.

wrongAnswers.name: Adrenal insufficiency (primary)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) causes hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation but occurs in older patients (autoimmune destruction); neonatal salt-wasting with elevated 17-OHP and ambiguous genitalia in females specifically points to CAH.

wrongAnswers.name: Pyloric stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pyloric stenosis causes projectile vomiting and a metabolic alkalosis (not hyponatremia/hyperkalemia) with hypokalemia; it does not cause hyperpigmentation, hypoglycemia, or endocrine abnormalities.

wrongAnswers.name: Salt-losing nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Salt-losing nephropathy causes hyponatremia but without the hormonal pattern of elevated 17-OHP, elevated ACTH, and low cortisol; it would not cause ambiguous genitalia or hyperpigmentation.

clues: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his family for progressive confusion, extreme thirst, and frequent urination developing over the past week.
He has a history of type 2 diabetes managed with metformin alone, and he was treated for a urinary tract infection five days ago but his mental status has continued to decline.

Exam reveals a profoundly obtunded elderly man with dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, tachycardia of 118 bpm, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, no Kussmaul respirations, and right-sided upper and lower extremity weakness.

Serum glucose is 1,080 mg/dL; serum osmolality is 365 mOsm/kg; sodium is 148 mEq/L; BUN 68 mg/dL; creatinine 2.4 mg/dL; bicarbonate is 22 mEq/L; urinalysis shows glycosuria without ketonuria; serum ketones are absent.
Serum glucose 842 mg/dL, calculated effective osmolality 348 mOsm/kg, arterial pH 7.31, serum bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.8 mmol/L, and anion gap 14 in a type 2 diabetic patient.
explanation: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) is a life-threatening hyperglycemic emergency of type 2 diabetes characterized by extreme hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL), hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), severe dehydration, and altered mental status WITHOUT significant ketoacidosis. The key distinction from DKA is the absence of acidosis and ketones (residual insulin prevents ketogenesis).
keyFact: HHS has a higher mortality than DKA (10–20% vs. 1–5%) due to its occurrence in elderly patients with comorbidities; the mortality is largely from the underlying precipitant (infection, MI) and the degree of hyperosmolality rather than the metabolic acidosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DKA features anion-gap metabolic acidosis, significant ketonemia/ketonuria, and typically occurs in type 1 diabetics with higher insulin deficiency; glucose is usually lower (250–500 mg/dL) and osmolality less extreme than in HHS.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic encephalopathy causes altered mental status with infection but would not explain the glucose of 1,080 mg/dL and osmolality of 365 mOsm/kg; the UTI here is the precipitant of HHS, not the primary cause of encephalopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: While HHS can cause focal neurological deficits (mimicking stroke), the profound hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality are the primary abnormality requiring correction; stroke workup should be performed after stabilization.

clues: A 54-year-old woman presents with a chronic migratory blistering skin rash, significant unintentional weight loss, and new-onset diabetes.
The rash heals in one area but appears in another, leaving behind bronze-colored scars; she also reports a persistently sore tongue and cracking at the corners of her mouth.

Exam reveals a cachectic woman with widespread erythematous patches showing central blistering and crusting on the abdomen, groin, and thighs with areas of bronze hyperpigmentation where prior lesions healed; glossitis and angular cheilitis are present; bilateral lower extremity edema is noted.
Fasting glucose is 245 mg/dL; plasma glucagon is markedly elevated at greater than 1,000 pg/mL; amino acid levels are diffusely low; CT abdomen shows a 4 cm mass in the tail of the pancreas.

Skin biopsy of an active lesion shows superficial epidermal necrosis with a necrolytic pattern, and the pancreatic tail mass on biopsy is a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor of alpha-cell origin.
explanation: Glucagonoma is a rare pancreatic alpha-cell neuroendocrine tumor causing the '4 D's': dermatitis (necrolytic migratory erythema — pathognomonic), diabetes, deep vein thrombosis, and depression, along with weight loss and hypoaminoacidemia. Most are malignant at presentation.
keyFact: Necrolytic migratory erythema (NME) — a migratory, blistering rash with central healing leaving bronze hyperpigmentation — is pathognomonic for glucagonoma; plasma glucagon > 500–1,000 pg/mL is diagnostic.

wrongAnswers.name: VIPoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VIPoma (Verner-Morrison syndrome) causes massive watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome) via vasoactive intestinal peptide; it does not cause the skin rash, diabetes, or glucagon elevation of glucagonoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Insulinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Insulinoma causes hypoglycemia (Whipple's triad) due to excess insulin secretion; it does not cause hyperglycemia, the skin rash, or elevated glucagon.

wrongAnswers.name: Pemphigus vulgaris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pemphigus vulgaris causes blistering skin disease but is an autoimmune condition not associated with elevated glucagon, pancreatic mass, diabetes, or the migratory pattern of NME.

clues: A 48-year-old woman presents with several months of profuse watery diarrhea, severe dehydration, and electrolyte abnormalities; stool studies are negative for infection.
She has been hospitalized twice for dehydration; the diarrhea is entirely watery without blood or mucus, persists even when she stops eating, and does not improve with dietary changes.
Exam reveals severe dehydration with tenting skin, diffuse muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, diffuse abdominal tenderness without organomegaly, and facial flushing.

Serum potassium is 2.1 mEq/L; bicarbonate is 14 mEq/L; gastric pH is 7.0; stool osmotic gap is low; plasma VIP level is markedly elevated at greater than 200 pg/mL; CT abdomen shows a 3 cm pancreatic body mass.

Plasma vasoactive intestinal peptide level exceeds 200 pg/mL, with secretory diarrhea volume exceeding 3 liters per day that persists during a 48-hour fast, and a well-circumscribed pancreatic body mass on cross-sectional imaging.
explanation: VIPoma (Verner-Morrison syndrome) is a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor secreting vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), causing the WDHA syndrome: Watery Diarrhea (>3L/day), Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria (or hypochlorhydria). The massive secretory diarrhea persists even with fasting, distinguishing it from osmotic diarrhea.
keyFact: The key distinguishing feature of secretory diarrhea (as in VIPoma) from osmotic diarrhea is that the diarrhea PERSISTS with fasting; the osmotic gap in stool is low (<50 mOsm/kg) in secretory diarrhea.

wrongAnswers.name: Glucagonoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Glucagonoma causes the '4 D's' including necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, and weight loss due to glucagon excess; it does not cause the massive secretory diarrhea and achlorhydria of VIPoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Carcinoid syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoid syndrome causes episodic flushing, watery diarrhea, bronchospasm, and right-sided heart disease from serotonin; it is diagnosed by elevated 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA, and CT would show a hepatic or small bowel primary, not an isolated pancreatic mass with elevated VIP.

wrongAnswers.name: Microscopic colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Microscopic colitis causes watery non-bloody diarrhea (often in middle-aged women) but does not cause the extreme hypokalemia, achlorhydria, or the degree of volume loss seen here; colonoscopy with biopsy would show collagen or lymphocytic changes, and plasma VIP would be normal.

clues: A 29-year-old woman presents with recurring headaches centered at the back of her head and upper neck that worsen when she coughs, sneezes, or strains.
She also reports episodes of dizziness, difficulty swallowing, and brief visual disturbances triggered by Valsalva maneuvers; she has noticed increasing clumsiness in her hands over the past year.

Exam reveals downbeat nystagmus on downgaze, bilateral upper extremity weakness with hyperreflexia, a cape-like distribution of pain and temperature loss over the shoulders and arms with preserved light touch, and a positive Romberg sign.

MRI brain sagittal view shows herniation of the cerebellar tonsils 8 mm below the foramen magnum into the upper cervical spinal canal; MRI cervical spine shows a fluid-filled cavity within the central cord from C3 to C7.
Cerebellar tonsillar descent greater than 5 mm below the foramen magnum on sagittal MRI with an associated central cord cavity spanning multiple cervical segments.
explanation: Chiari I malformation is the most common Chiari variant, characterized by herniation of the cerebellar tonsils >5 mm below the foramen magnum, often presenting in young adults with cough-headache, cerebellar dysfunction, and syringomyelia. The syrinx causes the characteristic dissociated sensory loss (pain and temperature lost, light touch preserved) in a cape-like distribution.
keyFact: Headaches in Chiari malformation are pathognomonic when they are triggered or worsened by Valsalva maneuvers (coughing, sneezing, straining) — this Valsalva-provoked headache is the most common presenting symptom.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS can cause dissociated sensory loss and cerebellar findings but would show periventricular white matter lesions on MRI (not tonsillar herniation), and symptoms would be episodic and disseminated in time and space.

wrongAnswers.name: Posterior fossa tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Posterior fossa tumors can cause obstructive hydrocephalus and cerebellar signs but would show an enhancing mass on MRI rather than tonsillar descent below the foramen magnum.

wrongAnswers.name: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervical myelopathy from spondylosis causes upper motor neuron signs and myelopathy but would show cord compression from disc/osteophyte complex on MRI, not tonsillar herniation or a syrinx.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with progressive hand weakness and reports that he has burned himself on multiple occasions without feeling any pain.
The sensory changes began in his hands and have slowly spread to involve his arms and upper back over two years; he has noticed increasing difficulty with fine motor tasks like buttoning shirts.

Exam reveals bilateral thenar and hypothenar muscle wasting, absent pain and temperature sensation over the C4 through T1 dermatomes in a cape-like distribution with fully preserved light touch and vibration, upper extremity hyporeflexia, lower extremity hyperreflexia, and bilateral Babinski signs.
MRI cervical spine shows a fusiform fluid-filled cavity within the central cord from C2 to T4; the cerebellar tonsils are displaced 6 mm below the foramen magnum.
A fusiform central cord cavity spanning C2 to T4 on MRI with selective loss of pain and temperature in a cape distribution while dorsal column function remains intact.
explanation: Syringomyelia is a fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord that expands centrally, first disrupting the crossing spinothalamic fibers at the level of the lesion (causing cape-like pain/temperature loss with preserved dorsal column function), then compressing anterior horn cells (LMN weakness) and corticospinal tracts (UMN signs below). Common causes include Chiari malformation, trauma, and tumors.
keyFact: The pathognomonic sensory finding is dissociated sensory loss — loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic) with PRESERVED light touch, vibration, and proprioception (dorsal columns) — in a bilateral cape-like distribution corresponding to the syrinx level.

wrongAnswers.name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ALS causes combined UMN and LMN signs but does not cause sensory loss (purely motor disease); a syrinx would be absent on MRI and the pattern of sensory dissociation is not seen in ALS.

wrongAnswers.name: Cervical cord compression from myelopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervical myelopathy causes UMN and LMN signs but typically causes a non-dissociated sensory level (all modalities lost below the lesion), not a selective cape-like loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch.

wrongAnswers.name: Peripheral neuropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Peripheral neuropathy causes stocking-glove distal sensory loss with reduced reflexes throughout; it does not cause the central cape-like dissociated pattern, the UMN signs in the lower extremities, or the central cord cavity on MRI.

clues: A 72-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty walking, forgetfulness, and episodes of urinary incontinence developing over the past 18 months.
His wife reports that the walking difficulty came first, followed by memory problems, and most recently urinary urgency progressing to frank incontinence.

Examination reveals a wide-based, shuffling gait with small steps and marked difficulty initiating movement as though his feet are magnetically attached to the ground; there is psychomotor slowing with impaired recall, brisk leg reflexes without Babinski signs, and no rigidity or resting tremor.

MRI brain shows disproportionately enlarged lateral and third ventricles with an Evans ratio greater than 0.3, out of proportion to sulcal atrophy, with tight high-convexity sulci and periventricular FLAIR hyperintensities.
After removal of 40 mL of CSF via lumbar puncture, gait speed improves by 20 percent and step length increases measurably within two hours of the procedure.
explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with the classic triad of magnetic gait apraxia, dementia (frontal/subcortical), and urinary incontinence — 'wet, wacky, wobbly.' Despite enlarged ventricles on imaging, CSF pressure is normal. The tap test (improvement after large-volume LP) predicts surgical response to VP shunting.
keyFact: In NPH, gait disturbance (magnetic gait — wide-based, small shuffling steps, difficulty initiating gait) is typically the FIRST symptom and the most prominent; the classic teaching is that if only one symptom is present, it is almost always gait disturbance.

wrongAnswers.name: Alzheimer disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alzheimer disease causes memory loss as the predominant feature but does not cause the characteristic magnetic gait or early urinary incontinence; ventricular enlargement in AD is proportionate to cortical atrophy.

wrongAnswers.name: Parkinson disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Parkinson disease causes a shuffling gait but with rigidity, resting tremor, bradykinesia, and a stooped posture; there is no early prominent dementia or incontinence in early Parkinson's, and MRI does not show disproportionate ventriculomegaly.

wrongAnswers.name: Vascular dementia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vascular dementia causes stepwise cognitive decline with white matter changes and lacunar infarcts; gait abnormality is present but the ventricles are not disproportionately enlarged, and the tap test does not produce acute gait improvement.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of excruciating unilateral pain around and behind one eye that wake him from sleep at the same time each night.

He describes the pain as unbearable, lasting 45 to 90 minutes; during attacks he paces the room and cannot sit still; between episodes he is completely pain-free, and the attacks have been occurring daily for three weeks.

Exam during an attack reveals ptosis and miosis of the left eye, left conjunctival injection with profuse tearing, ipsilateral nasal congestion, and marked psychomotor agitation; between attacks the exam is entirely normal.
MRI brain is normal; there is no aura; attacks occur with strict clocklike regularity at the same time nightly in a period lasting weeks, separated by months of complete remission.

Functional neuroimaging during an attack demonstrates ipsilateral posterior hypothalamic activation with stereotyped unilateral periorbital pain and autonomic features occurring in a temporal cluster pattern.
explanation: Cluster headache is a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia characterized by unilateral severe periorbital pain lasting 15–180 minutes with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features (lacrimation, ptosis, miosis, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection). It is more common in men, occurs in cluster periods of weeks to months, and the affected patient is typically agitated (unlike migraine patients who prefer darkness and rest).
keyFact: The two most important distinguishing features of cluster headache: (1) the patient is AGITATED and paces during attacks (unlike migraine patients who prefer to lie still in a dark room), and (2) the ipsilateral autonomic features (partial Horner syndrome: ptosis + miosis) with the severe periorbital pain.

wrongAnswers.name: Migraine with aura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Migraine lasts 4–72 hours (not 45–90 min), has bilateral or unilateral throbbing pain, nausea/photophobia, and the patient prefers to lie still in a dark room; autonomic features are not prominent and it does not cluster nightly in predictable seasons.

wrongAnswers.name: Trigeminal neuralgia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief (seconds) electric-shock pain triggered by light touch in a V2/V3 distribution; it does not cause autonomic features, last minutes, or wake patients from sleep in a cluster pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SAH causes a sudden 'thunderclap' headache reaching peak intensity in seconds, with meningismus and photophobia; it is a single severe event (not recurrent nightly attacks) and CT/LP would show blood.

clues: A 65-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of severe, lancinating right-sided facial pain that she describes as electric shocks; she avoids touching her face, eating, and talking because these activities provoke the pain.

The pain lasts only 1 to 2 seconds per jolt but occurs in rapid volleys; it is triggered by light touch to her right cheek, chewing, or a gentle breeze; there is no tearing, nasal congestion, or other autonomic symptoms.

Neurological exam is entirely normal between attacks with no sensory loss or motor weakness; touching specific trigger zones on the right cheek and upper lip immediately provokes a brief severe paroxysm of pain.
MRI with high-resolution FIESTA/CISS sequences shows a vascular loop of the superior cerebellar artery compressing the right trigeminal nerve at its root entry zone into the pons.
Brief electric-shock paroxysms triggered by light touch to specific trigger zones in the V2/V3 distribution with a vascular loop compressing the nerve root entry zone on high-resolution MRI.
explanation: Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) is characterized by paroxysmal, unilateral, electric-shock facial pain in the V2 and/or V3 trigeminal distribution, triggered by innocuous stimuli. Most cases result from neurovascular compression (superior cerebellar artery) at the trigeminal root entry zone. Carbamazepine is first-line medical treatment.
keyFact: The presence of any objective sensory loss (numbness, decreased corneal reflex) in a patient presenting with 'trigeminal neuralgia' should prompt concern for a secondary cause such as multiple sclerosis or a posterior fossa tumor compressing the nerve.

wrongAnswers.name: Cluster headache
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cluster headache causes periorbital pain lasting 15–180 minutes with prominent autonomic features (lacrimation, ptosis, miosis) and agitation; it is not triggered by light touch and does not cause the brief second-long shock-like paroxysms.

wrongAnswers.name: Postherpetic neuralgia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Postherpetic neuralgia follows a herpes zoster eruption (dermatomal rash), causes constant burning/dysesthetic pain (not brief paroxysms), and does not have identifiable trigger zones for touch.

wrongAnswers.name: Temporomandibular joint disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TMJ disorder causes jaw pain with clicking and tenderness over the joint; it is dull and aching rather than electric-shock paroxysms, and is not triggered by skin touch to the cheek.

clues: A 44-year-old man presents with acute confusion, unsteady gait, and visual complaints developing over two days; he appears malnourished.
He has a long history of heavy alcohol use and has not eaten a proper meal in several weeks; his friend reports he has been unable to walk without falling and sees objects moving.

Exam reveals a confused, disoriented man with horizontal nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus palsy producing diplopia on lateral gaze, a broad-based ataxic gait, hypothermia at 36°C, and diminished deep tendon reflexes.
CBC shows macrocytic anemia; MRI brain FLAIR/DWI sequences show symmetric hyperintensity and restricted diffusion in the periaqueductal gray matter, mammillary bodies, and medial thalami.

Symmetric signal abnormalities on MRI involving the periaqueductal gray, mammillary bodies, and medial thalami in a malnourished patient presenting with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and altered mental status.
explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy is an acute neurological emergency caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, classically presenting with the triad of ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia, and confusion. It is most common in alcoholics but occurs in any malnourished state. Thiamine must be given BEFORE glucose (glucose administration can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's by depleting residual thiamine).
keyFact: The classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy is ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + confusion — but all three are present in only 10–16% of cases; always give thiamine empirically to any alcoholic or malnourished patient presenting with neurological symptoms, BEFORE glucose.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatic encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hepatic encephalopathy causes confusion and asterixis in the setting of liver failure, with elevated ammonia; it does not cause ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, or the specific MRI changes in periaqueductal gray matter.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Delirium tremens occurs 48–96 hours after alcohol cessation, features autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia), hallucinations, and seizures; it does not cause ophthalmoplegia or the specific MRI changes of Wernicke's.

wrongAnswers.name: Miller Fisher syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Miller Fisher syndrome (GBS variant) causes ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia following an infection; CSF shows cytoalbuminous dissociation and anti-GQ1b antibodies; it is not associated with nutritional deficiency or the periventricular MRI changes of Wernicke's.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 10-day progressive severe headache unlike any she has experienced before, along with nausea, vomiting, and new-onset seizures.

She started combined oral contraceptive pills six weeks ago and smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily; the headache has been constant, worsening, and she has developed left arm weakness and blurred vision over three days.
Exam reveals bilateral papilledema, left arm weakness graded 3 out of 5, left facial droop, brisk left-sided reflexes with a Babinski sign; she is afebrile without meningismus.

CT head shows a hyperdense cord sign in the superior sagittal sinus region and a hemorrhagic infarct in the right parietal lobe; MRI/MRV shows absent flow signal in the superior sagittal and right transverse sinuses.
MR venography demonstrates complete absence of flow in the superior sagittal sinus with extensive intraluminal thrombus and a hemorrhagic venous infarct not conforming to an arterial territory.
explanation: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) is a rare but important cause of stroke, most common in young women on oral contraceptives. It presents with progressive headache, raised ICP (papilledema, visual symptoms), focal deficits, and seizures. Anticoagulation is the mainstay of treatment, even when hemorrhagic transformation is present.
keyFact: Unlike arterial strokes, anticoagulation (heparin) is indicated even in CVST with hemorrhagic transformation because the hemorrhage results from venous hypertension, and treating the thrombosis is more important than the risk of expanding the hemorrhage.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacterial meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningitis causes fever, headache, and meningismus; it can cause focal deficits but does not cause the specific MRV finding of absent dural sinus flow or cortical venous infarction; CSF would show pleocytosis and bacteria.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic arterial stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Arterial stroke causes acute focal neurological deficits in a specific arterial territory; it does not cause progressive headache over days, papilledema, or the specific MRV pattern of sinus occlusion; DWI would show a wedge-shaped cortical infarct in an arterial distribution.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IIH causes chronic headache and papilledema in young obese women but does not cause focal deficits, seizures, or cortical venous infarcts; MRI/MRV would show patent sinuses (though sinus stenosis can occur secondarily) and a normal or small brain.

clues: A 58-year-old immunocompromised man presents with progressive confusion, focal neurological deficits, and headache worsening over several weeks.

He has advanced HIV (not on antiretroviral therapy) and has had progressive forgetfulness, word-finding difficulty, and left arm clumsiness; he has lost 20 pounds over three months without fever or neck stiffness.
Exam reveals confusion, left hemiparesis graded 3 out of 5, left hemispatial neglect, oral candidiasis plaques, no papilledema, and no meningismus.

MRI brain with contrast shows a single homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass in the right parietal lobe crossing the corpus callosum with surrounding edema; CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows no systemic disease.
Stereotactic biopsy of the periventricular mass reveals large B-cell lymphoma and CSF PCR detects EBV DNA, with the tumor confined to the central nervous system.
explanation: Primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL) is a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma confined to the CNS and vitreous, strongly associated with EBV in immunocompromised patients (HIV, transplant). It presents with cognitive changes, focal deficits, and periventricular enhancing lesions crossing the corpus callosum. Steroids should be withheld until biopsy as they cause rapid tumor dissolution and prevent diagnosis.
keyFact: In CNS lymphoma, corticosteroids should NOT be given before biopsy because they cause rapid tumor lysis ('ghost tumor'), resulting in a non-diagnostic biopsy; EBV-DNA in the CSF is highly specific for CNS lymphoma in HIV patients.

wrongAnswers.name: Cerebral toxoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii) also causes ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS patients with CD4 <100, but typically produces MULTIPLE lesions (not single) in the basal ganglia; positive Toxoplasma IgG serology and empiric response to pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine within 2 weeks help distinguish it from CNS lymphoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Glioblastoma multiforme
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBM causes ring-enhancing periventricular lesions in immunocompetent patients but does not associate with EBV, occurs primarily in HIV-negative patients, and would not show malignant lymphocytes on CSF cytology.

wrongAnswers.name: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PML (JC virus) causes non-enhancing white matter lesions without mass effect in immunocompromised patients; it does not produce the ring-enhancing lesion with perilesional edema seen in CNS lymphoma.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with a 3-year history of frequent unexplained falls, progressive stiffness, and personality changes including emotional lability.

He falls backward without warning like a felled tree, has difficulty looking down at his plate while eating and trouble descending stairs; a neurologist had tried levodopa but it produced no improvement.

Exam reveals marked axial rigidity exceeding limb rigidity with an erect extended posture, inability to look downward on command with preserved downward eye movement on passive head flexion, a wide-eyed staring facial expression, and severe postural instability on the pull test.

MRI brain sagittal view shows selective midbrain atrophy with relative preservation of the pontine volume, creating a distinctive silhouette of the brainstem; the midbrain-to-pons ratio is markedly reduced.

Early postural instability with unprovoked backward falls, vertical gaze palsy predominantly affecting downgaze with preserved oculocephalic reflexes, axial-predominant rigidity, and selective midbrain atrophy on sagittal MRI.
explanation: Progressive supranuclear palsy is a 4-repeat tauopathy (parkinsonian syndrome) characterized by early postural instability and backward falls, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (especially downgaze), axial rigidity, and frontal-subcortical dementia. The 'hummingbird sign' on MRI (midbrain atrophy) and poor levodopa response distinguish it from Parkinson disease.
keyFact: The hallmark finding of PSP is a vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (inability to voluntarily look down) with PRESERVED vertical oculocephalic reflexes (doll's head maneuver intact) — demonstrating the problem is supranuclear (above the oculomotor nuclei) rather than a nuclear or internuclear lesion.

wrongAnswers.name: Parkinson disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Parkinson disease features resting tremor, asymmetric bradykinesia, flexed posture, and FORWARD falls; it responds well to levodopa and does not cause vertical gaze palsy or early postural instability with backward falls.

wrongAnswers.name: Corticobasal degeneration
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CBD causes asymmetric cortical features (alien limb phenomenon, apraxia, cortical sensory loss) with unilateral parkinsonism; gaze palsy is less prominent and symmetric than in PSP, and falls are less common early.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple system atrophy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MSA causes parkinsonism with early prominent autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence) and/or cerebellar ataxia; vertical gaze palsy and backward falls are not characteristic.

clues: A 62-year-old woman presents with rapidly worsening cognitive decline, visual disturbances, behavioral changes, and involuntary jerking movements over several months; she has gone from fully independent to completely dependent.

She initially developed memory problems and depression, then over weeks progressed to difficulty walking, visual hallucinations, and involuntary limb jerking; her family is alarmed at the speed of deterioration.
Exam reveals a severely demented, nearly mute woman with startle-induced myoclonic jerks, cerebellar ataxia, extrapyramidal rigidity, and akinetic mutism; she is afebrile with no nuchal rigidity.

MRI DWI shows cortical ribboning with restricted diffusion in the cortex and bilateral caudate and putamen hyperintensity; EEG shows periodic sharp wave complexes at approximately 1 Hz; CSF shows elevated 14-3-3 protein and tau.
An ultrasensitive seeding assay performed on CSF detects misfolded prion protein, in the setting of cortical ribboning on DWI and periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG.
explanation: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a fatal prion disease characterized by rapidly progressive dementia (weeks to months), myoclonus, cerebellar ataxia, and visual disturbances. The prion protein (PrPSc) is the causative agent; diagnosis is supported by MRI DWI cortical ribboning, periodic sharp waves on EEG, CSF 14-3-3 protein, and confirmed by RT-QuIC or brain autopsy/biopsy.
keyFact: The key diagnostic clues are the combination of rapidly progressive dementia (months, not years) + myoclonus + DWI cortical ribboning on MRI + periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG; median survival from symptom onset is 4–6 months.

wrongAnswers.name: Alzheimer disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alzheimer disease progresses over years (not months), does not cause myoclonus early in the course, lacks the EEG PSWCs and DWI cortical ribboning, and is not associated with positive 14-3-3 or RT-QuIC.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA receptor)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis causes rapidly progressive encephalopathy, psychosis, and seizures in young women, but is treatable with immunotherapy; it would show CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and positive NMDAR antibodies, unlike the prion disease pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Frontotemporal dementia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FTD causes behavioral changes and language dysfunction over years, primarily in the frontal and temporal lobes; it does not cause myoclonus, periodic EEG changes, DWI cortical ribboning, or the rapid months-long trajectory of CJD.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with cola-colored urine that appeared within a day of developing a sore throat; he has no other complaints.
He had a similar episode of dark urine during an upper respiratory infection one year ago that resolved spontaneously.
Exam reveals blood pressure of 145/90 mmHg and mild bilateral flank tenderness; no edema, rash, or joint swelling.
Urinalysis shows 3+ blood with 2+ protein and red blood cell casts on microscopy; serum complement levels are normal; ASO titer is negative.

Kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence shows bright mesangial deposits, and electron microscopy confirms electron-dense deposits limited exclusively to the mesangial region without subendothelial or subepithelial involvement.
explanation: IgA nephropathy results from deposition of poorly glycosylated IgA1 immune complexes in the mesangium, triggering complement activation and glomerular inflammation. It classically presents with synpharyngitic hematuria — gross hematuria concurrent with or immediately after an upper respiratory infection.
keyFact: IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Hematuria occurs DURING the URI (synpharyngitic), distinguishing it from post-streptococcal GN which occurs 1–3 weeks after infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Post-streptococcal GN
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSGN follows streptococcal infection by 1–3 weeks (latent period), not concurrently; also more common in children with low complement levels.

wrongAnswers.name: Thin basement membrane disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Causes persistent microscopic hematuria, not episodic gross hematuria synpharyngitic with URIs.

wrongAnswers.name: Alport Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Also presents with recurrent hematuria but is X-linked, typically associated with sensorineural hearing loss and ocular abnormalities, and shows thinning/splitting of GBM on EM.

clues: A 52-year-old man presents with progressive swelling of both legs and frothy urine worsening over the past month.
He reports no joint pain, skin rashes, recent infections, or use of NSAIDs; he has no history of hepatitis or autoimmune conditions.
Exam reveals periorbital puffiness worse in the morning, pitting edema of both lower extremities, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, and no rash or lymphadenopathy.
24-hour urine protein is 7.2 g; serum albumin is 1.9 g/dL; serum anti-PLA2R antibody titer is elevated; complement levels are normal.
Kidney biopsy electron microscopy shows subepithelial immune deposits with a spike-and-dome pattern along the glomerular basement membrane.
explanation: Primary membranous nephropathy is caused by autoantibodies (most commonly anti-PLA2R) targeting antigens on podocytes, leading to subepithelial immune complex deposition, complement activation, and disruption of the filtration barrier.
keyFact: Anti-PLA2R antibodies are positive in ~70% of primary membranous nephropathy. Always rule out secondary causes (HBV, malignancy, lupus, drugs) especially in older patients — new-onset membranous nephropathy in a patient over 50 warrants cancer screening.

wrongAnswers.name: Minimal Change Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCD causes nephrotic syndrome but is most common in children; biopsy shows normal light microscopy and effacement of foot processes without immune deposits.

wrongAnswers.name: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS also causes nephrotic syndrome but biopsy shows segmental sclerosis of glomeruli, not subepithelial deposits.

wrongAnswers.name: Lupus Nephritis (Class V)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus membranous nephritis looks identical on biopsy but would require positive ANA/anti-dsDNA and systemic lupus features; anti-PLA2R is typically negative.

clues: A 4-year-old boy presents with periorbital puffiness, a swollen belly, and foamy urine noticed by his parents over the past two weeks.
He had a viral upper respiratory infection three weeks ago and has since been less active and eating poorly.
Exam reveals prominent periorbital edema, abdominal distension with a positive fluid wave, and pitting edema of the lower extremities; blood pressure is normal for age.
Urinalysis shows 4+ protein with no blood; serum albumin is 1.4 g/dL; total cholesterol is 340 mg/dL; complement levels are normal.
Kidney biopsy shows entirely normal glomeruli on light microscopy and immunofluorescence, with electron microscopy revealing diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes.
explanation: Minimal change disease results from T-cell dysfunction releasing a circulating factor that injures podocytes, causing diffuse foot process effacement and selective loss of the negatively charged glomerular filtration barrier, leading to massive proteinuria.
keyFact: MCD is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. It is highly steroid-responsive (hallmark). Secondary causes include NSAIDs, lithium, Hodgkin lymphoma (paraneoplastic).

wrongAnswers.name: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS also shows foot process effacement on EM but additionally demonstrates segmental sclerosis on light microscopy; more common in older children and adults.

wrongAnswers.name: Membranous Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Membranous nephropathy is uncommon in young children and shows subepithelial deposits on EM, not isolated foot process effacement.

wrongAnswers.name: Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Presents at birth or within the first 3 months of life; caused by mutations in nephrin (NPHS1) and is steroid-resistant.

clues: A 34-year-old Black man presents with bilateral leg swelling and 15 pounds of weight gain over six weeks.
He has a history of hypertension controlled with amlodipine; he denies joint pain, rashes, recent illness, or drug use.
Exam reveals blood pressure 162/98 mmHg, 3+ pitting edema to the knees bilaterally, and no rash, joint swelling, or lymphadenopathy.
Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 9.2; serum creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL; HIV test is negative; complement levels C3 and C4 are normal; ANA is negative.
Kidney biopsy shows collapse and sclerosis of portions of some glomeruli in a segmental pattern, with electron microscopy showing diffuse podocyte foot process effacement.
explanation: FSGS is caused by podocyte injury from various insults (genetic, circulating permeability factors, viral, adaptive) leading to segmental scarring of glomeruli, proteinuria, and progressive loss of nephrons.
keyFact: FSGS is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in Black adults in the US. Secondary causes include HIV (collapsing variant), heroin, pamidronate, obesity, and single kidney. APOL1 risk variants are strongly associated in patients of African ancestry.

wrongAnswers.name: Minimal Change Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCD shows normal light microscopy without segmental sclerosis; less likely in adults with hypertension and elevated creatinine.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetic Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No history of diabetes; diabetic nephropathy would show Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules and diffuse mesangial expansion on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis causes subnephrotic proteinuria and arteriolar thickening on biopsy; nephrotic-range proteinuria with segmental sclerosis points to FSGS.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with bilateral leg swelling, foamy urine, and painful swollen joints in her hands and wrists over three weeks.
She reports intermittent hair loss over the past year and a facial rash across her cheeks and nose that flares with sun exposure.
Exam reveals an erythematous butterfly-shaped rash sparing the nasolabial folds, blood pressure 154/92 mmHg, bilateral ankle edema, and swollen metacarpophalangeal joints.
ANA titer is 1:640 with a homogeneous pattern; anti-dsDNA antibody is strongly positive; C3 and C4 are both low; urinalysis shows red blood cell casts with 3+ protein.
Kidney biopsy shows diffuse proliferative changes in all glomeruli with immunofluorescence demonstrating deposition of IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, and C1q.
explanation: In lupus nephritis, circulating anti-dsDNA immune complexes deposit in the glomerulus (mesangium and subendothelial/subepithelial space), activating complement and triggering inflammatory injury that ranges from mild mesangial changes to severe crescentic GN.
keyFact: Class IV (diffuse proliferative) lupus nephritis is the most severe and common form requiring aggressive immunosuppression. 'Full house' immunofluorescence and low complement are hallmarks. Anti-dsDNA titers correlate with disease activity.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy lacks the systemic features of SLE, ANA positivity, and complement consumption; IF shows isolated mesangial IgA, not full house pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: ANCA Vasculitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ANCA vasculitis is pauci-immune (little/no immune deposits on IF) and would not show full house immunofluorescence; ANA is typically negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease Nephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCTD has anti-U1 RNP antibodies and less severe renal involvement; full-house IF and high-titer anti-dsDNA are more specific for SLE.

clues: A 61-year-old man presents with one week of dramatically decreased urine output, blood in his urine, and generalized joint aches.
He has had several months of persistent bloody nasal discharge and sinus congestion that did not respond to antibiotics; he has lost 12 pounds unintentionally.
Exam reveals blood pressure 168/102 mmHg, a nasal septal perforation on anterior rhinoscopy, and bilateral crackles on lung auscultation.
Serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 4.8 mg/dL over 10 days; urinalysis shows dysmorphic red cells with red blood cell casts; c-ANCA with anti-PR3 specificity is positive.
Kidney biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with necrotizing features and no significant immune complex deposits on immunofluorescence.
explanation: ANCA-associated vasculitis involves ANCA-mediated neutrophil activation causing necrotizing inflammation of small vessels, leading to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and systemic organ involvement (lungs, sinuses, kidneys). The pauci-immune pattern reflects direct cellular rather than immune complex-mediated injury.
keyFact: c-ANCA/anti-PR3 is associated with GPA (granulomatosis with polyangiitis); p-ANCA/anti-MPO with MPA and EGPA. Rapidly progressive GN with pauci-immune pattern on biopsy is the histologic hallmark. Treat with cyclophosphamide or rituximab plus glucocorticoids.

wrongAnswers.name: Anti-GBM Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anti-GBM also causes RPGN with crescents but shows linear IgG deposits on IF (not pauci-immune); anti-GBM antibody would be positive instead.

wrongAnswers.name: Lupus Nephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus nephritis has immune complex deposits (full house IF) and would have positive ANA/anti-dsDNA; nasal septal perforation is not a lupus feature.

wrongAnswers.name: Endocarditis-Associated GN
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Infectious endocarditis can cause immune complex GN with hematuria but would present with fever, murmur, and positive blood cultures; nasal/sinus involvement is absent.

clues: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with hemoptysis, worsening shortness of breath, and markedly decreased urine output developing over five days.
He smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily, works in a metal fabrication shop with hydrocarbon exposure, and had a mild flu-like illness three weeks ago.
Exam reveals blood pressure 172/104 mmHg, oxygen saturation 91% on room air, diffuse bilateral crackles on auscultation, and pallor.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates; creatinine is 7.2 mg/dL; urinalysis shows 4+ blood with red blood cell casts; serum anti-GBM antibody titer is markedly elevated.
Kidney biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with smooth linear IgG staining along the entire length of the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence.
explanation: Anti-GBM disease is caused by autoantibodies targeting the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the GBM and alveolar basement membrane, leading to complement-mediated destruction of glomeruli and alveoli. Pulmonary hemorrhage is triggered or worsened by smoking.
keyFact: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome) = pulmonary-renal syndrome with linear IgG on IF. Bimodal peak: young men (smoking/hydrocarbon exposure) and older women. 10–38% also have ANCA positivity (double-positive). Treat urgently with plasmapheresis + immunosuppression.

wrongAnswers.name: ANCA Vasculitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ANCA vasculitis causes pulmonary-renal syndrome but shows pauci-immune pattern on biopsy, not linear IgG; ANCA would be positive instead of anti-GBM.

wrongAnswers.name: Lupus Nephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE can cause nephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage but shows granular immune deposits on IF and positive ANA/anti-dsDNA, not linear IgG.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Vasculitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA vasculitis causes nephritis with IgA deposits but does not cause pulmonary hemorrhage or show linear IgG on immunofluorescence.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive bilateral leg swelling, persistent fatigue, and increasingly foamy urine over several months.
He has had worsening vision over the past year and was recently told he is losing sensation in both feet; he takes metformin and insulin for a chronic condition.
Exam reveals blood pressure 158/96 mmHg, bilateral pitting edema of the lower extremities, and absent monofilament sensation in both feet in a stocking distribution.

Serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 1,850 mg/g; HbA1c is 10.2%; dilated fundoscopic exam shows neovascularization, microaneurysms, and dot-blot hemorrhages bilaterally.

Kidney biopsy shows nodular glomerulosclerosis with eosinophilic acellular nodules in the mesangium, diffuse mesangial matrix expansion, and arteriolar hyalinosis of both afferent and efferent arterioles.
explanation: Chronic hyperglycemia leads to advanced glycation end-product accumulation, activation of PKC and TGF-beta pathways, causing mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, and ultimately nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions) with progressive nephron loss.
keyFact: Diabetic nephropathy is the most common cause of end-stage renal disease in the US. Triad: diabetic retinopathy + neuropathy + nephropathy suggests microvascular disease. Absence of retinopathy in a diabetic patient with proteinuria should prompt biopsy to rule out alternative diagnoses.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis causes subnephrotic proteinuria and arteriolar changes but lacks the specific Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules and the diabetic context.

wrongAnswers.name: Membranous Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic-range proteinuria but shows subepithelial deposits and spike-and-dome pattern on biopsy without the microvascular diabetic triad.

wrongAnswers.name: FSGS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS shows segmental sclerosis without nodular pattern; lacks the retinopathy/neuropathy context and Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules.

clues: A 32-year-old woman presents with persistent headaches, dizziness, and fatigue despite taking three different antihypertensive medications at maximum doses.
She has no family history of hypertension, has never smoked, and has no cardiovascular risk factors; her elevated blood pressure was first discovered incidentally one year ago.
Exam reveals blood pressure 178/106 mmHg in the right arm and an audible bruit over the right flank on abdominal auscultation.
Serum creatinine rose from 1.0 to 1.7 mg/dL after starting an ACE inhibitor; plasma renin activity is markedly elevated; serum aldosterone is elevated.
CT angiography of the renal arteries shows alternating areas of narrowing and dilation in the mid and distal segments of the right renal artery creating a string-of-beads appearance.
explanation: Fibromuscular dysplasia causes non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory fibrous proliferation of arterial walls (typically renal and carotid arteries), leading to luminal narrowing, reduced renal perfusion, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and secondary hypertension.
keyFact: Fibromuscular dysplasia is the most common cause of renovascular hypertension in young women. Beaded 'string of beads' appearance on angiography reflects alternating stenoses and aneurysms in the medial layer. ACE inhibitor-induced AKI is a classic clue to bilateral RAS or RAS in a solitary kidney.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Conn syndrome causes resistant hypertension with hypokalemia and suppressed renin activity; renovascular hypertension has elevated renin.

wrongAnswers.name: Pheochromocytoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pheochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension with palpitations, diaphoresis, and pallor; plasma/urine catecholamines would be elevated; no renal artery abnormality.

wrongAnswers.name: Atherosclerotic Renal Artery Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atherosclerotic RAS occurs in older patients with cardiovascular risk factors and affects the proximal renal artery; FMD is the diagnosis in young women with a beaded mid-arterial pattern.

clues: A 67-year-old man reports producing almost no urine and feeling increasingly fatigued two days after a routine surgical procedure.
The operative record documents 45 minutes of sustained hypotension requiring vasopressor support; he also received an aminoglycoside antibiotic for surgical prophylaxis.
Exam reveals blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, euvolemic status with no edema or signs of dehydration, and urine output of only 180 mL over the past 24 hours.
Serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 3.6 mg/dL; urine sodium is 68 mEq/L; fractional excretion of sodium is 3.2%; urine osmolality is 285 mOsm/kg.
Urine microscopy reveals numerous muddy brown granular casts and sloughed renal tubular epithelial cells.
explanation: Acute tubular necrosis results from ischemic or nephrotoxic injury to the renal tubular epithelium, impairing tubular reabsorption and concentrating ability. Muddy brown granular casts represent sloughed, necrotic tubular cells and are pathognomonic.
keyFact: ATN is the most common cause of intrinsic AKI in hospitalized patients. FENa >2% and muddy brown casts distinguish it from prerenal AKI (FENa <1%, hyaline casts). Common causes: ischemia (shock, surgery), nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, contrast, cisplatin, myoglobin).

wrongAnswers.name: Prerenal AKI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prerenal AKI shows FENa <1%, concentrated urine (osmolality >500), and responds to volume resuscitation; patient is now euvolemic and urine is isosthenuric.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Interstitial Nephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIN typically shows WBC casts and eosinophiluria; classically caused by drug hypersensitivity with rash, fever, and eosinophilia — not primarily by ischemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Postrenal Obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Postrenal obstruction would show hydronephrosis on ultrasound; urine sodium and FENa are less helpful since ATN develops after prolonged obstruction anyway.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with decreased urine output and a new diffuse skin rash that appeared five days ago.
She was started on a proton pump inhibitor six weeks ago for gastroesophageal reflux disease and has no prior kidney problems or allergies.
Exam reveals a temperature of 38.4°C, a diffuse maculopapular rash across the trunk and extremities, and bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness.
Serum creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL up from a baseline of 0.9; CBC shows peripheral eosinophilia; urinalysis shows sterile pyuria with white blood cell casts.
Kidney biopsy shows dense interstitial infiltration by lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils with tubulitis, while glomeruli and vasculature appear normal.
explanation: Acute interstitial nephritis is a T-cell–mediated hypersensitivity reaction to drugs (most commonly PPIs, NSAIDs, antibiotics) or infections, causing inflammatory cell infiltration of the renal interstitium and tubules, leading to AKI without significant glomerular damage.
keyFact: Classic triad of AIN: fever, rash, and eosinophilia (present in only 10–30%). PPIs are now the most common drug cause. Eosinophiluria (Hansel stain) is suggestive but not sensitive. Treatment is drug cessation; steroids used in severe or non-improving cases.

wrongAnswers.name: Pyelonephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pyelonephritis also causes fever, flank pain, and pyuria but would show positive urine culture (bacteria) not sterile pyuria; no drug exposure context.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ATN causes muddy brown casts from tubular injury, not WBC casts with eosinophilia; ATN follows ischemia or nephrotoxin exposure, not drug hypersensitivity.

wrongAnswers.name: ANCA Vasculitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ANCA vasculitis causes AKI with RBC casts and systemic vasculitis features; WBC casts with eosinophilia and drug exposure points strongly to AIN.

clues: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department for confusion that developed over two to three days; her daughter reports she has been much less active.
She has had profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting for four days; she takes lisinopril and furosemide for heart failure.
Exam reveals blood pressure 88/54 mmHg lying down with a further drop on sitting, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, tachycardia, and minimal urine output.
BUN is 68 mg/dL; serum creatinine is 2.8 mg/dL from a baseline of 1.0; BUN-to-creatinine ratio is 24; urine sodium is 8 mEq/L; urine osmolality is 620 mOsm/kg.
Fractional excretion of sodium is 0.4%, urine osmolality 680 mOsm/kg, BUN-to-creatinine ratio 28, and urine sodium 6 mEq/L — all indicating intact tubular reabsorptive function.
explanation: Prerenal AKI occurs when renal perfusion is insufficient to maintain GFR, triggering tubular sodium and water conservation (low urine Na, high urine osmolality). The kidney tubules are structurally intact; AKI reverses rapidly with restoration of adequate volume.
keyFact: Prerenal AKI: FENa <1%, BUN:Cr >20, urine osmolality >500, rapid response to fluids. FENa can be falsely elevated in patients on diuretics — use FeUrea (<35% suggests prerenal) instead.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ATN follows ischemia but shows tubular injury markers: FENa >2%, muddy brown casts, isosthenuria; does not reverse within 48 hours of fluids alone.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatorenal Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HRS also shows low urine sodium but requires underlying cirrhosis/liver failure and does not respond to volume resuscitation — key distinguishing feature.

wrongAnswers.name: Addisonian Crisis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adrenal insufficiency can cause AKI with hypotension and hyponatremia but would show hyperkalemia and requires cortisol deficiency context; responds to steroids not just fluids.

clues: A 71-year-old man presents with decreased urine output and dull lower abdominal discomfort worsening over four days.
He has had progressive difficulty initiating urination, a weak stream, and terminal dribbling for the past year, with nocturia three to four times per night.
Exam reveals suprapubic fullness with a palpable, dull mass above the pubic symphysis; digital rectal exam shows an enlarged, smooth, rubbery, non-tender prostate.
Serum creatinine is 4.2 mg/dL; urinalysis is unremarkable with no casts or significant proteinuria; PSA is 6.2 ng/mL; a bedside bladder scan shows 850 mL of retained urine.
Renal ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter; bladder scan reveals 850 mL of retained urine; ureteral jets are absent on Doppler.
explanation: Bladder outlet obstruction (most commonly from BPH) causes urinary retention, increased intravesical pressure that is transmitted retrograde to the collecting system, leading to bilateral hydronephrosis and obstructive nephropathy that is reversible with prompt decompression.
keyFact: Post-obstructive diuresis can occur after relief of bilateral obstruction — monitor urine output closely and replace fluids to prevent hypovolemia. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging. Unilateral obstruction does not cause AKI if the contralateral kidney is functional.

wrongAnswers.name: Prerenal AKI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prerenal AKI would show concentrated urine and respond to fluids; no hydronephrosis or urinary retention; patient lacks volume depletion signs.

wrongAnswers.name: Prostate Cancer with Metastases
wrongAnswers.whyNot: While an elevated PSA and urinary obstruction could suggest malignancy, smooth non-tender prostate on DRE and rapid creatinine normalization after catheterization point to BPH-related obstruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Neurogenic Bladder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Neurogenic bladder can also cause urinary retention and hydronephrosis but requires a neurological history; BPH is far more common in elderly men with lower urinary tract symptoms.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe right-sided flank pain radiating to the groin, nausea, and vomiting.
He had a similar episode two years ago that resolved after he passed something in his urine; he drinks only about one liter of fluid daily and lives in a hot, arid climate.
Exam reveals a man writhing in pain unable to find a comfortable position, heart rate 108 bpm, blood pressure 148/88 mmHg, and right costovertebral angle tenderness.
Urinalysis shows 3+ blood; urine microscopy reveals dumbbell-shaped and envelope-shaped crystals; non-contrast CT shows a 4 mm calculus at the right ureterovesical junction.
Passed stone analysis reveals calcium oxalate monohydrate composition, and 24-hour urine collection shows elevated calcium and oxalate excretion.
explanation: Calcium oxalate stones form when urinary saturation of calcium and oxalate exceeds solubility, typically from hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, low urine volume, or low urine citrate. They are the most common kidney stone type and are radiopaque on X-ray.
keyFact: Calcium oxalate is the most common kidney stone (80%). Risk factors: low fluid intake, hot climate, hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria (Crohn's disease, short bowel), low citrate. Dumbbell/envelope-shaped crystals on microscopy. Treatment: increased fluids, thiazides (hypercalciuria), low-oxalate diet.

wrongAnswers.name: Uric Acid Nephrolithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Uric acid stones are radiolucent and form in acidic urine (pH <5.5); crystals are rhomboid or needle-shaped; associated with gout and hyperuricemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Struvite Nephrolithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Struvite stones are associated with urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella) causing UTI and form staghorn calculi; dumbbell-shaped crystals are not typical.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Papillary Necrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Papillary necrosis causes hematuria and flank pain but is associated with analgesic overuse, diabetes, or sickle cell disease; no discrete stone on CT.

clues: A 55-year-old obese man presents with acute colicky right-sided flank pain and blood in his urine.
He has a history of gout with poor medication adherence, follows a high-protein diet, and drinks beer regularly.
Exam reveals moderate distress, right costovertebral angle tenderness, no fever, and a BMI of 38.
Urinalysis shows 2+ blood; urine pH is 4.9; non-contrast CT confirms a 6 mm calculus in the right ureter; plain abdominal radiograph shows no visible stone.
The stone is invisible on plain radiograph but visible on CT, and analysis after passage shows pure uric acid composition with elevated 24-hour urine uric acid excretion.
explanation: Uric acid stones form in persistently acidic urine (pH <5.5) because uric acid is poorly soluble in acidic conditions; the undissociated form precipitates. Conditions associated with high uric acid production (gout, high-protein diet, myeloproliferative disorders) and acidic urine (metabolic syndrome, diarrhea) are risk factors.
keyFact: Uric acid stones are radiolucent (invisible on plain X-ray) but visible on CT. Unique treatment: urinary alkalinization with potassium citrate or sodium bicarbonate (target urine pH 6–7) can dissolve existing stones. Associated with gout, metabolic syndrome, and high-purine diet.

wrongAnswers.name: Calcium Oxalate Nephrolithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Calcium oxalate stones are radiopaque and would be visible on plain X-ray; occur in normal or alkaline urine and are not dissolved by alkalinization.

wrongAnswers.name: Cystine Nephrolithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cystine stones also form in acidic urine and can be faintly radiopaque; require cyanide-nitroprusside test to distinguish; associated with cystinuria genetic disorder not gout.

wrongAnswers.name: Struvite Nephrolithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Struvite stones form in alkaline urine (pH >7) due to urease-producing organisms; no infection history here, and urine pH is acidic.

clues: A 44-year-old woman presents with right flank pain, burning with urination, and generalized malaise over the past week.

She has had four urinary tract infections in the past year that recur shortly after completing antibiotics; she has a neurogenic bladder from a prior spinal cord injury requiring intermittent catheterization.
Exam reveals a temperature of 38.6°C, right costovertebral angle tenderness, and suprapubic tenderness on palpation.

Urinalysis shows 4+ bacteria, 4+ WBCs, and urine pH of 8.2; urine culture grows Proteus mirabilis; non-contrast CT shows a large calculus filling the right renal pelvis and extending into the calyces.
Stone analysis shows magnesium ammonium phosphate composition with a branching morphology conforming to the shape of the renal collecting system.
explanation: Struvite (infection) stones form when urease-producing bacteria (Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas) split urea into ammonia, alkalinizing urine and causing precipitation of magnesium ammonium phosphate. They can grow rapidly to fill the renal pelvis (staghorn calculi) and are difficult to eradicate without complete stone removal.
keyFact: Struvite stones are the classic 'staghorn calculus.' They only form in alkaline urine secondary to urease-producing organisms. More common in women and patients with neurogenic bladder or anatomic abnormalities. Treatment requires both antibiotic therapy AND stone removal (percutaneous nephrolithotomy).

wrongAnswers.name: Calcium Oxalate Nephrolithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Calcium oxalate stones do not fill the renal pelvis in a staghorn pattern and are not associated with urease-producing organisms or chronically alkaline urine.

wrongAnswers.name: Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XGP is a destructive renal infection associated with staghorn calculi and can mimic stone disease, but is a tissue diagnosis showing lipid-laden macrophages; stone analysis confirms struvite.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RCC can cause hematuria and a renal mass but would not produce a calculus filling the collecting system; urine culture and stone analysis definitively identify struvite.

clues: A 17-year-old boy presents with severe flank pain and blood in his urine; this is his third such episode.
His older sister also had recurrent kidney stones beginning in her teenage years; both parents are healthy.
Exam reveals right costovertebral angle tenderness, no fever, and normal blood pressure; he appears in moderate distress.
Non-contrast CT shows bilateral renal calculi; urine microscopy reveals hexagonal crystals; urine pH is 5.5.
A urine screening test using sodium cyanide and nitroprusside produces a positive purple color, and 24-hour urine shows cystine excretion of 1,200 mg/day.
explanation: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of renal tubular transport of dibasic amino acids (cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine — 'COLA'), causing urinary cystine accumulation. Cystine is poorly soluble, precipitating as hexagonal crystals and recurrent calculi.
keyFact: Cystinuria: recurrent stones in children/young adults; autosomal recessive; hexagonal ('benzene ring') crystals on urinalysis. Treatment: high fluid intake, urinary alkalinization (pH >7.5), d-penicillamine or tiopronin for refractory cases. Mnemonic: COLA amino acids (Cystine, Ornithine, Lysine, Arginine).

wrongAnswers.name: Calcium Oxalate Nephrolithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common but occur in adults; hexagonal crystals and family history of early-onset stones in adolescents is not typical.

wrongAnswers.name: Uric Acid Nephrolithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Uric acid stones also form in acidic urine but show rhomboid/needle-shaped crystals and are associated with gout/hyperuricemia, not a hereditary transporter defect.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperoxaluria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary hyperoxaluria also causes recurrent childhood stones but is due to glyoxylate metabolism errors; shows calcium oxalate stones, not hexagonal crystals.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with generalized muscle weakness, painful cramping, and a history of recurrent kidney stones composed of calcium phosphate.
She has been diagnosed with Sjogren syndrome and reports chronic dry eyes and dry mouth; her serum potassium has been low on multiple prior lab draws.
Exam reveals mild proximal muscle weakness with intact neurological exam, no peripheral edema, and blood pressure 110/68 mmHg.
ABG shows pH 7.29 with bicarbonate 14 mEq/L and pCO2 30 mmHg; serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L; anion gap is normal at 10; urine pH is 6.5 despite the systemic acidosis.
An acid-loading challenge fails to lower urine pH below 5.5, and the urine anion gap is positive at +12 mEq/L, indicating impaired renal acid excretion.
explanation: Type 1 (distal) RTA results from failure of alpha-intercalated cells in the collecting duct to secrete H+ ions, leading to inability to acidify urine below pH 5.5. This causes normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia, hypercalciuria, and nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis.
keyFact: Distal RTA (Type 1): cannot acidify urine, urine pH >5.5 despite acidosis, hypokalemia, hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis. Associated with Sjogren syndrome, primary biliary cholangitis, medullary sponge kidney. Treatment: oral bicarbonate or citrate supplementation.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Tubular Acidosis Type 2
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Type 2 (proximal) RTA involves bicarbonate wasting; urine can be acidified normally once serum HCO3 drops below the reabsorption threshold; associated with Fanconi syndrome, not nephrocalcinosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Tubular Acidosis Type 4
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Type 4 RTA causes HYPERKALEMIA due to aldosterone deficiency/resistance; hypokalemia rules out Type 4.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Diarrhea-Induced Acidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diarrhea causes bicarbonate loss (NAGMA) with hypokalemia but the kidney would appropriately acidify urine (pH <5.5); urine anion gap would be negative.

clues: A 62-year-old man with longstanding diabetes presents with fatigue and palpitations; his ECG shows peaked T waves.
He was recently started on an ACE inhibitor for diabetic nephropathy, and his creatinine has been mildly elevated at 1.8 mg/dL for years.
Exam reveals no edema, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, and no signs of volume depletion; ECG confirms tall peaked T waves in the precordial leads.
