Serum potassium is 6.2 mEq/L; ABG shows pH 7.32 with bicarbonate 16 mEq/L and a normal anion gap; serum aldosterone and plasma renin activity are both suppressed.
Despite the metabolic acidosis, urine pH is appropriately acidic at 5.1, and the combination of hyperkalemia with low renin and low aldosterone points to impaired distal potassium and acid secretion.
explanation: Type 4 RTA results from aldosterone deficiency or resistance, most commonly from hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism in diabetic nephropathy. Aldosterone is required for potassium secretion and ammoniagenesis; its deficiency leads to hyperkalemia and reduced urinary ammonium, causing normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
keyFact: Type 4 RTA is the most common RTA. Key: hyperkalemia + NAGMA + preserved ability to acidify urine (pH <5.5). Causes: diabetic nephropathy (most common), ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, heparin, adrenal insufficiency. Unlike Type 1, patients can acidify their urine but cannot excrete potassium.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Tubular Acidosis Type 1
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Type 1 RTA causes hypoKALEMIA and urine pH >5.5 (inability to acidify urine); here potassium is high and urine is appropriately acidic.

wrongAnswers.name: CKD-Related Metabolic Acidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Advanced CKD causes high anion gap acidosis (uremic acid accumulation); this patient has a normal anion gap, and isolated NAGMA with hyperkalemia points to aldosterone deficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: Addison Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary adrenal insufficiency also causes hyperkalemia and low aldosterone but would show hyponatremia, low cortisol, and positive ACTH stimulation test; not typical in a diabetic on ACE inhibitor.

clues: A 41-year-old man presents with dull bilateral flank pain and intermittent episodes of blood in his urine over the past two months.
His father died of a stroke at age 52 and had been on dialysis for several years before his death; the patient takes no medications.
Exam reveals blood pressure 164/98 mmHg and bilaterally palpable, enlarged, irregularly nodular kidneys on deep abdominal palpation.

Serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL; urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria; renal ultrasound shows markedly enlarged kidneys bilaterally studded with innumerable cysts of varying sizes replacing normal parenchyma.
MR angiography of the brain reveals a small unruptured saccular aneurysm at an arterial bifurcation, and genetic testing identifies a mutation in the PKD1 gene on chromosome 16.
explanation: ADPKD is caused by mutations in PKD1 or PKD2 (polycystin proteins), leading to progressive cyst development in the kidneys and extrarenal manifestations. Polycystin dysfunction disrupts tubular cell polarity and proliferation, resulting in progressive cyst enlargement and nephron destruction.
keyFact: ADPKD: most common hereditary kidney disease; bilateral cysts, hypertension, hematuria, flank pain. Extrarenal: intracranial aneurysms (10%), liver cysts, mitral valve prolapse. PKD1 mutations (chr 16) are more severe than PKD2 (chr 4). Tolvaptan (V2 receptor antagonist) slows progression in rapidly progressive disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RCC can cause hematuria and a renal mass but is unilateral; bilateral enlarged nodular kidneys with innumerable cysts and strong family history point to ADPKD.

wrongAnswers.name: Autosomal Recessive PKD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ARPKD (PKD in infancy/childhood) presents much earlier with smaller kidneys and fusiform cysts; it is associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis, not intracranial aneurysms.

wrongAnswers.name: Acquired Cystic Kidney Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acquired cystic disease occurs in patients on long-term dialysis; this patient has no dialysis history and has a strong family history suggesting an inherited disorder.

clues: A 16-year-old boy is brought in by his parents who noticed persistently dark urine and are concerned that he has been having difficulty hearing in class.
His maternal uncle received a kidney transplant at age 32; the patient recently was fitted for hearing aids after audiometry confirmed bilateral hearing loss.
Exam reveals blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and ophthalmologic exam shows an abnormally shaped anterior lens with conical protrusion.
Urinalysis shows persistent microscopic hematuria with mild proteinuria; serum creatinine is normal; complement levels are normal; anti-GBM antibodies are negative.

Kidney biopsy electron microscopy shows irregular thickening, thinning, and lamellation of the glomerular basement membrane in a basket-weave pattern, and immunohistochemistry shows absence of the alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen.
explanation: Alport syndrome is caused by mutations in COL4A3, COL4A4, or COL4A5 genes encoding type IV collagen, leading to abnormal GBM structure with progressive nephritis, sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities (anterior lenticonus, macular flecks).
keyFact: Alport syndrome: X-linked (most common, COL4A5 mutation) — boys more severely affected; triad of nephritis + sensorineural hearing loss + ocular abnormalities (anterior lenticonus). EM shows GBM basket-weave splitting. Risk of anti-GBM disease post-transplant due to absent collagen acting as a neoantigen.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy causes hematuria (often gross, synpharyngitic) but lacks sensorineural hearing loss and ocular findings; biopsy shows mesangial IgA deposits, not GBM splitting.

wrongAnswers.name: Thin Basement Membrane Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TBMD also shows GBM thinning on EM and persistent hematuria but lacks hearing loss, ocular findings, and family history of renal failure; has a benign prognosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Anti-GBM Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anti-GBM disease causes rapidly progressive GN with hemoptysis and linear IgG on IF; anti-GBM antibodies are negative here and presentation is chronic hematuria not RPGN.

clues: A 6-year-old girl is brought in with dramatically decreased urine output, pallor, and fatigue developing over two days following a recent gastrointestinal illness with bloody diarrhea.
The family attended a barbecue last week where undercooked hamburgers were served; two other children from the same event have reportedly become ill with similar symptoms.
Exam reveals pallor, scattered petechiae on the lower extremities, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, and diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs.
Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL; platelets are 42,000/uL; peripheral blood smear shows fragmented red cells; direct Coombs test is negative; serum creatinine is 3.8 mg/dL; LDH is markedly elevated.
Stool culture isolates a Shiga toxin-producing organism, and ADAMTS13 activity level returns as greater than 50%.
explanation: Shiga toxin produced by E. coli O157:H7 enters the bloodstream, damages endothelial cells (particularly in the kidney and gut), and promotes platelet aggregation and fibrin thrombus formation in small vessels, causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and AKI (the classic triad of HUS).
keyFact: HUS triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + AKI. Most common in children after STEC (O157:H7) infection. Antibiotics are CONTRAINDICATED (may increase Shiga toxin release). ADAMTS13 >10% distinguishes from TTP (<10% in TTP). Treatment: supportive; dialysis if needed.

wrongAnswers.name: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP shows the same triad but predominantly affects adults; ADAMTS13 activity is severely reduced (<10%); neurological symptoms (not renal failure) predominate.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia without hemolytic anemia, AKI, or schistocytes; Coombs negative hemolysis with renal failure rules out isolated ITP.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningococcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningococcemia can cause petechiae and shock but does not follow a diarrheal prodrome; septic workup and absence of meningismus/purpura fulminans make HUS more likely.

clues: A 59-year-old man presents with dull left-sided flank pain, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss worsening over several months.
He has a 30-pack-year smoking history and has lost 15 pounds without trying; he has not had fevers or chills.
Exam reveals blood pressure 162/96 mmHg, a palpable left flank mass, and a left-sided varicocele that does not collapse when the patient lies flat.
CBC shows hemoglobin 18.2 g/dL; serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL; PTH is suppressed; urinalysis shows gross hematuria without casts or protein.
CT abdomen with contrast reveals a 9 cm heterogeneous, enhancing left renal mass with central necrosis and tumor thrombus extending into the left renal vein.
explanation: Renal cell carcinoma (most commonly clear cell type, driven by VHL mutation) arises from proximal tubular epithelium and can produce paraneoplastic hormones including EPO (polycythemia), PTHrP (hypercalcemia), and renin (hypertension). Left-sided varicocele occurs when the tumor obstructs the left gonadal vein draining into the left renal vein.
keyFact: RCC classic triad: hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass (present in only 10%). Paraneoplastic syndromes: polycythemia (EPO), hypercalcemia (PTHrP), hypertension (renin). Non-decompressing left varicocele = renal vein thrombosis until proven otherwise. Associated with VHL syndrome and smoking.

wrongAnswers.name: Transitional Cell Carcinoma of the Renal Pelvis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TCC causes hematuria but rarely presents as a palpable mass with paraneoplastic polycythemia; strongly associated with phenacetin and cyclophosphamide exposure.

wrongAnswers.name: Polycystic Kidney Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ADPKD causes bilateral palpable masses with hematuria and hypertension but shows multiple cysts on imaging, not a solid necrotic mass; no polycythemia or hypercalcemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Angiomyolipoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AML is a benign renal tumor associated with tuberous sclerosis; contains fat on CT and does not cause paraneoplastic syndromes or venous invasion.

clues: A 71-year-old man presents with nausea, decreased appetite, and markedly reduced urine output beginning two days after a cardiac catheterization procedure.
He has type 2 diabetes with a baseline creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL and takes metformin; he received a large volume of iodinated dye during the procedure.
Examination reveals blood pressure 146/88 mmHg, euvolemic status with no peripheral edema, clear lung fields, and no jugular venous distension; urine output has been 400 mL in the past 24 hours.

Serum creatinine has risen from 2.1 to 3.4 mg/dL over 48 hours; urinalysis shows muddy brown granular casts; fractional excretion of sodium is 2.1%; renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis.
Creatinine peaks at 72 hours post-procedure and begins trending downward by day 5, with the entire trajectory fitting a self-limited course of acute tubular injury.
explanation: Contrast-induced nephropathy results from direct tubular toxicity of iodinated contrast agents and contrast-induced renal vasoconstriction, causing medullary ischemia. Patients with CKD, diabetes, and reduced renal perfusion are at highest risk.
keyFact: Contrast nephropathy: AKI within 24–48h of contrast, peaks at 72h, resolves in 7–10 days. Risk factors: CKD (Cr >1.5), diabetes, dehydration, high contrast volume, NSAIDs. Prevention: IV hydration (NS or bicarb), hold metformin (lactic acidosis risk). N-acetylcysteine evidence is weak.

wrongAnswers.name: Prerenal AKI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prerenal AKI would respond rapidly to fluids alone; FENa <1% and concentrated urine are more typical; this patient is euvolemic with a non-resolving creatinine over days.

wrongAnswers.name: Cholesterol Emboli Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cholesterol emboli can also cause AKI after catheterization but occurs 1–4 weeks later and shows livedo reticularis, eosinophilia, eosinophiluria, and progressive (not self-resolving) renal failure.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis (Aminoglycoside)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ATN from aminoglycosides would require aminoglycoside exposure and shows muddy brown casts; temporal relationship to contrast exposure without another offending drug points to contrast nephropathy.

clues: A 19-year-old man who recently started treatment for a newly diagnosed malignancy develops nausea, vomiting, and muscle cramps within a day of his first chemotherapy dose.
He was diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma one week ago with a very high tumor burden; he received his first cycle of combination chemotherapy yesterday.
Exam reveals an uncomfortable young man with blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, heart rate 112 bpm, and ECG showing tall peaked T waves in the precordial leads.
Serum potassium is 6.8 mEq/L; phosphorus is 7.2 mg/dL; calcium is 6.9 mg/dL; uric acid is 14.2 mg/dL; creatinine is 3.6 mg/dL; LDH is markedly elevated.
Urine microscopy shows birefringent uric acid crystals within tubular lumina; renal ultrasound shows echogenic medullary pyramids from crystal deposition.
explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome occurs when rapid tumor cell death releases intracellular contents (potassium, phosphate, nucleic acids) into circulation; nucleic acids are catabolized to uric acid which precipitates in renal tubules causing AKI, while hypocalcemia results from calcium-phosphate binding.
keyFact: TLS: hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia (4H's). Most common with high-grade lymphomas (Burkitt) and ALL. Prevention: aggressive IV hydration, allopurinol (or rasburicase for high-risk patients). Rasburicase converts uric acid to allantois (more soluble). Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: Rhabdomyolysis-Induced AKI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rhabdomyolysis also causes hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and AKI but occurs after muscle injury and shows markedly elevated CK and myoglobinuria; no tumor lysis context.

wrongAnswers.name: Addisonian Crisis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adrenal crisis can cause hyperkalemia, hypotension, and AKI but would show hyponatremia and low cortisol; hyperuricemia and hyperphosphatemia are not features.

wrongAnswers.name: Crush Injury AKI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Crush injury causes rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia and AKI but lacks the chemotherapy/malignancy context, hyperphosphatemia, and markedly elevated uric acid.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with severe bilateral lower extremity pain, muscle swelling, and dark tea-colored urine after unusually intense physical exertion.
He started a new military boot camp program three days ago and was exercising in extreme heat; he has been taking ibuprofen for the soreness.
Exam reveals diffusely swollen and tender thigh and calf muscles bilaterally, temperature 37.9°C, and markedly decreased urine output over the past 12 hours.
Urinalysis dipstick is 4+ positive for blood, but urine microscopy shows no red blood cells; serum potassium is 5.8 mEq/L; creatinine is 2.9 mg/dL.

Serum creatine kinase is 48,000 U/L with urine myoglobin detected, and the discrepancy between a heme-positive dipstick and absent red cells on microscopy is explained by a non-hemoglobin heme pigment in the urine.
explanation: Rhabdomyolysis causes myoglobin release from injured skeletal muscle; myoglobin is directly toxic to proximal tubular cells and causes tubular obstruction in acidic urine. The urine dipstick detects heme pigment (myoglobin) yielding a false-positive for blood without corresponding RBCs on microscopy.
keyFact: Rhabdomyolysis: dipstick positive blood + NO RBCs on microscopy = myoglobinuria (pathognomonic discordance). CK >5,000 U/L diagnostic; >10,000 has high risk of AKI. Causes: exercise, crush, statins, alcohol, seizures, heat stroke. Treatment: aggressive IV hydration to maintain urine output 200–300 mL/hr.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis (Ischemic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic ATN follows hypoperfusion and shows muddy brown casts; the dipstick-microscopy heme discordance and markedly elevated CK specifically indicate myoglobinuria.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemolytic Anemia with Hemoglobinuria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemoglobinuria also causes heme-positive urine without RBCs, but would show a low hemoglobin, elevated LDH, and positive Coombs; CK elevation points to muscle injury.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Papillary Necrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Papillary necrosis can cause gross hematuria and AKI but is associated with NSAID overuse, diabetes, or sickle cell; the markedly elevated CK and exercise context are diagnostic of rhabdomyolysis.

clues: A 55-year-old man with known liver disease presents with progressive weakness, decreased urine output, and worsening abdominal swelling over the past week.
He has had no recent diarrhea, vomiting, hemorrhage, or nephrotoxic drug exposure; he has been hospitalized three times previously for tense ascites.
Examination shows jaundice, spider angiomata on the chest, tense ascites, asterixis, blood pressure 88/56 mmHg, and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema.
Serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.8 mg/dL over five days; urinalysis shows completely bland sediment with no casts or protein; urine sodium is less than 10 mEq/L; renal ultrasound is normal.
Creatinine continues to rise despite two days of intravenous albumin at 1 g/kg/day with no improvement in urine output, and plasma renin activity is markedly elevated.
explanation: Hepatorenal syndrome results from severe splanchnic vasodilation in cirrhosis causing underfilling of the systemic circulation, reflexive renal vasoconstriction via renin-angiotensin and sympathetic activation, and profound reduction in GFR. The kidneys are structurally normal and function normally if transplanted.
keyFact: HRS: AKI in cirrhosis with urine Na <10, no proteinuria/casts (bland), normal renal ultrasound, failure to respond to 1–1.5g/kg albumin. HRS Type 1 (HRS-AKI) is rapidly progressive; HRS Type 2 is slower. Treatment: terlipressin + albumin (or norepinephrine); definitive treatment is liver transplantation.

wrongAnswers.name: Prerenal AKI from Hypovolemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prerenal AKI also shows low urine Na and concentrated urine, but it responds to volume resuscitation with albumin; HRS is defined by failure to respond to adequate volume challenge.

wrongAnswers.name: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis-Associated AKI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SBP can precipitate HRS and AKI; however, SBP diagnosis requires >250 PMNs in ascitic fluid; this patient's AKI follows paracentesis without albumin, not a documented infection.

wrongAnswers.name: ATN from Sepsis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic ATN would show muddy brown casts on urinalysis; this patient has a bland urinalysis without infection signs; functional renal failure distinguishes HRS from structural ATN.

clues: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her son for confusion and unsteadiness developing over two days.
She was started on sertraline six weeks ago for depression and has a 40-pack-year smoking history; she denies excessive thirst or urinary frequency.
Exam reveals euvolemic status with no edema, no orthostatic blood pressure changes, no dry mucous membranes, and disorientation to place and time.
Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L; serum osmolality is 242 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality is 580 mOsm/kg; urine sodium is 52 mEq/L; TSH and morning cortisol are both normal.

Chest CT reveals a central lung mass, and biopsy of the mass shows small cell carcinoma in a euvolemic patient with hyponatremia, inappropriately concentrated urine, and normal thyroid and adrenal function.
explanation: SIADH occurs when ADH is secreted inappropriately (ectopically by tumor or from CNS/drug stimulation), causing water retention without sodium retention, resulting in euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine relative to dilute plasma.
keyFact: SIADH criteria: euvolemic hyponatremia, low serum osmolality, urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg (inappropriately concentrated), urine Na >40 mEq/L, normal TSH/cortisol. Causes: SCLC (most common malignant cause), CNS disorders, SSRIs, pain, nausea, pulmonary disease. Treatment: fluid restriction; tolvaptan for severe/chronic.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroid-Induced Hyponatremia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism can cause hyponatremia via SIADH mechanism but TSH is normal here; chest CT finding of SCLC provides an ectopic ADH source.

wrongAnswers.name: Adrenal Insufficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adrenal insufficiency causes hyponatremia (with possible hyperkalemia) but would show low cortisol and elevated ACTH; cortisol is normal in this case.

wrongAnswers.name: Psychogenic Polydipsia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psychogenic polydipsia causes dilute hyponatremia with very dilute urine (low urine osmolality); here urine is highly concentrated (580 mOsm/kg), which is the hallmark of SIADH.

clues: A 31-year-old woman presents with persistent fatigue, waking multiple times at night to urinate, and unquenchable thirst over the past three weeks.
She was involved in a motor vehicle accident with significant head trauma two months ago; she reports waking four to five times per night to urinate and immediately drinks large amounts of water.
Exam reveals blood pressure 118/74 mmHg with mild orthostatic changes on standing, mildly dry mucous membranes, and no focal neurological deficits.
Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L; serum osmolality is 306 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality is only 85 mOsm/kg despite hypernatremia; 24-hour urine volume is 9 liters.

Water deprivation test shows failure to concentrate urine above 300 mOsm/kg despite serum osmolality rising to 305 mOsm/kg; administration of desmopressin produces a greater than 50% increase in urine osmolality within 2 hours.
explanation: Central diabetes insipidus results from insufficient ADH production or secretion by the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary, leading to inability to concentrate urine and massive water losses. Causes include head trauma, pituitary surgery, tumors, infiltrative diseases, and idiopathic.
keyFact: Central DI vs. Nephrogenic DI: both cause polyuria, polydipsia, dilute urine. Key distinction: desmopressin (ADH analog) CORRECTS central DI (urine osmolality increases >50%) but NOT nephrogenic DI. MRI may show loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot in central DI.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nephrogenic DI also causes polyuria with dilute urine but does NOT respond to desmopressin; caused by renal resistance to ADH (lithium, hypercalcemia, V2R mutations).

wrongAnswers.name: Psychogenic Polydipsia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psychogenic polydipsia causes similar polyuria but serum sodium/osmolality are low or normal (primary polydipsia suppresses ADH); water deprivation corrects urine concentration in polydipsia.

wrongAnswers.name: SIADH
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SIADH causes hyponatremia and concentrated urine, the exact opposite of DI; polyuria is not a feature of SIADH.

clues: A 38-year-old man on a long-term psychiatric medication presents with excessive thirst and frequent urination that has worsened progressively over several weeks.
He has been on lithium for bipolar disorder for 12 years with good mood control; he has no history of kidney disease, diabetes, or calcium abnormalities.
Exam reveals blood pressure 112/70 mmHg with an orthostatic drop to 94/62 on standing, mildly dry mucous membranes, and no focal neurological deficits.
Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L; serum osmolality is 302 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality is only 72 mOsm/kg despite hypernatremia; plasma ADH level is appropriately elevated at 12 pg/mL.
Plasma ADH level is appropriately elevated at 12 pg/mL despite urine osmolality of 72 mOsm/kg; desmopressin administration produces less than 10% increase in urine osmolality after 2 hours.
explanation: Lithium enters collecting duct principal cells via ENaC channels, accumulating intracellularly and blocking ADH-mediated aquaporin-2 insertion; this impairs urinary concentration. Long-term lithium use can cause irreversible downregulation of AQP2, leading to permanent nephrogenic DI.
keyFact: Lithium is the most common acquired cause of nephrogenic DI. Nephrogenic DI: elevated ADH + failure to concentrate urine + no response to desmopressin. Treatment: stop lithium if possible; amiloride (blocks ENaC, reduces lithium entry); thiazide diuretics + low-salt diet (paradoxically reduce polyuria via volume contraction).

wrongAnswers.name: Central Diabetes Insipidus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Central DI responds to desmopressin with >50% increase in urine osmolality; here ADH is appropriately elevated and desmopressin produces no response, indicating renal resistance.

wrongAnswers.name: Psychogenic Polydipsia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psychogenic polydipsia produces dilute urine secondary to excessive water intake but serum sodium would be low/normal; hypernatremia indicates net water loss, not excess intake.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypercalcemia-Induced Polyuria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypercalcemia also causes nephrogenic DI but would show elevated serum calcium; lithium exposure with normal calcium and poor desmopressin response identifies the cause.

clues: A 26-year-old woman presents with recurrent painful muscle cramps, generalized weakness, and fatigue that have been worsening over the past year.
She has had low potassium on several prior lab draws attributed to poor diet; she takes no medications, denies vomiting or laxative use, and has no diarrhea.
Exam reveals blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, mild proximal muscle weakness, no Chvostek or Trousseau sign, and no peripheral edema.
Serum potassium is 2.6 mEq/L; magnesium is 1.1 mg/dL; bicarbonate is 30 mEq/L; urine potassium-to-creatinine ratio is elevated indicating renal wasting; urinary calcium excretion is very low.
Genetic testing reveals biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule.
explanation: Gitelman syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NCC cotransporter (same target as thiazide diuretics), leading to impaired sodium chloride reabsorption in the DCT, secondary hyperaldosteronism causing renal potassium and magnesium wasting, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and hypocalciuria.
keyFact: Gitelman syndrome: hypokalemia + hypomagnesemia + metabolic alkalosis + HYPOcalciuria + low-normal blood pressure. Distinguishable from Bartter by hypocalciuria (Bartter has hypercalciuria/normocalciuria) and milder clinical course. Think 'Gitelman = distal, like thiazide.'

wrongAnswers.name: Bartter Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bartter syndrome is a loop-diuretic equivalent tubular defect causing hypokalemic alkalosis with HYPERcalciuria/normocalciuria (not hypocalciuria); presents earlier in childhood with more severe volume depletion.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Conn syndrome causes hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis and hypertension (not low-normal BP); aldosterone is elevated with suppressed renin, not secondary hyperaldosteronism.

wrongAnswers.name: Surreptitious Diuretic Use
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thiazide abuse mimics Gitelman syndrome clinically and biochemically but can be detected by urine diuretic screen; genetic testing identifies SLC12A3 mutations confirming the inherited disorder.

clues: A 3-year-old boy is brought in for poor weight gain and frequent episodes of fussiness and muscle cramping.
He was born premature at 32 weeks due to severe polyhydramnios and has required potassium supplements since infancy.
Blood pressure is 86/52 mmHg; weight and height are below the 5th percentile; mild dehydration is noted; no dysmorphic features are present.
Serum potassium is 2.3 mEq/L with serum bicarbonate of 34 mEq/L; urine calcium is elevated; plasma renin and aldosterone are both markedly elevated.
Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the KCNJ1 gene encoding the ROMK channel in the thick ascending limb of Henle.
explanation: Bartter syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in proteins of the thick ascending limb of Henle (NKCC2, ROMK, chloride channels, Barttin), functionally mimicking loop diuretic use. This leads to sodium wasting, secondary hyperaldosteronism, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and hypercalciuria due to impaired paracellular calcium reabsorption.
keyFact: Bartter syndrome: hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis + hypercalciuria + low blood pressure + elevated renin and aldosterone. Presents in infancy/childhood, often with polyhydramnios. Distinguishable from Gitelman (DCT defect) by hypercalciuria and earlier/more severe presentation. Treatment: NSAIDs (reduce prostaglandin-mediated effects), potassium/magnesium supplementation.

wrongAnswers.name: Gitelman Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gitelman causes hypocalciuria (not hypercalciuria) and typically presents in adolescence/adulthood with milder symptoms; Bartter presents in infancy with polyhydramnios and failure to thrive.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Conn syndrome causes hypertension (not hypotension) with suppressed renin; both renin and aldosterone are elevated in Bartter due to the secondary hyperaldosteronism from volume depletion.

wrongAnswers.name: Cystic Fibrosis with Electrolyte Abnormalities
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CF can cause metabolic alkalosis via chloride loss in sweat but does not cause hypokalemia, hypercalciuria, or the specific tubular transport defect; genetic testing confirms CFTR vs KCNJ1.

clues: A 63-year-old man presents for routine follow-up with no new complaints, but his physician is concerned about a gradual decline in kidney function over several years.
He admits poor medication adherence, and home blood pressures have been running 170 to 190 systolic for years; he denies hematuria, foamy urine, or joint pain.
Blood pressure is 178/106 mmHg; fundoscopy reveals arteriovenous nicking and copper-wiring of retinal vessels; no peripheral edema is present.

Serum creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL, up from 1.2 five years ago; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 180 mg/g; urinalysis shows no casts or hematuria; renal ultrasound shows bilateral small, echogenic kidneys.
Kidney biopsy demonstrates arteriolar hyalinosis, intimal thickening of interlobular arteries, and global glomerulosclerosis without immune complex deposits on immunofluorescence.
explanation: Chronic hypertension causes intimal hyperplasia and hyalinosis of afferent arterioles, reducing glomerular perfusion and leading to ischemic glomerulosclerosis and tubular atrophy. This is the second most common cause of ESRD in the United States.
keyFact: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis: slowly progressive CKD with subnephrotic proteinuria, bland urinalysis, small echogenic kidneys. Pathology: arteriolar hyalinosis + global glomerulosclerosis. Differentiate from renovascular disease (which causes elevated renin). APOL1 variants increase risk in Black patients. Target BP <130/80 with ACE inhibitor or ARB.

wrongAnswers.name: FSGS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS causes nephrotic-range proteinuria (not mildly elevated) and shows segmental (not global) sclerosis on biopsy; more common in younger Black adults.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetic Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Diabetic nephropathy also causes progressive CKD with proteinuria but requires diabetes diagnosis and shows Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules on biopsy; no diabetes mentioned here.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Artery Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RAS causes resistant hypertension with elevated renin and can cause ischemic nephropathy; however, biopsy would show global ischemic changes without arteriolar hyalinosis characteristic of chronic hypertension.

clues: A 34-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of flank pain and blood in her urine since her early twenties.
She has passed multiple small kidney stones, and urine cultures have periodically been positive for E. coli; her father also has a history of kidney stones.
Mild right costovertebral angle tenderness is present; blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg; no palpable abdominal masses are found.
Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria; non-contrast CT reveals bilateral medullary calcifications; 24-hour urine shows hypercalciuria; urine pH is 6.0 despite a mild metabolic acidosis.
CT urography with contrast demonstrates dilated medullary collecting tubules with contrast pooling in a radiating pattern from the papillae.
explanation: Medullary sponge kidney is a congenital malformation characterized by cystic dilation of the medullary and papillary collecting tubules, leading to urinary stasis, nephrocalcinosis, hypercalciuria, incomplete distal RTA, and recurrent urolithiasis and UTIs.
keyFact: Medullary sponge kidney: 'bouquet of flowers' on contrast urography; bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis on CT; associated with hypercalciuria and incomplete distal RTA (Type 1). Usually not progressive to ESRD. May be associated with hemihypertrophy and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Distal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Primary)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary distal RTA causes nephrocalcinosis and recurrent stones with hypokalemia and alkaline urine; but does not show dilated collecting tubules or the paintbrush pattern on urography.

wrongAnswers.name: Autosomal Dominant PKD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ADPKD causes bilateral enlarged kidneys with large cortical and medullary cysts; does not produce medullary nephrocalcinosis or the specific paintbrush collecting tubule pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperparathyroidism-Induced Nephrocalcinosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis but would show elevated calcium and PTH; MSK is the cause of the structural changes seen on urography.

clues: A 67-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath on exertion over several months and a persistent nonproductive cough.
He has never smoked and has no history of occupational dust exposure, bird ownership, or regular medication use that could explain his symptoms.
Auscultation of the lung bases reveals fine, end-inspiratory "Velcro" crackles bilaterally; clubbing of the fingernails is noted.

Pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO; high-resolution CT shows bilateral, predominantly basal, subpleural reticular opacities with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis.

Multidisciplinary review identifies the imaging pattern as showing peripheral honeycombing with architectural distortion in a basal-predominant distribution; surgical lung biopsy reveals fibroblastic foci with temporal heterogeneity of fibrosis.
explanation: IPF is characterized by progressive fibrosis of the lung parenchyma in a UIP pattern, driven by aberrant epithelial repair responses leading to fibroblast activation and collagen deposition, ultimately destroying alveolar architecture.
keyFact: IPF is the most common idiopathic interstitial pneumonia; UIP pattern on HRCT (honeycombing + basal subpleural reticulation) is sufficient for diagnosis without biopsy in the right clinical context. Anti-fibrotic agents (nintedanib, pirfenidone) slow progression.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HP typically requires antigen exposure (birds, mold, farming); this patient has none, and HP more commonly shows upper/mid-lung predominance and ground-glass opacities rather than basal honeycombing.

wrongAnswers.name: Asbestosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asbestosis mimics UIP but requires confirmed asbestos exposure with pleural plaques, neither of which is present here.

wrongAnswers.name: Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NSIP shows ground-glass and reticulation without honeycombing on CT and lacks fibroblastic foci on biopsy; it is more common in younger women and those with connective tissue disease.

clues: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of dry cough, mild shortness of breath, fatigue, and aching in her ankles.
She has no history of smoking, recent travel, or sick contacts; she reports that her eyes have been intermittently red and irritated for the past month.
Chest examination reveals scattered faint crackles; skin exam shows raised, tender, erythematous nodules on both shins.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar enlargement; serum ACE level is elevated; calcium is mildly elevated at 10.8 mg/dL.
Transbronchial biopsy of a hilar lymph node reveals well-formed granulomas without central necrosis; special stains for fungi and acid-fast bacilli are negative.
explanation: Sarcoidosis results from an exaggerated granulomatous immune response to an unidentified antigen, forming non-caseating granulomas predominantly in the lungs and lymph nodes, but capable of involving virtually any organ.
keyFact: Lofgren syndrome (bilateral hilar adenopathy + erythema nodosum + ankle periarthritis) is a classic acute sarcoid presentation with an excellent prognosis. ACE is elevated in ~75% but is nonspecific.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma can cause bilateral hilar adenopathy but does not cause erythema nodosum or hypercalcemia, and biopsy would show malignant lymphocytes rather than non-caseating granulomas.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB can cause hilar adenopathy and granulomas, but granulomas are typically caseating; AFB stain and cultures are negative here, and bilateral symmetric hilar adenopathy is less typical.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HP causes granulomas and dyspnea but does not produce bilateral hilar adenopathy, erythema nodosum, or hypercalcemia; antigen exposure history would typically be present.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, and fatigue over four months that seems to fluctuate in severity.
She works as an office manager in a building that recently had water damage and visible mold growth; she has no history of atopy or smoking.
Lung auscultation reveals fine inspiratory crackles bilaterally, most prominent at the mid-lung zones; no clubbing or wheezing is noted.

HRCT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities with mid-lung predominance, poorly defined centrilobular nodules, and air trapping on expiratory images; serum precipitins to thermophilic actinomycetes are positive.
Surgical lung biopsy shows peribronchiolar granulomas and lymphocytic alveolitis; symptoms and imaging substantially improve after the patient is relocated to a different building.
explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a T-cell mediated immune response to inhaled organic antigens, leading to peribronchiolar inflammation and granuloma formation; chronic exposure can result in progressive fibrosis.
keyFact: The occupational/environmental history is crucial — classic antigens include bird droppings (bird fancier's lung), thermophilic actinomycetes in moldy hay (farmer's lung), and mold in water-damaged buildings. Air trapping on expiratory CT is a key finding.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis can show similar granulomas and dyspnea, but lacks the clear antigen exposure, work-related symptom pattern, and positive precipitins; bilateral hilar adenopathy would be more characteristic of sarcoidosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ABPA is associated with asthma and elevated IgE, involves central bronchiectasis and mucus plugging, and is not characterized by peribronchiolar granulomas or the occupational trigger seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COP shows patchy consolidations and peribronchovascular distribution rather than centrilobular nodules and air trapping; it lacks the antigen-exposure temporal relationship and positive precipitins.

clues: A 52-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of right-sided chest pain that worsens with deep breathing and mild shortness of breath that began 2 hours ago.
She returned from a 14-hour international flight 3 days ago and has been less active than usual since returning; she takes oral contraceptive pills.
Heart rate is 112 bpm and oxygen saturation is 93% on room air; the right calf is mildly swollen and tender compared to the left.
ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a new S1Q3T3 pattern; D-dimer is elevated at 3.2 mcg/mL; chest X-ray is unremarkable.
CT pulmonary angiography demonstrates filling defects in the right main pulmonary artery and multiple segmental branches bilaterally.
explanation: Pulmonary embolism occurs when thrombus, most often from deep vein thrombosis, lodges in the pulmonary vasculature, causing increased dead space, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and right ventricular pressure overload.
keyFact: Risk factors follow Virchow's triad (stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury). S1Q3T3 on ECG and Hampton's hump/Westermark sign on CXR are classic but insensitive. CTPA is the gold standard for diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pneumothorax causes pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea but chest X-ray would show absent lung markings and a visceral pleural line; calf swelling and DVT risk factors are not features.

wrongAnswers.name: Pleuritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pleuritis causes pleuritic chest pain but does not explain tachycardia, hypoxia, calf swelling, or elevated D-dimer; CTPA would be normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute MI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute MI can cause chest pain and dyspnea, but the pleuritic quality, hypoxia, unilateral calf swelling, and S1Q3T3 pattern point more strongly to PE; troponin and ECG changes would differ.

clues: An 18-year-old male presents with sudden onset left-sided sharp chest pain and mild shortness of breath that began 2 hours ago.
He is tall and thin with no prior lung disease or recent trauma; he had a similar episode on the right side two years ago.
Breath sounds are diminished over the left hemithorax; trachea is midline; percussion over the left chest is hyperresonant.
Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air; chest X-ray shows a left-sided pleural line with absence of lung markings lateral to it, estimated at approximately 25%.
CT chest shows a left apical bleb with the pleural defect and no underlying parenchymal disease or secondary cause identified.
explanation: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs due to rupture of subpleural blebs or bullae, most commonly at the lung apex, allowing air to enter the pleural space without an identifiable precipitating lung disease.
keyFact: PSP classically affects tall, thin young males. Recurrence risk is ~30% ipsilateral and higher after a second episode, prompting consideration of pleurodesis. Absence of underlying lung disease distinguishes PSP from secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE can cause sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, but breath sounds would be preserved, percussion would be normal, and CXR typically does not show a pleural line.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Dissection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aortic dissection presents with tearing pain and hemodynamic instability; it does not explain diminished breath sounds or hyperresonance and is uncommon in healthy 18-year-olds.

wrongAnswers.name: Pleuritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pleuritis causes pleuritic pain but not diminished breath sounds, hyperresonance, or a visible pleural line on chest X-ray.

clues: A 58-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of worsening cough, mild right-sided chest aching, and unintentional weight loss of 8 pounds.
She smoked half a pack per day for 15 years but quit 10 years ago; she has no occupational exposures and no family history of lung cancer.
Breath sounds are decreased in the right lower lobe; there is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.

CT chest shows a 3.2 cm irregular, spiculated peripheral mass in the right lower lobe with a small right-sided pleural effusion; PET scan reveals FDG avidity in the mass and in two ipsilateral mediastinal lymph nodes.
CT-guided biopsy demonstrates malignant cells forming acinar structures; immunohistochemistry is positive for TTF-1 and napsin A; molecular testing shows an EGFR exon 19 deletion.
explanation: Lung adenocarcinoma arises from peripheral bronchial epithelial cells and is the most common lung cancer subtype; EGFR mutations are targetable driver mutations found predominantly in never/light smokers and are associated with response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
keyFact: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer in never-smokers and women. TTF-1 and napsin A positivity confirms lung primary. EGFR mutations (most common in Asian, female, never-smokers) predict response to osimertinib.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCC typically arises centrally near the hilum and is strongly associated with heavy smoking; peripheral spiculated masses with EGFR mutations and TTF-1 positivity are not characteristic of SCC.

wrongAnswers.name: Small Cell Lung Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCLC is typically central, rapidly growing, and associated with paraneoplastic syndromes; it is TTF-1 positive but napsin A negative, does not harbor EGFR mutations, and has a distinct neuroendocrine histology.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Carcinoid
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoids are slow-growing neuroendocrine tumors that are typically central and do not show EGFR mutations or TTF-1/napsin A staining patterns consistent with adenocarcinoma.

accept: small cell carcinoma of the lung
clues: A 62-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of cough, progressive shortness of breath, and new facial puffiness.
He has a 50 pack-year smoking history and has recently noticed weakness in his legs along with increased thirst and frequent urination.

The face and bilateral upper extremities are edematous and ruddy; prominent dilated veins are visible over the anterior chest wall; proximal lower limb weakness with decreased deep tendon reflexes is found on neurological exam.

Chest CT demonstrates a large central hilar mass with bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy compressing the superior vena cava; serum sodium is 122 mEq/L with serum osmolality 260 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality 580 mOsm/kg.
Bronchoscopic biopsy shows sheets of small round cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, and high mitotic rate; immunostaining is positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and CD56.
explanation: SCLC is a highly aggressive neuroendocrine tumor arising from Kulchitsky cells; it frequently causes paraneoplastic syndromes through ectopic hormone production (SIADH, Cushing's, Lambert-Eaton) and commonly presents with bulky mediastinal disease causing SVC syndrome.
keyFact: SCLC is strongly associated with smoking and is staged as limited vs. extensive rather than TNM. Classic paraneoplastic syndromes include SIADH (hyponatremia), Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (proximal weakness, hyporeflexia), and ectopic ACTH. It is the most common cause of SVC syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome from Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma can cause SVC syndrome and mediastinal masses, but the neuroendocrine biopsy features, heavy smoking history, and combined SIADH with Lambert-Eaton syndrome point to SCLC.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Adenocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adenocarcinoma is typically peripheral and rarely causes SVC syndrome; it does not produce neuroendocrine paraneoplastic syndromes like SIADH or Lambert-Eaton, and biopsy would show glandular rather than neuroendocrine morphology.

wrongAnswers.name: Thymoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thymoma can cause SVC syndrome and is an anterior mediastinal mass, but is not associated with heavy smoking, does not produce SIADH, and biopsy would show epithelial thymocytes rather than neuroendocrine cells.

clues: A 71-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of progressive left-sided chest pain that is constant and non-pleuritic, along with worsening shortness of breath and a 15-pound weight loss.
He worked as a shipyard pipefitter for 30 years, retiring in 1998; he smoked one pack per day for 20 years but quit at age 50.
Breath sounds are markedly reduced over the entire left hemithorax; the left chest is dull to percussion throughout; no clubbing is noted.

Chest CT shows a large left-sided pleural effusion with diffuse irregular pleural thickening encasing the left lung and extending into the fissures; a pleural-based mass with lobulated contour is noted; thoracentesis yields bloody fluid.

Video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy shows malignant cells with biphasic epithelioid and sarcomatoid components; immunostaining is positive for calretinin, WT-1, and D2-40 and negative for CEA and TTF-1.
explanation: Malignant pleural mesothelioma arises from mesothelial cells lining the pleura and is causally linked to asbestos exposure, with a latency period of 20–50 years; the tumor encases the lung rather than forming a discrete mass.
keyFact: Mesothelioma has a 20–50 year latency after asbestos exposure. Calretinin, WT-1, and D2-40 positivity with CEA/TTF-1 negativity distinguishes it from metastatic adenocarcinoma. Circumferential pleural thickening on CT is a key imaging feature.

wrongAnswers.name: Pleural Metastases from Lung Adenocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastatic adenocarcinoma can cause pleural thickening and bloody effusions, but immunostaining would be TTF-1 and CEA positive; diffuse encasing pleural thickening without a discrete primary lung mass favors mesothelioma.

wrongAnswers.name: Asbestosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asbestosis causes interstitial fibrosis and pleural plaques from asbestos exposure, not a pleural-encasing mass or bloody effusion; it does not present with a pleural-based malignant tumor.

wrongAnswers.name: Empyema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Empyema causes pleural effusion and pleural thickening but presents with fever, infection, and purulent fluid rather than a bloody effusion, weight loss, and the malignant biopsy findings seen here.

clues: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 1-year history of progressive exertional dyspnea, easy fatigability, and two episodes of near-syncope with exertion.
She has no history of lung disease, heart disease, or connective tissue disease; she does not smoke and takes no medications; she now avoids walking more than one block.
Cardiac exam reveals a loud P2, a right ventricular heave, and a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration; mild bilateral ankle edema is present.
Echocardiogram shows estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 72 mmHg, right ventricular dilation with septal flattening in systole; V/Q scan is low probability for PE.
Right heart catheterization demonstrates a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mmHg with a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 10 mmHg and a pulmonary vascular resistance of 9 Wood units.
explanation: Idiopathic PAH results from progressive obliterative remodeling of small pulmonary arterioles, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance, leading to right ventricular pressure overload, dilation, hypertrophy, and ultimately right heart failure.
keyFact: PAH is defined by mean PA pressure >20 mmHg with PCWP ≤15 mmHg and PVR ≥3 Wood units on right heart cath. It predominantly affects young women. BMPR2 mutations are found in ~70% of familial PAH. Treatments include prostacyclins, endothelin antagonists, and PDE-5 inhibitors.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic thromboembolic disease can cause pulmonary hypertension, but V/Q scan is low probability here; right heart cath with low PCWP and high PVR without segmental perfusion defects is more consistent with idiopathic PAH.

wrongAnswers.name: Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HFpEF causes elevated PCWP (>15 mmHg) indicating postcapillary pulmonary hypertension; this patient has a normal PCWP of 10 mmHg, ruling out left-sided heart disease as the cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD-associated pulmonary hypertension occurs in older smokers with airflow obstruction; this young non-smoker has no obstructive physiology and the degree of PAP elevation is disproportionate to what COPD alone would cause.

clues: A 48-year-old man is referred for evaluation of uncontrolled hypertension and significant daytime fatigue despite seemingly adequate sleep duration.
He has a BMI of 34 kg/m2, a neck circumference of 44 cm, and reports waking up with headaches most mornings; he takes lisinopril and amlodipine.
Oropharyngeal exam shows a Mallampati class III airway with a crowded posterior pharynx and enlarged tonsils; he scores 14 out of 24 on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale.
Overnight pulse oximetry shows recurrent desaturation events with time below 90% SpO2 of 22%; morning arterial blood gas shows PaCO2 44 mmHg and PaO2 78 mmHg.
In-laboratory polysomnography reveals an apnea-hypopnea index of 42 events per hour, predominantly obstructive in character with associated arousal and desaturation events.
explanation: OSA results from repetitive collapse of the upper airway during sleep, causing intermittent hypoxia, hypercapnia, and arousal from sleep, leading to fragmented sleep, daytime somnolence, and sympathetically-driven hypertension.
keyFact: OSA is the most common cause of secondary hypertension. Diagnosis requires AHI ≥5 events/hour with symptoms or AHI ≥15 regardless of symptoms on polysomnography. CPAP is first-line treatment and can improve blood pressure control.

wrongAnswers.name: Central Sleep Apnea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Central sleep apnea features apneas without respiratory effort and is associated with heart failure or opioid use; the obstructive character on PSG, obesity, and crowded airway point to OSA.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes fatigue, weight gain, and can predispose to OSA, but does not directly cause the obstructive apneic events seen on polysomnography; TSH was not mentioned as abnormal.

wrongAnswers.name: Narcolepsy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Narcolepsy causes excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy but does not cause obstructive apneic events, choking sounds, nocturnal desaturation, or hypertension; polysomnography would show REM abnormalities rather than obstructive events.

clues: A 44-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of persistent nasal congestion, bloody nasal discharge, cough with occasional blood-streaked sputum, and new-onset shortness of breath.
He has had recurrent sinus infections over the past year requiring multiple antibiotic courses; he recently noticed joint pain and swelling along with a new rash on his legs.
Nasal examination reveals a saddle-nose deformity and crusting of the nasal mucosa with areas of ulceration; lung auscultation reveals scattered crackles; urinalysis shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein.
Chest CT shows multiple bilateral pulmonary cavitary nodules; serum creatinine is elevated at 2.4 mg/dL; ANCA testing returns positive for c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) with a titer of 1:320.

Renal biopsy demonstrates a pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis without immune complex deposition; open lung biopsy reveals necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with vasculitis of small and medium vessels.
explanation: GPA is an ANCA-associated vasculitis primarily targeting the upper and lower respiratory tracts and kidneys; PR3-ANCA-mediated neutrophil activation causes necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and pauci-immune glomerulonephritis.
keyFact: GPA classically presents as the triad of upper respiratory (sinusitis, saddle-nose), lower respiratory (cavitary nodules, hemoptysis), and renal disease (crescentic GN). c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA is ~90% specific. Treatment is rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids.

wrongAnswers.name: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EGPA (Churg-Strauss) features asthma, eosinophilia, and p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA rather than c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA; saddle-nose deformity and cavitary nodules are not typical of EGPA.

wrongAnswers.name: Goodpasture Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Goodpasture causes pulmonary-renal syndrome with hemoptysis and glomerulonephritis but is mediated by anti-GBM antibodies rather than ANCA; it does not cause upper airway disease or cavitary nodules.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Abscess with Septic Emboli
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic emboli can cause cavitary pulmonary nodules, but do not explain saddle-nose deformity, sinusitis, ANCA positivity, or pauci-immune GN; an infectious source would be identifiable.

clues: A 38-year-old woman with a history of asthma presents with worsening respiratory symptoms and a new painful rash on her lower legs.
Over the past 3 months she has developed tingling and weakness in her right foot and left hand in a pattern affecting multiple individual nerves; she also reports low-grade fevers and joint pain.
Lung exam reveals diffuse expiratory wheezing; the skin shows palpable purpura on bilateral lower legs; neurological exam shows right foot drop and decreased sensation in a stocking distribution.
Complete blood count shows eosinophils at 4,800 per microliter; chest CT shows patchy migratory ground-glass opacities and bronchial wall thickening; p-ANCA (MPO-ANCA) is positive.
Sural nerve biopsy shows eosinophilic infiltration and necrotizing vasculitis of the epineurial vessels with surrounding granulomatous inflammation.
explanation: EGPA is an ANCA-associated vasculitis characterized by asthma, tissue eosinophilia, and granulomatous necrotizing vasculitis affecting small and medium vessels, with a three-phase progression from atopic to eosinophilic to vasculitic disease.
keyFact: EGPA classically progresses through three phases: allergic (asthma/rhinitis), eosinophilic (organ infiltration), and vasculitic. Mononeuritis multiplex is a key feature. p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA is positive in ~40%. Distinguish from GPA by asthma and prominent eosinophilia.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypereosinophilic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HES also causes eosinophilia and multi-organ damage, but lacks the asthma-dominant history, pANCA positivity, and granulomatous vasculitis on biopsy; cardiac involvement is more prominent in HES.

wrongAnswers.name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GPA is c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA positive and lacks the longstanding asthma history, nasal polyps, and marked peripheral eosinophilia; cavitary nodules rather than ground-glass opacities are more typical of GPA.

wrongAnswers.name: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ABPA causes eosinophilia and asthma exacerbations but does not cause vasculitis, mononeuritis multiplex, palpable purpura, or MPO-ANCA positivity.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with two days of progressive shortness of breath and cough productive of blood-tinged sputum.
He has been feeling fatigued for 3 weeks and noticed his urine has been dark and foamy; he smokes half a pack per day and has no known lung or kidney disease.
He appears pale and in mild respiratory distress; oxygen saturation is 91% on room air; lung auscultation reveals bilateral crackles; blood pressure is 148/94 mmHg.

Serum creatinine is 4.2 mg/dL with an upward trend; urinalysis reveals dysmorphic red blood cells and red cell casts; chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates; ANCA testing is negative.

Serum testing reveals markedly elevated antibodies targeting the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen; kidney biopsy demonstrates linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence.
explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by autoantibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, leading to immune-mediated pulmonary hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
keyFact: Goodpasture is a pulmonary-renal syndrome. Anti-GBM antibodies cause linear IgG deposits on immunofluorescence (vs. pauci-immune in ANCA vasculitis). Smoking is a risk factor for pulmonary involvement. Treatment requires urgent plasmapheresis plus immunosuppression.

wrongAnswers.name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GPA also causes pulmonary-renal syndrome with hemoptysis and GN, but is ANCA positive (c-ANCA/PR3) and shows pauci-immune GN on biopsy; the linear IgG deposits confirm anti-GBM disease.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA Nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy causes hematuria and can worsen with respiratory infections, but does not cause diffuse alveolar hemorrhage; IF would show mesangial IgA deposits rather than linear GBM deposits.

wrongAnswers.name: Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage from SLE
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus can cause DAH and nephritis, but would show granular immune deposits on IF (not linear), is associated with ANA/dsDNA positivity, and does not show anti-GBM antibodies.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with a 5-year history of progressive exertional dyspnea, productive cough, and more recently weight loss and night sweats.
He has worked as a sandblaster in a metal foundry for 25 years and has smoked one pack per day since age 20; he has no prior diagnosis of lung disease.
Lung exam reveals decreased breath sounds bilaterally at the bases with occasional crackles; he appears cachectic; there is no clubbing.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral upper-lobe-predominant small nodular opacities with bilateral hilar calcification in an eggshell pattern; PFTs show a mixed obstructive-restrictive pattern.
HRCT demonstrates bilateral upper lobe conglomerate masses with surrounding emphysema; transbronchial biopsy shows whorled collagenous nodules with birefringent particles under polarized light.
explanation: Silicosis results from macrophage-mediated inflammatory response to inhaled crystalline silica, leading to collagen deposition, silicotic nodules in the upper lobes, and progressive massive fibrosis in advanced disease; silica exposure also markedly increases the risk of tuberculosis.
keyFact: Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes is pathognomonic for silicosis. Upper lobe predominance distinguishes it from asbestosis (lower lobe). Silicosis dramatically increases TB risk (Silicotuberculosis). Sandblasting carries the highest exposure risk.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB can cause upper lobe cavitary disease, weight loss, and night sweats in this demographic, but does not produce eggshell hilar calcification, silicotic nodules, or the occupational exposure history; cultures are negative here.

wrongAnswers.name: Coal Worker's Pneumoconiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CWP results from coal dust exposure and can progress to PMF, but the occupational exposure here is sandblasting (silica), eggshell hilar calcification is more specific to silicosis, and the birefringent particles confirm silica.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis can cause bilateral upper lobe opacities and hilar adenopathy, but eggshell calcification is not typical; the prolonged occupational exposure and birefringent particles on biopsy confirm a pneumoconiosis rather than a granulomatous disease.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with a 3-year history of progressive shortness of breath with exertion and a dry cough; he denies fever, hemoptysis, or significant weight loss.
He worked as an insulation installer in commercial buildings from 1968 to 1995; he has never smoked and has no history of connective tissue disease.
Bilateral end-inspiratory crackles are heard at the lung bases; mild finger clubbing is present; no lymphadenopathy is noted.
PFTs show a restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO; HRCT demonstrates bilateral subpleural basal reticular opacities with traction bronchiectasis and calcified pleural plaques bilaterally.
Surgical lung biopsy reveals interstitial fibrosis with golden-brown, dumbbell-shaped iron-coated fibers visible on light microscopy; bronchoalveolar lavage shows an increased fiber count.
explanation: Asbestosis results from asbestos fiber-induced macrophage activation and persistent inflammatory response leading to progressive interstitial fibrosis, predominantly in the lower lobes; pleural plaques are a marker of asbestos exposure but are distinct from asbestosis.
keyFact: Asbestosis histologically resembles UIP but is distinguished by asbestos bodies (ferruginous bodies) on biopsy. Calcified pleural plaques are a marker of asbestos exposure, not asbestosis itself. Asbestos exposure dramatically increases the risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer, especially in smokers.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IPF has identical HRCT and histologic patterns (UIP) but lacks the definitive occupational asbestos exposure history and the presence of asbestos/ferruginous bodies on biopsy, which distinguish asbestosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Mesothelioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mesothelioma is also related to asbestos exposure and can cause pleural disease, but presents as a malignant pleural mass rather than interstitial lung fibrosis; biopsy here shows fibrosis with ferruginous bodies, not malignant mesothelial cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HP causes interstitial lung disease with a history of antigen exposure, but asbestos is not a typical HP antigen; HP shows upper/mid-lung predominance and lacks pleural plaques or asbestos bodies.

clues: A 52-year-old woman presents with a 10-year history of daily productive cough with large amounts of purulent sputum, recurrent respiratory infections, and intermittent blood-streaked sputum.
She had severe whooping cough as a child followed by recurrent pneumonias throughout adolescence; she has never smoked and reports that sputum volume increases with positional changes.
Coarse crackles are heard bilaterally on auscultation, most prominent in the lower lobes; mild clubbing is present; no wheezing is noted.
PFTs show a mixed obstructive-restrictive pattern with FEV1/FVC of 0.62; sputum culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa; chest X-ray shows increased bronchial markings with areas of ring shadows.

HRCT demonstrates bilateral lower-lobe-predominant cylindrical and varicose airway dilation with bronchial wall thickening, mucus plugging, and airways whose diameter exceeds that of their accompanying pulmonary artery.
explanation: Bronchiectasis results from a vicious cycle of recurrent infection and inflammation causing irreversible structural bronchial dilation, impaired mucociliary clearance, and chronic bacterial colonization, most commonly following childhood respiratory infections.
keyFact: Signet ring sign on HRCT (bronchus diameter > adjacent pulmonary artery) is the hallmark. Postinfectious bronchiectasis (TB, whooping cough) is most common worldwide. Pseudomonas colonization indicates more severe disease. Chronic airway clearance and macrolide prophylaxis are key management strategies.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes airflow obstruction and productive cough but does not cause the structural bronchial dilation seen on HRCT; the childhood whooping cough, daily purulent sputum, and signet ring sign confirm bronchiectasis.

wrongAnswers.name: Cystic Fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CF also causes bronchiectasis and Pseudomonas colonization, but typically presents in childhood with upper-lobe predominance and would require genetic testing showing CFTR mutations; this adult with a postinfectious childhood history and lower-lobe disease is more consistent with non-CF bronchiectasis.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lung abscess causes purulent sputum and can cause hemoptysis, but presents as a localized cavitary lesion rather than diffuse bilateral bronchial dilation on HRCT.

clues: A 26-year-old man presents with a 2-month worsening of chronic cough, increased sputum production, dyspnea on exertion, and a 10-pound unintentional weight loss.
He has had recurrent pulmonary infections since childhood and requires enzyme supplements for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency; he has been unable to father children despite 2 years of trying.
He appears thin and malnourished; bilateral upper-lobe-predominant crackles and expiratory wheezing are heard; mild clubbing of the fingers is present.

PFTs show severe obstructive pattern with FEV1 42% predicted; chest CT shows upper-lobe-predominant bronchiectasis with mucus plugging; sputum cultures grow Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus.
Sweat chloride testing on two separate occasions reveals values of 78 mEq/L; genetic testing identifies compound heterozygous mutations in the CFTR gene.
explanation: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, leading to dysfunctional chloride channels, thickened airway secretions, impaired mucociliary clearance, recurrent infections, progressive bronchiectasis, and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
keyFact: Sweat chloride >60 mEq/L on two occasions is diagnostic. F508del is the most common mutation. G551D responds to ivacaftor (CFTR potentiator). Male infertility (bilateral absence of vas deferens), upper-lobe bronchiectasis, and Pseudomonas colonization are hallmarks.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PCD also causes recurrent infections and bronchiectasis but does not cause pancreatic exocrine insufficiency; it features ciliary ultrastructural defects and nasal nitric oxide testing would be abnormal rather than a positive sweat chloride test.

wrongAnswers.name: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A1AT deficiency causes early-onset emphysema (basal predominant) and liver disease, but not upper-lobe bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, or a positive sweat chloride; diagnosis is made by serum A1AT level and Pi typing.

wrongAnswers.name: Non-CF Bronchiectasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Non-CF bronchiectasis has similar imaging and clinical features, but lacks the pancreatic insufficiency, male infertility, and the positive sweat chloride/CFTR mutations that define CF.

clues: A 54-year-old man in the ICU develops increasing oxygen requirements and worsening respiratory status 48 hours after an abdominal surgical procedure.
He developed septic shock intraoperatively requiring vasopressor support and received 8 liters of crystalloid resuscitation; his post-operative course was complicated by Gram-negative bacteremia.
He is intubated and mechanically ventilated with FiO2 of 0.80 and PEEP of 12 cmH2O; auscultation reveals diffuse bilateral crackles; he is on norepinephrine.
Arterial blood gas shows PaO2 of 58 mmHg on FiO2 0.80 yielding a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 73; chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse airspace opacities; echocardiogram shows preserved LV function.

Pulmonary artery catheter shows a wedge pressure of 8 mmHg; the bilateral opacities and severe hypoxemia developed within 7 days of the septic insult with no evidence of left heart failure or volume overload.
explanation: ARDS results from direct or indirect lung injury triggering massive neutrophil activation, alveolar-capillary barrier disruption, and protein-rich edema flooding the alveoli, causing severe non-cardiogenic hypoxemic respiratory failure with diffuse inflammatory lung injury.
keyFact: Berlin Definition requires: bilateral opacities on CXR/CT, PF ratio <300 with PEEP ≥5, onset within 1 week of insult, and exclusion of heart failure/fluid overload. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg IBW) and prone positioning reduce mortality in severe ARDS.

wrongAnswers.name: Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cardiogenic edema causes bilateral opacities and hypoxemia but requires elevated PCWP (>18 mmHg) and evidence of left heart dysfunction; this patient has preserved LV function and PCWP of 8 mmHg, ruling out cardiogenic cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Bilateral Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bilateral pneumonia can cause bilateral opacities and hypoxemia and can trigger ARDS, but ARDS specifically represents the diffuse alveolar damage syndrome meeting Berlin criteria; here the bilateral opacities are attributed to ARDS from the septic insult.

wrongAnswers.name: Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TACO causes bilateral opacities after transfusion due to volume overload, but would show elevated PCWP and respond to diuresis; normal filling pressures and PCWP of 8 mmHg exclude this diagnosis.

clues: A 29-year-old woman with a history of asthma presents with worsening respiratory symptoms, productive cough, and recurrent low-grade fevers over the past 4 months.

Her asthma was previously well-controlled on medium-dose inhaled corticosteroids, but she has required two courses of systemic steroids in the past 3 months; she recalls coughing up a rubbery brown plug last week.
Lung exam reveals diffuse expiratory wheezing and coarse crackles in the left upper lobe; there is no clubbing or cyanosis.

CBC shows peripheral eosinophilia at 1,200 per microliter; total serum IgE is markedly elevated at 2,800 IU/mL; skin prick test to Aspergillus fumigatus is positive; chest CT shows left upper lobe central bronchiectasis with high-attenuation mucus plugging.

Specific IgE and IgG to Aspergillus fumigatus are elevated; bronchoalveolar lavage shows eosinophils and fungal hyphae; the combination of total IgE above 1000, central bronchiectasis, and peripheral eosinophilia occurs in an asthmatic patient with Aspergillus sensitization.
explanation: ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus colonizing the airways in susceptible patients with asthma or CF, driven by a Th2 response and IgE-mediated inflammation causing central bronchiectasis, mucus plugging, and recurrent pulmonary infiltrates.
keyFact: ABPA occurs in ~2% of asthma patients and ~10% of CF patients. High-attenuation mucus plugging on CT is highly specific. Key criteria: asthma, Aspergillus sensitization, total IgE >1000 IU/mL, elevated Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG, central bronchiectasis, eosinophilia. Treatment: systemic corticosteroids ± itraconazole.

wrongAnswers.name: Eosinophilic Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eosinophilic pneumonia causes peripheral eosinophilia and pulmonary infiltrates, but does not cause central bronchiectasis, markedly elevated IgE, or specific Aspergillus sensitization; it typically shows peripheral consolidation on CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HP can occur with fungal antigen exposure, but presents with restrictive physiology, centrilobular nodules and air trapping rather than central bronchiectasis, and does not involve IgE-mediated sensitization or eosinophilia.

wrongAnswers.name: Aspergilloma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aspergilloma is a fungal ball colonizing a pre-existing cavity and does not cause the immunologic criteria (elevated IgE, eosinophilia, Aspergillus-specific IgE) or central bronchiectasis that define ABPA.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of progressive dyspnea, dry cough, night sweats, and weight loss of 6 pounds.
She has no significant occupational exposures, no recent travel, no sick contacts, and does not smoke; she has a history of mild allergic rhinitis but no asthma; no new medications in the past year.
Temperature is 37.9 degrees Celsius; lung auscultation reveals crackles bilaterally in the upper and mid zones; no wheezing is noted; no lymphadenopathy.

CBC shows eosinophilia of 2,600 per microliter; ESR is 68 mm/hr; chest X-ray and CT show bilateral peripheral subpleural consolidations with upper and mid-lung predominance described as the photographic negative of pulmonary edema.

Bronchoalveolar lavage differential shows 42% eosinophils; transbronchial biopsy reveals eosinophilic infiltration of alveolar spaces and interstitium with no organisms identified; the peripheral consolidations are bilateral and upper-lobe predominant.
explanation: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia involves tissue eosinophilia with alveolar and interstitial eosinophilic infiltration, of unknown etiology, associated with atopy; the dramatic and rapid response to corticosteroids is characteristic and diagnostic.
keyFact: The 'photographic negative of pulmonary edema' (peripheral upper-lobe consolidations) on CXR is classic for CEP. BAL eosinophilia >25% is diagnostic. CEP has a dramatic response to steroids but a high relapse rate on tapering. It is distinct from acute eosinophilic pneumonia which is more severe and often requires ICU care.

wrongAnswers.name: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COP shows similar peripheral consolidations and responds to steroids, but BAL would not show >25% eosinophils; peripheral eosinophilia is not a feature of COP, and COP rarely shows upper-lobe predominance.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis can cause upper-zone opacities and night sweats, but BAL characteristically shows a CD4:CD8 lymphocyte elevation rather than eosinophilia; bilateral hilar adenopathy would be expected and non-caseating granulomas found on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EGPA features eosinophilia and pulmonary infiltrates but requires asthma history, ANCA positivity, and systemic vasculitic features (mononeuritis, purpura); this patient has none of these and no vasculitic features on biopsy.

clues: A 34-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath that began 2 hours ago while at rest.
She had a spontaneous left pneumothorax 18 months ago that was managed conservatively; she has no smoking history, no occupational exposures, and is not pregnant.
Breath sounds are decreased on the right; percussion is hyperresonant over the right hemithorax; no wheezing or crackles are noted; trachea is midline.

Chest X-ray confirms a right-sided pneumothorax; after chest tube placement, HRCT shows diffuse bilateral thin-walled cysts of uniform size distributed throughout all lung zones; bilateral renal masses with fat density are also noted.
Serum VEGF-D level is greater than 800 pg/mL in the setting of diffuse thin-walled pulmonary cysts, recurrent pneumothoraces, and bilateral fat-containing renal masses in a woman of reproductive age.
explanation: LAM is caused by somatic or germline mutations in TSC1/TSC2 genes leading to uncontrolled proliferation of smooth muscle-like LAM cells that infiltrate the lungs, lymphatics, and kidneys, causing cyst formation, pneumothorax, and chylous effusions.
keyFact: LAM exclusively affects women of reproductive age. Bilateral uniform thin-walled cysts on HRCT plus VEGF-D >800 pg/mL is diagnostic without biopsy. Recurrent pneumothoraces in a young woman should prompt consideration of LAM. Bilateral angiomyolipomas suggest tuberous sclerosis-associated LAM. Sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) slows progression.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSP explains the pneumothorax but does not account for the diffuse bilateral cysts on HRCT, elevated VEGF-D, and bilateral angiomyolipomas; recurrent pneumothoraces in a young woman require CT to evaluate for underlying cystic lung disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis
