wrongAnswers.whyNot: PLCH also causes cystic lung disease and pneumothorax in young patients, but is strongly associated with smoking, shows upper-lobe-predominant irregular nodules evolving to bizarrely shaped cysts, and does not cause angiomyolipomas or elevated VEGF-D.

wrongAnswers.name: Emphysema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Emphysema causes cystic/bullous changes on HRCT but is associated with smoking, shows upper-lobe predominance (centrilobular) or lower-lobe predominance (panacinar), and does not occur in young non-smoking women with angiomyolipomas.

clues: A 41-year-old man presents with an insidious 6-month history of progressive dyspnea on exertion and a dry cough; he feels well at rest but is increasingly limited by breathlessness.
He works as a sandblaster but notes his colleagues doing the same job are not experiencing similar symptoms; he smokes half a pack per day and has no fever, weight loss, or night sweats.
His oxygen saturation drops from 97% at rest to 88% with 6-minute walk; lung auscultation reveals no crackles; chest examination is otherwise unremarkable.

LDH is elevated at 380 IU/L; chest CT shows bilateral geographic ground-glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening in a pattern of superimposed ground-glass and reticular lines without consolidation or nodules.

Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid appears milky and opalescent; PAS staining reveals abundant acellular eosinophilic material filling the alveolar spaces; serum autoantibodies targeting GM-CSF are significantly elevated.
explanation: Autoimmune PAP is caused by anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies that block alveolar macrophage maturation, impairing surfactant clearance and leading to accumulation of surfactant-derived lipoprotein material in the alveolar spaces.
keyFact: Crazy paving pattern on HRCT (ground-glass + septal thickening) is the hallmark of PAP but is not specific. Milky BAL fluid with PAS-positive material is diagnostic. Anti-GM-CSF antibodies confirm autoimmune PAP (~90% of cases). Whole-lung lavage is the treatment of choice.

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumocystis Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PCP causes bilateral ground-glass opacities and can show crazy paving pattern, but requires immunosuppression (HIV, transplant); the milky BAL with PAS-positive acellular material and elevated anti-GM-CSF antibodies are specific to PAP.

wrongAnswers.name: Silicosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Silicosis from sandblasting can cause similar work exposure but presents with upper-lobe nodular opacities and progressive massive fibrosis, not crazy paving; BAL would not show acellular PAS-positive lipoprotein material.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HP can cause ground-glass opacities in workers with environmental exposures, but the crazy paving pattern, milky BAL fluid, and anti-GM-CSF antibodies specifically point to PAP rather than HP.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea and mild right-sided chest discomfort over 3 weeks following a recent thoracic surgical procedure.
He was discharged 3 weeks ago and has been eating normally since; he has lost 12 pounds since the operation and has noticed his clothes fitting loosely.
Decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right hemithorax from the mid-zone downward; no fever; mild tachycardia at 98 bpm.
Chest X-ray confirms a large right-sided pleural effusion; thoracentesis yields a milky white fluid with LDH 180 IU/L, protein 4.2 g/dL, pH 7.4, and a cell count that is predominantly lymphocytes.
Pleural fluid triglyceride level is 285 mg/dL with a cholesterol of 45 mg/dL; lipoprotein electrophoresis demonstrates chylomicrons in the pleural fluid.
explanation: Chylothorax results from disruption or obstruction of the thoracic duct or its tributaries, allowing chyle (lymph rich in dietary triglycerides and chylomicrons) to accumulate in the pleural space; it most commonly occurs following thoracic surgery or malignancy.
keyFact: Pleural fluid triglycerides >110 mg/dL strongly suggests chylothorax (>50 mg/dL possible, <50 mg/dL excludes it). Milky appearance is not specific — pseudochylothorax (cholesterol effusion) can also be milky. Chylomicrons on lipoprotein electrophoresis are definitive. Treatment: NPO/low-fat diet, octreotide, or thoracic duct ligation.

wrongAnswers.name: Empyema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Empyema causes a pleural effusion after thoracic surgery but fluid would be purulent with low pH, high LDH, and predominantly neutrophils; triglycerides would be normal and fluid would not be milky white.

wrongAnswers.name: Pseudochylothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pseudochylothorax also produces a milky effusion but is characterized by elevated cholesterol (>200 mg/dL), low triglycerides, and no chylomicrons; it is associated with longstanding effusions (TB, RA) rather than recent thoracic surgery.

wrongAnswers.name: Transudative Pleural Effusion from Heart Failure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Heart failure causes transudative effusions with low protein and LDH by Light's criteria; it does not produce milky fluid, elevated triglycerides, or chylomicrons.

clues: A 17-year-old female competitive swimmer presents with recurrent episodes of sudden-onset throat tightness, noisy breathing, and difficulty getting air in during intense exercise that resolve within minutes of stopping.

She has been treated for exercise-induced asthma for two years with no improvement despite escalating inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators; she has a history of significant academic stress and anxiety.

During a routine visit her lung examination is entirely normal; during a spontaneous episode, auscultation of the neck reveals inspiratory stridor loudest over the larynx, with clear lung fields bilaterally.
Spirometry between episodes is normal; a flow-volume loop obtained during a symptomatic episode shows truncation and flattening of the inspiratory limb with a preserved normal expiratory limb.
Direct laryngoscopy performed during a symptomatic episode reveals paradoxical adduction of both true vocal folds during inspiration with a posterior diamond-shaped glottic chink.
explanation: VCD results from paradoxical adduction of the vocal cords during inspiration (instead of abduction), causing episodic upper airway obstruction; it is often triggered by exercise, strong odors, or psychological stress and is frequently misdiagnosed as asthma.
keyFact: VCD is distinguished from asthma by: stridor (not wheezing), inspiratory flow loop truncation (not expiratory), no response to bronchodilators, normal spirometry between episodes, and laryngoscopic confirmation. It is overrepresented in young athletic females with anxiety. Treatment is speech therapy and breathing exercises.

wrongAnswers.name: Exercise-Induced Bronchoconstriction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EIB causes wheezing (expiratory) that responds to albuterol, with truncation of the expiratory flow-volume loop; stridor over the larynx, inspiratory truncation, and lack of bronchodilator response rule out EIB.

wrongAnswers.name: Anaphylaxis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anaphylaxis can cause acute throat tightness and stridor, but requires an allergen trigger, has systemic features (urticaria, hypotension, GI symptoms), and does not recur with exercise exclusively.

wrongAnswers.name: Tracheomalacia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tracheomalacia causes expiratory stridor and airway collapse that is positional rather than exercise-induced; flow-volume loops show expiratory flow limitation and laryngoscopy would show tracheal rather than glottic abnormality.

clues: A 72-year-old man with Parkinson's disease presents with a 3-week history of persistent cough, intermittent low-grade fever, and right-sided chest discomfort.
He has progressive dysphagia to solid foods and has had two episodes of aspiration pneumonia in the past year; he is on medications for Parkinson's disease.
Lung auscultation reveals decreased breath sounds in the right lower lobe with occasional coarse crackles; no stridor; he has mild resting tremor and cogwheel rigidity.

Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe collapse with a right pleural effusion; CT chest demonstrates post-obstructive pneumonia with complete obstruction of the right lower lobe bronchus but no discrete radiopaque density.
Flexible bronchoscopy reveals a solid organic object completely occluding the right lower lobe bronchus with surrounding granulation tissue and post-obstructive mucopurulent secretions.
explanation: Foreign body aspiration in adults most commonly involves food (nuts, meat) and tends to lodge in the right lower lobe bronchus due to its more vertical course; impaired swallowing (neurological disease, sedation, dental procedures) predisposes to aspiration, and post-obstructive pneumonia or atelectasis is the typical complication.
keyFact: In adults, aspirated foreign bodies most commonly lodge in the right lower lobe bronchus. The majority of aspirated food material is radiolucent; post-obstructive atelectasis or pneumonia on CT suggests the diagnosis even without a visible density. Flexible bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lung abscess can complicate foreign body aspiration and presents similarly, but would show a cavity with an air-fluid level rather than complete bronchial obstruction; bronchoscopy would not reveal a mechanical obstruction.

wrongAnswers.name: Endobronchial Malignancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Endobronchial tumor can cause post-obstructive pneumonia and bronchial obstruction on bronchoscopy, but the acute onset after a choking episode and the retrieval of a peanut fragment are pathognomonic for foreign body aspiration.

wrongAnswers.name: Mucus Plug
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mucus plugging causes lobar collapse and can appear as bronchial obstruction but would not be removable as a peanut fragment; bronchoscopy would show thick mucus rather than a solid food particle.

clues: A 62-year-old man with a long history of COPD presents with worsening dyspnea, a barking cough, and recurrent respiratory infections over the past 2 years despite optimized therapy.
He underwent a prolonged intubation for 18 days following cardiac surgery 3 years ago; he notes that his breathing difficulty worsens when bending forward or lying flat.
Biphasic stridor is audible without a stethoscope; auscultation over the trachea reveals inspiratory and expiratory stridor; wheezing is absent on peripheral lung auscultation.

Spirometry shows a sawtooth pattern on both inspiratory and expiratory limbs of the flow-volume loop; chest CT with expiratory phase images shows greater than 50% reduction in the tracheal cross-sectional area during expiration.
Dynamic bronchoscopy during forced exhalation demonstrates greater than 50% collapse of the posterior membranous tracheal wall with near-complete expiratory luminal narrowing.
explanation: Tracheomalacia results from weakening of the tracheal cartilaginous support or membranous posterior wall, causing dynamic airway collapse during expiration or coughing; it may be acquired after prolonged intubation, tracheostomy, or result from extrinsic compression.
keyFact: Acquired tracheomalacia is a common complication of prolonged intubation or tracheostomy. Expiratory CT showing >50% tracheal luminal narrowing is diagnostic. A sawtooth flow-volume loop pattern and barking cough are characteristic. Dynamic bronchoscopy is the gold standard. Severe cases may require tracheal stenting or tracheoplasty.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD Exacerbation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes expiratory airflow obstruction but does not produce central stridor, sawtooth flow-volume loops, or >50% tracheal collapse on expiratory CT; the post-intubation history and dynamic tracheal changes are not explained by COPD alone.

wrongAnswers.name: Vocal Cord Dysfunction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VCD produces inspiratory stridor and inspiratory flow-volume loop truncation from paradoxical vocal cord motion at the glottis; tracheomalacia affects the trachea below the cords and produces expiratory collapse seen on dynamic CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Goiter-related Tracheal Compression
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A compressive goiter can cause tracheal narrowing and stridor, but would show a fixed extrinsic compression on CT rather than dynamic collapse; the post-intubation history and >50% expiratory collapse indicate intrinsic tracheal wall weakness.

clues: A 48-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of fever, right-sided pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with thick greenish sputum, and fatigue that worsened after initial antibiotic treatment.
He has type 2 diabetes, drinks alcohol heavily, and is a current smoker; he was initially diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia 2 weeks ago and started on oral amoxicillin.
Temperature is 39.2 degrees Celsius; heart rate is 108 bpm; breath sounds are absent in the right lower lobe; percussion is dull over the right base.

Chest X-ray shows a right lower lobe opacity with a loculated right pleural effusion; CT chest shows loculated fluid collections with enhancing visceral and parietal pleural layers; WBC is 18,400 per microliter with 89% neutrophils.
Thoracentesis yields thick turbid yellow-green fluid with pH 7.12, glucose 32 mg/dL, and LDH 2,800 IU/L; Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
explanation: Empyema is a suppurative infection of the pleural space, most commonly complicating bacterial pneumonia; it progresses from exudative to fibrinopurulent to organized stages, requiring drainage in addition to antibiotics for effective treatment.
keyFact: Empyema criteria (Frank's criteria): pH <7.2, glucose <60 mg/dL, LDH >1000 IU/L, or positive Gram stain/culture — all mandate pleural drainage. Split pleura sign on CT (enhancing visceral and parietal pleura) suggests empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusion. Risk factors: pneumonia, aspiration, diabetes, alcoholism.

wrongAnswers.name: Simple Parapneumonic Effusion
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Uncomplicated parapneumonic effusions are free-flowing, have pH >7.2, glucose >60 mg/dL, and do not require drainage; the low pH, low glucose, high LDH, positive culture, and loculation indicate frank empyema.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lung abscess causes a localized cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level within the lung parenchyma, not a loculated pleural collection; the split pleura sign and pleural fluid analysis confirm a pleural rather than parenchymal abscess.

wrongAnswers.name: Malignant Pleural Effusion
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malignant effusions are typically exudative and may cause pleural thickening, but would not present with fever, purulent fluid, or the extremely low pH and glucose of a frank empyema.

answer: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lung
accept: squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
clues: A 67-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of persistent cough, hemoptysis on three occasions, and progressive shortness of breath.
He has a 55 pack-year smoking history and has lost 14 pounds over 3 months; he also mentions increased thirst, frequent urination, and constipation for the past 6 weeks.
Decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion in the right upper lobe; no lymphadenopathy or clubbing.

Chest CT shows a 4.5 cm centrally located right hilar mass with endobronchial extension and post-obstructive right upper lobe collapse; serum calcium is 12.6 mg/dL with suppressed PTH and elevated PTHrP.
Bronchoscopic biopsy of the endobronchial mass shows malignant cells with intercellular bridges and keratinization; immunostaining is positive for p40 and CK5/6 and negative for TTF-1.
explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma arises from bronchial epithelium in central airways, is strongly linked to smoking, and can cause hypercalcemia of malignancy via ectopic PTHrP secretion; it typically presents with endobronchial disease, hemoptysis, and obstructive atelectasis.
keyFact: SCC is the most common lung cancer to cause hypercalcemia via PTHrP (not bone metastases). It is central, strongly smoking-associated, and positive for p40/p63/CK5/6 while negative for TTF-1. It is the most common lung cancer to cavitate. Pancoast tumors are usually SCC.

wrongAnswers.name: Small Cell Lung Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCLC is also central and smoking-related, but causes different paraneoplastic syndromes (SIADH, Lambert-Eaton, ectopic ACTH); biopsy would show neuroendocrine histology (synaptophysin+) rather than squamous features (keratin pearls, p40+).

wrongAnswers.name: Carcinoid Tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoid can present as a central endobronchial lesion causing hemoptysis and obstructive pneumonia, but is not associated with heavy smoking or PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia; biopsy would show neuroendocrine cells without keratin pearls.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lung abscess can cause hemoptysis and upper lobe disease in smokers, but presents with fever, purulent sputum, and a cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level; biopsy would show necrotic tissue and organisms rather than malignant squamous cells.

clues: A 21-year-old man presents with a 10-day history of low-grade fever, persistent dry cough, headache, and sore throat.
Three of his dormitory roommates had a similar illness in the past 3 weeks; he has no significant medical history, no recent travel, and no sick animal contact.

Temperature is 37.9 degrees Celsius; oxygen saturation is 97% on room air; lung auscultation reveals diffuse crackles over the left lower lobe, but the patient appears comfortable and in no acute distress.

CBC shows a mildly elevated WBC with lymphocyte predominance; chest X-ray shows patchy interstitial infiltrates in the left lower lobe that appear much worse than the patient's clinical appearance would suggest; cold agglutinin titer is elevated at 1:64.
PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab is positive for M. pneumoniae with significantly elevated organism-specific IgM antibodies.
explanation: Atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae results from direct cytotoxic injury to respiratory epithelium and immune-mediated inflammation; it lacks the typical lobar consolidation of bacterial pneumonia and is characterized by a clinical-radiographic dissociation (imaging worse than the patient appears).
keyFact: Mycoplasma is the most common cause of atypical (walking) pneumonia in young adults. Radiographic-clinical dissociation (patient looks well despite bilateral infiltrates) is the classic finding. Cold agglutinins (IgM vs. RBC I antigen) are elevated in ~50%. Treatment: macrolides or tetracyclines (beta-lactams are ineffective — no cell wall).

wrongAnswers.name: Streptococcal Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: S. pneumoniae typically causes lobar consolidation with a productive rusty sputum, higher fever, and pleuritic chest pain; patients appear more acutely ill, CBC would show leukocytosis with neutrophilia, and Mycoplasma PCR would be negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Upper Respiratory Infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: URTI causes similar prodromal symptoms but does not produce audible crackles, significant chest X-ray infiltrates, or elevated cold agglutinin titers; positive Mycoplasma PCR confirms a specific bacterial etiology.

wrongAnswers.name: COVID-19 Pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COVID-19 pneumonia can cause bilateral interstitial infiltrates and a mildly symptomatic presentation in young adults, but SARS-CoV-2 PCR/antigen would be positive rather than Mycoplasma PCR; COVID-19 typically shows bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities on CT rather than unilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fever, productive cough with copious foul-smelling sputum, and right-sided chest pain with weight loss.
He has a history of alcohol dependence and was found unresponsive 4 weeks ago after a suspected aspiration event; he has poor dentition with several decayed teeth.
Temperature is 38.8 degrees Celsius; heart rate is 102 bpm; dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds in the right lower lobe; there is a pronounced fetid odor to his breath.

WBC is 22,000 per microliter with 87% neutrophils; CRP is 180 mg/L; chest X-ray shows a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level in the posterior segment of the right lower lobe; sputum Gram stain reveals mixed flora.

CT chest shows a 5 cm thick-walled cavitary lesion in the right lower lobe posterior segment with surrounding consolidation and an air-fluid level; anaerobic cultures from protected specimen brush grow Fusobacterium nucleatum and Peptostreptococcus species.
explanation: Lung abscess from aspiration results from aspiration of anaerobic oral flora, typically in dependent lung segments (right lower lobe posterior segment when supine), causing necrotizing pneumonia that liquefies and cavitates; risk factors include impaired consciousness, poor dentition, and dysphagia.
keyFact: Aspiration lung abscess classically involves the posterior segment of the right lower lobe or posterior segment of the right upper lobe (gravity-dependent when supine). Anaerobes from oral flora are the primary pathogens. Foul-smelling sputum is a hallmark. Distinguish from empyema (pleural vs. parenchymal) and malignant cavitation (irregular walls, no fever).

wrongAnswers.name: Empyema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Empyema is a pleural space infection showing fluid within the pleural cavity; CT here shows a parenchymal cavity with an air-fluid level surrounded by lung consolidation, not a pleural collection; the split pleura sign of empyema is absent.

wrongAnswers.name: Cavitary Lung Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lung cancer can cavitate and present with weight loss and cough, but typically shows irregular thin or thick walls without surrounding acute consolidation; the acute infectious presentation, fever, leukocytosis, and anaerobic culture results support abscess over malignancy.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB causes upper-lobe cavitary disease and can present with similar systemic symptoms, but AFB stain and culture would be positive and the history of aspiration with poor dentition, dependent location, and anaerobic organisms favor aspiration lung abscess.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with episodes of chest tightness and shortness of breath that have been worsening over the past 8 months, along with nasal congestion.
He works as a baker and notes his symptoms are significantly worse on workdays and improve on weekends and during vacations.
Between episodes, lung exam is normal; during a visit following a work shift, mild end-expiratory wheezing is heard bilaterally; no clubbing or cyanosis.

Serial peak expiratory flow measurements over 3 weeks show consistently decreased PEFR on workdays with recovery on days off and greater than 20% diurnal variability on work days; spirometry post-shift shows a 15% improvement in FEV1 after bronchodilator.
Specific inhalation challenge testing with wheat flour extract under controlled conditions reproduces symptoms and shows a dual early and late asthmatic response with greater than 20% fall in FEV1.
explanation: Occupational asthma is caused by workplace sensitization to high-molecular-weight allergens (such as flour proteins in bakers) or low-molecular-weight chemical sensitizers, leading to IgE-mediated (high-MW) or non-IgE-mediated airway inflammation and bronchospasm.
keyFact: Baker's asthma (wheat/rye flour sensitization) is one of the most common occupational asthma types. Key diagnostic criteria: work-related symptom pattern, serial PEFR variability (>20% on workdays), and specific inhalation challenge (gold standard). Early removal from exposure is critical — delayed diagnosis leads to persistent asthma.

wrongAnswers.name: Exercise-Induced Bronchoconstriction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EIB is triggered by exercise rather than specific workplace exposures; PEFR would not consistently drop only on workdays, and specific inhalation challenge to flour would not be positive in EIB.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HP can also show work-related symptoms from organic dust exposure, but presents with flu-like systemic symptoms (fever, myalgia), restrictive rather than obstructive physiology, and centrilobular nodules on HRCT rather than reversible airflow obstruction.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD causes fixed or partially reversible airflow obstruction in older smokers and does not show work-related symptom variability, a positive specific inhalation challenge, or dramatic improvement with bronchodilators in a 38-year-old non-smoker.

answer: Major Depressive Disorder with Atypical Features
clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with 4 months of low energy, excessive sleeping, and gaining 15 pounds.

She reports her mood noticeably improves when she receives good news or spends time with friends, but crashes again afterward; she also describes a pattern of intense emotional pain in response to perceived interpersonal rejection.
Psychomotor slowing is noted with prolonged response latency; her affect becomes notably brighter when discussing positive topics; no psychotic features are elicited on mental status examination.
TSH and complete metabolic panel are normal; PHQ-9 score is 18 with prominent hypersomnia and increased appetite endorsed.

Structured interview reveals sustained mood reactivity to positive events, leaden paralysis, interpersonal rejection sensitivity, hypersomnia, and hyperphagia persisting for more than 2 weeks with significant functional impairment.
explanation: Atypical depression involves dysregulation of mood reactivity, with preserved ability to experience pleasure in response to positive events.
keyFact: Mood reactivity is the hallmark feature required for the atypical specifier. MAOIs historically show superior efficacy over TCAs for this subtype.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal TSH rules this out and mood reactivity is not a feature of hypothyroidism.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar II Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No history of hypomanic episodes is present.

wrongAnswers.name: Persistent Depressive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dysthymia involves chronic low-level depression for 2+ years; this presentation is 4 months with moderate-severe severity.

clues: A 24-year-old man is brought to the ED by his roommate because of increasingly erratic and grandiose behavior over the past several days.
His roommate says this started abruptly about a week ago after months of being notably withdrawn and sleeping excessively; the patient has not slept more than 2 hours per night all week.
He speaks rapidly without pause, jumps between unrelated topics, and becomes irritable when interrupted; he is oriented and denies any drug use.
Urine drug screen is negative; serum glucose, electrolytes, and TSH are normal; brain MRI is unremarkable.

Collateral history reveals a prior 3-month depressive episode; the current episode of grandiosity, pressured speech, decreased need for sleep, and flight of ideas has persisted for greater than 7 days with marked functional impairment and no substance use.
explanation: Bipolar I disorder requires at least one lifetime manic episode, which by definition causes marked functional impairment or requires hospitalization.
keyFact: A manic episode must last at least 7 days. Unlike Bipolar II, a depressive episode is NOT required for Bipolar I diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Substance-Induced Mood Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Negative urine drug screen and absence of substance use history make this unlikely.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prominent mood episode is the primary feature; schizophrenia requires psychotic symptoms in the absence of mood episodes.

wrongAnswers.name: ADHD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ADHD does not cause episodic decreased need for sleep or abrupt onset after a depressive period.

clues: A 32-year-old woman presents after her third antidepressant was discontinued because she became agitated and overly energized on each one within weeks of starting.

On further questioning, she describes several distinct stretches of 4 to 5 days where she felt unusually productive, needed only 4 hours of sleep, and started multiple new projects; she never required hospitalization during these periods.
She is currently euthymic; mental status exam is unremarkable; she denies any periods of reckless spending, psychosis, or behavior causing serious consequences.
PHQ-9 today is 6; no manic-level impairment has ever been documented.

Structured interview identifies distinct 4-to-5-day periods of elevated mood, decreased sleep need, and increased goal-directed activity without psychosis or hospitalization, alternating with documented major depressive episodes.
explanation: Bipolar II is characterized by recurrent depressive episodes and at least one hypomanic episode.
keyFact: Bipolar II is often misdiagnosed as MDD. Antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate a hypomanic or manic switch.

wrongAnswers.name: Major Depressive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The history of hypomanic episodes rules out unipolar MDD.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar I Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No manic episode with marked impairment or hospitalization occurred.

wrongAnswers.name: Cyclothymic Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: This patient has full major depressive episodes, ruling out cyclothymia.

clues: A 30-year-old man is brought to the psychiatric emergency department after neighbors called police because he was shouting that his building's water was poisoned.
His mother reports he has had at least two prior hospitalizations and that he hears voices and holds paranoid beliefs even during periods when his mood appears stable.
He has a blunted affect, is guarded, and endorses auditory hallucinations telling him the water is contaminated even now when his mood is at baseline.
Urine toxicology is negative; symptom timeline review with family reveals psychotic symptoms present for at least 2 weeks in the absence of any mood episode.
Longitudinal review shows concurrent mood episodes present for the majority of total illness duration alongside persistent psychotic symptoms that continue between mood episodes.
explanation: Schizoaffective disorder requires concurrent mood and psychotic symptoms, with psychosis persisting for at least 2 weeks independent of mood episodes.
keyFact: In schizoaffective disorder, mood episodes are present for the majority of the total illness duration; in schizophrenia, mood episodes are brief relative to the psychotic illness.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia would not have prominent mood episodes constituting the majority of illness duration.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar I with Psychotic Features
wrongAnswers.whyNot: In bipolar I with psychosis, psychotic symptoms occur only during mood episodes; here psychosis persists outside of mood episodes.

wrongAnswers.name: Substance-Induced Psychosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Negative toxicology and longitudinal illness course make substance induction implausible.

clues: A 22-year-old woman with no psychiatric history is brought to the ED by family because she has been confused, disorganized, and claiming to communicate with a deceased relative.
Family reports she began hearing her deceased mother's voice guiding her and believes her mother is living inside the television; the mother died unexpectedly just days ago.
She is disorganized, tearful, and intermittently responds to internal stimuli; her behavior was entirely normal prior to her mother's death.
Urine drug screen is negative; metabolic panel and head CT are unremarkable; symptoms began acutely within 24 hours of the bereavement.
All psychotic symptoms fully resolve within 10 days with supportive care; no prior psychotic, manic, or depressive episodes are identified on comprehensive review.
explanation: Brief psychotic disorder involves sudden onset of psychotic symptoms lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to premorbid functioning.
keyFact: Brief psychotic disorder resolves within 1 month by definition. Duration distinguishes it from schizophreniform (1-6 months) and schizophrenia (6+ months).

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Grief Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal grief does not include frank hallucinations or disorganized behavior.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophreniform Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophreniform requires symptoms lasting 1-6 months; this case resolves within 10 days.

wrongAnswers.name: Substance-Induced Psychosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Negative drug screen and clear temporal relationship to stressor rule out substance etiology.

clues: A 55-year-old man is referred by his attorney after multiple complaints to law enforcement about a neighbor he believes is targeting him.
He has held this belief with absolute certainty for 3 years; he remains employed as an accountant and maintains his daily routines without difficulty.
He is well-groomed, speaks coherently, and demonstrates logical reasoning on all topics except the neighbor; he has no hallucinations or disorganized thought.
Neuropsychological testing is within normal limits; MRI brain is unremarkable; no depressive or manic symptoms are identified.
A single fixed belief about the neighbor's surveillance activities has persisted for over 1 month with no hallucinations, disorganization, negative symptoms, or decline in global functioning.
explanation: Delusional disorder involves one or more fixed delusions lasting at least 1 month without the other characteristic symptoms of schizophrenia.
keyFact: Delusional disorder subtypes: persecutory (most common), erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, somatic.

wrongAnswers.name: Paranoid Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Paranoid PD involves pervasive distrust without fixed delusions; this patient has a specific fixed delusion.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia requires prominent hallucinations or disorganization and significant functional impairment.

wrongAnswers.name: OCD with Poor Insight
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OCD involves ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts; this patient's belief is ego-syntonic.

clues: A 34-year-old man presents to cardiology after multiple emergency department visits for recurrent episodes of acute distress lasting 10 to 20 minutes with palpitations, chest tightness, and a sense of impending doom.
He has started avoiding driving on highways and crowded shopping malls because several episodes occurred in those places; he worries constantly about having another episode.
Between episodes he is in no distress; heart rate and blood pressure are normal; he is persistently anxious about recurrence.
Holter monitor, echocardiogram, thyroid function tests, and basic metabolic panel are all within normal limits.

Structured psychiatric interview identifies recurrent unexpected episodes with at least one month of persistent concern about future attacks and maladaptive avoidance behavior in the absence of another medical or psychiatric explanation.
explanation: Panic disorder involves recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by at least one month of persistent concern about additional attacks or maladaptive behavioral change.
keyFact: Panic disorder patients are high utilizers of emergency and cardiology services. SSRIs are first-line; CBT with interoceptive exposure is highly effective.

wrongAnswers.name: Arrhythmia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal Holter monitor and echocardiogram make cardiac arrhythmia unlikely.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperthyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal TSH rules out thyrotoxicosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Social Anxiety Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Social anxiety involves fear tied to social scrutiny; this patient's attacks are unexpected and occur in non-social contexts.

clues: A 40-year-old woman presents with a year of frequent headaches, poor sleep, muscle tension, and difficulty concentrating at work.
She worries excessively about her children's safety, job performance, finances, and her own health, finding it nearly impossible to control the worry.
She is visibly tense with furrowed brow; palpation reveals increased tone in the trapezius and neck muscles; resting heart rate is mildly elevated at 92 bpm.
Complete metabolic panel, CBC, and TSH are normal; GAD-7 score is 16; no depressive symptoms dominate the clinical picture.

Excessive worry across multiple life domains has been present more days than not for over 6 months with associated muscle tension, irritability, and sleep disturbance causing significant occupational impairment.
explanation: GAD involves persistent, excessive, and difficult-to-control worry across multiple life domains lasting at least 6 months.
keyFact: GAD must involve worry across multiple domains. It is highly comorbid with MDD. First-line: SSRIs/SNRIs and CBT.

wrongAnswers.name: Major Depressive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No depressed mood, anhedonia, or neurovegetative symptoms dominate here.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperthyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal TSH rules out thyroid etiology.

wrongAnswers.name: Somatic Symptom Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SSD centers on physical symptoms; this patient's distress is about life-domain worries.

clues: A 26-year-old man is referred by his employer after declining new responsibilities and avoiding certain workplace tasks.
He reports avoiding work meetings, eating alone to avoid the cafeteria, and turning down social invitations for years due to fear of being negatively judged.
He is cooperative and articulate in the one-on-one interview; he describes significant anticipatory anxiety before any situation where others might evaluate him.
PHQ-9 is 5; SPIN score is 38; no agoraphobia or unexpected panic attacks are reported.
A persistent pattern of avoidance of social and performance situations driven specifically by fear of negative evaluation is documented over multiple years with significant occupational impairment.
explanation: Social anxiety disorder involves intense, persistent fear of social or performance situations driven by fear of humiliation or negative evaluation.
keyFact: The 'performance only' specifier applies when fear is restricted to public speaking. First-line: SSRIs + CBT. Beta-blockers for performance-only subtype.

wrongAnswers.name: Avoidant Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AvPD involves a more pervasive pattern across all relationships; social anxiety disorder can be more circumscribed.

wrongAnswers.name: Agoraphobia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Agoraphobia involves fear of situations where escape is difficult; this patient's fear is about negative evaluation.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizoid Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizoid PD involves indifference to relationships; this patient desires connection but avoids due to fear.

clues: A 19-year-old pre-nursing student is referred after three syncopal episodes in the past year, the most recent causing her to miss several weeks of class.
She has fainted three times in her life, each time when exposed to blood or needles, and has avoided medical procedures for as long as she can remember.
When shown an image of a needle in session, she becomes pale and diaphoretic; her heart rate drops from 80 to 52 bpm.
ECG shows no conduction abnormalities; Holter monitor is normal; tilt-table testing is unremarkable; episodes are entirely triggered by a specific stimulus.

Marked immediate fear and a biphasic cardiovascular response occur exclusively upon exposure to blood, injection, or injury stimuli, persisting for more than 6 months and causing occupational avoidance.
explanation: Blood-injection-injury phobia uniquely triggers a vasovagal response: initial sympathetic activation followed by parasympathetic rebound causing bradycardia and syncope.
keyFact: BII phobia is the only specific phobia with a vasovagal response causing fainting. Treatment: applied tension technique.

wrongAnswers.name: Vasovagal Syncope
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal tilt-table test and strictly stimulus-specific episodes indicate psychological rather than structural etiology.

wrongAnswers.name: Panic Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Panic disorder involves unexpected panic attacks; this response is exclusively cued by blood/needle stimuli.

wrongAnswers.name: PTSD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No identifiable traumatic exposure meeting Criterion A.

clues: A 17-year-old boy is brought in by his parents because he has been late to school every day for 3 months due to time-consuming morning routines he cannot explain.
He confides he must check that the faucet is fully off exactly 12 times in sequence, and if interrupted he must restart; he finds these rituals senseless but cannot stop.
His hands are dry and cracked; he appears distressed and embarrassed; he denies depressed mood and does not endorse hallucinations.
CY-BOCS score is 28; streptococcal titers are normal; brain MRI is unremarkable.
Intrusive thoughts about contamination that the patient recognizes as irrational drive repetitive checking rituals consuming more than 3 hours daily with significant academic and social impairment.
explanation: OCD involves recurrent, intrusive, ego-dystonic obsessions that drive repetitive compulsive behaviors aimed at reducing anxiety.
keyFact: OCD compulsions are ego-dystonic. First-line: SSRIs + ERP. PANDAS is considered when onset is acute and strep-associated.

wrongAnswers.name: PANDAS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal ASO titers and gradual onset over 3 months make PANDAS unlikely.

wrongAnswers.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD rituals are ego-syntonic; OCD rituals are ego-dystonic.

wrongAnswers.name: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OCPD involves ego-syntonic perfectionism; OCD involves ego-dystonic obsessions and compulsions.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with 6 months of insomnia, recurrent disturbing dreams, and progressive emotional withdrawal from his wife and children.
He returned from military deployment 8 months ago and was involved in a blast injury that killed two members of his unit; he avoids news coverage of the military.
He appears hypervigilant, startles easily at sounds in the hallway, has a constricted affect, and reports recurrent intrusive images of the blast.
PCL-5 score is 52; toxicology is negative; no psychotic symptoms are elicited.

CAPS-5 interview documents intrusion symptoms including flashbacks and nightmares, avoidance of trauma-related stimuli, negative cognitions with emotional numbing, and hyperarousal with exaggerated startle persisting for greater than 1 month following a life-threatening traumatic event.
explanation: PTSD involves a maladaptive stress response following traumatic exposure, characterized by dysregulation of fear extinction via hippocampal-amygdala-prefrontal circuits.
keyFact: PTSD requires all four symptom clusters: intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, hyperarousal. First-line: sertraline or paroxetine. Prazosin for nightmares.

wrongAnswers.name: Adjustment Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adjustment disorder does not include intrusion symptoms or the full four-cluster profile.

wrongAnswers.name: Major Depressive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The intrusion symptoms and hyperarousal tied to a specific traumatic event define PTSD over MDD.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Stress Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute stress disorder resolves within one month; this patient has had symptoms for 6 months.

clues: A 29-year-old woman presents saying she has felt strange and unlike herself for several days and is having trouble focusing at work.
She describes repeated intrusive images of her attacker's face, avoids parking garages, and is unable to sleep due to nightmares; she was assaulted less than a week ago.
She appears dazed, describes watching herself from outside her body, and has difficulty maintaining a linear narrative of events.
No prior psychiatric history; urine drug screen and metabolic panel are normal; head CT is unremarkable.

Intrusive images, avoidance of assault-related locations, depersonalization, dissociative amnesia for portions of the event, and hyperarousal are all present within days of the assault, persisting for 5 days but less than 1 month.
explanation: Acute stress disorder shares symptom clusters with PTSD but is defined by duration of 3 days to 1 month and includes prominent dissociative symptoms.
keyFact: ASD requires dissociative symptoms, which are not required for PTSD. Duration: 3 days to 1 month. ~50% of ASD cases progress to PTSD.

wrongAnswers.name: PTSD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PTSD requires symptom duration of more than 1 month; this patient is only 5 days post-trauma.

wrongAnswers.name: Adjustment Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adjustment disorder does not include dissociative symptoms or the full intrusion/avoidance/arousal cluster.

wrongAnswers.name: Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DPDR involves chronic depersonalization not linked to a specific traumatic event.

clues: A 45-year-old man is referred by his employer after three weeks of poor work performance, frequent absences, and tearfulness.
He reports low mood and poor concentration clearly tied to being passed over for a promotion; he has no prior psychiatric history.
He is tearful when discussing the promotion but brightens when discussing his family; he denies suicidal ideation, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, appetite change, or psychomotor retardation.
PHQ-9 score is 9; GAD-7 is 6; thyroid function and CBC are normal.

Emotional and behavioral symptoms developed within three months of the identifiable stressor, with distress out of proportion to the event and functional impairment, but without meeting full criteria for a major depressive or anxiety disorder.
explanation: Adjustment disorder is a stress-related condition where symptoms emerge in response to an identifiable stressor, exceeding what would be expected but not meeting criteria for a more specific disorder.
keyFact: Adjustment disorder is a diagnosis of exclusion. It resolves within 6 months of stressor termination. Most common psychiatric diagnosis in medically ill patients.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Stress Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute stress disorder requires a Criterion A traumatic event (life-threatening), not a career setback; dissociative symptoms would also be expected.

wrongAnswers.name: Normal Disappointment
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The degree of functional impairment is out of proportion, meeting adjustment disorder threshold.

wrongAnswers.name: Persistent Depressive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dysthymia requires 2+ years; this is 3 weeks following a discrete stressor.

clues: A 42-year-old woman presents to her fifth physician this year with persistent lower back pain, intermittent nausea, and fatigue that have not been adequately explained.
She carries multiple diagnoses from different providers, spends hours daily reading about her symptoms online, and has missed 40 days of work this year.
She is distressed and tearful; she reports symptoms are the central focus of her life and feels her doctors do not take her seriously.
Extensive labs, MRI, endoscopy, and rheumatologic panel are unremarkable or show only minor nonspecific findings.
Structured assessment reveals disproportionate and persistent thoughts about symptom severity, high health-related anxiety, and excessive time and energy devoted to symptoms for more than 6 months.
explanation: Somatic symptom disorder involves distressing somatic symptoms accompanied by abnormal thoughts, feelings, and behaviors related to those symptoms.
keyFact: SSD does NOT require medically unexplained symptoms. A patient with a real medical condition can still have SSD if the psychological response is disproportionate.

wrongAnswers.name: Illness Anxiety Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IAD involves minimal somatic symptoms; SSD is characterized by prominent, distressing somatic symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Fibromyalgia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The key here is the disproportionate psychological response that defines SSD beyond any medical diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Factitious Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Factitious disorder requires intentional feigning; SSD symptoms are genuinely experienced.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with persistent worry about his health and requests additional testing despite multiple recent evaluations with normal results.

Over the past 3 years he has been convinced at various times that he had brain cancer, ALS, and multiple sclerosis; each normal workup provides only brief reassurance before a new health fear emerges.
He is anxious and repeatedly checks the back of his neck; he denies significant physical symptoms currently but states the absence of symptoms does not mean anything.
PHQ-9 is 7; GAD-7 is 11; a validated illness anxiety inventory score is markedly elevated.
Preoccupation with having a serious illness has persisted for more than 6 months despite repeated negative workups, with high health-related anxiety in the absence of significant somatic symptoms.
explanation: Illness anxiety disorder involves excessive preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness, driven by high health anxiety.
keyFact: IAD is distinguished from SSD by minimal somatic symptoms. Two subtypes: care-seeking and care-avoidant.

wrongAnswers.name: Somatic Symptom Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SSD requires prominent somatic symptoms; this patient's distress centers on fear of disease with minimal actual symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: GAD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GAD involves worry across multiple life domains; here worry is exclusively focused on health.

wrongAnswers.name: OCD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The pattern of reassurance-seeking without ego-dystonic compulsions better fits IAD.

clues: A 33-year-old woman is admitted after sudden onset of left arm paralysis without pain, trauma, or sensory changes.
She has no prior neurological history and appears notably unconcerned about her inability to move the limb.
When asked to lift her left arm she cannot, but when distracted and asked to push down her right leg against resistance, involuntary hip extension occurs on the paralyzed side.
Brain MRI is normal; EEG is unremarkable; nerve conduction studies show no peripheral nerve or motor neuron pathology.
Positive Hoover sign demonstrates incompatibility between the reported weakness and voluntary motor pathways.
explanation: Conversion disorder involves neurological symptoms that are incompatible with recognized neurological disease.
keyFact: DSM-5 requires a positive clinical sign of incompatibility (e.g., Hoover sign, tremor entrainment) rather than diagnosis by exclusion.

wrongAnswers.name: Stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal brain MRI makes stroke extremely unlikely.

wrongAnswers.name: Malingering
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malingering involves conscious simulation; conversion disorder symptoms are not consciously produced.

wrongAnswers.name: Peripheral Nerve Injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Normal nerve conduction studies rule out peripheral nerve injury.

clues: A 27-year-old woman is referred after coworkers report intermittent episodes of markedly altered behavior with significant memory gaps she cannot explain.
She frequently finds clothing she does not remember buying, wakes up in unexplained places, and receives messages referencing conversations she has no recall of.
During the interview her voice pitch and posture change abruptly and she introduces herself by a different name, denying knowledge of initial interview questions.
EEG is normal; brain MRI is unremarkable; toxicology is negative; structured psychiatric evaluation reveals no primary psychotic, mood, or substance-induced disorder.
Structured interview reveals two or more distinct personality states with recurrent amnesia between states causing significant functional impairment.
explanation: DID involves disruption of identity characterized by two or more distinct personality states and recurrent amnesia between states.
keyFact: DID is highly associated with severe childhood abuse. DSM-5 no longer requires amnesia to be reported by the patient — it can be observed by others.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia does not involve shifts in identity or amnesia.

wrongAnswers.name: Borderline Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BPD involves identity disturbance but not discrete alternate identity states with amnesia.

wrongAnswers.name: Complex PTSD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: C-PTSD does not involve distinct personality states with inter-state amnesia.

clues: A 21-year-old male college student reports four months of persistent perceptual disturbances and emotional detachment causing academic difficulties.
The sensation began after heavy cannabis use, persists despite cessation, and he finds it profoundly distressing.
He is alert, oriented, and coherent; he describes watching his hands move as if they belong to someone else; reality testing is fully intact.
Urine drug screen is negative; EEG is normal; brain MRI is unremarkable; no depressive, manic, or psychotic episodes are identified.
Symptoms persist unchanged for four months despite confirmed cannabis cessation, with no alteration in consciousness or perceptual distortion of external objects.
explanation: DPDR involves persistent experiences of detachment from one's mind/body or surroundings with preserved reality testing.
keyFact: Reality testing is INTACT in DPDR, distinguishing it from psychosis. Cannabis use is a common precipitant.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia involves a break from reality testing; DPDR patients retain insight.

wrongAnswers.name: Substance-Induced Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Symptoms persist after confirmed cannabis cessation.

wrongAnswers.name: Panic Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Derealization in panic disorder occurs in discrete episodes; this patient has persistent, continuous symptoms.

clues: A 16-year-old girl is brought in by her parents after noticeable weight loss over five months; she appears fatigued and has become increasingly socially withdrawn.
She insists she is overweight and needs to lose more weight; she has stopped menstruating and becomes angry when her weight loss is raised as a concern.
BMI is 15.2; she is bradycardic at 48 bpm; she has lanugo on her forearms and cold, mottled hands.
CBC shows mild leukopenia; metabolic panel reveals hypokalemia and low phosphate; ECG shows prolonged QTc; DEXA shows osteopenia.
Despite a BMI of 15.2, she insists she looks overweight when shown her reflection and refuses caloric supplementation.
explanation: Anorexia nervosa involves persistent restriction of energy intake, intense fear of weight gain, and disturbed body image.
keyFact: AN has the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric disorder. Refeeding syndrome must be monitored. Amenorrhea is no longer required for DSM-5 diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Bulimia Nervosa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bulimia involves binge-purge cycles with normal weight; this patient has significantly low BMI with restriction.

wrongAnswers.name: Major Depressive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDD can cause weight loss but does not involve distorted body image or ego-syntonic restriction.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperthyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyperthyroidism causes tachycardia, not the bradycardia seen here.

clues: A 20-year-old college woman presents with chronic sore throat, dental complaints, and irregular periods over the past year.
She discloses episodes of consuming very large amounts of food followed by self-induced vomiting at least twice per week; her weight is within normal range.
Dental enamel erosion is present on the lingual surface of her upper teeth; calluses are visible on the dorsum of her right hand; bilateral parotid glands are enlarged.
Metabolic panel shows hypokalemia and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; amylase is mildly elevated; ECG shows T-wave flattening.
She rates her self-worth almost entirely on the number on the scale, despite maintaining a BMI of 22.
explanation: Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent binge-purge cycles driven by overvaluation of shape and weight.
keyFact: Russell's sign, parotid hypertrophy, and dental enamel erosion are classic. Hypokalemia and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis result from vomiting HCl.

wrongAnswers.name: Anorexia Nervosa Binge-Purge Type
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AN binge-purge type requires significantly low body weight; this patient is at normal weight.

wrongAnswers.name: Binge Eating Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BED involves binge eating without compensatory purging.

wrongAnswers.name: GERD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GERD could explain enamel erosion but not parotid hypertrophy, Russell's sign, and the electrolyte pattern.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents requesting help with his eating habits, reporting he has gained 40 pounds over two years and feels out of control around food.
He describes recurring episodes of eating large amounts very quickly, well past fullness, often alone due to embarrassment, followed by disgust and guilt, but he does not vomit or use laxatives.
BMI is 34; blood pressure is 138/88; no calluses on the hands, no parotid enlargement, and no signs of purging behavior.
Fasting glucose is 108; lipid panel shows elevated triglycerides; metabolic panel is otherwise normal with no electrolyte abnormalities.
He has gained weight steadily because the episodes are never followed by vomiting, laxative use, fasting, or excessive exercise.
explanation: Binge eating disorder is characterized by recurrent binge episodes with marked distress but without compensatory purging behaviors.
keyFact: BED is the most common eating disorder. Unlike bulimia, there are NO compensatory behaviors. Lisdexamfetamine is FDA-approved for BED.

wrongAnswers.name: Bulimia Nervosa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bulimia requires recurrent compensatory behaviors; this patient has none.

wrongAnswers.name: Obesity without Eating Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The recurrent discrete binge episodes with loss of control and distress meet formal BED criteria.

wrongAnswers.name: Night Eating Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Night eating syndrome involves eating after awakening from sleep, not discrete binge episodes throughout the day.

clues: A 35-year-old female attorney presents after her supervisor placed her on a performance improvement plan for repeatedly missing deadlines and losing important documents.
She reports these problems have been lifelong; she barely graduated college and was always described as bright but disorganized.
During the interview she interrupts frequently, loses track of her own sentences, and her desk is visibly chaotic; she is energetic and engaged, not dysthymic.
PHQ-9 is 4; GAD-7 is 5; neuropsychological testing reveals significant deficits in sustained attention and working memory with preserved IQ; childhood report cards note not reaching potential.
Childhood report cards from three separate schools consistently note difficulty sustaining attention in class with unfinished assignments, dating back to first grade.
explanation: Adult ADHD predominantly inattentive type involves persistent deficits in executive function, sustained attention, and working memory.
keyFact: Adult ADHD often presents without hyperactivity. DSM-5 requires onset before age 12. First-line: stimulants. Non-stimulant alternatives: atomoxetine, bupropion.

wrongAnswers.name: Major Depressive Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDD involves depressed mood/anhedonia; deficits here are lifelong, not episodic.

wrongAnswers.name: GAD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GAD-7 is low and symptoms predate any anxious period.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar II Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bipolar II involves episodic mood changes; ADHD is persistent and non-episodic.

clues: A 28-year-old man is referred after a relationship ended due to interpersonal difficulties; he reports a lifelong pattern of struggling with social cues.
He describes always preferring routines, becoming distressed when plans change, and having an extensive specialized interest in railway timetables that occupies most evenings.
He maintains minimal eye contact, speaks in a formal monotone, does not modulate facial expression, and appears unaware of conversational turn-taking cues.
ADOS-2 reveals deficits in social-emotional reciprocity and nonverbal communication; IQ testing shows above-average intelligence with a significant verbal-performance split.
Home videos from age 2 show repetitive hand-flapping and no pointing or joint attention behaviors during play.
explanation: ASD involves persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, plus restricted/repetitive behaviors, present from early development.
keyFact: ASD diagnosis in adults requires retrospective evidence of early developmental onset. DSM-5 collapsed Asperger's into one spectrum. No FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for core symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizoid Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizoid PD lacks the restricted/repetitive behaviors and special interests of ASD.

wrongAnswers.name: Social Anxiety Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Social anxiety involves fear of negative evaluation; this patient has fundamental deficits in social reciprocity.

wrongAnswers.name: ADHD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ADHD lacks the specific pattern of social reciprocity deficits and rigid routines defining ASD.

clues: A 24-year-old woman presents to the ED after a self-inflicted injury; this is her fourth visit this year, each following an interpersonal conflict.
She describes her boyfriend as perfect last week but now the worst person alive; she reports chronic emptiness, unstable relationships, and impulsive spending.
She is alternately tearful and hostile; she describes dissociative episodes under stress and an unstable sense of who she is.
Mood charting reveals rapid mood shifts lasting hours, not days; no manic or hypomanic episodes are identified; suicide risk assessment indicates moderate-risk chronic suicidality.
She has had 15 romantic relationships in 4 years, impulsively overdrew her bank account last week, and describes feeling like a completely different person day to day.
explanation: BPD involves pervasive instability in affect, self-image, and interpersonal relationships driven by fear of abandonment and emotional dysregulation.
keyFact: BPD mood shifts last hours (not days), distinguishing from bipolar. First-line: DBT. ~10% lifetime completed suicide risk.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar II Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bipolar mood episodes last days to weeks; BPD mood shifts last hours and are reactive to interpersonal events.

wrongAnswers.name: Histrionic Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HPD lacks the self-harm, abandonment fears, and identity disturbance seen in BPD.

wrongAnswers.name: PTSD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The pervasive personality pattern of identity instability and unstable relationships defines BPD beyond trauma-linked symptoms.

clues: A 32-year-old man is referred by his primary care physician after his partner expressed concern about a pattern of impulsive, reckless behavior and apparent lack of conscience since adolescence.
Medical records show two prior incarcerations for fraud, multiple job terminations for theft, and several abandoned partners and children; he was diagnosed with conduct disorder at age 10.
He is charming and articulate, flatters the examiner, and shows no visible distress when describing harm to others; he minimizes all actions and rationalizes his fraud.

Neuropsychological testing shows intact cognition with specific deficits in recognition of fearful facial expressions; polysubstance use is documented but began after age 18, postdating the behavioral pattern.
When confronted with evidence that his fraud resulted in an elderly woman losing her home, he shrugs and says she should have been smarter.
explanation: ASPD involves a pervasive pattern of disregard for others' rights with deceitfulness, impulsivity, and lack of remorse.
keyFact: ASPD requires Conduct Disorder before age 15. ASPD prevalence within prison populations is approximately 40-70%. No FDA-approved medications.

wrongAnswers.name: Narcissistic Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NPD involves grandiosity without repeated criminal behavior and conduct disorder history.

wrongAnswers.name: Substance Use Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Substance use does not account for the longstanding pattern of criminal behavior predating substance use.

wrongAnswers.name: Malingering
wrongAnswers.whyNot: While secondary gain is present, the lifelong pattern of antisocial behavior is genuine and meets ASPD criteria.

clues: A 45-year-old male surgeon is referred after multiple nursing staff complaints about belittling behavior and an episode where he exploded at a resident in front of patients.
He dismisses complaints as jealousy from people who could never achieve what he has; he demands to see only senior administrators.
He is poised and immaculately dressed, dominates the interview, describes a colleague's recognition as undeserved, and expresses rage when his own behavior is questioned.
Personality inventories reveal elevated scores on grandiosity, entitlement, exploitativeness, and lack of empathy across all assessed domains.
He has terminated three friendships this year after each friend received professional recognition he felt he deserved more.
explanation: NPD involves a pervasive pattern of grandiosity, need for admiration, and lack of empathy.
keyFact: NPD involves narcissistic injury — rage reactions to perceived slights. Comorbid depression is common when external validation diminishes.

wrongAnswers.name: Antisocial Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASPD involves criminal behavior and conduct disorder history; this patient has workplace misconduct driven by entitlement.

wrongAnswers.name: Histrionic Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HPD involves attention-seeking through emotional expressiveness; NPD is driven by grandiosity.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar I Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bipolar I involves episodic mood elevation; this patient's grandiosity is persistent, not episodic.

clues: A 30-year-old woman is referred after five years of working exclusively from home, reporting she has no close friends and experiences significant distress about this.
She desperately wants friendships but is unable to initiate social contact because she is certain she will be rejected or humiliated.
She is visibly anxious but engaged; she reports feeling inferior, is hypersensitive to criticism, and is preoccupied with appearing foolish; she denies indifference to relationships.
Social anxiety screening score is elevated; structured interview reveals avoidance pervasive across all relationships and a self-view of being socially incompetent since early adulthood.
She rehearsed calling her neighbor to say hello for two weeks, then hung up immediately when the neighbor answered, sobbing afterward.
explanation: AvPD involves pervasive social inhibition driven by fear of rejection and feelings of personal inadequacy.
keyFact: AvPD vs Social Anxiety: AvPD is more pervasive, involves a stable self-concept of inadequacy. Distinguished from Schizoid PD by the desire for connection.

wrongAnswers.name: Social Anxiety Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Social anxiety can be situationally specific; AvPD involves a pervasive personality-level pattern with a chronic self-schema of inferiority.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizoid Personality Disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizoid PD involves genuine indifference to social relationships; this patient deeply desires connection.

wrongAnswers.name: Agoraphobia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Agoraphobia involves fear of situations where escape is difficult; this patient's avoidance is driven by fear of rejection.

clues: A 26-year-old man is brought to the ED after two days of believing microphones are hidden throughout his apartment and that people outside are watching him.
His roommate reports he has been awake for four days, was seen ingesting a powder substance, and has no prior psychiatric history.
He is agitated, tachycardic at 118 bpm, hypertensive, diaphoretic, with dilated pupils; he is responding to unseen stimuli and is convinced the examiner is surveilling him.
Urine drug screen is positive for amphetamines; glucose, electrolytes, HIV, and RPR are normal; brain CT is unremarkable.
Paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations that developed during active stimulant intoxication, with no prior psychotic history, remitting completely within 72 hours of cessation.
explanation: Stimulant-induced psychosis results from excess dopamine release, producing paranoid delusions and hallucinations.
keyFact: Key differentiators from primary psychosis: positive toxicology, acute onset, autonomic arousal, rapid resolution with abstinence.

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Schizophrenia requires symptoms lasting 6+ months in the absence of substance use; rapid resolution confirms substance etiology.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar I Mania with Psychosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Positive toxicology and complete resolution within 72 hours point to substance-induced disorder.

wrongAnswers.name: Delirium
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Delirium involves fluctuating consciousness; this patient is alert and oriented with specific paranoid delusions.

clues: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her family after becoming increasingly unresponsive and difficult to engage over the past two days.
She was hospitalized two weeks ago for a first manic episode, and the current state emerged two days after her antipsychotic dose was increased.

She is mute and immobile in bed; when the examiner repositions her arm overhead it remains fixed in that position for several minutes; she grimaces when approached but does not speak or follow commands.
Vitals show a mild fever of 37.9 degrees Celsius and heart rate of 92 bpm; CK is mildly elevated at 280 U/L; EEG shows diffuse slowing without epileptiform discharges.
Intravenous lorazepam 2 mg produces dramatic resolution of mutism and immobility within ten minutes, with the patient beginning to speak and move spontaneously.
explanation: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome of motor dysregulation. GABA-A hypofunction is the proposed mechanism; benzodiazepines and ECT are definitive treatments.
keyFact: Catatonia occurs more commonly in bipolar disorder and MDD than in schizophrenia. Benzodiazepine challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

wrongAnswers.name: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NMS presents with severe hyperthermia (>38.5C), markedly elevated CK (often >1000), and profound lead-pipe rigidity with autonomic instability; the mild fever, modest CK, and dramatic lorazepam response here favor catatonia, though overlap exists and both must be considered.

wrongAnswers.name: Nonconvulsive Status Epilepticus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EEG shows only diffuse slowing without epileptiform activity, ruling out NCSE.

wrongAnswers.name: Stuporous Depression
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Waxy flexibility and the dramatic benzodiazepine response are specific to catatonia.

clues: A 67-year-old man's wife calls 911 because he suddenly could not finish his morning coffee and his speech stopped making sense.
He has a history of atrial fibrillation and hypertension; the symptoms began abruptly approximately 90 minutes ago.
Neurological exam reveals right-sided facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and inability to repeat phrases or follow commands.
Non-contrast head CT is negative for hemorrhage; blood glucose is 98 mg/dL; ECG confirms atrial fibrillation.
MRI diffusion-weighted imaging shows restricted diffusion in the left middle cerebral artery territory.
explanation: Cardioembolic ischemic stroke in the left MCA territory is a common consequence of atrial fibrillation, where stasis promotes thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage. Embolism causes abrupt focal neurological deficits corresponding to the affected vascular territory.
keyFact: Atrial fibrillation is the most common cardiac cause of embolic stroke; DWI-MRI is the most sensitive early imaging modality.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemorrhagic Stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Non-contrast CT showed no blood, and the clinical syndrome with AF points to embolism rather than hemorrhage.

wrongAnswers.name: Todd's Paralysis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No witnessed seizure preceded the deficits, and DWI confirms structural infarction.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypoglycemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Blood glucose was normal at 98 mg/dL, ruling out metabolic mimicry.

clues: A 58-year-old woman is brought to the ED after suddenly collapsing at work; coworkers say she appeared well earlier that day.
She has a long-standing history of poorly controlled hypertension and has been noncompliant with her medications for several months.
Vital signs show BP 220/130 mmHg; exam reveals a GCS of 8, left gaze deviation, and right hemiplegia with extensor posturing.
Head CT shows a large hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia with surrounding edema and 8 mm midline shift.
CT angiography identifies no vascular malformation; the hyperdense mass is located in the putamen, arising from a ruptured lenticulostriate artery.
explanation: Hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage most commonly occurs in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum due to rupture of small penetrating arteries damaged by chronic hypertension. Rapid neurological deterioration and markedly elevated BP are characteristic.
keyFact: The most common location for hypertensive ICH is the putamen/basal ganglia, supplied by the lenticulostriate arteries.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic Stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The hyperdense lesion on CT confirms blood, not infarction, and hyperdensity is the hallmark of acute hemorrhage.

wrongAnswers.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Blood is parenchymal, not in the subarachnoid space, and no aneurysm was found on CTA.

wrongAnswers.name: Brain Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Abscesses appear as ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema, not hyperdense acute blood products.

clues: A 71-year-old man presents to urgent care reporting an episode earlier today where he was unable to speak and his right hand felt weak.
He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia; the episode lasted approximately 20 minutes and fully resolved before arrival.
Current neurological exam is completely normal; carotid auscultation reveals a left-sided bruit.
Non-contrast CT head is unremarkable; MRI DWI shows no restricted diffusion; carotid ultrasound reveals 75 percent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery.
Repeat MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging at 24 hours remains negative for acute infarction, with complete resolution of the transient focal neurological deficit in under one hour.
explanation: A TIA is a transient neurological deficit caused by focal brain ischemia that resolves completely without infarction on imaging. High-grade carotid stenosis is a major modifiable risk factor, and TIA is a neurological emergency due to imminent stroke risk.
keyFact: Up to 10-15% of patients with TIA will have a stroke within 90 days; half of those strokes occur within the first 48 hours.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic Stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Symptoms fully resolved and DWI MRI showed no infarction, which is required to diagnose stroke.

wrongAnswers.name: Focal Seizure with Todd's Paralysis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No witnessed convulsive activity, and speech impairment with hand weakness is more consistent with ischemia than postictal deficit.

wrongAnswers.name: Complex Migraine
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No headache was reported, and the patient's vascular risk factor burden makes ischemic etiology far more likely.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with a two-week history of progressive unilateral visual changes and mild periorbital discomfort.
She reports a similar episode two years ago involving numbness in her left leg that resolved over several weeks; she is otherwise healthy.
Visual acuity in the right eye is 20/100; fundoscopic exam is normal; a relative afferent pupillary defect is present in the right eye; vibration sense is reduced in both lower extremities.
MRI brain and spine with gadolinium reveals multiple periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintensities and one enhancing lesion in the right optic nerve; CSF shows oligoclonal bands not present in serum.
Visual evoked potentials show prolonged P100 latency in the right eye; MRI shows periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial lesions with some enhancing and some not.
explanation: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the CNS characterized by episodes of neurological dysfunction separated in time and space. Optic neuritis with a prior sensory episode satisfies dissemination in time and space per McDonald criteria.
keyFact: Oligoclonal bands in CSF but not serum, and periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson's fingers on sagittal FLAIR), are hallmarks of MS.

wrongAnswers.name: Neuromyelitis Optica
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NMO typically causes more severe, bilateral optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions; anti-AQP4 antibody testing would be needed to confirm.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ADEM is monophasic, typically follows infection or vaccination, and does not fulfill dissemination in time criteria.

wrongAnswers.name: Optic Neuritis Alone
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The prior sensory episode, spinal cord findings, and periventricular lesions confirm dissemination in time and space, pointing to MS rather than isolated optic neuritis.

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with three days of progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness and paresthesias in his distal upper extremities.
Three weeks ago he had a self-limited diarrheal illness; the weakness is symmetric and he notes difficulty climbing stairs.
Neurological exam reveals symmetric proximal and distal lower extremity weakness at 3/5, absent ankle and knee reflexes bilaterally, and mild distal sensory loss.
Nerve conduction studies show markedly prolonged distal latencies, reduced conduction velocities, and conduction block in multiple motor nerves.
CSF analysis reveals protein of 180 mg/dL with only 2 white blood cells per microliter.
explanation: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy often triggered by preceding infection (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV). It presents with ascending flaccid weakness, areflexia, and albuminocytologic dissociation in the CSF.
keyFact: Albuminocytologic dissociation (high CSF protein, normal cell count) peaks at 2-4 weeks after onset and is the classic CSF finding in GBS.

wrongAnswers.name: Myasthenia Gravis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MG causes fatigable weakness predominantly at the neuromuscular junction, not areflexia or sensory symptoms, and NCS would be normal.

wrongAnswers.name: Spinal Cord Compression
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cord compression causes upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity), not the areflexia and demyelinating NCS pattern seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Transverse Myelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Transverse myelitis causes a spinal cord level with UMN findings below the lesion, not ascending peripheral demyelination.

clues: A 42-year-old woman presents with a six-week history of intermittent double vision and fluctuating eyelid drooping.
