She also reports difficulty chewing tough foods by the end of a meal and occasional nasal speech when she talks for extended periods.
Sustained upgaze for 60 seconds produces worsening bilateral ptosis; strength in the extremities is 5/5 and reflexes are intact and symmetric.

Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz shows a decremental response greater than 10 percent in the orbicularis oculi; ice pack test applied to the closed eye for 2 minutes produces significant improvement in ptosis.
Serum anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies return markedly elevated, and chest CT reveals an anterior mediastinal mass.
explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease caused by antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable weakness. Thymoma is found in approximately 15% of patients and should always be screened for.
keyFact: Fatigable ptosis worse with sustained upgaze or at end of day, and improvement with the ice pack test, are highly specific clinical features of ocular MG.

wrongAnswers.name: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LEMS causes proximal limb weakness with initial augmentation on repetitive stimulation, not ocular symptoms, and is associated with small cell lung cancer.

wrongAnswers.name: Multiple Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS can cause diplopia but not fatigable ptosis, decremental NMJ responses, or AChR antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitochondrial Myopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia from mitochondrial disease does not fatigue with activity and does not respond to the ice pack test.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with a one-year history of progressive weakness in his right hand that has made it difficult to button shirts and type.
Over the past three months he has noticed his speech is becoming slurred and his voice sounds strained; he denies any sensory symptoms.
Exam shows right hand intrinsic muscle atrophy, fasciculations in bilateral upper and lower extremities, brisk reflexes throughout, and a spastic dysarthric voice with a hyperactive jaw jerk.
EMG reveals widespread active denervation and chronic reinnervation in cervical, thoracic, and lumbar myotomes.

MRI brain and spine shows no structural lesion to explain the combined upper and lower motor neuron findings across bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral regions, and all metabolic and inflammatory workup is negative.
explanation: ALS is a fatal neurodegenerative disease involving progressive loss of both upper and lower motor neurons. The coexistence of UMN signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity, pathological reflexes) and LMN signs (atrophy, fasciculations, denervation on EMG) in multiple regions is diagnostic.
keyFact: The simultaneous presence of UMN and LMN signs in bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral regions is pathognomonic for ALS.

wrongAnswers.name: Multifocal Motor Neuropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MMN causes pure LMN findings without hyperreflexia or bulbar UMN signs, and responds to IVIG.

wrongAnswers.name: Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cervical myelopathy would not explain bulbar symptoms, and EMG would not show thoracolumbar denervation.

wrongAnswers.name: Kennedy Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kennedy disease (SBMA) is a pure LMN disease with androgen insensitivity features and no UMN signs.

clues: A 68-year-old man is brought by his wife for evaluation of gradually worsening motor difficulties and recent balance problems over the past two years.
His wife notes that his handwriting has become progressively smaller and he has lost facial expressiveness; he also reports difficulty initiating movements and a softer voice.

Exam shows masked facies, reduced arm swing on the right, a 4 to 5 Hz pill-rolling tremor of the right hand at rest that diminishes with intentional movement, and cogwheel rigidity in the right upper extremity.
Neuropsychological testing shows intact cognition; MRI of the brain is unremarkable for structural lesions or atypical patterns.
DaTscan SPECT imaging shows asymmetrically reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the left posterior putamen, contralateral to his predominantly right-sided symptoms.
explanation: Parkinson's disease is caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The cardinal features are asymmetric rest tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability, with a robust response to levodopa.
keyFact: Asymmetric onset and a robust, sustained response to levodopa are key features distinguishing idiopathic PD from atypical parkinsonian syndromes.

wrongAnswers.name: Essential Tremor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Essential tremor is an action/postural tremor, not a resting tremor, and lacks the bradykinesia and rigidity of PD.

wrongAnswers.name: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSP features early falls, axial rigidity, and supranuclear gaze palsy with a poor levodopa response — not present here.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-Induced Parkinsonism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No antidopaminergic medications were reported; drug-induced parkinsonism is typically symmetric and reversible upon drug discontinuation.

clues: A 60-year-old woman presents with a five-year history of shaking hands that has become progressively disabling and embarrassing in social situations.
Her father had the same problem; she reports that drinking a glass of wine before dinner noticeably reduces the shaking for a few hours.
Tremor is bilateral, symmetric, and present when she holds a cup or writes but absent when her hands rest in her lap; no bradykinesia or rigidity is detected.
Thyroid function tests, serum ceruloplasmin, and a medication review are all unremarkable; DaTscan is normal.
Accelerometry confirms the tremor is purely postural and kinetic with a frequency of 6-8 Hz and no resting component; no cogwheel rigidity or bradykinesia is detected on repeat testing.
explanation: Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder, characterized by bilateral action and postural tremor without other neurological features. It frequently has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and is dramatically suppressed by alcohol and beta-blockers.
keyFact: Essential tremor is an action/postural tremor (worsens with movement) that is absent at rest, distinguishing it from the rest tremor of Parkinson's disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Parkinson's Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PD features a rest tremor that diminishes with movement, plus bradykinesia and rigidity not seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Physiologic Tremor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Physiologic tremor is fine, high-frequency, and triggered by stimulants, anxiety, or metabolic causes — this patient has a persistent bilateral tremor with a positive family history.

wrongAnswers.name: Wilson's Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wilson's disease presents in younger patients with liver disease and Kayser-Fleischer rings; ceruloplasmin was normal here.

clues: A 42-year-old man is referred for evaluation of worsening involuntary movements and cognitive decline over the past three years.
His mother died in a psychiatric institution in her late 40s; his maternal uncle also had abnormal movements; he is divorced and recently lost his job due to erratic behavior.

Exam shows brief, irregular, non-repetitive jerking movements of the face, trunk, and limbs that flow from one body part to another; he has impaired saccadic eye movements and frontal-subcortical cognitive deficits.
MRI brain shows bilateral caudate nucleus atrophy with corresponding enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles.
Genetic testing reveals 48 CAG trinucleotide repeats in the HTT gene on chromosome 4.
explanation: Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene. It presents with the triad of chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbance, with caudate atrophy on imaging.
keyFact: Greater than 40 CAG repeats in HTT confers full penetrance; anticipation occurs, with paternal transmission causing earlier onset in subsequent generations.

wrongAnswers.name: Wilson's Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wilson's disease occurs in younger patients, involves liver disease and Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is not caused by CAG repeat expansion.

wrongAnswers.name: Sydenham's Chorea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sydenham's chorea follows streptococcal infection, is self-limited, occurs in children, and has no family history of neurodegeneration.

wrongAnswers.name: Tardive Dyskinesia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tardive dyskinesia is caused by chronic antidopaminergic drug exposure; this patient has no such history and has a strong genetic pedigree.

clues: A 19-year-old male college student presents to the ED with a six-hour history of severe headache, high fever, and vomiting that has been rapidly worsening.
He was well yesterday; his roommate in the dormitory was recently hospitalized with a similar febrile illness.
Temperature is 39.8 degrees C, BP 88/60, HR 118; exam reveals neck stiffness, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, and a non-blanching petechial rash on the trunk and lower extremities.
Lumbar puncture reveals CSF with WBC 4200 at 95 percent neutrophils, protein 280, glucose 28 with serum glucose 110; Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci.
CSF and blood cultures grow Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B.
explanation: Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency most commonly caused by Neisseria meningitidis in young adults and Streptococcus pneumoniae in adults. Non-blanching petechiae or purpura in the setting of meningismus strongly suggests meningococcal disease.
keyFact: Empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone) must be given within 30 minutes of presentation — do not delay for LP if CT is needed first.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral meningitis causes lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose; the neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, and Gram-negative diplococci on CSF Gram stain are inconsistent with viral meningitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SAH presents with thunderclap headache but without fever, meningismus signs, petechiae, or a markedly abnormal CSF cell count.

wrongAnswers.name: Fungal Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fungal meningitis (cryptococcal) is subacute, occurs in immunocompromised hosts, and shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with positive India ink on CSF.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents in August with a two-day history of headache, low-grade fever, and neck stiffness.
Several of his college classmates have had similar illnesses over the past month; he had a mild diarrheal illness one week ago that has since resolved.
Temperature is 38.2 degrees C; he has mild photophobia and meningismus; he is alert and oriented with no rash and no focal neurological deficits.
LP shows CSF with WBC 210 at 92 percent lymphocytes, protein 65, glucose 62 with serum glucose 90; Gram stain is negative; bacterial cultures are negative at 48 hours.
CSF enterovirus PCR returns positive.
explanation: Viral meningitis, most commonly caused by enteroviruses, presents with meningismus, fever, and headache but lacks the neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, and toxic appearance of bacterial meningitis. It is typically self-limited with supportive care.
keyFact: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose on CSF strongly favors viral over bacterial meningitis; enterovirus PCR of CSF is the fastest confirmatory test.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacterial Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial meningitis shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, low CSF glucose, and elevated protein; this patient's CSF is lymphocytic with normal glucose.

wrongAnswers.name: Herpes Encephalitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSV encephalitis presents with fever plus altered mental status and temporal lobe involvement on MRI — this patient has intact cognition.

wrongAnswers.name: Fungal Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cryptococcal meningitis is chronic, insidious, and occurs in immunocompromised patients; CSF India ink and cryptococcal antigen would be positive.

clues: A 41-year-old man presents with three weeks of progressive headache, mild confusion, and blurred vision.
He has known HIV infection with a CD4 count of 32 cells per microliter and has been non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy; he keeps pigeons on his apartment rooftop.
Examination reveals temperature 38.0 degrees Celsius, neck stiffness on passive flexion, papilledema on fundoscopy, and subtle left sixth cranial nerve palsy with lateral gaze limitation.
Lumbar puncture shows opening pressure of 38 cmH2O, CSF WBC 18 with lymphocytic predominance, glucose 32 mg/dL, protein 88 mg/dL; India ink preparation demonstrates encapsulated yeast forms.
Mucicarmine stain of centrifuged CSF sediment highlights a thick magenta-staining polysaccharide capsule surrounding narrow-based budding yeast.
explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis is the most common cause of fungal meningitis and a major AIDS-defining illness in patients with CD4 counts below 100. Elevated intracranial pressure from impaired CSF reabsorption is a major cause of morbidity and vision loss.
keyFact: Opening pressure management with serial LPs or lumbar drain is critical in cryptococcal meningitis — elevated ICP is the leading cause of early mortality.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculous Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB meningitis also causes lymphocytic meningitis with low glucose, but India ink and cryptococcal antigen are negative; AFB stain and culture or TB PCR would be positive.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacterial Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial meningitis is acute with neutrophilic pleocytosis; this is a subacute illness in an immunocompromised host with lymphocytic CSF.

wrongAnswers.name: CNS Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CNS lymphoma in HIV can cause headache and cranial nerve palsies but would not show encapsulated yeast on India ink staining.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with two weeks of progressive right-sided weakness, headache, and low-grade fever.
He recently had a tooth extraction three weeks ago without antibiotic prophylaxis; he also has a known patent foramen ovale.
Temperature is 37.9 degrees C; neurological exam reveals right hemiparesis at 4/5 and subtle right facial droop; he is alert and oriented.
MRI brain with gadolinium shows a 3 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe with surrounding vasogenic edema; MR spectroscopy shows a lactate and amino acid peak with absent NAA.
Stereotactic aspiration yields thick pus; culture grows Streptococcus viridans and Fusobacterium nucleatum.
explanation: Brain abscesses form via direct spread (sinusitis, otitis, dental infection), hematogenous seeding, or trauma. Ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema in a patient with a dental source and PFO is classic for hematogenous brain abscess.
keyFact: The MR spectroscopy signature of a brain abscess — lactate, amino acid, and acetate peaks with absent N-acetylaspartate — helps distinguish abscess from necrotic tumor.

wrongAnswers.name: Glioblastoma Multiforme
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBM causes ring-enhancing lesions but MR spectroscopy shows elevated choline and absent NAA without the amino acid and lactate peaks of infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Brain Metastasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastases present with multiple lesions at the gray-white junction in a patient with known malignancy — not with a dental source and MRS spectroscopy of infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Tumefactive MS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tumefactive MS produces an incomplete ring of enhancement with mass effect, occurring in younger MS patients, without fever or an infectious source.

clues: A 22-year-old man is brought to the ED after a head injury; he is found to be increasingly drowsy and confused.
He was initially alert and complaining of a headache; thirty minutes later nursing staff note he is becoming increasingly somnolent.
Repeat exam reveals GCS 10, right pupil 6 mm and non-reactive, and left hemiplegia representing rapid neurological deterioration.
Emergent non-contrast CT head shows a biconvex hyperdense collection overlying the left temporal lobe with 12 mm midline shift and a linear temporal bone fracture.
Emergent craniotomy identifies the middle meningeal artery as the bleeding source beneath the biconvex collection.
explanation: Epidural hematoma is typically caused by rupture of the middle meningeal artery following temporal bone fracture. The classic lucid interval — brief loss of consciousness followed by temporary recovery and then rapid deterioration — reflects expanding arterial bleeding.
keyFact: The lucid interval followed by rapid herniation is the classic presentation of epidural hematoma; the biconvex (lenticular) shape on CT is due to the dura being stripped from the inner table.

wrongAnswers.name: Subdural Hematoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute SDH presents as a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection that crosses suture lines; EDH is biconvex and bounded by sutures.

wrongAnswers.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SAH blood fills the sulci and cisterns; it does not form the focal extra-axial biconvex collection with midline shift seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Diffuse Axonal Injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DAI causes immediate and prolonged loss of consciousness from the moment of impact, without the lucid interval; CT may be normal or show microhemorrhages at gray-white junctions.

clues: A 79-year-old man on anticoagulation therapy presents with gradually progressive cognitive decline and psychomotor slowing over the past three weeks.
His daughter recalls he slipped and hit his head on a cabinet about a month ago but seemed fine and refused to go to the hospital.
Exam reveals mild left-sided weakness at 4/5, subtle left facial droop, and a score of 18/30 on the MMSE; his INR is 3.2.
Non-contrast CT head shows a right-sided crescent-shaped isodense to hypodense collection with 7 mm midline shift to the left.
The collection extends across the entire right cerebral convexity, crosses the coronal suture, and is bounded medially by the inner cortical surface.
explanation: Chronic subdural hematoma results from tearing of bridging veins, often following minor head trauma in elderly anticoagulated patients. Blood liquefies over days to weeks, appearing isodense then hypodense on CT, and presents with insidious cognitive decline and focal deficits.
keyFact: Chronic SDH appears crescent-shaped, crosses suture lines (unlike EDH), and is isodense to hypodense on CT; elderly patients on anticoagulants are at highest risk.

wrongAnswers.name: Epidural Hematoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EDH is biconvex, bounded by sutures, and typically arterial with rapid acute deterioration — not the subacute, crescent-shaped collection seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Alzheimer's Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alzheimer's causes insidious cortical atrophy without focal motor deficits or a mass lesion on CT.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic Stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stroke causes a focal infarct in a vascular territory, not a compressive crescent-shaped extra-axial fluid collection.

clues: A 51-year-old woman calls 911 after developing the worst headache of her life with sudden onset while doing yard work.
She has a family history of a brother who died of a brain aneurysm at age 45; she has smoked one pack per day for 25 years.
She is mildly confused with GCS 14; blood pressure is 190/105; nuchal rigidity is present; bilateral fundoscopic exam shows subhyaloid hemorrhages.
Non-contrast CT head shows diffuse hyperdensity in the basal cisterns, sylvian fissures, and interhemispheric fissure.
CT angiography identifies a 9 mm saccular aneurysm at the junction of the left internal carotid artery and posterior communicating artery.
explanation: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage is a neurosurgical emergency presenting with an instantaneous thunderclap headache, the worst of the patient's life. CT sensitivity for SAH is 98% within 6 hours; LP for xanthochromia is needed if CT is negative.
keyFact: The 'sentinel headache' — a sudden severe headache days before major rupture — occurs in 20-40% of aneurysmal SAH cases and is often misdiagnosed as migraine.

wrongAnswers.name: Migraine
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Migraine builds over minutes to hours; SAH is instantaneous (thunderclap). Nuchal rigidity and subhyaloid hemorrhages do not occur in migraine.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertensive Encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypertensive encephalopathy causes gradual confusion and blurred vision with posterior FLAIR changes (PRES), not thunderclap headache and basal cistern blood.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningitis has fever and CSF pleocytosis; SAH has xanthochromia, RBCs on LP, and blood in the basal cisterns on CT.

clues: A 26-year-old woman presents reporting recurrent debilitating headaches since age 18 that occur two to three times per month.
Each episode begins with 20 to 30 minutes of visual disturbances she describes as a shimmering zigzag arc in her right visual field that slowly expands, followed by a unilateral throbbing headache.
The headache is severe at 8/10 on the left side, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and extreme sensitivity to light and sound; it lasts 12 to 24 hours and forces her to lie in a dark room.
Neurological exam between episodes is completely normal; head MRI is unremarkable; no papilledema or focal deficits are found.
A headache diary confirms at least five lifetime attacks meeting the same pattern of unilateral pulsation, nausea, and photo-phonophobia lasting 4 to 72 hours.
explanation: Migraine with aura is a primary headache disorder defined by recurrent, unilateral, throbbing headaches with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia, preceded by a transient neurological aura. Triptans (5-HT1B/D agonists) are first-line abortive therapy.
keyFact: The migraine aura is caused by cortical spreading depression — a slow wave of neuronal depolarization followed by suppression propagating at 2-6 mm/min across the cortex.

wrongAnswers.name: TIA
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TIA visual symptoms are negative (loss of vision), not positive (scintillating scotoma), and do not resolve to be predictably followed by a headache.

wrongAnswers.name: Cluster Headache
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cluster headache is unilateral periorbital pain with autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhea), lasts 15-180 minutes, and does not have aura or nausea.

wrongAnswers.name: Tension Headache
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tension headache is bilateral, non-pulsating, mild-to-moderate, and without nausea or photophobia — it does not have an aura.

clues: A 32-year-old woman presents reporting near-daily headaches for the past three months since starting a new stressful job.
The headaches are diffuse and she describes a pressing or tightening sensation like a band around her head; she denies nausea, vomiting, or visual changes.
She has mild tenderness on palpation of the pericranial muscles bilaterally; neurological exam is normal; there is no photophobia or phonophobia during her headaches.
CBC, ESR, TSH, and brain MRI are all normal; no papilledema or focal neurological findings.
Over-the-counter ibuprofen provides complete relief, and the headache pattern remains bilateral, pressing, mild-to-moderate, with no associated nausea.
explanation: Tension-type headache is the most prevalent primary headache disorder, characterized by bilateral, non-pulsating, mild-to-moderate headache without the nausea, vomiting, or sensitivity features of migraine. Pericranial muscle tenderness and stress are common associations.
keyFact: ICHD-3 criteria for tension-type headache require bilateral pressing/tightening quality, mild-to-moderate intensity, no nausea, and no more than one of photophobia or phonophobia.

wrongAnswers.name: Migraine
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Migraine is unilateral, throbbing, moderate-to-severe, accompanied by nausea and photophobia/phonophobia — this patient's headache lacks these features.

wrongAnswers.name: Medication Overuse Headache
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Medication overuse headache requires intake of acute headache medications more than 10-15 days/month for over 3 months — this patient uses OTC NSAIDs infrequently.

wrongAnswers.name: Intracranial Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Raised ICP headache is worse in the morning, worsens with Valsalva, and is associated with papilledema — not present here.

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents to urgent care reporting that she woke up this morning and noticed the right side of her face was drooping.

She reports that her right eye would not fully close overnight and she woke with it dry and irritated; she also noticed drooling from the right side of her mouth and food collecting in her right cheek.

Examination shows complete right-sided facial weakness involving both the upper and lower face, including inability to raise the right eyebrow, wrinkle the right forehead, or close the right eye completely; the right nasolabial fold is flattened; no vesicles are seen in the ear canal.
Lyme serology is negative; CBC and CMP are normal; MRI of the temporal bone with gadolinium shows enhancement of the labyrinthine segment of the right facial nerve.
Electromyography at day 10 shows absent voluntary motor unit potentials in the right orbicularis oculi and orbicularis oris with preserved direct nerve excitability on the affected side.
explanation: Bell's palsy is the most common cause of acute unilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy, thought to be caused by reactivation of HSV-1 in the geniculate ganglion. Involvement of the forehead distinguishes peripheral (Bell's) from central facial palsy (e.g., stroke).
keyFact: In Bell's palsy, the forehead is involved because the facial nerve's forehead fibers have only contralateral cortical representation; in a central stroke, forehead sparing is the rule.

wrongAnswers.name: Central Facial Palsy from Stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Central stroke causes contralateral lower-face weakness with forehead sparing because the forehead receives bilateral cortical input — Bell's palsy involves the entire ipsilateral face including the forehead.

wrongAnswers.name: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV reactivation) presents with painful vesicles in the external auditory canal or soft palate — otoscopy was normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Lyme Disease Facial Palsy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lyme facial palsy is clinically identical but must be excluded by history of tick exposure, rash, and serologic testing in endemic areas.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with a one-year history of progressive burning pain and altered sensation in both feet.
He describes the pain as worse at night, like walking on hot coals, and notes it has gradually ascended to his lower calves.

Exam reveals reduced pinprick and light touch sensation in a stocking distribution to mid-shin bilaterally; vibration sense is absent at the great toes and reduced at the ankles; ankle reflexes are absent; motor strength is intact.
HbA1c is 10.2 percent; nerve conduction studies show reduced sural nerve sensory amplitudes bilaterally with mildly prolonged distal latencies in a length-dependent pattern.
Skin punch biopsy of the distal leg shows markedly reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density.
explanation: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is the most common neuropathy worldwide, caused by polyol pathway activation and oxidative stress from chronic hyperglycemia. It follows a length-dependent stocking-and-glove distribution beginning distally.
keyFact: The symmetric length-dependent pattern of diabetic neuropathy reflects the fact that longer axons are more metabolically vulnerable to hyperglycemic damage.

wrongAnswers.name: Guillain-Barre Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBS is acute, ascending, and associated with areflexia and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation; this patient has a chronic, length-dependent progression without systemic illness.

wrongAnswers.name: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication worsened by walking and relieved by flexion, affecting dermatomal distributions — not bilateral symmetric distal sensory loss.

wrongAnswers.name: Vasculitic Neuropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vasculitic neuropathy causes asymmetric, painful mononeuropathy multiplex — not symmetric distal sensory loss in the setting of longstanding diabetes.

clues: A 23-year-old man is brought in by EMS for a prolonged episode of generalized tonic-clonic activity that has not ceased.
His roommate reports he has a known seizure history but ran out of his levetiracetam four days ago; he had no fever or illness recently.
On arrival he is still actively seizing with generalized tonic-clonic activity; temperature is 38.4 degrees C, BP 160/90, HR 128, O2 sat 88 percent on room air.
Fingerstick glucose is 94 mg/dL; levetiracetam serum level is undetectable; basic metabolic panel shows no electrolyte abnormality.
Continuous EEG monitoring shows ongoing electrographic seizure activity persisting for over 30 minutes despite initial benzodiazepine administration.
explanation: Status epilepticus is defined as continuous or recurrent seizures without return to baseline for more than 5 minutes. Benzodiazepines are first-line; failure mandates urgent second-line therapy (fosphenytoin, valproate, levetiracetam) and continuous EEG monitoring.
keyFact: The operational definition of status epilepticus is seizure duration over 5 minutes, because spontaneous termination is unlikely after this point and neuronal injury begins.

wrongAnswers.name: Psychogenic Non-Epileptic Seizure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PNES can mimic convulsions but typically lacks post-ictal confusion, hypoxia, and the prolonged generalized motor activity unresponsive to benzodiazepines.

wrongAnswers.name: Syncope with Myoclonic Jerks
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Syncopal convulsions last under 30 seconds and self-terminate; this patient had continuous activity for 28 minutes unresponsive to initial therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypoglycemic Seizure
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Glucose was normal at 94 mg/dL, ruling out hypoglycemia as the cause of this breakthrough seizure from antiepileptic non-compliance.

clues: A 42-year-old woman presents with several weeks of bilateral hand pain and joint stiffness that is worst in the morning.
The stiffness lasts more than 90 minutes each morning and improves with activity throughout the day.
Exam reveals symmetric swelling and tenderness of the MCP and PIP joints bilaterally with sparing of the DIP joints.
RF is positive at 1:320 and anti-CCP antibody is elevated; X-ray shows periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions at the MCPs.
Synovial biopsy shows pannus formation with CD4-positive T-cell and plasma cell infiltration eroding into the adjacent cartilage and bone.
explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune disease causing symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, characteristically affecting MCPs and PIPs with DIP sparing. Anti-CCP antibody is highly specific and pannus formation drives joint destruction.
keyFact: Anti-CCP antibody has ~95% specificity for RA and predicts more erosive disease; DIP sparing distinguishes RA from osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthritis.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteoarthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OA causes DIP and PIP involvement (Heberden/Bouchard nodes), not MCP predominance, and lacks prolonged morning stiffness or elevated inflammatory markers.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriatic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriatic arthritis frequently involves DIPs and can be asymmetric; it is seronegative for RF/anti-CCP and associated with psoriatic skin lesions.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE arthritis (Jaccoud arthropathy) is typically non-erosive; SLE is distinguished by multi-system involvement, ANA positivity, and characteristic serologies like anti-dsDNA.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue, joint pain, and a new facial rash.
She reports recurrent oral ulcers, hair loss over the past two months, and pleuritic chest pain last month.
Exam shows a malar erythema sparing the nasolabial folds, non-scarring alopecia, and mild synovitis of bilateral wrists without erosions.
CBC reveals leukopenia with WBC 2800 and hemolytic anemia; urinalysis shows 3-plus protein and RBC casts.
ANA titer is 1:1280 homogeneous pattern; anti-dsDNA is markedly elevated and complement C3 and C4 levels are consumed.
explanation: SLE is a systemic autoimmune disease driven by immune complex deposition, classically presenting in young women with photosensitive rash, serositis, cytopenias, nephritis, and positive ANA/anti-dsDNA. RBC casts indicate proliferative lupus nephritis.
keyFact: Anti-dsDNA antibody titers correlate with lupus nephritis disease activity; low complement (C3/C4) during flares reflects consumption by immune complexes.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA lacks photosensitive rash, renal involvement, and cytopenias; its arthritis is erosive and symmetric with anti-CCP positivity rather than anti-dsDNA.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatomyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatomyositis causes proximal muscle weakness with heliotrope rash and Gottron papules over knuckles, not malar rash or nephritis.

wrongAnswers.name: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCTD features overlap of SLE, myositis, and scleroderma with high-titer anti-U1-RNP; it lacks the prominent nephritis and anti-dsDNA seen here.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents to the ED with sudden-onset severe pain and swelling in his right foot that began overnight.
He drinks four to six beers nightly, takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension, and recently started a low-calorie diet.
Exam shows the first MTP joint is exquisitely tender, erythematous, warm, and swollen; he cannot bear weight on the foot.
Serum uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL; X-ray shows soft tissue swelling but no erosions; joint aspiration is performed.
Polarized microscopy of synovial fluid reveals negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals within neutrophils.
explanation: Gout results from monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints, classically causing acute monoarthritis of the first MTP (podagra). Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals are diagnostic; thiazide diuretics impair urate excretion and precipitate attacks.
keyFact: Gout crystals are negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the compensator) and needle-shaped; thiazides, alcohol, and fasting all raise serum uric acid.

wrongAnswers.name: Pseudogout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pseudogout crystals are positively birefringent, rhomboid-shaped calcium pyrophosphate crystals; it preferentially affects the knee and wrist, not the first MTP.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic arthritis must be excluded but synovial fluid WBC in gout is typically 10,000–100,000 with crystals present; gram stain and culture are negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis is a soft tissue infection without joint involvement; it does not cause intra-articular crystals and typically lacks the abrupt nocturnal onset pattern of gout.

clues: A 74-year-old man presents with acute swelling and pain in his right knee that developed over 24 hours.
He has a history of hyperparathyroidism and hemochromatosis; he notes similar but milder episodes in the same knee over the past few years.
Exam reveals a warm, erythematous knee with a large effusion and limited range of motion; he is afebrile.
X-ray of the knee shows linear calcification of the menisci; synovial fluid WBC is 28,000 with 90 percent PMNs.
Polarized microscopy shows weakly positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals within neutrophils.
explanation: Pseudogout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition, most commonly affecting the knee in older adults. It is associated with metabolic conditions including hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, and hypomagnesemia; chondrocalcinosis on X-ray is a hallmark.
keyFact: CPPD crystals are weakly positively birefringent (blue when parallel to the compensator) and rhomboid-shaped; always screen for metabolic causes in patients under 60.

wrongAnswers.name: Gout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gout crystals are negatively birefringent and needle-shaped; gout preferentially attacks the first MTP and is associated with hyperuricemia, not chondrocalcinosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic arthritis would show organisms on gram stain or culture; the presence of crystals does not exclude infection but crystal identification confirms CPPD in this context.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteoarthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: OA causes chronic degenerative joint changes without acute inflammatory flares, high synovial WBC, or crystals on polarized microscopy.

clues: A 24-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain and stiffness that has gradually worsened over several years.
The pain is worse in the morning and with rest but improves significantly with exercise; he also reports alternating buttock pain.
Exam reveals decreased lumbar flexion with Schober test at 3 cm, reduced chest expansion, and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints bilaterally.
ESR and CRP are elevated; HLA-B27 is positive; pelvis X-ray shows bilateral sacroiliac joint sclerosis and irregularity.
MRI of the sacroiliac joints shows bone marrow edema and erosions bilaterally; later spine X-ray shows marginal syndesmophytes bridging vertebral bodies.
explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy characterized by inflammatory low back pain, sacroiliitis, and progressive spinal fusion. HLA-B27 is present in ~90% of patients and the classic radiographic end-stage is bamboo spine.
keyFact: Ankylosing spondylitis affects young men, improves with exercise (unlike mechanical back pain), and HLA-B27 is positive in ~90%; bamboo spine reflects complete spinal fusion.

wrongAnswers.name: Mechanical Low Back Pain
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mechanical back pain worsens with activity and improves with rest — the opposite pattern; it lacks sacroiliitis, elevated inflammatory markers, and HLA-B27 association.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriatic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriatic arthritis can cause sacroiliitis but tends to be asymmetric and is associated with psoriatic skin/nail changes; it lacks the degree of spinal involvement seen in AS.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis follows a preceding infection (GI or GU), is typically self-limited, and does not cause progressive sacroiliitis or bamboo spine.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with pain and swelling in multiple fingers and toes over the past three months.
He notes that his entire right index finger and left third toe are diffusely swollen, and he has had a scaly rash on his elbows and scalp for years.
Exam reveals dactylitis of the right index finger and left third toe, nail pitting, and onycholysis of multiple fingernails.
RF and anti-CCP are negative; X-ray shows DIP erosions with adjacent bone proliferation creating a pencil-in-cup deformity.
Skin biopsy of an elbow plaque shows parakeratosis, neutrophilic microabscesses in the stratum corneum, and elongated rete ridges.
explanation: Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis, characteristically causing dactylitis, nail changes, DIP involvement, and enthesitis. Pencil-in-cup deformity on X-ray reflects severe erosive disease with bone resorption.
keyFact: Dactylitis (entire digit swelling from tenosynovitis) and nail pitting are hallmark features of psoriatic arthritis; skin disease may precede, follow, or occur simultaneously with joint disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA spares the DIP joints, is seropositive (RF/anti-CCP), symmetric, and does not cause dactylitis or nail pitting.

wrongAnswers.name: Gout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gout causes acute monoarticular attacks with urate crystals; it does not cause dactylitis, nail changes, or the pencil-in-cup radiographic deformity.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis follows a GI or GU infection, is typically self-limited, and does not cause the chronic nail changes, psoriatic skin plaques, or pencil-in-cup erosions.

clues: A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive skin tightening, color changes in her fingers with cold exposure, and joint discomfort over six months.
She reports episodic color changes in her fingers going white then blue then red with cold, and new difficulty swallowing solid foods.
Exam reveals diffuse non-pitting skin thickening extending from fingers to the trunk, digital pitting scars at the fingertips, and a friction rub heard over the wrists.
Anti-Scl-70 antibody is positive; PFTs show a restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO; echocardiogram shows early pulmonary hypertension.
Nail-fold capillaroscopy reveals capillary dropout and dilated loops; skin biopsy shows excessive collagen deposition in the dermis with loss of adnexal structures.
explanation: Diffuse systemic sclerosis is a connective tissue disease characterized by widespread fibrosis of skin and internal organs. Anti-Scl-70 antibody is associated with diffuse skin involvement and a higher risk of ILD; pulmonary hypertension and ILD are leading causes of death.
keyFact: Diffuse SSc (anti-Scl-70) carries high risk for ILD and renal crisis, while limited SSc (anti-centromere) carries higher risk for pulmonary arterial hypertension as a late complication.

wrongAnswers.name: Limited Systemic Sclerosis (CREST)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Limited SSc has skin thickening confined to distal extremities and face (not trunk), positive anti-centromere antibody, and lower ILD risk; diffuse involvement and anti-Scl-70 indicate diffuse SSc.

wrongAnswers.name: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MCTD overlaps features of SLE, myositis, and scleroderma with high-titer anti-U1-RNP positivity; anti-Scl-70 and the extent of fibrosis point to diffuse SSc.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NSF occurs exclusively in patients with severe renal failure exposed to gadolinium MRI contrast; it causes skin thickening but lacks Raynaud phenomenon, serologic findings, and internal organ fibrosis pattern of SSc.

clues: A 48-year-old woman presents with chronic eye discomfort, difficulty swallowing dry foods, and fatigue over two years.

She reports needing to drink water to swallow dry foods, waking at night to sip water, and having three dental cavities in the past year despite good hygiene; she also has bilateral parotid enlargement.
Schirmer test shows less than 5 mm of wetting in 5 minutes; slit-lamp exam reveals corneal punctate staining with rose bengal.
ANA is positive; anti-SSA and anti-SSB antibodies are both positive; RF is positive; ESR is elevated.
Minor salivary gland biopsy of the lower lip shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score of 1 or greater.
explanation: Primary Sjogren syndrome is an autoimmune exocrinopathy causing keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia due to lymphocytic destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands. Anti-SSA/Ro and anti-SSB/La antibodies are characteristic; focus score on lip biopsy confirms diagnosis.
keyFact: Sjogren syndrome carries a 44-fold increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (particularly MALT type); persistent parotid swelling, cryoglobulinemia, and low C4 are risk factors for lymphoma development.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE can have anti-SSA/Ro positivity and sicca symptoms but the primary presentation with predominantly exocrine gland involvement, lip biopsy findings, and absence of major organ manifestations points to primary Sjogren.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis can cause parotid enlargement and dry eyes (uveoparotid fever/Heerfordt syndrome) but would show non-caseating granulomas on biopsy, not focal lymphocytic sialadenitis; ACE level would be elevated.

wrongAnswers.name: Medication-Induced Xerostomia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anticholinergic medications cause dry mouth and eyes but would lack the autoantibodies, parotid enlargement, and positive lip biopsy with focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.

clues: A 34-year-old man presents with three weeks of progressive cough, fatigue, and a 10-pound unintentional weight loss.
He emigrated from the Philippines two years ago and shares a one-bedroom apartment with six family members.
Exam reveals dullness to percussion at the right apex and post-tussive crackles; no lymphadenopathy.
Chest X-ray shows a right upper lobe cavitary lesion with surrounding nodular infiltrates and ipsilateral hilar prominence.
Three consecutive early-morning sputum samples stain positive for acid-fast bacilli.
explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread by respiratory droplets, and classically produces upper lobe cavitary disease with constitutional symptoms. Crowded living conditions and origin from an endemic country are well-established risk factors.
keyFact: Upper lobe cavitation reflects high local oxygen tension favoring mycobacterial growth; acid-fast stain positivity on sputum is sufficient to initiate airborne precautions and empiric four-drug therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lung abscess typically follows aspiration, involves dependent segments (posterior upper or lower lobes), and sputum culture grows mixed oral flora rather than acid-fast bacilli.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis can cause bilateral hilar adenopathy and upper lobe infiltrates but does not produce AFB-positive sputum and rarely cavitates.

wrongAnswers.name: Histoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Histoplasmosis can mimic TB radiographically but is endemic to the Ohio-Mississippi River valley, not the Philippines, and is diagnosed by urinary antigen or fungal culture rather than AFB smear.

clues: A 28-year-old man presents with two months of profound fatigue, oral lesions, and a 15-pound weight loss.
He reports unprotected intercourse with multiple male partners and has never been tested for sexually transmitted infections.
Exam reveals white plaques on the buccal mucosa that wipe off with a tongue blade, bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and seborrheic dermatitis across the nasolabial folds.
CBC shows lymphopenia; chest X-ray is clear; absolute CD4 count returns at 87 cells per microliter.
Fourth-generation antigen/antibody combination assay is reactive and RNA viral load returns at 220,000 copies per mL.
explanation: HIV destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes; a count below 200 cells/µL defines AIDS and places patients at risk for opportunistic infections including oral candidiasis. Antiretroviral therapy initiated promptly reduces transmission and prevents AIDS-defining illnesses.
keyFact: Oral candidiasis (thrush) in an otherwise healthy young adult is a sentinel finding for advanced HIV; CD4 <200 qualifies as AIDS regardless of symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBV mononucleosis causes pharyngeal exudates and lymphadenopathy but resolves within weeks, does not cause CD4 depletion, and the heterophile antibody test would be positive.

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma can cause lymphadenopathy and weight loss but does not explain oral candidiasis or profound CD4 lymphopenia without an underlying immunodeficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary syphilis causes a diffuse rash and lymphadenopathy but not oral candidiasis or CD4 depletion; RPR would be positive.

clues: A 32-year-old man presents with three weeks of fevers, chills, night sweats, and progressive fatigue.
He injects heroin intravenously daily and reports no recent dental work or hospitalization.
Exam reveals a temperature of 39.4 degrees C, a new holosystolic murmur loudest at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration, and scattered conjunctival petechiae.
Three sets of blood cultures drawn over 24 hours all grow Staphylococcus aureus; ECG shows a new first-degree AV block.
Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrates a 1.2 cm mobile vegetation on the tricuspid valve.
explanation: Infective endocarditis in people who inject drugs most commonly involves the tricuspid valve and is predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus introduced via non-sterile injection. The modified Duke criteria require two major criteria (positive blood cultures plus echocardiographic evidence) for definite diagnosis.
keyFact: Right-sided endocarditis from IV drug use classically presents with septic pulmonary emboli causing multiple peripheral nodular infiltrates on chest imaging, even when the chest X-ray appears normal initially.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic thrombophlebitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic thrombophlebitis causes bacteremia and fever but does not produce valvular vegetations or a new cardiac murmur.

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatic fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis, affects left-sided valves, and would not account for S. aureus bacteremia in an IV drug user.

wrongAnswers.name: Marantic endocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis is a sterile process seen in advanced malignancy or hypercoagulable states and would not yield positive blood cultures.

clues: A 9-year-old boy is brought in by his parents for five days of right leg pain, refusal to bear weight, and low-grade fever.
He had a skin abscess on his right forearm three weeks ago that was drained at an urgent care clinic.
Exam shows point tenderness over the distal right femoral metaphysis, overlying warmth, and passive range of motion limited by pain; the knee joint itself moves freely without effusion.
ESR is 88, CRP 7.4, and plain X-ray is normal; MRI of the right femur reveals periosteal elevation and bone marrow edema at the distal metaphysis without joint involvement.
Bone aspiration yields purulent material; Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters and culture grows methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus.
explanation: Hematogenous osteomyelitis preferentially seeds the metaphyses of long bones in children because of sluggish blood flow in metaphyseal sinusoidal vessels. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism at all ages.
keyFact: The metaphysis, not the diaphysis or epiphysis, is the classic site in children due to terminal capillary loops that lack phagocytic lining cells, creating a nidus for bacterial seeding.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic arthritis produces a joint effusion and markedly restricted passive motion in all planes; MRI here shows metaphyseal involvement with a normal joint space.

wrongAnswers.name: Ewing sarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ewing sarcoma can cause pain and fever but typically shows an 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction on plain films and does not yield purulent aspirate on bone biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Transient synovitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Transient synovitis is a self-limited hip condition in children and does not cause periosteal elevation, elevated inflammatory markers, or purulent bone aspirate.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with one week of fatigue, diffuse myalgias, and a skin finding on her left thigh she noticed four days ago.
She spent a weekend hiking in the Connecticut woods three weeks ago and recalls removing a small tick from her thigh the following day.
Exam reveals a 12 cm oval erythematous plaque on the left thigh with central clearing and a deeper red outer border; no lymphadenopathy.
Two-tier serology is sent; ELISA returns positive with an IgM Western blot showing two of three required bands reactive.
Repeat IgG Western blot at six weeks shows five of ten required bands reactive.
explanation: Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi transmitted by Ixodes scapularis ticks in the northeastern United States. Erythema migrans at the tick bite site is pathognomonic and sufficient to initiate treatment without confirmatory testing.
keyFact: Erythema migrans is the only Lyme disease manifestation that is diagnosed clinically without serology; two-tier testing can be negative in early localized disease because antibody responses may not yet be detectable.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis is an acute spreading skin infection without central clearing and is not associated with tick exposure; it would not produce the concentric ring morphology of erythema migrans.

wrongAnswers.name: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RMSF causes a petechial rash beginning on wrists and ankles with high fever and rapid systemic deterioration, not a slowly expanding annular skin lesion.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea corporis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea corporis is a superficial fungal infection that can produce annular plaques but has a scaly border, responds to antifungals, and is not associated with tick bites or systemic symptoms.

clues: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the ED with four days of high fever, severe headache, and diffuse malaise.
His family returned from a camping trip in North Carolina one week ago; his parents recall finding an attached tick on his scalp.
Exam reveals temperature 40.1 degrees C, blanching erythematous macules on both wrists and ankles that have begun spreading centrally to the trunk; mild periorbital edema is noted.
CBC shows thrombocytopenia with platelets at 68,000, hyponatremia at 129, and elevated transaminases; head CT is normal.
Skin biopsy immunofluorescence demonstrates rickettsial organisms within endothelial cells; paired serology shows fourfold rise in titers.
explanation: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii transmitted by Dermacentor ticks and carries high mortality if treatment is delayed beyond the first five days. The classic triad of fever, headache, and rash beginning peripherally is present in only 60% of cases.
keyFact: Treatment with doxycycline must begin empirically before serologic confirmation, as delay beyond day 5 of illness dramatically increases mortality; doxycycline is safe even in children under 8 for this indication.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningococcemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningococcemia can cause a petechial or purpuric rash and thrombocytopenia but begins on the trunk and spreads outward, the opposite direction of RMSF; blood cultures would grow Neisseria meningitidis.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral exanthem
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral exanthems are usually benign, self-limited, and do not cause thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, and transaminitis in this combination or begin on the distal extremities.

wrongAnswers.name: Ehrlichiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ehrlichiosis also follows tick exposure and causes leukopenia and thrombocytopenia but characteristically does NOT produce a rash (the 'spotless' tick fever), distinguishing it from RMSF.

clues: A 31-year-old woman presents to the ED with three days of high fevers, rigors, and severe headache.
She returned from a six-week humanitarian mission in sub-Saharan Ghana eight days ago and reports inconsistent use of her prescribed chemoprophylaxis.
Exam reveals temperature 40.3°C, splenomegaly, scleral icterus, and marked pallor; no skin rash or lymphadenopathy.
CBC shows hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, platelets 55,000, total bilirubin 4.8, and creatinine 2.1; peripheral blood smear shows parasitized red cells with 4% parasitemia.
Thick and thin blood smears reveal ring forms with double chromatin dots and 'appliqué' forms adherent to the RBC membrane; no Schüffner's dots are seen.
explanation: Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe form of malaria through cytoadherence of parasitized erythrocytes to vascular endothelium, leading to microvascular obstruction. Complications include cerebral malaria, severe anemia, acute kidney injury, and respiratory failure.
keyFact: P. falciparum is distinguished on smear by ring forms with double chromatin dots, 'appliqué' (accolé) forms at the RBC margin, and lack of visible Schüffner's dots seen in P. vivax and P. ovale.

wrongAnswers.name: Typhoid fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Typhoid fever (Salmonella typhi) also follows travel to endemic areas and causes sustained fever, but produces relative bradycardia, rose spots on the trunk, and positive blood cultures — not parasitemia on smear.

wrongAnswers.name: Dengue fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dengue causes thrombocytopenia and fever after tropical travel but presents with retro-orbital pain, a maculopapular rash, and is a viral illness — no intraerythrocytic parasites are seen on smear.

wrongAnswers.name: Visceral leishmaniasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) causes splenomegaly and fever but has a subacute course over months, and diagnosis requires demonstration of Leishmania amastigotes in bone marrow, not peripheral smear parasitemia.

clues: A 24-year-old man presents with five days of abrupt-onset high fever, severe headache, and diffuse body pain.
He returned from a two-week trip to Bangkok, Thailand, ten days ago and reports being heavily bitten by mosquitoes during the day.

Exam reveals temperature 39.8°C, severe retro-orbital pain on lateral eye movement, a faint erythematous flush on the trunk, and a positive tourniquet test with greater than 20 petechiae per square inch.
CBC shows leukopenia (WBC 2,800) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 62,000); liver enzymes are mildly elevated; no peripheral parasites on smear.
NS1 antigen ELISA returns positive on day 5 of illness with detectable IgM antibody.
explanation: Dengue is caused by a flavivirus transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and is the most common arboviral illness globally. Severe dengue (dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome) is mediated by antibody-dependent enhancement in secondary infections with a different serotype.
keyFact: The tourniquet test (Rumpel-Leede) is a simple bedside indicator of capillary fragility in dengue; thrombocytopenia nadir typically occurs around days 4–6 of illness and precedes plasma leakage.

wrongAnswers.name: Chikungunya
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chikungunya also spreads via Aedes mosquitoes and causes fever and rash but is dominated by debilitating polyarthritis/arthralgia that can persist for months, and NS1 antigen testing is negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Malaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malaria causes fever and thrombocytopenia after tropical travel but would show intraerythrocytic parasites on peripheral smear, which were absent here.

wrongAnswers.name: Leptospirosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Leptospirosis follows water exposure (not mosquito bites), causes conjunctival suffusion and can produce Weil's disease with jaundice and renal failure, and is diagnosed by serology or PCR — NS1 would be negative.

clues: A 52-year-old woman presents with six months of progressive exertional dyspnea, palpitations, and two syncopal episodes.
She was born in rural Bolivia and lived there until age 30; she recalls unilateral periorbital swelling as a child that resolved spontaneously.
Exam reveals an irregular pulse, elevated JVP, bilateral lower extremity edema, an S3 gallop, and a soft holosystolic murmur at the apex.
ECG shows right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block; echocardiogram reveals severe dilated cardiomyopathy with an apical aneurysm and an EF of 22%.
IgG ELISA for Trypanosoma cruzi is positive on two separate assays using different antigen platforms.
explanation: Chagas disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by triatomine bugs, and is endemic in Latin America. Chronic cardiomyopathy develops decades after acute infection and is characterized by a dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm, conduction abnormalities, and thromboembolic risk.
keyFact: The classic ECG triad of Chagas cardiomyopathy is right bundle branch block, left anterior fascicular block, and ventricular ectopy; an apical left ventricular aneurysm in a Bolivian or Brazilian patient is pathognomonic.

wrongAnswers.name: Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Idiopathic DCM lacks the geographic exposure history, the characteristic ECG pattern with RBBB+LAFB, or a positive T. cruzi serology.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic cardiomyopathy causes regional wall motion abnormalities in coronary distributions but would not produce an apical aneurysm with normal epicardial arteries or T. cruzi seropositivity.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoid cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cardiac sarcoidosis can cause heart block and ventricular arrhythmias but is not linked to Latin American origin, does not produce T. cruzi antibodies, and FDG-PET would show patchy myocardial uptake.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with two weeks of worsening headache, confusion, and progressive left-sided weakness.
He is known to have HIV infection and has not taken antiretroviral therapy for over a year; he has two cats at home that he adopted as strays.
Neurologic examination reveals left hemiparesis with 3/5 strength in the left upper and lower extremities, left facial droop, and mild dysarthria; fundoscopy shows no papilledema.

CD4 count is 54 cells per microliter; brain MRI with gadolinium shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding vasogenic edema in the basal ganglia and at the gray-white matter junction bilaterally.
On T1 post-gadolinium sequences the ring-enhancing lesions demonstrate an eccentric nodular target sign with asymmetric wall thickness, and serum IgG antibody to the causative organism is positive.
explanation: Cerebral toxoplasmosis results from reactivation of latent T. gondii cysts in patients with advanced HIV (CD4 <100). Multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions in a seropositive patient with CD4 <100 are treated empirically, with clinical and radiographic response confirming the diagnosis.
keyFact: The two main causes of ring-enhancing brain lesions in HIV patients are toxoplasmosis (multiple, responds to treatment) and primary CNS lymphoma (often solitary, FDG-PET avid, EBV-positive in CSF); empiric anti-toxoplasma therapy and reassessment at 2 weeks distinguish them.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary CNS lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CNS lymphoma in AIDS also causes ring-enhancing lesions but is typically solitary, periventricular, FDG-avid on PET, EBV DNA-positive in CSF, and does not respond to anti-toxoplasma therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Cryptococcal meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cryptococcal meningitis in HIV presents with diffuse meningitis and 'soap bubble' lesions in basal ganglia (cryptococcomas) but does not produce the multiple ring-enhancing lesions with hemiparesis seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PML causes non-enhancing white matter lesions due to JC virus reactivation and presents with focal deficits but without ring enhancement or mass effect; lesions do not respond to empiric anti-toxoplasma therapy.

clues: A 27-year-old man presents with three weeks of fever, dry cough, and fatigue.
He recently cleaned out an old barn in rural Kentucky that had a large bat colony roosting in the rafters.
Exam reveals temperature 38.5°C, mild splenomegaly, and diffuse fine crackles bilaterally; no skin lesions.
Chest CT shows diffuse bilateral small pulmonary nodules with mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy; serum LDH is elevated; standard bacterial sputum culture is negative.
Urine polysaccharide antigen is positive at 5.2 ng/mL, and bronchoalveolar lavage fungal culture grows a dimorphic fungus displaying tuberculate macroconidia at 25°C.
explanation: Histoplasmosis is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, found in soil enriched by bird and bat guano. Immunocompetent hosts develop self-limited pulmonary illness; disseminated disease occurs in immunocompromised patients.
keyFact: Urinary Histoplasma antigen has the highest sensitivity for diagnosis of disseminated and moderate-to-severe pulmonary histoplasmosis and is the fastest way to confirm the diagnosis while awaiting cultures.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB also causes upper lobe infiltrates and mediastinal adenopathy but would not be linked to bat guano exposure, and diagnosis relies on AFB smear/culture, not urinary fungal antigen.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes bilateral hilar adenopathy and pulmonary nodules but is a non-infectious granulomatous disease; urinary Histoplasma antigen would be negative and there is no epidemiologic exposure link.

wrongAnswers.name: Blastomycosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Blastomycosis also occurs in the central US and can cause pulmonary nodules but classically produces skin lesions with verrucous borders and would grow Blastomyces dermatitidis on culture with a negative Histoplasma antigen.

clues: A 35-year-old construction worker presents with six weeks of cough, fatigue, chest pain, and a skin rash.
He moved to Phoenix, Arizona three months ago and has been doing excavation work at a new housing development site in the desert.
Exam shows tender erythematous nodules on both shins, diffuse arthralgias, and decreased breath sounds at the right base.
Chest X-ray reveals a right lower lobe infiltrate with a small pleural effusion; CBC shows eosinophilia at 12%; serum fungal antigen testing is sent.
IgM complement fixation titer is positive at 1:32, and bronchoalveolar lavage cytology demonstrates large spherules containing endospores.
explanation: Coccidioidomycosis is caused by Coccidioides immitis/posadasii, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the desert Southwest (San Joaquin Valley, Arizona). The 'desert rheumatism' syndrome of cough, erythema nodosum, and arthralgias following soil disturbance is classic.
keyFact: Eosinophilia on CBC in a patient with pneumonia after residence in the desert Southwest is a key clue to coccidioidomycosis; complement fixation titers above 1:16 correlate with disseminated disease risk.

wrongAnswers.name: Community-acquired pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Typical bacterial CAP does not cause erythema nodosum, eosinophilia, or spherules on BAL cytology; it responds to antibiotics and lacks fungal serology positivity.

wrongAnswers.name: Histoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Histoplasmosis is endemic to the Ohio-Mississippi River valley, not the Sonoran Desert, and would not grow Coccidioides spherules or produce a positive Coccidioides complement fixation titer.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis can cause erythema nodosum and pulmonary infiltrates but is a non-infectious process with negative fungal serologies and no occupational exposure link to soil disturbance.

clues: A 50-year-old man presents with eight weeks of productive cough, night sweats, and a 12-pound weight loss.
He is an avid hunter who spends weekends along the banks of the Wisconsin River and recently cleared brush near a beaver dam.
Exam reveals temperature 38.2°C, decreased breath sounds at the right base, and two verrucous skin plaques on his left forearm with crusted, heaped-up borders and central scarring.
Chest CT shows a right lower lobe mass-like consolidation and pleural effusion; multiple sputum cultures for bacteria and mycobacteria are negative; KOH preparation of skin scrapings is sent.
KOH preparation shows broad-based budding yeast with a thick refractile double-contoured cell wall.
explanation: Blastomycosis is caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the north-central and southeastern US, especially along river valleys. The combination of pulmonary and skin involvement with verrucous plaques is characteristic.
keyFact: Blastomyces yeast is identified by its unique broad-based bud (vs. the narrow-based pinching bud of Cryptococcus) and thick double-contoured cell wall on KOH preparation; this distinguishes it from all other dimorphic fungi.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous cell carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCC can cause a lung mass and skin lesions but would not produce fever, broad-based budding yeast on KOH, or a positive fungal culture.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB can mimic blastomycosis with pulmonary infiltrates and skin involvement (scrofuloderma) but is diagnosed by AFB smear/culture and mycobacterial PCR, not broad-based budding yeast.

wrongAnswers.name: Histoplasmosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Histoplasma causes diffuse nodular infiltrates rather than mass-like consolidation and does not produce verrucous skin plaques; it also lacks broad-based budding yeast morphology.

clues: A 36-year-old woman presents with three weeks of gradually worsening exertional dyspnea, non-productive cough, and low-grade fevers.
She was recently diagnosed with HIV infection but has not yet started antiretroviral therapy; her CD4 count from last month was 78 cells/µL.
Exam reveals temperature 38.3°C, oxygen saturation 88% on room air that drops to 80% with ambulation, and fine bibasilar crackles; no lymphadenopathy.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates in a 'bat-wing' distribution; LDH is markedly elevated at 520 U/L; serum beta-D-glucan is positive.
Bronchoalveolar lavage with Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain reveals cyst forms with a characteristic 'crushed ping-pong ball' appearance.
explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is the most common AIDS-defining opportunistic infection in the US, occurring when CD4 falls below 200 cells/µL. The hallmark is progressive hypoxia out of proportion to radiographic findings, exacerbated by exertion.
keyFact: A-a gradient elevation with exertional desaturation out of proportion to the chest X-ray, combined with an elevated LDH and a CD4 <200, gives PJP a probability high enough to justify empiric TMP-SMX while awaiting BAL results.

wrongAnswers.name: Community-acquired pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial CAP typically presents with lobar consolidation and productive cough, causes acute rather than subacute illness, and would not show GMS-positive Pneumocystis cysts on BAL.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB in HIV-positive patients can cause bilateral infiltrates but usually shows upper lobe predominance or miliary pattern and is diagnosed by AFB smear/culture, not GMS staining.

wrongAnswers.name: Cytomegalovirus pneumonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CMV pneumonitis in HIV is far less common than PJP and is diagnosed by BAL demonstrating CMV inclusion-containing cells (owl-eye inclusions), not Pneumocystis cysts.

clues: A 44-year-old man presents with two weeks of gradually worsening vision in his left eye, describing increasing floaters and a dark area in his peripheral vision; he denies eye pain.
He has AIDS with a CD4 count of 18 cells per microliter and a detectable HIV viral load; he is not currently on antiretroviral therapy or any prophylactic medications.

Visual acuity is 20/200 in the left eye and 20/25 in the right eye; anterior segment slit lamp examination shows no cells or flare; dilated fundoscopy reveals areas of yellow-white retinal opacification with scattered hemorrhages along the vascular arcades.
Optical coherence tomography shows full-thickness retinal necrosis along the inferotemporal arcade with overlying vitreous debris; aqueous humor PCR for the causative virus is positive.
Fluorescein angiography shows perivascular blockage with late staining and vascular leakage in the affected retinal territories, and plasma viral DNA PCR returns at 8,400 IU/mL.
explanation: CMV retinitis is the most common cause of blindness in AIDS patients and occurs almost exclusively when CD4 falls below 50 cells/µL. It is a progressive, painless retinitis that will cause retinal detachment and permanent blindness if untreated.
keyFact: CMV retinitis is painless (unlike herpetic anterior uveitis), begins peripherally, and progresses centrally toward the macula and optic nerve; initiation of ART can paradoxically worsen inflammation through immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).

wrongAnswers.name: Toxoplasma chorioretinitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Toxoplasma chorioretinitis causes a focal necrotizing lesion adjacent to an old pigmented scar ('headlight in the fog') and is associated with significant vitritis and pain, unlike the painless full-thickness retinitis of CMV.

wrongAnswers.name: Retinal detachment
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Retinal detachment can cause a 'curtain' visual defect but lacks the characteristic retinal hemorrhage and infiltrate pattern; it is a complication of CMV retinitis rather than a separate diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Ocular syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ocular syphilis can affect any part of the eye in HIV patients but typically causes anterior or posterior uveitis with inflammation, and RPR/VDRL would be positive; it does not produce the 'pizza pie' funduscopic pattern.

clues: A 67-year-old woman develops diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, and low-grade fever during a prolonged hospitalization.
She completed a 10-day course of clindamycin for a dental abscess two weeks ago and was hospitalized for a hip fracture six weeks prior.
Exam reveals temperature 38.4°C, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding, and hyperactive bowel sounds; she appears mildly dehydrated.
WBC is 22,000 with 15% bands; creatinine is 1.8 (baseline 0.9); CT abdomen/pelvis shows marked colonic wall thickening and pericolonic stranding from cecum to sigmoid without free air.
Stool PCR assay for toxigenic genes returns positive for both toxin A and toxin B gene targets.
explanation: Clostridioides difficile infection results from disruption of normal colonic flora (typically by antibiotics), allowing C. difficile spores to germinate and produce toxins A and B that cause mucosal injury. Risk factors include prior antibiotic use, advanced age, and recent hospitalization.
keyFact: Leukocytosis exceeding 15,000 or acute kidney injury in C. difficile colitis are markers of severe disease requiring oral vancomycin rather than metronidazole; toxic megacolon (colonic dilation >6 cm) mandates surgical consultation.

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic colitis occurs in the watershed zones of the colon (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid), often follows hypotension or vascular disease, and would not be linked to recent antibiotic use or produce a positive C. difficile PCR.

wrongAnswers.name: Inflammatory bowel disease flare
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IBD flares occur in patients with established diagnoses, do not follow antibiotic use specifically, and C. difficile PCR would be negative; however, C. diff can complicate IBD flares.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious gastroenteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacterial gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Campylobacter) typically causes bloody diarrhea with fecal leukocytes and follows food exposure rather than recent antibiotic use; stool culture would grow the causative organism and C. difficile PCR would be negative.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with severe right thigh pain and swelling that began yesterday; he rates the pain 10/10.
He has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and sustained a minor laceration on his thigh while gardening four days ago.

Exam reveals temperature 39.6°C, tachycardia, and a tense, woody-hard right thigh with overlying dusky erythema extending beyond visible skin margins; the patient reports exquisite pain out of proportion to the skin findings, and gentle palpation produces crepitus.
CT of the right thigh shows gas tracking along the fascial planes from mid-thigh to the gluteal region; WBC is 28,000, creatinine 2.6, and sodium 129.
Intraoperative findings reveal gray necrotic fascia with 'dishwater' fluid that dissects easily along tissue planes; wound cultures grow mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms.
explanation: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressive infection of the deep fascial planes characterized by tissue necrosis, systemic toxicity, and high mortality without urgent surgical debridement. Pain out of proportion to skin findings and crepitus are the most important early clinical clues.
keyFact: The LRINEC (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis) score uses CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose; a score ≥6 suggests necrotizing fasciitis and warrants immediate surgical exploration — never delay surgery for diagnostic certainty.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis is a superficial skin infection without fascial involvement, does not cause crepitus, bony-hard tissue, or gas on CT; it responds to antibiotics alone without surgical intervention.

wrongAnswers.name: Deep vein thrombosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DVT causes leg swelling, erythema, and pain but without systemic toxicity, fever, crepitus, or gas on CT; D-dimer would be elevated but imaging would show venous thrombosis rather than fascial gas.

wrongAnswers.name: Pyomyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pyomyositis is a purulent infection within the muscle belly (not the fascia), progresses more slowly, lacks crepitus, and CT shows focal intramuscular abscess without tracking fascial gas.

clues: A 34-year-old woman presents with 12 hours of difficulty swallowing and progressive weakness in both arms.
She and two family members ate a home-canned meal together last night; both relatives have developed similar symptoms.
Neurologic exam reveals bilateral ptosis, lateral gaze palsy, absent gag reflex, dysarthria, and symmetric descending flaccid weakness; she is afebrile and fully alert.

Bedside spirometry shows FVC 1.4 L (52% predicted) with rapid downward trend; CSF analysis is normal; EMG shows incremental response of compound muscle action potentials at high-frequency repetitive stimulation.
Serum and stool specimens sent to the CDC reference laboratory return positive on mouse bioassay for type A neurotoxin.
explanation: Foodborne botulism results from ingestion of preformed Clostridium botulinum toxin, which cleaves SNARE proteins at the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia, causing a descending flaccid paralysis beginning with cranial nerves. Home-canned foods are the classic vehicle.
keyFact: Botulism classically presents with the '4 Ds': Diplopia, Dysarthria, Dysphagia, and Descending weakness — it is afebrile and causes flaccid (not spastic) paralysis; autonomic dysfunction (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention) is also present.

wrongAnswers.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GBS causes ascending (not descending) flaccid paralysis with albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF (elevated protein with normal WBC) and typically follows infection or vaccination; it does not present acutely after a shared meal.

wrongAnswers.name: Myasthenia gravis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness that worsens with activity, positive anti-AChR antibodies, and decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation — the opposite of the incremental response seen in botulism.

wrongAnswers.name: Brainstem stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A brainstem stroke could cause cranial nerve palsies and bulbar symptoms but would not cause a symmetric descending peripheral paralysis, would not affect multiple family members simultaneously, and would show abnormalities on brain MRI.
