clues: A 67-year-old man presents with three days of progressive muscle stiffness and painful spasms beginning in his jaw and spreading to his neck and trunk.
He punctured his foot on a rusty nail while working in his garden two weeks ago and did not seek medical care; he cannot remember receiving a vaccination in the past 30 years.
Exam reveals marked trismus with jaw opening less than 1 cm, a fixed sardonic grin (risus sardonicus), rigid abdomen, and opisthotonus triggered by light stimulation; he is fully conscious.
CBC and comprehensive metabolic panel are normal; CSF analysis is unremarkable; EMG shows continuous motor unit firing at rest without evidence of neuromuscular junction disease.
Wound culture from the foot puncture site grows gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobic bacilli under strict anaerobic conditions.
explanation: Tetanus is caused by tetanospasmin, a toxin produced by Clostridium tetani that ascends peripheral nerves to block inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord and brainstem, causing sustained muscle spasm. It is entirely preventable by vaccination.
keyFact: Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis — laboratory tests including CSF are typically normal; trismus (lockjaw) is the presenting sign in 75% of cases, and the spatial pattern of involvement (descending after initial jaw stiffness) distinguishes it from strychnine poisoning, which has similar spasms but no trismus predominance.

wrongAnswers.name: Strychnine poisoning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Strychnine blocks glycine receptors similarly to tetanospasmin and causes generalized muscle spasms, but unlike tetanus there is complete muscle relaxation between spasms and trismus is not a predominant feature; a toxicology screen would be positive.

wrongAnswers.name: Meningitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Meningitis causes neck stiffness and headache but does not produce trismus, risus sardonicus, or opisthotonus; CSF would show pleocytosis rather than a normal result.

wrongAnswers.name: Dystonic reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dystonic reactions (e.g., from antipsychotics or metoclopramide) cause acute muscle spasms and trismus but are associated with recent drug exposure, respond immediately to diphenhydramine or benztropine, and lack the wound history and normal CSF characteristic of tetanus.

clues: A 9-month-old infant is brought in for a third episode of pneumonia this year along with recurrent infections since birth.
His maternal uncle died in childhood from overwhelming sepsis; the infections began around 6 months of age.
The boy has no palpable lymph nodes and his tonsils are notably absent on oral exam.
Serum protein electrophoresis shows a near-complete absence of the gamma globulin fraction; lymphocyte count is normal.
Flow cytometry shows CD19+ B cells are less than 1% of peripheral lymphocytes with a mutation identified in the gene encoding a tyrosine kinase essential for pre-B cell receptor signaling.
explanation: A mutation in Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) arrests B-cell maturation at the pro-B cell stage, resulting in a near-complete absence of circulating B cells and all immunoglobulin classes. Maternal IgG provides protection for the first 6 months of life.
keyFact: XLA classically presents after 6 months when maternal IgG wanes, with recurrent bacterial (not viral/fungal) infections, absent tonsils/lymph nodes, and absent B cells with normal T-cell count. BTK mutation on X chromosome → affects males.

wrongAnswers.name: Common variable immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID typically presents in the second or third decade of life, not in infancy, and has detectable but dysfunctional B cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Transient hypogammaglobulinemia has low but present immunoglobulins and B cells, and resolves spontaneously; it does not cause this severity of infections.

wrongAnswers.name: SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCID involves absent T cells in addition to B-cell dysfunction and would present with opportunistic (viral, fungal) infections, not purely encapsulated bacterial pathogens.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with her fourth episode of sinopulmonary infection in the past 18 months along with intermittent diarrhea and unintentional weight loss.
She had a similar cluster of respiratory infections in her early twenties; she reports a sibling with an autoimmune condition.
Splenomegaly is noted on abdominal exam; scattered crackles are heard at bilateral lung bases.
Serum IgG, IgA, and IgM are all markedly reduced; B cells are present in normal numbers on flow cytometry.
Vaccination with pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine shows no rise in specific antibody titers at 4 weeks despite adequate B-cell numbers.
explanation: CVID is characterized by B cells that fail to differentiate into plasma cells and memory B cells, resulting in severely reduced immunoglobulins despite normal B-cell counts. The etiology is multifactorial and typically manifests in the second or third decade.
keyFact: CVID is the most common symptomatic primary antibody deficiency in adults. Associated with autoimmune disease, granulomatous disease, splenomegaly, and increased lymphoma risk. Normal B-cell count distinguishes it from XLA.

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked agammaglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLA presents in male infants after 6 months and features absent B cells; this patient is female, adult-onset, and has normal B-cell numbers.

wrongAnswers.name: Selective IgA deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Selective IgA deficiency affects only IgA with normal IgG and IgM, whereas this patient has pan-hypogammaglobulinemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia from hematologic malignancy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: While lymphoma can cause hypogammaglobulinemia, the normal B-cell count without malignant morphology and the lifelong infection pattern favor a primary immunodeficiency.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with recurrent sinopulmonary infections and intermittent diarrhea over the past 3 years.
She has a first-degree relative with celiac disease and has herself had documented Giardia infections twice; she reports no prior transfusions.
Vital signs are currently normal; she has mild eczema on her forearms bilaterally.
Complete metabolic panel and CBC are normal; serum IgG and IgM levels are normal.
Serum IgA is undetectable on two separate measurements, and anti-IgA antibodies are detected in her serum.
explanation: Selective IgA deficiency results from a block in terminal B-cell differentiation affecting only the IgA isotype, leaving mucosal immunity impaired. Patients can develop anti-IgA IgE antibodies, which cause anaphylaxis upon exposure to IgA-containing blood products.
keyFact: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency overall. Key associations: anaphylaxis to blood products (due to anti-IgA antibodies), celiac disease, Giardia infection, and autoimmune conditions. IgG and IgM are normal.

wrongAnswers.name: CVID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID features pan-hypogammaglobulinemia with reduced IgG and IgM in addition to IgA, whereas this patient has isolated IgA deficiency.

wrongAnswers.name: Allergic transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ABO incompatibility causes hemolytic reactions, not IgE-mediated anaphylaxis; anti-IgA antibodies explain the anaphylactic mechanism here.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyper-IgM syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyper-IgM syndrome features elevated IgM but absent IgG and IgA, not isolated IgA deficiency with normal IgG.

clues: A 14-month-old boy presents with recurrent bacterial ear infections and chronic diarrhea, now admitted with respiratory distress.
The infections began around 6 months of age; his maternal grandfather had similar childhood infections; he is fully vaccinated per schedule.
The child appears cachectic; cervical lymphadenopathy is present; liver and spleen are enlarged.
IgG, IgA, and IgE are all undetectable; IgM level is markedly elevated at 850 mg/dL.
Flow cytometry shows absence of CD154 expression on activated T cells after stimulation with PMA and ionomycin.
explanation: In X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome, a mutation in CD40L prevents the CD40–CD40L interaction required for B-cell isotype class switching, resulting in elevated IgM but absent IgG, IgA, and IgE. The defect also impairs macrophage activation, predisposing to opportunistic infections.
keyFact: Hyper-IgM syndrome: high IgM, absent IgG/IgA/IgE, susceptibility to Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium (hallmarks), sclerosing cholangitis from Cryptosporidium biliary involvement, neutropenia common. X-linked via CD40L mutation.

wrongAnswers.name: XLA
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLA features absent B cells and all immunoglobulin classes including IgM, whereas hyper-IgM syndrome has a markedly elevated IgM.

wrongAnswers.name: SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCID has absent T cells and would not show normal lymphadenopathy; also does not have elevated IgM.

wrongAnswers.name: CVID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID presents in adults, not infancy, and does not cause Pneumocystis pneumonia or have the characteristic IgM elevation.

clues: A 2-day-old girl develops a seizure; she is an otherwise full-term infant with an uncomplicated delivery.
Prenatal care was adequate; there is no family history of congenital heart disease; the mother had no infections during pregnancy.
Dysmorphic facies with hypertelorism, a short philtrum, and low-set ears are noted; the palate has a submucous cleft.
Serum calcium is 5.8 mg/dL; complete blood count shows markedly reduced lymphocyte count.
FISH testing reveals a microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2; flow cytometry shows severely reduced CD3+ T cells.
explanation: DiGeorge syndrome results from failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches due to 22q11.2 deletion, causing thymic aplasia/hypoplasia, parathyroid hypoplasia, and conotruncal cardiac defects. Absent thymus leads to T-cell lymphopenia and recurrent infections.
keyFact: DiGeorge triad: cardiac defects (tetralogy of Fallot most common), hypocalcemia (hypoparathyroidism), T-cell deficiency. Neonatal hypocalcemic seizures are a classic presentation. FISH for 22q11.2 is diagnostic.

wrongAnswers.name: Transient neonatal hypoparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Transient neonatal hypoparathyroidism does not explain the cardiac defect, dysmorphic features, absent thymus, or T-cell lymphopenia.

wrongAnswers.name: CHARGE syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CHARGE syndrome involves coloboma, choanal atresia, and ear anomalies but is caused by CHD7 mutations, not 22q11.2 deletion, and has a distinct constellation of features.

wrongAnswers.name: Noonan syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Noonan syndrome can cause cardiac defects and dysmorphic features but does not cause hypocalcemia, absent thymus, or T-cell deficiency.

clues: A 3-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive and an interstitial pneumonia that has not responded to standard treatment.
He developed a diffuse erythematous rash shortly after a blood transfusion last month; he has had no live vaccines.
He is below the 3rd percentile for weight and length; no lymph nodes are palpable; the chest X-ray shows absent thymic shadow.
CBC shows profound lymphopenia; mitogen stimulation assay shows no T-cell proliferative response.

Flow cytometry shows absent T cells and NK cells with present but nonfunctional B cells (T- B+ NK- pattern); genetic testing reveals a mutation in the gene encoding the common gamma chain shared by multiple cytokine receptors.
explanation: X-linked SCID results from mutations in IL2RG (common gamma chain), which is shared by receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21. Loss of IL-7 signaling blocks T-cell development; loss of IL-15 blocks NK-cell development, leaving nonfunctional B cells.
keyFact: SCID presents in the first year with opportunistic infections, absent thymic shadow, profound lymphopenia, and failure to thrive. Graft-versus-host disease from non-irradiated blood products is a critical complication. Newborn screening via TREC assay detects it early.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyper-IgM syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyper-IgM syndrome has elevated IgM and preserved T cells; it does not cause absent T and NK cells or the T-B+NK- pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: DiGeorge syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DiGeorge syndrome has partial T-cell deficiency with characteristic cardiac and hypocalcemic features and does not typically present with this degree of lymphopenia or NK-cell absence.

wrongAnswers.name: HIV infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Perinatal HIV can cause T-cell deficiency but presents with a CD4 decline over months to years, not neonatal absent T cells, and would not explain the transfusion-associated rash (GvHD).

clues: An 18-month-old boy is evaluated for easy bruising and a persistent skin rash since infancy.
He had prolonged bleeding after circumcision as a newborn; a maternal cousin had similar symptoms and died in childhood.
Petechiae and purpura are scattered across his trunk; weeping eczematous plaques cover his flexural surfaces.
CBC shows thrombocytopenia with a markedly reduced mean platelet volume (MPV); serum IgM is low; IgA and IgE are elevated; IgG is normal.

Flow cytometry shows reduced expression of a cytoskeletal regulatory protein in lymphocytes and platelets; genetic testing identifies a mutation in the gene encoding this actin-polymerization regulator on the X chromosome.
explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is caused by mutations in the WAS gene encoding the WASp protein, which regulates actin polymerization in hematopoietic cells. Defective cytoskeletal reorganization impairs T-cell and NK-cell function, platelet formation, and leads to microthrombocytopenia.
keyFact: Classic triad: thrombocytopenia with small platelets (low MPV), eczema, recurrent infections. Immunoglobulin pattern: low IgM, normal IgG, elevated IgA and IgE. X-linked. Increased risk of autoimmunity and lymphoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura with atopic dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ITP has normal or large platelet size (not small), no combined immunodeficiency, and no X-linked family history pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyper-IgE syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyper-IgE syndrome features markedly elevated IgE with recurrent abscesses and coarse facies but does not cause thrombocytopenia or small platelets.

wrongAnswers.name: Ataxia-telangiectasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ataxia-telangiectasia causes cerebellar ataxia and telangiectasias, not thrombocytopenia with small platelets; bleeding is not a feature.

clues: A 6-year-old girl is brought in for progressive difficulty walking and frequent falls over the past two years.
Her parents first noticed unsteadiness when she began walking; her infections are predominantly bacterial respiratory infections; she has a family history of childhood lymphoma.
Bilateral conjunctival telangiectasias are noted; she has a wide-based, ataxic gait and dysmetria on finger-nose testing.
Serum IgA and IgE are absent; IgG is reduced; AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) level is markedly elevated for age.
Genetic testing reveals a homozygous mutation in a gene encoding a kinase critical for DNA double-strand break repair.
explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in ATM, a kinase critical for DNA double-strand break repair. Failure of DNA repair causes progressive cerebellar degeneration, radiation sensitivity, immunodeficiency, and a markedly elevated cancer risk.
keyFact: AT: cerebellar ataxia starting ~2 years, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, IgA/IgE deficiency, elevated AFP, extreme radiosensitivity, and high risk of lymphoma/leukemia. ATM mutation; autosomal recessive.

wrongAnswers.name: Friedreich ataxia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Friedreich ataxia causes cerebellar ataxia but does not feature telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, elevated AFP, or increased cancer risk.

wrongAnswers.name: CVID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID causes antibody deficiency and sinopulmonary infections but does not produce cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, or elevated AFP.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HHT causes mucocutaneous and visceral telangiectasias with bleeding but is not associated with ataxia, immunodeficiency, or elevated AFP.

clues: A 4-year-old boy presents with a second deep-seated abscess and recurrent lymphadenitis requiring drainage.
He has had Aspergillus pneumonia once; his maternal uncle had similar recurrent infections in childhood; the abscesses have required surgical drainage each time.
Hepatomegaly is present; a draining lymph node in the right axilla is noted.
CBC and differential show normal neutrophil count with no morphologic abnormalities; serum immunoglobulins are elevated; nitroblue tetrazolium test shows absent color change in neutrophils.
Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry shows absent oxidative burst in neutrophils; genetic testing shows a mutation in the gene encoding a component of the NADPH oxidase complex on the X chromosome.
explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by mutations in NADPH oxidase components, most commonly gp91phox (X-linked), resulting in failure to generate the oxidative burst required to kill catalase-positive organisms. Catalase-positive pathogens (Staph, Aspergillus, Nocardia, Serratia) destroy hydrogen peroxide, leaving them resistant to killing.
keyFact: CGD: recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms (SANES: Staphylococcus, Aspergillus, Nocardia, Enterobacteriaceae, Serratia). NBT and DHR tests are diagnostic. X-linked (gp91phox) most common; autosomal recessive forms exist. Prophylactic TMP-SMX and itraconazole used.

wrongAnswers.name: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LAD causes recurrent bacterial infections without pus formation and delayed umbilical cord separation, but does not cause Aspergillus infection or absent oxidative burst.

wrongAnswers.name: Chediak-Higashi syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chediak-Higashi has giant lysosomes, partial albinism, and neuropathy; the NBT test is normal as the oxidative burst is intact.

wrongAnswers.name: Myeloperoxidase deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myeloperoxidase deficiency rarely causes severe infections and the NBT/DHR tests show a delayed but present oxidative burst, not absent.

clues: A 3-week-old infant is evaluated for a persistent wound that has been slow to heal and recurrent skin infections.
The umbilical cord stump has not yet separated at 4 weeks of age, which is significantly delayed.
A necrotic skin ulcer on the thigh shows no pus on incision and drainage; the wound edge is erythematous but firm, without fluctuance.
CBC during infection shows marked leukocytosis with WBC of 75,000/µL; CBC between infections shows persistent leukocytosis of 25,000/µL.
Flow cytometry shows absence of CD18 (beta-2 integrin) expression on neutrophils.
explanation: LAD type 1 is caused by mutations in ITGB2 encoding CD18 (beta-2 integrin), which is required for LFA-1 and Mac-1 expression. Without these integrins, neutrophils cannot undergo firm adhesion to endothelium and fail to migrate to sites of infection, resulting in bloodstream neutrophilia and absent pus.
keyFact: LAD type 1: delayed umbilical cord separation (>3 weeks), recurrent bacterial infections without pus, persistent leukocytosis, absent CD18 on flow cytometry. Autosomal recessive. Infections without neutrophil infiltration leads to gangrenous ulcers.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic granulomatous disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CGD causes absent oxidative burst but neutrophils can still migrate to infection sites and produce pus; persistent baseline leukocytosis is not a feature.

wrongAnswers.name: Chediak-Higashi syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chediak-Higashi has giant granules, partial albinism, and neuropathy; neutrophils do migrate but have impaired degranulation, and pus can form.

wrongAnswers.name: Neonatal omphalitis without immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Isolated omphalitis does not explain absent pus, persistent leukocytosis, and recurrent gangrenous wounds; this pattern requires a systemic immune defect.

clues: A 5-year-old boy presents with recurrent skin infections requiring hospitalization and easy bruising.
He has had recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin infections; his parents note he squints in bright light and his hair has always appeared silver-gray.
Partial ocular albinism with nystagmus is noted; peripheral neuropathy findings are present on neurological exam; no hepatosplenomegaly at this visit.
Peripheral blood smear shows abnormally large granules in neutrophils and lymphocytes; NK-cell cytotoxicity assay shows markedly reduced activity.
Electron microscopy of peripheral leukocytes shows giant lysosomal inclusions; genetic testing reveals a homozygous mutation in LYST on chromosome 1q42.
explanation: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by mutations in LYST, which regulates lysosomal trafficking. Defective lysosomal fusion results in giant granules in all granule-containing cells, impairing NK-cell cytotoxicity, neutrophil degranulation, and melanocyte melanin distribution.
keyFact: Chediak-Higashi: giant lysosomal granules on blood smear, partial oculocutaneous albinism, recurrent bacterial infections, neuropathy, and NK-cell deficiency. Most patients develop a fatal accelerated phase (EBV-driven hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis). LYST mutation, autosomal recessive.

wrongAnswers.name: Griscelli syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Griscelli syndrome also causes silvery hair and immunodeficiency but lacks giant lysosomal granules on blood smear; it is caused by RAB27A or MYO5A mutations.

wrongAnswers.name: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hermansky-Pudlak causes albinism and platelet dysfunction (bleeding) but not giant granules on smear, significant immunodeficiency, or neuropathy.

wrongAnswers.name: CGD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CGD causes recurrent pyogenic infections via absent oxidative burst but does not cause albinism, giant granules, or neuropathy.

clues: A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of facial and lip swelling and severe abdominal pain requiring ED visits.
Episodes began in her late teens and are often triggered by minor trauma, stress, or dental procedures; her father and brother have had similar episodes; antihistamines have never helped.
Non-pitting, non-pruritic edema of the lips and tongue is present; no urticaria is visible on skin exam.
C4 level is persistently low even between attacks; C3 level is normal; total complement (CH50) is reduced.
Functional assay of the serine protease inhibitor regulating the contact/kinin and complement pathways shows markedly reduced activity; genetic testing shows a SERPING1 mutation.
explanation: Hereditary angioedema type 1 results from C1-inhibitor deficiency due to SERPING1 mutations, leading to uncontrolled activation of the contact/kinin system and complement with excess bradykinin production, causing episodic non-histaminergic angioedema.
keyFact: HAE: non-pitting, non-pruritic, non-urticarial angioedema; no response to antihistamines or epinephrine; low C4 even between attacks; low C1 inhibitor; autosomal dominant. Laryngeal edema is life-threatening. Treat attacks with C1-INH concentrate, icatibant, or ecallantide.

wrongAnswers.name: Anaphylaxis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anaphylaxis is IgE-mediated, features urticaria and responds to epinephrine and antihistamines; it does not present with persistently low C4 or a hereditary pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated but is acquired, not hereditary, and resolves with drug cessation; no C1-INH mutation.

wrongAnswers.name: Acquired angioedema from C1q antibody
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acquired C1-INH deficiency from anti-C1q antibodies presents in older adults, often with lymphoma, and features low C1q levels not seen in hereditary forms.

clues: A 19-year-old man collapses at a restaurant; bystanders report he became flushed and had difficulty breathing before losing consciousness.
He has a known allergy to tree nuts; he was not aware his meal contained any; he carries an epinephrine auto-injector but it was not used before collapse.
Blood pressure is 68/40 mmHg with tachycardia at 130 bpm; diffuse urticaria and lip angioedema are visible; diffuse expiratory wheezing on auscultation.
Serum tryptase drawn at presentation is markedly elevated.
Specific IgE testing to cashew and pistachio antigens is markedly elevated, and repeat serum tryptase at 4 hours remains above baseline.
explanation: Anaphylaxis is an IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity reaction in which cross-linking of allergen-bound IgE on mast cells triggers massive degranulation, releasing histamine, tryptase, and other mediators causing systemic vasodilation, bronchospasm, and urticaria.
keyFact: Anaphylaxis diagnosis requires involvement of 2+ organ systems or hypotension after allergen exposure. Serum tryptase is elevated. Epinephrine IM (lateral thigh) is first-line. Biphasic reactions can occur 4-12 hours later.

wrongAnswers.name: Vasovagal syncope
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vasovagal syncope does not cause urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, or elevated tryptase; it is preceded by prodromal symptoms and resolves with supine positioning.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary angioedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HAE does not cause urticaria or wheezing, does not respond to epinephrine, and is not IgE-mediated with elevated tryptase.

wrongAnswers.name: Scombroid fish poisoning
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scombroid causes histamine poisoning with flushing and urticaria but not IgE-mediated anaphylaxis, not elevated tryptase, and is linked to improperly stored fish, not tree nuts.

clues: A 31-year-old man presents with joint pain, a widespread rash, and low-grade fever 10 days after starting a new medication.
He had no prior reactions; the rash began at the wrists and ankles and is spreading proximally; he also notes puffy hands and painful swollen knees.
A serpiginous, erythematous band along the lateral aspects of his feet is noted; bilateral knee effusions are palpable; temperature is 38.2°C.
CBC shows leukopenia; erythrocyte sedimentation rate and CRP are elevated; complement levels (C3, C4, CH50) are markedly decreased.
Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgG and C3 deposits on immunofluorescence; circulating immune complexes containing the offending foreign protein are detected in serum.
explanation: Serum sickness is a type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction in which IgG antibodies form complexes with foreign proteins, depositing in vessel walls and activating complement, causing fever, urticaria/rash, arthralgia, and vasculitis.
keyFact: Serum sickness occurs 7-21 days after exposure to foreign proteins (antisera, monoclonal antibodies, certain drugs). Key lab: low complement (C3, C4), elevated ESR, leukopenia. Pathological hallmark: leukocytoclastic vasculitis with immune complex deposition.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DRESS typically occurs 2-8 weeks after drug exposure and features prominent eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, and internal organ involvement without low complement.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus flare
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE can cause similar features but would not acutely develop 10 days post-ATG in a patient without prior SLE history; however, the timeline after ATG strongly supports serum sickness.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis follows a genitourinary or GI infection, not administration of foreign protein, and does not cause low complement or immune complex vasculitis.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue, jaundice, and dark urine over 3 weeks.
She takes hydroxychloroquine but no other medications; she has no family history of hemolytic anemia or blood disorders.
Scleral icterus and pallor of the conjunctivae are noted; mild splenomegaly is palpable; no lymphadenopathy.
CBC shows hemoglobin of 7.2 g/dL with elevated reticulocyte count; total and indirect bilirubin are elevated; LDH is elevated and haptoglobin is undetectable.
Direct antiglobulin test (Coombs) is positive for IgG and C3d coating the red blood cell surface.
explanation: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is a type II hypersensitivity reaction in which IgG autoantibodies bind RBC surface antigens (often Rh antigens) at body temperature, leading to extravascular hemolysis via Fc-receptor-mediated phagocytosis by splenic macrophages.
keyFact: Warm AIHA: positive DAT (IgG +/- C3d), elevated indirect bilirubin and LDH, low haptoglobin, reticulocytosis, spherocytes on smear. Associated with SLE, CLL, and drugs. Extravascular hemolysis (spleen). Treat with steroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (TTP)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TTP causes hemolysis from mechanical RBC destruction; the DAT is negative, and it features thrombocytopenia and neurological symptoms not explained by this presentation.

wrongAnswers.name: G6PD deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: G6PD deficiency causes episodic hemolysis triggered by oxidant stress (drugs, infections, fava beans); DAT is negative and it is X-linked, affecting males predominantly.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary spherocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hereditary spherocytosis is a congenital RBC membrane defect; the DAT is negative and it would not newly develop in the context of SLE.

clues: A 26-year-old man presents with hemoptysis and progressive dyspnea over 3 weeks, along with lower extremity edema.
He smoked one pack per day for 5 years; he had no prior kidney or lung disease; he does not use illicit drugs and has no recent infections.
Crackles throughout both lung fields; blood pressure is 158/96 mmHg; urine dipstick shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein.
Serum creatinine is 5.8 mg/dL (up from 0.9 mg/dL three months ago); urinalysis shows RBC casts; chest CT shows diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities.
Serum antibodies targeting the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen are detected; kidney biopsy shows linear IgG deposits along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence.
explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is a type II hypersensitivity reaction in which IgG autoantibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.
keyFact: Goodpasture: anti-GBM antibodies, linear IgG on renal IF, concurrent pulmonary hemorrhage and RPGN. Smoking triggers pulmonary involvement by exposing alveolar BM antigens. HLA-DR2 association. Treat with plasmapheresis + cyclophosphamide + steroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GPA causes pulmonary-renal syndrome but features c-ANCA (PR3 antibodies), granulomatous inflammation, and sinusitis; renal biopsy shows pauci-immune (not linear) deposits.

wrongAnswers.name: Microscopic polyangiitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MPA causes pauci-immune RPGN with p-ANCA (MPO antibodies) and lacks the defining anti-GBM antibody and linear IF pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: SLE nephritis with pulmonary hemorrhage
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE can cause nephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage but features granular (not linear) immune deposits on IF and anti-dsDNA/ANA antibodies, not anti-GBM antibodies.

clues: A 7-year-old boy develops facial puffiness, dark urine, and decreased urination over the past few days.
He was treated for impetigo with topical antibiotics 2 weeks ago; his blood pressure at his pediatrician's office last week was noted to be elevated.
Periorbital edema is present bilaterally, worse in the morning; blood pressure is 140/92 mmHg; urine dipstick shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein.
Complement C3 is markedly reduced; C4 is normal; anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer is elevated; urinalysis shows RBC casts.
Kidney biopsy shows mesangial and subepithelial electron-dense deposits ('humps') on electron microscopy, with granular C3 deposits on immunofluorescence.
explanation: PSGN is a type III hypersensitivity reaction where immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens deposit in the glomerulus, activating complement and causing proliferative nephritis. Skin infections (impetigo) cause PSGN; throat infections cause both PSGN and rheumatic fever.
keyFact: PSGN: 2-4 weeks post-impetigo (1-3 weeks post-pharyngitis), low C3 with normal C4 (alternate pathway activation), elevated ASO, granular IgG/C3 deposits on IF, subepithelial 'humps' on EM. Usually self-limited; complete recovery common in children.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy presents concurrent with or 1-2 days after an upper respiratory infection (synpharyngitic), features mesangial IgA deposits, and has normal complement levels.

wrongAnswers.name: Henoch-Schönlein purpura nephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HSP nephritis features purpuric rash, arthralgia, and abdominal pain with IgA deposits; it does not cause low C3 or follow impetigo by 2 weeks.

wrongAnswers.name: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MPGN also causes low C3 but presents chronically without a preceding streptococcal infection history and has a 'tram-track' appearance on light microscopy.

clues: A 34-year-old woman presents with an intensely itchy, blistering rash on her wrists and neck that appeared three days ago; she has no prior history of skin disease.
She recently received a new jewelry set as a gift and has been wearing the bracelet and necklace daily for the past week.

Well-defined, linear and geometric vesicular plaques are present on the dorsal wrists and lateral neck exactly matching the areas where the jewelry contacts skin; surrounding erythema and edema are present; no lesions are found elsewhere.
Skin scraping KOH preparation is negative for fungal elements; CBC shows mild peripheral eosinophilia; total IgE is normal.
Patch testing at 96 hours shows a strongly positive vesicular reaction to nickel sulfate at the application site, with no reaction to the 23 other standard allergens tested.
explanation: Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction in which sensitized CD4+ T cells recognize hapten-protein complexes presented by epidermal Langerhans cells, triggering cytokine-mediated inflammation 48-72 hours after re-exposure.
keyFact: Type IV hypersensitivity: T-cell mediated, 48-72 hour delay, diagnosed by patch testing. Classic examples: urushiol (poison ivy), nickel, rubber accelerants (thiuram). Spongiotic dermatitis with lymphocytic infiltrate on biopsy. Distinguished from irritant contact dermatitis by prior sensitization.

wrongAnswers.name: Irritant contact dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Irritant contact dermatitis is not immunologically mediated, occurs on first exposure, typically affects areas of highest chemical concentration, and does not give a positive patch test result.

wrongAnswers.name: Dyshidrotic eczema (pompholyx)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dyshidrotic eczema involves the palms and lateral fingers, is not tied to a specific contactant, and would not show a positive patch test to a rubber chemical.

wrongAnswers.name: Latex allergy (type I hypersensitivity)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Latex IgE-mediated allergy causes immediate urticaria, angioedema, or anaphylaxis within minutes; this patient uses latex-free gloves and the reaction is delayed, ruling out type I latex allergy.

clues: A 40-year-old man who recently underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant presents with a new rash, watery diarrhea, and yellowing of his eyes over the past five days.
The rash started on the palms and soles and has been spreading centrally; he is on tacrolimus for prophylaxis; stool studies and CMV PCR are negative.
Exam reveals a maculopapular erythematous rash covering approximately 40% of body surface area, scleral icterus, and diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs.

Total bilirubin is 6.2 mg/dL (conjugated predominant); stool volume exceeds 1 liter per day; skin biopsy shows vacuolar interface dermatitis with dyskeratotic keratinocytes and lymphocytic infiltration.
Liver biopsy demonstrates bile duct destruction with lymphocytic infiltration and endotheliitis; chimerism analysis confirms the infiltrating lymphocytes are of donor origin.
explanation: Acute GvHD results from donor T cells recognizing host minor histocompatibility antigens as foreign and mounting a cytotoxic immune response against host tissues, primarily affecting skin, liver, and gastrointestinal tract.
keyFact: Acute GvHD: occurs within 100 days post-transplant; triad of rash (palms/soles → trunk), diarrhea, and cholestatic hepatitis. Higher risk with matched unrelated donors. Treat with high-dose corticosteroids. Chronic GvHD resembles autoimmune diseases (sicca, scleroderma, lichen planus).

wrongAnswers.name: Engraftment syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Engraftment syndrome occurs at time of neutrophil engraftment with fever and rash but does not cause significant diarrhea, cholestatic hepatitis, or the degree of GI involvement described.

wrongAnswers.name: CMV colitis and hepatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CMV is an important post-transplant complication but has been excluded by negative CMV antigenemia and viral PCR; it would not explain the skin rash.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-induced hepatitis and rash from tacrolimus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tacrolimus toxicity can cause hepatitis but was tapered, not started; the combination of rash with palmar involvement, diarrhea, and bile duct destruction on biopsy is characteristic of GvHD, not drug toxicity.

clues: A 52-year-old woman undergoes deceased-donor kidney transplantation; shortly after surgery, the transplanted kidney produces no urine and Doppler shows absent blood flow.

She had received multiple blood transfusions following a motor vehicle accident 10 years ago; pre-transplant crossmatch was reported as negative at the regional lab, though the sample was collected 3 weeks prior.
Intraoperatively, urine output abruptly ceases; the kidney becomes cyanotic and firm; the surgeon notes sludging of blood in the renal vasculature.
Intraoperative biopsy shows neutrophil margination in glomerular and peritubular capillaries with fibrin thrombi in arterioles.
Post-operative flow cytometry crossmatch reveals high-titer preformed donor-specific IgG antibodies against donor HLA class I antigens that were undetectable on the outdated crossmatch sample.
explanation: Hyperacute rejection is a type II hypersensitivity reaction mediated by preformed recipient antibodies (against donor HLA, ABO, or endothelial antigens) that immediately activate complement and coagulation upon graft reperfusion, causing irreversible thrombotic occlusion.
keyFact: Hyperacute rejection: minutes to hours post-transplant; due to preformed donor-specific antibodies (DSA); irreversible—graft must be removed. Risk factors: prior transfusions, pregnancies, previous transplants. The crossmatch test is designed to prevent this.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute tubular necrosis from ischemia-reperfusion injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ATN causes delayed graft function over days, not immediate intraoperative graft cyanosis, and does not show fibrin thrombi with neutrophil margination on immediate biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal artery thrombosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Renal artery thrombosis can cause acute graft loss but is a surgical/vascular complication; it would not show preformed DSA or the histologic pattern of antibody-mediated rejection.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute cellular rejection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute cellular rejection occurs days to weeks post-transplant and is T-cell mediated with lymphocytic interstitial nephritis (tubulitis), not immediate fibrin thrombi from preformed antibodies.

clues: A 48-year-old man with a kidney transplant presents for routine follow-up with gradually worsening renal function and new proteinuria.

He has had two treated episodes of acute rejection in the first year; he reports medication adherence difficulties 3 years ago due to financial issues; his current tacrolimus levels have been therapeutic.
Blood pressure is 162/98 mmHg despite three antihypertensive agents; he has 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities.
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 800 mg/g; donor-specific antibodies to HLA-DQ antigens are detected at moderate titer.
Kidney biopsy shows transplant glomerulopathy (double-contour glomerular basement membrane), peritubular capillary C4d deposition, and arterial intimal fibrosis.
explanation: Chronic antibody-mediated rejection is caused by de novo or persistent donor-specific antibodies that chronically injure the graft microvasculature through complement activation and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, leading to transplant glomerulopathy and progressive fibrosis.
keyFact: Chronic rejection: occurs months to years post-transplant; insidious rise in creatinine, hypertension, proteinuria; C4d deposits in peritubular capillaries; transplant glomerulopathy on biopsy; donor-specific antibodies present. No proven treatment; desensitization strategies under study.

wrongAnswers.name: Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CNI toxicity causes interstitial fibrosis and arteriolar hyalinosis but does not produce transplant glomerulopathy, C4d deposition, or donor-specific antibodies.

wrongAnswers.name: Recurrent IgA nephropathy in the graft
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Recurrent IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits, not C4d in peritubular capillaries or transplant glomerulopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: BK virus nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BK nephropathy causes tubulitis and can be confused with rejection, but BK virus inclusions and positive BK PCR in urine/blood would be present; C4d and DSA would be absent.

accept: immune dysregulation polyendocrinopathy enteropathy x-linked syndrome
clues: A 3-week-old infant presents with intractable watery diarrhea, failure to thrive, and a widespread skin rash.
He developed insulin-dependent diabetes in the first week of life; a maternal uncle died in infancy from severe enteritis.
Severe wasting; generalized eczematous dermatitis; thyroid gland is enlarged.
Blood glucose is 420 mg/dL; anti-insulin antibodies, anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and anti-enterocyte antibodies are present; IgE level is markedly elevated.
Genetic testing reveals a hemizygous loss-of-function mutation in the gene encoding the master transcription factor for regulatory T-cell development on chromosome Xp11.23.
explanation: IPEX syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in FOXP3, the transcription factor required for regulatory T-cell (Treg) development and function. Without Tregs, self-reactive T cells are unchecked, causing severe multiorgan autoimmunity in neonates.
keyFact: IPEX: FOXP3 mutation, X-linked; neonatal triad of immune dysregulation (autoimmune enteropathy), polyendocrinopathy (neonatal diabetes, hypothyroidism), and eczema. Fatal without HSCT. Elevated IgE, autoantibodies. Tregs are absent or nonfunctional.

wrongAnswers.name: SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCID causes opportunistic infections from absent T cells, not autoimmune multiorgan disease; SCID patients lack autoantibodies and would not develop neonatal diabetes.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy (APECED)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: APECED is autosomal recessive via AIRE mutations, presents in older children with candidiasis and Addison disease/hypoparathyroidism, not as a neonatal presentation with enteropathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Congenital rubella syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Congenital rubella can cause neonatal diabetes and thyroiditis but is acquired via maternal infection, features cataracts, deafness, and cardiac defects, and would not cause this severity of enteropathy.

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with painless jaundice, weight loss, and a hard pancreatic mass on imaging, prompting concern for malignancy.
He also reports bilateral painless eye swelling over the past year and was previously treated for autoimmune pancreatitis at another institution; he does not smoke or drink alcohol.
Scleral icterus; firm, non-tender bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement; mild bilateral submandibular gland enlargement.
CA 19-9 is mildly elevated; CT shows a diffusely enlarged 'sausage-shaped' pancreas with a capsule-like rim and retroperitoneal fibrosis; serum IgG4 level is 8-fold above the upper limit of normal.
Pancreatic core biopsy shows dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells exceeding 10 per high-power field, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis.
explanation: IgG4-related disease is an immune-mediated fibroinflammatory condition characterized by tissue infiltration with IgG4-secreting plasma cells, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis, affecting multiple organs including the pancreas, salivary glands, orbit, and retroperitoneum.
keyFact: IgG4-RD: middle-aged men; pancreas (autoimmune pancreatitis type 1), salivary glands (Mikulicz), orbits, kidneys, aorta, retroperitoneum. Elevated serum IgG4 (>135 mg/dL). Biopsy: storiform fibrosis + obliterative phlebitis + >10 IgG4+ plasma cells/HPF. Responds dramatically to steroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pancreatic cancer rarely causes bilateral lacrimal/salivary gland swelling, prior autoimmune pancreatitis history, or sausage-shaped pancreatic morphology; it does not respond to steroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis can cause parotid and lacrimal gland enlargement with multiorgan disease but features non-caseating granulomas on biopsy and elevated ACE, not storiform fibrosis or IgG4+ plasma cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Sjögren syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sjögren causes exocrine gland involvement but features anti-SSA/SSB antibodies, lymphocytic infiltrate (not IgG4-rich), and sicca symptoms rather than obstructive jaundice from pancreatic involvement.

clues: A 16-year-old girl is referred for her third pneumonia this year, all requiring drainage of associated abscesses.
She reports her skin infections produce large amounts of pus but are relatively painless; she had a prior episode of esophageal fungal infection; her primary teeth were late to fall out.
Coarse facial features with a broad nasal bridge and prominent forehead; scoliosis is noted on spinal exam; active eczematous plaques on her arms.
Serum IgE is greater than 10,000 IU/mL; peripheral blood eosinophilia is present; CBC shows normal neutrophil count.
Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous dominant-negative mutation in a transcription factor critical for Th17 cell differentiation and IL-17 signaling.
explanation: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (AD-HIES) is caused by dominant-negative STAT3 mutations that impair Th17 differentiation, reducing IL-17-mediated neutrophil recruitment to mucosal surfaces and skin. Markedly elevated IgE results from dysregulated cytokine signaling.
keyFact: Hyper-IgE (Job's) syndrome: STAT3 mutation, AD; markedly elevated IgE (>2000 IU/mL), eczema, recurrent cold (non-inflammatory) staphylococcal abscesses, pneumatoceles, coarse facies, retained primary teeth, scoliosis. Th17 deficiency underlies susceptibility.

wrongAnswers.name: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: WAS features thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and IgE elevation is moderate not extreme; no coarse facies, dental anomalies, or pneumatoceles.

wrongAnswers.name: Atopic dermatitis with secondary infections
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atopic dermatitis does not cause markedly elevated IgE >10,000, coarse facies, retained primary teeth, scoliosis, or cold abscesses without inflammatory signs.

wrongAnswers.name: CGD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CGD causes recurrent staphylococcal and fungal infections via absent oxidative burst, but does not produce markedly elevated IgE, eczema, coarse facies, or pneumatoceles.

clues: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent oral lesions and recent onset of muscle cramping and tingling around her mouth.
She has had nail dystrophy and a whitening of areas of her skin over the past year; her older brother has similar oral candidiasis and was recently diagnosed with adrenal insufficiency.
Vitiligo patches on the dorsal hands; dystrophic fingernails; Chvostek sign is positive.
Serum calcium is 6.1 mg/dL with elevated phosphorus and undetectable PTH; serum cortisol fails to rise with ACTH stimulation.
Genetic testing reveals biallelic loss-of-function mutations in a thymic transcription factor gene on chromosome 21q22.3.
explanation: APECED is caused by biallelic AIRE mutations, which abrogate central T-cell tolerance by preventing thymic expression of peripheral self-antigens. Without AIRE-mediated negative selection, self-reactive T cells escape and cause autoimmunity at multiple endocrine and epithelial sites.
keyFact: APECED diagnostic triad: Addison disease, hypoparathyroidism, chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. At least 2 of 3 required, or 1 if a sibling is affected. AIRE mutation, autosomal recessive. Ectodermal features: vitiligo, alopecia, nail dystrophy, dental enamel hypoplasia.

wrongAnswers.name: DiGeorge syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DiGeorge causes hypoparathyroidism and T-cell deficiency from thymic aplasia due to 22q11.2 deletion, but not Addison disease, candidiasis, or AIRE mutation; it presents in infancy.

wrongAnswers.name: IPEX syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IPEX is X-linked (affects males), presents in neonates with enteropathy and neonatal diabetes, not with hypoparathyroidism and mucocutaneous candidiasis in a school-age girl.

wrongAnswers.name: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 (Schmidt syndrome)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: APS-2 involves Addison disease and type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease in adults; it does not cause hypoparathyroidism, candidiasis, or AIRE mutation.

clues: A 6-month-old girl presents with persistent diarrhea and failure to thrive; a recent CBC shows a markedly low CD4+ T-cell count despite normal total lymphocyte count.
The infections began at 3 months of age; she has had Cryptosporidium-associated cholangitis and one episode of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
Severely malnourished; hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy.
CBC shows normal to slightly reduced lymphocyte count; flow cytometry shows normal total T-cell count but markedly reduced CD4+ T-cell subset; immunoglobulins are low.
Flow cytometry of peripheral blood mononuclear cells shows absent HLA-DR, HLA-DP, and HLA-DQ expression; genetic testing identifies a homozygous mutation in the CIITA gene.
explanation: Bare lymphocyte syndrome type II is caused by mutations in MHC class II transactivator genes (CIITA, RFX5, RFXANK, RFXAP), leading to absent MHC class II expression. Without MHC class II, CD4+ T cells cannot be positively selected in the thymus, causing a combined immunodeficiency with selective CD4+ T-cell deficiency.
keyFact: BLS type II: absent MHC class II (HLA-DR/DP/DQ) on all APCs; selective CD4+ T-cell lymphopenia with normal total T-cell count; predominantly affects North African populations; autosomal recessive. Resembles SCID clinically but has normal lymphocyte count. CIITA is the most common mutated gene.

wrongAnswers.name: SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Classic SCID has profoundly absent T cells on flow cytometry and an absent thymic shadow; BLS type II has normal total T cells but selectively absent CD4+ cells and normal lymphocyte count.

wrongAnswers.name: HIV infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HIV causes selective CD4+ depletion but would be acquired, not autosomal recessive from birth, and HIV serology would be positive; also would not show absent HLA-DR on APCs.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyper-IgM syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyper-IgM syndrome has elevated IgM with absent IgG/IgA due to class-switch deficiency, but does not feature absent MHC class II expression or selective CD4 lymphopenia.

clues: A 2-year-old girl is brought in for recurrent hospitalizations for serious bacterial infections; her immunoglobulin levels and lymphocyte subsets are normal.
Her parents are healthy; newborn screen was normal; no family history of immunodeficiency; she received all vaccines on schedule, including pneumococcal and Hib vaccines.
Between infections, she appears well-nourished and developmentally normal; no lymphadenopathy; no hepatosplenomegaly.

Serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM) are normal for age; lymphocyte subset counts are normal; CH50 is normal; AP50 (alternative pathway) is normal; lectin pathway-specific assay shows absent activity.
Serum concentration of the pattern-recognition molecule that initiates the lectin complement pathway is undetectable; genetic testing shows a homozygous structural variant in the MBL2 gene.
explanation: MBL is a pattern-recognition molecule of the lectin complement pathway that binds carbohydrate patterns on pathogen surfaces and activates complement via MASP-1 and MASP-2. Deficiency impairs opsonization of encapsulated bacteria, particularly during early childhood before adaptive immunity matures.
keyFact: MBL deficiency: recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria in early childhood; CH50 and AP50 are normal (classical and alternative pathways intact); only lectin pathway assay is abnormal; serum MBL undetectable. Often identified by exclusion. May be more clinically significant in immunosuppressed patients.

wrongAnswers.name: CVID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID presents in adults (or older children), with low IgG/IgA/IgM; this child has normal immunoglobulins, making CVID unlikely.

wrongAnswers.name: Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Terminal complement deficiency causes susceptibility to Neisseria specifically, not broadly to encapsulated organisms; CH50 would be absent in terminal complement deficiencies.

wrongAnswers.name: Splenic dysfunction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asplenia/hyposplenia also increases susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria but requires physical or functional absence of spleen; this child has no evidence of splenic disease.

clues: A 7-year-old boy presents with persistent oral lesions and thickened, discolored nails that have not responded to standard treatments.
He has had no serious bacterial or viral infections; he was evaluated for SCID as a newborn, which was negative; his parents are healthy but are first cousins.
Thick, hyperkeratotic plaques on the scalp and face; nail dystrophy of all 10 fingernails; oral thrush with white plaques.
CBC, immunoglobulins, and lymphocyte subsets are normal; T-cell proliferation to mitogens is normal; Candida-specific T-cell proliferation assay shows absent response.
Genetic testing reveals a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in a gene encoding an adaptor protein in the dectin-1/CARD9 anti-fungal signaling pathway; anti-IL-17 antibodies are not detected.
explanation: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis results from defects in Th17 cell function or IL-17 signaling, impairing mucosal antifungal immunity. Causes include CARD9, STAT1 gain-of-function, AIRE, and IL-17RA/IL-17F mutations, with the common pathway being absent IL-17-mediated neutrophil and epithelial defense against Candida.
keyFact: CMC: persistent Candida of skin/nails/mucosa without systemic dissemination; normal T-cell counts and immunoglobulins; absent Candida-specific T-cell response; associated with CARD9, STAT1 GOF, AIRE mutations, and thymoma (acquired). Invasive candidiasis is rare.

wrongAnswers.name: APECED
wrongAnswers.whyNot: APECED (AIRE mutation) also causes CMC but is defined by at least two of three: Addison disease, hypoparathyroidism, and CMC; this boy has no endocrinopathy, and CARD9 mutation was found.

wrongAnswers.name: HIV/AIDS with oral candidiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HIV causes acquired immunodeficiency with low CD4 count; this boy has normal lymphocyte subsets, normal T-cell function to mitogens, and isolated Candida susceptibility from birth.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyper-IgE syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyper-IgE syndrome causes staphylococcal abscesses, eczema, and markedly elevated IgE alongside Candida susceptibility; this boy has isolated Candida susceptibility with normal IgE and normal skin/pulmonary findings.

clues: A 4-year-old boy is brought in for progressive abdominal fullness and recurrent nosebleeds.
He was previously evaluated for lymphoma, which was negative on biopsy; he has required transfusions for anemia; a sibling has similar lymphadenopathy.
Massive splenomegaly extending 8 cm below the costal margin; bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy; jaundice.
CBC shows anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia (cytopenias); Coombs test is positive; serum B12 is markedly elevated; serum IgG and IgA are elevated.
Flow cytometry shows expansion of CD3+CD4-CD8- double-negative T cells comprising greater than 1.5% of total lymphocytes; in vitro FAS-mediated lymphocyte apoptosis assay shows absent cell death.
explanation: ALPS is caused by defects in the FAS apoptosis pathway (most commonly FAS mutations), impairing activation-induced cell death of lymphocytes. The resulting failure of lymphocyte homeostasis leads to accumulation of double-negative T cells, lymphoproliferation, and autoimmune cytopenias.
keyFact: ALPS: massive splenomegaly + lymphadenopathy + autoimmune cytopenias (hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia); elevated DNT cells (CD3+CD4−CD8−); elevated serum B12 and IL-10 as biomarkers; FAS mutation most common. Increased risk of lymphoma. Treat with sirolimus.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HLH causes fever, cytopenias, and splenomegaly but presents acutely with hyperferritinemia, not chronic lymphadenopathy since infancy; DNT cells are not elevated.

wrongAnswers.name: Niemann-Pick disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Niemann-Pick causes organomegaly and cytopenias from sphingolipid storage but is a metabolic disease without autoimmune cytopenias, DNT cell expansion, or FAS mutations.

wrongAnswers.name: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma was excluded by prior biopsy; ALPS nodes show preserved architecture with polyclonal lymphoid hyperplasia, not malignant clonal proliferation; DNT cell expansion and FAS-apoptosis defect confirm ALPS.

clues: A 14-year-old girl presents with her fourth episode of severe, disseminated herpes simplex virus infection requiring hospitalization along with two prior episodes of severe varicella.
She had a life-threatening disseminated VZV infection at age 5; her bacterial infections have been routine for her age; she is HIV-negative.
Widespread herpetic lesions across the trunk and extremities; hepatomegaly is noted; she is afebrile.
CBC, IgG, IgA, IgM are all normal; T-cell and B-cell counts are normal; viral-specific T-cell assay to HSV shows normal function.
Flow cytometry shows markedly reduced CD56+CD16+CD3- cells at 0.2% of lymphocytes (normal 5-15%); cytotoxicity assay against K562 target cells shows absent killing activity.
explanation: Selective NK-cell deficiency causes a narrow susceptibility to herpesvirus family infections (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV), as NK cells provide the critical innate immune surveillance against herpesvirus-infected cells via recognition of MHC-I downregulation. Bacterial and fungal resistance is preserved through intact T and B-cell immunity.
keyFact: NK cell deficiency: selective severe herpesvirus infections (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV) with normal T cells, B cells, and immunoglobulins; absent CD56+CD16+ NK cells on flow; absent K562 killing. Rare; autosomal recessive. Distinct from Chediak-Higashi (which also has NK deficiency but other features).

wrongAnswers.name: SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCID causes absent T cells with susceptibility to all pathogens (bacterial, viral, fungal); this patient has normal T cells and only herpesvirus susceptibility.

wrongAnswers.name: DOCK8 deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DOCK8 deficiency also causes herpesvirus susceptibility but additionally features eczema, elevated IgE, sinopulmonary infections, and reduced T-cell memory, not seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Chediak-Higashi syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chediak-Higashi has NK-cell dysfunction but also features giant lysosomal granules, partial albinism, and neuropathy; NK-cell numbers may be normal with impaired function.

clues: A 19-year-old college student presents with sudden fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness.

She is her family's third member to develop meningococcal disease; her brother had meningococcemia at age 17 and her father had meningococcal meningitis in his twenties; she received meningococcal vaccine at age 11.
Temperature 39.8°C; non-blanching petechiae and purpura on the trunk; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are positive.
Blood cultures grow Neisseria meningitidis serogroup W; CSF shows gram-negative diplococci; CH50 (total hemolytic complement) is undetectable.

Individual complement component assays identify absent protein and function at a specific late-cascade step required for membrane attack complex assembly; genetic testing identifies the responsible mutation.
explanation: Terminal complement deficiencies (C5-C9) prevent formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC), which is the primary mechanism for killing gram-negative encapsulated bacteria, particularly Neisseria species. Affected individuals are specifically susceptible to recurrent Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections.
keyFact: Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9): absent CH50; selective susceptibility to Neisseria (meningitidis/gonorrhoeae); recurrent and familial pattern; vaccinated patients still at risk; autosomal recessive. Eculizumab (anti-C5) causes similar acquired susceptibility.

wrongAnswers.name: Asplenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asplenia causes susceptibility to multiple encapsulated bacteria (Strep pneumoniae, Hib, Meningococcus) but CH50 would be normal; family history of specifically meningococcal disease is not expected.

wrongAnswers.name: Properdin deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Properdin deficiency is X-linked and also causes meningococcal susceptibility via impaired alternative pathway amplification, but CH50 may be normal or mildly reduced; this patient has absent CH50.

wrongAnswers.name: MBL deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MBL deficiency predisposes to encapsulated bacteria in early childhood; CH50 and AP50 would be normal as only the lectin pathway is affected, whereas CH50 is absent here.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with 3 weeks of progressive fatigue, recurrent fevers, and easy bruising.
He reports drenching night sweats and has had two episodes of spontaneous gum bleeding over the past week.
Exam reveals pallor, scattered petechiae on the lower extremities, and mild splenomegaly; no significant lymphadenopathy.
CBC shows WBC 45,000 with a left shift, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, and platelets 28,000; peripheral smear shows large cells with prominent nucleoli and scant cytoplasm.
Bone marrow biopsy reveals greater than 20% blasts that are myeloperoxidase-positive; cytogenetics show t(8;21)(q22;q22).
explanation: AML is a clonal expansion of myeloid blasts in the bone marrow, causing cytopenias through marrow replacement. t(8;21) is associated with AML-M2 and carries a relatively favorable prognosis.
keyFact: AML diagnosis requires ≥20% blasts in the bone marrow or peripheral blood; t(8;21), inv(16), and t(15;17) are recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities with prognostic significance.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CML typically presents with a much higher WBC, more granulocyte precursors at all stages (not predominantly blasts), and the hallmark BCR-ABL t(9;22) translocation; blast crisis would be needed for >20% blasts.

wrongAnswers.name: Myelodysplastic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDS shows dysplastic marrow elements and cytopenias but by definition has <20% blasts; progression to >20% blasts redefines the diagnosis as AML.

wrongAnswers.name: Aplastic Anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aplastic anemia presents with pancytopenia and a hypocellular marrow with no increase in blasts, rather than a hypercellular marrow packed with leukemic cells.

clues: A 7-year-old girl is brought in by her parents for 4 weeks of fatigue, pallor, and limping.
Her parents note she has had recurrent ear infections over the past 2 months and unusual bruising on her shins without significant trauma.
Exam reveals diffuse anterior and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, a palpable spleen tip, and point tenderness over the sternum.
CBC shows WBC 85,000, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, platelets 40,000; peripheral smear reveals numerous small cells with scant cytoplasm, condensed chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli.
Bone marrow biopsy shows greater than 90% blasts; immunophenotyping shows B-cell precursor origin with CD10, CD19, and TdT positivity.
explanation: ALL is the most common childhood malignancy, arising from clonal proliferation of lymphoid precursors. B-cell ALL with favorable cytogenetics (e.g., hyperdiploidy, ETV6-RUNX1) has excellent cure rates exceeding 90% in children.
keyFact: Sternal tenderness from medullary expansion is a classic physical finding in ALL; bone pain that disrupts sleep in a child should raise immediate concern for leukemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Myeloid Leukemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AML blasts are larger with more cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and Auer rods; myeloid markers (MPO, CD13, CD33) would be positive rather than lymphoid markers.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious Mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBV causes lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly but produces reactive lymphocytes (not blasts), a positive monospot test, and does not cause thrombocytopenia of this severity.

wrongAnswers.name: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NHL in children can present similarly but is defined by a dominant tissue mass; when marrow involvement exceeds 25% blasts, the diagnosis is reclassified as ALL.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents for evaluation of early satiety and a sensation of left-sided abdominal fullness over the past 2 months.
He also reports night sweats and a 6-pound unintentional weight loss; he has no lymphadenopathy and his past medical history is unremarkable.
Abdominal exam reveals a spleen palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin; the liver is also mildly enlarged.
CBC shows WBC 210,000 with a full spectrum of myeloid precursors (myelocytes, metamyelocytes, bands), hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, and platelets 650,000; LAP score is markedly decreased.
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) detects a BCR-ABL1 fusion gene resulting from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22.
explanation: CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase, which promotes uncontrolled granulocyte proliferation. Imatinib and subsequent TKIs have transformed CML from a fatal disease to a chronic, manageable condition.
keyFact: A low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score distinguishes CML from a leukemoid reaction, which shows an elevated LAP score despite similar WBC counts.

wrongAnswers.name: Leukemoid Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A leukemoid reaction is a reactive granulocytosis from infection or inflammation with a high LAP score, no BCR-ABL fusion, and an identifiable underlying cause; it lacks basophilia and rarely exceeds 50,000 WBC.

wrongAnswers.name: Myelofibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myelofibrosis causes massive splenomegaly and a leukoerythroblastic picture with teardrop cells, but the WBC is not typically this high and BCR-ABL is absent; marrow fibrosis defines the diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Essential Thrombocythemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ET presents with isolated thrombocytosis without the marked leukocytosis, left-shift granulocytosis, or BCR-ABL fusion seen in CML.

clues: A 68-year-old woman is referred after routine bloodwork shows an abnormal complete blood count; she feels well.
On directed questioning, she notes mild fatigue over the past year and recurrent sinusitis episodes; she recalls feeling a lump in her neck for several months.
Exam shows multiple small, rubbery, non-tender lymph nodes in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions; the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.
CBC shows WBC 68,000 with 85% lymphocytes; peripheral smear shows small mature lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm and numerous smudge cells.
Flow cytometry of peripheral blood shows a clonal B-cell population co-expressing CD5, CD19, CD23, and dim CD20, with kappa light chain restriction.
explanation: CLL is the most common adult leukemia in the Western world, characterized by accumulation of functionally incompetent mature B lymphocytes. The co-expression of CD5 and CD23 on B cells is the immunophenotypic hallmark that distinguishes CLL from mantle cell lymphoma.
keyFact: Smudge cells on peripheral smear are a classic finding in CLL, resulting from the fragility of malignant lymphocytes during slide preparation.

wrongAnswers.name: Mantle Cell Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mantle cell lymphoma can leukemize and co-expresses CD5 but is CD23-negative and cyclin D1-positive due to t(11;14); it has a more aggressive course than CLL.

wrongAnswers.name: Follicular Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Follicular lymphoma is CD10-positive and CD5-negative, and rarely presents as a primary leukemia; it typically presents with painless lymphadenopathy and marrow involvement.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Lymphocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral infections cause polyclonal reactive lymphocytosis with atypical (not mature small) lymphocytes; clonality by flow cytometry confirms malignancy and excludes a reactive process.

clues: A 24-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of fatigue and generalized itching that worsens after hot showers.
He reports fever, drenching night sweats, and a 12-pound weight loss over the past 2 months; he also notes intense generalized pruritus.
Exam reveals a firm, non-tender, 4 cm left supraclavicular lymph node mass; mediastinal dullness is noted on percussion.
Chest CT shows a large anterior mediastinal mass with bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy; CBC shows mild eosinophilia and elevated ESR; LDH is mildly elevated.
Excisional lymph node biopsy shows large binucleated cells with prominent 'owl-eye' nucleoli in a background of mixed inflammatory infiltrate including eosinophils, plasma cells, and fibroblasts.
explanation: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma is characterized by the pathognomonic Reed-Sternberg cell, which is a malignant B cell that has lost B-cell marker expression and creates an inflammatory microenvironment. It is highly curable with ABVD chemotherapy, even in advanced stages.
keyFact: B symptoms (fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss) in Hodgkin lymphoma confer a worse prognosis and upstage the disease classification.

wrongAnswers.name: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: NHL in a young person can present with mediastinal mass but lacks Reed-Sternberg cells; DLBCL or primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma would show sheets of large B cells without the characteristic mixed inflammatory background.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and granulomas on biopsy, not Reed-Sternberg cells; it typically lacks the B symptom complex and affects older patients with pulmonary symptoms.

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious Mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBV can cause cervical lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms in young adults, but lymph nodes are tender, the monospot is positive, and biopsy shows reactive immunoblasts rather than Reed-Sternberg cells.

clues: A 62-year-old woman presents with rapidly enlarging masses in her right neck and groin over the past 3 weeks, accompanied by fever and night sweats.
She reports a 15-pound weight loss and notes that one cervical node became painful after she drank a glass of wine at dinner, though this has not recurred.
Exam shows firm, matted, 5 cm right cervical and 4 cm right inguinal lymph node masses; abdominal exam reveals hepatosplenomegaly.
LDH is markedly elevated at 3x the upper limit of normal; PET/CT shows hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy in multiple nodal regions above and below the diaphragm with bone marrow involvement.
Core biopsy of the cervical node shows sheets of large lymphoid cells with vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli; immunohistochemistry is CD20+, CD10-, BCL6+, MUM1+.
explanation: DLBCL is the most common aggressive lymphoma in adults, with two molecular subtypes: germinal center B-cell (GCB) and activated B-cell (ABC), the latter carrying a worse prognosis. R-CHOP immunochemotherapy remains the backbone of treatment.
keyFact: Markedly elevated LDH in DLBCL reflects rapid tumor cell turnover and is a key component of the International Prognostic Index (IPI), a tool that predicts overall survival.

wrongAnswers.name: Hodgkin Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hodgkin lymphoma in young adults presents with mediastinal mass and Reed-Sternberg cells; it does not typically present with rapidly enlarging peripheral nodes at multiple sites and markedly elevated LDH in this clinical pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Follicular Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Follicular lymphoma is an indolent lymphoma that grows slowly over years; rapid lymph node enlargement over weeks with markedly elevated LDH suggests aggressive disease. Transformation to DLBCL should be considered when follicular lymphoma behaves aggressively.

wrongAnswers.name: Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PTCL can present similarly but immunohistochemistry would show T-cell markers (CD3, CD4, CD8) rather than CD20; PTCL has a worse prognosis and different treatment approach.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with bilateral inguinal swelling that he first noticed 3 years ago; it has been slowly enlarging and is painless.
He denies fever, night sweats, or significant weight loss; he recalls that the lymph nodes seemed to shrink briefly when he had a viral illness last winter.
Exam reveals bilateral inguinal and axillary lymphadenopathy with soft, mobile, non-tender nodes up to 3 cm; the spleen is palpable at the left costal margin.
CBC is normal; bone marrow biopsy shows paratrabecular lymphoid aggregates; LDH is normal; PET/CT shows moderately hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy in multiple nodal regions.
Excisional lymph node biopsy shows a nodular growth pattern with centrocytes and centroblasts; immunohistochemistry is CD20+, CD10+, BCL2+, BCL6+; cytogenetics show t(14;18).
explanation: Follicular lymphoma arises from germinal center B cells and is characterized by t(14;18), which juxtaposes BCL2 to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, driving antiapoptotic BCL2 overexpression. It is an indolent but incurable lymphoma with a waxing and waning clinical course.
keyFact: The spontaneous waxing and waning of lymphadenopathy is a classic clinical feature of follicular lymphoma that can mislead clinicians into attributing it to a reactive process.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Follicular Hyperplasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive hyperplasia shows polyclonal B cells and preserved lymph node architecture; BCL2 expression within follicles is absent because normal germinal center B cells downregulate BCL2.

wrongAnswers.name: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DLBCL grows aggressively over weeks, not years; the clinical course of slow, waxing and waning lymphadenopathy over years is characteristic of an indolent lymphoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Mantle Cell Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mantle cell lymphoma has a nodular pattern but is CD5-positive and cyclin D1-positive with t(11;14); it is not indolent and does not show the slow multi-year course seen here.

clues: A 70-year-old man presents with 3 months of worsening low back pain and increasing fatigue; he also reports two episodes of confusion that resolved spontaneously.
He notes decreased urine output and has lost 10 pounds; he has a history of recurrent bacterial pneumonias over the past year.
Exam shows midline spinal tenderness at L2-L3, pallor, and he appears older than his stated age; no significant lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

Labs show calcium 12.8 mg/dL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL; X-rays show multiple punched-out lytic lesions in the skull and compression fracture at L2; serum protein electrophoresis shows a large M-spike in the gamma region.
Bone marrow biopsy shows 40% clonal plasma cells; serum immunofixation identifies an IgG kappa monoclonal protein with suppressed uninvolved immunoglobulins.
explanation: Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of terminally differentiated plasma cells that produce monoclonal immunoglobulin, causing the CRAB criteria: hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, and bone lesions. The recurrent bacterial infections result from suppression of normal immunoglobulin production (immunoparesis).
keyFact: Punched-out lytic lesions in myeloma are osteoclast-mediated and classically do not show uptake on bone scintigraphy (bone scan is falsely negative); PET/CT or whole-body low-dose CT is preferred for staging.

wrongAnswers.name: Metastatic Prostate Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Prostate cancer metastases are typically osteoblastic (sclerotic) rather than lytic, and PSA would be elevated; there is no M-spike or abnormal plasma cells on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: MGUS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance) is an asymptomatic precursor state with <10% plasma cells and no CRAB criteria; this patient's hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, and bone lesions define active myeloma.

wrongAnswers.name: Waldenstrom Macroglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Waldenstrom's is an IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma; it does not cause lytic bone lesions and presents with hyperviscosity syndrome rather than CRAB criteria.

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with persistent headaches, facial flushing, and a recent episode of digital ischemia.
He has a history of a deep vein thrombosis 2 years ago with no identified provoking cause; he also reports intense itching after warm showers.
Exam shows plethora of the face, injected conjunctivae, and a spleen palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin; blood pressure is 158/94 mmHg.
CBC shows hemoglobin 19.8 g/dL, hematocrit 61%, WBC 14,000 with basophilia, and platelets 520,000; erythropoietin level is undetectable.
Molecular testing detects a gain-of-function mutation in JAK2 at position V617F; bone marrow biopsy shows hypercellularity with trilineage hyperplasia.
explanation: Polycythemia vera is a JAK2-driven myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by erythrocytosis independent of erythropoietin. Aquagenic pruritus, caused by mast cell degranulation after warm water exposure, is a highly characteristic symptom that often precedes diagnosis by years.
keyFact: The JAK2 V617F mutation is found in >95% of PV cases; a suppressed erythropoietin level in the setting of erythrocytosis is a key distinguishing feature from secondary polycythemia, where EPO is elevated.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Polycythemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary polycythemia is driven by elevated erythropoietin from hypoxia (COPD, sleep apnea) or EPO-secreting tumors; EPO is elevated, JAK2 is negative, and there is no trilineage hyperplasia or splenomegaly.

wrongAnswers.name: Essential Thrombocythemia
