Exam shows point tenderness over the radial styloid and the first dorsal extensor compartment; no joint swelling or erythema.
The pain is sharply reproduced when the patient makes a fist over her thumb and the wrist is passively deviated toward the ulnar side.
Ultrasound shows thickening and fluid surrounding the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons in the first dorsal compartment.
explanation: De Quervain tenosynovitis is stenosing inflammation of the first dorsal compartment tendons (APL and EPB), commonly triggered by repetitive pinching or grasping — classically seen in new mothers. The Finkelstein test is diagnostic. Treatment includes thumb spica splinting and corticosteroid injection.
keyFact: De Quervain: radial wrist pain + positive Finkelstein test (ulnar deviation with fist over thumb reproduces pain); involves APL and EPB tendons; classic in new mothers.

wrongAnswers.name: Scaphoid Fracture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scaphoid fracture causes anatomical snuffbox tenderness after trauma (fall on outstretched hand); it is diagnosed by MRI when X-rays are negative and does not involve tendon sheaths.

wrongAnswers.name: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CTS causes median nerve compression with numbness/tingling in the first three fingers, positive Phalen and Tinel signs at the wrist, not radial-sided pain or a positive Finkelstein test.

wrongAnswers.name: Intersection Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Intersection syndrome involves the crossing of the first and second dorsal compartment tendons, causing pain 4-6 cm proximal to the wrist (not at the radial styloid) with a characteristic crepitus.

clues: A 28-year-old male soccer player presents with left knee pain and intermittent locking after twisting his knee during a game.
The next morning, his knee is swollen and he cannot fully extend it; he reports pain along the inner joint line with deep knee bending.
Exam shows a knee effusion; there is tenderness along the medial joint line; no varus or valgus instability is present.
McMurray test with external rotation produces a palpable clunk and medial joint line pain; Lachman test shows a firm endpoint with normal anterior translation.
MRI knee demonstrates a complex tear of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus with increased signal extending to the articular surface on two consecutive slices.
explanation: Meniscal tears occur from rotational mechanisms in athletes or degenerative changes in older patients. The medial meniscus is more commonly injured. MRI is the gold standard for diagnosis, and management ranges from physical therapy to arthroscopic repair or partial meniscectomy.
keyFact: Medial meniscal tear: joint line tenderness + McMurray test (clunk with rotation) + MRI confirmation; Lachman test negative (stable ACL) distinguishes from ACL tear.

wrongAnswers.name: ACL Tear
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ACL tear causes immediate hemarthrosis, positive Lachman and anterior drawer tests from anterior tibial instability; an ACL tear does not cause the positive McMurray test or meniscal clunk.

wrongAnswers.name: Lateral Collateral Ligament Sprain
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LCL sprain causes lateral knee instability with varus stress testing, not joint-line tenderness medially or a positive McMurray test.

wrongAnswers.name: Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Patellofemoral syndrome causes anterior knee pain with stairs and prolonged sitting, not joint-line tenderness, effusion, or a positive McMurray test.

clues: A 22-year-old female basketball player presents with acute right knee swelling and inability to bear weight after a non-contact pivoting injury during a game.

She heard a pop at the moment of injury and was unable to continue playing; within one hour the knee became markedly swollen; she now reports a sensation of the knee giving way when she tries to walk.
Examination shows a tense effusion of the right knee; the Lachman test reveals increased anterior tibial translation with a soft, mushy endpoint; the anterior drawer test is also positive.
X-rays of the right knee show no fracture; aspiration of the knee joint yields 40 mL of bloody fluid.

MRI shows complete discontinuity of the ligament fibers originating from the lateral femoral condyle, with bone contusions on the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau in a pivot-shift pattern.
explanation: ACL tears occur from non-contact deceleration/pivoting mechanisms and are more common in females. Immediate hemarthrosis, positive Lachman test, and anterior drawer test are characteristic. MRI confirms the diagnosis; reconstruction is typically offered to active patients.
keyFact: ACL tear: non-contact deceleration mechanism + pop + immediate hemarthrosis + positive Lachman test (most sensitive) + pivot shift; MRI shows bone contusions on lateral compartment.

wrongAnswers.name: Posterior Cruciate Ligament Tear
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PCL tear occurs from direct posterior force on the tibia (dashboard injury), causes posterior drawer test positivity and posterior tibial sag, not anterior instability or positive Lachman.

wrongAnswers.name: Patella Dislocation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Patella dislocation causes lateral knee instability with apprehension on lateral patella translation and medial retinaculum tenderness, not anterior tibial instability or positive Lachman test.

wrongAnswers.name: Tibial Plateau Fracture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tibial plateau fracture causes hemarthrosis from high-energy or valgus impact, seen on CT/X-ray as articular depression; it does not cause Lachman instability or pivot shift.

clues: A 58-year-old man with known chronic liver disease is brought in by family for behavioral changes over 48 hours.
He had a large upper GI bleed one week ago; family notes he recently stopped his lactulose and was given sedatives for anxiety.
Exam shows jaundice, spider angiomata, a flapping tremor elicited with outstretched hands, and altered mental status; he is disoriented to time and place.
Serum ammonia is 148 mcmol/L; CT head is unremarkable; EEG shows diffuse triphasic waves.
After lactulose and rifaximin are initiated and the precipitating factors are addressed, his mental status improves over 72 hours with ammonia trending down to 42 mcmol/L.
explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy results from impaired hepatic clearance of gut-derived toxins (primarily ammonia) in cirrhosis, causing neuropsychiatric dysfunction. Common precipitants include GI bleeding, infection, constipation, medications, and electrolyte disturbances. Treatment involves lactulose and rifaximin.
keyFact: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis + elevated ammonia + precipitating factor (GI bleed, infection, constipation, sedatives) in cirrhotic patient; EEG triphasic waves; treat with lactulose + rifaximin.

wrongAnswers.name: Wernicke Encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia from thiamine deficiency; it lacks asterixis, elevated ammonia, and is not specifically triggered by GI bleeding in a cirrhotic.

wrongAnswers.name: Subdural Hematoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Subdural hematoma causes confusion and focal neurologic signs in a patient at fall risk, but CT head would show a crescent-shaped hyperdensity; it does not explain ammonia elevation or asterixis.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcohol Withdrawal Delirium
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alcohol withdrawal causes agitation, tremor, tachycardia, and seizures typically 24-72 hours after cessation; it does not cause elevated ammonia, asterixis, or triphasic EEG waves.

clues: A 62-year-old woman presents with six months of watery, non-bloody diarrhea with 6-10 loose stools per day and significant weight loss.
She has a history of a chronic autoimmune condition and reports that the diarrhea has been unresponsive to dietary modifications; no fever or blood in stool.
Exam shows mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound; no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.
Colonoscopy reveals a grossly normal-appearing colon without visible lesions, erythema, or ulceration.
Random biopsies from the ascending and transverse colon show a thickened subepithelial collagen band (greater than 10 micrometers) and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.
explanation: Microscopic colitis (collagenous or lymphocytic subtypes) presents with chronic watery non-bloody diarrhea with a grossly normal colonoscopy; diagnosis requires mucosal biopsies. It is associated with NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, and autoimmune conditions. Budesonide is the most effective treatment.
keyFact: Microscopic colitis: watery non-bloody diarrhea + normal colonoscopy appearance + abnormal colonic biopsy (collagen band greater than 10 mcm or increased intraepithelial lymphocytes); associated with NSAIDs and PPIs.

wrongAnswers.name: Irritable Bowel Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IBS-D causes chronic diarrhea with abdominal cramping but does not cause significant weight loss, and colonoscopic biopsies are normal without collagen band thickening.

wrongAnswers.name: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IBD shows visible endoscopic lesions (ulceration, erythema, granularity) and deeper histologic inflammation; microscopic colitis has a grossly normal colonoscopy with only microscopic changes.

wrongAnswers.name: Active Celiac Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Active celiac disease causes diarrhea with villous atrophy on small bowel biopsy; the colon biopsy in celiac is normal (though celiac is a comorbidity, it does not explain the colonic histologic changes here).

clues: A 52-year-old woman presents with colicky right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and yellowing of her skin.
She had a cholecystectomy two years ago; she now has dark urine and pale stools; the pain comes in waves and radiates to her right shoulder.
Exam shows scleral icterus, right upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs, and a low-grade temperature of 37.9 degrees Celsius.

Labs show elevated direct bilirubin (6.2 mg/dL), elevated ALP and GGT, and mildly elevated ALT/AST in a cholestatic pattern; RUQ ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct (11 mm) without visible stones.
MRCP reveals a 9 mm filling defect in the distal common bile duct; ERCP with sphincterotomy extracts the stone.
explanation: Choledocholithiasis occurs when gallstones (or retained stones post-cholecystectomy) lodge in the common bile duct, causing obstructive jaundice with a cholestatic biochemical pattern. MRCP is the preferred non-invasive diagnostic test; ERCP is therapeutic. Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) indicates cholangitis.
keyFact: Choledocholithiasis: obstructive jaundice (elevated direct bilirubin, ALP, GGT) + dilated CBD on US; MRCP diagnoses; ERCP treats; Charcot triad (+ fever) = cholangitis; Reynolds pentad (+ shock/AMS) = severe cholangitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Cholecystitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute cholecystitis causes RUQ pain, fever, and positive Murphy sign from gallbladder inflammation; it does not cause obstructive jaundice, dilated CBD, or cholestatic lab pattern unless stones migrate to the CBD.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PSC causes cholestatic liver disease with multifocal biliary strictures on MRCP ('beaded appearance'), is associated with IBD, and does not present acutely with a discrete filling defect representing a stone.

wrongAnswers.name: Pancreatic Cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pancreatic head cancer causes painless progressive obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign); MRCP shows a mass with double-duct sign rather than a discrete CBD filling defect.

clues: A 55-year-old man with a distended abdomen presents with fever and worsening abdominal pain.
He has a history of chronic liver disease and has not had a paracentesis in three months.
Abdomen is diffusely tender with shifting dullness and a fluid wave; asterixis is present on exam.
Diagnostic paracentesis yields turbid fluid with a WBC of 800 cells/mcL and a PMN count of 420 cells/mcL; ascitic fluid culture grows Escherichia coli.
Serum-to-ascites albumin gradient is 1.5 g/dL with ascitic PMN count of 420 cells/mcL and no evidence of a surgically treatable intra-abdominal focus on imaging.
explanation: SBP is a bacterial infection of ascitic fluid without an intra-abdominal source, occurring in cirrhotic patients with ascites. Diagnosis requires ascitic PMN count of 250 cells/mcL or greater. E. coli and Klebsiella are most common organisms. Albumin infusion reduces the risk of hepatorenal syndrome.
keyFact: SBP diagnosis: ascitic fluid PMN 250 cells/mcL or more; treat with IV cefotaxime + IV albumin (reduces hepatorenal syndrome); long-term norfloxacin or TMP-SMX for secondary prophylaxis.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Bacterial Peritonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary peritonitis from gut perforation shows very high ascitic WBC, multiple organisms on culture, and glucose less than 50 mg/dL in ascites — requires surgical intervention, not antibiotics alone.

wrongAnswers.name: Hepatic Encephalopathy (isolated)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hepatic encephalopathy causes confusion and asterixis in cirrhosis but does not cause peritoneal signs or turbid ascites with PMN greater than 250; SBP can precipitate HE but they are distinct diagnoses.

wrongAnswers.name: Tuberculous Peritonitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TB peritonitis causes ascites with lymphocytic predominance, elevated adenosine deaminase, and is associated with TB exposure in endemic areas — not an acute presentation with E. coli on culture.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset left flank pain radiating to the groin and gross hematuria.
She has a history of nephrotic syndrome with membranous nephropathy and worsening bilateral leg edema.
Left costovertebral angle tenderness is present; significant pitting edema is noted in both lower extremities.
Creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 2.4 mg/dL; LDH is elevated; CT abdomen with contrast shows a filling defect in the left renal vein extending toward the IVC.
Antithrombin III levels are markedly low from urinary losses in a patient with heavy proteinuria exceeding 8 g/day.
explanation: Renal vein thrombosis is a serious complication of nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy, due to loss of antithrombin III and other anticoagulant proteins in the urine. It presents with flank pain, hematuria, and worsening renal function. CT venography confirms the diagnosis.
keyFact: Renal vein thrombosis: classic complication of membranous nephropathy; caused by urinary loss of antithrombin III + hypercoagulable state; flank pain + worsening proteinuria; diagnosed by CT venography.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Artery Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Renal artery stenosis causes hypertension and renal insufficiency with a bruit over the flank; it does not cause acute flank pain, hematuria, or venous filling defects, and is associated with atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia.

wrongAnswers.name: Ureterolithiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ureteral stones cause colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria, but CT would show a stone rather than a venous filling defect, and is not specifically associated with nephrotic syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Pyelonephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pyelonephritis causes flank pain with fever, dysuria, pyuria, and positive urine culture from bacterial infection; it does not cause a venous filling defect or occur in the context of nephrotic syndrome.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with six months of left flank pain, fever, and unintentional weight loss.
She has a history of diabetes and recurrent urinary tract infections with Proteus mirabilis.
Left costovertebral angle tenderness is present with a palpable tender flank mass; there is no peritoneal irritation.
CT abdomen shows a markedly enlarged left kidney replaced by multiple low-density masses in a 'bear paw' pattern surrounding a central staghorn calculus.
Nephrectomy specimen shows complete replacement of renal parenchyma by lipid-laden foamy macrophages (xanthoma cells) with chronic inflammatory infiltrate.
explanation: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a destructive chronic renal infection characterized by replacement of normal parenchyma by lipid-laden macrophages (xanthoma cells), typically associated with staghorn calculi and Proteus or E. coli infection. The 'bear paw' CT sign and nephrectomy for treatment are characteristic.
keyFact: XGP: 'bear paw' CT sign (enlarged kidney with low-density masses surrounding staghorn calculus) + chronic UTI (Proteus/E. coli) + diabetes; lipid-laden macrophages on pathology; treated by nephrectomy.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RCC presents with the classic triad of flank pain, hematuria, and palpable mass; CT shows a solid enhancing renal mass without the 'bear paw' pattern or staghorn calculus; no foamy macrophages on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Renal abscess causes focal fluid collection within the kidney with fever and flank pain, but CT shows a discrete single abscess cavity rather than diffuse parenchymal replacement with a 'bear paw' pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Transitional Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Urothelial carcinoma involves the renal pelvis/collecting system with hematuria and filling defects on imaging; it is not associated with staghorn calculi, lipid-laden macrophages, or the 'bear paw' CT appearance.

clues: A 68-year-old man presents with progressively worsening whole-body itching and generalized redness over the past three years.
He reports severe, unremitting pruritus; the redness now covers more than 90% of his body surface area.
Skin is diffusely erythematous and thickened; alopecia, nail dystrophy, fissured leathery palms and soles, and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy are noted on exam.
Flow cytometry of peripheral blood shows an expanded population of CD4+ CD7- CD26- T-cells with a CD4:CD8 ratio of 22:1 and more than 1,000 atypical cells per mcL.
Skin biopsy shows epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei and a clonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangement.
explanation: Sezary syndrome is the leukemic phase of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, defined by the triad of erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and circulating Sezary cells (greater than 1000/mcL) with a clonal T-cell population. It carries a poor prognosis; treatment includes extracorporeal photopheresis, bexarotene, and mogamulizumab.
keyFact: Sezary syndrome triad: erythroderma + lymphadenopathy + circulating Sezary cells (cerebriform nuclei, CD4+CD7-CD26-, greater than 1000/mcL); clonal TCR rearrangement; treat with extracorporeal photopheresis.

wrongAnswers.name: Erythrodermic Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Erythrodermic psoriasis causes diffuse erythema with scaling but lacks circulating malignant T-cells, Sezary cells on biopsy, or clonal TCR rearrangement; it is an inflammatory, not neoplastic, condition.

wrongAnswers.name: Severe Atopic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Severe atopic dermatitis causes erythroderma and pruritus but occurs in younger patients, lacks malignant T-cell clones, and does not produce circulating Sezary cells or lymphadenopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Mycosis Fungoides
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mycosis fungoides is the non-leukemic form of CTCL presenting with patches and plaques progressing to tumors; Sezary syndrome is specifically the leukemic variant with erythroderma and more than 1000 circulating Sezary cells.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with acute joint pain, swelling, and difficulty bearing weight over the past 2 days.
He has a history of diabetes and a recent skin infection near the affected joint.
The knee is warm, erythematous, and exquisitely tender with any passive range of motion; fever of 38.9°C is noted.
Joint aspiration yields cloudy fluid with 85,000 WBC/mm³, greater than 90% neutrophils; Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters.
Synovial fluid culture grows Staphylococcus aureus.
explanation: Septic arthritis is a surgical emergency caused by bacterial seeding of the joint space, most commonly by S. aureus. It requires urgent joint washout and IV antibiotics to prevent cartilage destruction.
keyFact: Synovial WBC >50,000/mm³ with >90% PMNs is strongly suggestive of septic arthritis; immediate joint aspiration and IV antibiotics are required.

wrongAnswers.name: Gout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gout typically shows needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid and does not grow bacteria on culture

wrongAnswers.name: Pseudogout
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pseudogout shows rhomboid positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals and does not cause bacterial growth in joint fluid

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis follows infection at a distant site and synovial fluid is sterile; WBC is typically <20,000/mm³

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with right shoulder pain and progressive weakness that began after he heard a pop while lifting a heavy box three months ago.
The pain is worst with overhead reaching and at night when he rolls onto the affected side; he has worked as a painter for over 30 years.

There is weakness with resisted abduction and external rotation of the right shoulder; the drop arm test is positive, with the arm falling to his side when lowered from 90 degrees of abduction; active range of motion is limited but passive range is full.
Shoulder X-ray shows superior migration of the humeral head with a decreased acromiohumeral distance of 5 mm; no fracture is seen.

MRI shows complete discontinuity of the supraspinatus tendon with retraction of the musculotendinous junction to the level of the glenoid face and grade 2 fatty infiltration of the muscle belly on sagittal images.
explanation: Rotator cuff tears most commonly involve the supraspinatus tendon and present with pain and weakness with overhead activity. Full-thickness tears often require surgical repair, especially in active patients.
keyFact: The drop arm test (inability to slowly lower the abducted arm) and positive empty can test are highly specific for supraspinatus tear.

wrongAnswers.name: Shoulder impingement syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Impingement causes pain without significant weakness and does not show tendon discontinuity on MRI

wrongAnswers.name: Biceps tendon rupture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Biceps rupture presents with a Popeye deformity and weakness in supination/flexion, not abduction

wrongAnswers.name: Acromioclavicular joint injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AC joint injury causes focal tenderness at the AC joint and is diagnosed by cross-body adduction test, not weakness in abduction

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with hand tingling and pain that wakes her from sleep several times per week.
Symptoms are worse in the dominant hand; she reports that shaking the hand relieves the tingling temporarily.
Tingling localizes to the first three digits and the lateral half of the fourth digit; Phalen test and Tinel sign at the wrist are both positive.
Two-point discrimination is reduced in the median nerve distribution; thenar muscle atrophy is beginning.
Nerve conduction studies show prolonged distal motor and sensory latency of the median nerve at the wrist.
explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from median nerve compression at the wrist and is the most common peripheral neuropathy. Night symptoms and symptom relief with wrist shaking are characteristic.
keyFact: Carpal tunnel syndrome spares thenar eminence sensation because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve branches proximal to the carpal tunnel; nerve conduction studies are the gold standard.

wrongAnswers.name: Cervical radiculopathy C6
wrongAnswers.whyNot: C6 radiculopathy causes neck pain radiating to the thumb but is not worsened by wrist flexion and Tinel sign at the wrist is negative

wrongAnswers.name: Cubital tunnel syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cubital tunnel syndrome involves ulnar nerve compression causing fourth and fifth digit symptoms, not the first three digits

wrongAnswers.name: Thoracic outlet syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thoracic outlet syndrome causes diffuse arm symptoms exacerbated by arm elevation, not localized to the median nerve distribution

clues: A 48-year-old woman who works on her feet all day presents with heel pain for 2 months.
The pain is worst with the first few steps in the morning and after prolonged sitting; it improves with continued walking.
Point tenderness is elicited at the medial calcaneal tuberosity; pain worsens with passive dorsiflexion of the toes (windlass test).
Ultrasound shows plantar fascia thickening to 6 mm at its calcaneal insertion with surrounding hypoechogenicity and loss of normal fibrillar pattern.
MRI shows increased T2 signal within the proximal plantar fascia at its calcaneal insertion with surrounding periplantar soft tissue edema and partial tearing of the medial band.
explanation: Plantar fasciitis is the most common cause of heel pain, caused by degenerative microtears at the calcaneal insertion of the plantar fascia. First-step morning pain is the hallmark symptom.
keyFact: Morning first-step pain that improves with walking but returns after rest is the classic pattern; calcaneal spurs on x-ray are common but are not causative.

wrongAnswers.name: Calcaneal stress fracture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stress fracture pain worsens with activity throughout the day and squeeze test is positive; MRI confirms trabecular edema

wrongAnswers.name: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tarsal tunnel syndrome involves tibial nerve compression causing burning and tingling on the sole with a positive Tinel sign at the medial ankle

wrongAnswers.name: Achilles tendinopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Achilles tendinopathy causes pain at the posterior heel and tendon, not the plantar medial calcaneus

clues: A 22-year-old male with a recent lower extremity injury reports rapidly increasing leg pain despite adequate immobilization and analgesia.
The pain is described as out of proportion to the injury, with a sensation of tightness and pressure building in the leg.
The leg is tense, swollen, and firm to palpation; pain is markedly worsened with passive dorsiflexion of the toes.
Compartment pressure measurement reveals anterior compartment pressure of 42 mmHg with a diastolic BP of 75 mmHg, yielding a delta pressure of 33 mmHg.
Repeat compartment pressure measurements show anterior 48 mmHg, lateral 44 mmHg, deep posterior 46 mmHg, and superficial posterior 40 mmHg with delta pressure below 30 mmHg in all four compartments.
explanation: Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency caused by elevated intracompartmental pressure compromising perfusion. Delta pressure (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) less than 30 mmHg is an absolute indication for fasciotomy.
keyFact: Delta pressure (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) <30 mmHg is the indication for fasciotomy; loss of pulse is a late sign and should not be awaited before operative intervention.

wrongAnswers.name: Deep vein thrombosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DVT causes swelling and calf pain but does not cause extreme tenderness with passive stretch or elevated compartment pressures

wrongAnswers.name: Arterial injury
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Arterial injury may coexist but compartment syndrome primarily causes pain with passive stretch before pulse loss occurs

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis presents with skin erythema, warmth, and fever but not with firm compartments or pain on passive muscle stretch

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with progressive right hip pain and stiffness over the past 4 months.
He has a history of systemic lupus erythematosus treated with prolonged high-dose corticosteroids over several years.
Internal rotation of the hip is restricted and painful; gait is antalgic; no overlying skin changes or warmth.
X-ray shows flattening of the femoral head with a subchondral lucency (crescent sign).
MRI shows a serpiginous low-signal band surrounding a segment of subchondral bone with evidence of femoral head collapse.
explanation: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head results from interruption of blood supply to the femoral head, commonly caused by corticosteroids, alcohol, or trauma. MRI is the most sensitive modality for early detection.
keyFact: The crescent sign on x-ray represents subchondral fracture and indicates collapse; MRI is required for early diagnosis before x-ray changes appear.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteoarthritis of the hip
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteoarthritis typically affects older patients, shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes on x-ray, and lacks the subchondral crescent sign

wrongAnswers.name: Femoral neck stress fracture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stress fracture shows a distinct fracture line on MRI and typically occurs in young athletes or elderly osteoporotic patients

wrongAnswers.name: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Transient osteoporosis is self-limiting, shows marrow edema on MRI without subchondral collapse, and resolves spontaneously over months

clues: A 25-year-old woman presents with chronic widespread joint pain, easy bruising, and joints that seem to move too far.
She reports frequent shoulder and patellar dislocations with minimal trauma since childhood, and her skin stretches abnormally far and heals poorly, leaving wide scars.
Skin extends more than 1.5 cm at the volar forearm; Beighton score is 8 out of 9; multiple hyperpigmented, atrophic, papyraceous scars are present over the shins and knees.
Echocardiogram shows no aortic root dilation or mitral valve prolapse; ophthalmologic exam shows no lens subluxation; coagulation studies are normal.
Genetic testing reveals a heterozygous pathogenic variant in COL5A1.
explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a group of heritable connective tissue disorders caused by collagen defects, characterized by skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility, and tissue fragility. The hypermobile subtype is most common.
keyFact: Classical EDS (COL5A1/COL5A2 mutations) features skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, and joint hypermobility. Hypermobile EDS is clinically diagnosed without a known gene. Vascular EDS (COL3A1) is the most dangerous subtype.

wrongAnswers.name: Marfan syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Marfan syndrome features aortic root dilation and lens subluxation but does not cause skin hyperextensibility or the degree of joint instability seen in EDS

wrongAnswers.name: Hypermobility spectrum disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypermobility spectrum disorder lacks the additional EDS features of skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, and confirmed pathogenic collagen variants

wrongAnswers.name: Loeys-Dietz syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Loeys-Dietz syndrome features hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and aortic aneurysms and is caused by TGFBR1/2 mutations, not collagen gene mutations

clues: A 17-year-old unusually tall male presents with chest pain, a recent spontaneous pneumothorax, and blurry vision in one eye.
He reports occasional palpitations; his father died suddenly at age 42 from an unknown cause.
Arm span exceeds height; pectus excavatum, high-arched palate, and superotemporal lens subluxation are found on exam.
Echocardiogram shows aortic root dilation at 4.8 cm with moderate aortic regurgitation.
FBN1 gene sequencing identifies a pathogenic fibrillin-1 variant.
explanation: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by FBN1 mutations affecting fibrillin-1. Aortic root dilation is the major cause of morbidity and mortality, necessitating regular imaging and beta-blocker therapy.
keyFact: Ectopia lentis (superotemporal lens subluxation) combined with aortic root dilation and a positive family history meets Ghent criteria for Marfan syndrome; competitive sports restriction is required.

wrongAnswers.name: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EDS features skin hyperextensibility and joint instability without lens subluxation or significant aortic root dilation in most subtypes

wrongAnswers.name: Homocystinuria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Homocystinuria causes lens subluxation but inferiorly and is autosomal recessive; elevated plasma homocysteine distinguishes it from Marfan

wrongAnswers.name: Loeys-Dietz syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Loeys-Dietz syndrome features bifid uvula, hypertelorism, and arterial tortuosity and is caused by TGFBR mutations, not FBN1

clues: A 62-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of non-pruritic swelling of the face, lips, and tongue over the past 8 months.
Episodes last 48-72 hours and do not respond to antihistamines or epinephrine; she has no family history of similar episodes.
Laryngeal edema requiring intubation during one episode; during another attack, severe colicky abdominal pain from bowel wall involvement is noted on exam.
C4 is persistently low between attacks; C1q is markedly reduced; C1 inhibitor level and function are both low.
Anti-C1 inhibitor antibodies are detected; workup reveals an underlying B-cell lymphoma.
explanation: Acquired C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency differs from hereditary angioedema in that it occurs after age 40, is associated with lymphoproliferative disorders or anti-C1q antibodies, and C1q levels are low (which is normal in the hereditary form).
keyFact: Low C1q is the key distinguishing feature of acquired versus hereditary C1 inhibitor deficiency; treatment of the underlying malignancy may resolve attacks.

wrongAnswers.name: Hereditary angioedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hereditary angioedema has autosomal dominant inheritance, positive family history, onset in childhood or young adulthood, and normal C1q levels

wrongAnswers.name: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ACE inhibitor angioedema occurs in patients on ACE inhibitors, is bradykinin-mediated, and resolves after drug discontinuation; complement levels are normal

wrongAnswers.name: Allergic angioedema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Allergic angioedema is IgE-mediated, occurs with urticaria and pruritus, responds to epinephrine, and complement levels are normal

clues: A 3-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive and recurrent infections since birth.
She has had recurrent oral candidiasis and persistent diarrhea; her parents are consanguineous.
No thymic shadow is visible on chest X-ray; costochondral junction abnormalities are noted on skeletal survey; lymphocyte count is markedly low with absent T, B, and NK cells.
Lymphocyte proliferation assays show no response to mitogens; immunoglobulin levels are very low across all classes.
Adenosine deaminase enzyme activity in red blood cells is undetectable; gene sequencing shows biallelic pathogenic variants in ADA.
explanation: ADA-SCID is an autosomal recessive form of SCID caused by toxic deoxyadenosine metabolite accumulation that destroys developing lymphocytes. It accounts for approximately 15% of SCID cases and was the first disease treated with gene therapy.
keyFact: ADA-SCID shows absent T, B, and NK cells (T-B-NK- phenotype); treatment options include PEG-ADA enzyme replacement, allogeneic HSCT, or gene therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked SCID
wrongAnswers.whyNot: X-linked SCID (IL2RG mutation) shows a T-B+NK- pattern, occurs only in males, and is not caused by ADA enzyme deficiency

wrongAnswers.name: DiGeorge syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DiGeorge syndrome causes selective T-cell deficiency with normal B and NK cells, and is associated with 22q11 deletion and cardiac defects

wrongAnswers.name: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome presents with thrombocytopenia, eczema, and progressive combined immunodeficiency but does not cause absent B and NK cells from birth

clues: A 7-year-old child presents with disseminated mycobacterial infection despite appropriate vaccination and no known immunodeficiency.
She has had two prior episodes of Salmonella bacteremia; she now presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly.
Mycobacterium avium complex is cultured from bone marrow; standard T and B cell counts, immunoglobulin levels, and neutrophil oxidative burst are all normal.
IFN-gamma production by T cells is absent after stimulation with IL-12; NK cell cytotoxicity is impaired.
Biallelic loss-of-function mutations affecting the IL-12 receptor beta-1 chain are identified on gene sequencing.
explanation: IL-12 receptor deficiency is the most common single-gene defect causing Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD). IL-12 drives Th1 responses and IFN-gamma production; its absence impairs macrophage activation against intracellular pathogens.
keyFact: IL-12/IL-12R pathway defects cause selective susceptibility to weakly virulent mycobacteria and Salmonella while preserving overall T and B cell numbers; IFN-gamma therapy is a treatment option.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic granulomatous disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CGD involves NADPH oxidase defects causing susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms; DHR assay is abnormal and the IL-12 pathway is intact

wrongAnswers.name: IFN-gamma receptor deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IFN-gamma receptor deficiency also causes MSMD but is differentiated by normal IL-12-induced IFN-gamma production with defective IFN-gamma receptor signaling downstream

wrongAnswers.name: STAT1 deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: STAT1 deficiency causes MSMD and viral susceptibility; IFN-gamma signaling downstream of its receptor is impaired, not IL-12 receptor function

clues: A 19-year-old college student presents with a second serious bacterial meningitis episode within 3 years; she was previously healthy.
A sibling had a meningococcal infection; she has no asplenia and her vaccination history is up to date.
Meningismus and scattered petechiae are present on exam; no features of autoimmune disease are noted.
CH50 (total hemolytic complement) is undetectable; AH50 (alternative pathway) is also absent; C3 level is normal.
Individual complement component testing reveals undetectable C5 with biallelic C5 null mutations on sequencing.
explanation: Terminal complement deficiencies (C5-C9) cause selective susceptibility to Neisseria species due to failure to form the membrane attack complex. Recurrent meningococcal or gonococcal infections in an otherwise healthy person should prompt complement evaluation.
keyFact: Undetectable CH50 with normal C3 points to a terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9); these patients require lifelong prophylactic antibiotics and vaccination against encapsulated organisms.

wrongAnswers.name: Asplenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Asplenia also predisposes to encapsulated organisms but CH50 is normal; susceptibility spans pneumococcus, H. influenzae, and meningococcus equally

wrongAnswers.name: C3 deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: C3 deficiency causes broad susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria with low C3 and low CH50, and also impairs opsonization causing immune complex disease

wrongAnswers.name: Properdin deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Properdin deficiency is X-linked and causes absent AH50 with normal CH50, affecting only the alternative pathway

clues: A 9-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of repetitive involuntary movements and vocalizations noticed by his teacher.
His parents report the movements increase with stress and can be briefly suppressed but always return; they wax and wane over time.
Multiple motor tics (eye blinking, head jerking, shoulder shrugging) and at least one vocal tic (throat clearing, sniffing) are observed on exam; no focal neurological deficits.
EEG is normal; brain MRI is normal; OCD and ADHD screening questionnaires are positive.

Video-recorded observation across multiple visits documents simultaneous eye blinking, head jerking, shoulder shrugging, throat clearing, and sniffing tics persisting across all documented sessions spanning 14 months.
explanation: Tourette syndrome requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, present for more than 12 months with onset before age 18. It is highly comorbid with ADHD (50-60%) and OCD (40-50%). Most cases improve in adulthood.
keyFact: Coprolalia (obscene vocalizations) occurs in only approximately 10% of patients and is not required for diagnosis; the defining criteria are multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic lasting >12 months.

wrongAnswers.name: Provisional tic disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Provisional tic disorder has tics present for less than 12 months; this patient has had tics for over a year

wrongAnswers.name: Persistent motor tic disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Persistent motor tic disorder has only motor OR vocal tics, not both; Tourette requires both motor and vocal tics

wrongAnswers.name: Stereotypic movement disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stereotypic movements are repetitive but not suppressible, not preceded by a premonitory urge, and do not fluctuate; they are not classified as tics

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with episodic severe headaches, palpitations, and profuse sweating occurring several times per week.
Episodes last 15-30 minutes and are sometimes triggered by bending over or emotional stress; blood pressure during one episode reaches 210/120 mmHg.
Between episodes she is normotensive; thyroid exam is normal; no abdominal bruit or cushingoid features on exam.
24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines are markedly elevated at 3-4 times the upper limit of normal.
CT abdomen reveals a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass with heterogeneous enhancement and functional imaging uptake localizing to that mass.
explanation: Pheochromocytoma classically presents with the triad of episodic headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis with paroxysmal hypertension. Pre-operative alpha-blockade followed by beta-blockade is mandatory before surgical resection.
keyFact: Alpha-blockade MUST precede beta-blockade in pheochromocytoma; giving a beta-blocker first can cause paradoxical hypertensive crisis by unmasking unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary hyperaldosteronism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes sustained (not episodic) hypertension with hypokalemia; catecholamines are not elevated

wrongAnswers.name: Carcinoid syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoid syndrome causes flushing and diarrhea with elevated urine 5-HIAA, not metanephrines, and does not typically cause hypertensive crises

wrongAnswers.name: Panic disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Panic disorder can mimic pheochromocytoma symptoms but does not produce elevated urine metanephrines or an adrenal mass on imaging

clues: A 47-year-old man with resistant hypertension on 3 agents presents with muscle weakness and cramping.
He has persistent hypokalemia of 2.9 mEq/L on repeat testing despite oral supplementation.
Blood pressure is 158/94 mmHg; no peripheral edema, no cushingoid features, no abdominal bruit on exam.
Plasma aldosterone is elevated at 32 ng/dL with suppressed plasma renin activity less than 0.5 ng/mL/hr; aldosterone-to-renin ratio exceeds 30; confirmatory testing fails to suppress aldosterone.
Adrenal CT shows a 1.5 cm left adrenal adenoma; adrenal vein sampling lateralizes aldosterone secretion to the left side.
explanation: Primary hyperaldosteronism is the most common secondary cause of hypertension. Aldosterone-secreting adenoma accounts for approximately 35% and is treated with adrenalectomy; bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is treated with mineralocorticoid antagonists.
keyFact: ARR >30 (with aldosterone >15 ng/dL) is the preferred screening test; adrenal vein sampling is the gold standard to differentiate unilateral adenoma from bilateral hyperplasia before surgery.

wrongAnswers.name: Pheochromocytoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pheochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension with elevated catecholamines; aldosterone and renin are not the primary abnormality

wrongAnswers.name: Cushing syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cushing syndrome causes hypertension through cortisol excess; hypercortisolism labs including elevated UFC and failed dexamethasone suppression distinguish it

wrongAnswers.name: Renovascular hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Renovascular hypertension causes elevated renin (not suppressed) due to renal artery stenosis and does not cause hypokalemia through aldosterone excess

clues: A 32-year-old woman presents with scaly, scarring plaques on her face and scalp that have been slowly progressive over 2 years.
She has no joint pain, oral ulcers, or systemic symptoms; previously affected areas show permanent scarring and hypopigmentation.
Adherent scale with follicular plugging (carpet-tack sign) is present on the cheeks, nose, and ears; scarring alopecia is noted on the scalp.
ANA is weakly positive at 1:80; anti-dsDNA is negative; complement levels and urinalysis are normal.

Skin biopsy shows vacuolar interface dermatitis with basement membrane thickening and perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate; direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 at the dermal-epidermal junction.
explanation: Discoid lupus erythematosus is the most common chronic cutaneous lupus, primarily affecting sun-exposed areas. It causes permanent scarring and alopecia. Only 5-10% progress to systemic lupus. Hydroxychloroquine and sun protection are first-line.
keyFact: The carpet-tack sign (follicular plugging with adherent scale) and scarring with hypopigmentation are hallmarks of DLE. Progression to SLE is more likely with widespread lesions, leukopenia, or strongly positive ANA.

wrongAnswers.name: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCLE presents with non-scarring photosensitive annular or psoriasiform lesions and positive anti-Ro/SSA antibodies; it does not cause follicular plugging

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatomyositis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatomyositis features heliotrope rash and Gottron papules with proximal muscle weakness; skin biopsy lacks follicular plugging

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriasis plaques have silvery-white scale on an erythematous base, do not cause scarring or follicular plugging, and DIF is negative

clues: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with severe vulvar itching, burning, and dyspareunia that has been progressive over 18 months.
She has been treated for presumed yeast infections multiple times without improvement.
Porcelain-white, atrophic plaques are distributed in a figure-of-eight pattern around the vulva and perianal area; fissures and loss of normal labial architecture are present on exam.
KOH preparation is negative; vaginal pH is mildly elevated; the skin appears parchment-like with complete effacement of the labia minora.
Punch biopsy shows epidermal atrophy, homogenized collagen in the upper dermis, and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate below the zone of fibrosis.
explanation: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis most common in postmenopausal women and prepubertal girls. It carries a 4-5% lifetime risk of squamous cell carcinoma. First-line treatment is high-potency topical corticosteroids.
keyFact: Lichen sclerosus carries a 4-5% risk of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma; patients need long-term surveillance. Biopsy is essential to confirm diagnosis and exclude malignancy in atypical areas.

wrongAnswers.name: Lichen simplex chronicus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lichen simplex chronicus shows skin thickening from chronic rubbing without the atrophy, white color, or figure-of-eight distribution of lichen sclerosus

wrongAnswers.name: Vulvar candidiasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Candidiasis causes satellite lesions, whitish discharge, and responds to antifungals; KOH is positive and permanent architectural changes do not occur

wrongAnswers.name: Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VIN is associated with HPV, shows acetowhitening, and is distinguished by dysplastic epithelial cells on biopsy; it can coexist with but is not the same as lichen sclerosus

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with leg swelling, foamy urine, and blood-tinged urine over the past several weeks.
She has a known history of hepatitis C infection; she also reports arthralgias and a rash on her lower extremities.
Palpable purpura is present on both legs; blood pressure is elevated; urinalysis shows red cell casts and 4+ protein on exam.

C3 and C4 are both low; cryoglobulin screen is positive; rheumatoid factor is elevated; renal biopsy shows mesangial expansion with lobular accentuation and double contour (tram-track) appearance of glomerular basement membranes.
Immunofluorescence shows C3, IgG, and IgM deposits; electron microscopy shows subendothelial and mesangial electron-dense deposits.
explanation: MPGN is characterized by mesangial proliferation and GBM duplication. Type I (immune complex-mediated) is associated with hepatitis C, cryoglobulinemia, and other infections. Low C3 and C4 reflect classical pathway activation.
keyFact: The tram-track double contour on silver stain represents GBM splitting by mesangial interposition. Both C3 and C4 being low suggests classical pathway activation; isolated low C3 suggests C3 glomerulopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: IgA nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits with normal complement and typically presents with episodic gross hematuria after upper respiratory infection

wrongAnswers.name: Lupus nephritis class IV
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lupus nephritis class IV shows wire-loop lesions and requires anti-dsDNA positivity and clinical SLE features; ANA should be strongly positive

wrongAnswers.name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: FSGS shows segmental sclerosis without double-contour GBM or mesangial proliferation; complement levels are normal and immunofluorescence is nonspecific

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with excessive thirst, frequent urination, and progressive fatigue over the past year.
She has bipolar disorder and has been on a mood stabilizer for many years; she reports polyuria of 5-6 liters per day.
Urine osmolality after overnight water deprivation is only 180 mOsm/kg; there is no adequate concentration response after desmopressin administration.
Renal ultrasound shows bilateral small kidneys with cortical and medullary microcysts; 24-hour urine protein is 850 mg.
Renal biopsy reveals tubular atrophy with interstitial fibrosis, focal glomerulosclerosis, and characteristic tubular microcysts in the cortex and medulla.
explanation: Long-term lithium use causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (blocking aquaporin-2 insertion) and chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy progressing to CKD. Tubular microcysts on biopsy or imaging are highly characteristic.
keyFact: Lithium-induced nephrogenic DI is caused by downregulation of aquaporin-2 water channels and does not respond adequately to desmopressin (unlike central DI). Amiloride is preferred treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Central diabetes insipidus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Central DI responds completely to desmopressin; lithium nephropathy causes nephrogenic DI with partial or absent response to desmopressin

wrongAnswers.name: Analgesic nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Analgesic nephropathy is caused by analgesic overuse, features papillary necrosis and calcification, and lacks tubular microcysts

wrongAnswers.name: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ADPKD features much larger and more numerous cysts, PKD1/2 mutations, and family history; lithium nephropathy cysts are small microcysts correlating with lithium duration

clues: A 38-year-old woman presents with early satiety, nausea, and postprandial bloating for 8 months.
She has longstanding diabetes with erratic blood glucose levels despite consistent insulin use; symptoms worsen with high-fat and high-fiber meals.
Upper endoscopy shows a large amount of retained food in the stomach after an overnight fast; no mechanical obstruction is identified on exam.
Autonomic neuropathy is noted on cardiovascular reflex testing; an upper GI series shows retained barium at 4 hours.
Wireless motility capsule study confirms markedly prolonged gastric emptying time of 8.2 hours with antroduodenal manometry showing absent phase III migrating motor complexes.
explanation: Diabetic gastroparesis results from autonomic neuropathy disrupting gastric motility, causing delayed emptying without mechanical obstruction. Gastric emptying scintigraphy is the gold standard. Metoclopramide and domperidone are prokinetic agents used for treatment.
keyFact: Gastric emptying scintigraphy with solid-phase meal is the gold standard; >10% retention at 4 hours is diagnostic. Metoclopramide (dopamine antagonist) is FDA-approved for gastroparesis but carries tardive dyskinesia risk with long-term use.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastric outlet obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gastric outlet obstruction shows a mechanical narrowing on endoscopy or imaging; scintigraphy shows mechanical delay rather than a motility-based pattern

wrongAnswers.name: Functional dyspepsia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Functional dyspepsia causes epigastric discomfort but gastric emptying scintigraphy is normal or borderline; it is not associated with diabetic neuropathy or retained food on endoscopy

wrongAnswers.name: Rumination syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rumination syndrome involves effortless regurgitation of recently ingested food immediately postprandially with re-chewing; gastric emptying is normal

clues: A 29-year-old man presents at the urging of his wife, reporting that he cannot stop placing bets despite losing their savings and facing eviction.
He describes needing to wager increasingly larger amounts to achieve the same excitement, and he has made multiple unsuccessful attempts to cut back over the past two years.

Mental status exam shows an alert, well-groomed man with anxious affect who becomes agitated and restless when discussing attempts to reduce the behavior; no psychomotor abnormalities, hallucinations, or grandiosity are present.
Urine drug screen is negative; PHQ-9 score is 8 suggesting mild depressive symptoms; structured clinical interview reveals no history of manic episodes or psychotic symptoms.

A behavioral monitoring log over 14 months documents escalating wager amounts from 50 dollars to 2,000 dollars per session, return visits to the casino within hours of large losses, fabricated explanations for missing funds, and a formal workplace disciplinary action for absenteeism.
explanation: Gambling disorder is characterized by persistent, problematic gambling causing distress or impairment across at least 4 of 9 DSM-5 criteria over 12 months. It is classified as a behavioral addiction with neurobiological overlap with substance use disorders.
keyFact: Gambling disorder is the only behavioral (non-substance) addiction formally recognized in DSM-5 under 'Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders.'

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar disorder (manic episode)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mania can include impulsive spending but requires distinct elevated/expansive mood episodes; this patient shows no episodic mood cycling

wrongAnswers.name: Alcohol use disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: No substance is driving the behavior; financial and relational consequences stem specifically from gambling, not intoxication

wrongAnswers.name: Antisocial personality disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lying and financial harm are present but remorse is evident and the pattern does not reflect a pervasive disregard for others' rights starting in childhood

clues: A 24-year-old man is referred by his employer after multiple incidents of disproportionate angry outbursts resulting in property damage at work and strained relationships.
He describes the outbursts as uncontrollable, grossly out of proportion to any provocation, lasting less than 30 minutes each, and followed by genuine remorse and embarrassment.

Mental status exam between episodes shows a calm, cooperative man with euthymic mood, no psychomotor abnormalities, no evidence of psychosis, and a normal neurological examination including cranial nerves and coordination.
Urine drug screen is negative; structured clinical interview confirms no history of sustained mood episodes, psychotic symptoms, or pervasive personality disturbance; brain MRI is unremarkable.

A documented outburst log shows 28 discrete episodes over three months, each lasting under 20 minutes, triggered by minor provocations such as traffic delays, with property damage in 8 episodes and expressed remorse documented after each event.
explanation: Intermittent explosive disorder involves recurrent, impulsive, and disproportionate aggressive outbursts. It is diagnosed only after excluding mood disorders, ADHD, conduct disorder, and substance-related causes.
keyFact: In IED, outbursts are ego-dystonic — the individual feels remorse afterward — distinguishing it from antisocial or borderline personality disorder patterns.

wrongAnswers.name: Bipolar disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bipolar-related aggression occurs within discrete mood episodes with associated neurovegetative symptoms, not as isolated brief outbursts with normal interepisode function

wrongAnswers.name: Antisocial personality disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASPD involves a pervasive pattern of rights violations beginning before age 15; IED episodes are ego-dystonic with remorse, not callous disregard

wrongAnswers.name: Borderline personality disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BPD aggression is embedded in identity disturbance and fear of abandonment; IED lacks the chronic affective instability and relationship pattern of BPD

clues: A 5-year-old child is referred because they have not spoken at school despite speaking normally at home since age 2.
Parents confirm the child speaks in full sentences at home and with close family members; the silence is confined to school and public settings.
Hearing test is normal; speech-language evaluation shows age-appropriate language; the child communicates through nodding, pointing, and writing at school.
The pattern has persisted for over one month; academic achievement is affected; the child is not unfamiliar with the spoken language used at school.

Standardized behavioral assessment (Selective Mutism Questionnaire) scores above the clinical threshold with video-documented fluent conversational speech at home contrasting with zero spoken words across 12 consecutive school observation sessions.
explanation: Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder in which a child consistently fails to speak in specific situations where speaking is expected, despite speaking normally elsewhere. It most commonly manifests at school entry.
keyFact: Selective mutism is classified as an anxiety disorder in DSM-5, not a communication disorder; CBT with gradual exposure and parental involvement is first-line treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Autism spectrum disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD involves deficits in social communication across all settings with restricted behaviors; this child speaks normally at home without social communication deficits

wrongAnswers.name: Social anxiety disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Social anxiety disorder can co-occur but does not by itself explain the complete absence of speech in specific contexts; selective mutism is the primary diagnosis when mutism is the dominant feature

wrongAnswers.name: Expressive language disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Language testing is normal and the child speaks fluently at home, ruling out a structural language production deficit

clues: A 3-year-old with developmental delay presents with recurrent abdominal pain, irritability, and unexplained microcytic anemia.
The behavior has persisted for over a month and is not part of a culturally normative practice; nutritional intake appears adequate otherwise.
Abdominal tenderness is present without guarding; developmental milestones are delayed; no acute distress on exam.
Blood lead level is elevated at 38 mcg/dL; CBC shows microcytic anemia; abdominal X-ray shows radiopaque material in the colon.

Direct observation on three separate occasions documents the child actively seeking and ingesting paint chips and soil from the floor, each time requiring physical intervention to redirect the behavior.
explanation: Pica is the persistent ingestion of non-nutritive substances (e.g., dirt, paint, clay) inappropriate to developmental level. It is associated with intellectual disability, ASD, iron deficiency, and lead poisoning.
keyFact: Lead poisoning is a key complication of pica involving paint chip ingestion and must be screened for with blood lead level in all suspected cases.

wrongAnswers.name: Rumination disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rumination involves regurgitation and re-chewing of previously swallowed food, not ingestion of non-food substances

wrongAnswers.name: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ARFID involves restriction of food intake based on sensory features or fear, not consumption of non-nutritive non-food items

wrongAnswers.name: Iron deficiency anemia (isolated)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Iron deficiency can co-occur with pica but does not explain the behavioral diagnosis; pica is the primary DSM-5 diagnosis driving clinical management here

clues: A 14-year-old presents with progressive weight loss, dental enamel erosion, and food returning to the mouth after meals over the past 3 months.
The patient describes the process as effortless; food is brought back into the mouth, re-chewed, and either re-swallowed or spit out.
Weight loss of 4 kg; dental enamel erosion noted; upper endoscopy is unremarkable with no structural abnormality on exam.
pH-impedance study shows postprandial retrograde events without acid; the behavior does not occur exclusively during episodes of an eating disorder.
High-resolution esophageal manometry shows postprandial retrograde contractions originating in the proximal stomach, occurring repeatedly within 30 minutes of meals without nausea or retching.
explanation: Rumination disorder involves repeated, effortless regurgitation of recently ingested food, not explained by a GI condition. It is distinct from GERD and bulimia; diaphragmatic breathing is the primary treatment.
keyFact: Rumination disorder characteristically occurs within minutes of eating, is effortless (no retching), and ceases when the regurgitated food becomes acidic.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastroparesis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gastroparesis causes nausea, vomiting of undigested food hours after eating, and delayed gastric emptying on scintigraphy — not effortless postprandial regurgitation

wrongAnswers.name: Bulimia nervosa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bulimia involves intentional purging driven by body image disturbance and guilt; rumination is effortless and not motivated by weight control

wrongAnswers.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GERD produces heartburn/acid symptoms with pH study showing acidic reflux; rumination occurs with normal pH and no structural pathology

clues: A 28-year-old reports waking from sleep multiple times per week for 4 months with vivid, disturbing dreams involving threats to survival.
The patient becomes fully alert upon awakening, recalls dream content in detail, and has difficulty returning to sleep afterward.
No focal neurological deficits; no abnormal movements during sleep per bed partner report; no history of trauma on exam.
Polysomnography shows awakenings from REM sleep with tachycardia; no abnormal motor activity is recorded during episodes.

Sleep diary over 4 months documents 3-4 awakenings per week with immediate detailed narrative recall of threat-themed dreams, each followed by sustained wakefulness exceeding 45 minutes and inability to return to sleep.
explanation: Nightmare disorder involves recurrent distressing dreams causing impairment. Unlike sleep terrors, full alertness and recall on awakening are characteristic. Image Rehearsal Therapy is first-line.
keyFact: Nightmare disorder occurs during REM sleep (typically in the second half of the night) with full recall upon awakening — contrasting with sleep terrors, which occur in NREM and have no recall.

wrongAnswers.name: Sleep terror disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sleep terrors occur during NREM slow-wave sleep with inconsolable arousal, autonomic activation, and no dream recall upon awakening

wrongAnswers.name: REM sleep behavior disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RBD involves acting out dreams with abnormal motor behavior during REM; this patient has no abnormal motor activity on PSG

wrongAnswers.name: PTSD-related nightmares
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PTSD nightmares are a specifier requiring a traumatic stressor; this patient has no trauma history and meets criteria for nightmare disorder as a primary diagnosis

clues: A 16-year-old assigned female at birth presents expressing strong discomfort with their body and a persistent desire to be recognized and treated as male.
There has been a strong preference for male roles, clothing, and peer groups since early childhood; the discomfort has intensified since puberty.
Physical exam shows normal female pubertal development; the patient reports significant distress specifically related to breast development and menstruation.
No psychotic features on mental status exam; identity is stable and consistent over years; psychological testing does not identify a mood disorder as the primary explanation.

Longitudinal clinical documentation spanning 4 years across multiple providers shows consistent male gender identification with escalating distress scores on the Utrecht Gender Dysphoria Scale correlating with pubertal development.
explanation: Gender dysphoria describes the distress arising from incongruence between experienced/expressed gender and assigned gender at birth. DSM-5 focuses on the distress rather than the identity itself.
keyFact: DSM-5 intentionally separated gender dysphoria from sexual dysfunctions and paraphilic disorders, recognizing that gender nonconformity alone is not a mental disorder — it is the distress that warrants clinical attention.

wrongAnswers.name: Body dysmorphic disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BDD involves preoccupation with perceived defects in physical appearance, not a pervasive sense of belonging to another gender

wrongAnswers.name: Schizophrenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: The patient's beliefs are consistent, ego-syntonic, culturally coherent, and long-standing — not delusional in nature

wrongAnswers.name: Major depressive disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Depression may co-occur but the gender incongruence predates and is independent of mood; the identity distress is the primary diagnosis

clues: A 22-year-old presents with acute chest pain and a sensation of fullness in the neck that began during vigorous exercise.
He was exercising intensely when the symptoms started suddenly; he also notes that his voice sounds muffled.
Crepitus is palpable over the neck and anterior chest wall; mild dyspnea is present without hypoxia on exam.
Chest X-ray shows radiolucent streaks outlining the mediastinal structures and extending into the soft tissues of the neck; CT confirms air tracking along fascial planes.
Esophagram with water-soluble contrast is negative for perforation; air is present exclusively within the mediastinal space without pleural involvement.
explanation: Pneumomediastinum results from alveolar rupture with air dissecting along perivascular sheaths into the mediastinum. Spontaneous cases in young adults are usually benign and self-limited; Boerhaave syndrome must be excluded.
keyFact: Hamman's sign — a crunching sound synchronous with the heartbeat on auscultation — is a classic physical finding in pneumomediastinum.

wrongAnswers.name: Boerhaave syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Boerhaave (esophageal perforation) presents with severe chest pain, fever, and pleural effusion; esophagram here is negative, and there is no pleural contamination

wrongAnswers.name: Pneumothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pneumothorax shows lung collapse with absent breath sounds on the affected side; imaging here shows mediastinal, not pleural, air

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic dissection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aortic dissection presents with tearing pain radiating to the back, pulse differentials, and mediastinal widening — not crepitus or radiolucent fascial streaks

clues: A 58-year-old man with occupational dust exposure presents with mild exertional dyspnea and a dull ache in his left chest over the past few months.
He has a history of prolonged asbestos exposure at his previous workplace decades ago.
Spirometry shows mild restriction; no fever, weight loss, hemoptysis, or lymphadenopathy on exam.
CT chest shows a rounded peripheral mass in the lower lobe with a comet-tail sign — bronchovascular structures curving into the lesion — and adjacent pleural thickening.
Serial CT imaging over 2 years shows no growth, with the same comet-tail morphology and pleural tethering unchanged.
explanation: Round atelectasis is a benign form of lung collapse in which pleural disease (classically asbestos-related) causes folding of adjacent lung into a rounded opacity. The comet-tail sign on CT is pathognomonic.
keyFact: The comet-tail (or crow's feet) sign on CT — bronchovascular bundles curving toward a pleural-based round opacity — is pathognomonic for round atelectasis and avoids unnecessary biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Lung adenocarcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Malignancy lacks the comet-tail sign and pleural-based adhesion, typically shows growth on serial imaging, and does not have the characteristic folded-lung morphology

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary carcinoid
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoid is usually central with endobronchial features or vascular blush on CT; it lacks the pleural association and comet-tail morphology

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary hamartoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hamartoma presents as a discrete coin lesion, often with popcorn calcification or fat density on CT, without the pleural tethering or comet-tail sign

clues: A 19-year-old is referred for evaluation of recurrent left lower lobe pneumonia that keeps occurring in the same location.
He has been treated for community-acquired pneumonia twice in the past 5 years; each episode resolves with antibiotics but recurs in the identical spot.
Chest CT shows a hyperdense mass in the left lower lobe with no visible communication to the tracheobronchial tree on exam.
CT angiography reveals a systemic arterial vessel arising directly from the descending thoracic aorta supplying the mass; venous drainage is to the pulmonary veins.

Surgical specimen confirms a demarcated mass of lung parenchyma with a 6 mm systemic arterial pedicle from the thoracic aorta, no bronchial communication on serial sectioning, and venous drainage to the inferior pulmonary vein.
explanation: Pulmonary sequestration is a congenital lung malformation in which a mass of non-functioning lung tissue is supplied by a systemic (not pulmonary) artery and lacks normal tracheobronchial connection. Intralobar type drains to pulmonary veins.
keyFact: The hallmark of pulmonary sequestration is a systemic arterial supply (usually from the descending aorta) to a non-communicating lung mass — demonstrable on CT angiography.

wrongAnswers.name: Recurrent aspiration pneumonia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aspiration affects dependent segments and lacks a discrete mass with anomalous vasculature; it is not confined to one lobe over years

wrongAnswers.name: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CPAM consists of cystic lesions with normal pulmonary arterial supply — no anomalous systemic vessel is present

wrongAnswers.name: Lung abscess
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Abscess is an acquired infectious cavity with air-fluid level; it resolves with antibiotics and does not recur in the same location with an anomalous vessel

clues: A 55-year-old non-smoker has an incidental 1.8 cm lung nodule found on CT done for an unrelated reason.
The nodule has been stable on serial imaging for 2 years; the patient reports no respiratory symptoms.
The nodule is well-circumscribed and smooth; PFTs are normal; no lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion on exam.
CT shows internal fat attenuation (-40 to -120 HU) and stippled 'popcorn' calcification within the nodule.
Biopsy (if performed) shows disorganized cartilage, fat, smooth muscle, and epithelial clefts within a single well-demarcated nodule.
explanation: Pulmonary hamartoma is the most common benign lung tumor in adults. The combination of fat density and popcorn calcification on CT is diagnostic, avoiding invasive biopsy in most cases.
keyFact: Fat attenuation on CT (-40 to -120 HU) within a smooth pulmonary nodule is virtually diagnostic of hamartoma and is the key feature distinguishing it from malignancy.

wrongAnswers.name: Carcinoid tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoids are highly vascular with intense contrast enhancement, typically central or endobronchial, and lack fat density or popcorn calcification

wrongAnswers.name: Solitary pulmonary metastasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Metastases lack fat content, are rarely calcified, and require a known primary malignancy; hamartoma is benign with characteristic fat/calcium on CT

wrongAnswers.name: Granuloma (histoplasmosis)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Granulomas calcify centrally or diffusely (not popcorn pattern), lack fat, and have an epidemiologic/exposure history

clues: A 40-year-old non-smoker presents with a 6-month history of recurrent cough and two episodes of small-volume hemoptysis.
She has no weight loss, night sweats, or tobacco use history; symptoms have not responded to multiple courses of antibiotics.
Breath sounds are diminished over the right middle lobe zone; no wheezing, clubbing, or lymphadenopathy on exam.
Octreotide scintigraphy shows focal uptake in the right hilar region; 24-hour urine 5-HIAA is mildly elevated.
Bronchoscopic biopsy shows uniform cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin and low mitotic index; chromogranin A and synaptophysin are positive; Ki-67 is less than 2%.
explanation: Pulmonary carcinoid is a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor arising from bronchial epithelium. Typical carcinoids have low mitotic rate (< 2/10 HPF) and Ki-67 < 2%, with a favorable prognosis after resection.
keyFact: Pulmonary carcinoids are the most common primary lung tumor in patients under 40, and typical carcinoid (Ki-67 < 2%) has a 5-year survival > 90% after surgical resection.

wrongAnswers.name: Small cell lung cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCLC also has neuroendocrine markers but is highly aggressive with high Ki-67, central necrosis, and rapid growth — not a low-mitotic endobronchial tumor in a young non-smoker

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary hamartoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hamartoma is a peripheral nodule with fat/calcification on CT; it is not endobronchial, does not enhance intensely, and lacks neuroendocrine markers

wrongAnswers.name: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the bronchus is rare, lacks neuroendocrine differentiation, and does not show octreotide uptake or elevated 5-HIAA

clues: A 60-year-old presents with progressive hoarseness, stridor, and recurrent obstructive pneumonias over 3 years.
Symptoms have been gradually worsening; there are no systemic complaints such as edema, neuropathy, or organomegaly.

Spirometry shows a flattened flow-volume loop suggesting fixed upper airway obstruction; CT shows circumferential submucosal wall thickening and calcification of the trachea and main bronchi without a discrete mass.
Bronchoscopy reveals diffuse, waxy, submucosal plaques narrowing the airway lumen; biopsies show apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining.
Immunohistochemistry identifies AL-type amyloid deposits confined to the tracheobronchial tree; bone marrow biopsy is negative for systemic involvement.
explanation: Tracheobronchial amyloidosis involves AL amyloid deposition in the airway submucosa, causing progressive obstruction. It is often localized to the airway without systemic involvement and is distinct from systemic amyloidosis.
keyFact: Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence under polarized light is the histologic hallmark of amyloid regardless of organ or type.

wrongAnswers.name: Relapsing polychondritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Relapsing polychondritis destroys cartilage with floppy airway collapse and associated auricular/nasal chondritis; it does not produce Congo-red positive submucosal deposits

wrongAnswers.name: Wegener granulomatosis (GPA)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GPA causes subglottic stenosis with necrotizing granulomas and is ANCA-positive; it lacks the diffuse calcified plaques and amyloid deposits

wrongAnswers.name: Tracheobronchomalacia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tracheobronchomalacia is dynamic collapse on expiration, not fixed narrowing with calcified plaques; no submucosal deposits are present

clues: A 62-year-old presents with bilateral lower extremity swelling, chronic productive cough, and recurrent pleural effusions of unclear etiology over 2 years.
She reports that her fingernails and toenails have become discolored, thickened, and grow very slowly over the same time period.
Nails are thickened, yellow-green, over-curved with loss of the lunula and onycholysis; bilateral non-pitting lower extremity edema is present; lymphoscintigraphy demonstrates lymphatic obstruction.
Pleural fluid is an exudate with high lymphocyte count; cultures are negative; cytology shows no malignant cells.

Lymphoscintigraphy confirms bilateral lower extremity lymphatic hypoplasia with dermal backflow, and nail clipping histology shows thickened nail plate with absent lunula and subungual hyperkeratosis without fungal elements.
explanation: Yellow nail syndrome is characterized by the triad of yellow/dystrophic nails, lymphedema, and respiratory manifestations (pleural effusions, bronchiectasis). It results from lymphatic hypoplasia.
keyFact: Yellow nail syndrome is defined by the triad of dystrophic yellow nails + lymphedema + respiratory manifestations; all three may not be present simultaneously, but nails are almost always involved.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrotic syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nephrotic syndrome causes edema and effusions but does not produce nail changes; urinalysis would show heavy proteinuria, which is absent here

wrongAnswers.name: Primary lymphedema (Milroy disease)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Milroy disease presents in childhood with lower limb lymphedema alone and lacks nail changes or pleural effusions

wrongAnswers.name: Onychomycosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fungal nail infection causes nail thickening and discoloration but is unilateral or patchy, responds to antifungals, and does not cause lymphedema or pleural effusions

clues: A 15-year-old presents with persistent severe neutropenia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and extensive cutaneous warts unresponsive to multiple treatments.
The warts are widespread and refractory to cryotherapy, topical treatments, and immunomodulators; infections have required multiple hospitalizations.
CBC shows severe neutropenia (ANC less than 500) with hypersegmented or bilobed neutrophils on peripheral smear; immunoglobulins are low; lymphocyte counts are reduced.
Bone marrow biopsy shows myelokathexis with abundant mature but retained myeloid cells; mature neutrophils have pyknotic nuclei with long filamentous nuclear lobes.
CXCR4 gain-of-function mutation is identified, impairing neutrophil and lymphocyte egress from bone marrow.
