explanation: WHIM syndrome (Warts, Hypogammaglobulinemia, Infections, Myelokathexis) is caused by autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutations in CXCR4, leading to retention of mature neutrophils in the bone marrow.
keyFact: Myelokathexis — hypersegmented, pyknotic neutrophils with long filamentous nuclear lobes retained in the bone marrow — is the pathognomonic bone marrow finding of WHIM syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Cyclic neutropenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cyclic neutropenia has regular 21-day cycles of neutropenia driven by ELANE mutations; it lacks HPV warts, myelokathexis, and CXCR4 mutation

wrongAnswers.name: Common variable immunodeficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CVID presents with hypogammaglobulinemia and recurrent infections but lacks neutropenia, myelokathexis, and severe HPV wart susceptibility

wrongAnswers.name: Severe congenital neutropenia (Kostmann)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kostmann disease has myeloid maturation arrest at promyelocyte stage without myelokathexis, and HPV warts are not a feature

clues: A 25-year-old presents with recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia, arthralgias, and a photosensitive rash.
A family history reveals a sibling who had meningococcal disease at age 12; the patient has a lupus-like phenotype but no prior autoimmune diagnosis.
ANA is positive at 1:320; anti-dsDNA is negative; no encapsulated organism vaccinations are documented on exam.
C4 and C2 levels are undetectable; C3 is low-normal; CH50 is nearly zero; AP50 (alternative pathway) is normal.
Genetic testing shows a homozygous 28-bp deletion in the C2 gene.
explanation: C2 deficiency is the most common inherited complement deficiency in Caucasians. It impairs the classical pathway, predisposing to encapsulated organism infections and SLE-like autoimmunity due to impaired immune complex clearance.
keyFact: C2 deficiency is the most common complement deficiency in Caucasians and classically presents with the combination of recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections AND lupus-like autoimmunity.

wrongAnswers.name: C5-C9 (terminal complement) deficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Terminal complement deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal/gonococcal) infections, not pneumococcal disease, and does not cause lupus-like illness

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE can present similarly but is not the primary diagnosis; the complement pathway defect (absent CH50, confirmed C2 deletion) drives both the infections and the lupus phenotype

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked agammaglobulinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLA causes absent B cells and very low immunoglobulins; complement levels would be normal, and there is no autoimmune overlap

clues: A 16-year-old with a BMI of 34 is referred for evaluation of asymptomatic, progressive skin darkening in the neck and underarm areas.
The changes are bilateral, symmetric, and have developed gradually over the past 2 years.
Velvety, dark, thickened skin is present in the posterior cervical and axillary folds; no satellite lesions, scale, or tenderness on exam.
Fasting insulin is markedly elevated with HOMA-IR indicating significant insulin resistance; fasting glucose is 108 mg/dL; HbA1c is 5.9%.
Biopsy (if performed) shows papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis of the epidermis with accentuation of normal skin markings in flexural areas.
explanation: Acanthosis nigricans is a dermatologic marker of insulin resistance most commonly seen in obesity. Rapid onset in a non-obese adult warrants workup for occult malignancy (paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans).
keyFact: Rapid-onset acanthosis nigricans in a lean adult — especially involving the oral mucosa or palms — should prompt workup for gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma (paraneoplastic).

wrongAnswers.name: Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (Gougerot-Carteaud)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CRP is a superficial papillomatosis with reticulate pattern on the trunk, typically in young women; it lacks the metabolic associations and responds to minocycline

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea versicolor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea versicolor presents with hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules with fine scale and a positive KOH prep for Malassezia; it lacks velvety texture

wrongAnswers.name: Dowling-Degos disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dowling-Degos is an AD genodermatosis causing reticulate hyperpigmentation in flexures but lacks velvety texture, metabolic associations, and insulin resistance

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with a sudden eruption of firm, non-tender papules on the buttocks and arms over the past 2 weeks along with new epigastric discomfort.
He has poorly controlled diabetes; the papules appeared abruptly coinciding with worsening glycemic control.
Papules are 2-5 mm, yellow-orange, firm, and some are surrounded by an erythematous halo; no joint pain or tendon thickening on exam.
Fasting triglycerides are 1,850 mg/dL; total cholesterol is 390 mg/dL; glucose is 320 mg/dL; lipase is mildly elevated.
Skin biopsy shows collections of lipid-laden foam cells (macrophages) within the dermis.
explanation: Eruptive xanthomas are cutaneous deposits of triglyceride-laden macrophages that appear suddenly during severe hypertriglyceridemia (usually >1,000 mg/dL). Treating the underlying lipid disorder leads to resolution.
keyFact: Eruptive xanthomas are pathognomonic for severe hypertriglyceridemia (chylomicronemia syndrome) and signal an acute pancreatitis risk — triglyceride reduction is urgent.

wrongAnswers.name: Molluscum contagiosum
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Molluscum lesions are umbilicated, flesh-colored papules in clusters caused by poxvirus; they lack yellow color and are not associated with hyperlipidemia

wrongAnswers.name: Gout (tophus)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tophi are white-yellow nodular deposits of uric acid near joints with gout history; they are firm/chalky and associated with hyperuricemia, not hypertriglyceridemia

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatofibroma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatofibromas are solitary, firm, pigmented nodules with a positive dimple sign; they are not multiple, yellow, or lipid-laden

clues: A 35-year-old presents with a slowly enlarging, firm, indurated plaque on the trunk that has been present for 5 years.
The lesion has recurred twice after local excision at the same site.
The plaque has a red-brown, protuberant nodular surface firmly attached to the skin but mobile over underlying fascia; no regional lymphadenopathy on exam.
Biopsy shows a storiform pattern of spindle cells extending into the subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern; CD34 is positive and Factor XIIIa is negative on immunohistochemistry.
FISH demonstrates a COL1A1-PDGFB fusion from translocation t(17;22).
explanation: DFSP is a locally aggressive, low-grade dermal sarcoma characterized by high local recurrence, CD34 positivity, and the pathognomonic COL1A1-PDGFB translocation driving PDGFR-beta signaling. Imatinib is used for unresectable disease.
keyFact: DFSP harbors a COL1A1-PDGFB translocation t(17;22) that constitutively activates PDGFR-beta — making it uniquely sensitive to imatinib (a PDGFR inhibitor) among skin tumors.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatofibroma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatofibroma is Factor XIIIa-positive and CD34-negative — the reverse of DFSP; it is benign, does not recur after excision, and lacks the COL1A1-PDGFB translocation

wrongAnswers.name: Kaposi sarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 driven, presents as violaceous vascular plaques in immunocompromised or elderly Mediterranean patients, and is CD31/CD34 positive but lacks the t(17;22)

wrongAnswers.name: Atypical fibroxanthoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AFX arises on sun-damaged skin of elderly patients as a rapidly growing nodule on the head/neck; it is CD34-negative and lacks the translocation

clues: A 70-year-old presents with a painless upper eyelid lesion that has been growing for 8 months despite being treated conservatively twice.
The lesion was previously managed as a chalazion twice without resolution; eyelash loss (madarosis) is noted in the affected area.
Eyelid thickening is present; slit-lamp exam shows abnormal cells spreading within the conjunctival epithelium; no cervical lymphadenopathy on exam.
Biopsy shows lobules of cells with foamy cytoplasm and lipid vacuoles; oil red O stain is positive for intracellular lipid.
Immunohistochemistry is positive for EMA and androgen receptor with pagetoid spread of tumor cells within the conjunctival epithelium.
explanation: Sebaceous carcinoma most commonly arises from the meibomian glands of the eyelid, mimicking chalazion. Pagetoid spread and madarosis are hallmarks; it may be associated with Muir-Torre syndrome.
keyFact: Sebaceous carcinoma should be considered in any recurrent 'chalazion' — especially in elderly patients with madarosis (eyelash loss) — as it frequently mimics benign eyelid conditions and delays diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Basal cell carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BCC of the eyelid is typically a pearly, ulcerated nodule with rolled edges affecting the lower lid; it lacks lipid-laden foamy cells and oil red O positivity

wrongAnswers.name: Chalazion
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chalazion is a lipogranulomatous reaction to inspissated meibomian secretions; it resolves or responds to incision/drainage and lacks malignant cytology

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous cell carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCC is keratinizing with intercellular bridges on biopsy; it lacks the foamy lipid-laden cytoplasm, oil red O positivity, and androgen receptor staining of sebaceous carcinoma

clues: A 6-year-old presents with persistent skin roughness on the arms and legs that does not improve with standard moisturizers.
The child also has atopic dermatitis and seasonal allergies; the father has similar skin findings.
Fine, white, fish-like scaling is present on the extensor surfaces; palms show accentuated skin markings (hyperlinear palms); flexural creases are spared on exam.
Skin biopsy shows a thin or absent granular layer with compact orthohyperkeratosis.
FLG (filaggrin) gene mutation is identified on genetic testing.
explanation: Ichthyosis vulgaris is the most common inherited ichthyosis, caused by FLG mutations causing reduced or absent filaggrin production. It is strongly associated with atopic dermatitis, asthma, and allergic rhinitis.
keyFact: FLG (filaggrin) mutations causing ichthyosis vulgaris are the strongest known genetic risk factor for atopic dermatitis — filaggrin is essential for skin barrier function.

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked ichthyosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: X-linked ichthyosis is caused by steroid sulfatase deficiency, affects males only, spares the palms, and has larger, darker scales — distinguished by elevated serum cholesterol sulfate and absent flexural sparing pattern

wrongAnswers.name: Lamellar ichthyosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lamellar ichthyosis (TGM1 mutations) presents at birth as a collodion membrane, with large plate-like scales covering the entire body including flexures — much more severe than ichthyosis vulgaris

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriasis has well-demarcated, salmon-pink plaques with silver scale, Auspitz sign, and nail changes; it does not begin in infancy or show the absent granular layer on biopsy

clues: A 55-year-old woman with chronic pain presents with slowly progressive renal insufficiency and sterile pyuria over 5 years.
She reports daily use of combined analgesic preparations (aspirin, acetaminophen, and caffeine) for over 10 years.
Blood pressure is elevated; urinalysis shows sterile pyuria and mild proteinuria; urine culture is negative on exam.
CT without contrast shows bilateral small kidneys with cortical scarring, calyceal deformity, and papillary calcifications.
Retrograde pyelography confirms papillary necrosis with ring shadows (ring sign) and medullary cavities communicating with the collecting system bilaterally.
explanation: Analgesic nephropathy results from chronic use of combination analgesics (classically phenacetin, now NSAID + acetaminophen combinations), causing papillary ischemia and necrosis. CT showing papillary calcification and bilateral renal scarring is diagnostic.
keyFact: The combination of analgesics (not single agents alone) is required to cause analgesic nephropathy — phenacetin-containing preparations were the classic culprit; the CT finding of papillary calcification is pathognomonic.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic pyelonephritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Chronic pyelonephritis causes asymmetric cortical scarring overlying dilated calyces from recurrent bacterial infection; sterile pyuria and papillary calcifications without infection point to analgesic nephropathy

wrongAnswers.name: Medullary sponge kidney
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Medullary sponge kidney shows medullary tubular ectasia with nephrocalcinosis on imaging; it is congenital and does not cause papillary necrosis or cortical scarring

wrongAnswers.name: IgA nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: IgA nephropathy causes episodic hematuria and proteinuria; imaging shows normal-sized kidneys without papillary calcifications, and there is no analgesic use pattern

clues: A 62-year-old man presents with progressive renal insufficiency, bilateral renal enlargement, and submandibular gland swelling.
He also reports abdominal fullness; the pancreas appears enlarged on imaging done at another facility.
Eosinophilia is present; ESR and CRP are elevated; CT shows bilateral renal masses and wedge-shaped low-attenuation lesions along with pancreatic enlargement with a capsule-like rim.
Serum IgG4 is markedly elevated at 680 mg/dL; renal biopsy shows storiform fibrosis, dense IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltrate with more than 10 IgG4+ cells per HPF, and obliterative phlebitis.
Immunofluorescence of tubular basement membranes shows granular IgG4, C3, and kappa/lambda light chain deposits in a unique pattern distinct from other immune-complex nephritides.
explanation: IgG4-related kidney disease most commonly presents as tubulointerstitial nephritis with storiform fibrosis and IgG4+ plasma cell infiltration. It is part of the systemic IgG4-related disease spectrum and responds dramatically to steroids.
keyFact: The histologic triad of IgG4-related disease is: (1) dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with IgG4+ plasma cells, (2) storiform fibrosis, and (3) obliterative phlebitis — all three in the correct clinical context are diagnostic.

wrongAnswers.name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: GPA causes necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, pauci-immune crescentic GN, and is ANCA-positive; it lacks storiform fibrosis, IgG4 plasma cells, and salivary/pancreatic involvement

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sarcoidosis causes non-caseating granulomas in the kidney with hypercalcemia; it lacks IgG4+ plasma cell infiltrate, elevated serum IgG4, and obliterative phlebitis

wrongAnswers.name: Lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma can cause renal masses but lacks storiform fibrosis and IgG4 plasma cells; clonal B-cell proliferation and LDH elevation would distinguish it

clues: A 50-year-old man undergoing cancer treatment presents with nausea, hearing changes, and markedly decreased urine output over three days.
His chemotherapy was administered several days ago; no contrast agents or NSAIDs have been used recently.
Urinalysis shows granular casts and tubular epithelial cells; urine sodium is elevated with FeNa greater than 2%; blood pressure is stable on exam.
Serum magnesium is low despite normal intake; urine magnesium is inappropriately elevated indicating renal magnesium wasting.
Renal biopsy (if done) shows proximal tubular necrosis concentrated in the S3 segment of the outer medulla with a clear temporal relationship to a platinum-based chemotherapy infusion.
explanation: Cisplatin nephrotoxicity targets the S3 proximal tubular segment in the outer medulla, causing ATN and Fanconi-like tubular dysfunction including renal magnesium wasting. Hypomagnesemia may persist long after treatment ends.
keyFact: Cisplatin-induced hypomagnesemia is caused by tubular magnesium wasting and can persist for months to years after cisplatin is stopped — making it a chronic consequence, not just acute toxicity.

wrongAnswers.name: Contrast-induced nephropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Contrast nephropathy peaks 24-72 hours after contrast exposure, is typically transient, and does not cause persistent renal magnesium wasting

wrongAnswers.name: Tumor lysis syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TLS causes hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia — not isolated hypomagnesemia with tubular casts

wrongAnswers.name: Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aminoglycosides cause proximal tubular toxicity but produce hypokalemia and polyuria (Bartter-like) rather than hypomagnesemia as the dominant electrolyte disturbance; no aminoglycosides are documented here

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with dull back and flank pain, lower extremity edema, and new-onset hypertension over 6 months.
Symptoms have been gradually progressive; he has no history of malignancy, radiation, or medication exposures known to cause retroperitoneal disease.
CT shows a periaortic soft-tissue mass encasing the aorta and inferior vena cava from L2 to the aortic bifurcation with bilateral ureteral obstruction on exam.
Creatinine is 3.2 mg/dL; ESR is 85 mm/hr; serum IgG4 is elevated at 240 mg/dL; ANA and ANCA are negative.
Biopsy of the periaortic mass shows storiform fibrosis with IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltrate and obliterative phlebitis.
explanation: Retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF) encases retroperitoneal structures causing ureteral obstruction and renal failure. The IgG4-related subtype (most common) responds to steroids; drug-induced (methysergide) and idiopathic forms also exist.
keyFact: Retroperitoneal fibrosis that encases but does not invade the aorta (the mass is anchored anterior to the aorta) is a key imaging feature distinguishing it from malignant retroperitoneal tumors, which tend to displace the aorta anteriorly.

wrongAnswers.name: Retroperitoneal lymphoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma forms discrete nodal masses, displaces rather than encases great vessels, and would show clonal lymphoid cells on biopsy — not storiform fibrosis with IgG4 plasma cells

wrongAnswers.name: Abdominal aortic aneurysm with periaortic hematoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AAA with periaortic hematoma has an aortic lumen > 3 cm with discontinuous outer wall; it does not produce the fibrous encasing tissue or bilateral ureteral obstruction seen here

wrongAnswers.name: Urolithiasis with ureteral obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Urolithiasis obstructs one ureter at a time at specific anatomical points; bilateral simultaneous obstruction by an encasing soft-tissue mass is not explained by stones

clues: A 22-year-old African-American man presents with three weeks of painless blood in his urine and vague right-sided flank discomfort.
He has sickle cell trait documented on a prior hemoglobin electrophoresis.
A firm, non-tender right flank mass is palpable on deep palpation; no costovertebral angle tenderness is elicited.
CT abdomen shows a 5 cm infiltrative right renal mass centered in the medulla with retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and bilateral pulmonary nodules on chest CT.
Biopsy shows reticular and adenoid growth pattern with yolk sac-like architecture; immunohistochemistry demonstrates complete loss of INI1 (SMARCB1) nuclear staining.
explanation: Renal medullary carcinoma is an aggressive malignancy almost exclusively in patients with sickle cell trait, caused by SMARCB1 (INI1) inactivation. Metastatic disease is present in 95% at diagnosis.
keyFact: Renal medullary carcinoma is the 'almost exclusive' tumor of sickle cell trait — over 95% of cases occur in individuals with HbSC or HbS trait — and is universally SMARCB1-deficient.

wrongAnswers.name: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Clear cell RCC has VHL mutations, rich vascularity, occurs in older patients, and is not associated with sickle cell trait; it lacks the medullary location and INI1 loss

wrongAnswers.name: Transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TCC arises from urothelium, is associated with smoking/aniline dye exposure, and shows urothelial histology — not the reticular pattern with SMARCB1 loss

wrongAnswers.name: Collecting duct carcinoma (Bellini)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Collecting duct carcinoma is histologically similar but lacks the sickle cell trait association and SMARCB1 inactivation; it occurs in older patients and is distinguished by immunohistochemistry

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive bone pain, multiple stress fractures, and difficulty climbing stairs over the past three years.
He has a history of recreational sports and reports proximal muscle weakness that has been worsening over the past year.
He has proximal muscle weakness bilaterally, waddling gait, and diffuse bony tenderness; no joint swelling or deformity is noted.
Serum phosphate is profoundly low; plain films show pseudofractures (Looser zones) in the femoral necks and ribs; Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT localizes a 1.2 cm soft tissue mass at the right knee.
Elevated FGF23 level with renal phosphate wasting confirmed on 24-hour urine; functional imaging localizes the mass to a site expressing somatostatin receptors.
explanation: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor (PMT) is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm that secretes FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting and tumor-induced osteomalacia. Surgical resection is curative.
keyFact: Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) caused by FGF23-secreting PMTs is confirmed by elevated FGF23 with hypophosphatemia; Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT is the imaging of choice to localize occult tumors.

wrongAnswers.name: X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: XLH is an inherited FGF23 excess disorder from birth with dental abscesses and enthesopathy; TIO is acquired in adulthood without family history — requiring tumor localization, not genetic testing

wrongAnswers.name: Primary hyperparathyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PHPT causes hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated PTH; here PTH is normal and FGF23 is elevated — the mechanism is phosphate wasting, not PTH-driven

wrongAnswers.name: Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vitamin D deficiency causes low 25-OH-D with secondary hyperparathyroidism and normal-to-low phosphate; FGF23 is not elevated and there is no occult tumor

clues: A 52-year-old woman presents with intermittent catching and difficulty straightening her right ring finger, particularly in the morning, along with palm-side hand discomfort for three months.
She works as a seamstress with repetitive hand use and has type 2 diabetes.
A tender, palpable nodule is present at the base of the ring finger on the palm side at the level of the metacarpophalangeal joint; no joint swelling, erythema, or warmth is noted.
Plain radiographs of the hand are normal with no joint space narrowing, erosions, or calcifications.
Ultrasound of the affected finger demonstrates thickening of the A1 pulley with a visible nodule on the flexor tendon that catches during dynamic assessment of finger extension.
explanation: Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis) results from a size mismatch between the flexor tendon nodule and the A1 pulley, causing catching or locking. Diabetes is the strongest risk factor; corticosteroid injection is first-line treatment.
keyFact: Trigger finger is caused by stenosis at the A1 pulley (not the A2 pulley or elsewhere); surgical release of the A1 pulley is the definitive treatment when injection fails.

wrongAnswers.name: Dupuytren contracture
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dupuytren produces progressive painless fixed flexion contracture due to palmar fascia fibrosis — there is no catching, nodule at A1 pulley, or locking-unlocking phenomenon

wrongAnswers.name: De Quervain tenosynovitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: De Quervain affects the first dorsal compartment (APL and EPB) at the radial styloid with positive Finkelstein test; it does not cause finger locking

wrongAnswers.name: Flexor digitorum profundus avulsion (Jersey finger)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Jersey finger causes inability to flex the DIP joint actively after a hyperextension injury — it is an acute traumatic avulsion, not a chronic locking phenomenon

accept: tenosynovial giant cell tumor diffuse type
clues: A 30-year-old man presents with a two-year history of recurrent knee swelling without significant trauma.
The knee swelling recurs after each drainage and the aspirated fluid has always appeared dark brown or bloody; he denies trauma or infection.
The knee is diffusely swollen with a palpable boggy synovium; range of motion is mildly limited; no warmth or erythema is present.
Plain films show juxta-articular erosions on both sides of the joint with preserved joint space; MRI shows diffuse synovial thickening with marked low signal on both T1 and T2 sequences.
Synovial biopsy shows villonodular proliferation with hemosiderin-laden macrophages, foam cells, and multinucleated giant cells; CSF1 translocation is identified.
explanation: PVNS (now reclassified as diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor) is characterized by hemosiderin-laden synovial proliferation, recurrent bloody effusions, and dark signal on MRI due to hemosiderin. It is driven by CSF1 overexpression.
keyFact: The MRI 'blooming artifact' — marked hypointensity on all sequences from hemosiderin — in a young patient with recurrent bloody effusions and preserved joint space is pathognomonic for PVNS.

wrongAnswers.name: Hemophilic arthropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemophilic arthropathy causes hemarthroses with hemosiderin deposition but requires a known bleeding diathesis; factor levels are normal here

wrongAnswers.name: Synovial chondromatosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Synovial chondromatosis shows multiple calcified loose bodies on imaging; it lacks hemosiderin deposition and the villonodular histology

wrongAnswers.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RA causes symmetric polyarthritis with pannus formation and joint space loss; it does not produce recurrent bloody effusions, preserved joint space, and hemosiderin-laden histology

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with difficulty fully straightening his ring and small fingers on his right hand that has been gradually worsening over the past year.
His father had a similar hand condition requiring surgery; the patient drinks alcohol socially and has no history of hand trauma or diabetes.

Firm, non-tender cord-like bands are palpable in the palmar fascia extending to the ring and small fingers bilaterally; palmar pitting and nodules are present at the distal palmar crease; the right ring finger MCP joint is fixed in 40 degrees of flexion and cannot be passively extended.
Plain radiographs of both hands show no bony abnormality, joint narrowing, or calcification.

MRI shows nodular thickening and cord-like fibrous bands continuous with the palmar aponeurosis inserting onto the proximal phalanges of the ring and small fingers, with no tendon sheath involvement or joint capsule abnormality.
explanation: Dupuytren contracture is a fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia causing progressive finger flexion contracture. Risk factors include Northern European ancestry, male sex, diabetes, alcohol use, and manual labor.
keyFact: The Hueston tabletop test — inability to place the hand flat on a table — is the clinical threshold for intervention in Dupuytren contracture (MCP > 30 degrees or any PIP contracture).

wrongAnswers.name: Trigger finger
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trigger finger causes catching/locking at the A1 pulley with a palpable nodule at the MCP but no palmar cord, and the finger is not fixed in flexion — it can be passively extended

wrongAnswers.name: Camptodactyly
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Camptodactyly is a congenital flexion deformity of the PIP joint of the little finger, present from birth or adolescence, without palmar cords or the adult onset risk factors

wrongAnswers.name: Flexor tendon adhesion (post-traumatic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Post-traumatic flexor adhesion causes restricted active finger flexion/extension following a known injury, without the characteristic palmar fascial cords or pitting of Dupuytren disease

clues: A 72-year-old man presents with fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and recurrent mouth sores over the past several months.
He has no prior hematologic history and takes no medications known to cause cytopenias.
He appears pale with scattered oral aphthous ulcers; mild splenomegaly is palpable; no lymphadenopathy is noted.
CBC shows WBC 18,000 with absolute monocyte count 2,800; mild anemia and thrombocytopenia are present; peripheral smear shows monocytosis with dysplastic neutrophils and blasts under 5%.

Bone marrow biopsy shows hypercellularity with dysplastic changes in two or more lineages, persistent absolute monocytosis greater than 1x10^9/L, less than 20% blasts, and no Philadelphia chromosome; next-generation sequencing identifies TET2 and SRSF2 mutations.
explanation: CMML is a clonal myeloid neoplasm with features of both myelodysplastic syndrome and myeloproliferative neoplasm, defined by persistent absolute monocytosis > 1x10^9/L. It carries a risk of transformation to AML.
keyFact: CMML is classified as an MDS/MPN overlap syndrome in the WHO classification — it has both dysplastic (MDS-like) and proliferative (MPN-like) features, with persistent absolute monocytosis > 1x10^9/L as the defining criterion.

wrongAnswers.name: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CML has the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL1), basophilia, and left-shifted granulocytosis without significant monocytosis; it lacks dysplasia and BCR-ABL1 is absent in CMML

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive monocytosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive monocytosis can occur in infections, autoimmune disease, and recovery from neutropenia; it lacks clonal cytogenetics, dysplasia, and the persistent > 3-month duration

wrongAnswers.name: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDS has < 1x10^9/L monocytes and lacks the monocytic expansion; CMML is distinguished by absolute monocytosis exceeding the MDS/MPN threshold

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue and pallor requiring repeated blood transfusions over the past three months.
She has a known anterior mediastinal mass found incidentally on imaging two years ago that has not been resected.
She is markedly pale; no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae, or bruising is present.

CBC shows hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL with normal WBC and platelets; reticulocyte count is less than 0.1%; peripheral smear shows normochromic normocytic red cells without dysplastic changes or hemolysis markers.
Bone marrow biopsy shows complete absence of erythroid precursors with normal myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages; anti-erythropoietin antibodies are detected.
explanation: Pure red cell aplasia is characterized by selective absence of erythroid precursors in the marrow with normal WBC and platelets. It is associated with thymoma, parvovirus B19, large granular lymphocyte leukemia, and EPO therapy.
keyFact: The classic association of pure red cell aplasia with thymoma — present in 5% of thymoma cases and requiring thymectomy as part of treatment — is a high-yield board fact.

wrongAnswers.name: Aplastic anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia with hypocellular marrow affecting all lineages; PRCA selectively eliminates only erythroid precursors

wrongAnswers.name: Myelodysplastic syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MDS causes multilineage dysplasia with variable cytopenias and dysplastic cells on biopsy; PRCA shows a cellular marrow with absent erythroid precursors only

wrongAnswers.name: Hemolytic anemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hemolytic anemia features elevated reticulocyte count, schistocytes or spherocytes, elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin — the opposite of PRCA's absent reticulocyte response

clues: A 58-year-old man undergoing chemotherapy for lymphoma presents with sudden onset of chills, malaise, and feeling feverish ten days after his last treatment cycle.
He received CHOP chemotherapy; he has no localizing symptoms such as cough, dysuria, diarrhea, or skin lesions and no sick contacts.
Temperature is 38.6 degrees C; heart rate is 102; blood pressure is 118/72; no oral mucositis, skin breakdown, or perianal tenderness is found and no clear source of infection is identified.
CBC shows WBC 0.3 with absolute neutrophil count of 180 cells per microliter; chest X-ray and urinalysis are unremarkable.
Repeat CBC confirms absolute neutrophil count below 500 cells/uL; procalcitonin is elevated at 1.8 ng/mL despite negative initial cultures, and the MASCC risk score is calculated at 15.
explanation: Febrile neutropenia is defined as a single temperature >= 38.3 degrees C (or >= 38.0 degrees C sustained for 1 hour) with ANC < 500/uL. Empirical anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam therapy (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime) is initiated immediately.
keyFact: MASCC score >= 21 identifies low-risk febrile neutropenia patients eligible for oral antibiotics and outpatient management; MASCC < 21 requires inpatient IV antibiotics.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug fever from CHOP
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion and should not delay empirical antibiotics in a neutropenic patient; ANC < 500 mandates immediate treatment regardless of suspected etiology

wrongAnswers.name: Tumor fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lymphoma can cause B-symptoms including fever, but fever in a neutropenic post-chemotherapy patient must be treated as infectious until proven otherwise

wrongAnswers.name: Viral upper respiratory infection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral URI does not account for the urgency in a patient with ANC 180; febrile neutropenia management requires empirical antibacterial coverage regardless of viral suspicion

clues: A 35-year-old man on long-term immunosuppression following a kidney transplant presents with fever, unintentional weight loss, and new lumps in his neck over the past month.
He was EBV-seronegative before receiving his transplant from an EBV-seropositive donor three years ago; he takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate.
Firm, non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy is present bilaterally with an enlarged right tonsil; no hepatosplenomegaly is noted.
EBV viral load is markedly elevated; CT shows multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, mediastinum, and mesentery with a 3 cm tonsillar mass.
Excisional lymph node biopsy shows a monomorphic proliferation of large B cells expressing CD20 with a high Ki-67 index; EBER in situ hybridization is strongly positive.
explanation: PTLD encompasses a spectrum from polyclonal EBV-driven lymphoid proliferations to frank monomorphic B-cell lymphomas in transplant recipients. Reduction of immunosuppression is the first step in management.
keyFact: PTLD most commonly arises in EBV-seronegative recipients who receive an EBV-seropositive organ — the highest-risk group — and occurs preferentially in the first year post-transplant when immunosuppression is most intense.

wrongAnswers.name: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (de novo)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: De novo DLBCL occurs in immunocompetent patients; the transplant context, elevated EBV load, and EBER positivity establish PTLD as the specific diagnosis

wrongAnswers.name: Infectious mononucleosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EBV mononucleosis in an immunocompetent host is self-limited with heterophile antibodies; in a transplant recipient the clonal proliferation and CD20+ biopsy distinguish PTLD

wrongAnswers.name: Graft rejection (acute cellular)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute rejection presents with rising creatinine, allograft tenderness, and biopsy showing T-cell tubulitis — not extragraft lymphadenopathy with B-cell proliferation

clues: A 40-year-old man who underwent allogeneic stem cell transplant six months ago presents with a new skin rash, watery diarrhea, and yellowing of his eyes.
The rash started on his palms and soles and has been spreading toward his trunk; stool cultures are negative and CMV PCR is negative.
Maculopapular erythema involves the palms, soles, and upper trunk; the skin is tender; scleral icterus is present; abdomen is soft with hyperactive bowel sounds.
Liver function tests show elevated total bilirubin with a conjugated predominance; stool volume exceeds 1 liter per day; CMV PCR is negative.
Liver biopsy demonstrates bile duct destruction with lymphocytic infiltration and endotheliitis; chimerism analysis confirms the infiltrating lymphocytes are of donor origin.
explanation: Acute GVHD is a T-cell mediated alloreaction against host tissues, classically involving skin, liver, and GI tract within 100 days of allogeneic HSCT. Grading determines steroid dosing and prognosis.
keyFact: Acute GVHD grading (I-IV) uses the extent of skin rash (% BSA), bilirubin level, and daily stool volume — Grade III-IV has > 30% mortality and requires second-line therapy when steroid-refractory.

wrongAnswers.name: CMV enteritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CMV enteritis causes diarrhea and colonic ulceration in immunosuppressed patients; CMV PCR is negative here, and the triad of skin/liver/GI involvement with biopsy findings points to GVHD

wrongAnswers.name: Veno-occlusive disease (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VOD/SOS presents with hepatomegaly, weight gain, ascites, and hyperbilirubinemia without the skin rash or diarrhea triad — liver biopsy shows sinusoidal obstruction, not bile duct lymphocytic infiltration

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-induced liver injury (tacrolimus/cyclosporine)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CNI toxicity causes nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity rather than the multi-organ skin/liver/GI presentation; biopsy would show drug-induced pattern, not bile duct lymphocytic damage

clues: A 32-year-old woman presents with sudden pain and swelling in her left leg that developed over the past day.
She has had three unexplained pregnancy losses and a prior deep vein thrombosis in the opposite leg two years ago.
The left leg is swollen, warm, and tender along the medial thigh; Homan sign is positive; no skin rash or joint findings are present.
Doppler ultrasound confirms left femoral DVT; CBC shows mild thrombocytopenia; hypercoagulable workup is otherwise negative.
Anti-cardiolipin IgG, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I IgG, and lupus anticoagulant are all positive on two separate occasions drawn 14 weeks apart.
explanation: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia caused by antibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins, causing arterial/venous thrombosis and obstetric complications. Anticoagulation is the cornerstone of treatment.
keyFact: The APS diagnosis requires both a clinical criterion (thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity) AND a laboratory criterion (positive lupus anticoagulant, aCL, or anti-beta-2-GPI on 2 occasions >= 12 weeks apart).

wrongAnswers.name: Factor V Leiden thrombophilia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Factor V Leiden causes venous thrombosis but not recurrent pregnancy loss or lupus anticoagulant positivity; it is a fixed genetic variant, not an acquired antibody

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE may coexist with APS ('secondary APS') but is not required for the diagnosis; this patient meets primary APS criteria without evidence of SLE

wrongAnswers.name: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HIT requires prior heparin exposure with new thrombocytopenia and anti-PF4 antibodies; the patient has no documented heparin use and positive antiphospholipid antibodies

clues: A 75-year-old woman presents with three days of intermittent crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, and abdominal distension; symptoms seem to transiently improve then worsen.
She has no prior abdominal surgery; she reports the pain comes and goes in waves.
Abdomen is distended with high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds; mild diffuse tenderness without peritoneal signs; no surgical scars are present.
Plain abdominal X-ray shows small bowel air-fluid levels, air in the biliary tree, and an ectopic calcified density in the right iliac fossa.
CT shows a 3.5 cm gallstone impacted at the ileocecal valve with small bowel obstruction and a fistulous tract between the gallbladder fundus and the second portion of the duodenum.
explanation: Gallstone ileus is a mechanical small bowel obstruction caused by a large gallstone eroding through a cholecystoenteric fistula. The CT triad (pneumobilia, ectopic gallstone, SBO) is diagnostic. Surgical enterolithotomy is definitive.
keyFact: Rigler's triad — pneumobilia + small bowel obstruction + ectopic gallstone visible on imaging — is pathognomonic for gallstone ileus; it accounts for 25% of SBO in patients over 65 without prior surgery.

wrongAnswers.name: Adhesive small bowel obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adhesive SBO requires a history of prior abdominal surgery or peritonitis; this patient has no prior surgery and the imaging shows pneumobilia and an ectopic gallstone

wrongAnswers.name: Colorectal cancer with obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Colorectal cancer causes large bowel obstruction, not small bowel; it would not produce pneumobilia or an ectopic calcified density in the ileum

wrongAnswers.name: Acute cholecystitis with CBD obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute cholecystitis causes RUQ pain, Murphy sign, and CBD dilation on ultrasound — not SBO; pneumobilia here indicates a cholecystoenteric fistula, not uncomplicated cholecystitis

clues: A 22-year-old woman with a recent 15-pound weight loss presents with six weeks of progressive post-prandial nausea, bilious vomiting, and epigastric pain.
She reports that symptoms improve when she lies on her left side or gets into a knee-chest position.
She is cachectic with a BMI of 16; abdomen shows epigastric distension with a succussion splash; no peritoneal signs are present.
Upper GI series shows dilation of the first and second portions of the duodenum with abrupt cutoff at the third portion and to-and-fro peristalsis.

CT angiography with 3D reconstruction shows an aortomesenteric angle of 18 degrees and aortomesenteric distance of 6 mm with the third duodenal segment compressed between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery.
explanation: SMA syndrome results from compression of the third portion of the duodenum in the aortomesenteric angle following loss of mesenteric fat. It is precipitated by rapid weight loss, prolonged supine position, or spine surgery.
keyFact: SMA syndrome is precipitated by anything reducing the aortomesenteric angle (normally 25-60 degrees): rapid weight loss, body casting after spinal surgery, prolonged bed rest — the 'cast syndrome' after spinal body casts is a classic trigger.

wrongAnswers.name: Gastroparesis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gastroparesis causes delayed gastric emptying with vomiting of undigested food; UGI series would show gastric retention, not duodenal obstruction at the third portion with aortomesenteric compression

wrongAnswers.name: Duodenal ulcer with obstruction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Peptic ulcer obstruction occurs at the pylorus/first duodenum due to scarring; SMA syndrome compresses the third portion of the duodenum — a more distal location — without ulcer crater on imaging

wrongAnswers.name: Achalasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Achalasia involves esophageal dysmotility with a bird-beak sign at the GEJ; it does not cause duodenal obstruction and is unrelated to weight loss or mesenteric fat

clues: A 68-year-old woman presents with worsening fatigue and exercise intolerance; her stools are dark but she has not seen frank blood.
She has a history of cirrhosis and a connective tissue disorder; stool is guaiac-positive without overt melena or hematochezia.
She appears pale with signs of chronic liver disease including palmar erythema and spider angiomata; abdomen shows mild ascites; no active bleeding is seen on rectal exam.
Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL with iron studies showing iron deficiency; upper endoscopy shows linear red stripes radiating from the pylorus to the antrum resembling a watermelon rind.

Biopsy of antral lesions shows dilated mucosal capillaries with intravascular fibrin thrombi and fibromuscular hyperplasia of the lamina propria; narrow-band imaging confirms dilated collecting venules in parallel longitudinal rows converging at the pylorus.
explanation: GAVE is characterized by ectatic mucosal vessels in the gastric antrum causing chronic occult GI bleeding. It is associated with cirrhosis, systemic sclerosis, and renal failure. Argon plasma coagulation is first-line endoscopic treatment.
keyFact: GAVE is distinguished from portal hypertensive gastropathy by its antral distribution (not fundus/body), watermelon endoscopic appearance, and persistence/worsening despite TIPS — whereas PHG improves with TIPS.

wrongAnswers.name: Portal hypertensive gastropathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PHG affects the fundus and body with a mosaic/snake-skin pattern; it improves with TIPS or propranolol, whereas GAVE is antral, does not respond to TIPS, and requires endoscopic ablation

wrongAnswers.name: Gastric antral ulcer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Peptic ulcers are discrete mucosal defects with erythematous bases; they do not produce the longitudinal red stripe pattern from pylorus to antrum or the dilated capillary histology of GAVE

wrongAnswers.name: Gastric vascular malformation (AVM)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gastric AVMs are solitary pulsatile lesions with large vessels on histology; GAVE is a diffuse, linear, antrum-limited pattern with fibrin thrombi — not a focal AV communication

clues: A 7-year-old boy from a rural tropical community presents with recurrent abdominal pain and abdominal distension.
He has a history of playing in soil and eating unwashed vegetables; he has not traveled outside his community.
Mild periumbilical tenderness is present with a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant; bowel sounds are hyperactive; lungs are clear.
CBC shows eosinophilia at 12%; abdominal X-ray shows a tubular mass causing partial small bowel obstruction with a coiled-spring appearance.
Stool microscopy shows large fertilized ova with a mammillated outer coat measuring 60-70 micrometers, and abdominal imaging confirms a bolus of tubular filling defects within the small bowel lumen.
explanation: Ascariasis is the most common helminthic infection worldwide, caused by Ascaris lumbricoides. Large worm burdens cause intestinal obstruction; Loeffler syndrome (pulmonary eosinophilia) occurs during larval lung migration.
keyFact: Ascaris lumbricoides is the largest intestinal nematode; during larval migration through the lungs it causes Loeffler syndrome — transient pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia — which precedes the intestinal stage by weeks.

wrongAnswers.name: Intussusception
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Intussusception typically causes intermittent colicky pain with currant-jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass; plain films would show a soft-tissue lead point, not coiled tubular filling defects from worms

wrongAnswers.name: Trichuriasis (whipworm)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trichuris trichiura causes rectal prolapse and bloody diarrhea with lemon-shaped eggs on stool exam; worm mass obstruction and the large mammillated eggs are features of Ascaris, not Trichuris

wrongAnswers.name: Appendicitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Appendicitis causes focal RLQ tenderness with fever and elevated WBC; the worm visualization, eosinophilia, and imaging showing tubular filling defects establish Ascaris as the cause

clues: A 35-year-old man presents with three weeks of profuse, non-bloody watery diarrhea and significant weight loss.
He has not been adherent with his antiretroviral medications for several months.
He is cachectic and dehydrated with dry mucous membranes; abdomen is soft with diffuse mild tenderness and hyperactive bowel sounds; no hepatosplenomegaly.
Stool cultures for bacteria are negative; fecal leukocytes are absent; stool microscopy with modified acid-fast staining reveals pink-red oocysts 4-6 micrometers in diameter.
CD4 count returns at 38 cells/uL; stool antigen EIA is positive; modified acid-fast stain confirms 4-6 micrometer pink-red oocysts.
explanation: Cryptosporidiosis causes self-limited diarrhea in immunocompetent hosts but can cause life-threatening cholera-like diarrhea in patients with CD4 < 50. ART to restore CD4 count is the most effective treatment; nitazoxanide has limited efficacy in AIDS.
keyFact: Cryptosporidium oocysts are identified by modified acid-fast stain (not routine O&P); the oocysts are acid-fast positive (pink/red) at 4-6 um — much smaller than Cyclospora (8-10 um) and Isospora (25 um).

wrongAnswers.name: Isosporiasis (Cystoisospora belli)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cystoisospora also causes watery diarrhea in AIDS but has much larger oocysts (25 um), is acid-fast positive, and responds well to TMP-SMX — unlike Cryptosporidium

wrongAnswers.name: Microsporidiosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Microsporidium causes diarrhea in AIDS but requires modified trichrome or Calcofluor staining to visualize the much smaller (1-2 um) spores; acid-fast stain is negative

wrongAnswers.name: CMV colitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CMV colitis causes bloody diarrhea with mucosal ulceration and intranuclear inclusions on biopsy; Cryptosporidium produces watery diarrhea with brush-border parasites, not ulceration

clues: A newborn boy appears dusky and breathes rapidly shortly after delivery; supplemental oxygen does not improve his color.
There is no family history of congenital heart disease; the pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal prenatal ultrasounds.
A single loud S2 is heard with no audible tricuspid valve component; a holosystolic murmur is present at the left lower sternal border; peripheral cyanosis is noted.
ECG shows left axis deviation and left ventricular hypertrophy; chest X-ray shows decreased pulmonary vascular markings; pulse oximetry reads 72% on room air with no improvement on 100% FiO2.
Echocardiogram demonstrates complete absence of the tricuspid valve with an atretic plate, a hypoplastic right ventricle, and obligatory right-to-left shunting through an atrial septal defect.
explanation: Tricuspid atresia is the absence of the tricuspid valve causing complete obstruction to right ventricular inflow. Survival depends on an ASD (for right-to-left shunting) and a PDA or VSD. ECG showing LVH/LAD in a cyanotic neonate is characteristic.
keyFact: Tricuspid atresia is the only cyanotic congenital heart disease that classically shows LEFT axis deviation and LEFT ventricular hypertrophy on ECG — all other cyanotic CHDs cause right axis deviation and RVH.

wrongAnswers.name: Tetralogy of Fallot
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ToF causes cyanosis with right ventricular hypertrophy and right axis deviation on ECG; the boot-shaped heart on CXR and RV outflow obstruction distinguish it from tricuspid atresia's LVH/LAD pattern

wrongAnswers.name: Transposition of the great arteries
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TGA causes cyanosis with an egg-on-a-string CXR and parallel great vessel arrangement on echo; ECG shows RVH, not the LVH/LAD characteristic of tricuspid atresia

wrongAnswers.name: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TAPVR causes cyanosis with snowman-sign CXR (supracardiac type) and RVH; pulmonary veins drain anomalously but the tricuspid valve is present and normal

clues: A 15-year-old boy presents with persistent knee pain and swelling for six weeks that is worse at night and not relieved by rest; there is no history of trauma.
He is in the middle of a growth spurt and recently joined the track team; the pain has been steadily worsening despite over-the-counter pain relievers.
Point tenderness is present over the distal femur metaphysis; a firm, fixed mass is palpable with warm overlying skin and dilated veins; no fever; knee range of motion is limited by pain.
Alkaline phosphatase and LDH are elevated; X-ray shows a mixed lytic and blastic lesion in the distal femur metaphysis with periosteal elevation forming a triangular shape and a sunburst pattern.
MRI defines intramedullary extension and a large soft tissue mass; biopsy shows malignant cells producing osteoid matrix.
explanation: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor, predominantly arising in the metaphysis of long bones around the knee in adolescents during periods of rapid bone growth. The Codman triangle (periosteal elevation) and sunburst pattern on X-ray are classic radiographic features.
keyFact: Osteosarcoma peaks in the second decade of life during adolescent growth spurts and is the most common bone tumor in children; it has a bimodal age distribution with a second peak in Paget disease patients.

wrongAnswers.name: Ewing sarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ewing sarcoma arises in the diaphysis, shows an 'onion skin' periosteal reaction on X-ray, and carries the EWS-FLI1 translocation t(11;22), unlike the metaphyseal Codman triangle of osteosarcoma.

wrongAnswers.name: Osteomyelitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Osteomyelitis typically presents with fever, leukocytosis, and bone edema on MRI; it does not produce malignant osteoid on biopsy.

wrongAnswers.name: Giant cell tumor of bone
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Giant cell tumors arise in the epiphysis of skeletally mature adults and show a soap-bubble lytic appearance without the bone-forming matrix of osteosarcoma.

clues: A 34-year-old woman presents with six months of progressive fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and intermittent nausea.
She reports episodes of dizziness when standing and has developed a strong craving for salty foods.
Blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg supine with further drop on standing; diffuse hyperpigmentation is noted on the buccal mucosa, palmar creases, and areas of friction.
Sodium is 128 mEq/L, potassium is 5.8 mEq/L, and morning cortisol is 3.2 mcg/dL with ACTH elevated at 980 pg/mL.
Cosyntropin stimulation test shows a peak cortisol of 8 mcg/dL at 60 minutes, failing to rise above 18 mcg/dL.
explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency results from destruction of the adrenal cortex, causing deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone. Elevated ACTH drives hyperpigmentation via melanocortin receptor stimulation.
keyFact: Hyperpigmentation in primary (not secondary) adrenal insufficiency distinguishes it from central causes; aldosterone deficiency causes hyperkalemia and hyponatremia.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary adrenal insufficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pituitary/hypothalamic causes produce low ACTH and no hyperpigmentation; aldosterone is preserved so hyperkalemia is absent.

wrongAnswers.name: Anorexia nervosa
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Causes weight loss and fatigue but lacks hyperpigmentation, hyperkalemia, or an impaired cortisol response to ACTH stimulation.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Can cause fatigue and hyponatremia but does not produce hyperpigmentation, hyperkalemia, or orthostatic hypotension from volume depletion.

clues: A 42-year-old woman presents with progressive weight gain concentrated in her face and abdomen over the past year, along with easy bruising.
She has developed new-onset high blood pressure and was recently found to have elevated blood sugar on routine labs.
Central obesity with a dorsocervical fat pad, facial plethora, and wide violaceous striae greater than 1 cm on the abdomen are present; proximal muscle weakness is noted.
24-hour urine free cortisol is four times the upper limit of normal; overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test shows a morning cortisol of 18 mcg/dL.
ACTH is suppressed at less than 5 pg/mL; adrenal CT reveals a 2.1 cm right adrenal adenoma with attenuation less than 10 Hounsfield units.
explanation: Cushing syndrome from an autonomous adrenal adenoma produces excess cortisol independent of ACTH, causing suppression of the pituitary-adrenal axis. Clinical features reflect glucocorticoid excess across multiple organ systems.
keyFact: ACTH-independent Cushing (adrenal adenoma) shows suppressed ACTH, whereas ACTH-dependent causes (pituitary adenoma, ectopic) show normal or elevated ACTH.

wrongAnswers.name: Cushing disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma would show elevated, not suppressed, ACTH levels.

wrongAnswers.name: Metabolic syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Shares central obesity and diabetes but does not cause violaceous striae, dorsocervical fat pad, or failure to suppress cortisol.

wrongAnswers.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Can cause weight gain and insulin resistance but does not produce hypercortisolism, striae, or plethora.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with a slowly growing lump in her neck, intermittent diarrhea, and episodes of flushing.
Her mother died of thyroid cancer at age 35; she also endorses occasional headaches and episodic high blood pressure readings.
A firm, non-tender 2 cm thyroid nodule is palpable in the right lobe; blood pressure is 168/95 mmHg during the visit; no exophthalmos or tremor is present.
Serum calcitonin is markedly elevated at 1,840 pg/mL; 24-hour urine metanephrines are elevated; calcium is 11.0 mg/dL with elevated PTH.
FNA of the thyroid nodule shows polygonal cells in an amyloid stroma; germline testing identifies a pathogenic RET proto-oncogene mutation.
explanation: MEN2A is caused by germline RET mutations and comprises medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism. Elevated calcitonin is a sensitive marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma.
keyFact: Pheochromocytoma must be excluded and treated before thyroid surgery in MEN2 patients to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis.

wrongAnswers.name: MEN1
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MEN1 features pituitary adenoma and gastrinoma, not medullary thyroid carcinoma or RET mutations.

wrongAnswers.name: Papillary thyroid cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Papillary thyroid cancer does not secrete calcitonin, is not associated with pheochromocytoma, and is not linked to RET germline mutations in this pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Carcinoid syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoid produces serotonin-mediated flushing and diarrhea but does not cause elevated calcitonin or concurrent pheochromocytoma.

clues: A 30-year-old woman presents with unintentional weight loss despite a good appetite, difficulty sleeping, and a visible swelling in the front of her neck.
She has noticed a racing heartbeat and irregular menstrual periods over the past three months.
A diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid gland is palpable; a fine resting tremor is present; mild bilateral proptosis with lid lag is noted.
TSH is undetectable; free T4 is 3.8 ng/dL and free T3 is markedly elevated; radioactive iodine uptake scan shows diffusely increased homogeneous uptake.
TSH receptor antibodies are positive at 12 IU/L.
explanation: Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism, driven by IgG antibodies that stimulate TSH receptors. Diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy, and occasionally pretibial myxedema are distinguishing features.
keyFact: TRAb (TSH receptor antibodies) are both diagnostic and pathogenic in Graves disease; ophthalmopathy can worsen with radioactive iodine treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Toxic multinodular goiter
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Causes hyperthyroidism in older patients with a nodular, not diffusely enlarged, thyroid and absent TRAb; no ophthalmopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Subacute thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Causes transient hyperthyroidism with a tender thyroid and LOW radioactive iodine uptake due to follicular destruction, not increased uptake.

wrongAnswers.name: Anxiety disorder
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Accounts for anxiety and palpitations but not weight loss, proptosis, diffuse goiter, or suppressed TSH.

clues: A 44-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight gain, and difficulty concentrating over the past year.
She has a family history of autoimmune conditions and has noticed her hair has been thinning and her skin feels dry.
Skin is dry with delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes; a mildly enlarged, firm, rubbery, non-tender thyroid gland is palpable; mild periorbital puffiness is present.
TSH is elevated at 14.2 mIU/L; free T4 is low-normal at 0.7 ng/dL; CBC shows mild normocytic anemia.
Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are markedly elevated at greater than 1,000 IU/mL; thyroid ultrasound shows a diffusely heterogeneous, hypoechoic gland.
explanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions, caused by autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicular cells. Elevated anti-TPO antibodies and a heterogeneous thyroid on ultrasound are characteristic.
keyFact: Anti-TPO antibodies are present in over 95% of patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis and correlate with the degree of lymphocytic infiltration and fibrosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Central hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pituitary or hypothalamic hypothyroidism causes low TSH with low T4; this patient has elevated TSH indicating primary thyroid failure.

wrongAnswers.name: Subacute thyroiditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Subacute thyroiditis presents with a tender thyroid and transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism; it lacks high anti-TPO antibodies and the thyroid is acutely painful.

wrongAnswers.name: Depression
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fatigue and cognitive changes can overlap, but depression does not cause elevated TSH, anti-TPO antibodies, or characteristic thyroid changes.

clues: A 32-year-old woman is referred for evaluation of a neck mass noticed incidentally during a routine physical exam; she has no symptoms.
She received low-dose radiation to the head and neck as a teenager for a benign condition.
A firm, solitary 2.4 cm thyroid nodule is palpable in the right lobe with a firm, non-tender ipsilateral cervical lymph node; the rest of the neck exam is unremarkable.
Thyroid ultrasound shows a hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications, irregular margins, and taller-than-wide shape; thyroid function tests are normal.
Fine needle aspiration cytology shows cells with large, clear, grooved nuclei containing intranuclear pseudoinclusions; molecular testing identifies a BRAF V600E mutation.
explanation: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy and has an excellent prognosis. It frequently spreads to regional lymph nodes but distant metastases are rare.
keyFact: Papillary thyroid cancer has the best prognosis of thyroid malignancies; Orphan Annie eye nuclei and BRAF V600E mutation are characteristic pathologic findings.

wrongAnswers.name: Follicular thyroid cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Follicular carcinoma spreads hematogenously to lung and bone rather than lymph nodes first, and FNA cannot distinguish follicular carcinoma from adenoma — capsular invasion on histology is required.

wrongAnswers.name: Medullary thyroid cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Medullary thyroid cancer secretes calcitonin and shows amyloid stroma on pathology; it does not have Orphan Annie nuclei or BRAF mutations.

wrongAnswers.name: Benign thyroid adenoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Adenomas are encapsulated without malignant cytologic features; microcalcifications, irregular margins, and lymphadenopathy indicate malignancy.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with a firm neck lump and a several-month history of intermittent diarrhea and facial flushing; he has no symptoms of hyper- or hypothyroidism.
His father had thyroid cancer and died from a hypertensive crisis during surgery.
A firm, irregular 3 cm right thyroid nodule is palpable with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy; blood pressure is elevated at 158/94 mmHg.
Serum calcitonin is 2,400 pg/mL; CEA is elevated; 24-hour urine metanephrines are within normal limits; TSH and free T4 are normal.
FNA of the thyroid nodule shows polygonal cells with granular cytoplasm embedded in an amyloid stroma; RET mutation testing reveals a C634F pathogenic variant.
explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C-cells and secretes calcitonin. It occurs sporadically in 75% of cases but in 25% occurs in the context of MEN2 or familial MTC due to RET mutations.
keyFact: Calcitonin is the most sensitive and specific tumor marker for medullary thyroid cancer; amyloid deposits in the stroma are pathognomonic on histology.

wrongAnswers.name: Papillary thyroid cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Papillary cancer does not secrete calcitonin, lacks amyloid stroma, and is not associated with RET germline mutations in this pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Carcinoid tumor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carcinoid causes flushing and diarrhea via serotonin with elevated 5-HIAA; calcitonin is not elevated and the lesion is not in the thyroid.

wrongAnswers.name: Anaplastic thyroid cancer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Anaplastic cancer presents in elderly patients with rapid, painful thyroid enlargement and aggressive local invasion; it does not secrete calcitonin.

clues: A 26-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual periods for eight months and unexpected fluid discharge from both breasts.
She denies pregnancy and has not started any new medications; she also reports occasional headaches and mild blurring of her peripheral vision.
Bilateral galactorrhea is expressed on breast compression; confrontational visual field testing reveals bitemporal visual field narrowing.
Serum prolactin is 980 ng/mL; FSH and LH are low; TSH is normal; pregnancy test is negative.
MRI of the sella with gadolinium shows a 1.8 cm mass with suprasellar extension abutting the optic chiasm.
explanation: Prolactinoma is the most common functional pituitary adenoma. Prolactin inhibits GnRH pulsatility, causing hypogonadism; macroadenomas can compress surrounding structures including the optic chiasm.
keyFact: Dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) are first-line treatment for prolactinomas and can shrink even large tumors; the hook effect can falsely lower prolactin in very large tumors requiring sample dilution.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Antipsychotics and dopamine antagonists can raise prolactin, but levels rarely exceed 150-200 ng/mL and there is no pituitary mass.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism raises TRH which stimulates prolactin, but TSH would be elevated and prolactin levels are usually modestly elevated, not in the hundreds.

wrongAnswers.name: Craniopharyngioma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Craniopharyngioma compresses the stalk causing mild hyperprolactinemia (stalk effect, usually less than 150 ng/mL) rather than the markedly elevated levels from a prolactin-secreting adenoma.

clues: A 47-year-old man presents with persistent headaches and progressive joint pain over the past three years.
His wife notes his facial features have coarsened and his shoe size has increased by two sizes; he was recently diagnosed with sleep apnea and carpal tunnel syndrome.
Enlarged hands with doughy texture, frontal bossing, prognathism with dental spacing, and macroglossia are present on examination.
IGF-1 is three times the upper limit of normal for age; random GH is 12 ng/mL; fasting glucose is 118 mg/dL.
GH fails to suppress below 1 ng/mL after a 75 g oral glucose challenge; MRI shows a 1.4 cm pituitary macroadenoma.
explanation: Acromegaly results from excess GH secretion (almost always from a pituitary adenoma) after epiphyseal closure, causing progressive soft tissue and bony changes. Elevated IGF-1 is the best screening test; failure of GH suppression on OGTT is confirmatory.
keyFact: Complications of acromegaly include sleep apnea, cardiomyopathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, and increased colon cancer risk; cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death.

wrongAnswers.name: Gigantism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Gigantism occurs when GH excess begins before epiphyseal closure, causing linear growth; acromegaly occurs after fusion, causing acral and soft tissue enlargement without height increase.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism can cause soft tissue swelling and coarse features but does not enlarge acral structures or suppress GH on oral glucose, and IGF-1 is not elevated.

wrongAnswers.name: Familial large stature
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Constitutional tall stature is not associated with coarsening of facial features, carpal tunnel, sleep apnea, or elevated IGF-1.

clues: A 30-year-old man presents with several months of excessive thirst and frequent urination, including waking multiple times at night to drink water and urinate.
He had a severe traumatic head injury in a motor vehicle collision eight months ago requiring hospitalization.
He appears well-hydrated from excessive water intake; mucous membranes are moist; no papilledema; neurologic exam is nonfocal.
Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L; serum osmolality is 302 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality during a symptomatic episode is 65 mOsm/kg; during water deprivation urine osmolality remains below 200 mOsm/kg.
Urine osmolality rises to 620 mOsm/kg after administration of desmopressin.
explanation: Central diabetes insipidus results from deficient ADH secretion, often from hypothalamic-pituitary damage due to trauma, surgery, or infiltrative disease. DDAVP responsiveness distinguishes it from nephrogenic DI.
keyFact: In central DI, urine osmolality rises greater than 50% after DDAVP; in nephrogenic DI, the kidney cannot respond to ADH so urine osmolality fails to rise.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nephrogenic DI shows no response to DDAVP because the kidney tubules are resistant to ADH; central DI shows a robust response to desmopressin.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary polydipsia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psychogenic polydipsia causes dilute urine but serum sodium and osmolality are typically low-normal or low; during water deprivation, urine can eventually concentrate.

wrongAnswers.name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis with polyuria and polydipsia, but urine osmolality is elevated due to glycosuria and there is no failure to concentrate with DDAVP.

clues: A 19-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and rapid breathing that developed over the past day.
She has been drinking large amounts of water and urinating frequently for several weeks, and has lost 15 pounds without trying.
She is tachycardic at 118 bpm and breathing deeply and rapidly; mucous membranes are dry; skin turgor is decreased; a fruity odor is noted on her breath.
Glucose is 498 mg/dL; ABG shows pH 7.18, bicarbonate 9 mEq/L, pCO2 22 mmHg; anion gap is 28; urine ketones are large.
Anti-GAD65 and anti-IA2 antibodies are positive; C-peptide is undetectable.
explanation: DKA results from absolute or relative insulin deficiency causing hyperglycemia, ketonemia, and high anion gap metabolic acidosis. It is a common presentation of new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus.
keyFact: The anion gap in DKA reflects accumulation of beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate; Kussmaul respirations represent respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HHS occurs in type 2 diabetes with glucose typically greater than 600 mg/dL, minimal ketosis, and severe hyperosmolality; significant acidosis is absent.

wrongAnswers.name: Alcoholic ketoacidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AKA occurs in chronic alcohol users with low to normal glucose; anti-GAD antibodies are absent and the clinical setting involves alcohol abuse rather than new-onset polyuria.

wrongAnswers.name: Starvation ketosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Starvation produces mild ketonemia and low glucose without the severe hyperglycemia or anion gap acidosis seen in DKA.

clues: An 82-year-old woman in a nursing home is brought to the ED for progressive confusion and decreased oral intake over five days.
She has type 2 diabetes and was treated for a urinary tract infection with antibiotics one week ago; she had not been drinking well during this period.
She is profoundly lethargic with dry mucous membranes; blood pressure is 92/60 mmHg supine; no deep rapid breathing is noted; skin tenting is present.
Glucose is 1,120 mg/dL; sodium is 148 mEq/L; serum osmolality is 374 mOsm/kg; ABG shows pH 7.34 with near-normal bicarbonate; urine ketones are trace.
BUN is 68 mg/dL and creatinine is 2.8 mg/dL from a baseline of 0.9 mg/dL; head CT is unremarkable; calculated effective serum osmolality exceeds 320 mOsm/kg.
explanation: HHS is a hyperglycemic emergency of type 2 diabetes characterized by extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and severe dehydration without significant ketoacidosis, due to residual insulin preventing lipolysis.
keyFact: Serum osmolality greater than 320 mOsm/kg with altered mental status is the hallmark of HHS; mortality is higher than DKA (10-20% vs 1-5%) due to older age and underlying precipitants.

wrongAnswers.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DKA presents with significant ketosis, pH below 7.30, and anion gap metabolic acidosis; glucose is typically lower and Kussmaul respirations are present.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute ischemic stroke
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Stroke can cause altered mental status but does not produce glucose over 1,000 mg/dL, hyperosmolality, or the profound dehydration seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic encephalopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Infection precipitated this event, but the metabolic derangements of extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality are the direct cause of the altered mental status.

clues: A 45-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of shakiness, confusion, and sweating occurring most often when she has not eaten for several hours.
Her symptoms consistently resolve within minutes of eating or drinking juice; she has gained 12 pounds over the past year from frequent snacking to prevent episodes.
During an episode she appears pale and diaphoretic with a heart rate of 108; no focal neurologic deficits are present.

Supervised 72-hour fast: at hour 32 she becomes symptomatic with glucose 41 mg/dL, insulin 18 mIU/mL, C-peptide 4.2 ng/mL, and elevated proinsulin; sulfonylurea screen is negative and exogenous insulin antibodies are absent.
CT abdomen shows a 1.4 cm hypervascular lesion in the pancreatic body; intraoperative ultrasound confirms the solitary mass.
explanation: Insulinoma is the most common functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, causing endogenous hyperinsulinism with Whipple's triad: symptoms of hypoglycemia, documented low glucose, and relief with glucose administration.
keyFact: Elevated C-peptide and proinsulin during hypoglycemia confirm endogenous insulin secretion; absent insulin antibodies exclude exogenous insulin injection as the cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Factitious hypoglycemia from insulin injection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Exogenous insulin injection would suppress C-peptide and proinsulin, and insulin antibodies may be detectable; C-peptide is elevated here confirming endogenous production.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive hypoglycemia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive hypoglycemia occurs 2-4 hours after meals in the postprandial state; this patient has fasting hypoglycemia confirmed on a 72-hour fast.

wrongAnswers.name: Adrenal insufficiency
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cortisol deficiency can cause hypoglycemia but would also cause hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and fatigue without the elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemic episodes.

clues: A 38-year-old man presents with persistent, itchy patches on his elbows and knees for several months that are not responding to moisturizers.
The patches worsen during periods of high stress and improve slightly in summer with sun exposure.
Well-demarcated, erythematous plaques covered with silvery-white scale are present on bilateral elbows, knees, and lower back; gentle scraping of the scale produces pinpoint bleeding.
Nail examination reveals pitting and onycholysis in several fingernails.

Skin biopsy shows regular epidermal hyperplasia with parakeratosis, elongated rete ridges, thinned suprapapillary plates, dilated dermal capillaries, and neutrophilic collections (Munro microabscesses) in the stratum corneum.
explanation: Plaque psoriasis results from T-cell mediated inflammation that drives keratinocyte hyperproliferation, reducing epidermal turnover from 28 days to 3-4 days, producing the characteristic thickened, scaly plaques.
keyFact: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on scale removal) and nail pitting are classic associations; psoriasis is linked to psoriatic arthritis in up to 30% of patients.

wrongAnswers.name: Eczema/Atopic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atopic dermatitis favors flexural surfaces and produces ill-defined, weeping patches rather than well-demarcated, thick silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Corporis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea corporis typically presents as an annular, expanding ring with central clearing and raised scaly borders, not persistent thick bilateral plaques on elbows and knees.

wrongAnswers.name: Lichen Planus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lichen planus produces flat-topped, violaceous papules with Wickham striae, not thick silvery-scaled plaques, and does not show nail pitting pattern.

clues: A 19-year-old woman presents with a sudden outbreak of multiple small pink spots scattered across her trunk and arms over the past two weeks.
Three weeks prior she had a sore throat with fever that resolved on its own without antibiotics.
The lesions are 0.5 to 1.5 cm teardrop-shaped papules with a fine loose scale overlying an erythematous base, distributed on the trunk and proximal extremities.
Throat culture is currently negative, but antistreptolysin O titer is markedly elevated.
Skin biopsy demonstrates psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with parakeratosis, mild spongiosis, and a dermal perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.
explanation: Guttate psoriasis is triggered by streptococcal pharyngitis in genetically susceptible individuals; streptococcal antigens mimic skin proteins, activating T-cells that drive keratinocyte hyperproliferation in a widespread eruptive pattern.
keyFact: Guttate psoriasis classically follows streptococcal pharyngitis by 2-3 weeks; up to 40% of patients subsequently develop chronic plaque psoriasis.

wrongAnswers.name: Pityriasis Rosea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pityriasis rosea typically begins with a single herald patch before the secondary eruption, and lesions follow skin cleavage lines in a Christmas-tree distribution, unlike the random teardrop distribution seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary syphilis rash classically involves the palms and soles and is associated with systemic symptoms; RPR/VDRL would be positive, and the ASO titer elevation points to streptococcal, not treponemal, infection.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Exanthem
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral exanthems are typically morbilliform, non-scaly macules and papules that resolve within days; the scaling, teardrop shape, and elevated ASO titer argue against a viral cause.

clues: A 52-year-old obese man presents with a red, moist rash in his groin and under his abdominal fold that has been present for two months and is moderately itchy.
He has tried over-the-counter antifungal cream for one month without improvement; he has a family history of a chronic skin condition.
Bright red, smooth, well-demarcated plaques without significant scale are present in the inguinal folds and under the abdominal pannus; the skin is macerated in the folds.
