KOH preparation of skin scrapings is negative for hyphae or spores; fungal culture is also negative.
Skin biopsy shows psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with parakeratosis, dilated dermal capillaries, and neutrophilic collections in the stratum corneum; PAS staining is negative for fungal elements.
explanation: Inverse psoriasis affects intertriginous areas where friction and moisture suppress the scale formation typical of plaque psoriasis, resulting in smooth, bright red, well-demarcated plaques that mimic fungal or bacterial intertrigo.
keyFact: Inverse psoriasis lacks the typical silvery scale due to moisture in skin folds; it is often misdiagnosed as candidiasis, and negative KOH prep with family history of psoriasis raises suspicion.

wrongAnswers.name: Candidal Intertrigo
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Candidal intertrigo would show satellite pustules beyond the main lesion border and positive KOH prep or culture; antifungal failure and negative KOH argue against this diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Cruris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea cruris shows an advancing scaly border with central clearing and a positive KOH prep; the negative KOH and lack of scale with well-demarcated smooth plaques are inconsistent.

wrongAnswers.name: Contact Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Contact dermatitis would correlate with exposure to a specific allergen or irritant, typically shows vesiculation or weeping, and responds to topical steroids differently without the psoriasiform histology.

clues: A 7-year-old boy is brought in for intensely itchy, red, rough patches that have been coming and going for two years.
He has a history of asthma diagnosed at age 3 and seasonal allergic rhinitis; his mother and maternal aunt have similar skin problems.
Lichenified, erythematous patches with excoriations are present in the antecubital and popliteal fossae; the skin is diffusely dry; an extra skin fold is noted under each lower eyelid.
Serum IgE is markedly elevated at 1,200 IU/mL; skin prick testing shows sensitization to dust mites and cat dander.
Skin biopsy demonstrates spongiotic dermatitis with eosinophilic infiltrate; genetic testing identifies a filaggrin gene loss-of-function mutation.
explanation: Atopic dermatitis results from mutations in filaggrin and other barrier proteins that allow allergen penetration, triggering a Th2-dominant inflammatory response with IgE sensitization, leading to chronic pruritic inflammation in characteristic flexural distributions.
keyFact: The atopic triad is atopic dermatitis, asthma, and allergic rhinitis; Dennie-Morgan lines (extra infraorbital fold) are a classic physical finding; filaggrin mutations are the most common genetic risk factor.

wrongAnswers.name: Contact Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Allergic contact dermatitis would be localized to areas of allergen exposure and would not follow a bilateral flexural distribution or be associated with asthma and elevated IgE.

wrongAnswers.name: Scabies
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scabies causes diffuse pruritus with burrows in web spaces, wrists, and genitals, and would not show the flexural lichenification or the chronic relapsing-remitting course seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriasis favors extensor surfaces and presents with well-demarcated thick silvery plaques rather than the flexural, lichenified spongiotic patches with elevated IgE seen in this child.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with persistent flaking and redness on his scalp and face that waxes and wanes; it worsens in winter and during stressful periods.
He has been diagnosed with a neurologic movement disorder and takes levodopa.
Greasy, yellowish scales on an erythematous base are present along the nasolabial folds, eyebrows, and behind the ears, with diffuse scalp scaling.
KOH preparation of scalp scale shows budding yeast forms without pseudohyphae.
Skin biopsy reveals parakeratosis with neutrophils within scale crust, spongiosis, and follicular plugging with a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.
explanation: Seborrheic dermatitis results from an abnormal immune response to Malassezia yeast species that colonize sebaceous gland-rich skin, producing lipases that break down sebum into irritating free fatty acids causing inflammation.
keyFact: Seborrheic dermatitis is significantly more severe and widespread in patients with Parkinson's disease and HIV/AIDS; it affects sebaceous-rich areas including nasolabial folds, eyebrows, retroauricular skin, and scalp.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scalp psoriasis produces thicker, drier, silvery-white scales rather than greasy yellow ones, and typically extends beyond the hairline; nasolabial fold involvement and association with Parkinson's favor seborrheic dermatitis.

wrongAnswers.name: Rosacea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Rosacea involves central facial erythema with telangiectasias and papulopustules but does not produce scaling or involve the scalp, eyebrows, or retroauricular skin.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Capitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea capitis causes patchy scalp hair loss with broken hairs and cervical lymphadenopathy; KOH would show hyphae, not budding yeast, and facial involvement in this distribution is uncharacteristic.

clues: A 42-year-old woman presents with intensely itchy, purple bumps on her inner wrists and ankles for six weeks; she also notes a painful lesion inside her cheek.
She noticed a painful white lacy patch on the inside of her cheek around the same time as the skin lesions; she takes no medications.

Flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules with a shiny surface are present on the flexor wrists and ankles; fine white lines are visible on the surface of several papules under dermatoscopy; a white reticular patch is present on the buccal mucosa.
Hepatitis C antibody test returns positive; liver enzymes are mildly elevated.
Skin biopsy demonstrates a dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction with basal cell vacuolization, saw-tooth rete ridges, and colloid (Civatte) bodies.
explanation: Lichen planus is a T-cell mediated autoimmune condition in which cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells attack basal keratinocytes at the dermoepidermal junction; it is associated with hepatitis C virus in a significant subset of patients.
keyFact: The 6 P's of lichen planus: Pruritic, Planar (flat-topped), Polygonal, Purple Papules with Wickham striae; oral mucosal involvement and hepatitis C association are high-yield.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriasis produces thick silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces, not flat-topped violaceous papules with oral lacy lesions; the histology and hepatitis C association are not features of psoriasis.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug Eruption
wrongAnswers.whyNot: A lichenoid drug eruption can mimic lichen planus histologically but requires offending medication exposure; this patient takes no medications, making idiopathic lichen planus more consistent.

wrongAnswers.name: Pityriasis Rosea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pityriasis rosea presents with oval scaly macules following skin lines with a herald patch; it does not produce flat-topped violaceous papules or oral mucosal lesions.

clues: A 22-year-old woman presents with an itchy rash on her trunk that has been spreading for two weeks; she recalls a single larger patch appearing before the rest.
She recalls a single larger oval pink patch on her left flank about ten days before the current rash appeared; she had a mild upper respiratory illness three weeks ago.

Multiple 1-2 cm oval, salmon-colored macules with a collarette of scale along the inner border are distributed on the trunk and proximal arms following skin cleavage lines; palms, soles, and face are spared.
RPR is negative; KOH prep of scale is negative; CBC is normal.
Skin biopsy shows focal spongiosis with extravasated erythrocytes in the papillary dermis and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate without interface change or atypical cells.
explanation: Pityriasis rosea is a self-limited exanthem thought to be triggered by reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 or 7, producing a characteristic herald patch followed by a secondary eruption along Langer's lines.
keyFact: The herald patch precedes the secondary eruption by 1-2 weeks; secondary syphilis must be excluded with RPR; the rash self-resolves in 6-8 weeks without treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Secondary Syphilis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Secondary syphilis produces a similar truncal rash but classically involves the palms and soles and is associated with positive RPR/VDRL; the negative RPR here rules it out.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Corporis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea corporis produces annular plaques with advancing scaly edges and central clearing; it does not produce the Christmas-tree distribution or the collarette scale pattern seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug Eruption
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug eruptions (morbilliform) produce symmetric pink macules and papules but lack the collarette scale, herald patch, and Christmas-tree distribution; no offending drug is identified here.

clues: A 16-year-old boy who wrestles presents with a round, expanding patch on his upper arm that has been slowly growing over three weeks.
Several teammates have had similar lesions; he showers at the gym but shares towels occasionally.
A 4 cm annular, erythematous plaque with a raised, scaly, vesicular leading edge and relative central clearing is present on the right upper arm.
KOH preparation of scale from the advancing border shows branching septate hyphae.
Fungal culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar grows a dermatophyte identified as Trichophyton tonsurans after two weeks of incubation.
explanation: Tinea corporis is caused by dermatophyte fungi that invade keratinized tissue; they produce keratinases enabling colonization of the stratum corneum, with centrifugal spread creating the characteristic annular lesion with active advancing border.
keyFact: Tinea gladiatorum (T. tonsurans on the body of wrestlers) is transmitted by skin-to-skin contact; the active border with central clearing and positive KOH are diagnostic; avoid topical steroids alone as they cause tinea incognito.

wrongAnswers.name: Granuloma Annulare
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Granuloma annulare presents as a flesh-colored or red annular ring without scale and has a negative KOH; it is not contagious and does not have a vesicular advancing border.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriasis produces thick, silvery-scaled well-demarcated plaques without the central clearing or advancing vesicular border; KOH would be negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Nummular Eczema
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nummular eczema produces coin-shaped, oozing, crusted plaques but lacks an annular advancing scaly border with central clearing; KOH would be negative.

clues: A 24-year-old man presents with multiple discolored patches on his chest and back that become more noticeable in summer; mild itching is present occasionally.
He is otherwise healthy and active; he reports that the patches do not tan like the surrounding skin.

Multiple 0.5-2 cm hypopigmented macules with very fine, branny scale are scattered across the upper chest, back, and proximal arms; some lesions in non-sun-exposed areas appear faintly hyperpigmented.
Wood lamp examination shows yellow-green fluorescence of the affected patches.
KOH preparation of scale demonstrates short curved hyphae intermixed with round spores in a pattern described as spaghetti and meatballs.
explanation: Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur overgrowth, which produces azelaic acid that inhibits tyrosinase in melanocytes, causing hypopigmentation; in darker skin the inflammatory response can cause hyperpigmentation.
keyFact: KOH shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' (short hyphae + round spores); lesions are hypopigmented in sun-exposed skin and may be hyperpigmented in non-exposed skin; recurrence is common in hot, humid climates.

wrongAnswers.name: Vitiligo
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vitiligo produces completely depigmented (not merely hypopigmented) macules with no scale; Wood's lamp shows bright blue-white fluorescence and KOH is negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Pityriasis Rosea
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pityriasis rosea produces salmon-colored oval macules with collarette scale in a Christmas-tree distribution and includes a herald patch; KOH is negative and lesions are not hypopigmented.

wrongAnswers.name: Guttate Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Guttate psoriasis produces pink, scaly papules, not hypopigmented macules, and follows a streptococcal infection; KOH is negative and lesions are not related to sun exposure.

clues: A 6-year-old girl is brought in for patches of hair loss on her scalp with some scaliness noticed over two weeks.
Several children in her class have similar hair loss; her family recently adopted a kitten.
One to two areas of partial alopecia with broken-off hairs at the scalp surface, mild erythema, and gray-white scaling are present; a tender posterior cervical lymph node is palpable.
Wood lamp examination shows no fluorescence; KOH preparation of hair shafts shows spores filling the interior of the hair shaft.
Fungal culture grows Trichophyton tonsurans after 14 days.
explanation: Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte infection of the scalp and hair shaft predominantly affecting prepubertal children; T. tonsurans causes endothrix infection and does not fluoresce under Wood's lamp, unlike Microsporum species.
keyFact: T. tonsurans (most common in the US) causes endothrix infection with no Wood's lamp fluorescence; oral antifungals are required (topical agents do not penetrate the hair shaft); cervical lymphadenopathy is common.

wrongAnswers.name: Alopecia Areata
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Alopecia areata causes smooth, completely bald patches without scaling or broken hairs, and there is no infectious spread among contacts; lymphadenopathy would not be present.

wrongAnswers.name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Seborrheic dermatitis causes diffuse scalp scaling without discrete patches of alopecia, broken hairs, or cervical lymphadenopathy, and is less common in young children.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scalp psoriasis produces thick silvery plaques that extend to the hairline but does not cause hair breakage or posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and is not contagious.

clues: A 74-year-old man presents with a moderately itchy eruption of fluid-filled lesions on his abdomen and thighs appearing over three weeks; he denies any mouth sores.
He has a neurologic condition and takes several medications; he denies any oral sores.
Multiple tense, intact bullae on an erythematous and urticarial base are present on the lower abdomen, inner thighs, and flexor arms; oral mucosa is clear and uninvolved.
ELISA serology shows markedly elevated IgG antibodies against BP180 and BP230.
Perilesional skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone.
explanation: Bullous pemphigoid results from IgG autoantibodies targeting hemidesmosomal proteins BP180 and BP230 at the dermoepidermal junction, activating complement and eosinophil recruitment that causes subepidermal blister formation.
keyFact: Bullous pemphigoid: tense bullae, spares mucosa, linear IgG at BMZ on DIF; pemphigus vulgaris: flaccid bullae, involves mucosa, IgG in intercellular spaces; BP180 antibody titer correlates with disease activity.

wrongAnswers.name: Pemphigus Vulgaris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pemphigus vulgaris produces flaccid, easily ruptured bullae with prominent oral mucosal involvement and shows intercellular (fishnet) IgG pattern on DIF, contrasting with the tense bullae and linear BMZ pattern here.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatitis Herpetiformis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatitis herpetiformis causes small, intensely pruritic papulovesicles on extensor surfaces, not large tense bullae; DIF shows granular IgA at the BMZ, not linear IgG.

wrongAnswers.name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SJS is an acute, drug-triggered reaction with epidermal necrosis, mucosal involvement, and systemic toxicity; it would not present as a chronic urticarial-bullous eruption with positive BP180 serology.

clues: A 55-year-old woman presents with painful mouth sores for two months and more recent skin blistering; the blisters are fragile and leave raw, painful erosions.
She reports the blisters rupture easily and leave raw erosions; she has had difficulty eating due to the oral lesions, resulting in a 5-pound weight loss.

Multiple shallow oral erosions are present on the buccal mucosa and palate; on the skin, fragile blisters are noted; applying lateral pressure to a blister causes it to extend into adjacent uninvolved skin.
Anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies are significantly elevated on ELISA serology.
Perilesional skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposition throughout the epidermis in a fishnet pattern with suprabasal acantholysis.
explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris results from IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein-3 (and desmoglein-1 in widespread disease), disrupting desmosomal adhesion between keratinocytes and causing suprabasal acantholysis and flaccid blister formation.
keyFact: Nikolsky sign (lateral blister extension on pressure) is positive in pemphigus vulgaris; oral mucosa involvement often precedes skin disease; DIF shows intercellular IgG in a fishnet/tombstone pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Bullous Pemphigoid
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bullous pemphigoid produces tense, intact bullae on a urticarial base, spares the mucosa, and shows linear IgG at the basement membrane zone on DIF rather than intercellular staining.

wrongAnswers.name: Erythema Multiforme
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Erythema multiforme produces targetoid lesions with central blistering in an acral distribution and is typically triggered by HSV; oral involvement occurs but the skin lesions are distinct from fragile widespread bullae.

wrongAnswers.name: Aphthous Stomatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aphthous ulcers are confined to oral mucosa, self-limited, and do not produce skin blistering or show autoantibodies on serology.

clues: A 32-year-old man presents with intensely itchy, burning blisters recurring on his elbows, knees, and buttocks for several months.
He reports chronic intermittent diarrhea and bloating; the rash improves somewhat when he avoids bread and pasta.
Symmetric clusters of small papules and vesicles on erythematous bases are present over the extensor elbows, knees, and buttocks; many lesions are excoriated.
Serology shows elevated IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies; IgA anti-epidermal transglutaminase antibodies are also elevated.
Perilesional skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence demonstrates granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae.
explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease; IgA antibodies against epidermal transglutaminase-3 deposit in the dermal papillae and activate neutrophils, causing subepidermal microabscess formation and blistering.
keyFact: Granular IgA in dermal papillae on DIF is pathognomonic; virtually all patients have underlying celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy); dapsone provides rapid symptom relief; gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Bullous Pemphigoid
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bullous pemphigoid produces large tense bullae predominantly in elderly patients with linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ on DIF; it is not associated with celiac disease or granular IgA deposits.

wrongAnswers.name: Scabies
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Scabies causes pruritic burrows in web spaces and flexural areas with mite visualization on scraping; it is infectious, not autoimmune, and lacks the gluten association and granular IgA pattern.

wrongAnswers.name: Contact Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Contact dermatitis is localized to allergen exposure sites, is not associated with gastrointestinal symptoms or gluten sensitivity, and does not show IgA deposits on DIF.

clues: A 27-year-old woman presents with a symmetric rash on her hands and forearms that appeared suddenly over 24 hours.
She had a cold sore on her lip one week ago that has since resolved; she takes no regular medications.

Multiple round, concentric lesions with a dusky central zone, a pale middle ring, and an outer red ring are present on the dorsal hands, palms, and forearms; two small oral ulcers are noted on the lips.
HSV PCR from the healed cold sore site returns positive for HSV-1; Mycoplasma IgM is negative.
Skin biopsy shows interface dermatitis with individual keratinocyte apoptosis, lymphocytic satellitosis at the dermoepidermal junction, and focal epidermal necrosis.
explanation: Erythema multiforme is a T-cell mediated hypersensitivity reaction most commonly triggered by HSV infection; viral DNA fragments are deposited in skin, inducing cytotoxic CD4+ T-cell responses against HSV antigen-expressing keratinocytes.
keyFact: HSV is the most common trigger for EM (especially recurrent EM); targetoid lesions are classic; EM minor spares mucosa or has minimal involvement; EM major has two or more mucosal sites involved.

wrongAnswers.name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SJS involves more than 10% BSA with epidermal detachment, severe mucosal involvement of two or more sites, and systemic toxicity; it is triggered by medications, not HSV, and lesions show atypical targets.

wrongAnswers.name: Urticaria
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Urticaria produces transient, migratory wheals lasting less than 24 hours without epidermal changes; the fixed concentric targetoid lesions here persisting over days are inconsistent with urticaria.

wrongAnswers.name: Fixed Drug Eruption
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Fixed drug eruption produces solitary or few dusky red-violet plaques that recur at the same site with drug re-exposure; it is not multifocal or acral-predominant and requires an offending drug.

clues: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the ED with a rapidly worsening painful rash, eye redness, and mouth sores over two days.
She started a new sulfonamide antibiotic for a urinary tract infection 12 days ago; she feels systemically unwell with fevers.

Extensive erythematous and purpuric macules with epidermal sloughing are present over less than 10% of body surface area; bilateral conjunctival injection with pseudomembrane formation is noted; hemorrhagic crusting of lips and oral erosions are present.
Skin biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis with minimal dermal inflammation.
Frozen section of detached epidermis confirms a subepidermal split with necrotic keratinocytes at all epidermal levels; granulysin concentration in blister fluid is markedly elevated.
explanation: SJS/TEN results from cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell and NK-cell mediated apoptosis of keratinocytes, driven by drug-specific immune activation; granulysin is the primary mediator of widespread epidermal necrosis.
keyFact: SJS involves less than 10% BSA epidermal detachment; TEN involves greater than 30%; SJS-TEN overlap is 10-30%; sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs, and allopurinol are common triggers; SCORTEN score predicts mortality.

wrongAnswers.name: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TEN is on the same spectrum as SJS but involves greater than 30% BSA epidermal detachment; the less than 10% BSA involvement here classifies this as SJS.

wrongAnswers.name: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SSSS occurs predominantly in children under 5, is caused by staphylococcal exotoxin, and spares mucous membranes; it would not be triggered by antibiotic initiation and affects a younger population.

wrongAnswers.name: Erythema Multiforme Major
wrongAnswers.whyNot: EM major is typically HSV-triggered with classic targetoid lesions and limited mucosal involvement; drug-triggered widespread atypical targets with epidermal detachment classify as SJS rather than EM.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with painful, tender bumps on both shins appearing over the past week.
She has been experiencing a cough and mild shortness of breath for three weeks; a recent chest X-ray showed bilateral hilar enlargement.
Multiple 2-4 cm warm, tender, ill-defined erythematous nodules are present bilaterally on the anterior shins; the lesions are not fluctuant and have not ulcerated.
ESR and CRP are markedly elevated; angiotensin-converting enzyme level is elevated; PPD skin test is negative.
Skin biopsy of a nodule shows septal panniculitis without vasculitis, with granulomatous inflammation in the fibrous septa of subcutaneous fat.
explanation: Erythema nodosum is a reactive septal panniculitis representing a delayed hypersensitivity response to various antigenic triggers including sarcoidosis, infections, and medications; immune complex deposition in septal blood vessels drives the inflammatory infiltrate.
keyFact: Erythema nodosum combined with bilateral hilar adenopathy is called Löfgren syndrome (a form of acute sarcoidosis with a favorable prognosis); other triggers include streptococcal infections, TB, IBD, and oral contraceptives.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis is typically unilateral, spreading, and associated with a wound or entry site; bilateral symmetric tender nodules on the shins with hilar adenopathy and elevated ACE strongly favor a systemic reactive process.

wrongAnswers.name: Nodular Vasculitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nodular vasculitis (erythema induratum) occurs on the posterior calves, may ulcerate, and shows lobular panniculitis with vasculitis on biopsy; the anterior shin location and septal panniculitis pattern argue against it.

wrongAnswers.name: Kaposi Sarcoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Kaposi sarcoma produces violaceous, non-tender nodules and plaques, not painful erythematous nodules on the shins; it is associated with HHV-8 and immunosuppression, not sarcoidosis.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with a ring-shaped rash on the back of her hand that has been slowly growing for four months and causes no symptoms.
She is otherwise healthy with no skin conditions. She denies any trauma to the area, and the lesion is completely asymptomatic.
A 3 cm annular, flesh-colored to faintly erythematous ring of coalescing papules is present on the dorsal right hand. There is no scale, vesiculation, or central clearing, and the surface is smooth.
KOH preparation is negative. Fasting glucose is 105 mg/dL (borderline). Serology for sarcoidosis (ACE level) is normal.
Punch biopsy demonstrates palisading granulomas with central mucin deposition and histiocytic infiltrate surrounding degenerated collagen in the mid-dermis.
explanation: Granuloma annulare is a benign granulomatous reaction pattern in the dermis of unclear etiology; T-cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity and collagen degeneration lead to histiocyte recruitment forming palisading granulomas with mucin accumulation.
keyFact: Granuloma annulare is associated with diabetes mellitus in the generalized form; it is asymptomatic, self-limited, and distinguished from tinea corporis by the absence of scale and negative KOH.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Corporis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea corporis has a scaly, raised advancing border with central clearing and a positive KOH prep; the smooth, non-scaly surface and negative KOH here are inconsistent.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cutaneous sarcoidosis can form annular plaques but typically involves the face and is associated with systemic sarcoidosis findings; the normal ACE level and mid-dermal mucin on biopsy favor granuloma annulare.

wrongAnswers.name: Necrobiosis Lipoidica
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Necrobiosis lipoidica presents as yellow-brown atrophic plaques with telangiectasias, predominantly on the anterior shins; it shows full-thickness dermal collagen degeneration without mucin on biopsy.

clues: A 40-year-old woman presents with a hardening, discolored patch on her left abdomen that she first noticed six months ago.
The patch has been slowly expanding. She denies Raynaud's phenomenon, difficulty swallowing, or any joint complaints.

A 6 cm oval plaque with an ivory-white, waxy, indurated center and a surrounding violaceous (lilac) ring is present on the left lateral abdomen. The skin cannot be pinched into a fold over the lesion.
ANA is positive at low titer (1:40). Anti-Scl-70 and anti-centromere antibodies are negative. CBC and metabolic panel are normal.
Skin biopsy demonstrates thickened, homogenized collagen bundles in the dermis with loss of appendageal structures and a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate at the border.
explanation: Morphea results from fibroblast activation driven by Th2 cytokines and TGF-β, leading to excessive collagen deposition in the dermis; unlike systemic sclerosis, it is confined to skin without internal organ involvement or Raynaud's phenomenon.
keyFact: Morphea differs from systemic sclerosis by sparing acral skin, lacking Raynaud's phenomenon and internal organ involvement; the lilac ring (lilac ring of active disease) indicates active inflammation; anti-Scl-70 is negative.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic Sclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Systemic sclerosis causes acral sclerosis with Raynaud's phenomenon, internal organ fibrosis, and positive anti-Scl-70 or anti-centromere antibodies; the localized abdominal plaque without systemic features argues against it.

wrongAnswers.name: Lichen Sclerosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lichen sclerosus predominantly affects anogenital skin and shows thin, atrophic white plaques with wrinkling; extragenital lesions lack the thickened collagen on biopsy seen in morphea.

wrongAnswers.name: Lipodermatosclerosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Lipodermatosclerosis affects lower legs in the setting of venous insufficiency, causing fibrosis of subcutaneous fat with an inverted champagne-bottle appearance; abdominal involvement without venous disease is inconsistent.

clues: A 24-year-old woman notices slowly expanding white patches on her hands and around her mouth over the past year.
She has a history of an underactive thyroid and her maternal aunt had a similar skin condition.
Sharply demarcated, completely depigmented, chalk-white macules are present symmetrically on the dorsal hands, fingers, and perioral skin with no scale or induration.
Wood lamp examination dramatically accentuates the lesions, showing bright blue-white fluorescence with sharp borders.
Skin biopsy demonstrates complete absence of melanocytes in the epidermis with preservation of the overall epidermal architecture.
explanation: Vitiligo results from autoimmune destruction of melanocytes mediated by autoreactive CD8+ T-cells; it is associated with other autoimmune conditions including thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, and Addison's disease.
keyFact: Vitiligo associated with thyroid disease (Hashimoto's or Graves'), type 1 diabetes, and pernicious anemia; Wood's lamp distinguishes vitiligo (complete depigmentation) from tinea versicolor (hypopigmentation); JAK inhibitors are an emerging therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Versicolor
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea versicolor causes hypopigmentation (not complete depigmentation) with fine scale and a positive KOH; it does not have the sharp borders or autoimmune associations seen in vitiligo.

wrongAnswers.name: Albinism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Albinism is a congenital condition causing diffuse hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes from birth due to melanin synthesis defects; it is not acquired or patchy, unlike vitiligo.

wrongAnswers.name: Pityriasis Alba
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pityriasis alba presents as faintly hypopigmented, slightly scaly macules on the face in children and is associated with atopic dermatitis; it is not completely depigmented and resolves spontaneously.

clues: A 28-year-old man presents with a sudden patch of hair loss on his scalp noticed two weeks ago; he has been under significant work stress and has a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
He has no family history of hair loss and has not started any new medications. There is no itching, burning, or pain in the area.

A 3 cm smooth, completely bald, circular patch is present on the vertex scalp with no visible inflammation, scarring, or scaling. At the margin of the patch, short hairs that taper toward the scalp (exclamation point hairs) are visible.
Dermoscopy reveals yellow dots (empty follicular openings), black dots, and broken hairs at the patch margin.
Scalp biopsy demonstrates a lymphocytic peribulbar infiltrate around anagen follicles ('swarm of bees' pattern) with preservation of the follicular architecture and no scarring.
explanation: Alopecia areata results from collapse of immune privilege in hair follicles, exposing auto-antigens to autoreactive CD8+ T-cells that attack the hair bulb, driving follicles from anagen to catagen and causing non-scarring alopecia.
keyFact: Exclamation point hairs at the patch border are characteristic; association with autoimmune diseases (thyroid, vitiligo, type 1 DM); regrowth is possible as follicles are preserved; JAK inhibitors (baricitinib) are approved for severe alopecia areata.

wrongAnswers.name: Tinea Capitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tinea capitis causes scaling, broken hairs, and cervical lymphadenopathy in children; the smooth non-scaly patch and exclamation point hairs in an adult without cervical nodes argue against a fungal cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Trichotillomania
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Trichotillomania produces irregular, geometric patches with hairs of different lengths due to compulsive pulling; the perfectly circular patch with exclamation point hairs and peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate on biopsy are inconsistent.

wrongAnswers.name: Discoid Lupus Erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Discoid lupus causes scarring alopecia with follicular plugging, dyspigmentation, and atrophy; histology shows interface dermatitis with scarring, not the non-scarring peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate seen here.

clues: A 52-year-old fair-skinned woman with a history of sun exposure presents with a pigmented lesion on her back that her partner says has been changing over the past year.
She has a history of significant sun exposure and multiple prior sunburns. She has fair skin and red hair. A first-degree relative had a skin cancer removed.
A 1.2 cm pigmented lesion on the upper back with irregular, asymmetric borders, variegated colors including brown, black, and areas of red and white, and a notched periphery is identified.
Dermoscopy reveals atypical pigment network, regression structures (blue-white veil), and irregular streaks at the periphery.
Excisional biopsy shows malignant melanocytes with pagetoid spread through the epidermis and invasion into the papillary dermis; Breslow thickness is 0.9 mm.
explanation: Melanoma arises from malignant transformation of melanocytes, commonly driven by UV-induced DNA mutations in BRAF and NRAS; pagetoid spread (upward migration of malignant cells) and deep invasion determine staging and prognosis.
keyFact: ABCDE criteria: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution; Breslow thickness is the most important prognostic factor; BRAF V600E mutation found in ~50% enables targeted therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Dysplastic Nevus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dysplastic nevi can show some ABCDE features but are benign with uniform cytology on biopsy; the pagetoid spread and dermal invasion on histology confirm malignancy rather than atypia.

wrongAnswers.name: Seborrheic Keratosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Seborrheic keratoses are benign epidermal lesions with a 'stuck-on' waxy appearance, horn cysts on dermoscopy, and uniform keratinocyte proliferation on biopsy; they do not show pagetoid spread or melanocytic atypia.

wrongAnswers.name: Blue Nevus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Blue nevi are uniformly blue-gray, symmetric, and show benign spindle melanocytes in the deep dermis on biopsy without pagetoid spread; they lack the variegated multicolor and irregular border seen here.

clues: A 67-year-old man with extensive occupational sun exposure presents with a slow-growing bump on his nose that occasionally bleeds; he has fair skin.
He spent most of his career as an outdoor construction worker. He has fair skin and does not regularly use sunscreen.
A 0.8 cm flesh-colored to pearly, dome-shaped papule with a smooth surface and subtle overlying telangiectasias is present on the left nasal ala. A small central area of ulceration is noted.
Dermoscopy reveals arborizing (tree-like) telangiectasias on a white-pink background with an ulcerated center.
Shave biopsy demonstrates nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, mucinous stroma retraction artifact, and stromal desmoplasia arising from the epidermis.
explanation: Basal cell carcinoma arises from follicular stem cells in the basal layer of the epidermis via UV-induced PTCH1 mutation activating the Hedgehog signaling pathway; it rarely metastasizes but causes significant local tissue destruction.
keyFact: BCC is the most common human cancer; pearly papule with arborizing telangiectasias and rolled border on the nose/face; peripheral palisading of basaloid cells on biopsy; vismodegib targets Hedgehog pathway for advanced/unresectable BCC.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCC typically presents as a keratotic, scaly, or crusted papule or plaque with less pearly quality; histology shows atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls rather than basaloid nests with peripheral palisading.

wrongAnswers.name: Intradermal Nevus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Intradermal nevi are flesh-colored dome-shaped papules but lack telangiectasias, ulceration tendency, and the basaloid histology with peripheral palisading; they appear in younger patients without the solar damage history.

wrongAnswers.name: Sebaceous Hyperplasia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sebaceous hyperplasia presents as yellowish, donut-shaped papules with a central dell on sebaceous-rich facial skin; it lacks arborizing telangiectasias on dermoscopy and shows enlarged lobulated sebaceous glands, not basaloid nests.

clues: A 72-year-old long-term transplant recipient presents with a firm, growing lesion on his right hand that has been present for three months.
He has been on tacrolimus and prednisone for eight years following a kidney transplant. He has multiple prior actinic keratoses that have been treated.
A 1.5 cm firm, indurated, hyperkeratotic papule with a central crust is present on the dorsal right hand. Palpation reveals induration extending beyond the visible lesion.
Dermoscopy shows white circles (keratin-filled follicular openings), hairpin vessels, and a structureless white area at the center.
Punch biopsy shows full-thickness keratinocyte atypia with keratin pearl formation, individual cell keratinization, and invasion into the dermis.
explanation: Cutaneous SCC arises from malignant keratinocytes driven by UV-induced TP53 mutations and is accelerated by chronic immunosuppression; it carries a higher metastatic rate in transplant recipients than in the general population.
keyFact: Organ transplant recipients have a 65-100x increased risk of SCC compared to the general population; SCC in transplant patients is more aggressive and more likely to metastasize; keratin pearls and individual cell keratinization are histologic hallmarks.

wrongAnswers.name: Actinic Keratosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Actinic keratosis is a precursor lesion with intraepidermal atypia without dermal invasion; the indurated, deeply palpable lesion with full dermal invasion on biopsy confirms progression to invasive SCC.

wrongAnswers.name: Keratoacanthoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing, crateriform, self-involuting tumor histologically similar to SCC; its rapid 6-8 week growth cycle and symmetric cup-shape differ from the slower-growing indurated plaque seen here, and many now consider it a variant of SCC.

wrongAnswers.name: Verruca Vulgaris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Common warts (HPV-induced) present as hyperkeratotic papules but show koilocytosis and papillomatous architecture without cytologic atypia or dermal invasion; however, HPV can co-exist with SCC in immunosuppressed patients.

clues: A 65-year-old farmer presents with multiple rough spots on his face and scalp that he has noticed over the past year; they feel like sandpaper and have not responded to moisturizers.
He has worked outdoors his entire life without sun protection. He notes the spots feel rough like sandpaper. He has no bleeding or ulceration from the lesions.
Multiple 0.3-0.8 cm pink-red macules and thin papules with adherent, rough, yellowish scale are scattered on the forehead, temples, and bald scalp. Marked background solar elastosis is noted.
Dermoscopy shows a strawberry pattern with red pseudonetwork and white follicular openings with scale on the scalp lesions.
Shave biopsy demonstrates atypical keratinocytes in the lower epidermis with parakeratosis, sparing follicular ostia, without breakthrough into the dermis.
explanation: Actinic keratoses are caused by UV-induced TP53 mutations in epidermal keratinocytes leading to intraepidermal dysplasia; they represent precancerous lesions with an estimated 0.1-10% annual risk of progression to invasive SCC.
keyFact: Actinic keratoses are markers of cumulative UV damage; the 'field cancerization' concept describes diffuse epidermal dysplasia in sun-damaged skin; treatment options include cryotherapy, 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, and photodynamic therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Seborrheic Keratosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Seborrheic keratoses are benign, have a 'stuck-on' warty surface with horn cysts, are not precancerous, and do not show atypical keratinocytes on biopsy; they can occur on covered skin.

wrongAnswers.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SCC shows full dermal invasion on biopsy with indurated palpable lesion; the thin, non-indurated lesions here with intraepidermal atypia only represent precancerous actinic keratosis, not invasive cancer.

wrongAnswers.name: Discoid Lupus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Discoid lupus produces erythematous, scaly plaques with follicular plugging and scarring; it would show interface dermatitis on biopsy and be associated with ANA positivity, unlike actinic keratosis.

clues: A 34-year-old man presents with multiple painless discolored spots on his legs and one on the roof of his mouth appearing over two months; he has had significant weight loss.
He has lost 15 pounds over the past four months, has had recurrent oral thrush, and has not seen a doctor in several years.
Multiple 0.5-2 cm violaceous macules and papules are present on the lower extremities and hard palate. The lesions are non-blanching, non-tender, and some appear nodular.
CD4 count returns at 62 cells/µL and HIV viral load is markedly elevated. Serum LDH is elevated.

Punch biopsy demonstrates a proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated erythrocytes and hemosiderin deposition; immunohistochemistry is positive for HHV-8 LANA-1.
explanation: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV) infection driving spindle cell proliferation from lymphatic endothelial progenitors; in HIV-associated KS, profound immunosuppression (low CD4) removes immune control of HHV-8 replication.
keyFact: HHV-8 is necessary but not sufficient for KS; HIV-associated KS occurs at CD4 <200 cells/µL; four epidemiological forms: classic (elderly Mediterranean men), endemic (African), iatrogenic (transplant), and AIDS-associated; LANA-1 IHC is diagnostic.

wrongAnswers.name: Bacillary Angiomatosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella spp. in immunocompromised patients and can mimic KS clinically; however, biopsy shows lobular capillary proliferation with neutrophilic infiltrate and Warthin-Starry staining identifies bacteria, not HHV-8 spindle cells.

wrongAnswers.name: Purpura (Thrombocytopenic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Thrombocytopenic purpura causes petechiae and ecchymoses from bleeding, not raised nodular violaceous papules; lesions would be completely flat and a low platelet count rather than HHV-8 infection would be the cause.

wrongAnswers.name: Melanoma (Amelanotic)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Amelanotic melanoma could present as pink-violaceous nodules but would not produce multiple lesions simultaneously or involve the oral mucosa in this pattern; HHV-8 LANA-1 positivity on IHC distinguishes KS definitively.

clues: A 58-year-old man presents with persistent, mildly pruritic patches on his trunk and proximal thighs that have been slowly enlarging over years, resistant to topical steroids prescribed by multiple dermatologists.
He has seen multiple dermatologists and been treated for eczema and psoriasis without lasting improvement. The patches have slowly enlarged over time.

Multiple 5-10 cm flat, thin, atrophic, poikilodermatous patches with mottled hypo- and hyperpigmentation, telangiectasias, and fine wrinkling are present on the buttocks, lower trunk, and inner thighs in a bathing suit distribution.
Flow cytometry of peripheral blood shows a small abnormal CD4+/CD8- T-cell population with loss of CD7. LDH is mildly elevated.

Skin biopsy shows epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes with Pautrier microabscesses in the epidermis and a band-like infiltrate of cerebriform lymphocytes in the upper dermis with T-cell receptor gene rearrangement confirmed by PCR.
explanation: Mycosis fungoides is the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, representing a clonal proliferation of epidermotropic CD4+ T-cells; it progresses through patch, plaque, and tumor stages over years and can evolve to Sézary syndrome with blood involvement.
keyFact: Mycosis fungoides classically presents in a 'bathing suit distribution'; Pautrier microabscesses (intraepidermal atypical lymphocyte clusters) and cerebriform nuclei on biopsy are hallmarks; misdiagnosis as eczema or psoriasis is common in early stages.

wrongAnswers.name: Psoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Psoriasis produces well-demarcated, thick silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces that respond to standard therapies; the poikilodermatous atrophic patches, bathing suit distribution, and epidermotropic lymphocytic infiltrate are inconsistent with psoriasis.

wrongAnswers.name: Atopic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Atopic dermatitis is typically associated with personal or family history of atopy, flexural distribution, elevated IgE, and responds to conventional eczema therapies; the clonal T-cell population and Pautrier microabscesses are not features of eczema.

wrongAnswers.name: Parapsoriasis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Large-plaque parapsoriasis is now considered a precursor to or early form of mycosis fungoides; the clonal T-cell proliferation, epidermotropism, and Pautrier microabscesses on biopsy confirm progression to established mycosis fungoides.

clues: A 44-year-old woman with inflammatory bowel disease presents with a rapidly expanding, painful leg ulcer that began two weeks ago at a site of minor skin trauma.
She has a known diagnosis of Crohn's disease managed with infliximab. She recalls a minor insect bite at the site where the ulcer began.

A 6 cm ulcer with a necrotic, violaceous, undermined border and purulent base is present on the left shin. Surrounding erythema and edema extend several centimeters beyond the ulcer edge. There is exquisite tenderness.
Wound cultures show no significant pathogen growth. CBC shows leukocytosis. Blood cultures are negative. Vascular studies show intact arterial flow.
Skin biopsy of the ulcer edge shows a dense sterile neutrophilic infiltrate with dermal necrosis and no vasculitis; wound cultures remain negative on repeat.
explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis in which dysregulated innate immunity drives sterile neutrophilic tissue destruction; it is associated with IBD, rheumatoid arthritis, and hematologic malignancies.
keyFact: Pathergy (worsening with trauma or debridement) is a key feature; the undermined, violaceous border is characteristic; association with IBD, RA, and hematologic malignancy; debridement worsens the ulcer due to pathergy — avoid surgery.

wrongAnswers.name: Necrotizing Fasciitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressive bacterial infection with systemic sepsis, crepitus, and positive wound cultures; surgical debridement is life-saving (not harmful), and the sterile cultures with IBD association here favor PG.

wrongAnswers.name: Venous Stasis Ulcer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Venous stasis ulcers occur at the medial malleolus with surrounding lipodermatosclerosis in the setting of chronic venous insufficiency; they are not exquisitely tender, lack the violaceous undermined border, and are not associated with IBD.

wrongAnswers.name: Antiphospholipid Syndrome Ulcer
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Antiphospholipid syndrome causes livedo reticularis and painful ulcers from thrombotic occlusion; biopsy would show thrombi in vessels rather than sterile neutrophilic infiltrate, and antiphospholipid antibodies would be elevated.

clues: A 50-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset tender, edematous red plaques on her arms and face associated with high fevers for four days; she was recently treated for a respiratory infection and a routine blood count three weeks ago was normal.
She was recently treated for a respiratory infection with antibiotics. Her CBC from a routine check-up three weeks ago was normal.
Multiple 2-4 cm edematous, bright red to violaceous, tender papules and plaques with a mammillated (pseudovesicular) surface are present on the dorsal arms, neck, and face. Temperature is 38.7°C.
CBC shows leukocytosis with neutrophilia. ESR and CRP are markedly elevated. Repeat CBC shows a new left shift. Peripheral blood smear review is ordered due to concern.
Skin biopsy demonstrates a dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate with papillary dermal edema without vasculitis; bone marrow biopsy reveals 25% blasts.
explanation: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) results from cytokine-driven (IL-1, G-CSF, IL-6) massive dermal neutrophil recruitment; paraneoplastic Sweet syndrome is associated with myeloid malignancies in up to 20% of cases.
keyFact: Sweet syndrome triggers: infection (URI, GI), IBD, pregnancy, and malignancy (especially AML); new-onset or refractory Sweet syndrome should prompt investigation for hematologic malignancy; responds dramatically to systemic corticosteroids.

wrongAnswers.name: Cellulitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cellulitis is typically unilateral, follows a spreading pattern from an entry wound, responds to antibiotics, and does not produce the symmetric multi-site tender plaques with sterile neutrophilic biopsy findings seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Erythema Multiforme
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Erythema multiforme produces targetoid lesions in an acral distribution triggered by HSV, not edematous pseudovesicular plaques with dense dermal neutrophilia on biopsy; EM is not associated with leukemia.

wrongAnswers.name: Drug Hypersensitivity Reaction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Drug reactions can cause neutrophilic eruptions (DRESS involves eosinophils), but Sweet syndrome with paraneoplastic AML requires a thorough malignancy workup; the left shift and blast cells on peripheral smear point beyond a simple drug reaction.

clues: A 29-year-old woman presents with chronic, recurrent painful nodules in her axillae and inguinal folds that have not responded to multiple courses of antibiotics.
The lumps frequently drain foul-smelling fluid. She is a smoker with a BMI of 32. She has tried multiple courses of antibiotics without lasting improvement.

Bilateral axillary skin shows multiple tender inflammatory nodules, open comedones ('tombstone' double-headed comedones), and rope-like fibrotic bands. Sinus tracts draining seropurulent material are present in both axillae and bilateral inguinal folds.
Wound cultures show mixed polymicrobial growth including Staphylococcus epidermidis and anaerobes. No single pathogen predominates. CBC shows mild leukocytosis.
Skin biopsy demonstrates follicular occlusion with follicular rupture, chronic granulomatous inflammation, sinus tract formation, and extensive dermal fibrosis.
explanation: Hidradenitis suppurativa begins with follicular occlusion, not primary apocrine gland infection; follicular rupture triggers an intense innate immune response with IL-1β and TNF-α driving abscess formation, sinus tract development, and progressive scarring.
keyFact: HS is classified by Hurley staging (I: isolated nodules, II: recurrent nodules with sinus tracts, III: diffuse involvement); smoking and obesity are major modifiable risk factors; TNF-α inhibitors (adalimumab) and IL-17 inhibitors are approved biologics.

wrongAnswers.name: Furuncles/Carbuncles
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Furunculosis is caused by S. aureus, is not restricted to intertriginous areas, does not produce sinus tracts and fibrotic bands, and responds to antibiotics; the bilateral axillary and inguinal pattern with tombstone comedones is specific to HS.

wrongAnswers.name: Crohn's Disease Perianal Fistulas
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Crohn's disease can cause perianal fistulas but would not involve bilateral axillary skin; the axillary and inguinal distribution with follicular occlusion and tombstone comedones points specifically to HS (though HS and Crohn's can co-exist).

wrongAnswers.name: Infected Epidermal Inclusion Cysts
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Infected inclusion cysts are isolated, not recurring in multiple intertriginous sites, do not form sinus tracts, and lack tombstone comedones; the bilateral pattern with fibrosis is specific to HS.

clues: A 46-year-old woman presents with persistent facial redness and inflammatory papules on her cheeks and nose that worsen with certain triggers; she also reports intermittent eye redness.
She reports facial flushing triggered by spicy food, alcohol, sun, and heat. She notes her eyes have been intermittently red and irritated for the past year. No blackheads are present.

Diffuse centrofacial erythema with telangiectasias is present across both cheeks and the nose. Inflammatory papules and pustules are scattered in the same distribution. No comedones are visible. Meibomian gland dysfunction and lid margin telangiectasias are noted on eye exam.
Demodex folliculorum mite density on skin surface biopsy is significantly elevated above normal thresholds.
Skin biopsy shows perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation with Demodex mites within dilated follicular infundibula and granulomatous dermal response.
explanation: Rosacea involves dysregulation of innate immune responses to Demodex mites and their bacteria (Bacillus oleronius), along with neurovascular hyperreactivity causing flushing; cathelicidin (LL-37) overproduction drives the inflammatory cascade.
keyFact: Rosacea subtypes: ETR (flushing/telangiectasias), papulopustular (acne-like without comedones), phymatous (rhinophyma), ocular; ocular rosacea affects up to 50% of patients; metronidazole, azelaic acid, and low-dose doxycycline are first-line treatments.

wrongAnswers.name: Acne Vulgaris
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acne vulgaris requires comedones (open/closed) as the primary lesion and predominantly affects teenagers; the absence of comedones, adult onset, centrofacial distribution, and flushing triggers distinguish rosacea.

wrongAnswers.name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Seborrheic dermatitis produces greasy, yellowish scale in the nasolabial folds and eyebrows; it does not cause flushing episodes, papulopustules without comedones, or ocular surface disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SLE malar rash spares the nasolabial folds, is triggered by sunlight, and is associated with ANA positivity and systemic symptoms; papulopustules and telangiectasias without the butterfly distribution are more consistent with rosacea.

accept: drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
clues: A 38-year-old man presents with a widespread rash, fever, and facial swelling that started several weeks after beginning a new medication for a chronic condition.
He started allopurinol for gout six weeks ago. Over the past two weeks he has developed a rash that started on the face and spread downward, accompanied by facial swelling and swollen lymph nodes.
Diffuse morbilliform erythema covering more than 50% BSA with facial edema is present. Bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy is palpable. Temperature is 39.1°C.
CBC reveals leukocytosis with eosinophilia (2,800/µL) and atypical lymphocytes. Liver function tests show AST 480 U/L, ALT 520 U/L. HHV-6 IgM serology is positive.
Skin biopsy shows interface dermatitis with eosinophilic infiltrate; peripheral blood shows eosinophilia of 2,800/uL, atypical lymphocytes, and HHV-6 reactivation by PCR.
explanation: DRESS results from defective detoxification of drug metabolites triggering T-cell activation and reactivation of herpesvirus family members (HHV-6, EBV, CMV); the virus-drug interaction amplifies immune activation causing multi-organ inflammation.
keyFact: DRESS onset is 2-8 weeks after drug initiation (distinguishing it from morbilliform drug eruption onset at days); allopurinol, anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, and minocycline are common triggers; HHV-6 reactivation is characteristic; mortality up to 10%.

wrongAnswers.name: Morbilliform Drug Eruption
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Simple morbilliform drug eruptions appear within 1-2 weeks of drug initiation, lack systemic involvement (organ damage, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia), and resolve within days of drug discontinuation; the 6-week latency and multi-organ involvement here indicate DRESS.

wrongAnswers.name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SJS presents with epidermal detachment, mucosal involvement, and skin pain/tenderness rather than morbilliform erythema; SJS does not produce eosinophilia or HHV-6 reactivation, and the RegiSCAR criteria differentiate them.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Exanthem
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral exanthems follow acute viral symptoms and are self-limited without organ involvement; while HHV-6 can cause exanthem subitum in children, DRESS involves drug-triggered HHV-6 reactivation with eosinophilia and hepatitis, not primary viral infection.

clues: A 30-year-old woman presents with raised, itchy red welts appearing all over her body intermittently for the past six weeks, with each individual welt lasting a few hours before disappearing.
She has not changed soaps, detergents, or foods. She began ibuprofen for knee pain around the time the welts started but has since stopped without improvement. No lip or throat swelling has occurred.
Multiple 1-5 cm erythematous, edematous, blanching wheals with surrounding flare are present on the trunk and extremities. Dermatographism is present. No angioedema is noted today.
CBC, thyroid function, and ANA are all within normal limits. Total IgE is mildly elevated. Specific IgE RAST testing for common food and environmental allergens is negative.
Skin biopsy of a wheal shows perivascular mast cell degranulation with dermal edema and eosinophilic infiltrate; individual wheals resolve within 24 hours leaving no residual mark.
explanation: Chronic spontaneous urticaria results from mast cell degranulation triggered by IgG autoantibodies against FcεRI or IgE (in autoimmune CSU) or idiopathic activation, releasing histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins causing transient dermal edema.
keyFact: Individual urticarial wheals last less than 24 hours and leave no residual mark (unlike urticarial vasculitis); chronic urticaria persists more than 6 weeks; 2nd-generation H1 antihistamines are first-line; omalizumab (anti-IgE) is approved for refractory CSU.

wrongAnswers.name: Urticarial Vasculitis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Urticarial vasculitis produces wheals lasting more than 24 hours that leave bruising or hyperpigmentation; biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis, not simple mast cell degranulation with dermal edema.

wrongAnswers.name: Dermatitis Herpetiformis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dermatitis herpetiformis causes fixed, clustered papulovesicles on extensor surfaces with granular IgA on DIF; it does not produce transient migratory wheals and is associated with celiac disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Erythema Multiforme
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Erythema multiforme produces fixed, targetoid lesions that persist for days rather than transient wheals that resolve within hours; it is triggered by HSV or mycoplasma and shows interface dermatitis on biopsy.

answer: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction
accept: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
clues: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive exercise intolerance and bilateral lower extremity swelling over three months; he reports disturbed sleep from respiratory symptoms.
He reports waking up at night gasping for air and needing two pillows to sleep comfortably.
Bilateral crackles are heard at the lung bases, and jugular venous distension is noted at 45 degrees.
BNP is markedly elevated at 980 pg/mL and chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with bilateral pleural effusions.
Echocardiogram reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% with global hypokinesis and a dilated left ventricle.
explanation: HFrEF results from impaired systolic contractility, leading to reduced stroke volume, compensatory neurohormonal activation, and progressive ventricular remodeling with dilation.
keyFact: EF <40% defines HFrEF. Associated with prior MI, dilated cardiomyopathy, or myocarditis. Treated with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta-blockers, and aldosterone antagonists.

wrongAnswers.name: Cardiac Tamponade
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tamponade causes hypotension and muffled heart sounds, not pulmonary crackles, and would show equalization of pressures without the dilated LV on echo.

wrongAnswers.name: COPD Exacerbation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: COPD can cause dyspnea and JVD, but would not produce bilateral crackles, elevated BNP, or a low EF on echocardiogram.

wrongAnswers.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Nephrotic syndrome causes ankle edema and can cause dyspnea, but BNP would not be markedly elevated and echocardiogram would show preserved EF.

answer: Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction
accept: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
clues: A 72-year-old woman with obesity and hypertension presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and bilateral ankle swelling for two months.
She reports no chest pain but notices her symptoms worsen significantly when she misses her blood pressure medications.
She has elevated blood pressure at 160/95 mmHg, bibasilar crackles, and pitting edema to the knees.
BNP is elevated at 420 pg/mL and chest X-ray shows mild pulmonary vascular congestion without significant cardiomegaly.
Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 62% with a markedly elevated E/e' ratio of 18 and left atrial enlargement.
explanation: HFpEF results from impaired ventricular relaxation and increased stiffness, causing elevated filling pressures despite preserved systolic function, commonly in elderly hypertensive patients.
keyFact: EF ≥50% with signs/symptoms of heart failure and elevated filling pressures. Strongly associated with hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and age. No proven mortality-reducing therapy exists, though SGLT2 inhibitors show benefit.

wrongAnswers.name: HFrEF
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HFrEF requires an EF <40%; echocardiogram here shows preserved EF of 62%.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PAH can cause dyspnea and edema, but would show right heart strain on echo rather than left atrial enlargement with elevated E/e' ratio.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypothyroidism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypothyroidism can cause edema and dyspnea, but the elevated BNP, elevated filling pressures on echo, and hypertensive history favor HFpEF.

clues: A 65-year-old man presents with a two-day history of palpitations and mild shortness of breath.
He has a history of hypertension and drinks four to five glasses of wine nightly; symptoms worsened after a particularly heavy weekend.
His pulse is noted to be irregular in rate and rhythm at approximately 110 beats per minute.
ECG shows no discernible P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular response at a rate of 112 bpm.
Repeat ECG after rate control shows chaotic baseline fibrillatory waves replacing organized atrial activity with variable RR intervals.
explanation: Atrial fibrillation results from disorganized rapid electrical impulses from multiple re-entrant circuits or ectopic foci (commonly pulmonary veins), causing irregular ventricular response and loss of atrial kick.
keyFact: Most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia. Risk factors include hypertension, alcohol ('holiday heart'), sleep apnea, valvular disease. CHA2DS2-VASc score guides anticoagulation. Irregularly irregular rhythm is the hallmark.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrial Flutter
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Flutter typically produces a regular or regularly irregular ventricular rate (often 150 bpm with 2:1 block) and shows sawtooth flutter waves on ECG, not chaotic fibrillatory baseline.

wrongAnswers.name: Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MAT is also irregularly irregular but requires at least three distinct P wave morphologies; it does not produce absent P waves with a fibrillatory baseline.

wrongAnswers.name: Frequent PVCs
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PVCs produce isolated wide-complex beats with compensatory pauses but not sustained irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves.

clues: A 60-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset palpitations and mild lightheadedness that began three hours ago.
She has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and recently completed a course of bronchodilator and steroid therapy for an exacerbation.
Her pulse is regular at 150 beats per minute and blood pressure is 108/72 mmHg.
ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm with a ventricular rate that does not vary with vagal maneuvers.
Adenosine transiently slows the ventricular rate, unmasking sawtooth-shaped atrial waves at 300 bpm in the inferior leads.
explanation: Atrial flutter is caused by a macroreentrant circuit in the right atrium, typically around the tricuspid annulus, producing organized atrial activity at 300 bpm with variable AV block.
keyFact: Classic atrial flutter rate is 300 bpm with 2:1 block producing ventricular rate of 150 bpm. Sawtooth pattern is best seen in leads II, III, aVF. Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is highly curative.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrial Fibrillation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AFib is irregularly irregular with no discernible P waves; this patient has a regular pulse and organized flutter waves.

wrongAnswers.name: AVNRT
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AVNRT typically terminates with adenosine rather than unmasking underlying atrial activity, and does not show sawtooth flutter waves.

wrongAnswers.name: Sinus Tachycardia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Sinus tachycardia would have identifiable upright P waves before each QRS and typically does not reach 150 bpm without significant physiologic stress.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of rapid heartbeat that start and stop suddenly; she reports neck pulsations during episodes.
She reports identical episodes in the past that terminated abruptly on their own, with one episode resolving after bearing down.
Her pulse is 178 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure is 100/68 mmHg, and she appears anxious but hemodynamically stable.
ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 178 bpm; P waves are not visible before the QRS complexes.
IV adenosine 6 mg terminates the tachycardia immediately, and sinus rhythm reveals retrograde P waves buried within or just after the QRS complexes.
explanation: AVNRT results from a reentrant circuit using dual pathways within or near the AV node, causing near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation and retrograde P waves.
keyFact: Most common cause of paroxysmal SVT. Retrograde P waves in or just after the QRS (RP interval <70ms) are characteristic. Responds to vagal maneuvers, adenosine, and long-term beta-blockers or ablation.

wrongAnswers.name: Atrial Flutter
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Flutter shows sawtooth flutter waves at 300 bpm and does not terminate abruptly with adenosine; instead adenosine unmasks the flutter.

wrongAnswers.name: WPW Syndrome with Orthodromic AVRT
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Orthodromic AVRT in WPW also terminates with adenosine but shows a delta wave on baseline ECG after conversion, which is absent here.

wrongAnswers.name: Ventricular Tachycardia
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VT produces wide-complex tachycardia; this patient has a narrow-complex tachycardia that terminates immediately with adenosine.

clues: A 22-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of sudden-onset rapid heartbeat that begin and end abruptly, occasionally associated with lightheadedness during exercise.
His episodes have been occurring since his teenage years; one lasted 20 minutes during intense weightlifting before stopping on its own; he has never been evaluated before.
Between episodes he appears well; during a brief captured episode in clinic, heart rate is 190 bpm with a regular rhythm that terminates abruptly to a normal rate of 72 bpm.
Resting 12-lead ECG shows a PR interval of 100 ms, a slurred upstroke at the onset of the QRS complex, and a widened QRS duration of 130 ms; echocardiogram is structurally normal.
Electrophysiology study identifies an accessory pathway with anterograde conduction, and during induced atrial fibrillation, the shortest pre-excited RR interval is less than 250 ms.
explanation: WPW results from an accessory atrioventricular pathway (bundle of Kent) that bypasses the AV node, causing ventricular pre-excitation and predisposing to reentrant tachycardia and potentially lethal rapid conduction of atrial fibrillation.
keyFact: Delta wave + short PR + wide QRS on baseline ECG is classic. During AFib, the accessory pathway can conduct rapidly causing pre-excited AFib (wide, irregular) with risk of ventricular fibrillation. Avoid AV nodal blocking agents in pre-excited AFib. Ablation is curative.

wrongAnswers.name: AVNRT
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AVNRT does not show delta waves or a short PR interval on baseline ECG; the pre-excitation pattern here confirms an accessory pathway.

wrongAnswers.name: Bundle Branch Block
wrongAnswers.whyNot: BBB widens the QRS but does not shorten the PR interval or produce a delta wave; the slurred upstroke (delta wave) points to pre-excitation.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM can cause exercise-related syncope and arrhythmias but does not produce a delta wave or short PR interval on ECG.

clues: A 66-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease is brought to the ED after a brief syncopal episode at home; he recalls a sudden racing sensation before blacking out.
His wife reports he looked pale and unresponsive for about 30 seconds; he recalls a sudden racing sensation in his chest before blacking out.
He is awake and mildly diaphoretic with blood pressure 88/60 mmHg and a rapid, regular pulse at approximately 180 bpm.
ECG shows a wide-complex tachycardia at 182 bpm with a left bundle branch block morphology and AV dissociation visible in lead II.
Capture beats and fusion beats are identified on the rhythm strip.
explanation: Sustained ventricular tachycardia most commonly arises from reentrant circuits around post-infarction scar tissue, producing a wide-complex tachycardia with hemodynamic compromise.
keyFact: AV dissociation, capture beats, and fusion beats are diagnostic of VT. History of prior MI is the strongest risk factor. QRS >160ms, extreme axis deviation, and concordance in precordial leads favor VT over SVT with aberrancy.

wrongAnswers.name: SVT with Aberrant Conduction
wrongAnswers.whyNot: SVT with aberrancy can produce wide-complex tachycardia but AV dissociation, capture beats, and fusion beats confirm ventricular origin.

wrongAnswers.name: Accelerated Idioventricular Rhythm
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AIVR occurs at 60–100 bpm (a slow ventricular rhythm), not at 182 bpm, and is not associated with hemodynamic collapse.

wrongAnswers.name: Hyperkalemia with Widened QRS
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hyperkalemia causes diffuse QRS widening with sine wave pattern at slower rates; it does not produce a regular monomorphic tachycardia at 182 bpm.

clues: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the ED after losing consciousness during swim practice; she recovered within one minute without intervention; there is a family history of cardiac events.
Her older brother had a similar episode and was diagnosed with a cardiac condition; her mother carries a small device in her chest.
She is alert and fully oriented with a normal physical exam; vital signs show heart rate 72 bpm and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg.
12-lead ECG shows a corrected QT interval of 510 ms with a broad-based T wave morphology.
Genetic testing reveals a pathogenic variant in KCNQ1 affecting the slow delayed rectifier potassium channel.
explanation: Congenital long QT syndrome results from mutations in cardiac ion channels that prolong repolarization, increasing the risk of triggered early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes.
keyFact: QTc >470ms in women and >450ms in men is abnormal. LQT1 triggered by exercise (swimming), LQT2 by auditory stimuli, LQT3 at rest/sleep. Avoid QT-prolonging drugs. Beta-blockers and ICD for high-risk patients.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM causes exertional syncope but ECG shows LVH pattern; the markedly prolonged QTc and family history of a pacemaker/ICD point to channelopathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Vasovagal Syncope
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Vasovagal syncope occurs with prolonged standing or emotional triggers, is preceded by prodrome, and is not associated with QTc prolongation or family history of sudden cardiac events.

wrongAnswers.name: WPW Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: WPW shows delta waves and short PR interval on ECG; this patient has a normal PR with markedly prolonged QTc.

clues: A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being resuscitated from a cardiac arrest that occurred while he was sleeping.
His younger brother died suddenly in his sleep at age 32 with no identified cause; the patient has no prior cardiac history and takes no medications.
Post-resuscitation examination shows an alert, hemodynamically stable man; cardiac auscultation reveals regular rate and rhythm with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs; neurological exam is intact.

Echocardiogram shows structurally normal heart with preserved ejection fraction of 60 percent; coronary angiography reveals no obstructive disease; electrolyte panel including potassium, calcium, and magnesium are normal.
Resting 12-lead ECG shows a coved ST-segment elevation of greater than 2 mm in leads V1 and V2 followed by a negative T wave, with a normal QT interval.
explanation: Brugada syndrome results from mutations in SCN5A reducing sodium channel function, causing abnormal repolarization in the right ventricular outflow tract and predisposing to ventricular fibrillation, particularly during rest or sleep.
keyFact: Type 1 coved pattern (≥2mm coved ST elevation in V1–V2) is diagnostic. Predominantly affects young Southeast Asian men. Fever, sodium channel blockers, and vagal tone can unmask or worsen the pattern. ICD is the only proven therapy.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute MI with VF
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Coronary angiography showed no obstructive disease, ruling out ischemic cause for VF; the ECG pattern is not consistent with ST-elevation MI.

wrongAnswers.name: Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ARVC causes epsilon waves and RV structural changes; echocardiogram here is normal and the coved ST pattern in V1-V2 is characteristic of Brugada.

wrongAnswers.name: Long QT Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: LQTS prolongs the QT interval and causes torsades; the QT is not prolonged here and the coved ST morphology in V1-V2 is pathognomonic for Brugada.

clues: A 17-year-old male athlete is brought to the ED after collapsing during a competitive game; he had occasional exertional chest tightness.
His father died suddenly at age 42 while jogging; the patient had occasional chest tightness with exertion that he attributed to asthma.
After resuscitation, a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border that becomes louder when he stands up.
ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with deep Q waves in the lateral leads and diffuse T wave inversions.
Echocardiogram reveals asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a septal wall thickness of 22 mm, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, and an LVOT gradient of 70 mmHg at rest.
explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is caused by mutations in sarcomeric proteins leading to myocardial hypertrophy, particularly of the interventricular septum, causing LVOT obstruction, diastolic dysfunction, and a substrate for life-threatening arrhythmias.
keyFact: Most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes in the US. Murmur increases with Valsalva and standing (decreased preload). SAM of mitral valve causes LVOT obstruction. Avoid dehydration, vasodilators, and vigorous exercise.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AS murmur increases with squatting (increased preload) and decreases with standing; the murmur here does the opposite, and echo confirms septal hypertrophy without valvular pathology.

wrongAnswers.name: Commotio Cordis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Commotio cordis is a one-time event from blunt chest wall impact; this patient has a structural heart lesion with a family history of sudden death.

wrongAnswers.name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: DCM causes a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle with low EF; echocardiogram here shows a hyperdynamic, thickened, obstructive pattern.

clues: A 45-year-old man presents with four months of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and a dry cough; he recalls a viral illness about six months ago from which he never fully recovered.
He drinks two to three beers per night and notes his symptoms initially improved but never fully resolved after the viral illness six months ago.
He has an elevated JVP, bibasilar crackles, a displaced apical impulse at the anterior axillary line, and pitting edema to the mid-shin.
Chest X-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with pulmonary venous congestion; ECG shows sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block.
Echocardiogram demonstrates a markedly dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 20%, thinned walls, and 3+ functional mitral regurgitation.
explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricular dilation and impaired systolic function from diverse causes including viral myocarditis, alcohol toxicity, and genetic mutations, leading to progressive heart failure.
keyFact: Most common cardiomyopathy; causes include alcohol, viral (Coxsackievirus B), peripartum, genetic (TTN, LMNA mutations), and idiopathic. Functional MR is common due to annular dilation. LBB is an adverse prognostic sign (may indicate CRT benefit).

wrongAnswers.name: Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Ischemic cardiomyopathy shows regional wall motion abnormalities in coronary artery territories; this patient has global dilation without segmental changes.

wrongAnswers.name: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy
