wrongAnswers.whyNot: Restrictive cardiomyopathy shows normal or small ventricular size with diastolic dysfunction; dilation and low EF are not features.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute myocarditis can progress to DCM; if the acute inflammatory phase has resolved and remodeling has occurred, the diagnosis shifts to dilated cardiomyopathy.

clues: A 78-year-old man presents with worsening shortness of breath, leg swelling, and dizziness when standing up from his chair over the past year.
He has a history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome surgically released five years ago and recently developed tingling in his feet.
His blood pressure drops 20 mmHg upon standing; he has elevated JVP, a narrow pulse pressure, and bibasilar crackles.
ECG shows low voltage in the limb leads despite echocardiogram revealing markedly increased wall thickness of 18 mm; BNP is 1200 pg/mL.
Technetium pyrophosphate nuclear scan demonstrates grade 3 cardiac uptake, and genetic testing identifies a Val122Ile variant in the TTR gene.
explanation: Transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis results from misfolded transthyretin protein depositing in the myocardium, causing progressive diastolic heart failure with the characteristic low-voltage ECG to wall-thickness discordance.
keyFact: Low voltage on ECG with thick walls on echo is the hallmark mismatch. ATTR amyloid is underdiagnosed in elderly men; carpal tunnel syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, and lumbar spinal stenosis are important extracardiac clues. Tafamidis reduces mortality in ATTR-CM.

wrongAnswers.name: Hypertensive Heart Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Hypertensive cardiomyopathy causes LVH with increased voltage on ECG, not the characteristic low-voltage/thick-wall discordance; Tc-PYP scan would be negative.

wrongAnswers.name: HFpEF
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HFpEF does not explain the low-voltage/thick-wall discordance, positive Tc-PYP scan, or extracardiac amyloid features such as carpal tunnel and neuropathy.

wrongAnswers.name: Sarcoidosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cardiac sarcoidosis can cause conduction abnormalities and heart failure but would show patchy FDG uptake on PET and does not produce the Tc-PYP uptake pattern of ATTR.

clues: A 68-year-old woman with no cardiac history presents with acute substernal chest pain and dyspnea that began shortly after receiving news of a family member's death.
She has no prior cardiac history, does not smoke, and takes only a calcium supplement; the pain is substernal and radiates to her left arm.
She is diaphoretic with blood pressure 110/70 mmHg and heart rate 102 bpm; cardiac exam reveals a soft S3.
ECG shows ST elevation in the anterior leads and troponin is mildly elevated at 2.1 ng/mL; emergent coronary angiography shows no obstructive coronary artery disease.
Left ventriculogram reveals apical ballooning with hypercontractility of the basal segments, producing a shape resembling a Japanese octopus trap.
explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a catecholamine-mediated transient ventricular dysfunction triggered by acute emotional or physical stress, causing apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis in the absence of obstructive coronary disease.
keyFact: Predominantly affects postmenopausal women after emotional stress. ST elevation mimics anterior STEMI but coronary arteries are clean. Apical ballooning on ventriculography is diagnostic. Usually fully reversible within weeks.

wrongAnswers.name: Anterior STEMI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: STEMI shows obstructive coronary disease on angiography in the LAD territory; coronary angiography here showed no obstruction, ruling out ischemic infarction.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myocarditis can mimic ACS but typically affects younger patients, is associated with viral prodrome, and does not produce the classic apical ballooning pattern with basal hyperkinesis.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Dissection
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Aortic dissection can cause chest pain and ECG changes via coronary ostial involvement, but would not produce apical ballooning on ventriculography and coronary arteries would not be normal.

clues: A 24-year-old male college student presents with chest pain and fatigue for five days. The pain is sharp, varies with position, and woke him from sleep last night.
He had a sore throat and runny nose about two weeks ago that resolved spontaneously. He has no cardiac history, does not use drugs, and has no family history of sudden death.
Temperature is 38.2 degrees C. Cardiac auscultation reveals a faint S3 gallop. There is no pericardial friction rub. Vital signs are otherwise stable.
ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression in multiple leads. Troponin I is elevated at 4.8 ng/mL. CRP is markedly elevated. Echocardiogram shows mildly reduced ejection fraction.
Cardiac MRI demonstrates diffuse late gadolinium enhancement in a subepicardial, non-ischemic pattern involving the lateral and inferior walls, with myocardial edema on T2-weighted sequences.
explanation: Viral myocarditis results from direct cardiomyocyte injury by a cardiotropic virus (commonly Coxsackievirus B) and subsequent immune-mediated inflammation, causing myocyte necrosis and cardiac dysfunction.
keyFact: Most common cause is Coxsackievirus B in young adults. Cardiac MRI with LGE in a subepicardial, non-ischemic pattern is diagnostic. Can progress to dilated cardiomyopathy. Concomitant pericarditis (myopericarditis) is common.

wrongAnswers.name: Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Pericarditis can cause mild troponin elevation (myopericarditis), but the subepicardial LGE pattern on cardiac MRI and the degree of troponin rise here indicate primary myocardial involvement.

wrongAnswers.name: STEMI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: STEMI causes regional ST elevation in a coronary distribution; diffuse ST changes, preceding viral illness, age, and subepicardial LGE pattern are inconsistent with ischemic MI.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE can cause chest pain and troponin elevation but does not produce diffuse ST changes with PR depression or myocardial LGE on cardiac MRI.

clues: A 30-year-old woman presents with sharp chest pain that started two days ago and worsens when she lies flat or takes a deep breath.
She had flu-like symptoms with low-grade fever and fatigue one week ago that resolved on their own.
Temperature is 37.8 degrees C; a scratchy, triphasic sound is heard with the stethoscope placed firmly at the left sternal border.
ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation in multiple leads with PR segment depression in lead II and PR elevation in aVR; troponin is within normal limits.
Echocardiogram shows a trivial pericardial effusion without tamponade physiology, and the pericardium appears mildly thickened and echogenic.
explanation: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac, most commonly caused by viral infection, causing fibrinous pericardial inflammation and the characteristic pleuritic chest pain and ECG changes.
keyFact: Four diagnostic criteria: pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, ECG changes (diffuse saddle-shaped ST elevation + PR depression), and new/worsening effusion. Normal troponin distinguishes from myopericarditis. Ibuprofen + colchicine reduces recurrence.

wrongAnswers.name: Myocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myocarditis also presents post-virally with chest pain and ECG changes, but is distinguished by elevated troponin and myocardial LGE on MRI; troponin is normal here.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE causes pleuritic chest pain and can cause ST changes, but ECG would show S1Q3T3 pattern or right heart strain, not diffuse saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression.

wrongAnswers.name: STEMI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: STEMI produces regional convex ST elevation in a coronary distribution, not diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression throughout multiple unrelated leads.

clues: A 52-year-old man with a known malignancy presents with progressive shortness of breath, weakness, and lightheadedness for three days; he feels his heart racing.
He was recently started on immunotherapy; he has no chest pain but feels his heart racing and is unable to walk to the bathroom without feeling faint.
His blood pressure is 88/72 mmHg with an SBP drop of 18 mmHg on inspiration; heart sounds are distant and jugular veins are markedly distended.
ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low-voltage QRS complexes and electrical alternans.
Bedside echocardiogram shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse and exaggerated respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocity.
explanation: Cardiac tamponade occurs when pericardial fluid accumulates rapidly enough to raise intrapericardial pressure above cardiac filling pressures, compressing the cardiac chambers and severely impairing diastolic filling and cardiac output.
keyFact: Beck's triad: hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds. Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg SBP drop with inspiration) is sensitive. Electrical alternans on ECG is pathognomonic. Malignancy and uremia are common causes. Urgent pericardiocentesis is required.

wrongAnswers.name: Tension Pneumothorax
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tension pneumothorax also causes hypotension and JVD but produces absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation, not distant heart sounds and electrical alternans.

wrongAnswers.name: Constrictive Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Constrictive pericarditis causes similar hemodynamics chronically but does not produce electrical alternans, and echo would show pericardial thickening rather than a large effusion with chamber collapse.

wrongAnswers.name: Distributive Shock
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic or immunotherapy-related distributive shock would cause warm extremities with low SVR, not JVD and equalized pressures; electrical alternans would not be present.

clues: A 48-year-old man presents with progressive abdominal distension, bilateral leg swelling, and fatigue that has been worsening over the past year.
He underwent cardiac surgery for a coronary bypass six years ago and has had two prior episodes of pericarditis; he is not diabetic and does not drink alcohol.
He has markedly elevated JVP that increases with inspiration, a prominent dip-and-plateau waveform, ascites, and a sharp, early diastolic sound along the left sternal border.
Echocardiogram shows septal bounce with exaggerated interventricular dependence; BNP is mildly elevated at 180 pg/mL despite significant volume overload.
Cardiac catheterization reveals equalization of diastolic pressures in all four chambers with a dip-and-plateau (square root sign) in the right ventricular pressure tracing.
explanation: Constrictive pericarditis results from fibrous thickening and calcification of the pericardium, creating a rigid shell that prevents normal diastolic filling and causes equalization of diastolic pressures across all chambers.
keyFact: Kussmaul sign (JVP rises with inspiration) is classic. Pericardial knock is an early diastolic sound. Disproportionately low BNP for the degree of volume overload. Prior radiation, cardiac surgery, and TB are risk factors. Pericardiectomy is curative.

wrongAnswers.name: Cardiac Tamponade
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Tamponade causes pulsus paradoxus with JVP that lacks the prominent y descent; Kussmaul sign (JVP rising with inspiration) is characteristic of constriction, not tamponade.

wrongAnswers.name: Cirrhosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Cirrhosis causes ascites and edema but does not cause JVD, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, or equalization of cardiac pressures on catheterization.

wrongAnswers.name: HFpEF
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HFpEF does not produce Kussmaul sign, a pericardial knock, or the square root sign on catheterization; the post-surgical/pericarditis history and pericardial thickening point to constriction.

clues: A 42-year-old woman from South Asia presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and two episodes of coughing up blood over the past year.
She had recurrent episodes of sore throat and joint pain in childhood requiring prolonged courses of intramuscular antibiotics; she has been in the US for 15 years.
Her pulse is irregular at 88 bpm; a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur is heard at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position, preceded by a sharp opening sound.
Chest X-ray shows left atrial enlargement with straightening of the left heart border and Kerley B lines; ECG shows broad notched P waves in lead II and atrial fibrillation.
Echocardiogram shows a mitral valve area of 0.9 cm squared, hockey-stick deformity of the anterior mitral leaflet, and a mean gradient of 18 mmHg across the valve.
explanation: Rheumatic mitral stenosis results from autoimmune inflammation after group A Streptococcus pharyngitis, leading to leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and progressive narrowing of the mitral orifice that obstructs left atrial outflow.
keyFact: Most common cause is rheumatic heart disease in developing countries. Opening snap with short S2-OS interval indicates severe stenosis. Complications include AFib, pulmonary hypertension, hemoptysis, and systemic embolism. Balloon valvuloplasty for suitable anatomy.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MR causes a holosystolic murmur at the apex, not a diastolic rumble; hemoptysis from pulmonary hypertension and left atrial enlargement are more characteristic of stenosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PAH can cause dyspnea and hemoptysis but would not produce a diastolic rumble, opening snap, or the characteristic echo findings of mitral stenosis.

wrongAnswers.name: Left Atrial Myxoma
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myxoma can mimic MS with a 'tumor plop' and positional symptoms but would show a mobile mass on echocardiogram, not leaflet thickening and fusion.

clues: A 55-year-old man presents with gradually worsening exertional dyspnea and occasional palpitations over the past two years.
He was told years ago he had a heart murmur on a routine exam and was asked to follow up but never did; he has no chest pain or syncope.
A blowing holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla is heard at the cardiac apex; the apical impulse is displaced laterally and is hyperdynamic.
ECG shows left atrial enlargement and left ventricular hypertrophy; chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with a prominent left atrial silhouette.
Echocardiogram reveals a flail posterior leaflet due to chordal rupture with severe eccentric regurgitant jet, EROA of 0.5 cm2, and an EF of 52%.
explanation: Mitral regurgitation from chordal rupture causes volume overload of the left ventricle, which compensates through eccentric hypertrophy; EF may appear preserved while contractile function is actually impaired.
keyFact: Degenerative (myxomatous) disease and chordal rupture are the most common causes in the West. A 'normal' EF of 50–55% in severe MR actually represents impaired myocardial contractility. Surgical repair is preferred over replacement for degenerative MR.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AS causes a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to the carotids, not a holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.

wrongAnswers.name: VSD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VSD causes a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border, not the apex with axillary radiation; VSD is typically congenital and presents much earlier in life.

wrongAnswers.name: Tricuspid Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TR causes a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border that increases with inspiration (Carvallo's sign); the murmur here radiates to the axilla and is located at the apex.

clues: A 76-year-old man presents with chest tightness during his daily walks and occasional lightheadedness when climbing stairs.
He was told of a heart murmur 20 years ago and has had annual checkups; over the past year his cardiologist has been watching it more closely.
A harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is best heard at the right upper sternal border with radiation to the carotid arteries; the carotid upstroke is slow and delayed.
ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern; echo Doppler shows a peak jet velocity of 4.6 m/s across the aortic valve.
Echocardiogram shows a calcified bicuspid aortic valve with a mean gradient of 55 mmHg and a valve area of 0.7 cm².
explanation: Calcific aortic stenosis results from progressive calcium deposition on the aortic valve leaflets causing outflow obstruction, left ventricular hypertrophy, and ultimately the symptomatic triad of angina, syncope, and heart failure.
keyFact: Classic symptom triad: angina (survival 5 years), syncope (3 years), heart failure (1–2 years). AVA <1.0 cm² or mean gradient >40 mmHg defines severe AS. Pulsus parvus et tardus (weak, delayed pulse). TAVR or SAVR when symptomatic.

wrongAnswers.name: HCM
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HCM murmur increases with Valsalva and standing; the murmur here decreases with Valsalva. Echo confirms calcified valve pathology rather than septal hypertrophy.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AR causes a blowing diastolic murmur, not a systolic murmur, and produces a wide pulse pressure with a bounding pulse rather than pulsus parvus et tardus.

wrongAnswers.name: Carotid Artery Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Carotid stenosis can cause presyncope, but does not explain the systolic murmur with radiation and the echo findings of a calcified valve with high gradient.

clues: A 38-year-old man with a connective tissue disorder presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and awareness of his heartbeat, especially when lying down.
He was told of a murmur years ago and has a family member with a known connective tissue disorder; he recently noticed his pulse feels very strong.
His blood pressure is 155/55 mmHg; a blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border leaning forward, and his head appears to bob with each heartbeat.
ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy; chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with a prominent aortic knuckle and boot-shaped heart.
Echocardiogram shows aortic root dilation to 5.4 cm with prolapsed leaflets, holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta, and an LV end-systolic diameter of 52 mm.
explanation: Aortic regurgitation causes diastolic backflow into the left ventricle producing volume overload, eccentric LV hypertrophy, and a wide pulse pressure from elevated systolic and decreased diastolic pressures.
keyFact: Wide pulse pressure is the hallmark. Classic signs: de Musset (head bob), Quincke (nail-bed pulsations), Duroziez (femoral bruit), Corrigan (water-hammer pulse). Most common causes: bicuspid valve, Marfan syndrome, rheumatic disease, aortic root dilation. Surgery when symptomatic or LV dilates.

wrongAnswers.name: Aortic Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: AS causes a systolic murmur with pulsus parvus et tardus and a narrow pulse pressure; this patient has a diastolic murmur with a wide pulse pressure of 100 mmHg.

wrongAnswers.name: Patent Ductus Arteriosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PDA causes a continuous machine-like murmur loudest at the left clavicle; it does not produce aortic root dilation or a pure diastolic murmur at the left sternal border.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MS causes a diastolic murmur at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position with a narrow pulse pressure; this patient has a wide pulse pressure and a left sternal border diastolic murmur.

clues: A 50-year-old woman with known valvular heart disease presents with progressive abdominal distension, leg swelling, and fatigue worsening over six months.
She has a known history of severe mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension; she developed increasing right-sided symptoms after a recent hospitalization for respiratory infection.
She has marked jugular venous distension with a prominent CV wave, pulsatile hepatomegaly, ascites, and a soft holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border that increases with deep inspiration.
ECG shows right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy; echocardiogram demonstrates severe RV dilation and dysfunction.
Echocardiogram Doppler shows severe valvular insufficiency with systolic flow reversal in the hepatic veins, a regurgitant jet velocity of 4.2 m/s, and estimated RVSP of 75 mmHg.
explanation: Secondary tricuspid regurgitation results from right ventricular dilation and annular enlargement caused by pulmonary hypertension, leading to incomplete leaflet coaptation and regurgitant flow into the right atrium.
keyFact: Carvallo's sign: TR murmur increases with inspiration (distinguishes from MR). Pulsatile liver and systolic jugular CV wave are hallmarks. Most TR is functional/secondary (not primary valve disease). Associated with pulmonary HTN, left heart disease, and carcinoid syndrome.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Regurgitation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MR causes an apical holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla that does not increase with inspiration; the right-sided signs (pulsatile liver, CV wave) point to tricuspid pathology.

wrongAnswers.name: Right Heart Failure from Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Acute PE can cause RV failure and TR, but the chronic six-month course and known pulmonary hypertension from mitral stenosis point to secondary TR from longstanding RV pressure overload.

wrongAnswers.name: Constrictive Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Constriction also causes JVD and hepatomegaly, but would not produce a systolic murmur that increases with inspiration or the classic Doppler findings of TR.

clues: A 32-year-old man presents with three weeks of fevers, chills, night sweats, and progressive fatigue; he has a known cardiac valve abnormality and admits to intravenous drug use.
He has a known bicuspid aortic valve and admits to intravenous drug use; he had a dental procedure two months ago without antibiotic prophylaxis.
Temperature is 39.1°C; painless red spots are noted on his palms, small tender nodules on his fingertips, and splinter hemorrhages under two fingernails.
Three blood cultures drawn from separate sites all grow Staphylococcus aureus; ESR and CRP are markedly elevated.
Transesophageal echocardiogram demonstrates a 1.2 cm oscillating vegetation on the aortic valve with moderate aortic regurgitation and paravalvular abscess formation.
explanation: Infective endocarditis results from bacteremia seeding a structurally abnormal or prosthetic valve, forming platelet-fibrin vegetations that cause valvular destruction, embolic phenomena, and metastatic infection.
keyFact: Modified Duke criteria: major (positive blood cultures, echo evidence) + minor (fever, embolic phenomena, predisposing condition). Janeway lesions (painless, palmar) vs Osler nodes (painful, fingertips). S. aureus most common in IVDU. TEE superior to TTE for vegetations.

wrongAnswers.name: Acute Rheumatic Fever
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ARF affects younger patients after strep pharyngitis and produces migratory polyarthritis and chorea; it does not cause the peripheral embolic stigmata or positive blood cultures found here.

wrongAnswers.name: Septic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Septic arthritis localizes to joints and does not produce cardiac vegetations, peripheral embolic phenomena, or valvular regurgitation seen here.

wrongAnswers.name: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Libman-Sacks endocarditis in SLE can mimic IE but produces sterile vegetations without positive blood cultures; the history of IVDU and S. aureus bacteremia confirm infectious etiology.

clues: A 14-year-old girl presents with fever, joint pain, and chest discomfort that began two weeks after a sore throat; the joint pain seems to move between joints.
She reports her knees and ankles have been swollen and painful, and the pain migrates from joint to joint; she also notices involuntary jerky movements of her hands.
Temperature is 38.6 degrees C; she has warm, swollen, tender knee and ankle joints; a new apical systolic murmur is heard that was absent at her last visit.
ASO titer is markedly elevated; ECG shows a prolonged PR interval of 240 ms; throat swab culture is negative but anti-DNase B is elevated.
Echocardiogram shows mitral valve regurgitation with commissural fusion, leaflet thickening, and restricted leaflet motion.
explanation: Acute rheumatic fever results from molecular mimicry between group A Streptococcus M-protein antigens and cardiac tissue, triggering an autoimmune response that causes pancarditis, valvulitis, and long-term valve damage.
keyFact: Jones criteria: major (carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules) + minor (fever, elevated CRP/ESR, prolonged PR). Evidence of preceding GAS infection required. Penicillin prophylaxis prevents recurrence and progressive valve damage.

wrongAnswers.name: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: JIA causes chronic joint inflammation but does not follow streptococcal infection, does not produce migratory arthritis, and is not associated with elevated ASO titers or acute cardiac valve changes.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Myocarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Myocarditis can present with fever and a new murmur, but lacks the migratory polyarthritis, chorea, elevated ASO titer, and post-streptococcal temporal association of rheumatic fever.

wrongAnswers.name: Reactive Arthritis (Reiter Syndrome)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Reactive arthritis typically follows gastrointestinal or urogenital infection with the classic triad of urethritis, arthritis, and uveitis; it does not cause the carditis pattern or elevated streptococcal antibodies.

clues: A 19-year-old man presents for evaluation of leg cramps and fatigue during exercise that his teammates do not experience.
He has no prior cardiac history and was never told of any heart problems as a child; he has no headaches or nosebleeds.
Blood pressure in his right arm is 165/95 mmHg; blood pressure in both legs is 110/75 mmHg; femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared to radial pulses.
Chest X-ray shows rib notching on the undersurface of ribs 3–8 bilaterally and a figure-3 sign at the aortic knuckle.

CT angiography shows a severe discrete narrowing of the descending aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery with a peak gradient of 40 mmHg and extensive collateral intercostal artery formation.
explanation: Coarctation of the aorta is a congenital narrowing typically at the juxtaductal region, causing upper extremity hypertension, lower extremity hypoperfusion, and development of collateral intercostal vessels.
keyFact: Upper vs lower extremity blood pressure differential is the key finding. Rib notching from intercostal collaterals appears after age 5. Strongly associated with bicuspid aortic valve (~50%) and Turner syndrome. Intervention indicated for gradient >20 mmHg.

wrongAnswers.name: Essential Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Essential hypertension does not cause upper-lower limb blood pressure discrepancy, weak femoral pulses, rib notching, or a figure-3 sign on X-ray.

wrongAnswers.name: Renal Artery Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Renal artery stenosis causes systemic hypertension but does not cause differential arm-leg blood pressures, weak femoral pulses, or aortic narrowing on imaging.

wrongAnswers.name: Peripheral Artery Disease
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PAD is uncommon in a 19-year-old and would not cause upper extremity hypertension with rib notching; the brachial-femoral gradient and figure-3 sign confirm aortic coarctation.

clues: A 35-year-old woman presents with gradual onset exertional dyspnea and occasional palpitations over two years.
She was told of a murmur as a child but was reassured it was innocent; she has had several respiratory infections over the past three years requiring antibiotics.
A soft systolic murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border; S2 is widely and fixedly split regardless of the respiratory cycle.
Chest X-ray shows pulmonary plethora, enlarged pulmonary arteries, and a small aortic knuckle; ECG shows incomplete right bundle branch block and right axis deviation.
Transesophageal echocardiogram with bubble study shows a 2.2 cm defect in the fossa ovalis region with left-to-right shunting, RV dilation, and a Qp:Qs of 2.4:1.
explanation: An atrial septal defect allows left-to-right shunting due to lower right heart pressures, leading to right heart volume overload, pulmonary overcirculation, and eventual right heart failure or Eisenmenger syndrome if uncorrected.
keyFact: Fixed widely split S2 is the hallmark of ASD. Pulmonary flow murmur (not the defect itself) causes the systolic murmur. Secundum ASD is most common (70%). Recurrent respiratory infections in childhood are a clue. Transcatheter or surgical closure indicated for significant shunts.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PS causes a systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border but S2 splitting is variable with inspiration, not fixed; bubble study would not show atrial shunting.

wrongAnswers.name: VSD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VSD causes a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border without fixed S2 splitting; echocardiogram would show a ventricular-level shunt.

wrongAnswers.name: Mitral Valve Prolapse
wrongAnswers.whyNot: MVP causes a mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur at the apex, not fixed S2 splitting or right heart dilation with pulmonary plethora.

clues: A 2-year-old boy is brought in because he tires quickly during feeding and is not gaining weight.
He was noted to have a heart murmur at his newborn exam; his parents are concerned because several murmur checks resulted in different advice.
A harsh, pansystolic murmur is heard best at the left lower sternal border with a palpable thrill; he is below the 5th percentile for weight and has mild subcostal retractions.
Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascularity; ECG shows left ventricular and left atrial enlargement.
Echocardiogram demonstrates a 6 mm perimembranous ventricular defect with significant left-to-right shunting, a Qp:Qs of 2.8:1, and early signs of pulmonary hypertension.
explanation: A ventricular septal defect allows left-to-right shunting due to the higher left ventricular pressure, causing pulmonary overcirculation, left heart volume overload, heart failure symptoms, and failure to thrive in infants.
keyFact: Most common congenital heart defect. Harsh holosystolic murmur at LLSB with thrill. Small VSDs (maladie de Roger) may close spontaneously. Large VSDs cause failure to thrive, heart failure, and risk of Eisenmenger syndrome. LV/LA enlargement distinguishes from ASD (RV enlargement).

wrongAnswers.name: ASD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD causes right heart volume overload with RV enlargement and fixed split S2, not LV/LA enlargement or a harsh LLSB thrill; the murmur location and echocardiography confirm ventricular level.

wrongAnswers.name: Patent Ductus Arteriosus
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PDA causes a continuous machinery murmur loudest below the left clavicle, not a holosystolic murmur at the LLSB; echocardiography confirms the ventricular septal defect.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Stenosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PS causes a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border without the thrill at the LLSB or left heart volume overload seen here.

clues: A 3-week-old premature infant born at 28 weeks is noted to have increased work of breathing and difficulty weaning from the ventilator despite initial improvement after surfactant.
His respiratory status initially improved after surfactant therapy but has worsened over the past 48 hours despite adequate ventilator settings.
He has bounding peripheral pulses, a wide pulse pressure, and a continuous murmur heard below the left clavicle; he has mild hepatomegaly.
Chest X-ray shows increased pulmonary vascular markings and mild cardiomegaly; echocardiogram shows a dilated left atrium with a LA:Ao ratio of 1.6.

Echocardiogram with color Doppler shows a large communication between the descending aorta and pulmonary artery with continuous left-to-right flow from the descending aorta to the main pulmonary artery, with left heart volume overload.
explanation: In preterm infants, failure of the ductus arteriosus to close results from relative prostaglandin excess and immature smooth muscle, causing left-to-right shunting that increases pulmonary blood flow and worsens respiratory status.
keyFact: Continuous 'machinery' murmur below the left clavicle is classic. Bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure from aortic runoff. Premature infants at high risk; indomethacin/ibuprofen inhibits prostaglandin synthesis to promote closure. Surgical ligation if medical therapy fails.

wrongAnswers.name: VSD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: VSD causes a holosystolic murmur at the LLSB, not a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle; echo would show a ventricular-level defect, not aortopulmonary communication.

wrongAnswers.name: ASD
wrongAnswers.whyNot: ASD produces a soft systolic murmur with fixed S2 splitting and right heart volume overload, not a continuous murmur and the left heart dilation seen on echocardiography.

wrongAnswers.name: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: RDS from surfactant deficiency is expected in preterm infants, but improvement followed by deterioration with bounding pulses and continuous murmur indicates a hemodynamically significant PDA complicating recovery.

clues: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the ED after her parents noticed cyanotic episodes during agitation.
Her parents report she has been growing slowly and often squats to rest during play; she was noted to have a murmur at birth and cardiology follow-up was arranged but not yet completed.
She has mild cyanosis, clubbing of the fingertips, and a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border; the second heart sound is single.
Chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart with decreased pulmonary vascularity and right-sided aortic arch; ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy.

Echocardiogram reveals the four components: large perimembranous ventricular defect, overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction with subpulmonic stenosis, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterosuperior deviation of the infundibular septum causing RVOT obstruction, right-to-left shunting through the VSD, and cyanosis that worsens with decreased systemic vascular resistance or increased RV outflow obstruction.
keyFact: Most common cyanotic congenital heart disease after the neonatal period. Tet spells (hypercyanotic spells) are managed with knee-chest position, oxygen, IV morphine, and propranolol. Boot-shaped heart on X-ray from RVH. Total surgical repair is the definitive treatment.

wrongAnswers.name: Transposition of the Great Arteries
wrongAnswers.whyNot: TGA presents with severe cyanosis immediately at birth (not episodic spells), shows an egg-on-a-string X-ray with increased pulmonary vascularity, and is corrected in the first week of life.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Stenosis with Intact Ventricular Septum
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Isolated PS without VSD does not cause right-to-left shunting or cyanosis at rest; the boot-shaped heart and overriding aorta confirm the four anatomic components of TOF.

wrongAnswers.name: Eisenmenger Syndrome
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Eisenmenger syndrome is a late complication of longstanding left-to-right shunts causing irreversible pulmonary hypertension; it does not occur in a 6-month-old infant with decreased pulmonary vascularity.

clues: A 28-year-old woman presents with worsening exertional dyspnea, episodes of coughing up blood, bluish discoloration of her lips and fingers, fatigue, and occasional lightheadedness.
She was told as a child she had a hole in her heart but her parents declined early surgery; she was told in her teens the window for repair had passed.
She has central cyanosis, digital clubbing, and a right ventricular heave; the previously audible murmur from her childhood defect is now much softer.
CBC shows polycythemia with hemoglobin 19.8 g/dL; echocardiogram shows severely elevated RVSP of 110 mmHg with bidirectional shunting across the septal defect.
Right heart catheterization shows pulmonary vascular resistance of 14 Wood units that does not decrease with vasoreactivity testing.
explanation: Eisenmenger syndrome results from longstanding unrepaired left-to-right shunts causing progressive obliterative pulmonary arteriopathy and pulmonary hypertension until pulmonary pressures exceed systemic, reversing the shunt and causing cyanosis.
keyFact: Shunt reversal (left-to-right becomes right-to-left) causes central cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia. The original murmur becomes softer as shunt flow equalizes. Surgical correction is contraindicated. Pulmonary vasodilators (bosentan, sildenafil) improve symptoms. Heart-lung transplant is the only cure.

wrongAnswers.name: Primary Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Idiopathic PAH does not involve intracardiac shunts; the history of congenital heart defect and bidirectional shunting on echo confirm the Eisenmenger mechanism.

wrongAnswers.name: Cystic Fibrosis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: CF causes chronic pulmonary disease with cyanosis and clubbing but is associated with recurrent infections and bronchiectasis, not congenital heart defects and elevated RVSP from pulmonary vascular disease.

wrongAnswers.name: Polycythemia Vera
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Polycythemia vera causes elevated hemoglobin but is a bone marrow disorder; the cyanosis, clubbing, elevated pulmonary pressures, and congenital heart history confirm secondary polycythemia from Eisenmenger syndrome.

clues: A 55-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease presents with chest pain, low-grade fever, and shortness of breath; he has been missing his regular treatments recently.
He has been on renal replacement therapy for three years but has missed multiple sessions over the past two weeks due to transportation issues; he has no recent respiratory illness.
Temperature is 38.0 degrees C, blood pressure is 145/90 mmHg; a pericardial friction rub is heard in all positions and does not vary with respiration.
ECG shows no ST elevation or PR depression; BUN is 112 mg/dL and creatinine is 14.8 mg/dL; troponin is mildly elevated.
Echocardiogram shows a moderate pericardial effusion with fibrinous stranding; the absence of typical ECG changes despite a friction rub and severely elevated BUN and creatinine is noted.
explanation: Uremic pericarditis results from the irritant effect of retained uremic toxins on the visceral and parietal pericardium, causing fibrinous pericarditis that resolves with adequate dialysis.
keyFact: Unique feature: ECG does NOT show the classic ST/PR changes of viral pericarditis (uremic pericarditis causes hemorrhagic effusion without the typical electrolyte shifts). Occurs when BUN typically >60 mg/dL. Treatment is intensification of dialysis, not NSAIDs. Tamponade is a dangerous complication.

wrongAnswers.name: Viral Pericarditis
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Viral pericarditis shows the classic ECG pattern of diffuse ST elevation with PR depression; the absent ECG changes, markedly elevated BUN, and dialysis-dependent patient point to uremic etiology.

wrongAnswers.name: Post-MI Pericarditis (Dressler Syndrome)
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Dressler syndrome occurs weeks after myocardial infarction; there is no history of recent MI here, and the temporal link to missed dialysis sessions is the key differentiating factor.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE can cause chest pain, dyspnea, and mild troponin elevation, but would not cause a friction rub, pericardial effusion, or resolution with dialysis intensification.

clues: A 61-year-old man presents with pleuritic chest pain, fever, and dyspnea that began this week; he was hospitalized one month ago for an acute cardiac event and had been recovering well.
He was hospitalized one month ago for a large anterior myocardial infarction and underwent coronary stenting; he completed cardiac rehabilitation and was doing well until this week.
Temperature is 38.4 degrees C; a pericardial friction rub is audible at the left sternal border; lungs have decreased breath sounds at the right base.
ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression in multiple leads; troponin is mildly elevated; CBC shows leukocytosis and ESR is 78 mm/hr.
Echocardiogram shows a new moderate pericardial effusion without hemodynamic compromise and a right pleural effusion; anti-heart antibodies are detected in serum.
explanation: Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune inflammatory response triggered by the release of cardiac antigens after myocardial necrosis, causing pericarditis, pleuritis, and pericardial effusion typically two to ten weeks post-MI.
keyFact: Classically occurs 2–10 weeks after MI (or cardiac surgery). Autoimmune mechanism with anti-heart antibodies. Distinguished from early post-MI pericarditis (1–4 days, direct inflammation) by timing. Treated with NSAIDs and colchicine; steroids for refractory cases.

wrongAnswers.name: Recurrent MI
wrongAnswers.whyNot: Recurrent MI would cause localized ST elevation in the territory of the culprit vessel with a significant troponin rise; diffuse saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression and a friction rub indicate pericarditis.

wrongAnswers.name: Pulmonary Embolism
wrongAnswers.whyNot: PE is a consideration post-MI, but would not cause a friction rub, diffuse ST/PR changes, or anti-heart antibodies; the clinical picture is consistent with autoimmune pericarditis.

wrongAnswers.name: Heart Failure Exacerbation
wrongAnswers.whyNot: HF exacerbation after MI would cause bilateral pleural effusions and pulmonary edema, not a unilateral pleural effusion with pericarditis, fever, and inflammatory markers.
